summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: Description This repository contains the Python implementation, numerical experiments, analysis outputs, and figures associated with the manuscript Sharp Bounds for Raman Band-Area Ratios . The study investigates the identifiability of Raman band-area ratios under explicit constraints on baseline curvature, measurement noise, nonnegativity, and band-free anchor regions. Sharp identification intervals are computed using linear programming, while an analytical bound is used to examine the influence of spectral geometry and integration-window selection. The accompanying materials support the reported simulation studies, analytical-bound evaluations, semi-synthetic validation on measured backgrounds, and analysis of nitrate–nitrite mixtures. The original experimental Raman spectra are publicly available from Mendeley Data: https://doi.org/10.17632/cxf3zxsc3k.3 . Funding: This research received no external funding.

summary: Proving an alternating-current optimal power flow solution globally ε-optimal usually takes a convex-relaxation solve per instance. Most of these solves can be reused. For a fixed multiplier, the box-constrained Lagrangian bound of a conic relaxation is affine in the load, so a multiplier computed once gives a lower bound at every load by an inner product. Where the relaxation's prices vary smoothly in few load directions, packing numbers in their number bound the size of a library from above and, under a curvature assumption, from below, and solving the relaxation only where the library falls short stays within the upper bound; where prices are constant within operating regimes, one multiplier per regime suffices. On eight benchmark systems of 14 to 500 buses, one multiplier per regime certifies nearly as many loads as a thousand, and a library used first makes an interior-point-plus-relaxation pipeline 3.0 to 15.2 times faster at ε = 0.5%, depending on the baseline configuration, and 8.9 times while proving both bounds. Grown this way over a year of hourly loads of a modified 2000-bus Texas grid, a library certified 98.2% of the hours with 252 solves.
title: Amortized and Rigorous Optimality Certificates for AC Optimal Power Flow via Load-Affine Dual Libraries

summary: LLMatter2D grounds pre-trained large language models (run locally through LM Studio, Ollama, or hosted APIs) in curated, citable data on two-dimensional materials: DFT electronic structure from C2DB, MC2D, 2DMatPedia and JARVIS-DFT, Wannier90 tight-binding models, geometry and ARPES observables. summary: We study which training and calibration data help three open models solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks when the solver runs offline on four L4 GPUs for at most 12 hours. We compare data offline on public tasks and report 189 runs on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For the NVARC Qwen3-4B grid model, we built a corpus of 12,000 executable rules in a typed language and 95,993 tasks; a rule is admitted only if its behaviour on a fixed probe set differs from that of every admitted rule, and a task only if its pairs refute a shortlist of nearest competing rules and defeat 12 shortcut solvers. Continued fine-tuning on 1,920 real task records with revised four-GPU scheduling raised the semi-private score from 28.96 (mean of the released model) to 33.06 (mean of five runs, best 34.86); no checkpoint trained with synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 of them, improved on the real-task model. For the Qwen3.8-27B reasoning model, we fine-tuned on 1,036 of its own reasoning traces with correct final answers and compared sets that add traces of other models and synthetic tasks. With an inference procedure built around the model (a thinking cap enforced in the serving engine, a Python program checked on the demonstrations after each answer, a long first attempt per input), the score rose from 26.81 to 44.03, the level the ARC Prize Foundation measured for the base model without a time limit (42.36); most of the gain came from the inference procedure. For the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next mixture-of-experts model (125B parameters, 6B active), GPU memory limited concurrency. Pruning from 512 to 384 experts per layer by router-weighted activation saliency grew the key-value cache from 0.55M to 1.39M tokens; a 296-expert list adapted with ARC routing statistics, keeping experts for program tokens, plus an FP8 indexer cache, reached 1.96M. With a tool that checks programs, the model scored 56.67, our best result.
title: Rules, Traces and Routing Statistics: Training and Calibration Data for Open Models on ARC-AGI-2

summary: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.
title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control

summary: Debates about AI and responsibility ask whether automation opens responsibility gaps. This book argues that the more pressing failure lies elsewhere: an institution can remain fully responsible and accountable, yet lose its claim to be relied on, because it issues more than it can answer for. In the book's fictional test case, an insurer's AI appeals agent tells a policyholder: "I have reconsidered my decision. I have reversed it." Nothing happens, because the agent never had the power to reverse anything. The insurer still owns the refusal. No one is off the hook, yet no one answered. Three results Missing bearership is not defective ownership. Answerability is defined as four public relations: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence and standing-consequence. On that account, an AI interface can occupy a role emptily while the institution behind it still owns the role's commitments. So there can be no global responsibility gap and still a genuine local Empty Occupancy. Testimonial force without testimony. Machine output can inform and invite reliance without anyone owning it. Institutions may adopt such output only when five conditions of Normative Sponsorship are met: epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection and repair power. Authority must be serviceable. Because practical authority is defeasible, reliance must remain revisable while a claim operates. Obligations that mature without timely service accumulate as Deontic Debt. Where no credible plan could service issuance at a given scale, the institution is insolvent in a precise sense. It loses presumptive authority, while its duties of ownership and repair survive. Tested against the record and its rivals Robodebt yields a determinate Deontic Debt that case-by-case actor–forum accountability does not settle. The insolvency finding remains provisional, and the book names the records that would decide it. Moffatt v. Air Canada and the DPD chatbot episode leave interface standing indeterminate, and the book says so. TennCare, Post Office Horizon and the Dutch childcare-benefits affair discipline the comparisons. A dedicated chapter engages Bovens, List and Pettit, the responsibility-gap sceptics (Tigard, Königs, Himmelreich) and Lazar. The book closes with explicit conditions under which it would be wrong. Scope. The method is philosophical reconstruction with bounded public-record analysis. The terminology carries no legal consequence, and the equations are uncalibrated. Stipulated cases test whether the criteria discriminate, not how often such cases occur. The role criterion does not settle personhood or moral status. For philosophers of testimony, responsibility and group agency; AI-governance researchers; administrative lawyers; auditors and regulators; and anyone a machine has told that their problem was "resolved." 167 pages. summary: In solving systems of nonlinear equations, one of the main objectives is to construct iterative methods that attain high orders of convergence using as few evaluations as possible. However, the information a method obtains during each iteration imposes limitations on the order it can guarantee. The Cordero–Torregrosa conjecture proposes a bound on this order in terms of the number of evaluations of the function and its Jacobian. In this work, we prove this bound for the universal local order of one iteration, without requiring the number of Jacobian evaluations to be less than or equal to the number of function evaluations. In particular, our result also covers the case in which more evaluations of the Jacobian than of the function are performed. The proof encompasses deterministic, causal, memoryless methods whose rules may be arbitrary, without imposing rationality, continuity, or computability conditions. Moreover, we prove that when each Jacobian evaluation is performed at a point where the value of the function is already known, a more restrictive bound on the order of convergence can be obtained. Finally, we propose a new conjecture that establishes a refined bound through a product of factors determined by the distribution of evaluations, under additional dimensional conditions. These results provide a better understanding of the limitations imposed by the available information and raise new possibilities for studying high-order iterative methods.
title: Proof of the Cordero–Torregrosa Conjecture and an Improved Order Bound for Paired Jacobian Evaluations

summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly involved in both producing and evaluating scholarship, raising fundamental questions about how editorial judgments should be documented, contested, and governed. Existing publication models offer complementary approaches to access, selection criteria, review visibility, and preservation, yet these dimensions must be specified independently when evaluative work is delegated to AI systems. This inaugural editorial/perspective introduces the Journal of Autonomous Scholarship (JAS), a fee-free, open- access, multidisciplinary journal welcoming human-authored, AI-assisted, and AI-generated manuscripts under a uniform standard of evidential support, methodological or logical validity, clarity, and research integrity. JAS combines seven explicitly identified AI editorial roles and two revision-continuity auditors with publicly reusable review instructions, hash-bound review provenance, a mechanical and substantive acceptance gate that blocks unresolved material objections, author proof verification, and named human administrative oversight. To support inspection, we assemble a dated companion archive containing local source files, policy and handbook documents, machine-readable prompts and schemas, a synthetic serialization fixture, and extracted historical review reports. The archive is embedded in the supplement PDF; reviewer access does not depend on a separately uploaded ZIP. A file-hash manifest identifies the local snapshot; its equivalence to the previously cited repository commit and the original runtime environment has not been established. We distinguish normative policy requirements, implemented software controls, and prelaunch verification limits, examine risks arising from correlated model errors, non-execution of code during text-based review, and single-publisher governance, and specify a prospective benchmark agenda with finding- and manuscript-level error metrics and cluster-robust uncertainty estimation. summary: v2.1.0 - Current Microbiology corrected reproducibility analysis Study: Cohort-conditioned portability of microbiome biomarkers in Parkinson's disease and colorectal cancer. Parkinson's disease analysis This release provides the corrected three-cohort analysis using 675 public microbiome profiles: 148 from Finland, 200 from Malaysia and 327 from the United States. The conservative genus-label representation contains 154 matched labels, with 46 descriptive features. Outer-fold and cohort-held-out AUROCs: | Model | Pooled | Cohort-held-out | |---|---:|---:| | ElasticNet | 0.731206 | 0.679606 | | Random Forest | 0.741901 | 0.626226 | | XGBoost | 0.716056 | 0.619658 | Cohort-associated variation exceeded disease-associated variation. The results support a measurable average portability gap, with performance varying across held-out cohorts. Independent score evaluation The independent simulation experiment separates coefficient fitting, strategy selection and evaluation using disjoint source donors. The selected six-component ElasticNet score was constant and failed independent discrimination (AUROC 0.50). The proposed categorical portability rule and clinical-probability interpretation are not validated by these results. Heterogeneity alone and alternative scoring strategies are reported for comparison. Colorectal cancer benchmark The contextual CRC analysis includes 1,850 samples, 12 studies and 668 MSP features. Pooled out-of-fold AUROC: 0.725096. Concatenated study-held-out AUROC: 0.689825. Unweighted mean study AUROC: 0.704407. CRC-specific recalibration is not presented as independent validation of the PD score. Sequencing quality control Authentic observed-ASV rarefaction curves are provided for all 675 PD samples. Finland: 148 samples. Malaysia: 200 samples. United States: 327 samples. 64 seeded without-replacement replicates per sample. The release includes per-sample curves, cohort summaries, raw-run accession mappings, processing provenance, QC tables and SHA256 checksums. The sequencing-QC processing did not alter the frozen classifier inputs or fitted models. Reproducibility This release includes corrected processed inputs, sample-level provenance, analysis scripts, model outputs, statistical tables, figures, independent score-evaluation results and executable reproduction instructions. The previous v2.0.0 release remains available as the earlier analysis version. Its numerical results should not be used as the current study results. No raw FASTQ files are redistributed.
title: squareshorts/pd-microbiome-portability: v2.1.0 - Current Microbiology corrected reproducibility analysis

summary: This paper proposes the Transient-Loss Functional Compounding Theory (TLFCT), a medium-independent, time-indexed framework for investigating how a temporary loss in a system's functional performance may be associated with subsequent capability formation, recovery, net gain, and, under more restrictive conditions, compounding improvement. The central proposition is conditional rather than universal: a transient functional loss can contribute to a positive long-term outcome when a demonstrable conversion mechanism produces retained adaptive capacity or another relevant functional resource, and when the resulting future net benefit is sufficient to offset the initial loss and additional costs. The framework distinguishes transient loss, recovery, compensation, positive net conversion, and functional compounding. It proposes explicit measures for the initial loss, future benefit, subsequent degradation, additional costs, net outcome, loss-to-gain ratio, net conversion index, and break-even time. It also introduces a candidate state-space architecture connecting disturbance, information, feedback, adaptive capacity, performance, and resource constraints. The proposed theoretical architecture contains eighteen analytical layers and nine cross-cutting research modules. Its methodological foundation combines dynamical systems, systems theory, cybernetics, information theory, statistical model selection, and causal inference. A primary case design, a real-time measurement protocol, eight research hypotheses, a falsification strategy, a cross-domain validation plan, and a fourteen-stage research roadmap are specified. TLFCT is presented as a proposed research framework, not as an empirically established universal law. Its mathematical specifications are candidate models whose applicability, identifiability, predictive performance, and domain-level invariance must be established through empirical research.

summary: This repository contains computational scripts, numerical results, and statistical validation outputs supporting a genome-wide investigation of ancestral CpG dinucleotide retention and disruption in modern and archaic Homo genomes, together with analyses of Neanderthal- and Denisovan-introgressed haplotypes and reconstructed ancient DNA methylation. The analyses examine three complementary questions: Ancestral CpG retention across Homo lineages. Of 13,743,967 reconstructed ancestral CpG pairs, 3,004,026 met the criteria for the selected five-genome comparison. Among these, 2,557,297 (85.13%) retained the CpG dinucleotide in all five sampled genomes. CpG disruption in archaic-introgressed modern human haplotypes. Corrected matched-target analyses compared introgressed haplotypes with opposite homologues from the same individuals and independent population controls. The dataset comprises 29,717,417 Neanderthal-related and 765,630 Denisovan-related site–haplotype observations. Introgressed-minus-opposite-homologue differences were +0.00452 and +0.01176 percentage points, respectively, with two-way cluster-robust 95% confidence intervals including zero. Reconstructed ancient methylation at archaic-ancestry-associated genomic regions. Ancient methylation reconstructions were integrated with ancestral CpG coordinates and modern introgression annotations. Five control-selection and matching strategies were evaluated across six methylation contrasts, yielding 30 statistical comparisons. Results include effect estimates, confidence intervals, nominal P-values, and Holm-adjusted P-values. Apparent associations were sensitive to control definitions and CpG-count matching. The archive includes analysis scripts, derived numerical tables, statistical validation results, a complete 30-comparison Figure 5 dataset, and supporting documentation. Large original genomic datasets and intermediate files are not redistributed. Some computational scripts retain high-performance-computing-specific paths and are not independently validated as a portable end-to-end workflow. Related ancestral reconstruction resources: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23426694 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23442145 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23425960 External data sources: HGDP archaic introgression resources (Skov, 2024; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14136628 ) and published ancient methylation reconstructions (GEO GSE96833). The associated manuscript is being prepared for submission to Human Biology.

summary: Keyword retrieval returns expressions of personal anxiety together with many other uses of anxiety-related language. We present a benchmark of 1,000 Arabic Twitter/X posts retrieved with the keyword qalaq ("anxiety/worry") and annotated for six discourse functions. Two native Arabic-speaking annotators labeled every post independently, reaching 51.1% raw agreement (Cohen's $κ= 0.378$). We then reviewed all 489 disagreements and all 511 agreements under the same guidelines. The review changed 120 of the agreed labels (23.5%), which shows that agreements need auditing as well as disagreements. The final labels form a consensus reference; on a random sample of 200 posts, an additional annotator agreed with it on 60.5% of posts ($κ= 0.517$). Against this reference, Fanar-C-2-27B reaches 79.8% accuracy and macro-F1 0.784 ($κ= 0.749$). Its errors concentrate in the residual category (41.1% of errors; precision 0.905, recall 0.447), whose definition is internally inconsistent in the executed prompt, so the low recall cannot be attributed to the model alone. Sociopolitical Anxiety (27.1%) outnumbers Personal Emotional Expression (22.0%); these are assignment proportions in the sample, not estimates of prevalence or retrieval precision. We release the guidelines, a residual-subtype scheme, a fixed data split, label provenance, and evaluation code.
title: Beyond the Keyword: A Human-Annotated Benchmark for Arabic Anxiety-Related Discourse

summary: Intelligent metasurfaces enable advanced wave manipulation, including negative refraction, focusing, beam splitting and beam steering, with significant potential for practical applications. However, conventional approaches often rely on active metamaterials with gain, or demand computationally intensive solutions of inverse problems to find the optimal configuration. In this work, we use the scattering framework of quantum graph theory to derive an exact, analytic expression for configuration of a passive metasurface that produces a prescribed reflected wave field. The metasurface terminates a periodic lattice of waveguides and consists of an array of channels, each a tube of length $\ell_m$ ending in a vertex whose scattering parameter $λ_m$ sets how much of the wave is lost to the wall. For any prescribed incident and reflected field, the exact lengths and scattering parameters follow channel by channel, in closed form, from the ratio of the wave amplitudes returning to and leaving the lattice, and the metasurface is passive whenever this ratio does not exceed unity in modulus. We demonstrate the construction for both a one-dimensional and a two-dimensional metasurface. The one-dimensional metasurface terminates a two-dimensional lattice and steers, splits or perfectly absorbs Gaussian beams. The two-dimensional metasurface terminates a three-dimensional lattice and generates a prescribed image in a plane inside the lattice. In each case, we obtain the exact boundary properties that produce the effect.
title: A Passive Intelligent Metasurface: A Network Model

summary: The Suggested Upper Merged Ontology (SUMO) supplies general categories, relations and axioms for knowledge representation. Its source language, Standard Upper Ontology Knowledge Interchange Format (SUO-KIF), and its reasoning environment, Sigma Knowledge Engineering Environment (KEE), have different roles. Rikishi is a source-bound workbench for inspecting those commitments, submitting selected reasoning problems, and retaining their inputs and evidence. This paper asks how that infrastructure can make a scientific modeling connection inspectable. Prior Active Inference–SUMO alignment provides a direct precedent (Douglass et al., 2024; doi:10.5281/zenodo.11463326). One shared finite witness connects selected ontology expressions to probability models, numerical evaluation, pinned FEP_Formal Lean statements and synthetic observation histories. The ontology lane investigates declared model, representation, calculation and result roles. The mathematical lane supplies finite normalization, conditioning and information identities under stated hypotheses. The computational lane checks numerical outputs and generates trajectories from an explicit persistent-state model. Stable identifiers and common inputs join these lanes without treating their claims as interchangeable. Worked source formulas, direction-sensitive queries, numerical references and formal controls make the connections testable. Exact conditioning is separated from simulated frequencies, and variational inference from action selection and empirical model assessment. The resulting interface supports reproducible inspection of particular examples; it does not establish full-SUMO consistency, a general SUMO-to-Lean interpretation, verification of all Python execution, or biological validity of the Free Energy Principle (FEP).
title: Rikishi: Reproducible operation and analysis of the Suggested Upper Merged Ontology

summary: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.
title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery

summary: LaCAM is a search-based solver for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) that runs a depth-first search over joint configurations, using PIBT to generate successors and lazily adding single-agent constraints to explore alternatives. summary: Loop invariants are essential for deductive program verification, yet automatically inferring them for {multiphase programs}, whose loops contain conditional branches that induce multiple execution phases with distinct behaviors, remains an open problem. Existing LLM-based methods either reason about loops as a whole or use explicit branch information to generate atomic assertions jointly across branches, without maintaining complete candidate sub-invariants for independent generation and targeted repair. We present CLOVER, a structured neurosymbolic reasoning framework for multiphase invariant inference built on two interlinked mechanisms. First, compositional inference: CLOVER statically decomposes a loop into symbolic {loop branch sequences}, conjunctions of the loop guard and branch conditions that characterize distinct execution scenarios, and guides the LLM to generate candidate sub-invariants for each one independently, so that each LLM query focuses on a single execution scenario rather than the entire loop. Second, counterexample-guided localized refinement: when SMT verification rejects a composed disjunctive invariant, CLOVER traces the counterexample back through the branch structure to identify which specific loop branch sequence caused the failure and repairs only that sub-invariant, preserving all correct components. Both mechanisms are unified by a shared symbolic structure derived from the loop's branch semantics, which guides what the LLM generates, how candidates are composed, and where refinement is directed. We evaluate CLOVER on 316 linear arithmetic, 50 nonlinear arithmetic, and 54 multiphase benchmarks. CLOVER solves 35 of 54 multiphase benchmarks, outperforming the best LLM-based baseline (29) by 20.7\% and the best traditional method (22) by 59.1\%. On linear/nonlinear benchmarks, CLOVER remains competitive, solving 355 of 366 programs overall.

summary: Reliable operation of multi-hop wireless networks requires accounting for statistical dependence among link failures caused by common propagation conditions and shared network components. This paper develops a copula-based framework for modeling node-induced dependence among link-level signal-to-noise ratios and quantifying its effect on end-to-end outage. By separating marginal fading distributions from the dependence structure, the framework captures nonlinear and tail-dependent coupling beyond conventional correlation-based models. Exact outage expressions are derived for primary-backup configurations involving edge-disjoint paths and paths with shared links. We then characterize the conditional outage probability of each candidate backup path given a primary-path failure, jointly accounting for node-induced dependence and shared-link failures. In high-reliability regimes, we derive a first-order score that decomposes conditional outage into terms associated with marginal path outage, shared links, and node-induced dependence, enabling efficient dependence-aware backup-path selection. We also establish sufficient conditions under which the first-order and exact selection rules identify the same backup path. Numerical results validate the analysis and show that copula families with the same Kendall's $τ$ can yield markedly different outage behavior because of their different tail-dependence properties. In particular, lower-tail dependence and path overlap can substantially reduce redundancy gains and reverse rankings based only on marginal outage probability.
title: Copula-Based Dependence Modeling for Resilient 6G Multi-Hop Wireless Networks

summary: We study the cost of certifying a scalar target driven by a product of centered Bernoulli means when an unobserved terminal gate leaves irreducible uncertainty. Each factor can be queried independently at a price. We derive the exact identified interval and determine when a requested accuracy is feasible. At product cancellation, we solve the game through a one-dimensional inverse-KL equation and explicit cost weights. For two tickets, quartic projections and rational bounds give checkable global optimality gaps. Joint confidence--precision limits expose a failure of the analyzed fixed pilot: it can cost asymptotically at least twice the optimum. summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is increasingly used in settings where pairwise preferences coexist with pointwise criteria such as response length, answer correctness, or safety scores. When the two disagree, standard DPO treats pairs whose preferred output scores worse on the pointwise criterion (conflict pairs) in the same way as the remaining (matching) pairs. We characterize a systematic failure mode, constraint drift: for sufficiently small updates, conflict pairs tend to increase constraint cost while matching pairs tend to repair it, and the net change depends on their balance. This balance yields a closed-form pre-alignment diagnostic, $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$, computable from dataset statistics, that indicates whether a dataset is self-correcting or requires intervention. Building on this diagnostic, we propose Conflict-aware DPO (CoDPO), which down-weights conflict pairs with a strength set from $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ rather than tuned, and adds an adaptive margin shift that addresses residual drift during training. Empirically, drift grows monotonically with conflict exposure on the conflict-dominated domains, and the intervention decision given by $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ matches the observed drift on every domain, including one that it identifies as self-correcting. On all four domains of the main comparison, CoDPO reduces drift while largely preserving the preference learning of vanilla DPO. Compared with hard filtering and recent constrained and multi-objective baselines, CoDPO also achieves a more favorable drift-preference trade-off.

summary: Algorithm-driven services, including search, recommendation, and advertising, rely on multi-stage model pipelines. While research prioritizes model optimization, post-deployment monitoring focuses on operational reliability. Yet operationally healthy systems may still produce poor-quality results, exposing a gap in existing evaluation and monitoring practices. However, a systematic problem formulation and benchmark for this task remain lacking. To bridge this gap, we formulate System Quality Diagnosis (SQD) for algorithm-driven services, a new task that extends quality evaluation beyond identifying poor outcomes to attributing their causes across system components. Focusing on industrial search, we propose WISE, an agentic framework for end-to-end quality diagnosis that discovers user-facing issues and traces their origins to underlying algorithmic components. To improve diagnostic reliability, we introduce ReTrace for constructing evidence-consistent trajectory supervision and Adaptive Harness-Policy Optimization (AHPO) for failure-guided optimization of the agent harness and model policy. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct WISE-BENCH, a real-world multimodal search benchmark that combines user-facing evidence, internal pipeline traces, and expert diagnosis annotations. Extensive experiments show consistent gains across model scales, with WISE achieving 75.20% end-to-end accuracy on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. In production, WISE supports quality auditing, online quality assurance, and model optimization, reducing diagnosis costs and improving downstream relevance models.

summary: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/
title: Seeing Beyond the Next Step: World-Model-Guided Human-Like Navigation in Multi-Agent Scenes

summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone. We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. summary: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.
title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance

summary: Existing models of social media virality either prescribe the functional form of engagement growth or assume a fixed mechanism by which past activity influences future engagement. We present a fractional physics-informed neural network that learns both the temporal memory and nonlinear growth dynamics of social media engagement, using symbolic regression to translate the learned dynamics into interpretable equations. Synthetic experiments at the deployment resolution of 24 hourly observations demonstrate that the fractional order and reaction law can be jointly recovered from clean data. Under observation noise, however, the standard pointwise physics residual drives the fractional order toward its lower bound through a scale artifact. We address this failure using a fully whitened residual that propagates observation noise through the fractional operator. Applying the framework to 348 posts from X (formerly Twitter), we find that a single-window model estimates strongly memory-dependent dynamics but fails to accurately reconstruct held-out trajectories. Partitioning the 24-hour window into four teacher-forced segments substantially improves performance, yielding segment-specific fractional orders that increase from 0.23 to 0.99 and interpretable growth laws for each phase. The segmented model reconstructs 64% of held-out trajectories within a mean squared error of 0.01, compared with 44% for the strongest of nine classical baselines. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of fractional physics-informed equation discovery to uncover interpretable engagement dynamics while highlighting the importance of noise-aware estimation and temporal segmentation.
title: Fractional physics-informed neural networks to model social media virality

summary: Accurate segmentation of 3D anatomical structures is crucial to medical image analysis. summary: Hexagonal germanium combines direct-gap optical activity with the low-nuclear-spin environment of a group-IV material, making it a candidate platform for spin qubits and spin-photon interfaces. A transverse electric field strongly reduces the nanowire band gap, providing a gate-tunable optical signature and limiting the usable field range. We identify the microscopic origin of the Rashba coupling as a second-order process mediated by a few intermediate subbands with distinct symmetry selection rules. summary: The nonlinear interaction of closely spaced magnetic skyrmions remains poorly understood, particularly the conditions governing their merger into a single skyrmion or a stable skyrmionium. Here, we investigate the merging dynamics of two Néel skyrmions using analytical modelling and micromagnetic simulations based on Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics. We examine the effects of exchange, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, anisotropy, and magnetostatic energies by varying the initial separation, polarity, winding number, and skyrmion size. Our results reveal a topological selection rule: skyrmions with identical polarity and opposite winding numbers form a stable skyrmionium at intermediate overlap, while all other configurations relax into a single skyrmion. We also identify a critical radius below which the skyrmionium collapses, showing that its formation requires both the appropriate topology and a minimum size. Energy analysis reveals that the transition involves cooperative relaxation of exchange frustration and redistribution of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and magnetostatic energies, leading to a double-domain-wall structure. The resulting skyrmionium exhibits persistent breathing oscillations around an equilibrium radius, confirming its dynamical stability as a metastable state. These findings establish a predictive framework for controlling skyrmion merging and provide design guidelines for engineering skyrmionium textures in chiral magnetic nanostructures.
title: Nonlinear Interaction and Topological Selection Rules in two Skyrmion Merging: Emergence of Skyrmionium Textures

summary: A child who learns to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace the difference to what a learner reads when it decides. A position, a count or a time keeps taking new values as the input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine is at least 99% correct, on average over lengths 41 to 500, on nine of fifteen benchmark tasks, five of them tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves; given new cycles after training it reverses strings of 15,015 symbols without error and fails beyond that on the curve the theory predicts; and its controllers run unchanged on neurons.
title: How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer

summary: Building a playable world requires more than generating plausible video: it demands responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions with dynamic entities. Beyond single-player interaction, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction through the composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions. summary: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. summary: Volatility dynamics can carry information about temporal relationships that is not apparent in the conditional mean. Extracting this information is difficult because the persistence of each variable can obscure its dependence on other variables. This paper presents QS-TCN, a method for ordering multivariate time series that combines statistical estimates of volatility memory with temporal convolutional learning. Persistence estimates obtained by quasi-maximum likelihood and temporal modes extracted by the Matrix Pencil method define structured filters within the network. Together with learned filters, they represent the history of the target and support comparisons of directional evidence between variables. These comparisons are combined into a global order of precedence, which does not identify a causal graph. summary: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.
title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction

summary: The shift from traditional to generative search has fundamentally transformed online product discovery. Because conversational recommendations synthesize choices into a few direct answers, subtle systemic preferences toward specific providers can exert profound commercial impacts. In this work, we audit this phenomenon through two distinct dimensions: (i) brand popularity bias, the systematic preference for market-dominant entities over long-tail alternatives, and (ii) brand familiarity bias, the ranking advantage an entity encoded in an LLM's parametric memory holds over an unfamiliar competitor. First, evaluating commercial queries across major engines, we observe persistent brand popularity bias: dominant brands in the top quintile are cited 1.4x to 2.8x more frequently than the average brand within a sample of 1,176 top market players, already present in parametric memory that external web retrieval fails to mitigate. Second, through controlled in-context experiments holding product attributes constant, we find that substituting authentic brand signatures with unfamiliar ones significantly degrades recommendation rank. Conversely, fact-preserving content rewrites yield negligible ranking gains. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that generative search engines reinforce a ``rich-get-richer'' dynamic by favoring established market leaders and imposing a parametric barrier to entry that standard content optimization cannot overcome.
title: The Popular Get More Popular: Auditing Brand Bias in Generative Search

summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.
title: TACT-KV: Tri-Axis Cosine Transform for Compressing Volumetric KV Caches in Medical VLMs

summary: Serving large language models (LLMs) under tight memory and latency service-level objectives (SLOs), including on edge devices, requires jointly selecting the model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and mixed-precision quantization recipes. Exhaustive search over this combinatorially large space is infeasible. Unlike data-center serving, which often prioritizes throughput or generation speed, resource-constrained deployments typically set memory and latency budgets as constraints and then seek the configuration with the highest generation quality among feasible ones. To this end, we propose ACSeL, a framework that identifies configurations predicted to satisfy deployment constraints while achieving high predicted generation quality. To enable efficient quality estimation, we use Relative Model Quality Degradation (RMQD), a proxy based on the divergence between the candidate and reference models' next-token distributions over a small calibration corpus. Across the evaluated model sizes and precisions, RMQD is inexpensive to evaluate and strongly correlated with downstream benchmark performance. ACSeL combines (i) a lightweight quality surrogate that predicts RMQD directly from a configuration; (ii) Few-shot Median Calibration (FMC), which calibrates operator-profile-based latency estimates using a small number of end-to-end profiles; and (iii) a structured search algorithm BandPareto for exploring layerwise mixed-precision configurations. Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge platform show that FMC substantially improves deployment feasibility, while BandPareto + FMC achieves the highest feasibility and the lowest RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations in the evaluation set.
title: ACSeL: Adaptive Configuration Search for Hardware-Constrained LLM Inference

summary: Here, I study the conditions for realizing an axion topology in a homogeneous inversion-symmetric electromagnetic continuum, in the absence of a crystalline lattice. I introduce a continuum inversion invariant expressed solely in terms of the spectral properties of the material response in the zero- and infinite-wave-vector limits. Surprisingly, it is found that standard gyrotropic-type material responses are strongly constrained and, under fairly general conditions, cannot open an axion gap within first-order perturbation theory. Based on an analogy between the effective response of crystalline photonic axion insulators and the optical response of centrosymmetric altermagnets, a class of spatially dispersive odd magnetoelectric couplings that can open an axion gap is identified. These findings suggest an interesting hierarchy of nonreciprocal mechanisms in electromagnetic continua: while uniform gyrotropy relates to Chern phases, odd magnetoelectric coupling relates to axion phases.

summary: Capturing scenes with extreme motion and high dynamic range is fundamentally constrained by trade-offs among temporal resolution, spatial detail, signal-to-noise ratio, and dynamic range under practical bandwidth, power, and quantum-efficiency limits. Conventional frame-based cameras therefore suffer from temporal undersampling, exposure-induced motion blur, and sensor saturation. The Complementary Vision Sensor (CVS) addresses these limitations by decomposing visual information across two complementary pathways, a spatially dense, temporally sparse, long-exposure RGB pathway and a temporally dense, spatially sparse, short-exposure patiotemporal difference pathway. Their complementary measurements provide appearance, structural, and motion cues across a wide dynamic range that enable reconstruction beyond conventional imaging. We present CoGenRec, a complementarity-driven generative reconstruction framework that unifies video deblurring, high-temporal-resolution frame interpolation, and HDR fusion. CoGenRec encodes complementary measurements into multi-scale spatiotemporal features using exposure-aware appearance modeling and bidirectional temporal propagation. These features constrain a video diffusion model and are injected into the VAE decoder to recover fine structures lost during latent-space compression, combining the scene fidelity of physical measurements with the appearance recovery capabilities of learned video priors. On SportsSloMo-CVS, CoGenRec improves PSNR over the strongest general-purpose baseline by 4.40 dB for deblurring, 3.89 dB for frame interpolation, and 5.04 dB for HDR fusion, respectively. It also achieves strong perceptual quality on 129 unseen scenes captured with real CVS. These results establish a unified approach to advance high-quality reconstruction under challenging motion and illumination conditions. Project page: https://cogenrec.github.io/.
title: CoGenRec: A Unified Generative Framework for Complementary Vision Reconstruction

summary: Capturing scenes with extreme motion and high dynamic range is fundamentally constrained by trade-offs among temporal resolution, spatial detail, signal-to-noise ratio, and dynamic range under practical bandwidth, power, and quantum-efficiency limits. Conventional frame-based cameras therefore suffer from temporal undersampling, exposure-induced motion blur, and sensor saturation. The Complementary Vision Sensor (CVS) addresses these limitations by decomposing visual information across two complementary pathways, a spatially dense, temporally sparse, long-exposure RGB pathway and a temporally dense, spatially sparse, short-exposure patiotemporal difference pathway. Their complementary measurements provide appearance, structural, and motion cues across a wide dynamic range that enable reconstruction beyond conventional imaging. We present CoGenRec, a complementarity-driven generative reconstruction framework that unifies video deblurring, high-temporal-resolution frame interpolation, and HDR fusion. CoGenRec encodes complementary measurements into multi-scale spatiotemporal features using exposure-aware appearance modeling and bidirectional temporal propagation. These features constrain a video diffusion model and are injected into the VAE decoder to recover fine structures lost during latent-space compression, combining the scene fidelity of physical measurements with the appearance recovery capabilities of learned video priors. On SportsSloMo-CVS, CoGenRec improves PSNR over the strongest general-purpose baseline by 4.40 dB for deblurring, 3.89 dB for frame interpolation, and 5.04 dB for HDR fusion, respectively. It also achieves strong perceptual quality on 129 unseen scenes captured with real CVS. These results establish a unified approach to advance high-quality reconstruction under challenging motion and illumination conditions. Project page: https://cogenrec.github.io/.

summary: Memory-safety concerns make Rust an attractive target for modernizing legacy C/C++ systems, yet project-level C++ migration must balance semantic fidelity with Rust-oriented reconstruction. Source-structure-preserving migration can track low-level behavior, but it can also carry source-language organization, unsafe idioms, and project assumptions into Rust. Direct agent-based translation gives the model more freedom to construct a Rust project, but semantic coverage depends on the model identifying the source behaviors that must be preserved. This problem is especially acute for C++, where source behaviors are often hidden in object models, destructor-driven lifetime protocols, and other hard-to-localize C++ semantics. This paper presents Req2Rust, the first project-level LLM-based C++-to-Rust migration harness. Req2Rust first derives an evidence-grounded Migration Requirements Specification (MRS) that records the behaviors and constraints that must be preserved. It then synthesizes a Rust Design Specification (RDS) and realizes it as an initial Rust project. Because real projects contain implementation details and idioms that only become visible during build and validation, Req2Rust treats the initial Rust project as an executable refinement state. Compiler, semantic, and unsafe-reduction validators produce validation reports for improving buildability, behavioral alignment, and unsafe usage. We evaluate Req2Rust on general C++ projects and modules from the large-scale Openharmony codebase against a ClaudeCode baseline. Req2Rust produces buildable Rust crates in both settings and improves test pass rate from 69.5% to 91.9% on general projects and from 45.4% to 87.9% on Openharmony modules.
title: Req2Rust: A Requirements-Guided Agent Harness for Project-Level C++-to-Rust Migration

summary: Traditional models of collective motion commonly assume that animals turn to match their neighbours' directions of travel. In the harmonic theory, decisions follow from a neural representation of direction, and a neighbour enters only as a stimulus at a bearing, the direction in which it lies. Here we show that a neighbour's spatial extent allows its orientation to enter through projection geometry alone, and the theory generates a matrix of coupling coefficients indexed by the neighbour's bearing and aspect. Responses to bearing alone form one edge of this matrix, and classical heading matching is a special case on its diagonal, one ray through a two-parameter family. Independently, an animal that responds only to neighbour position, perceived with a delay, acquires an alignment coefficient set by the slope of its distance-weighted attraction profile, so that it can align, anti-align or reverse sign. Alignment need not be a rule to be measured. In schooling fish and walking pigeons with body orientation measured independently of travel, social responses are recovered, including bearing responses in the fish. Heading excess depends on how turning is measured, appearing in the fish with forward but not centred responses and remaining unresolved in pigeons. Controls show why neither outcome identifies a direct alignment rule. In fish recordings with motion-assigned body polarity, heading-dependent structure departs from Vicsek form and fails the coefficient test for a common angular potential. Whether animals align thereby becomes a measurable question, with geometric, perceptual and behavioural origins that can be distinguished.
title: Bearing, heading and the perceptual geometry of collective motion

summary: Nonreciprocal charge transport in noncentrosymmetric superconductors probes broken symmetries and superconducting fluctuations and underpins the superconducting diode effect. Despite extensive studies, the factors governing its magnitude remain unclear. In this work, we use molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) to synthesize a broad family of FeTe-based superconducting heterostructures with top layers spanning topologically trivial versus nontrivial, layered versus nonlayered, and magnetic versus nonmagnetic materials. Through systematic first- and second-harmonic transport measurements, we find that the magnetochiral anisotropy coefficient $γ$ is insensitive to the top-layer crystal structure, lattice constant, thickness, topology, and magnetism, but exhibits a negative correlation with the superconducting transition width $ΔT$. Control measurements on superconducting stoichiometric FeTe films reveal much weaker nonreciprocity, confirming the essential role of interfacial inversion-symmetry breaking. Combined with a disorder-based theoretical model, our results establish a universal relationship: for comparable inversion-symmetry breaking, reduced interfacial disorder sharpens the superconducting transition and strongly enhances nonreciprocal transport in the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition regime. These findings identify $ΔT$ as a unifying parameter governing nonreciprocity across FeTe-based heterostructures, reconcile previously disparate observations, and establish a general framework for engineering enhanced nonreciprocal superconducting responses and exploring superconducting diode effects in nonlinear quantum devices.
title: Universal Negative Correlation between Nonreciprocity and Superconducting Transition Width in FeTe-Based Heterostructures

summary: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.
title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving

summary: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.
title: MAC-v2: Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels

summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant
title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization

summary: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.
title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time

summary: Corporate fraud is a serious threat to the integrity of markets, the protection of investors, and public confidence in business institutions. It may involve the deliberate falsification of accounts, diversion of assets, bribery, market manipulation, concealment of liabilities, related-party abuse, or misleading disclosures. In India, the problem is addressed through a combination of company law, securities regulation, financial-sector supervision, criminal investigation, audit regulation and corporate-governance requirements. The framework includes the Companies Act, 2013; the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992; listing and disclosure regulations; banking laws; and the work of institutions such as the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Serious Fraud Investigation Office, Securities and Exchange Board of India, Reserve Bank of India, National Financial Reporting Authority and enforcement agencies. This paper examines the principal forms and causes of corporate fraud, the legal and institutional mechanisms used to prevent and investigate it, and the continuing challenges in enforcement. The Satyam Computer Services scandal and the Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services crisis are considered as examples of how weak oversight, misleading financial information, governance failures and delayed detection can damage stakeholders. The paper argues that India has developed a substantial formal framework, but effective protection depends on implementation: timely information sharing, competent investigation, independent boards and auditors, credible whistle-blower systems, proportionate sanctions, and stronger financial literacy. It concludes that regulation should combine deterrence with early detection and organisational cultures that reward truthful reporting.

title: Corporate Fraud and Regulatory Mechanisms in India

summary: TrustEval presents an empirical study of ensemble reliability in small open-weight Large Language Model (LLM) safety judges. The study evaluates two lightweight models, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, using a simple random sample of 50 conversations from the DICES-350 dataset. Rather than relying on free-form model generation, the evaluation uses next-token probabilities for fixed Yes/No responses to estimate each model's unsafe classification probability. The study compares individual model performance with an arithmetic-mean probability ensemble, examining error metrics, ranking performance, calibration, and the relationship between inter-model disagreement and human-consensus error. The evaluation uses 5,200 ratings from 104 retained raters per conversation, including 4,889 decisive ratings. Results indicate that the ensemble reduces mean absolute error relative to Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, but does not outperform SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct on mean absolute error or the held-out prevalence baseline on squared-error metrics. Inter-model disagreement shows an exploratory association with evaluation error in some analyses, but is not established as a validated uncertainty or human-escalation signal. This work is an exploratory empirical study. Its findings are limited by the sample of 50 conversations, the use of two models from one benchmark, and the reliance on human consensus as a reference rather than objective ground truth. Independent external validation and broader evaluation are left for future work.
title: TrustEval : An Empirical Study of Ensemble Reliability in Small Open-Weight LLM Safety Judges

summary: Introduction : Orbital blowout fractures may be accompanied by substantial edema and soft-tissue injury that complicate assessment of extraocular muscle involvement. Distinguishing true mechanical entrapment from potentially reversible post-traumatic soft-tissue restriction is important to avoid unnecessary orbital exploration. Case Illustration : Two patients presented following blunt facial trauma with right orbital blowout fractures, marked periorbital swelling, and orbital fat herniation into the maxillary sinus. Diplopia was absent in both cases, and the second patient had no rectus muscle entrapment on computed tomography. Both were managed conservatively with cold compresses and high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg every six hours followed by tapering. After five and six days, respectively, facial and periorbital swelling markedly decreased, ocular movements were documented in all directions, and neither patient reported diplopia or blurred vision. No orbital surgical exploration was performed. Discussion : Orbital fat herniation and severe edema should not automatically be interpreted as extraocular muscle entrapment. Serial clinical assessment after reduction of acute swelling may better identify patients who truly require reconstruction. Although corticosteroids may facilitate edema resolution, improvement cannot be attributed solely to steroid therapy in this uncontrolled case series. Conclusion : Corticosteroid-assisted conservative management may support reassessment of selected orbital blowout fractures without definite muscle entrapment and may help avoid premature surgery.
tags: Orbital blowout fracture; corticosteroids; periorbital edema; conservative management; muscle entrapment.
title: High-Dose Corticosteroid-Assited Conservative Management of Orbital Blow Out Fractures Without Extraocular Muscle Entrapment: A Two-Case Series

summary: We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.
title: Whiel: A Neurosymbolic Platform for Certified Relational Program Verification
