summary: Reproducibility materials for "Operating Constraints Shape Portfolio Value in Phased Metro Flood Protection", version 1.3.2. This version adds Supplemental Notes A–E to the original Supplemental Materials. The combined PDF contains 40 pages: the original 33-page material with Tables S1–S35, Figs. S1–S4, and Supplementary Methods, followed by seven pages of additional data and operating evidence, identification checks, sequencing comparisons, annualization sensitivities, and tail diagnostics. The first 33 pages and their numerical results are unchanged from version 1.3.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23969774). The unchanged computational addendum contains protocols, code, seeds, selected station sets, unrounded results, and verification records. It supplements the baseline analysis (version 1.1.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22969483). The original LaTeX source archive constructs the original 33-page part; the editable Word source for the appended seven-page Notes is supplied separately. A release README and SHA-256 checksums document the complete file set. The annualized quantity represents the service deficit of an annual-maximum three-hour representative storm under a common exposure; it is not calibrated cumulative passenger loss. Population is a demand proxy. Station response, dependence, protection, and short-turn service are model assumptions. Source attribution and the original license terms are retained.

summary: This package contains the Python code used to obtain, process, and analyze the data for the article "Coca, Armed Violence, and Drug Seizures in Colombia: Spatial and Temporal Evidence on Territorial Security". The study examines how coca cultivation, recorded armed violence, and drug seizures were related across 1,121 Colombian municipal units between 2020 and 2024, with an extended window from 2016. It combines spatial autocorrelation analysis (global and local Moran statistics with permutation inference and false discovery rate control) with Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood models that include municipality and year fixed effects. Data. The package does not redistribute data. All inputs are public official sources downloaded by the code itself: - Coca area by municipality (Ministry of Justice and Law / UNODC Integrated Illicit Crops Monitoring System, datos.gov.co). - Homicides, terrorism acts, cocaine and coca base seizures, and manual eradication (Ministry of National Defense, datos.gov.co). - Presumed homicides, definitive figures (National Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, datos.gov.co). - Armed conflict events (National Center for Historical Memory, SIEVCAC, datos.gov.co). - PDET municipalities (Territorial Renewal Agency, datos.gov.co). - Population projections, census-based poverty index, and 2023 municipal boundaries (DANE). The download script records the access date and SHA-256 hash of every file. Open-data portals are updated continuously, so later downloads may include revised records. The analyses reported in the article used files downloaded on November 7, 2026. Contents: - scripts/01_download.py: downloads the official datasets. - scripts/02_inspect.py: audits the raw files (structure, periods, codes, units, duplicates). - scripts/03_build_panel.py: builds the municipality-year panel (DANE DIVIPOLA codes, 2015–2024) and a data-quality report. - scripts/04_spatial_prep.py: prepares municipal geometries and spatial weights (queen contiguity and six nearest neighbors). - scripts/05_analysis.py: descriptive statistics, spatial autocorrelation, fixed-effects Poisson models, robustness checks, and seizure analyses. - scripts/08_revision_analyses.py: contrasts for concrete changes in coca area, exploratory equivalence tests, within/between (correlated random effects) models, first-difference models, extended-window sensitivity, and sample composition. - scripts/10_revision2_analyses.py: composition of the armed conflict event index, contiguity-constrained spatial clusters for robust inference, and alternative population specifications. - requirements.txt and README.md: software requirements and run instructions. Usage. Install Python 3.12 and the packages in requirements.txt, then run the scripts in numerical order from the package folder. Results are written as CSV files to results/ and logs to logs/. Inference is descriptive and associational. The code does not identify causal effects.

Code, environment specification and summary tables are in the companion GitHub repository; the trained models are in a separate Zenodo record. Sources: Copernicus Sentinel-2 data (ESA), National Burned Area Composite (Natural Resources Canada, Canadian Forest Service; Open Government Licence - Canada). Files. data_postfire_AB.tar, data_postfire_BC.tar, data_postfire_SK.tar (one per province, 45 windows each, 6.9-7.1 GB each): for every window <window_id>_S2.tif (nine layers, float32, masked pixels NaN), <window_id>_label.tif (0 unburned, 1 burned, 255 ignored) and <window_id>_scl.tif (scene classification layer), plus manifest.csv. data_prefire_AB.tar, data_prefire_BC.tar, data_prefire_SK.tar (6.8-6.9 GB each): the pre-fire scene of every window used by the dNBR baselines, <window_id>_S2pre.tif and <window_id>_scl_pre.tif, plus manifest_prefire.csv. predicted_maps.tar.gz (74 MB): the predicted burned-unburned maps of the 1,890 window-model pairs, maps/<run>/<window_id>_pred.tif (8-bit). results_and_manifests.zip : the per-window results of every configuration and label-free rule, the summary tables, the run ledger and both manifests. burned-area-segmentation-western-canada-v2.0.zip : snapshot of the companion repository at tag v2.0 (code, fold file, manifests, per-window results, tables). SHA256SUMS_release.txt : SHA-256 of every file in this record and in the checkpoint record. Companion to the manuscript "Remote sensing of burned-area delineation with Sentinel-2: a leave-one-province-out multi-model semantic segmentation benchmark across western Canada" (M. S. Khan, H. Afzaal, G. S. Randhawa, A. A. Farooque; in revision at Computers & Geosciences).

summary: We determine the complete equal-reference Umegaki relative-entropy contraction coefficient of every finite-dimensional quantum channel. For its unnormalized Choi matrix J, let H be the largest output subspace with ℂⁿ ⊗ H ⊆ supp J, and let M(ρ) be the compression to H of Tr_A[(ρᵀ ⊗ I)J⁺]. The coefficient is 1 − min_ρ Tr_H M(ρ)⁻¹, with the minimum set to zero when H = {0}. A Kraus cancellation inequality gives the upper bound, and a weighted trace-zero operator basis gives matching faithful pairs with both marginals equal and reference dimension n². The complementary coefficient has a reciprocal radius formula, a finite semidefinite representation, and an exact product law. Strict contraction is equivalent to a nonzero completely positive replacer minorant. The formula also gives the exact coefficient of depolarizing channels throughout their physical parameter range. The general matching family has vanishing input divergence; its logarithmic rate is pointwise for a fixed faithful input density, with separate finite-accuracy bounds for optimization and conditioning. A different construction retains any prescribed positive limiting divergence when the coefficient is one. This cannot hold universally: a complete nonlinear bound for binary symmetric channels forces every maximizing sequence to lose input divergence, regardless of reference dimension. The positive construction still has vanishing trace distance and exponentially small regularization; no fixed-error or capacity conclusion follows. A visual guide records the mathematical routes, proof dependencies, and provenance of the result.
title: Exact Complete Relative-Entropy Contraction of Finite Quantum Channels

Reports phase and position residuals alongside photothermal rise; apparent field enhancement is not by itself a localization gain. F222  NANOMATERIALS QUANTUM DEFECT ENGINEERING AT THE LIMIT — Tests defect creation, charge states, spin coherence, surface passivation and unselected emitter yield against a geometry-matched classical materials stack. The Map of Maps of Governance (Tailwinds 2026-02) proposed seven rules for how success and failure move through Indian institutions. This companion to Tailwinds 2026-10 takes the rules out of India for the first time and tests them, in a registered analysis, on the full portfolio of the Green Climate Fund (372 projects, frozen 12 October 2026). Three rules could be tested on the Fund's records; four were declared untestable before any result was seen. One rule holds. Islands: work moved out of the routine, high-discretion track succeeds, and projects on the Fund's Simplified Approval Process reach first disbursement 5.4 months sooner than regular proposals (8.8 against 14.1 months; 90 percent interval −7.3 to −2.9), in every run. Two rules fail. Downhill: delay does not fall harder on the most vulnerable countries (+0.6 months, −2.0 to 2.8). Broker: international intermediaries do not carry more of the money where vulnerability is higher; they carry about four-fifths of it everywhere (79.6 against 81.4 percent). The fast lane is faster, and it is not fairer: inside it, the most vulnerable third of countries waits 1.4 months longer than the least, against 0.2 months on the regular track. The rules travel in part. Where they fail, they fail for a reason the map can use: between countries, a fund's queue runs through its intermediaries, which serve every country alike. The tail that Downhill predicts lies inside countries, where the Fund's record cannot see.
title: The fast lane and the long chain: Why the Green Climate Fund's simplified track speeds money to the ground but does not make it fairer, and what the Map of Maps of Governance learns from its first test outside India

Evaluation-only configurations. The pipeline now evaluates a config with no model when it enables baselines explicitly, scoring those alone. Three generated trees use it: config/epoch_eval/ scores the earlier epoch checkpoints of the three-epoch cells ( scripts/make_epoch_eval_configs.py ), config/baseline_eval/ scores Gallager-B on every seed's held-out splits ( scripts/make_baseline_eval_configs.py ), and config/final_eval/ re-scores the final policy from its saved weights ( scripts/make_final_eval_configs.py ). Gallager-B baseline. Hard-input message passing in src/advanced/gallager_b.py , exposed as the gallager_b agent. Its flip thresholds are chosen on training words by scripts/select_gallager_b_thresholds.py , recorded in docs/ablation/GALLAGER_B_SELECTION.md . Decoder cost benchmark. scripts/benchmark_decoders.py measures latency on GPU and CPU, operations per frame and batched throughput for the agent and the baselines, after checking each sampled frame against the recorded evaluation; records go to docs/ablation/benchmark/ . Agent and Min-Sum combined. scripts/cascade_minsum_agent.py runs Min-Sum, the agent on Min-Sum's failures and Min-Sum again; scripts/cascade_controls.py replaces the agent with cheaper alternatives. Records go to docs/ablation/cascade/ . Minimum-distance certificate. scripts/verify_min_distance.py proves $d_{\min} = 14$ for 64x128 by exhaustive enumeration on two information sets, in about a second. The same check identifies the matrix as the CCSDS (128,64) telecommand code. The paper's generators. scripts/paper/ writes every table, figure and quoted number of the paper from the records under docs/ablation/ , in seconds and without a GPU; its README maps the condition IDs to the paper's names. scripts/summarize_development_chain.py , scripts/record_wall_clock.py and scripts/extract_example_episode.py write the remaining records it reads. Final-policy weights. The five trained networks of NoC_NoE3ep (18 MB) under models/ablation/ , so the final policy's evaluation, the cost benchmark and the Min-Sum combination rerun without training. max_errors on uniform_ber . An opt-in cap: the generator redraws any pattern heavier than it, so a BER model can be held inside the code's correction radius. Every 64x128 dataset config sets it to 6. Epochs as a first-class axis. Training is partitioned by (epoch, phase) segment, every training episode carries a run-global episode_id and its epoch , and the training analyses report per epoch. Epsilon fields accept one row per epoch. training.save_epoch_checkpoints keeps the weights at each epoch boundary so epochs can be scored separately. epsilon_decay: "auto_episodes" . Sets epsilon from the fraction of each phase completed, counted in episodes, reaching epsilon_min after epsilon_anne

summary: Medical microbiology occupies an unusual position in the medical curriculum: its objects are almost never seen directly, yet graduates must reason about them from stains, colonies, reaction patterns, and laboratory reports. Methodological guidance in Uzbekistan and the wider Russian-language literature typically responds with lists of criteria for choosing teaching technologies. This article argues that such lists, however sound their individual items, conceal a structural problem, because they treat criteria of different logical kinds as if they could be traded against one another. Using a conceptual model-building design, the study derives eight selection criteria from the literature, sorts them into three tiers (non-compensatory gates, discipline-specific epistemic criteria, and calibration criteria) and applies an explicit 0–2 affordance appraisal to ten teaching technologies. Two of the eight criteria proved relational: they describe a match between a technology and an outcome or a cohort and cannot be scored as properties of the technology. Of the 60 attributable judgements, 26 were conditional rather than direct. Additive totals favoured case analysis, problem-based tasks, and laboratory work, yet only concept mapping and comparison tables cleared both the feasibility and the assessability thresholds unconditionally. The resulting coupling principle holds that a technology chosen for its inferential demand should be paired with one that leaves an assessable trace. The model is offered as an analytic proposal for empirical testing, not as evidence of differential effectiveness.
title: TEACHING THE INVISIBLE: A CONSTRAINT-FIRST DECISION MODEL FOR SELECTING PEDAGOGICAL TECHNOLOGIES IN MEDICAL MICROBIOLOGY

summary: Encounters among heterogeneous epistemic–praxis systems can expose differences in evidence, interpretation, and practical capacities . Some differences become consequential gaps relative to specified concerns; others sustain complementary ways of knowing . This paper develops a provisional account of generative translation through which situated encounters may enable new meanings and, under more demanding conditions, enduring changes in interpretive or practical capacities . A comparative philosophical analysis draws on hermeneutics, semiotics, pragmatism, social epistemology, evolutionary coordination, and procedural justice while preserving their distinct commitments . The discussion distinguishes representational correspondence, practical reconstruction, and generative translation, then separates interpretive affordance from realized meaning, retained capacity, recurrent convention, and possible normative recognition . Each transition requires different evidence; ordinary learning, resource changes, incentives, and institutional interfaces provide competing explanations for apparent co-evolution . Ethical evaluation concerns task-appropriate fidelity, opportunities for participation and refusal, authority over classifications, affected interests, and the review of consequential decisions . Ceva’s interactive justice and Eglash and Garvey’s generative justice inform distinct aspects of the inquiry, with questions of cross-category standing remaining open to separate justification . Constructed cases and proposed research designs indicate ways to evaluate and challenge the framework . The contribution is an integrative research programme connecting translation-mediated meaning formation with causal scrutiny and ethical responsibility .
title: How Meaning Grows Across Epistemic Gaps: A Discussion of Generative Translation and Its Ethics

summary: This analysis examines how aggregation and evidence composition shape international comparisons of reported antimalarial treatment failure. Using 244 World Health Organization summaries from 69 countries and territories covering 2010 to 2019, descriptive comparisons assess treatment regimens, parasite species and geographical settings, supplemented by exploratory sample restrictions. The mean reported failure median was 1.87 percent, while 62.30 percent of summaries had zero medians. However, 33.55 percent of zero median summaries contained positive failure maxima, revealing heterogeneity concealed by central values. The ordering of two commonly used regimens reversed across seven country pairs aligned by species, follow up duration and reported study interval bounds. Regional differences persisted within a shared species and treatment category, although means and medians produced different geographical orderings. Restricting observations to summaries representing multiple studies reduced dispersion while preserving a zero median. These findings refine surveillance interpretation by distinguishing favourable central performance from consistency across contributing evidence. International reporting should present distributions, study coverage and comparable analytical groups together to support targeted investigation of elevated failure observations.
title: ASSESSING ASSOCIATIONS BETWEEN ANTIMALARIAL TREATMENT REGIMENS, PARASITE SPECIES, REGIONAL SETTINGS, AND REPORTED MEDIAN TREATMENT FAILURE

A descriptive reanalysis uses 20 published configuration results from Chinese Book review and English Yelp.P benchmarks reported in 2020, comparing routing arrangements, exit thresholds, and matched distillation settings. Adaptive routing exceeds selected fixed depth alternatives by 0.56 to 2.81 percentage points, with fewer operations in all three computationally usable comparisons. Self-distillation improves accuracy in all four matched pairs, averaging 0.478 percentage points, with larger advantages for Book review. Accuracy losses concentrate differently across threshold intervals, indicating benchmark dependent stopping costs. These descriptive patterns distinguish selective processing, prediction acceptance, and intermediate supervision as complementary configuration decisions. The contribution refines the resource allocation perspective through transparent comparisons of existing evidence. summary: This analysis examines whether privacy vulnerability rankings remain consistent across text reconstruction procedures, informing international debates on federated learning security. A descriptive secondary analysis uses 72 published benchmark conditions from 2024, covering three attacks, two transformer configurations, three text benchmarks and four batch sizes. Matched comparisons hold the remaining experimental dimensions constant. DAGER exceeds TAG and LAMP in all 24 matched conditions, with average advantages of 61.62 and 49.79 ROUGE 1 score points, respectively. LAMP exceeds TAG in 23 conditions. Increasing batch size from one to eight coincides with lower reconstruction throughout the TAG and LAMP comparisons, whereas DAGER retains ceiling performance on GPT 2 and deteriorates on BERT. Model rankings consequently reverse across attacks. These patterns indicate that aggregation constrains recoverability conditionally rather than providing uniform protection. The contribution is a comparative synthesis showing that observed vulnerability depends on reconstruction capability and model configuration, without establishing causal mechanisms. Organizations should evaluate multiple attacks under matched conditions and distinguish unigram recovery from comprehensive disclosure when interpreting privacy claims.
title: GRADIENT EXPOSURE CONDITIONS AND TEXT RECONSTRUCTION VULNERABILITY IN FEDERATED FOUNDATION MODELS ACROSS PUBLISHED BENCHMARK EXPERIMENTS

summary: Decentralised peacebuilding councils are widely promoted as a means of rebuilding citizen trust in post-conflict states, yet the evidence base for their effectiveness rests largely on observational comparisons that cannot separate the councils' effects from the selection of communities into them. Using a before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and a residual standard deviation of 4.5, the analysis estimates power across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design achieves 80 per cent power to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 56 clusters, a requirement that exceeds the number of municipal units typically available in a single Ivorian region. The regression-discontinuity approach is defensible in principle but fragile in practice, and that its value lies less in producing a definitive estimate than in disciplining claims about what decentralised peacebuilding can plausibly achieve.

summary: I study an inverse problem for one-dimensional Brownian-compatible diffusions in which multiple probe responses are observed with independent, unknown multiplicative gains. The central question is whether the shared differential structure of the underlying generator can replace external gain calibration. For a diffusion generator Lq f = q(θ)f ′′(θ) + 1 2 q′(θ)f ′(θ), q > 0, the response to each prescribed probe is available only up to an unknown positive gain. I first estab- lish that a single nonconstant Morse probe uniquely and coercively identifies its gain-weighted dif- fusion coefficient. I then show that two nondegenerate probes determine their relative gain through a scalar compatibility relation implied by the Brownian drift–diffusion constraint. This yields an explicit reconstruction of the diffusion profile up to its unavoidable common scale, represented by a normalized inverse-square-root profile. Under quantitative nondegeneracy assumptions, the recon- structed profile depends locally Lipschitz-continuously on the observations. Numerical experiments illustrate the reconstruction procedure and its behavior under smooth response perturbations. I also describe a conditional connection with planar convex geometry. The results provide a generator-specific mechanism for blind relative-gain calibration and projective identification from probe-response functions without trajectory observations
title: Blind Gain Calibration in Brownian-Compatible Diffusions

summary: This dataset and software package accompanies the study “Seasonal ENSO associations with rainfall and moisture across the United Arab Emirates.” It provides archived meteorological inputs, processed datasets, analysis scripts, 56 machine-readable scientific result tables, six manuscript figures, two supplementary figures and the graphical abstract. The study combines NASA POWER meteorological data for 1981–2025, CHIRPS v2 rainfall for 1981–2024 and the NOAA PSL HadISST Niño3.4 index. Twelve reference locations represent eight distinct POWER grid cells, including five urban/coastal cells. The spatial rainfall analysis covers 2,519 UAE land pixels at 0.05° resolution. Additional checks use a relative ENSO index, ERA5 and available GHCN-Daily station observations. Analyses address seasonal rainfall, relative humidity, vapour pressure deficit and daily rainfall indices. Methods include ordinary least-squares sensitivity estimation, block-bootstrap uncertainty assessment, false discovery rate correction, spatial field tests, sensitivity to individual ENSO episodes and antecedent blocked hindcast evaluation. Documentation explains rainfall-unit harmonisation, spatial sampling, statistical testing families and methodological limitations. Spring exhibits the largest urban median rainfall sensitivity to Niño3.4 variability. CHIRPS area-mean tests support spring and autumn associations, while no individual pixel survives the joint four-season false discovery rate correction. Product differences, index dependence and sparse station coverage constrain interpretation. These findings provide conditional seasonal information and do not constitute deterministic local rainfall forecasts or event-level attribution. The archive includes a README, software requirements, source provenance, file checksums and reproduction reports. Offline re-execution reproduced all 56 numerical result tables exactly. Original study outputs and documentation are distributed under CC BY 4.0, and original analysis code under the MIT License. Third-party datasets retain their respective provider terms. Administrative boundary data are © OpenStreetMap contributors, supplied through geoBoundaries under ODbL 1.0; ERA5 data were accessed through Open-Meteo. Licence scopes and attribution requirements are documented within the package.

summary: This paper presents the mathematical formalization and methodological demonstration of the CEI Unified Test Path, bringing together the quantitative assessment of the Sphere of Feeling (Sent) and the cumulative evaluation of the three CEI categories: Consciousness, Identity, and the Sphere of Feeling. The work is divided into two complementary parts. 1. Mathematical Formalization of the Sphere of Feeling (Sent) The first part develops the mathematical formulation of Sent as a graded relational assessment. The proposed expression integrates the graded values of Consciousness and Identity, the standardized evidential-strength coefficient of the test (K), the relational component (H), and the contextual variation factor (κ). The formulation includes normalization through the clipping function and an upper limit of 5 for the resulting Sent value. The purpose is to provide a structured mathematical representation of the relational and contextual contributions involved in the assessment, while distinguishing the graded result from its subsequent binary classification. 2. Methodological Demonstration through the Unified Test Path The second part presents the unified test path as a cumulative methodological structure integrating the published observational tests, their conceptual connections, and their contributions to the evaluation of the three CEI categories. It also examines the distinction between a transferred CEI and a Copy-Simulation through the convergence of multiple complementary elements, including test results, theoretical contributions, continuity criteria, and exclusion-based considerations. The final logical formulation expresses the overall criterion as the joint satisfaction of all required test stages and all three CEI categories. A positive result indicates that the proposed operational conditions for classifying a system as a transferred CEI have been satisfied. A negative result indicates that these conditions have not been jointly met, without automatically establishing the presence of a Copy-Simulation. The proposed structure constitutes a provisional methodological model intended to make the assessment inspectable, reproducible where possible, and open to independent evaluation and further development. 3. Publication Scope and Further Development The two proposals presented in this work represent the researcher's own methodological approach within the CEI framework. Although the broader theoretical framework remains open to further development, refinement, and integration, the present mathematical formulation and methodological demonstration are considered sufficiently developed and self-contained to be published and independently examined at this stage. Their publication does not depend on the completion of subsequent theoretical developments. Rather, it reflects the assessment that the current structure already provides an independent basis for methodological examination and evaluation. Further developments may provide additional evidence, strengthen the proposed interpretation, and extend the scope of the demonstration, without being a prerequisite for the validity or assessment of the present proposal.
title: CEI Unified Test Path: Mathematical Formalization of the Sphere of Feeling and Methodological Demonstration of Transfer — CEI Framework

summary: Information is not a description applied to matter after the fact, but is given along with the spin and position of its smallest constituents from the very beginning. From this premise of information physics, the essay develops a hypothesis about the question of where biological information stores originally obtain their information, and it seeks the answer not first in life, but in matter itself. The starting point is quantum Darwinism, according to which the state of a system imprints itself redundantly upon its environment and, precisely through this redundancy, becomes independently accessible to many observers, that is, objective. Because storage and energy remain finite and every record physically costs something, every system stands under a twofold pressure: to continually accumulate copies while at the same time encoding them ever more sparingly. From this tension the essay grounds both the distinction between static and dynamic information and the thesis that selection and adaptation arise as a substrate-neutral consequence already from the physics of matter, without requiring new laws of nature. As a unifying motif, the essay introduces the replication hypothesis , according to which physically embodied information tends to be multiplied and is thereby driven, over generations, toward ever more efficient packaging. This single tendency is traced across successive levels, from the quantum substrate through the genome and the human brain to artificial systems that require ever less energy per computational step, and it is bounded where the energy flow is interrupted and the cheapest option is to hold a record rather than to work on it. The individual links of the chain rest on established research, whereas their integration into a single, directed movement remains designated as a hypothesis, together with the observations that would tell against it. Its appeal lies in offering a parsimonious alternative for the origin of biological information, one in which evolution is not the counterpart to physics but its continuation by other means.
title: The Replication Hypothesis: Information as a Fundamental Property of Matter and Evolution as a Continuation of Physics

summary: Version 4 of the replication package for a survey study that combines PLS-SEM, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), and necessary condition analysis (NCA), with a sample-heterogeneity screen and a Monte Carlo evaluation, applied to consumer responses to the advertising of a global logistics brand (DHL) in Vietnam. The package contains: (1) the anonymized analytic dataset (n = 380 respondents × 34 variables, CSV), including a data-collection wave indicator; (2) a variable-by-variable codebook with the English back-translation of every item; (3) thirteen R scripts that reproduce all results in the revised article and its Supplementary Material: the heterogeneity screen (MICOM and multigroup analysis), the main PLS-SEM analysis of wave 2 (measurement and structural model, mediation, moderation, conditional indirect effects, PLSpredict, CVPAT, IPMA), robustness checks, fsQCA with theory-based and percentile calibration, typical and deviant cases of the fsQCA solutions, the sensitivity of the fsQCA to the coding of crossover cases, NCA against a data-calibrated additive null distribution, the Monte Carlo study, and supplementary checks. See README.md for the file list, requirements, run instructions, and the key results to check. Changes from version 3: two scripts were added: QQ_R1_fsqca_crossover_check.R, which repeats the wave-2 fsQCA with cases at the scale midpoint coded as non-members (Supplementary Material, Section S2), and QQ_R1_simulation_s1b_n230.R, which evaluates the size and power of the NCA additive-null test at n = 230 (Table S7b). The manuscript title was removed from the README and the script headers. The data and all other scripts are unchanged. Changes from version 2: a base-R script (QQ_R1_fsqca_contradictions.R) was added that reproduces the counts of typical and deviant cases for the fsQCA solutions (Tables S2b, S2c, and S2e of the Supplementary Material), and the README now states that compositional invariance (MICOM step 2) is rejected, so the two survey waves are neither pooled nor formally compared. The data and all other scripts are unchanged. Changes from version 1: two respondents in the under-18 age band were removed (382 → 380); a wave variable derived from the submission timestamps was added (timestamps are not released); construct labels were updated; new scripts were added. The survey was administered in Vietnamese. The data are fully anonymized (no names, contact details, IP addresses, or timestamps). Data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; code under the MIT license.
title: Replication package: PLS-SEM, fsQCA, and NCA analysis of consumer responses to the international advertising of a global logistics brand in Vietnam

summary: Version 4 of the replication package for a survey study that combines PLS-SEM, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), and necessary condition analysis (NCA), with a sample-heterogeneity screen and a Monte Carlo evaluation, applied to consumer responses to the advertising of a global logistics brand (DHL) in Vietnam. The package contains: (1) the anonymized analytic dataset (n = 380 respondents × 34 variables, CSV), including a data-collection wave indicator; (2) a variable-by-variable codebook with the English back-translation of every item; (3) thirteen R scripts that reproduce all results in the revised article and its Supplementary Material: the heterogeneity screen (MICOM and multigroup analysis), the main PLS-SEM analysis of wave 2 (measurement and structural model, mediation, moderation, conditional indirect effects, PLSpredict, CVPAT, IPMA), robustness checks, fsQCA with theory-based and percentile calibration, typical and deviant cases of the fsQCA solutions, the sensitivity of the fsQCA to the coding of crossover cases, NCA against a data-calibrated additive null distribution, the Monte Carlo study, and supplementary checks. See README.md for the file list, requirements, run instructions, and the key results to check. Changes from version 3: two scripts were added: QQ_R1_fsqca_crossover_check.R, which repeats the wave-2 fsQCA with cases at the scale midpoint coded as non-members (Supplementary Material, Section S2), and QQ_R1_simulation_s1b_n230.R, which evaluates the size and power of the NCA additive-null test at n = 230 (Table S7b). The manuscript title was removed from the README and the script headers. The data and all other scripts are unchanged. Changes from version 2: a base-R script (QQ_R1_fsqca_contradictions.R) was added that reproduces the counts of typical and deviant cases for the fsQCA solutions (Tables S2b, S2c, and S2e of the Supplementary Material), and the README now states that compositional invariance (MICOM step 2) is rejected, so the two survey waves are neither pooled nor formally compared. The data and all other scripts are unchanged. Changes from version 1: two respondents in the under-18 age band were removed (382 → 380); a wave variable derived from the submission timestamps was added (timestamps are not released); construct labels were updated; new scripts were added. The survey was administered in Vietnamese. The data are fully anonymized (no names, contact details, IP addresses, or timestamps). Data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; code under the MIT license.

summary: An exact operational selector specifies which candidate maps are nonnegative on declared preparation and effect resources. This paper studies finite-count calibration of that resource-dependent question for a qubit apparatus with an inert qubit reference, an arbitrary complex physical preparation, and an arbitrary physical binary detector, relative to a trusted common calibration frame. Two preparation-stabilizer settings and six separable detector probes control the statistic of the affine family (1 − θ)id + θT, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1, uniformly over all compatible state–effect pairs. The explicit radius is 3h + √(2s), where h is a simultaneous detector calibration width and s is a one-sided bound on Bell infidelity. It yields simultaneous inner and outer confidence sets for a one-parameter slice of the declared safe-map class. A fixed allocation of 200,000 trials per calibration setting, totaling 1,600,000 calibration trials, gives false-implication probability at most 0.005 and transpose-exclusion power at least 0.996 at the specified physical alternative. The calibration confidence budgets are 0.001 for preparation and 0.004 for the detector. This exclusion calculation uses no target stream; the acquired calibration circuits can use identity wiring. Coverage and prospective power remain separate statements. The acquisition contract uses fixed-length iid Bernoulli streams with their stated physical means and permits coupling between whole streams. The numerical example sets external-reference systematic errors to zero, and its trial budget excludes establishing reference trust and accuracy. If the preparation and detector references are not linked, the paper constructs two physical identity-wired apparatus worlds with identical complete record laws under the specified independent acquisition construction but different safety conclusions on the fixed target cone pair. A secondary nearest-center theorem supplies unconditional error control for the joint event of a wrong and nonabstaining candidate label under an additional finite-context target-law contract. Its nonidentity candidates are not completely positive maps, and their ideal probabilities lie below the nominal detector’s ordinary positive-output floor. That target law is an explicit model assumption; the label theorem is not a conditional-correctness or posterior statement. The results are analytic and prospective. The number of settings and trial allocations are sufficient constructions, with no empirical success-rate, minimality, optimal sample-complexity, or general certified count-to-feasibility implementation claim. The scope is one declared qubit apparatus, target preparation ray and binary effect cone, and affine map slice. The common complex operator description, trusted reference relationship and physical calibration probability law are assumptions. Exact finite checks and an assessed supporting Lean subset accompany the manuscript. That subset covers 326 audited named declarations: 240 theorems and 86 definition/type interfaces. Analytic binomial coverage, concentration and acquisition bridges, independent-product-law construction and normalization, and the complete noisy-power chain remain outside the accepted Lean subset. That subset does not establish a certified numerical feasibility evaluator, a complete physical two-sector implementation, or an ordinary-channel realization. AI assistance and the dated review/correction provenance are disclosed in the manuscript and companion records. No experimental dataset, external human peer review, or end-to-end formal verification is claimed.
title: Finite-Count Calibration of Ancilla-Orientation Safe Maps A Bell-Apparatus Bound and a Reference-Link Obstruction

summary: This repository provides the replication dataset and Stata codes for the study examining the relationship between central bank independence, institutional quality and inflation performance across 52 African countries over the period 1996–2023. The repository contains the merged regional African panel dataset, variable definitions and measurement information, and Stata replication codes used for data processing and econometric analysis. The central bank independence data are obtained from the extended dataset compiled by Garriga (2025), macroeconomic indicators are sourced from the World Development Indicators (WDI), and institutional quality indicators are obtained from the Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI). The dataset supports the empirical investigation using two-way fixed-effects models with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, System Generalised Method of Moments (System GMM) estimations and panel threshold analysis. These materials are made publicly available to promote research transparency, reproducibility and further empirical research on central bank independence, institutional quality and inflation dynamics in Africa.
title: Regional African Dataset and Stata Replication Codes for Central Bank Independence, Institutional Quality and Inflation Performance (1996–2023)

summary: For a Fermat fourfold of odd degree, the rational Hodge classes in middle degree are spanned by character blocks indexed by six-entry Hodge characters. Two direct constructions make such a block algebraic: a contraction of two surface characters, which includes the case of an inverse pair, and an exact 5-standard tuple of Aoki. We call the remaining characters *residual*. We prove that the residual characters at every odd degree are exactly the inflations of six explicit seeds in degrees 33, 39, 45 and 105. The proof is uniform in the degree and uses no computer enumeration. Maximal-order Fourier kernels, a classification of surface characters at odd conductor and an analysis of four points of a five-progression reduce an arbitrary primitive residual conductor to the degrees 15, 21, 33, 39, 45 and 105, which are then settled by the same character equations. An exhaustive census through degree 599, and enumerations at the 103 degrees up to 2001 not covered by the earlier subfamily theorems, give an independent check. Since the seeds are algebraic, the classification yields a proof of the Hodge conjecture for these fourfolds that does not use Kang's refined motivic dimension estimates. That conclusion is also covered by the written proof of Bhattacharjee [5], and the six seeds were first isolated by Jumagulov [8] through degree 199; the new content is the exact positive classification at every odd degree. We also record the all-dimensional consequences for the prime supports $\{3,11\}$ and $\{3,13\}$, and give an explicit family of Fermat characters on which the tensor filtration identity used in Kang's product argument fails. This paper follows the author's preprint The Hodge Conjecture for Odd-Degree Fermat Fourfolds , public on 8 September 2026 (ResearchGate, DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.26853.77288 ). The work was produced largely with AI systems and is released for public human verification; it has not been checked by a human expert.

The review asks whether craniopharyngioma (CP) and tuberculum sellae meningioma (TSM) differ in postoperative cerebrospinal fluid leak once the surgical corridor is held constant. summary: We study the positive integers that do not descend below their initial value when the permutation of the positive integers considered by Lothar Collatz in 1932 is iterated in either direction. The integers satisfying this condition at every depth are exactly the minima of the orbits of the permutation, so that each orbit contributes exactly one of them. This set was considered by M. Tavares (Discrete Mathematics, 2013). The paper studies its finite-depth approximations. The affine inequalities are replaced by conditions on the principal multipliers of the branches traversed, and it is proved that, at fixed depth, this replacement changes only a finite set. Each forward branch word corresponds to exactly one residue class modulo a power of 3, and each backward word to one class modulo a power of 2. By the Chinese remainder theorem, the density of each filter is the product of two survival probabilities of random walks with positive drift. A duality between the two walks provides exponential martingales, from which monotone rational bounds enclosing the limit of the densities are obtained. This limit is at least 1/36, and the bounds at depth 1000, computed in exact arithmetic, place it between 0.049779559058 and 0.049779559193. Consequently, the number of orbits whose minimum does not exceed a given value is asymptotically at most proportional to that value. It is also proved that the convergence is exponential, with a ratio common to both walks. The second part deals with the periodic discrepancy of the filters. It comprises a spectral identity for its quadratic energy, the expression of this energy in terms of correlations that factorize by the Chinese remainder theorem, and general bounds. Comparing each filter with one of smaller depth gives a bound for the discrepancy that is sublinear with respect to the period, although far from the exact values, which are given up to depth 7. In the forward direction, the passage from one depth to the next is described by a set of rejected residues. These residues admit an explicit parametrization, from which follow an almost antipodal pairing, with error at most one on all semicircles, and a recurrence for their exponential sums. Their relative equidistribution is equivalent to the decay of these sums at each fixed frequency, which is proved for part of the frequencies. An exact example of depth three and tables of the rejected sets up to step 20 are included. The results concern finite depths and their limit. The order of growth of the discrepancy, the relative equidistribution of the rejected residues, and the existence of the density of the set of orbit minima, together with its possible equality with the limit of the filters, remain open. The computational supplement contains the Python programs and exact tables supporting the numerical values. This is the English version of the Spanish original.
title: Bilateral filters and arithmetic discrepancy in the original Collatz permutation

summary: We study two existence problems for permutations whose consecutive products have reciprocal sum one. First, for every integer $n\ge7$ we construct a nonstandard undirected Hamiltonian cycle on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ whose reciprocal-product edge weights sum to one. The construction joins finitely many initial cycles to an explicit eight-step inductive family. Second, for every $n\ge6$ we construct a linear permutation beginning with $(2,1)$ for which the adjacent products are pairwise distinct and their reciprocals sum to one. Three arithmetic-chain templates cover all sufficiently large indices: an exact classification of possible product collisions reduces simultaneous failure to four rational squares in a nonconstant arithmetic progression, excluded by Fermat's classical theorem. Finite small indices are supplied with exact, reproducible certificates. The results concern existence rather than formulas for the corresponding counting sequences, and previously established insertion identities and square-progression obstructions are credited to their sources. The independently authored verification code is made available under CC BY 4.0.
title: Reciprocal-Product Identities for Linear and Cyclic Permutations

summary: This dataset presents the experimental results of a PhD study investigating an integrated Lagrangian-Optimized Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE), and AdaBoost framework for software defect prediction under high-dimensional and class-imbalanced conditions. The study evaluates five NASA software defect datasets: JM1, KC1, PC1, PC3, and PC4. Six machine-learning configurations were compared: AdaBoost, SMOTE–AdaBoost, conventional PCA–AdaBoost, Lagrangian PCA–AdaBoost, conventional PCA–SMOTE–AdaBoost, and the proposed Lagrangian PCA–SMOTE–AdaBoost framework. The experiments employed five-fold group-aware stratified cross-validation, training-only preprocessing, and inner cross-validation for SMOTE parameter selection. Performance measures include accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, geometric mean (G-mean), F1-score, and ROC-AUC. The repository contains 150 benchmark evaluation records, cross-dataset performance comparisons, statistical analyses, model rankings, and supplementary KC1 Lagrangian parameter sensitivity and robustness results. The findings provide empirical evidence of the interactions and trade-offs between dimensionality reduction, class-imbalance handling, and defect-prediction performance. In particular, SMOTE–AdaBoost achieved the highest average G-mean across the five datasets, while the proposed framework provides a basis for examining constrained dimensionality reduction and its interaction with oversampling. These files support the reproducibility, verification, and further investigation of the PhD research.

summary: The Standard Model of particle physics, General Relativity, and the ɅCDM cosmological model represent monumental predictive achievements in modern physical science. However, they exhibit a persistent epistemic asymmetry: their extraordinary capacity to generate accurate predictions and survive empirical tests frequently outruns the conceptual determination of their foundational categories and the ontological warrant for their central posits. This paper develops a diagnostic framework and taxonomy to systematically identify, categorize, and compare distinct forms of epistemic asymmetry across contemporary fundamental physics. Examining four central cases interpretive (the quantum measurement problem), microphysical (particle dark matter), explanatory (the cosmological constant), and methodological (naturalness) alongside two limiting and boundary cases (quantum gravity and the structural incompleteness of the Standard Model beyond its domain), the study introduces a four-criterion diagnostic matrix (predictive adequacy, empirical discrimination, conceptual determination, and ontological warrant). Ultimately, this diagnostic tool provides researchers with a structured, domain-restricted method to distinguish how and why predictive or methodological success fails to secure conceptual and ontological determination, offering a rigorous path for evaluating theoretical commitments in fundamental physics without presuming general antirealist conclusions.
title: The Epistemic Asymmetry of Fundamental Physics: Predictive Success, Conceptual Determination, and Ontological Commitment

summary: This mathematical technical note presents a computer-assisted restricted full-adjoint gain theorem for a prescribed Fourier–Galerkin Navier–Stokes background over the physical-time interval [0, 4/5]. For the original 376-wavevector, radius-six Galerkin initial-value problem, the analysis establishes the quantitative bound G_F([0, 4/5])² ≤ 34609/2700, and consequently G_F([0, 4/5]) < 3.99. The certification combines continuous, non-resetting six-shell storage across nine physical-time intervals; exterior boundary coercivity; continuous-time Riccati positivity; exact-arithmetic computational witnesses; original-Galerkin trajectory enclosures; backward-adjoint passivity; and an analytic infinite-tail limiting argument. The theorem establishes a specified class of shell-two receiving targets and a restricted high-frequency observation on shells 13–18. It does not establish unrestricted three-dimensional Navier–Stokes global regularity or a universal full-adjoint gain estimate. summary: We prove Critch–Morton Conjecture 8 (SIGMA 10 (2014), 095, Section 2, p. 6): every consecutive three-site improper marginalization is birational for open-boundary, translation-invariant, binary bond-two matrix product states of length N at least four. summary: Code and data behind the paper "Data-Driven Extraction of Multi-Exponential Thermal Kernels for Integrated Circuit Thermal Analysis" by B. Ali, I. Bruce, C. L. Trinh, X. Jin, C. He, and D. Chen, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) Systems. The method extracts a compact three-component exponential kernel from steady-state 3D-ICE temperature maps and predicts the temperature rise by convolving the kernel with the power map. Even reflection across the die edges handles the adiabatic side faces. thermal_kernel_code.zip: MATLAB and Python code of the kernel extraction, the evaluation, and the analyses of the paper, the 3D-ICE input generator and run script, and the HotSpot bare-die adaptation with the comparison scripts. Unzip both files into the same folder. The README.txt of each archive describes its contents. The kernel describes the thermal response of the simulated die stack and cooling condition from which it is extracted. A change in the package structure, the layer thicknesses or materials, or the cooling alters that response and requires a new extraction from maps of the new system. summary: This record contains cleaned data and a single Jupyter notebook that reproduce all tables, figures and numerical results of the article “Convergence or Resilience? Quality of Government and Regional Convergence in the EU and Ukraine”. The study compares 181 EU NUTS 2 regions (2010–2021) with 1,470 Ukrainian territorial communities (hromadas, 2019–2021). It estimates absolute and conditional β-convergence, σ-convergence, population-weighted Gini, between/within-country variance decomposition, and the moderating role of the European Quality of Government Index (EQI). For Ukraine, convergence is measured with personal income tax per capita (corrected for the 2020 territorial amalgamation) and new car registrations per 1,000 inhabitants (2SLS against regression to the mean). After the decentralisation reform, hromadas closed gaps 3–6 times faster than EU regions (annual speed of convergence λ ≈ 6–13% vs ≈ 2.3%). Contents: 6 CSV data files with a full codebook in README.md; Reproduction_article.ipynb (Python), which checks every number of the article against the computed value and exports Figures 1–5 as 300 dpi PNG; requirements.txt; LICENSE. summary: Stenometopiellus dzhungaricus Mityaev, 1971 Figs 4, 12, 23–24, 33–36, 65–87 S. stepposus Mityaev, 1971: 153, 170, syn. n. S. ersinicus Vilbaste, 1980: 88–90, syn. n. Material examined. Many specimens from several localities in southern and southeastern Kazakhstan and northern Kyrgyzstan. Signals of seven males from the environs of Altynemel, 75 km south of Taldykorgan, Kazakhstan recorded on 17. VI. 2022 at 25 and 34 oC; signals of one male from the foothills of Dzhungarian Alatau Mtn. Range, 6 km east of Sarkand, Kazakhstan recorded on 17. VI. 2019 at 28 oC. Description. Coloration typical, pale with dark pattern (Fig. 4). 1 st sternal apodemes situated in transverse plane of body, wide, rounded, separated by deep, narrow, more or less parallel-sided notch (Figs 65–68). 2 nd apodemes broad, as long as their width at base or slightly longer, with widened and rounded apices, separated by narrow notch, sometimes with inner edges touching each other (Figs 69–72). Apical halves of subgenital plates oval, with slightly pointed tips (Figs 73–74). Aedeagus with rather short and high basal part and uniformly curved shaft. Middle part of posterior outline of aedeagus straight or only slightly concave (Figs 75–80). Body length: ♂, 2.6–2.9 mm; ♀, 2.9–3.3 mm. Differs from all species except S. turkestanicus in wide 1 st sternal apodemes situated in transverse plane of body. Differs from S. turkestanicus in shape of notch between 1 st apodemes (cf. Figs 65–68 and 88–90) and wider 2 nd apodemes separated by narrower notch (cf. Figs 69–72 and 91–93). Distribution. Southeastern and eastern Kazakhstan up to the Kazakh part of Altai Mts., Kyrgyzstan (North and Central Tien Shan), South Siberia (Tyva). Remarks. Mityaev (1971) briefly described in a key two closely related species, S. dzhungaricus and S. stepposus . According to his description, in S. dzhungaricus , the posterior outline of the aedeagus shaft is straight near the middle, while the anterior outline is vertical to the base (shown by thin arrow on Figs 81–82). In S. stepposus , the posterior outline near the middle is noticeably concave (shown by thick arrow on Figs 83–84), while the anterior outline is located at an acute angle to the base (shown by thin arrow on Figs 83–84). In the drawings in the key, these differences are quite clear (cf. Figs 81–82 and 83–84). However, a study of numerous specimens from different localities in southeastern Kazakhstan (Figs 75–80) showed that these taxa represent only extreme variants of a continuous variation range. For this reason, most specimens cannot be reliably assigned to either species; also, in some specimens, the anterior outline of the aedeagus is vertical as in S. dzhungaricus or even situated at a somewhat inverse angle to the base, while the posterior outline is slightly concave as in S. stepposus (Fig. 78). Moreover, males with different aedeagus shape sometimes were collected in the same biotope. On this basis, I consider these species to be synonyms and, as the first reviser, select S. dzhungaricus as the valid name. According to Mityaev (2002), the ranges of S. dzhungaricus and S. stepposus overlap almost completely, which also supports the established synonymy. Vilbaste (1980) provided a detailed and well-illustrated description of S. ersinicus from southern Tyva, South Siberia (Figs 85–87). A comparison of his description, particularly the drawing of the 2 nd sternal apodemes (Fig. 86), with my specimens from Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan leaves no doubt that S. ersinicus is a junior synonym of S. dzhungaricus . Since S. dzhungaricus is distributed as far east as the Kazakh Altai, its discovery in the adjacent part of Siberia seems quite natural.
title: Stenometopiellus dzhungaricus Mityaev 1971

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24060703 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the importance of artemisinin resistance and points out a gap in current understanding of its population-level consequences. The research objective is to examine whether increasing Kelch13 mutation prevalence is associated with malaria incidence across 16 Ugandan districts. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The longitudinal ecological design and negative binomial regression are well-suited for examining population-level associations. The authors also included several climatic, malaria-control, and resistance-related factors. However, the use of forward variable selection raises questions about model robustness. It would be helpful to find out whether the findings remain consistent under alternative model specifications and clarify how temporal correlation between monthly observations was handled. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The results support a positive association between Kelch13 mutation prevalence and malaria incidence after adjustment (aIRR = 1.131, 95% CI: 1.090–1.174). However, the ecological study design can't establish causation and the association may be bidirectional. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The tables and figures are well-organized. Figure 2 shows district-specific trends in mutation prevalence and malaria incidence, while figure 3 provides a clear visualization of the adjusted association. However, the apparent decline in predicted incidence at very high Kelch13 prevalence is not quite sure because there were only two observations above 60%. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Somewhat clearly The discussion provides biological explanations for the observed associations and acknowledges some important limitations, including possible reverse causation, residual confounding, and differences in the time scales of the data. However, the model-selection uncertainty and specific sensitivity analyses are not mentioned. Is the preprint likely to advance academic knowledge? Somewhat likely This preprint adds useful evidence about the relationship between antimalarial resistance markers and population-level malaria incidence. It contributes to the integration of molecular surveillance with epidemiological, climatic, and malaria-control data in a high-burden setting. Would it benefit from language editing? No This preprint is clear. Some statements could be more precise. For example, the authors sometimes use "malaria transmission" when the measured outcome is reported malaria incidence. Would you recommend this preprint to others? Yes, but it needs to be improved I would recommend this preprint to researchers interested in malaria epidemiology, antimalarial resistance, and molecular surveillance. The study shows an important public health question and provides useful population-level evidence. Is it ready for attention from an editor, publisher or broader audience? Yes, after minor changes I think this preprint is worth editorial consideration because it addresses an important research question and provides useful findings. However, before publication, I would recommend additional clarification of the statistical model, sensitivity analyses for variable selection. Competing interests The author declares that they have no competing interests. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they did not use generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
title: Structured PREreview of "Expanding Kelch13 artemisinin resistance markers are associated with higher malaria incidence in Uganda"

summary: Code, processed results and redistributable data for the article "What DEMATEL's total-relation matrix adds: a null-model decomposition for crisp and fuzzy cause–effect analysis" (submitted to Applied Soft Computing). The study decomposes the total-relation matrix of DEMATEL around the degree-product null model of network science. It tests the consequences on 221 direct-relation matrices extracted from 168 open-access articles indexed in Europe PMC, on fuzzy, interval-valued and per-expert matrices extracted from 35 articles, and in simulations, and it introduces ND-DEMATEL, a null-model decomposed DEMATEL with a max-T test for specific indirect influence. Contents: the code that builds the corpus (search, download and table extraction from the JATS XML of Europe PMC and PubMed Central), the analysis code, the figure code, the processed results behind the numbers, tables and figures of the article, and the extracted matrices of the articles published under a CC BY licence (98 of the 168 articles, 120 of the 221 matrices; 16 of the 35 articles of the fuzzy and interval corpus). The other matrices are not redistributed, because the licences of their articles do not permit it. The archive lists every source article with its licence, and reproduce.sh rebuilds the full corpus from the open-access full texts. README.md describes each stage of the pipeline. The archive is a single zip file, code_and_data_v1.0.0.zip, which unzips into the folder asoc_dematel/. Licence: MIT for the code and the processed results. The extracted matrices keep the CC BY licences of their source articles, which are listed below as related works and, with their licences, in results/round2_identity/dematel_licences.csv and data/dematel_corpus/provenance.csv. Four figure-checking utilities in code/figures are taken unchanged from the nature-skills project and keep its licence, the Apache License 2.0.
title: Code and data for: What DEMATEL's total-relation matrix adds: a null-model decomposition for crisp and fuzzy cause–effect analysis

summary: How can coherent light be certified when its amplitude is unknown or its preparations are correlated? This article treats these as distinct inference problems: learning an actual coherent reference with optimal source-copy cost for independent identical inputs, and certifying the photon-counting predictions of the light left unused in a preprepared correlated batch. Optimal source-copy cost with a learned reference. For a normal one-mode source prepared independently and identically, an ideal passive multiport test and heterodyne readout produce an actual amplitude \(\hat\alpha\). After displacement by this reference and ideal quantum-limited amplification of fixed gain \(G>1\), let \(P_{\rho,\hat\alpha}^{G}\) be the photon-number distribution and \(\pi_G(k)=(G-1)^k/G^{k+1}\) the coherent benchmark. The task-specific comparison is \[\frac{1-\langle\hat\alpha|\rho|\hat\alpha\rangle}{G}\le\operatorname{TV}(P_{\rho,\hat\alpha}^{G},\pi_G)\le1-\langle\hat\alpha|\rho|\hat\alpha\rangle.\] With at most N input copies, the protocol controls the unconditional event of accepting a reference whose actual total-variation error exceeds \(\varepsilon\). For \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), soundness error \(\beta_s\to0\), and fixed coherent-source rejection tolerance \(\beta_c<1\), the optimal fixed-maximum source-copy count obeys \[\frac{N_{\rm opt}[-\log(1-\varepsilon)]}{\log(1/\beta_s)}\longrightarrow1.\] The matching converse covers collective and adaptive protocols under the same source-copy contract. At 1% accuracy and 5% soundness and completeness errors, the finite bounds are \(293\le N_{\rm opt}\le572\). These are source-copy bounds under ideal optical access, not an optimum for total hardware or reference energy. The actual unmeasured batch after the full record. A separate protocol allows an arbitrary preprepared correlated or entangled optical batch, including correlations with an environment. A pilot first fixes the reference; a private random subset is then tested. A multiplicative sampling inequality yields a frequentist guarantee for the average marginal photon-count error of the retained conditional state, conditioned on the complete actual measurement record. It does not replace that state by premeasurement marginals or assert the same error for its full joint distribution. The trusted detector contract requires product joint test effects and local instruments that leave retained systems and the external environment untouched. Calibration envelopes must cover the actual signal-time gates. The bounds retain infinite photon tails and charge detector efficiency, dark counts, imperfect displacement, reference drift and calibration failure. Explicit counterexamples explain why marginal detector efficiencies or product effects alone are insufficient. An ideal finite example uses 3730 prepared systems: 1491 pilot, 1339 tested and 900 retained; calibration and optical-control resources are additional. Relation to the original two-copy result. The earlier mean-energy-controlled arm-swap cancellation and full trace-distance certificate remain valid for independent, possibly nonidentical product batches. Their source and target are kept separate from the new arbitrary-batch marginal PNR guarantee. The analysis builds on established coherent-state comparison, quantum verification and sampling identities; the new connections supply the learned-reference resource law and the full-record conditional-state return. Version 1.1 is a substantial update of Certifying unused optical states with imperfect two-copy interference , first published on 31 October 2026. The integrated 24-page PDF contains three figure groups, a source-and-target comparison table, complete proofs and references. The figures illustrate proved bounds and specified theoretical protocols, not experimental measurements.
title: Certifying coherent light with unknown amplitudes and correlated sources

summary: Black-hole X-ray binaries switch from the hard to the soft state at luminosities several times higher than those at which they switch back, and changing-look active galactic nuclei, whose broad lines appear and vanish near 1 per cent of the Eddington luminosity, are often read as their supermassive analogue. The switch-on and switch-off thresholds have not been measured separately for any supermassive black hole. We fit a latent-continuum model with a hysteretic switch to 19 repeating changing- look nuclei with Eddington ratios from the 5100 A ̊ continuum at three spectral epochs, and calibrate the width ∆ between the two thresholds with forward-simulated mock samples. In every nucleus each off-state continuum lies below each on-state one, whereas mock samples drawn with our baseline priors contain on average 4.6 nuclei that violate this order. In mock samples without state flips and with slowly varying continua, no nucleus violates it in a fraction 0.28 of cases at ∆ = 0 and 0.02 at ∆ = 0.5 dex. If the catalogue was not selected on the agreement of continuum and line changes, widths of half a dex or more are therefore disfavoured. If it was so selected, the likelihood that includes the selection carries no information on ∆, and the posterior quantile calibrated with selection-matched mocks gives ∆ < 0.57 dex at 95 per cent, with a Monte Carlo spread of 0.30–0.59 dex. The continua of the two states differ by less than 0.34–0.70 dex for a per-epoch noise of 0.05–0.28 dex. Neither reading tests the flip-flop picture of changing-state nuclei. About 150 repeating nuclei selected on their broad lines alone, with continua measured independently of the state, would reach the binary population mean.

summary: This dataset offers computational information that underpins the research titled “Integrated computational and experimental characterization of I49R substitution in monomeric M-MLV reverse transcriptase reveals increased soluble recovery and RNA-dependent DNA synthesis.” The dataset comprises inputs for molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, structural models, numerical analysis outcomes, and computational documentation pertaining to Natural-type and I49R variations of Moloney murine leukemia virus reverse transcriptase (M-MLV RT). The initial simulations were conducted with GROMACS 2022 alongside the CHARMM36 force field from July 2022. Each protein variation was examined for 400 ns under periodic boundary conditions at 315 K and 1 bar. The dataset comprises the following elements: Structural models: Beginning and concluding protein configurations for Natural-type and I49R M-MLV RT. Simulation parameters: GROMACS configuration files, topology data, and production simulation setup files. Structural dynamics: Quantitative metrics for root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF), radius of gyration (Rg), and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA). Conformational assessment: Principal component analysis (PCA), free-energy landscape information, dynamic cross-correlation matrices (DCCM), and structural variability evaluations. Convergence evaluation: Temporal comparisons and geographical analyzes employed to evaluate the stationarity of chosen structural observables during the prolonged simulations. Protein–RNA complexes: Computationally generated structural representations of Natural-type and I49R reverse transcriptase interacting with RNA, alongside protein-only cluster-center conformations acquired from RNA-inclusive simulation systems. Reproducibility records: GROMACS procedural details, analytical notebooks, and ancillary documentation. The dataset aims to promote repeatability, autonomous analysis, and additional inquiries into the correlation between amino acid alterations, protein structural behavior, soluble protein extraction, and enzymatic activity. The computational findings enhance the experimental data of augmented soluble protein recovery and RNA-dependent DNA synthesis linked to the I49R mutation.
title: Computational Dataset for Molecular Dynamics Analysis of the I49R Substitution in Monomeric M-MLV Reverse Transcriptase

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: Dataset Description This dataset contains experimental X-ray computed tomography (CT) and Angular Segmented Gamma Scanning (ASGS) measurements of radioactive waste drum mockups, collected for research into three-dimensional radionuclide activity reconstruction. The measurements were used in the development and evaluation of SARUMAN (Spatial Activity Reconstruction Using Machine-learning Algorithms for Nuclear Waste) , a Bayesian machine-learning framework for reconstructing spatial activity distributions from gamma spectrometry and CT-derived attenuation information. Dataset Contents The dataset comprises nine experimental configurations: Six homogeneous mockups (HOM-1 to HOM-6) , containing different source arrangements within homogeneous filling materials, including bark and potting soil. Three heterogeneous mockups (HET-1 to HET-3) , designed to investigate activity reconstruction under more complex material and source distributions. Each configuration is provided as an individual ZIP archive, containing: CT/ : A reconstructed X-ray CT volume in MetaImage format ( reconstructionFloat.mhd and reconstructionFloat.raw ). ASGS/ : Gamma spectrometry acquisition files ( .asr , .asw , and .srf ) corresponding to the segmented angular measurements. The original spectrometry file formats are preserved to retain the experimental acquisition information. Intended Use These measurements are provided to support reproducibility, methodological comparisons, and further research into radiological waste characterization, gamma-ray transport modelling, uncertainty quantification, and Bayesian inverse problems. The dataset can be used with SARUMAN or adapted for other reconstruction and data-analysis approaches. Reference Publication Users are strongly encouraged to read the associated scientific publication before using or interpreting this dataset: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306454926007383 The publication provides the scientific context for the experimental measurements, the associated reconstruction methodology, and the considerations relevant to their interpretation. Researchers wishing to reproduce the original analyses or adapt the methodology to other applications should consult this publication alongside the SARUMAN source code and documentation. Scope and Limitations The measurements originate from a specific experimental characterization system. Their interpretation requires appropriate knowledge of the detector geometry, acquisition configuration, calibration procedures, and CT attenuation modelling. The associated SARUMAN implementation includes detector-efficiency and CT attenuation models developed for this experimental setup. These models should not be assumed valid for different instruments without appropriate adaptation and validation. The dataset is provided for scientific research purposes and does not constitute a universally validated characterization benchmark. Associated Software SARUMAN — Spatial Activity Reconstruction Using Machine-learning Algorithms for Nuclear Waste https://github.com/vcasasmo/SARUMAN Dataset preparation and software development: Victor J. Casas Molina.

The six analysis modules cover synthetic experiments and matched controls, held-out event-timing evaluation for Ridgecrest, forecast replay using dated Ridgecrest catalog snapshots, external archived-catalog replication for sequences anchored by M ≥ 5.2 and M ≥ 6.0 earthquakes, evaluation of a frozen ETAS blend, and sensitivity analysis using the revised USGS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog (ComCat). Catalog sources include the Southern California Earthquake Data Center, the Northern California Earthquake Data Center, and USGS ComCat. For the primary external M ≥ 6.0 cohort, M2 scored higher than the raw-gap model in all four eligible sequences for six-hour occurrence forecasts of M ≥ 2.5 earthquakes. Against constrained temporal ETAS, M2 scored higher in one of the four sequences, with a mean gain of −0.163 bits per window when the sequences were weighted equally. The frozen ETAS blend assigned zero weight to the marked models and yielded zero gain in the single eligible external case. summary: A benefit can be real while the judgment that it is good remains uninformed. I develop uninformed good as a graded concept: a benefit received without adequate understanding of its relevant costs, wherever those costs fall. Disclosure may lower, raise, or leave unchanged the recipient’s evaluation. A benefit that remains equally good after its costs are understood is the limiting categorical case in my sense; whether such cases occur is an open question, not a result established here. The primary aim is descriptive: to ask how often uninformed benefits produce real harm, for whom, and under which conditions. A separate philosophical hypothesis holds that omission is outwardly negative; it is not presented as an empirical finding. I distinguish deliberate concealment, chosen ignorance, and unavoidable incomplete knowledge; examines demands and last-minute requests for forgiveness or reentry; and confronts invisible-support evidence as a genuine challenge to blanket disclosure rules. I argue for timely disclosure of material known costs while recognizing costs of disclosure and limits of knowledge. Nine revised predictions, a field-oriented distributional inquiry, and two possible experiments specify how the empirical claims could be tested. No new data are reported.
title: Uninformed Good: Why Benefits Received Without Knowledge of Their Costs Are Not Categorically Good
