summary: I propose that wanting is shaped through the ways other people affect one’s existence. I retain two versions as the heart of the argument. The strong version claims that all desire content is socially imparted; the moderate version sets bare bodily states partly aside and concerns the content and strength of socially shaped wants. Needs lean toward bodily action and impulse, while wants lean toward thought-shaped objects and possibilities; this distinction is conceptual, not an established biological partition. I call the felt interpersonal draw pull and the proposed influence imparted force, without claiming a new physical force. Research on goal contagion, valuation, comparison, and social support motivates the account but does not establish that social shaping is total. I distinguish experienced connection from evidence of reciprocity, compatibility, or safety, and being influenced from freely endorsing a course of action. Eight predictions and two proposed studies address observable consequences, including the limits of tracing a desire’s source. A background glossary preserves my existing terminology without using it to explain away contrary results. A brief universe/fabric analogy remains philosophical speculation. No new data are reported.
title: Desire as Imparted Force: A Social-Origin Hypothesis of Wanting and Connection

summary: I propose an organizing model of the formal mind as knowledge and experience: reusable observations and techniques, and the lived history from which they develop. Skills are techniques trained through experience; habits are repeated patterns rather than a third substance. I call the architecture these processes train the metastructure: a proposed organization of heuristics, reconstruction, anticipation, and usable continuity of thought, not a newly identified neural network. The model predicts that relevant learning can reduce both avoidable errors and stalled thinking, while fixation and bodily disruption can limit or reverse that benefit. I also argue that bodily sensation, presence, and practical constraints matter as much to the person as mental personality. My earlier phrase “more than half” is a qualitative generalization about that interplay, not a measured percentage. The account draws on memory research, expertise, predictive processing, and interoception without treating their findings as proof of the whole model. Eight predictions and two proposed studies distinguish the organizing assumptions from testable consequences. Companion manuscripts address incomplete knowledge of costs, socially shaped wanting, association between perspectives, and the deliberate experience of ordinary boredom; those connections are proposals rather than independent evidence. summary: Bees play a crucial role in human agriculture, making the accurate characterization of their behavior essential. In the field of automatic bee traffic tracking, individual monitoring has been prevalent in the past two decades to collect detailed data on foraging behavior. To support analysis, these data must be classified into entry and exit events, and assembled into flight trajectories. However, existing classification methods largely consider only simple exits and entrances, which ignore the existence of U-turn or guarding movements which represent a non-trivial fraction of bee activity at the hive entrance. Identifying these movements as compound events is necessary to accurately track all movements over time while avoiding classifications which may produce misleading movement records. In this presentation, we analyze existing event classification methods to evaluate their accuracy for two different types of movements: simple and compound. We then propose extended event classification methods that explicitly account for compound events, enabling more accurate reconstruction of bee traffic dynamics.

summary: Bayesian inference is a predictive act. This book builds it from three ideas: de Finetti supplies the structure, writing exchangeable beliefs as mixtures of independent laws; Sanov supplies the asymptotics, the exponential concentration of empirical measures at a rate given by the Kullback Leibler divergence; and Bayes supplies the updating, an exponential tilt of the predictive law. Together they give a tilted de Finetti theorem: conditioning an exchangeable sequence on empirical moment constraints yields predictive laws that are I projections of a baseline measure, so parameters emerge as limits of empirical functionals and maximum entropy appears as a predictive limit rather than a postulate. Testing, shrinkage, asymptotics and decision are then read on one moderate deviation scale. Results the book proves, most first stated in the authors' papers with Daniel Zantedeschi and Jyotishka Datta: a finite sample total variation bound between a block drawn under a moment window and independent draws from the I projection, and the projected de Finetti limit behind it; a split of the predictive Kullback Leibler Bayes risk into a Sanov term and a posterior contraction term,; a condition for a scalar learning rate to calibrate credible sets at moderate scale, namely that model curvature and score covariance be proportional; one control variate form for Bayes linear and prediction powered inference estimators, with the optimal gain in closed form; the global posterior of federated learning as a product of local experts under exchangeability; and a convergence rate for the policy that maximizes posterior expected utility in generative Bayesian computation. Several results are stated conditionally or as open problems, and the book says which. Later chapters treat computation, universal portfolios, causal machine learning and medicine. Scripts reproducing every computed figure and number are in the repository.
title: Elements of Bayes and Information Theory: A Predictive Theory of Inference: Information, Algorithms, and Large Deviations

summary: Thermal Quantum Annealing (tQuA) is a quantum architecture in which a system coupled non-adiabatically to a thermodynamic reservoir evolves toward the thermal Gibbs state of a target Hamiltonian . This paper provides a rigorous and honest foundation for tQuA and its extension to Quantum Intelligent Matrix Methods (QIMM). We distinguish carefully among Theorems (proved in the cited literature, with proofs reproduced in Appendices A–D where necessary), Propositions (with explicitly identified gaps), Conjectures (with open steps), and Numerical Results (simulation evidence, explicitly labeled as obtained on a classical surrogate or on a quantum emulator). The work delivers four contributions. (1) Convergence, correctly scoped. A five-pillar chain establishes that, under the stated Born–Markov and Ohmic-bath assumptions, tQuA converges in trace norm to the unique Gibbs state from any initial condition, without Hamiltonian-adiabatic scheduling, and that the transition rate out of every local minimum is strictly positive at any finite . Ground-state convergence requires a cooling schedule whose rate is bounded by the spectral gap (Theorem 8), or, for the engineered-dissipation family ED-tQuA, follows directly from the dark-state condition (Theorem 7). (2) Honest scaling benchmarks, corrected. On a classical diagonal surrogate, the v2/v6 claim of a flat gap and a clean power law is corrected. At finite temperature ( ), the surrogate gap decays as : polynomial in the Hilbert dimension but exponential in qubit count . At low temperature ( ), the chain is numerically frozen; the value is attributable to a single-transition rate . The surrogate is exact for diagonal and deviates by for off-diagonal perturbation of size (Proposition 2 and Corollary). The trajectory (400 steps, §4.5) remains valid as a short-run diagnostic. (3) Engineered-dissipation tQuA. For the engineered-dissipation family (programmable, energy-lowering jump operators with a complete-graph core and a dark ground state), we prove a logarithmic gap , mixing time , monotonic energy decrease and ground-state convergence, and robustness to bounded control error. These convert the scaling claim from conjecture to theorem for the engineered-dissipation design , not the natural bath. (4) Adaptive policy, reframed. tQuA is identified as an adaptive policy system (temperature schedule, coupling, jump-operator structure, priors ). This is presented as a research direction, not a theorem. The earlier vs. query speedup claim is withdrawn ; Block–Lanczos matches the Simchowitz–Recht–Jordan lower bound. The quantum-advantage conjecture is reframed as a resource tradeoff (qubit count, device time, I/O), not query complexity.

summary: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range for uncooperative spacecraft pose estimation, but models trained on synthetic event streams must generalize to the noise, background activity, and contrast variation of physical sensors. We present a comparative systems study of two independently developed approaches to synthetic-to-real, event-based 6-DoF spacecraft pose estimation. The first is a modular pipeline that combines learned keypoint detection and unlabeled target-domain adaptation with geometry-based pose recovery and temporal smoothing. The second directly regresses translation and rotation from global and cropped event representations using an apparent-scale cue, physics-motivated synthetic corruptions, and feature-consistency regularization. We evaluate both systems under the same SPARK 2026 hidden-test protocol on the real-event split of SPADES, with predictions for all test frames. The results reveal a component-wise reversal concealed by the aggregate challenge score: direct regression reduces orientation error by 22.7% (1.1767 to 0.9101 rad) and obtains a 13.4% lower composite score, whereas the modular pipeline reduces relative translation error by 78.7% (0.1335 to 0.0285). Archived configurations and a qualitative failure case identify plausible explanations for these complementary error profiles, without isolating their causes. These findings motivate a testable hybrid design that combines direct orientation estimation with geometry-constrained translation recovery.
title: Direct Regression and Geometric Recovery for Event-based Spacecraft Pose Estimation

summary: High throughput computational databases such as Materials Project, the Open Quantum Materials Database, and Alexandria now each list on the order of 10^5 predicted stable compounds. However, the overall reliability of these predictions in terms of actual experimental synthesizability remains poorly understood. In this work we attempt to synthesize, via arc melting, 34 different predicted ternary compounds. The majority of these materials did not form in the predicted structure, instead resulting in disordered variants or multiphase mixtures. Four formed ordered structures not reported before, one of them at a composition reported earlier without a structure. We discuss both the failures and the successes, and identify simple filtering criteria that can help researchers avoid hypothetical materials that are unlikely to form.
title: Experimental Evaluation of High-Throughput Structure Predictions

summary: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.
title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates

summary: In many domains from species identification to cancer diagnosis, labelling data to train predictive models remains costly. In these settings, it is advantageous to intelligently select data points to label to achieve the maximum information gain, this is the motivation behind the study of active learning. summary: Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. These libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of training and inference across diverse GPU platforms, implementing attention, GEMM, quantization, and low-precision operators while managing tensor shapes, memory layouts, code generation, and hardware-specific dispatch. Problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs, prevent compilation, introduce deployment incompatibilities, or degrade performance, thereby reducing developer productivity and wasting expensive GPU resources. We present the first comprehensive empirical study of issues in GPU kernel libraries for LLM systems. We manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions, and available fixes from seven representative libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers, and bitsandbytes. The analysis characterizes symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. Our main findings are: (1) 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions, so validation must cover the deployment and execution stack, not just kernel code. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. We outline research opportunities and tooling directions to support future LLM GPU kernel development.
title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems

summary: Existing Korean benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) evaluate performance across diverse knowledge domains, but their accuracy scores cannot distinguish whether incorrect responses arise from a lack of required knowledge or a failure to apply that knowledge correctly. Our analysis of existing Korean benchmarks reveals that most questions can be answered through factual recall alone, while those demanding greater application also differ in required knowledge, making it difficult to isolate application ability. To address this, we introduce KLEAR, a framework that constructs knowledge-matched contrasts by varying application demand while preserving the required knowledge. During construction, KLEAR identifies the knowledge underlying each source question as an explicit anchor bundle to guide generation of questions requiring more complex application. Generated candidates then undergo automated and human validation, with iterative revision based on evaluation feedback. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting knowledge-matched sets largely satisfy the intended constraints, enabling controlled evaluation across diverse LLMs. These evaluations reveal that increasing application demand exposes failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided.

summary: Multi-agent systems become capable through institutional mechanisms, such as rules that route information to agents that act on it. These mechanisms are also natural places to restrict the system. Yet as agents learn, share memory, delegate, and repair failures, the collective can find other paths to the same effects: a restriction on the original mechanism still operates but no longer stops them, while routine performance and compliance checks pass. We propose \textbf{Reversible Multi-agent Systems} as a research agenda: collectives that grow while an authorized supervisor can still restrict specified effects, keep them restricted as agents adapt, and reconstitute useful cooperation under renewed authority. What is reversed is the ability to produce a specified effect; restrictions must hold even if learned knowledge persists. The goal is to preserve effective intervention, not a particular mechanism: at every step of growth, some authorized intervention must keep a specified prohibited effect rare while maintaining required service. We identify three research problems: tracking what capabilities depend on, handing off control before an old mechanism loses its effect, and separating legitimate repair from unauthorized reconstruction. We outline how to evaluate control across growth paths, back control claims with evidence, and allocate the rights to restrict and restore.
title: From Emergence to Reversibility: Toward Reversible Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.
title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection

summary: Walsh analysis connects ordered Fourier convergence, summability, nonlinear approximation, and universal representation through a common character algebra. This survey examines developments from 2000-2026 against their classical foundations. Binary kernel geometry explains Hardy-space losses and summability thresholds; interval and packet methods control spectral selection; localized blocks produce correction and universal representations with distinct coefficient and exceptional-set requirements. Quantitative thresholds, source conventions, and published theorem pointers are collected in comparative tables. Supplementary derivations preserve normalization checks and finite covariance calculations while keeping the main exposition focused on the analytic mechanisms.

summary: Unified multimodal models combine image understanding and generation within one system, creating an opportunity to improve both capabilities through paired image--text supervision. We examine the outputs of a pretrained unified model in both directions and observe a loss of specificity: generated images can contain the requested objects with incorrect attributes, while captions identify a scene without expressing its distinguishing details. These failures call for supervision that specifies both the visual content to realize and the descriptive differences to distinguish. We propose UniMore, a post-training method that derives these complementary learning tasks from the fine-grained content of image--text pairs. The generation route predicts grounded crops from their corresponding phrases, matching the scope of the condition and visual target while using the native visual objective. The understanding route combines positive-caption fitting with ranking against captions that omit or alter details, conditioned on the full image. The two routes are optimized independently, and their learned updates are combined into a single unified model without changing its inference procedure. Experiments show gains across multiple understanding and generation benchmarks.
title: UniMore: Fine-Grained Supervision for Unified Understanding and Generation

summary: This release avoids the import pykoopman failure caused by setuptools 82, which removed pkg_resources . pykoopman no longer uses pkg_resources itself and now requires setuptools < 82 , because the pinned lightning still imports that module. The release also corrects the rk4 integrator in pykoopman.common . That fix changes numerical results, so data generated with rk4 or with the example systems built on it will differ from 1.2.1. Import failure with setuptools 82 or newer (#71) setuptools 82.0.0 removed pkg_resources , and with setuptools 82 or newer installed, import pykoopman fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pkg_resources' . Every 1.x release up to 1.2.1 reads its version through pkg_resources . pykoopman 1.2.1 does not limit setuptools, so an environment that starts without it, such as one created with uv venv (the setup the README recommends), receives the newest setuptools and hits this error. pykoopman now reads __version__ with importlib.metadata . setuptools < 82 is a new runtime requirement, because the pinned lightning ~= 2.0.9 calls pkg_resources.declare_namespace when it is imported, and import pykoopman imports lightning for NNDMD. If setuptools 82 or newer is installed anyway, the import still fails inside lightning. The UserWarning that pkg_resources is deprecated, which importing pykoopman may still show, also comes from lightning and is harmless despite its advice to pin setuptools below 81. torch 2.1 also imports pkg_resources in torch.utils.cpp_extension , which import pykoopman does not load. The cap can be lifted once the pins require lightning >= 2.4 and torch >= 2.2. The outdated pins are discussed in #65. Because of the cap, installing 1.2.2 resolves setuptools to 81.0.0, the last release below 82, when it is absent and downgrades it to 81.0.0 when 82 or newer is installed. Dependency scanners may flag 81.0.0, which is in the affected ranges of GHSA-h35f-9h28-mq5c (sdist builds on macOS, fixed in 83.0.0) and GHSA-xmj3-9gf7-h52w (legacy wheel installation on Windows, fixed in 84.1.0). Neither concerns importing pykoopman. summary: GiriNeoEquipment™ is a single-file, offline, interactive clinical decision support system (CDSS). Equipment-by-level-of-care tables with back-up logic. A back-up and spares calculator with a busy-night stress test. A ten-step procurement pathway for India (GeM, CDSCO Medical Devices Rules 2017, Target Product Profile) with specification checklists. A total-cost-of-ownership comparator. Equipment governance and programme design. PM and calibration planning, and a daily shift readiness check. Consumables stock and reorder calculator; uptime, MTBF and MTTR with a contract-penalty calculator. Repair, replace or condemn guidance. Power, oxygen, medical air and vacuum (three-source) planning, plus environment and HVAC. A pre-filled FMEA; mock drills; alarm safety. Materiovigilance (MvPI) reporting. Reports phase and position residuals alongside photothermal rise; apparent field enhancement is not by itself a localization gain. F222  NANOMATERIALS QUANTUM DEFECT ENGINEERING AT THE LIMIT — Tests defect creation, charge states, spin coherence, surface passivation and unselected emitter yield against a geometry-matched classical materials stack. F223  MICROSCALE PHOTOTHERMAL CONVERSION SAFETY AT THE LIMIT — Constrains photothermal conversion in sealed microfluidic reference systems through spatially independent microthermometry, absorbed-power accounting, duty-cycle variation and physical shutdown tests. Beacon-phase drift, image interpolation, occlusion, flow reversal and independent trajectory truth challenge seemingly superior tracking; phase stability cannot replace physical pose evidence. Tracks chemical state, adhesion, insertion loss, intrinsic versus loaded quality factor and functional yield on unselected devices. Survivor selection and bulk-index drift remain rival explanations.     SECOND RESEARCH UNIT / SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE & SUCCESSION Research Unit II · F226–F230 F226  PHOTONIC-CRYSTAL MICROFLUIDIC SENSING AT THE LIMIT — Tests photonic-crystal microfluidic sensing against a commercial chip under equal optical power using concealed pressure, ionic and fouling challenges. F227  NANO-OPTICAL FIELD MULTI-TARGET MANIPULATION AT THE LIMIT — Examines whether optical-field control can manipulate several microscale targets without hidden collision, cross-trap force, laser dose or thermal burden. summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies

summary: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

summary: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support commonly focus on the clinical appropriateness of individual responses, potentially overlooking failures that emerge across extended interactions. As AI assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances and prior disclosures, this raises an accountability question: Do AI chatbots provide appropriate support as users' needs evolve? We investigate by analyzing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, examining how a memory-equipped assistant responds to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles. We introduce the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, to assess the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. Advice was less aligned with users' readiness after a crisis than in matched control stretches of the same conversation, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and users' communication style changed how often and when the assistant gave recommendations. Although explicitly unproductive advice was rare, the assistant frequently omitted clinician-expected support such as follow-up and planning for next steps. These findings show the limits of single response-level safety evaluation and the need to assess timing, omission, and consistency across users when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.
title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Evaluating Timing and Omission in Longitudinal AI Mental Health Support

summary: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents

summary: Zeolites are an important class of porous crystalline materials with broad applications in gas storage, separations, and catalysis. Although hundreds of thousands of experimentally realized and hypothetical zeolite structures are known, identifying materials optimized for a target application remains challenging because property labels are expensive to obtain and available only for limited structure-molecule pairs. While prior work has demonstrated that 3D neural representations can predict zeolite properties effectively, it remains unclear which representation-learning strategies are most effective in the low-data regime relevant to materials discovery. We present ZeoBench, a benchmark for self-supervised learning on dense 3D representations of all-silica zeolites, and evaluate the resulting features on six existing downstream adsorption-property prediction tasks, across a range of training set sizes. Our study compares self-supervised 3D pretraining on volumetric zeolite data, adaptations of image-pretrained 2D ConvNets and vision transformers to 3D via multiview and channel-inflation strategies, and 3D ConvNets pretrained on out-of-domain volumetric datasets, alongside hand-crafted descriptors and supervised baselines. Using our pretraining and evaluation framework, we find self-supervised 3D representations outperform existing methods and achieve state-of-the-art performance across both in-domain label regimes and for the unseen domain of metal organic frameworks. Learned representations consistently outperform hand-crafted descriptors, and convolutional architectures are generally more effective than vision transformers in this setting. These results establish ZeoBench as a practical benchmark for 3D representation learning in zeolites and provide guidance for data-limited adsorption property prediction.
title: ZeoBench: A Benchmark for Self-Supervised Learning on 3D Zeolite Representations

summary: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. summary: Quantum-state conversion between the ortho and para nuclear-spin states of H$_2$ is forbidden in the isolated molecule but these states can become connected through interactions with a surrounding environment. How that same environment governs the dynamics of the newly connected states remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this problem using H$_2$ confined in crystalline molecular solids, where the host environment selectively enables conversion between a pair of otherwise disconnected ortho-H$_2$ and para-H$_2$ states. Rotationally resolved infrared spectroscopy directly determines the state-specific conversion dynamics in crystalline CO$_2$ and N$_2$O at 10 K, revealing that increasing H$_2$ concentration suppresses nuclear-spin conversion by nearly an order of magnitude, reaching complete suppression by 20% H$_2$ loading. Molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations identify two complementary origins of this concentration dependence: changes in the thermally populated phonon modes available to mediate relaxation, and strain-driven H$_2$ clustering that progressively removes molecules from the host crystal field responsible for enabling conversion. The resulting picture connects a classical collective response of the host to microscopic quantum-state dynamics: H$_2$ loading generates strain that reorganizes the local molecular environment, thereby modifying both the phonon bath and the molecular coupling to that bath. These results establish a multiscale mechanism by which condensed-phase environments can govern the connectivity and dynamics of an effective two-level system.
title: Classical control of quantum-state relaxation in confined molecular hydrogen

summary: Plug-and-play (PnP) methods reconstruct images by alternating a data-fitting step with an image denoiser. Their performance depends on two parameters: the step size $γ$ and the measurement noise level $σ$. In practice, $γ$ is often tuned by grid search over validation images and must be retuned whenever the problem setting changes, and $σ$ is assumed known or estimated separately. We propose AdaptivePnP, a PnP framework that jointly estimates $σ$ and $γ$ at every iteration from the data-fitting residual. To do so, we apply the PnP virtual model to the data-fitting proximal map and show that the residual is zero-mean Gaussian with covariance parameterized by $γ$ and $σ$. However, when one parameter is much larger than the other, the residual carries little information about the smaller one and using the maximum likelihood (ML) estimator can degrade the PnP iterations. We therefore introduce the identifiable maximum likelihood (IML) estimator, which restricts the ML estimator to an identifiable window in which the normalized Cramér--Rao bound of every parameter is bounded by a user-specified tolerance. For the virtual model, this window is an interval of ratios $ρ= γ/σ$, so computing the IML estimate reduces to a one-dimensional search over $ρ$. We apply AdaptivePnP to two standard PnP methods, yielding algorithms that require neither a tuned $γ$ nor a known $σ$. On image deblurring and super-resolution, AdaptivePnP matches or outperforms PnP baselines tuned with the true $σ$. Code is available at https://github.com/hdubasullivan/AdaptivePnP.
title: AdaptivePnP: Fast Auto-Tuned Plug-and-Play for Deconvolution

summary: The pigs were bleeding. That was the point of the experiment: could airway pressure reveal hemorrhage before it became critical? In the UCR Time Series Classification Archive, the de facto benchmark for Time Series Classification (TSC), the same recordings ask a different question: "which of 52 pigs produced this trace?". summary: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly involved in software development, but their participation in real-world security remediation remains poorly understood. We investigate observable evidence of coding-agent involvement in commits referenced by reviewed GitHub Security Advisories (GHSAs), characterize the associated vulnerabilities, and examine review timing in relation to advisory disclosure routes. These findings demonstrate that coding-agent involvement is already observable across hundreds of security advisories and repositories, including high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities. By distinguishing direct attribution from repository-level adoption evidence and separating route-composition effects from within-route timing differences, we provide an empirical characterization of agent-associated remediation in the GHSA review pipeline.

summary: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.
title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks

summary: The reconstruction of the top-quark-pair ($t\bar{t}$) kinematics in the dilepton $t\bar{t}$ decay channel is challenging due to the presence of two undetected neutrinos. In this work, existing kinematic reconstruction methods used by the CMS Collaboration are studied using a Monte Carlo sample with $t\bar{t}$ events from CMS Open Data at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. An improved version of the loose kinematic reconstruction, LKRv2, is developed by imposing more stringent requirements on the jet-lepton pairing entering the reconstruction. A further modification, LKRv3, exploits the kinematic similarity between the dilepton and neutrino-pair systems and improves the resolution of the reconstructed $t\bar{t}$ invariant mass relative to the baseline LKR by $7\%$, with smaller improvements for the transverse momentum and rapidity of $t\bar{t}$. In addition, two machine-learning (ML) based approaches are developed using a residual multilayer perceptron and a conditional normalizing flow. Relative to LKRv3, they improve the resolution of the invariant mass, transverse momentum and rapidity by approximately $30\%$, $20\%$ and $15\%$, respectively. In particular, a resolution of 30 GeV is achieved for the reconstructed invariant mass of $t\bar{t}$ near the production threshold. A dedicated generator-level study and a generator-to-detector transfer test demonstrate that the ML approaches learn a genuine physics-driven correction to the $ν\barν$ approximation, rather than merely exploiting detector-specific effects. These results demonstrate the strong potential of ML-based approaches for improving the reconstruction of dilepton $t\bar{t}$ events, while identifying the neutrino-pair approximation as an important limitation on the achievable resolution.
title: Kinematic Reconstruction of Top-Quark Pairs Using Analytical and Machine-Learning Methods with CMS Open Data

summary: Vehicle telematics provides detailed observations of driving behaviour that can be useful for automobile insurance risk assessment. Existing approaches often summarize these data through counts of harsh events or individually unusual observations, although driving movements naturally develop over time. Building on a previously proposed hidden Markov model (HMM) framework that identifies pointwise anomalies, we identify short intervals in which a sequence of observations is unusual when considered together. We then examine the original acceleration signals to measure the magnitude and temporal concentration of these episodes and identify recurring patterns of vehicle movement. Temporal concentration describes whether acceleration activity is distributed evenly across an episode or concentrated in relatively few observations. Using a controlled telematics dataset containing normal, aggressive, and drowsy driving by the same drivers, we evaluate the proposed measures through comparisons matched by driver and road type. We find that statistical anomaly measures depend on the driving population used to train the HMM. More importantly, mean temporal concentration alone distinguishes normal from abnormal driving more effectively than the original pointwise anomaly indices across different reference populations. The recurring movement patterns further reveal different characteristics of abnormal driving, with stronger longitudinal acceleration during aggressive driving and more frequent lateral corrections or excursions during drowsy driving. The framework therefore goes beyond pointwise anomaly detection, providing interpretable behavioural features that can be calculated for unlabeled trips, used for trip-level assessment, aggregated across a driver's trip history, and subsequently evaluated alongside existing telematics and rating variables for insurance risk modelling and ratemaking.
title: From Point Anomalies to Anomalous Driving Episodes: Interpreting Abnormal Driving from Vehicle Telematics

summary: Extracting discriminative features from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) spectra is important for the classification of complex biological samples. This study evaluates continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based spectral peak extraction for distinguishing human plasma samples labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative. Plasma specimens from 181 individuals, comprising 53 positive samples and 128 negative controls, were deposited as 5 μL droplets on silicon substrates and dried before analysis. Spectra were acquired using a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser operating at 1064 nm, with 100 single-shot measurements collected per specimen and averaged after intensity-based outlier rejection. CWT-based peak detection was coupled with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The reported leave-one-out evaluation yielded an accuracy of 93.00%, sensitivity of 94.67%, and specificity of 91.61%; these estimates remain provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions. Features identified by the CWT pipeline included emission lines assigned to Ca II, K I, and N I. The workflow provides a basis for examining spectral features associated with the studied plasma groups. Independent validation and assessment of specimen, substrate, and acquisition-related variability are required to establish generalizability and diagnostic relevance.
title: Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples

summary: Recommendation systems often enter a new serving window before enough outcomes are available to retrain the deployed model. We study this regime with 0.05-1.0% target feedback, a range that spans our stress tests while keeping supervision far below the degrees of freedom of the source recommender. summary: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.
title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds

summary: Overview The script conducts the full end-to-end inferential and descriptive statistical analysis pipeline reported in the manuscript . It evaluates changes in commercial drivers' subjective states (sleepiness, physical fatigue symptoms, musculoskeletal discomfort, and blood pressure) alongside objective sustained attention measured via the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) before and after simulated driving sessions . Statistical Pipeline & Methodology Pre-Post Subjective Comparisons: Calculates median and interquartile ranges (Q1, Q3), Wilcoxon signed-rank test statistics, paired rank-biserial correlation effect sizes, and one-sample Hodges-Lehmann median difference estimates paired with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (5,000 resamples) . Fatigue Symptoms & Musculoskeletal Discomfort: Evaluates discrete fatigue symptoms using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni family-wise error rate corrections, and assesses anatomical discomfort changes across individual Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ) regions using exact McNemar tests . Objective Vigilance (PVT): Analyzes pre-to-post alterations in median reaction time (RT), mean RT, mean reciprocal reaction time (1/RT), fastest 10% RT, slowest 10% RT, lapses (RT >= 500 ms), and false starts, adjusted via Holm corrections . Cross-Domain Concordance & Associations: Computes Spearman rank correlations with 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (4,000 resamples), partial Spearman correlations controlling for prior sleep duration, and Cohen's kappa coefficient to quantify concordance across elevated symptom domains . Subjective Fatigue vs. Objective Vigilance: Tests associations between subjective self-reports and objective vigilance metrics with Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjustments, complemented by Kruskal-Wallis tests across composite elevated impairment levels . Sensitivity Power Analysis: Computes the minimal detectable paired Cohen's d effect size and minimal detectable correlation coefficient (|rho|) achievable at 80% statistical power and an alpha level of 0.05 . Files & Data Structure analisis_TSR.py : Standalone Python replication script . Input Data: Expects an Excel workbook named Dataset_Induk_n20_v2.xlsx containing participant records within the sheet named data . Generated Output: Automatically writes all formatted statistical output tables directly into a consolidated Excel file named Hasil_Analisis_TSR.xlsx . Execution & Reproducibility Deterministic Randomness: All resampling routines utilize a fixed pseudorandom number generator seed ( seed = 2026 ) to ensure exact reproducibility across runs . Execution: Run directly via terminal/command line: python analisis_TSR.py or within a Google Colab notebook by placing Dataset_Induk_n20_v2.xlsx in the active runtime directory and invoking !python analisis_TSR.py . Software Requirements The script prints active package versions directly to the console upon execution for reporting in manuscript methodology sections . Required dependencies: Python NumPy pandas SciPy statsmodels scikit-learn

The deposit is organised as five bundles, so a reader can take only the part they need: rog-ah-01-search-and-corpus : the locked Web of Science query, its per-branch counts, and the corpus index that screening ran over. rog-ah-02-prompts-and-schema : the screening and extraction prompts with their changelog, and the JSON schemas used to validate model output. rog-ah-03-model-runs : one directory per model run: inputs, outputs, and metadata recording the model identifier and prompt version, together with the structured per-paper extraction. rog-ah-04-figure-data-and-scripts : inputs, plotting scripts and the source manifest behind the figures, including the one compared dataset that has no persistent identifier. rog-ah-05-si-counts : the scripts that derive the counts reported in the supporting information, the reduced audit records they read, and the derived values. MANIFEST.sha256 lists a checksum for every bundle and for every file inside one. Figure 2 compares five global anthropogenic heat flux datasets; four resolve to their own DOIs and are not duplicated in full here, and sources.json records the identifier, filename, size and checksum of each. The figure bundle carries small cut-outs of all five around the three case cities, so the figure can be redrawn without the full rasters; these keep their sources' terms. The deposit also carries AHF_2005-2040_0.5x0.5.nc, the 0.5 degree gridded anthropogenic heat flux dataset of Flanner (2009, https://doi.org/10.1029/2008GL036465), inside the figure bundle at data/publication/figure2/qf_datasets/. That dataset is third-party work. It is redistributed here unmodified and with attribution because its original host, http://www.cgd.ucar.edu/tss/ahf/data/, went offline in July 2024 and the dataset has no persistent identifier of its own, so Figure 2 could not otherwise be reproduced from a citable source. The copy was retrieved on 2026-08-07 from the Internet Archive capture of 2012-04-13 and verified against the digest that the archive records for that capture; the full provenance is in AHF_2005-2040_0.5x0.5.nc.provenance.txt, which is deposited alongside the bundles as well as inside that one. summary: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. summary: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.

summary: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. summary: We study a Bayesian inverse problem in EUV reflectometry, where optical constants and layer thicknesses are inferred from angle- and wavelength-resolved reflection measurements. The physical process is modeled and evaluated using an efficient forward model based on the transfer matrix method. As an alternative to computationally expensive sampling-based inference, we employ an Eulerian, entropically regularized Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler divergence via proximal steps in the Wasserstein space. Using the Benamou--Brenier dynamic formulation and a Hopf-Cole transform, each JKO step is reformulated as a pair of heat equations coupled only through their initial and terminal conditions, enabling an efficient fixed-point solver. The resulting high-dimensional densities are discretized on tensor-product grids and represented in tensor-train format, exploiting Kronecker structure for scalable computation. Preconditioning based on estimated posterior moments further improves tractability. We test the method with numerical experiments on EUV reflectometry data for a ruthenium--silicon ($\ce{Ru}$ on $\ce{Si}$) specimen and compare the learned tensor-train posterior to ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) reference samples. We demonstrate a use case in which we are able to reuse the tensor-train posterior to obtain samples for shifted target distributions with less computational effort than a comparable MCMC method.
title: Bayesian Inverse Problems for EUV reflectometry with regularized JKO scheme

summary: Local response measurements track how perturbations spread in quantum simulators and nonequilibrium many-body systems. Locality bounds constrain the propagation speed, but do not determine whether the response can distinguish computational outcomes at fixed measurement precision as the distance increases. Here we construct time-independent dynamics with bounded nearest-neighbor interactions in which a fixed single-site detector responds to a remote bond phase after a time proportional to their separation. The susceptibility has a positive lower bound independent of distance. With product-state preparations, estimating this susceptibility to constant additive accuracy is complete for bounded-error quantum polynomial time (BQP), with a decision gap independent of distance. Two source-phase settings give the susceptibility with a distance-independent shot count at fixed accuracy and confidence. Inverse-polynomially weak local couplings between the computational register and the chain carrying the excitation preserve the gap. The leading correction vanishes when exchanging the two internal states of the excitation reverses the interaction. Varying the source and observation time makes all bond phases locally identifiable near the zero-phase reference setting. We also prove a conditional quantum advantage for distribution-free response prediction.
title: BQP-Complete Susceptibilities Observable at Ballistic Times in Local Quantum Dynamics

summary: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. summary: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.
title: Know What You Need: Efficient Activation Checkpointing

summary: Deep learning training is difficult to verify within a scientific workflow: its architecture, hyperparameters, and procedure are rarely fixed until training has been attempted, and two honest runs never produce the same weights, so recomputation cannot serve as a check. We present SciCheck, a framework in which the scientist explores training configurations freely and posts a blueprint to a provenance ledger for each candidate they want verified, and a verifying scientist judges the resulting run in two layers: a statistical judge model that compares per-step gradient statistics against the verifier's own reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly chosen training segments whose checkpoints are committed to the ledger one epoch at a time. On an MLP, a CNN, and an autoencoder at 100k-500k parameters, under gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fabricated runs, SciCheck reaches F1 of 0.966, 0.906, and 0.976 while rejecting 0-4.4% of honest runs. For the attacks we test, the spot-check accounts for most of this accuracy, and we characterize what each layer can detect. The effective-signal statistic falls as $(1-2s)^2$ under a sign flip of severity $s$, so gradient statistics alone catch strong enough sign flips, while fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics look no more anomalous than honest runs to any statistical detector we test. The spot-check catches fully fabricated segments with probability at least $1-(1-s)^k$ for $k$ sampled segments when the draws stay hidden until the run is committed, which roughly matches our measurements and lets a verifier choose $k$ for a target soundness. Verification costs 1.5-2.3x one retraining, mostly for the verifier's reference run; each submission's spot-check takes under 1.5 s, and per-epoch commitments reduce checkpoint storage 5-17x compared with keeping every checkpoint.
title: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training

summary: The natural environments habitable to life are inseparable from dissipative and entropic forces, which mandate active matter to operate on constant fluxes of energy and momentum to survive and propagate through spacetime. In contrast to fundamental particles which are characterized by energy and momentum, we postulate that energy expenditure rate and momentum generation rate are the fundamental dynamical quantities driving this evolution of swimming active matter and accordingly construct the corresponding Lagrangian and Hamiltonian of motion of the active matter. Furthermore, living systems broadly employ periodic, non-repeating motion for both locomotion and various biological functions, with meaningful information stored in the periods of these functions. Consequently, analyzing these dynamics in the Fourier space lands us at the familiar tools of the operator based, quantum mechanics. This is accomplished by introducing a complex field to describe the evolving probability distribution of a single unit, as well as the population density of mutually non-interacting active particles under the constraint of scarce resources. The resulting single-unit wavefunction evolves analogously to the Dirac equation with minimal coupling, wherein gauge symmetry reflects the generality of the governing equations across arbitrary resource landscapes. Additionally, we present a Schrödinger-like equation where the effective potential term represents the environmentally mandated, non-motile base metabolic rate. Finally, we formalize the bidirectional coupling between active swimmers and the surrounding fluid via a multipole expansion of the active force with an emphasis on force monopoles and dipoles, where each pole corresponds to a distinct mode of active motility.
title: A Quantum Mechanical Description of Active Matter

summary: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and schedule
title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part IV : Two Independent Checks and Endpoint-Side Reconstruction to Prevent Tool Misuse, Memory Poisoning, Unauthorized Delegation and Unlawful Data Use — Supporting EU AI Act Record-Keeping, Human Oversight and Cybersecurity, GDPR Purpose Limitation and DORA

summary: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. summary: This repository contains the analysis code accompanying the SPiCe paper (Genome Biology; secrierlab/SPiCe). It has three components. (i) merfish_analysis/ implements the graph neural network (GNN) framework. For each sample of the MERFISH mouse cortex dataset, it builds a spatial k-nearest-neighbour cell graph (k = 20, Euclidean-distance edge weights). It then holds out one cell type at a time and trains a three-layer graph convolutional network (PyTorch Geometric) on one-hot cell-type features to predict which remaining cells sit next to the removed type. Evaluation is inductive, on held-out tissue sections, and performance is measured by ROC-AUC. Predictions are interpreted with Integrated Gradients (Captum) for node-level (cell-type) importance, tested against a permutation baseline with Mann–Whitney U tests and multiple-testing correction. GNNExplainer is used for edge-level (cell-type-pair) importance. (ii) spatial_regression/ contains Python and R notebooks that model spatially varying relationships in Xenium breast cancer data. They regress an EMT hallmark score on tumour-microenvironment and CNV-derived predictors, such as distances to neighbouring cell populations and principal components. The notebooks fit spatial error models (spreg), geographically weighted regression (mgwr) and multiscale GWR (GWmodel in R), with VIF/correlation filtering and variable-specific bandwidth selection. (iii) figure_plotting/ holds the notebook and conda environment that reproduce the paper’s GNN performance, node/edge importance and network figures from the saved outputs. Conda environment files ( base_env_gnn.yml , figures_paper_gnn.yml ) specify the dependencies. The other notebooks show analyses regarding the generalisability, contender frameworks, etc.
title: Integrative Spatial Modelling of Cellular Plasticity using Graph Neural Networks and Geostatistics

summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can adapt O-RAN slice allocations to changing traffic and interference, but episode-average URLLC cost can hide failures during short traffic surges. We audit the maximum traffic-group mean cost; because the groups partition an episode, this worst-group constraint already implies the mean constraint. In a single-cell benchmark with burst traffic, selective jamming, impaired KPMs, and 105 discrete actions, 57 static actions satisfy the mean limit by point estimate but only 46 satisfy the worst-group limit on 100 fresh episodes; interval estimates classify 45 as supported, 10 as uncertain, and 50 as violating. The validation-selected mean-feasible action is worst-group uncertain on those traces. Across five seeds of PPO-Lagrangian, recurrent PPO-Lagrangian, and DQN, bootstrap intervals classify 13 of 15 final states as violating and two as uncertain; every recurrent final policy reduces to a constant catalogue action. A privileged oracle and a delayed-load heuristic, both a two-action rule tuned on validation episodes, safely recover about 4.2 return of adaptive headroom on training-matched and constant-jammer traces, which no evaluated learner or shield does. A calibrated risk ensemble has five supported evaluated runs on both scenarios, yet it loses return to the best safe static action and to the heuristic. Under an unseen sweep jammer, only 50% URLLC reservation remains supported. The resulting audit establishes traffic group, seed, checkpoint, and distribution shift as distinct dimensions of O-RAN DRL safety evaluation.
title: Auditing Deep Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Network Slicing: Worst-Group Safety under Traffic Bursts and Jamming

summary: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education requires sound instruments for identifying faculty development needs. This study reports the Portuguese adaptation and measurement-model evaluation of the Generative AI Competency Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers and Researchers (GAICS-TR), a 35-item self-report instrument designed to assess academics’ perceived self-efficacy in relation to GenAI competencies. The scale comprises nine dimensions conceptually organised into four domains: Basic GenAI Understanding, Teaching with GenAI, Research with GenAI, and Professional Engagement with GenAI. The Portuguese version was developed through a pragmatic, team-based translation and adaptation procedure informed by established cross-cultural adaptation guidance. The procedure included translation of the items, review of their wording and contextual suitability, discussion of discrepancies, and consensus within the PRODIGIA research team. The items were administered on a five-point agreement scale to faculty and researchers from three partner universities, yielding 105 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLSSEM) was used to assess indicator reliability, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The retained measurement model met the reported reliability and validity criteria, with the exception of the discriminant validity between GPD and GKG, which yielded a correlation of 0.923 (exceeding the standard 0.90 threshold). Item GPD2 was removed after presenting a loading of 0.482; after its removal, the professional-development dimension reached an Average Variance Extracted of 0.708 and a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.790. This item-level result should be interpreted cautiously because it may reflect wording, translation, or sample-specific effects. The adapted scale provides evidence for assessing self-reported GenAI competency self-efficacy in the participating institutions and for informing the diagnostic phase of PRODIGIA. Replication in larger, independent samples is needed.
title: Validating a Generative AI competency self-efficacy scale for higher education faculty: A PLS-SEM study

summary: Current research in the food industry highlights the importance of alternative protein sources in the context of global population growth and the need to reduce the negative impact of raising animals, producing animal proteins, on the environment. Plant proteins represent a sustainable, affordable and beneficial option for health, with high potential to replace animal proteins in the food industry. Plant sources rich in protein include legumes, cereals, pseudocereals, oilseeds, green leaves, algae and, more recently, insects. They differ considerably in protein content and amino acid profile, and their strategic combination can ensure a balanced intake of essential nutrients. Legumes offer high protein content, but are deficient in sulfur amino acids. Cereals, although lower in protein, bring technological benefits and can complement the amino acids missing from legumes. Pseudocereals have a higher nutritional value than conventional cereals, while green leaves and algae offer a high proteins intake and compounds with antioxidant potential, although they require advanced technologies to overcome extraction limitations. Extraction methods play a decisive role in the yield and quality of plant proteins. Conventional techniques are efficient but can cause denaturation and provide low yields. On the other hand, emerging methods allow the recovery of proteins in larger quantities, preserving their functional and technological properties.
title: Plant-based proteins: sources, extraction methods and functional perspectives for the sustainable food industry

summary: Replication package for a staged empirical study of whether a dependency upgrade changes the conclusions of machine-learning comparisons. Six scikit-learn classifiers (LR, SVC, kNN, RF, GB, HGB) were evaluated on all 63 eligible OpenML-CC18 tasks with frozen splits (6 × 5-fold cross-validation), across two real upgrades: 0.21.3 → 0.22.2.post1 (changed defaults) and 1.8.0 → 1.9.1 (negative control). The package contains: the frozen study protocol (v2.2.5) and pre-run amendment (v2.2.6), with SHA-256 manifests; the frozen plan (folds and seeds), environment lock files and provenance records for each scikit-learn release; the frozen changelog-coding frame used for blinding; all fold-level results (balanced accuracy and prediction hashes) and analysis reports; post-review analyses G0–G3 with all raw outputs: restoration of historical defaults, boosting interventions, bootstrap and winner-margin sensitivity, and the corrected six-estimator explicit map E2; scripts that verify every stored file and recompute every number and figure in the paper. Quick check, with no experiments required: python3 paper/verify_results.py and python3 postreview/verify_postreview.py --zip VersionShift_replication.zip . The attached VersionShift_replication.zip (SHA-256 5eb716b64c21ded6f979b0b1610bb68aee46ad2f24889a0d3b133bd430c6ff7d) is the frozen original-study archive that the post-review kits require. The OpenML-CC18 datasets are not redistributed. The scripts rebuild them from OpenML and check them against the frozen hashes.
tags: dependency upgrades; default arguments; breaking changes; scikit-learn; reproducibility; conclusion stability; empirical software engineering
title: When a Library Upgrade Changes the Verdict: Default-Configuration Drift and the Stability of Machine-Learning Comparisons
