The package contains: the frozen study protocol (v2.2.5) and pre-run amendment (v2.2.6), with SHA-256 manifests; the frozen plan (folds and seeds), environment lock files and provenance records for each scikit-learn release; the frozen changelog-coding frame used for blinding; all fold-level results (balanced accuracy and prediction hashes) and analysis reports; post-review analyses G0–G3 with all raw outputs: restoration of historical defaults, boosting interventions, bootstrap and winner-margin sensitivity, and the corrected six-estimator explicit map E2; scripts that verify every stored file and recompute every number and figure in the paper. Quick check, with no experiments required: python3 paper/verify_results.py and python3 postreview/verify_postreview.py --zip VersionShift_replication.zip . The attached VersionShift_replication.zip (SHA-256 5eb716b64c21ded6f979b0b1610bb68aee46ad2f24889a0d3b133bd430c6ff7d) is the frozen original-study archive that the post-review kits require. The OpenML-CC18 datasets are not redistributed. The scripts rebuild them from OpenML and check them against the frozen hashes.

summary: This record contains the data of the CascadeFQN Study, which asks when a language model is needed to resolve the fully qualified names of types in Java snippets that lack their import statements. It holds a SQLite database with the 467 runs of the study (predictions, costs, and gold labels) and a cache of the model replies, so the LLM runs can be repeated without cost. It also holds FQNs4J, a new benchmark of 1,224 snippets from code created in 2025 or later, together with StatType-SO and ThaliaType, and the dictionaries, usage statistics, trained scorers, and library jars the pipeline uses. The outputs of the external baselines (CKTyper, Scitix, SnR) and the repair rounds of ZS4C on our test parts are included, and the accompanying code repository ( https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cascade-fqn-replication/ ) regenerates every table and number of the paper from these files.

summary: Photonic Neural Networks (PNNs) are projected to be the next-generation AI platform, driving significant advances in compute energy and area efficiency by leveraging light’s parallelism across space, wavelength, and time. Here we present a Photonic Integrated Tensor Core (PITC) architecture that combines an Arrayed Waveguide Grating Router (AWGR)-enabled PNN with a SiGe electro-absorption modulator (EAM) array following a chiplet-based silicon photonic (SiPho) accelerator setup for multi-wavelength data and weight encoding. The 8×8 PITC architectural layout, was experimentally validated in two AI benchmark workloads at 20 Gbaud, successfully classifying the IRIS and MNIST datasets yielding Cohen’s kappa-scores of 0.8438 and 0.7421, respectively.
title: A Time-Space-Wavelength Multiplexed Photonic Tensor Core using WDM SiGe EAM array chiplets

summary: Code accompanying the paper Benchmarking DFT and Machine Learning Potentials for Heat of Formation and Combustion of High-Energy Materials . For a target molecule the script enumerates isodesmic reactions against a curated library of small reference species and ranks them. Bond conservation is encoded as bond signatures (bond order together with the hybridisation and aromaticity of the connected atoms) and solved with a linear programming solver under random cost-vector perturbations, so that many distinct valid schemes are found. A secondary ring-breaking relaxation is applied where strict conservation is impossible for fused ring systems. Candidates are ranked by an IsoScore that balances chemical simplicity, Tanimoto structural similarity to the reference library, and stoichiometric cost. The repository contains the generator, the input file with the twenty high-energy materials of the benchmark set, and a README.
title: Automated isodesmic reaction generator for high-energy materials

direction_title: Wolfram official open quantum research metadata — no Alpha API [FORWARD]
summary: Simultaneous tolerance certification asks whether every component of a dense latent vector lies within its prescribed range. This preprint studies noisy unit-norm linear measurements under pathwise resource budgets, with tolerances calibrated to a fixed prior membership probability. For independent Gaussian priors, every fixed linear channel is uniformly asymptotically equivalent, for the membership decision, to a coordinate-precision design at no greater total precision. A marked Poisson limit characterizes the complete family of feasible limiting experiments. The resulting allocation theory gives exact Brier-optimal designs and proves that every classification-optimal allocation has zero plus at most one positive normalized precision level. The global classification problem therefore reduces to a one-dimensional coverage choice. At low budgets, no allocation is most informative for every decision loss. At fixed row precision, adaptive screening yields a squared-logarithmic reduction in the order of measurements required for prescribed positive decision gain. For classification, sharp high-accuracy constants distinguish the inverse-square risk dependence of fixed designs from the logarithmic dependence of adaptive acquisition. Bounded-spectrum Gaussian dependence preserves the fixed-design frontier. Matching resource orders extend to exponential-power priors, including Laplace and lighter tails. A frozen Gaussian simulation, combined with certified deterministic bounds, establishes a finite-dimensional advantage over all fixed linear designs under the same affine acquisition budget, with one-sided 95% Monte Carlo confidence. This record contains the preprint, proof supplement, editable LaTeX sources, and a reproducibility archive with programs, experimental protocols, and saved results. The manuscript and proof supplement are licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0; original software is licensed under MIT. Third-party components retain their own licenses.
title: Simultaneous Tolerance Certification: Limit Experiments and Sharp Resource Laws

summary: This version combines two key updates. Significant reduction in model runtime by improving code efficiency. Function calls for ka,kw and kH are now only done once and archived for future reference as these remain constant for a given set of conditions. All occurrences of .loc have been replaced with .at which is ~10 times faster to return results. Additional performance improvements in the future could be achieved by using .iat. Corrections to rate constants. Work originally performed by Jennifer Lowrie in 2025. Detailed analysis of the chemistry scheme revealed several inconsistencies a) O3 + I- rate from Brown et al. 2024 has been updated to reflect the final published version and not the value from the pre-print. b) I2 + OH (and reverse) were raised to the incorrect power - this dates back to the original work of Carpenter et al. 2013. c) minor corrections to Reaction 19, 22 and 23 (using table from Pound et al. 2024). Note that there is a typo for the value of reaction 14 in this table, however it is correct in the code. These rate changes have resulted in some conditions having a decrease in total iodine emission rate, with the rate of I2 emission relative to HOI increasing at higher temperatures. Overall, the model results remain comparable between v1.2 and this release. <img width="692" height="698" alt="Chemistry_update_correlation" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d2f5e2eb-652b-40d3-b335-0497999bfbc1" /> <img width="1854" height="703" alt="Chemistry_update_T_comp" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/697304fd-cf65-4971-ae44-396608de3e1c" /> <img width="1854" height="707" alt="Chemistry_update_ws_comp" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/996f6e70-5f94-4aba-a84f-fc5370e10ac3" />

summary: Research code accompanying the paper Data-proximal null-space networks for inverse problems by Jürgen Frikel, Simon Göppel and Markus Haltmeier. Data-proximal networks extend null-space networks by learned corrections whose additional change of the predicted data is explicitly controlled. The repository contains the implementation of the synthetic limited-angle computed tomography study: ellipse phantom generation, the discrete Radon operator and the numerical row-space projection, Tikhonov and total-variation initializations, the residual (RES), null-space (NSN) and data-proximal (DP1, DP2) networks, Float64 training with checkpointing, the frozen evaluator, the public inference entry point for published checkpoints, and the compact scientific export from which the paper tables and figures are regenerated with scripts/reproduce_paper.py . Trained weights, the row-space basis, the operator and the sample data are not part of this record; they are intended for separate data records. The program code is licensed under GPL-3.0-only; see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for the U-Net attribution.

The repository contains the implementation of the synthetic limited-angle computed tomography study: ellipse phantom generation, the discrete Radon operator and the numerical row-space projection, Tikhonov and total-variation initializations, the residual (RES), null-space (NSN) and data-proximal (DP1, DP2) networks, Float64 training with checkpointing, the frozen evaluator, the public inference entry point for published checkpoints, and the compact scientific export from which the paper tables and figures are regenerated with scripts/reproduce_paper.py . Trained weights, the row-space basis, the operator and the sample data are not part of this record; they are intended for separate data records. The program code is licensed under GPL-3.0-only; see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for the U-Net attribution.

summary: Deep learning training is difficult to verify within a scientific workflow: its architecture, hyperparameters, and procedure are rarely fixed until training has been attempted, and two honest runs never produce the same weights, so recomputation cannot serve as a check. We present SciCheck, a framework in which the scientist explores training configurations freely and posts a blueprint to a provenance ledger for each candidate they want verified, and a verifying scientist judges the resulting run in two layers: a statistical judge model that compares per-step gradient statistics against the verifier's own reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly chosen training segments whose checkpoints are committed to the ledger one epoch at a time. On an MLP, a CNN, and an autoencoder at 100k-500k parameters, under gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fabricated runs, SciCheck reaches F1 of 0.966, 0.906, and 0.976 while rejecting 0-4.4% of honest runs. For the attacks we test, the spot-check accounts for most of this accuracy, and we characterize what each layer can detect. The effective-signal statistic falls as $(1-2s)^2$ under a sign flip of severity $s$, so gradient statistics alone catch strong enough sign flips, while fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics look no more anomalous than honest runs to any statistical detector we test. The spot-check catches fully fabricated segments with probability at least $1-(1-s)^k$ for $k$ sampled segments when the draws stay hidden until the run is committed, which roughly matches our measurements and lets a verifier choose $k$ for a target soundness. Verification costs 1.5-2.3x one retraining, mostly for the verifier's reference run; each submission's spot-check takes under 1.5 s, and per-epoch commitments reduce checkpoint storage 5-17x compared with keeping every checkpoint.
title: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training

summary: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and schedule
title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part IV : Two Independent Checks and Endpoint-Side Reconstruction to Prevent Tool Misuse, Memory Poisoning, Unauthorized Delegation and Unlawful Data Use — Supporting EU AI Act Record-Keeping, Human Oversight and Cybersecurity, GDPR Purpose Limitation and DORA

summary: This Supplemental Materials file accompanies the manuscript submitted to the Journal of Urban Planning and Development (ASCE). It contains eleven supplementary figures (Figs. S1–S11) and three supplementary tables (Tables S1–S3), whose numbering matches the in-text citations and supports every robustness, calibration, optimizer-comparison, PPO-training, MRIO-cross-check, and accounting-identity claim that does not fit in the main text. Gross mitigation-triggered leakage pressure and leakage-pressure-to-reduction ratio across S1–S5. Fig. S7. Temporal holdout performance of city log-linear, damped-trend, and last-observation benchmark models. Fig. S8. Performance of the neutral 70-variable, leakage-aware 70-variable, and leakage-aware 210-variable open-loop optimizers. Fig. S9. Paired effects of leakage penalty, domain randomization, and their joint use relative to matched S3. Fig. S10. Recorded PPO training outcomes and update diagnostics across six trained policies. Fig. S11. Active-versus-frozen S4 outcome differences and action-response magnitudes under identical shocks. Supplementary Tables (Tables S1–S3) Table S1. Disclosed transition and implementation-burden coefficients — per-policy-action GDP response, carbon-intensity-improvement response, net CO₂ response, PIB coefficient cₖ, and calibration basis (e.g., fixed-asset investment / industrial structure for industrial adjustment; municipal / public-utility and water-saving investment for energy efficiency). CO₂ consistency diagnostics and temporal holdout benchmark — GDP × CI accounting identity over 190 city–year observations (maximum relative error = 4.38 × 10⁻¹⁶, exact numerical consistency) and 2021–2022 continuity test (regional z = −0.52; maximum city |z| ≈ 0.64, no detected reconstruction breakpoint). summary: Current research in the food industry highlights the importance of alternative protein sources in the context of global population growth and the need to reduce the negative impact of raising animals, producing animal proteins, on the environment. Plant proteins represent a sustainable, affordable and beneficial option for health, with high potential to replace animal proteins in the food industry. Plant sources rich in protein include legumes, cereals, pseudocereals, oilseeds, green leaves, algae and, more recently, insects. They differ considerably in protein content and amino acid profile, and their strategic combination can ensure a balanced intake of essential nutrients. Legumes offer high protein content, but are deficient in sulfur amino acids. Cereals, although lower in protein, bring technological benefits and can complement the amino acids missing from legumes. Pseudocereals have a higher nutritional value than conventional cereals, while green leaves and algae offer a high proteins intake and compounds with antioxidant potential, although they require advanced technologies to overcome extraction limitations. Extraction methods play a decisive role in the yield and quality of plant proteins. Conventional techniques are efficient but can cause denaturation and provide low yields. On the other hand, emerging methods allow the recovery of proteins in larger quantities, preserving their functional and technological properties.
title: Plant-based proteins: sources, extraction methods and functional perspectives for the sustainable food industry

summary: Replication package for a staged empirical study of whether a dependency upgrade changes the conclusions of machine-learning comparisons. Six scikit-learn classifiers (LR, SVC, kNN, RF, GB, HGB) were evaluated on all 63 eligible OpenML-CC18 tasks with frozen splits (6 × 5-fold cross-validation), across two real upgrades: 0.21.3 → 0.22.2.post1 (changed defaults) and 1.8.0 → 1.9.1 (negative control). The package contains: the frozen study protocol (v2.2.5) and pre-run amendment (v2.2.6), with SHA-256 manifests; the frozen plan (folds and seeds), environment lock files and provenance records for each scikit-learn release; the frozen changelog-coding frame used for blinding; all fold-level results (balanced accuracy and prediction hashes) and analysis reports; post-review analyses G0–G3 with all raw outputs: restoration of historical defaults, boosting interventions, bootstrap and winner-margin sensitivity, and the corrected six-estimator explicit map E2; scripts that verify every stored file and recompute every number and figure in the paper. Quick check, with no experiments required: python3 paper/verify_results.py and python3 postreview/verify_postreview.py --zip VersionShift_replication.zip . The attached VersionShift_replication.zip (SHA-256 5eb716b64c21ded6f979b0b1610bb68aee46ad2f24889a0d3b133bd430c6ff7d) is the frozen original-study archive that the post-review kits require. The OpenML-CC18 datasets are not redistributed. The scripts rebuild them from OpenML and check them against the frozen hashes.
tags: dependency upgrades; default arguments; breaking changes; scikit-learn; reproducibility; conclusion stability; empirical software engineering
title: When a Library Upgrade Changes the Verdict: Default-Configuration Drift and the Stability of Machine-Learning Comparisons

summary: Simultaneous tolerance certification asks whether every component of a dense latent vector lies within its prescribed range. This preprint studies noisy unit-norm linear measurements under pathwise resource budgets, with tolerances calibrated to a fixed prior membership probability. For independent Gaussian priors, every fixed linear channel is uniformly asymptotically equivalent, for the membership decision, to a coordinate-precision design at no greater total precision. A marked Poisson limit characterizes the complete family of feasible limiting experiments. The resulting allocation theory gives exact Brier-optimal designs and proves that every classification-optimal allocation has zero plus at most one positive normalized precision level. The global classification problem therefore reduces to a one-dimensional coverage choice. At low budgets, no allocation is most informative for every decision loss. At fixed row precision, adaptive screening yields a squared-logarithmic reduction in the order of measurements required for prescribed positive decision gain. For classification, sharp high-accuracy constants distinguish the inverse-square risk dependence of fixed designs from the logarithmic dependence of adaptive acquisition. Bounded-spectrum Gaussian dependence preserves the fixed-design frontier. Matching resource orders extend to exponential-power priors, including Laplace and lighter tails. A frozen Gaussian simulation, combined with certified deterministic bounds, establishes a finite-dimensional advantage over all fixed linear designs under the same affine acquisition budget, with one-sided 95% Monte Carlo confidence. This record contains the preprint, proof supplement, editable LaTeX sources, and a reproducibility archive with programs, experimental protocols, and saved results. The manuscript and proof supplement are licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0; original software is licensed under MIT. Third-party components retain their own licenses.
title: Simultaneous Tolerance Certification: Limit Experiments and Sharp Resource Laws

summary: Version 5: Documentation corrections only; code, data, and results are unchanged from v4. Version 4  adds the analyses of the second revision: time-ordered and cross-project evaluation, structured label noise, a drop-one process-feature ablation, a Random Forest hyperparameter check, and label-provenance analyses (results/r2_experiments/), with the per-row revision metadata and commit dates they need. All Java runners now read the datasets from a configurable data directory (JML_DATA_DIR). Everything in v3 is otherwise unchanged; the audit labels are the same as in v3. Version 3. Supersedes version 2 (distributed as package v1.1) and version 1 (package v1.0). Prepared for the revised submission to Science of Computer Programming. Figures from earlier versions should not be cited. Manual validation re-run with a two-rater protocol. Estimated commit-level SZZ label precision is now  49.5% (197/398) with inter-rater agreement Cohen's κ = 0.799 , replacing the 29.2% reported in versions 1 and 2, which came from a single-rater audit with no documented agreement statistic. Per-project precision: Kafka 57.1%, Gson 48.5%, Commons-IO 42.9%. Both raters' blind passes, the disagreement-resolution record for the 10 conflicting cases, and a per-instance false-positive taxonomy of all 201 false positives are included. The labelling question changed, so labels are not directly comparable across versions. The is_valid_fix column has been renamed is_true_bic . The earlier audit recorded whether a candidate was itself a valid fix; the current audit records whether the candidate introduced the defect that its traced fix later repaired. These are different questions, and the resulting labels cannot be compared row by row with earlier versions. A central claim has been withdrawn. Earlier versions of the paper argued that feature-engineering quality has a stronger influence on predictive performance than label purity. A label-noise sensitivity experiment, included here, does not support that claim: adding 20 percentage points of label noise erases more MCC than the entire static-to-hybrid feature-engineering gain, in every project. The claim has been removed from the manuscript and replaced with the measured finding that process features hold a consistent advantage over static features at the observed noise level, while performance remains sensitive to further label degradation. Ablation and significance results re-derived from logged runs. All values now come from 270 independently seeded 10-fold cross-validation runs (30 seeds × 3 projects × 3 feature sets), with per-seed raw results, runner scripts and exact seeds included. The reported Hybrid-over-Static improvement on Commons-IO is 55%, not the 128% stated previously; Static-only MCC on Commons-IO is +0.166, not negative. Statistical testing is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test paired by seed with Cliff's delta and Holm-Bonferroni correction over nine comparisons per metric. MCC replaces F1 as the primary metric, and class prevalence, trivial baselines and confusion matrices are now reported. Prevalence differs by a factor of ~2.7 across the three projects (55.4% / 44.9% / 20.9%), so F1 is not comparable across them; all trivial baselines have MCC = 0. The reported pipeline does not use SMOTE. A direct comparison, included here, shows no benefit in any project and a measurable cost on Commons-IO. SMOTE remains available as a configuration option in the framework. Runtime and energy figures are measured, not extrapolated: 30.6 minutes wall-clock across all three projects for the reported configuration, with per-phase timings and logs. New in this version: the label-noise sensitivity sweep; an AGE-feature ablation; confusion matrices and specificity per project and feature set; a Process-versus-Static significance test; a read-only exporter for the SZZ fix-to-BIC mapping, which the original pipeline did not persist; and a replication configuration annotated with the exact s
title: JML-BugDB Dataset & JavaMLBugDetective Replication Package

summary: Se estudia la variante del algoritmo de Collatz que aplica 3m+1 a los impares congruentes con 1 módulo 4 y 3m−1 a los congruentes con 3 módulo 4, introducida por el autor en 2019. La regla equivale a elegir, entre 3m−1 y 3m+1, el término divisible por 4, de modo que cada paso impar va seguido al menos de dos divisiones por 2. Se demuestra que la distancia al punto fijo 1 se contrae al menos en el factor 3/4 en cada transición entre impares. De ello se siguen la convergencia a 1 de toda órbita, una cota explícita para el número de términos impares y una cota logarítmica para la longitud total de la trayectoria. Se establecen dos acoplamientos exactos. El primero relaciona, en un solo paso, la variante con la aplicación de Collatz acelerada y sitúa su diferencia en una única valuación 2-ádica. El segundo la relaciona con la permutación considerada por Collatz en 1932: sobre cada impar, la inversa de la permutación realiza en un paso el resultado de tres pasos elementales de la variante, y los retornos impares de ambos sistemas difieren en una potencia de 3 determinada por la valuación 2-ádica del paso. Se demuestra que el retorno impar de la permutación es biyectivo y que la variante se obtiene suprimiendo los factores de 3 de su resultado, y se precisa que esta factorización no es una conjugación. Se señalan además obstáculos a la conjugación de la variante con la aplicación de Collatz y con el retorno de la permutación. El resultado central es de naturaleza simbólica. El lenguaje de paridades de la variante es exactamente el conjunto de palabras binarias que evitan el factor 11, con entropía topológica igual al logaritmo de la razón áurea, y la densidad de las clases residuales que realizan cada palabra viene dada por una medida de Markov explícita y no uniforme. Ello contrasta con el teorema de paridades de Terras y Lagarias para la aplicación de Collatz, donde todas las palabras se realizan con la misma densidad. Se plantea como problema abierto la geometría de las clases residuales asociadas a cada palabra, con datos de enumeración exhaustiva. El escrito discute con precisión qué no se sigue de estos resultados acerca de la conjetura de Collatz, y propone controles positivos y negativos para evaluar argumentos generales. Los enunciados efectivos se han comprobado computacionalmente, y el suplemento contiene el programa en Python que reproduce esas comprobaciones con aritmética entera, junto con sus resultados. Versión 2. Se añaden un índice, las referencias a los escritos del autor sobre la permutación de Collatz de 1932 y sobre los filtros bilaterales de los mínimos de sus órbitas, y un suplemento computacional formado por el programa de verificación, un resumen de sus resultados y la tabla de las pruebas sobre las clases residuales. La sección de verificación numérica se reescribe para describir ese suplemento.
title: Una variación en el algoritmo de la conjetura de Collatz.

De ello se siguen la convergencia a 1 de toda órbita, una cota explícita para el número de términos impares y una cota logarítmica para la longitud total de la trayectoria. Se establecen dos acoplamientos exactos. El primero relaciona, en un solo paso, la variante con la aplicación de Collatz acelerada y sitúa su diferencia en una única valuación 2-ádica. El segundo la relaciona con la permutación considerada por Collatz en 1932: sobre cada impar, la inversa de la permutación realiza en un paso el resultado de tres pasos elementales de la variante, y los retornos impares de ambos sistemas difieren en una potencia de 3 determinada por la valuación 2-ádica del paso. Se demuestra que el retorno impar de la permutación es biyectivo y que la variante se obtiene suprimiendo los factores de 3 de su resultado, y se precisa que esta factorización no es una conjugación. Se señalan además obstáculos a la conjugación de la variante con la aplicación de Collatz y con el retorno de la permutación. El resultado central es de naturaleza simbólica. El lenguaje de paridades de la variante es exactamente el conjunto de palabras binarias que evitan el factor 11, con entropía topológica igual al logaritmo de la razón áurea, y la densidad de las clases residuales que realizan cada palabra viene dada por una medida de Markov explícita y no uniforme. Ello contrasta con el teorema de paridades de Terras y Lagarias para la aplicación de Collatz, donde todas las palabras se realizan con la misma densidad. Se plantea como problema abierto la geometría de las clases residuales asociadas a cada palabra, con datos de enumeración exhaustiva. El escrito discute con precisión qué no se sigue de estos resultados acerca de la conjetura de Collatz, y propone controles positivos y negativos para evaluar argumentos generales. Los enunciados efectivos se han comprobado computacionalmente, y el suplemento contiene el programa en Python que reproduce esas comprobaciones con aritmética entera, junto con sus resultados. Versión 2. Se añaden un índice, las referencias a los escritos del autor sobre la permutación de Collatz de 1932 y sobre los filtros bilaterales de los mínimos de sus órbitas, y un suplemento computacional formado por el programa de verificación, un resumen de sus resultados y la tabla de las pruebas sobre las clases residuales. La sección de verificación numérica se reescribe para describir ese suplemento.

summary: This record is the reference implementation released with COES-CD, built from the method and evaluation protocol described in the accompanying manuscript (Sections 5-6 and Appendices B/D). It is a clean implementation that follows the manuscript and the appendix, with fixed seeds, documented configurations and a uniform evaluation pipeline, and every measured number reported in this record was produced by running the code shipped here; values transcribed from the manuscript are marked as the manuscript's. The package contains the model source (coes_cd/), the experiment configurations (configs/), a deterministic synthetic data generator with fixed seeds (data_generation/, scripts/generate_data.py), acquisition scripts for the baselines actually obtained, and the scripts that rebuild the 10 tables and the 6 figures that README's asset table assigns a generation script to. NOTEARS and DAGMA are fetched at pinned commits by the shipped scripts; CSL-HNTS, DyCAST, Meta-D2AG and SPACETIME are not integrated, for the reasons given in Section 0 of docs/BASELINES.md. The pipeline is a six-step chain: generate the datasets, train stage 1, run the stage-2 stability readout, evaluate both stages into results/raw_results.csv, collect the training costs, and rebuild the assets. README's Quick start gives the exact commands, and its asset table lists the seeds and the measured per-run costs. Fixed hyperparameters, the seeds and the dataset count for each setting are listed in docs/HYPERPARAMETERS.md; the per-dataset checksums are stored in the manifests under data/synthetic/. No result files are shipped: the package has no results/ directory. Every asset whose README asset-table row names a generation script is produced by that script from the chain above; assets marked 'no generator in this release' are not, and any stored row whose source lies outside this release is identified in that table's note. NetSim is a public benchmark and is not redistributed; data/prepare_netsim.py records its public identity and implements the preprocessing, but the manuscript's N = 18 / K = 3 subset is not identified, so it is not re-run. Satellite telemetry is access-restricted and is not redistributed; the package ships the preprocessing procedure, the variable and regime schema, and a synthetic demo that exercises the pipeline end to end without the restricted input. Tables and figures that README's asset table does not list are not generated by this release. External baseline code is cloned at install time and is not redistributed with this record. Every measured cell in the rebuilt assets is the output of the code shipped here, and where an asset also carries a value transcribed from the manuscript, that value appears in a column marked as such. The measurement path of each cell (forward chain, stage-2 readout, gate, dataset coverage) and the protocol used for it are documented in README and in the table notes generated by the code. How the released runs differ from the submitted experiments: the released tables are measured at 800 epochs on a consumer GPU with one training seed per dataset and 10 datasets per setting, while the submitted tables were measured at 2000 epochs on an RTX 3090 with five training seeds and 20 datasets per setting. Where a table carries a manuscript column, it is marked as such, and each comparison can be read directly off the table. The stage-2 readout rows of Table 4 stay within 10% of the manuscript's F1 across K; the neural forward chain is reported separately in the asset table and is not the source of the reported Table 4 rows. Table 5 and Table 6 are rebuilt and compared cell by cell in the table notes. A diagnostic rerun of the K = 8 setting at the manuscript's 2000-epoch budget on the same generated data leaves the reported metric essentially unchanged, so the residual difference at K = 8 is not explained by the training budget alone; at K = 8 the average segment length falls below the manuscript's own Section 7 reliabil

summary: The KV cache is the bottleneck of long-context LLM inference.  Every modern serving system —  vLLM, SGLang, Mooncake  — is, at its core, a memory manager for the cache that grows one token at a time as the model decodes.  PagedAttention, RadixAttention , and the various  prefix caching  schemes each solve a piece of the problem, but none of them is  lock-free , none of them is  position-keyed , and none of them uses  structural sharing  to handle both beam-search branching and multi-tenant prefix sharing at the same time. This book introduces the  persistent rope  — a single data structure that does all of these things, derived from two pieces of prior art that were never combined before: the  persistent vector  (which gives the rope its branching semantics) and the  Bw-tree  (which gives the rope its lock-free properties). The book is a design document and API reference for the rope, written for engineers who build serving systems, GPU kernels, and lock-free data structures.  It is  not  a benchmark paper,  not  a tutorial, and  not  a complete serving system. The Python reference implementation is  correct but not lock-free ; the  lock-free Rust port is scaffolded in the repository  and described in detail in Chapter 22. The book covers the design (Ch 1–9), the Python reference (Ch 10–11), the verification (Ch 12–14), the public API (Ch 15–19), and the honest framing of what works, what doesn't, and what's left for future work (Ch 20–23). The appendices include a full  glossary, references, and index . Read it in order if you want to understand the design end-to-end; jump to Chapters 10–19 if you want to use the Python reference; read Chapter 22 if you're planning the Rust port.

summary: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and schedule
title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part IV : Two Independent Checks and Endpoint-Side Reconstruction to Prevent Tool Misuse, Memory Poisoning, Unauthorized Delegation and Unlawful Data Use — Supporting EU AI Act Record-Keeping, Human Oversight and Cybersecurity, GDPR Purpose Limitation and DORA

summary: This record accompanies Working Paper No. 9 of the Independent FAIR Evaluation Series of the ATLAS Framework , entitled Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation . The study examines the concentration of computational AACF susceptibility profiles derived from frozen PaccMann and DRPreter predictions for 95 unique registered configurations across 970 matched cancer cell-line profiles . Scores are transformed into normalized weights using a softmax transformation favouring lower AACF indices, with fixed model-specific reference scales. Profile characterization includes Shannon entropy, normalized entropy, effective configuration counts, and leading configuration weights. The evaluation addresses five normalization-scale multipliers, the effect of retaining 97 registered labels instead of 95 unique configurations, lineage comparisons covering 953 profiles in 21 groups, and variability across ten DRPreter checkpoints. It also distinguishes entropy calculated after median index aggregation from the median of checkpoint-wise entropies. At the reference scales, median normalized entropy was 0.9346 for PaccMann and 0.9528 for the DRPreter median consensus . These aggregate differences coexisted with weak cross-model agreement in cell-line entropy rankings ( Spearman ρ = −0.0788 ) and only six shared profiles among the 97 most concentrated profiles identified by each model. Normalization and checkpoint aggregation affected concentration summaries and rankings, demonstrating that entropy requires an explicitly specified computational representation. The accompanying computational materials document the six-stage workflow through analysis scripts, frozen input resources, configuration and profile mappings, normalization policies, numerical tables and arrays, saved bootstrap draws, and provenance and validation records. A README explains the directory structure, principal outputs, reproduction workflow, and interpretation limits. Resources inherited from ATLAS Working Papers 06–08 retain their upstream licensing and attribution requirements. The final technical audit recorded 2,363 passed checks and no failed checks , reviewing 206 distinct files in the selected analysis chain. This audit supports technical consistency and traceability within the implemented checks; it does not constitute independent experimental or clinical validation. The results establish entropy as a conditional descriptor of computational profile concentration . They do not establish therapeutic efficacy, measured mixture responses, biological mechanisms, or malignant-versus-normal selectivity. The materials support transparent inspection, reanalysis, and further methodological evaluation of the ATLAS framework.
title: Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation

summary: Resilience in psychology and public health is usually assessed through recovery or maintained functioning, outcomes that do not reveal whether desirable states have become self-maintaining or still depend on external support. Drawing on coerced-regime theory from social-ecological systems research, we develop aided mental health resilience (AMHR), a framework for desirable mental health states established or maintained through external inputs of resources, organisation, political capital and trust. We make three contributions. First, we frame population mental health as a dimension of social-ecological system states and define the external maintenance subsidy required to sustain desirable conditions. Second, using a dialectical reading of regime change, we distinguish reversion, permanent subsidy and sublation, in which the function initially supplied by aid becomes reproduced through reorganised capacities, practices or institutions. Displacement of harm is treated as a cross-cutting failure mode. Four cases illustrate these dynamics and their limits. Third, drawing on strange loop ethics, we argue that paradoxical outcomes should trigger review not only of intervention instruments but also of the premises that define desirable states and authorise intervention. We outline disconfirmation conditions and a research agenda centred on longitudinal evaluation, subsidy accounting, displacement monitoring and recursive premise review.

summary: This paper establishes the mathematical and methodological foundations of the GCT-STL research program on the P versus NP problem, using the decision Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP_dec) as a canonical NP-complete representative and its polynomial reduction to 3-SAT with an exact materialized 3-CNF artifact. The framework organizes nine provenance-controlled descriptors (D1–D9) across three computational-information domains: semantic/geometric (S), temporal/computational (T), and logical/syntactic (L). These descriptors form the canonical raw Valiant–González tensorial signature (R0), supported by explicit SourceMap and Provenance Bundle contracts and three foundational entropy results. Paper I-A situates R0 within a branched four-representation architecture: R1 is a componentwise logarithmic scale complement, R2 is the canonical entropic/information representation, and R3 is the exact-envelope normalized representation. The Full STL Tensorial Coupling Principle remains an open and falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established obstruction theorem. The logical-complexity architecture distinguishes the internal classes P_STL and NP_STL and the conditional F1–F4 route toward the classical P versus NP problem. F1 and F2 remain open mathematical obligations. Empirical robustness, tensorial diagnostics, and candidate obstructions do not constitute universal computational lower bounds. Accordingly, Paper I-A does not prove P ≠ NP. It establishes the representational, logical, methodological, and formal-certification foundations for subsequent research within the GCT-STL program.

summary: This deliverable presents practical and adaptable protocols for scaling citizen science initiatives, developed through a user-centred design (UCD) process informed by co-design and validation workshops, interviews with citizen science experts, researchers, and practitioners, and a literature review. Rather than proposing a single, one-size-fits-all model, the protocols are organised around five CROPS scaling strategies: institutional scaling (driving policy and governance change), expansion and replication scaling (extending reach and participation), transformative change scaling (influencing values, attitudes, and behaviours), downscaling (reducing scope while maintaining impact), and combined scaling (pursuing multiple pathways simultaneously). These strategies reflect a multidimensional understanding of scaling that extends beyond geographic or numerical growth. To support projects in deciding whether and how to scale, the deliverable also highlights the CROPS Scalability Framework, a diagnostic tool built around nine constructs relating to the intrinsic characteristics of a project, the scaling process itself, and the target context. This is complemented by a six-step Strategic Scaling Decision process that helps projects determine whether scaling is not only feasible but strategically appropriate. In this deliverable, the protocols are first presented through concise, visually structured informative briefs, providing accessible overviews of guidance for each scaling strategy. These are followed by more detailed guidance, including summary tables of protocols, pillars, and objectives, illustrative examples, and practical dos and don'ts. Additional resources, tools, and guidelines support implementation. The protocols are designed to be adopted in full or in part, depending on a project's context, resources, and objectives, and are intended to remain useful not only for scaling but also for the design of new citizen science initiatives from the outset. Ethical considerations, including privacy, inclusivity, fairness, and transparency, are treated as a cross-cutting requirement throughout. The primary audience for the protocols is the citizen science practitioner community, represented through personas developed as part of the UCD process, alongside researchers, policymakers, EU and international organisation representatives, and other stakeholders engaged in scaling citizen science, particularly in relation to the Horizon Europe EU Missions. The CROPS protocols are intended as an evolving, non-prescriptive resource rather than a definitive model for scaling. Their value lies in providing a structured basis for reflection, planning, and decision-making, while recognising that successful scaling also depends on a broader enabling ecosystem of institutional readiness, sustainable funding, and supportive technical and policy infrastructure. The methodology underpinning protocol development, including persona creation and the wider UCD process, is described in detail in Section 7 and the accompanying annexes.

The methodology underpinning protocol development, including persona creation and the wider UCD process, is described in detail in Section 7 and the accompanying annexes.

summary: tc-cwi is a lightweight Python toolbox for Environmental and Operational Condition (EoC) compensation in ultrasonic Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) using Coda Wave Interferometry (CWI) and the Time-Stretching method . Developed within the  USES2 project (Work Package 3, Deliverable D3.3), it estimates the relative velocity stretch factor ( eps ) and/or time shift ( dt ) that best realign a measured ultrasonic signal with a baseline reference (fixed or moving-average) and reports the remaining decorrelation. The package provides both clean Python functions ( stretch , shift , find_optimum , MovingAverageReference ) and a 1:1 MATLAB-compatible dispatch interface ( tc_cwi("findeps", ...) ). PyPI Package: https://pypi.org/project/tc-cwi/ ( pip install tc-cwi ) Source Repository (GitHub): https://github.com/aderaema/tc-cwi Workflows (EWSHM 2026): https://github.com/Zensor-BE/tc-cwi-workflows GitLab Entry Point: https://gitlab.com/uses2project/wp3/tc-cwi

summary: This record is the reference implementation released with COES-CD, built from the method and evaluation protocol described in the accompanying manuscript (Sections 5-6 and Appendices B/D). It is a reconstruction, not the original experiment code; the original code was developed iteratively and was not maintained as a release-ready artifact. It depended on internal paths and an undocumented environment and was not kept in a state that could be independently verified. This record therefore provides a clean implementation that follows the manuscript and the appendix, with fixed seeds, documented configurations, and a uniform evaluation pipeline. Every measured number reported in this record was produced by running the code shipped here; values transcribed from the manuscript are marked as the manuscript's. The package contains the model source (coes_cd/), the experiment configurations (configs/), a deterministic synthetic data generator with fixed seeds (data_generation/, scripts/generate_data.py), acquisition scripts for the baselines actually obtained, and the scripts that rebuild the 10 tables and the 6 figures that README's asset table assigns a generation script to. NOTEARS and DAGMA are fetched at pinned commits by the shipped scripts; CSL-HNTS, DyCAST, Meta-D2AG and SPACETIME are not integrated, for the reasons given in Section 0 of docs/BASELINES.md. The pipeline is a six-step chain: generate the datasets, train stage 1, run the stage-2 stability readout, evaluate both stages into results/raw_results.csv, collect the training costs, and rebuild the assets. README's Quick start gives the exact commands, and its asset table lists the seeds and the measured per-run costs. Fixed hyperparameters, the seeds and the dataset count for each setting are listed in docs/HYPERPARAMETERS.md; the per-dataset checksums are stored in the manifests under data/synthetic/. No result files are shipped: the package has no results/ directory. Every asset whose README asset-table row names a generation script is produced by that script from the chain above; assets marked 'no generator in this release' are not, and any stored row whose source lies outside this release is identified in that table's note. NetSim is a public benchmark and is not redistributed; data/prepare_netsim.py records its public identity and implements the preprocessing, but the manuscript's N = 18 / K = 3 subset is not identified, so it is not re-run. Satellite telemetry is access-restricted and is not redistributed; the package ships the preprocessing procedure, the variable and regime schema, and a synthetic demo that exercises the pipeline end to end without the restricted input. Tables and figures that README's asset table does not list are not generated by this release. External baseline code is cloned at install time and is not redistributed with this record. Every measured cell in the rebuilt assets is the output of the code shipped here, and where an asset also carries a value transcribed from the manuscript, that value appears in a column marked as such. The measurement path of each cell (forward chain, stage-2 readout, gate, dataset coverage) and the protocol used for it are documented in README and in the table notes generated by the code. How the released runs compare with the submitted experiments: the released tables are measured at 800 epochs on a consumer GPU with one training seed per dataset and 10 datasets per setting, while the submitted tables were measured at 2000 epochs on an RTX 3090 with five training seeds and 20 datasets per setting. Where a table carries a manuscript column, it is marked as such, and each comparison can be read directly off the table. The stage-2 readout rows of Table 4 stay within 10% of the manuscript's F1 across K; the neural forward chain is reported separately in the asset table and is not the source of the reported Table 4 rows. Table 5 and Table 6 are rebuilt and compared cell by cell in the table notes. A diagnostic rerun o

summary: GPU-native Julia framework for CT and photon-counting CT simulation, reconstruction, and quantitative spectral imaging. Provides distance-driven forward projection (with Siddon ray tracing as an alternative), polychromatic Beer-Lambert physics with vendor-realistic detector response (MC-derived LUTs for GE Gemstone scintillator and Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha CdTe), FDK, helical WFBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, sinogram and image-domain beam-hardening correction, projection-domain dual-kVp and PCCT material decomposition (K-channel profile likelihood, Cong 2022), spectral denoising, and virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI + Grant 2014 Mono+) — all dispatching transparently across CPU, Metal, CUDA, and ROCm via AcceleratedKernels.jl.

summary: This record contains the experimental datasets supporting the technical Key Performance Indicator (KPI) evaluation of the DETO-XR (Dynamic Edge Tracking Optimization for XR) use case developed within the 6G-PATH (6G Pilots and Trials Through Europe) project, Open Call 2. DETO-XR investigates a distributed edge–cloud architecture combining environment sensing, Multiple Object Tracking (MOT), GPU-accelerated cloud processing, and remote rendering for interactive Mixed Reality applications. The proposed MOT-as-a-Service (MOTaaS) concept enables multiple independent tracking sessions to access shared cloud processing resources. The dataset provides raw measurement traces, processed results, experimental configurations, and verification scripts covering five technical KPIs: Dataset Description KPI-1: Frame Drop Streaks HoloLens 2 client-side video-selection telemetry collected during 5G experiments, including a selected stable operating interval and a supplementary retrospective 30 Hz frame-availability analysis. KPI-2: Jitter Buffer and Frame Availability Evaluation of video-frame availability with a configured 30 ms jitter buffer, including per-stream frame-selection events, timestamped records, and full measurement-stage context. KPI-3: Pose Staleness Comparative experiments evaluating a tracking pose-staleness proxy using different cloud-based object-detection configurations. KPI-4: GPU Duty-Cycle Reduction GPU utilization measurements comparing continuous object detection with periodic detection refresh, supporting the evaluation of computational resource efficiency. KPI-5: Concurrent MOT Sessions Application traces and GPU monitoring data collected during experiments with one, two, and three concurrent MOT sessions sharing GPU-backed cloud services. The experiments were conducted between 18 October and 4 November 2026 , including measurements associated with the 6G-INCOGNICO experimentation environment in Greece. Dataset Organization Each KPI is documented in a dedicated directory containing the relevant raw and processed measurement data. The archive also includes: Detailed README files explaining the experimental setup, measurement methodology, and interpretation of results. A data dictionary describing measurement fields, timestamps, and derived metrics. Source provenance information and mappings between reported KPI results and supporting evidence. SHA-256 checksums and Python verification scripts supporting data integrity and reproducibility. Measurement Scope The KPI-1/KPI-2 dataset includes a retrospectively selected 5G operating interval evaluated using a 30 Hz frame-availability model, together with the original 13-minute measurement-stage records. The alternative frame-availability metric is distinct from native 60 Hz display-frame-loss measurements and does not establish full-run compliance with the original KPI targets. Similarly, KPI-3 uses a model-based pose-staleness proxy rather than direct HoloLens display measurements, while KPI-4 and KPI-5 evaluate specific GPU utilization and concurrency configurations. The datasets are intended to support reproducible performance evaluation, independent analysis, and further research into distributed object tracking, cloud-assisted XR applications, and efficient GPU resource utilization. Funding The 6G-PATH project has received funding from the Smart Networks and Services Joint Undertaking (SNS JU) under the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under Grant Agreement No. 101139172 . This dataset reflects only the authors' views. The European Commission is not responsible for any use that may be made of the information it contains.

summary: Replication package for a staged empirical study of whether a dependency upgrade changes the conclusions of machine-learning comparisons. Six scikit-learn classifiers (LR, SVC, kNN, RF, GB, HGB) were evaluated on all 63 eligible OpenML-CC18 tasks with frozen splits (6 × 5-fold cross-validation), across two real upgrades: 0.21.3 → 0.22.2.post1 (changed defaults) and 1.8.0 → 1.9.1 (negative control). The package contains: the frozen study protocol (v2.2.5) and pre-run amendment (v2.2.6), with SHA-256 manifests; the frozen plan (folds and seeds), environment lock files and provenance records for each scikit-learn release; the frozen changelog-coding frame used for blinding; all fold-level results (balanced accuracy and prediction hashes) and analysis reports; post-review analyses G0–G3 with all raw outputs: restoration of historical defaults, boosting interventions, bootstrap and winner-margin sensitivity, and the corrected six-estimator explicit map E2; scripts that verify every stored file and recompute every number and figure in the paper. Quick check, with no experiments required: python3 paper/verify_results.py and python3 postreview/verify_postreview.py --zip VersionShift_replication.zip . The attached VersionShift_replication.zip (SHA-256 5eb716b64c21ded6f979b0b1610bb68aee46ad2f24889a0d3b133bd430c6ff7d) is the frozen original-study archive that the post-review kits require. The OpenML-CC18 datasets are not redistributed. The scripts rebuild them from OpenML and check them against the frozen hashes.

summary: This version combines two key updates. Significant reduction in model runtime by improving code efficiency. summary: Research code accompanying the paper Data-proximal null-space networks for inverse problems by Jürgen Frikel, Simon Göppel and Markus Haltmeier. Data-proximal networks extend null-space networks by learned corrections whose additional change of the predicted data is explicitly controlled. The repository contains the implementation of the synthetic limited-angle computed tomography study: ellipse phantom generation, the discrete Radon operator and the numerical row-space projection, Tikhonov and total-variation initializations, the residual (RES), null-space (NSN) and data-proximal (DP1, DP2) networks, Float64 training with checkpointing, the frozen evaluator, the public inference entry point for published checkpoints, and the compact scientific export from which the paper tables and figures are regenerated with scripts/reproduce_paper.py . Trained weights, the row-space basis, the operator and the sample data are not part of this record; they are intended for separate data records. summary: Version 5: Documentation corrections only; code, data, and results are unchanged from v4. Version 4  adds the analyses of the second revision: time-ordered and cross-project evaluation, structured label noise, a drop-one process-feature ablation, a Random Forest hyperparameter check, and label-provenance analyses (results/r2_experiments/), with the per-row revision metadata and commit dates they need. All Java runners now read the datasets from a configurable data directory (JML_DATA_DIR). Everything in v3 is otherwise unchanged; the audit labels are the same as in v3. Version 3. Supersedes version 2 (distributed as package v1.1) and version 1 (package v1.0). Prepared for the revised submission to Science of Computer Programming. Figures from earlier versions should not be cited. Manual validation re-run with a two-rater protocol. Estimated commit-level SZZ label precision is now  49.5% (197/398) with inter-rater agreement Cohen's κ = 0.799 , replacing the 29.2% reported in versions 1 and 2, which came from a single-rater audit with no documented agreement statistic. Per-project precision: Kafka 57.1%, Gson 48.5%, Commons-IO 42.9%. Both raters' blind passes, the disagreement-resolution record for the 10 conflicting cases, and a per-instance false-positive taxonomy of all 201 false positives are included. The labelling question changed, so labels are not directly comparable across versions. The is_valid_fix column has been renamed is_true_bic . The earlier audit recorded whether a candidate was itself a valid fix; the current audit records whether the candidate introduced the defect that its traced fix later repaired. These are different questions, and the resulting labels cannot be compared row by row with earlier versions. A central claim has been withdrawn. Earlier versions of the paper argued that feature-engineering quality has a stronger influence on predictive performance than label purity. A label-noise sensitivity experiment, included here, does not support that claim: adding 20 percentage points of label noise erases more MCC than the entire static-to-hybrid feature-engineering gain, in every project. The claim has been removed from the manuscript and replaced with the measured finding that process features hold a consistent advantage over static features at the observed noise level, while performance remains sensitive to further label degradation. Ablation and significance results re-derived from logged runs. All values now come from 270 independently seeded 10-fold cross-validation runs (30 seeds × 3 projects × 3 feature sets), with per-seed raw results, runner scripts and exact seeds included. Statistical testing is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test paired by seed with Cliff's delta and Holm-Bonferroni correction over nine comparisons per metric. summary: This record accompanies Working Paper No. 9 of the Independent FAIR Evaluation Series of the ATLAS Framework , entitled Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation . The study examines the concentration of computational AACF susceptibility profiles derived from frozen PaccMann and DRPreter predictions for 95 unique registered configurations across 970 matched cancer cell-line profiles . Scores are transformed into normalized weights using a softmax transformation favouring lower AACF indices, with fixed model-specific reference scales. Profile characterization includes Shannon entropy, normalized entropy, effective configuration counts, and leading configuration weights. The evaluation addresses five normalization-scale multipliers, the effect of retaining 97 registered labels instead of 95 unique configurations, lineage comparisons covering 953 profiles in 21 groups, and variability across ten DRPreter checkpoints. It also distinguishes entropy calculated after median index aggregation from the median of checkpoint-wise entropies. At the reference scales, median normalized entropy was 0.9346 for PaccMann and 0.9528 for the DRPreter median consensus . These aggregate differences coexisted with weak cross-model agreement in cell-line entropy rankings ( Spearman ρ = −0.0788 ) and only six shared profiles among the 97 most concentrated profiles identified by each model. Normalization and checkpoint aggregation affected concentration summaries and rankings, demonstrating that entropy requires an explicitly specified computational representation. The accompanying computational materials document the six-stage workflow through analysis scripts, frozen input resources, configuration and profile mappings, normalization policies, numerical tables and arrays, saved bootstrap draws, and provenance and validation records. A README explains the directory structure, principal outputs, reproduction workflow, and interpretation limits. Resources inherited from ATLAS Working Papers 06–08 retain their upstream licensing and attribution requirements. The final technical audit recorded 2,363 passed checks and no failed checks , reviewing 206 distinct files in the selected analysis chain. This audit supports technical consistency and traceability within the implemented checks; it does not constitute independent experimental or clinical validation. The results establish entropy as a conditional descriptor of computational profile concentration . They do not establish therapeutic efficacy, measured mixture responses, biological mechanisms, or malignant-versus-normal selectivity. The materials support transparent inspection, reanalysis, and further methodological evaluation of the ATLAS framework.
title: Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation

summary: This paper establishes the mathematical and methodological foundations of the GCT-STL research program on the P versus NP problem, using the decision Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP_dec) as a canonical NP-complete representative and its polynomial reduction to 3-SAT with an exact materialized 3-CNF artifact. The framework organizes nine provenance-controlled descriptors (D1–D9) across three computational-information domains: semantic/geometric (S), temporal/computational (T), and logical/syntactic (L). These descriptors form the canonical raw Valiant–González tensorial signature (R0), supported by explicit SourceMap and Provenance Bundle contracts and three foundational entropy results. Paper I-A situates R0 within a branched four-representation architecture: R1 is a componentwise logarithmic scale complement, R2 is the canonical entropic/information representation, and R3 is the exact-envelope normalized representation. The Full STL Tensorial Coupling Principle remains an open and falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established obstruction theorem. The logical-complexity architecture distinguishes the internal classes P_STL and NP_STL and the conditional F1–F4 route toward the classical P versus NP problem. F1 and F2 remain open mathematical obligations. Empirical robustness, tensorial diagnostics, and candidate obstructions do not constitute universal computational lower bounds. Accordingly, Paper I-A does not prove P ≠ NP. It establishes the representational, logical, methodological, and formal-certification foundations for subsequent research within the GCT-STL program.
title: Three-Dimensional Entropic Domains for TSP Complexity via 3-SAT: Foundations of the GCT-STL Research Program on P versus NP

summary: This record contains the experimental datasets supporting the technical Key Performance Indicator (KPI) evaluation of the DETO-XR (Dynamic Edge Tracking Optimization for XR) use case developed within the 6G-PATH (6G Pilots and Trials Through Europe) project, Open Call 2. DETO-XR investigates a distributed edge–cloud architecture combining environment sensing, Multiple Object Tracking (MOT), GPU-accelerated cloud processing, and remote rendering for interactive Mixed Reality applications. The proposed MOT-as-a-Service (MOTaaS) concept enables multiple independent tracking sessions to access shared cloud processing resources. The dataset provides raw measurement traces, processed results, experimental configurations, and verification scripts covering five technical KPIs: Dataset Description KPI-1: Frame Drop Streaks HoloLens 2 client-side video-selection telemetry collected during 5G experiments, including a selected stable operating interval and a supplementary retrospective 30 Hz frame-availability analysis. KPI-2: Jitter Buffer and Frame Availability Evaluation of video-frame availability with a configured 30 ms jitter buffer, including per-stream frame-selection events, timestamped records, and full measurement-stage context. KPI-3: Pose Staleness Comparative experiments evaluating a tracking pose-staleness proxy using different cloud-based object-detection configurations. KPI-4: GPU Duty-Cycle Reduction GPU utilization measurements comparing continuous object detection with periodic detection refresh, supporting the evaluation of computational resource efficiency. KPI-5: Concurrent MOT Sessions Application traces and GPU monitoring data collected during experiments with one, two, and three concurrent MOT sessions sharing GPU-backed cloud services. The experiments were conducted between 18 October and 4 November 2026 , including measurements associated with the 6G-INCOGNICO experimentation environment in Greece. Dataset Organization Each KPI is documented in a dedicated directory containing the relevant raw and processed measurement data. The archive also includes: Detailed README files explaining the experimental setup, measurement methodology, and interpretation of results. A data dictionary describing measurement fields, timestamps, and derived metrics. Source provenance information and mappings between reported KPI results and supporting evidence. SHA-256 checksums and Python verification scripts supporting data integrity and reproducibility. Measurement Scope The KPI-1/KPI-2 dataset includes a retrospectively selected 5G operating interval evaluated using a 30 Hz frame-availability model, together with the original 13-minute measurement-stage records. The alternative frame-availability metric is distinct from native 60 Hz display-frame-loss measurements and does not establish full-run compliance with the original KPI targets. Similarly, KPI-3 uses a model-based pose-staleness proxy rather than direct HoloLens display measurements, while KPI-4 and KPI-5 evaluate specific GPU utilization and concurrency configurations. The datasets are intended to support reproducible performance evaluation, independent analysis, and further research into distributed object tracking, cloud-assisted XR applications, and efficient GPU resource utilization. Funding The 6G-PATH project has received funding from the Smart Networks and Services Joint Undertaking (SNS JU) under the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under Grant Agreement No. 101139172 . This dataset reflects only the authors' views. The European Commission is not responsible for any use that may be made of the information it contains.
title: 6G-PATH OC2 [DETO-XR]: Technical KPI Evaluation Datasets

summary: This paper develops a scale-spanning account of latent vibration and frequency manifestation within Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM). It examines the relationship between complete latent vibration, the negative and positive displacement domains around the manifestable origin, and the eligibility of positive displacement for progression towards physical manifestation. The development distinguishes the complete latent-vibration interval from the directed displacement associated with manifestation, establishing the proposed Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck threshold relationships in terms of the Planck length. The analysis further develops phase-dependent frequency relations below the Planck threshold and considers the proposed frequency increments associated with the Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck domains. It then presents a state-dependent sequence of energy–frequency transformations across latent, phase, and manifested states, including the reverse progression associated with dissolution. Within this framework, frequency and displacement are treated as related physical parameters whose coefficients depend on the corresponding phase domain. The paper also distinguishes the phase-state potential-energy mass representation from the mass contribution associated with the manifested domain. It formulates the effective-mass relationship and separates this ECM representation from the distinct dark-energy-related mass representation. Taken together, these developments present an integrated theoretical description of latent vibration, manifestation eligibility, threshold transitions, energy–frequency relations, and mass-state transformations within the proposed ECM framework.
title: Complete Latent Vibration and Frequency Manifestation Eligibility in Extended Classical Mechanics
