summary: Nicomachean Algorethics: Principles, Limits and Verification of Human and Artificial Transformative Decision-Making This monograph develops a philosophical and formal framework for examining the legitimacy, responsibility and verifiability of transformative decisions made by human agents, institutions and artificial systems. Drawing on Aristotelian practical philosophy, contemporary ethics, epistemology, decision theory and the challenges of artificial intelligence governance, Nicomachean Algorethics addresses a fundamental question: under what conditions may an agent legitimately make decisions that transform the lives, opportunities and futures of others? The proposed framework is organised around twelve normative laws and a Recognition Matrix designed to distinguish technical possibility, epistemic justification, normative admissibility and legitimate authority. Rather than attempting to calculate or optimise the Good, the framework investigates the conditions under which decisions may be justified, contested, corrected or withheld. Particular attention is given to uncertainty, the limitations of representation, delegated authority, corrigibility, reversibility, capability preservation, the distribution of responsibility, value pluralism and the prevention of harm. The work introduces formal definitions, mathematical formulations, verification contracts and operational procedures intended to make normative assumptions and decision-making constraints explicit. Its methodological approach distinguishes conceptual arguments, formal propositions, computational verification, illustrative examples and empirical claims, without treating these different forms of evidence as interchangeable. The monograph also examines recognition as a philosophical and practical problem, investigating the relationship between distinction, otherness, interpretation and responsibility in human and artificial decision-making. Through theoretical analysis and selected case studies, it explores how artificial systems and institutions may improve not only their decisions but also their capacity to identify, explain and correct errors. The work comprises twenty-three chapters, an epilogue and five technical appendices addressing verification contracts, retrospective analysis, comparative protocols, canonical terminology and formal mechanisation. Nicomachean Algorethics is intended as a contribution to moral philosophy, philosophy of technology, artificial intelligence ethics and the interdisciplinary study of responsible decision-making. Its central thesis is that responsibility requires more than selecting among available alternatives: it requires recognising who may be affected, what authority may legitimately be exercised and which possibilities must remain open to others and to future generations.

Drawing on Aristotelian practical philosophy, contemporary ethics, epistemology, decision theory and the challenges of artificial intelligence governance, Nicomachean Algorethics addresses a fundamental question: under what conditions may an agent legitimately make decisions that transform the lives, opportunities and futures of others? The proposed framework is organised around twelve normative laws and a Recognition Matrix designed to distinguish technical possibility, epistemic justification, normative admissibility and legitimate authority. Rather than attempting to calculate or optimise the Good, the framework investigates the conditions under which decisions may be justified, contested, corrected or withheld. Particular attention is given to uncertainty, the limitations of representation, delegated authority, corrigibility, reversibility, capability preservation, the distribution of responsibility, value pluralism and the prevention of harm. The work introduces formal definitions, mathematical formulations, verification contracts and operational procedures intended to make normative assumptions and decision-making constraints explicit. Its methodological approach distinguishes conceptual arguments, formal propositions, computational verification, illustrative examples and empirical claims, without treating these different forms of evidence as interchangeable. The monograph also examines recognition as a philosophical and practical problem, investigating the relationship between distinction, otherness, interpretation and responsibility in human and artificial decision-making. Through theoretical analysis and selected case studies, it explores how artificial systems and institutions may improve not only their decisions but also their capacity to identify, explain and correct errors. The work comprises twenty-three chapters, an epilogue and five technical appendices addressing verification contracts, retrospective analysis, comparative protocols, canonical terminology and formal mechanisation. Nicomachean Algorethics is intended as a contribution to moral philosophy, philosophy of technology, artificial intelligence ethics and the interdisciplinary study of responsible decision-making. Its central thesis is that responsibility requires more than selecting among available alternatives: it requires recognising who may be affected, what authority may legitimately be exercised and which possibilities must remain open to others and to future generations.

summary: In the article, the formation of the theory of territorial urban systems and urban agglomerations is scientifically and methodologically analyzed. Historical-comparative, structural-structural analysis and content-analysis methods were used. As a result, a three-stage periodization of theory evolution, a comparative classification of four methods of limiting agglomeration and a five-stage algorithm of their complex application are proposed. The initial approval in the case of Andijan agglomeration showed the possibility of practical application of the approach. The conclusions serve as a methodological basis for the quantitative and spatial study of agglomerations of the Fergana Valley.

summary: Reproducibility data and executable source for Accuracy, Storage, and Update Cost in Reference-Assisted Sensor Calibration , by Oleksandr Kuznetsov. Version 1.1.0 adds the completed seven-model common-fixture campaign: two validated sessions each on Mega2560, ESP32-C3 and ESP32-S3, 480 timing records and 42 numerical-accuracy checks. It preserves the three original acquisition ZIPs, firmware images, raw serial logs, source/image hashes and an executable audit. All models use one frozen synthetic distorted-NTC fixture; no coefficients, seeds or hyperparameters were retuned. The captured S3 executable uses native float32 instructions. The 4.2% polynomial-Horner timing advantage over LUT32 is specific to the recorded S3 build; optimization-level and code-layout robustness were not measured. The original 1.0.0 evidence archive is retained unchanged. It contains the matched synthetic calibration/adaptation records, cross-validation and sensitivity analyses, historical MCU fixtures and paired refinements using 32-pair block least squares and decaying NLMS. Earlier reanalysis reused separate development and confirmation seeds; it is not a new untouched holdout. Historical fixtures remain separate from the V2 frontier. This is an implementation and resource-cost study. Accuracy and drift are controlled synthetic quantities. Physical boards establish execution time and numerical agreement. No physical NTC/LDR calibration, S3 update timing, measured energy, WCET, peak stack or between-board uncertainty is claimed. The author photograph illustrates the development boards, not a sensor-calibration setup. Immutable V2 audit and results: commit df19065 . Each component archive supplies exact code provenance and SHA-256 manifests. The cleaned English documentation preserves all numerical evidence and the frozen benchmark source set. Author-created data and research documentation: CC BY 4.0. Software retains its included MIT license; third-party components retain their own terms. This is a dataset/software evidence release, not an accepted journal publication.

summary: Visual geo-localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in GNSS-denied environments remains challenging due to the lack of datasets with trajectory continuity, broad scene and geographic coverage, multimodal UAV imagery, wide altitude and geometric variation, and sufficient scale. Here we present UAV-VisLoc, a dataset for UAV geo-localization through image retrieval between UAV imagery and geo-referenced satellite tiles. UAV-VisLoc contains 14,998 UAV images organized into 30 flight trajectories, spanning six continents and seven scene types. The dataset preserves contiguous observations along each trajectory, enabling trajectory-level studies under realistic sequential flight conditions. It includes RGB and Infrared UAV imagery and covers altitudes from 160 to 2,500 m. The dataset comprises 21 real UAV flights collected across multiple provinces in China and 9 synthetic flights built from OpenAerialMap imagery for regions outside China. The dataset also provides image-level flight metadata and more than 120,000 geo-referenced satellite tiles. Baseline retrieval experiments and accompanying scripts are provided to validate data organization, ground-truth annotations, and benchmark usability under diverse real-world conditions.

summary: This paper examines the effectiveness of Uzbekistan's tax reforms in reducing the shadow economy. Drawing on macroeconomic indicators, firm-level data, and econometric estimates, the analysis reports model-based shadow-economy estimates of approximately 38.9–39.6% of GDP for 2025, alongside reductions in statutory tax rates. The reported average firm-level tax burden was 27.3%, compared with a macroeconomic indicator of 18.3%. Econometric findings suggest a conditional tax-burden benchmark of 19–20% of GDP. The study concludes that sustainable formalization may be supported by tax-rate optimization, equitable taxation, simplified compliance procedures, improved VAT administration, and effective institutional enforcement. UZ Mazkur tezisda O'zbekistonning yashirin iqtisodiyotni qisqartirishga qaratilgan soliq islohotlari samaradorligi o'rganilgan. Makroiqtisodiy ko'rsatkichlar, korxonalar darajasidagi ma'lumotlar va ekonometrik baholash natijalariga asoslanib, 2025-yilda yashirin iqtisodiyotning yalpi ichki mahsulotdagi ulushi modellar bo'yicha taxminan 38,9–39,6% darajasida baholangani, shu bilan birga qonunchilikda belgilangan soliq stavkalari pasaytirilgani qayd etilgan. Korxonalar darajasida o'rtacha soliq yuki 27,3% ni, makroiqtisodiy ko'rsatkich esa 18,3% ni tashkil etgani ko'rsatilgan. Ekonometrik natijalar soliq yukining YIMga nisbatan 19–20% darajasini shartli mo'ljal sifatida belgilash mumkinligini ko'rsatadi. Tadqiqotda iqtisodiy faoliyatni barqaror rasmiylashtirishga soliq stavkalarini optimallashtirish, adolatli soliqqa tortish, soliq majburiyatlarini bajarish tartib-taomillarini soddalashtirish, qo'shilgan qiymat solig'i ma'murchiligini takomillashtirish va institutsional nazorat samaradorligini oshirish orqali ko'maklashish mumkinligi xulosa qilingan.

Drawing on macroeconomic indicators, firm-level data, and econometric estimates, the analysis reports model-based shadow-economy estimates of approximately 38.9–39.6% of GDP for 2025, alongside reductions in statutory tax rates. The reported average firm-level tax burden was 27.3%, compared with a macroeconomic indicator of 18.3%. Econometric findings suggest a conditional tax-burden benchmark of 19–20% of GDP. The study concludes that sustainable formalization may be supported by tax-rate optimization, equitable taxation, simplified compliance procedures, improved VAT administration, and effective institutional enforcement. UZ Mazkur tezisda O'zbekistonning yashirin iqtisodiyotni qisqartirishga qaratilgan soliq islohotlari samaradorligi o'rganilgan. Makroiqtisodiy ko'rsatkichlar, korxonalar darajasidagi ma'lumotlar va ekonometrik baholash natijalariga asoslanib, 2025-yilda yashirin iqtisodiyotning yalpi ichki mahsulotdagi ulushi modellar bo'yicha taxminan 38,9–39,6% darajasida baholangani, shu bilan birga qonunchilikda belgilangan soliq stavkalari pasaytirilgani qayd etilgan. Korxonalar darajasida o'rtacha soliq yuki 27,3% ni, makroiqtisodiy ko'rsatkich esa 18,3% ni tashkil etgani ko'rsatilgan. Ekonometrik natijalar soliq yukining YIMga nisbatan 19–20% darajasini shartli mo'ljal sifatida belgilash mumkinligini ko'rsatadi. Tadqiqotda iqtisodiy faoliyatni barqaror rasmiylashtirishga soliq stavkalarini optimallashtirish, adolatli soliqqa tortish, soliq majburiyatlarini bajarish tartib-taomillarini soddalashtirish, qo'shilgan qiymat solig'i ma'murchiligini takomillashtirish va institutsional nazorat samaradorligini oshirish orqali ko'maklashish mumkinligi xulosa qilingan.

summary: This Zenodo repository contains the data for the following article: Molecular Signatures of Pressure-Induced Phase Transitions in a Lipid Bilayer (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcb.5c08607) by Yanna Gautier, Guillaume Stirnemann, and Jérôme Hénin   Abstract: Understanding how lipid bilayers respond to pressure is essential for interpreting the coupling between membrane proteins and their native environments. Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics to examine the pressure–temperature behavior of model membranes composed of dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) or its cis-unsaturated analogue Δ9-cis-PC. Within the studied range (288–308 K, 1–2000 bar), DMPC undergoes a liquid–gel transition, while Δ9-cis-PC remains fluid due to unsaturation. The CHARMM36 force field reproduces experimental boundaries with high fidelity: simulated DMPC transitions fall within 5–10 K and 100–300 bar of experimental values, and Δ9-cis-PC exhibits no transition. Hysteresis is modest but most pronounced when starting from low-temperature gels; we propose a split-phase simulation protocol that alleviates the hysteresis problem. We identify the area per lipid, bilayer thickness, and acyl-chain gauche fractions as sensitive phase markers; among these, the gauche fraction provides the most robust signature. Simulations indicate that an interdigitated gel is the equilibrium structure under finite-size conditions, and we propose a novel metric to quantify the extent of this phenomenon. However, at low temperature and high pressure, interdigitation decreases, consistent with the experimental lamellar gel phase. This long-lived interdigitation critically impacts standard order parameters, specifically, area per lipid and membrane thickness. Finally, we discuss in detail how finite-size effects influence phase transition and interdigitation. Overall, these results underscore the accuracy of modern force fields and highlight how simulations are essential to mechanistically complement experimental studies of pressure-sensitive membranes. Keywords : Molecular Dynamics, DMPC, lipid phase transition, high pressure, phase diagram   Detailed content of the repository: The directories contain the all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulation data generated for the different systems and simulation protocols investigated in this study. All atoms are retained in the trajectory files. To limit the overall size of the repository, the trajectories have been subsampled, with one frame retained for every three frames. DRPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic Δ9-cis-PC bilayer, which was used as the control system. Pressure_temperature_ramp : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer subjected to a pressure and temperature ramp. These simulations were performed for comparison with the pressure and temperature jump simulations used as reference. DMPC_Large_Small_Bilayers : Contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for periodic DMPC bilayers with different system sizes, corresponding to twice and half the size of the reference bilayer, respectively. The reference system consists of 57 DMPC molecules per leaflet. DMPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations used to construct the DMPC phase diagram. The directory is organized into subdirectories, with one folder per simulation replicate.  gel_to_fluid_simulations : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations performed to investigate the gel-to-fluid phase transition. The transition, starting from final gel phase configurations obtained from the DMPC simulations, was induced by independently varying either the pressure or the temperature
title: Molecular Signatures of Pressure-Induced Phase Transitions in a Lipid Bilayer

Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics to examine the pressure–temperature behavior of model membranes composed of dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) or its cis-unsaturated analogue Δ9-cis-PC. Within the studied range (288–308 K, 1–2000 bar), DMPC undergoes a liquid–gel transition, while Δ9-cis-PC remains fluid due to unsaturation. The CHARMM36 force field reproduces experimental boundaries with high fidelity: simulated DMPC transitions fall within 5–10 K and 100–300 bar of experimental values, and Δ9-cis-PC exhibits no transition. Hysteresis is modest but most pronounced when starting from low-temperature gels; we propose a split-phase simulation protocol that alleviates the hysteresis problem. We identify the area per lipid, bilayer thickness, and acyl-chain gauche fractions as sensitive phase markers; among these, the gauche fraction provides the most robust signature. Simulations indicate that an interdigitated gel is the equilibrium structure under finite-size conditions, and we propose a novel metric to quantify the extent of this phenomenon. However, at low temperature and high pressure, interdigitation decreases, consistent with the experimental lamellar gel phase. This long-lived interdigitation critically impacts standard order parameters, specifically, area per lipid and membrane thickness. Finally, we discuss in detail how finite-size effects influence phase transition and interdigitation. Overall, these results underscore the accuracy of modern force fields and highlight how simulations are essential to mechanistically complement experimental studies of pressure-sensitive membranes. Keywords : Molecular Dynamics, DMPC, lipid phase transition, high pressure, phase diagram   Detailed content of the repository: The directories contain the all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulation data generated for the different systems and simulation protocols investigated in this study. All atoms are retained in the trajectory files. To limit the overall size of the repository, the trajectories have been subsampled, with one frame retained for every three frames. DRPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic Δ9-cis-PC bilayer, which was used as the control system. Pressure_temperature_ramp : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer subjected to a pressure and temperature ramp. These simulations were performed for comparison with the pressure and temperature jump simulations used as reference. DMPC_Large_Small_Bilayers : Contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for periodic DMPC bilayers with different system sizes, corresponding to twice and half the size of the reference bilayer, respectively. The reference system consists of 57 DMPC molecules per leaflet. DMPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations used to construct the DMPC phase diagram. The directory is organized into subdirectories, with one folder per simulation replicate.  gel_to_fluid_simulations : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations performed to investigate the gel-to-fluid phase transition. The transition, starting from final gel phase configurations obtained from the DMPC simulations, was induced by independently varying either the pressure or the temperature

summary: This archive contains the complete, reproducible analysis pipeline accompanying the article by Bentounsi, Achour and Boufaida, currently under review. Purpose Clinical datasets often present expert labels as if they applied a published guideline. This work proposes an audit method that (i) measures the gap between a guideline-derived reference rule base and the expert labels, (ii) attributes the disagreements to an implicit criterion (Algorithm 1), and (iii) tests whether that criterion can be reconstructed out of sample, using an explicit acceptance criterion: an agreement gain of at least 5 points over the majority baseline, the same rule selected in at least 4 of 5 folds, and a family-wise permutation p-value below 0.01. The method is applied to an Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) dataset (270 records, six labels) and replicated on the UCI Cardiotocography dataset (2,126 segments) against the FIGO 2015 guideline. Contents src/ : Python modules (thresholds and protocol constants, data loading with hash check, generated rule trace, rules–expert gap and Algorithm 1, threshold and interval enumerations with permutation tests, learning control and Shapley attribution, cardiotocography replication, robustness analyses, figures). results/ : every result file used in the manuscript (CSV, TXT, JSON). figures/ : Figures 1–5 (PDF and PNG). tests/ : pytest suite (equivalence of fast and direct enumerations, regression tests on the published tables, checks of the FIGO rule base, and a test that every key figure of the manuscript matches the recomputed results). PROTOCOL.md : analysis protocol, including Amendment 1 for the replication.  PROTOCOL2.sha256 records the hash of Protocol 2. run_all.sh , requirements.txt (pinned versions with hashes, Python 3.13). Data (not redistributed) The input datasets are not included and must be downloaded from their original sources; the code refuses to run on any other version of the files. ABPM: Douibi K, Benabid MM, Settouti N, Chikh MA. Data for: An analysis of Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) . Mendeley Data, V1, 2017. https://doi.org/10.17632/y4dh3b3tfx.1 . File ABPM-dataset.arff , SHA-256 0ea0a53c86bd2564117913fe99dd6699579fc03b23acd118c0b33822db911e07 . Cardiotocography: Campos D, Bernardes J. Cardiotocography . UCI Machine Learning Repository, 2000. https://doi.org/10.24432/C51S4N . File CTG.xls , SHA-256 d6aa62e82625e59f9d5b05bc8fc52af9ea67bdf2a23f1faca8511d5618fcb421 . Reproduction Place both files in data/raw/ , then run: python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt ./run_all.sh The script verifies the dataset hashes, runs all modules, regenerates every result file and figure, and runs the test suite (about twelve minutes on an ordinary laptop). All randomness uses a fixed seed (0); the rule trace is deterministic. Licence Code released under the MIT licence. The datasets remain under the terms set by their authors.
title: Code and results for: Auditing Expert Annotations against Published Guidelines: Measuring, Attributing and Reconstructing Implicit Labelling Criteria in Clinical Datasets

summary: Description This record contains the data, code and source data supporting a Mendelian randomization (MR) study of smoking and obesity traits, with DNA methylation (CpG sites) and gut microbial features (species and pathways) as candidate mediators. Files Processed and formatted GWAS summary statistics (instrumental variables and outcome data) used in the analyses. Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx : sources of the original GWAS summary statistics (also listed in Table S1 of the article). Codes.zip : R code for instrument selection, two-sample MR and sensitivity analyses, mediation analysis, colocalization and the figures, with a README describing each script and the run order, software versions and R session information. Source_data.zip : source data underlying the main and supplementary figures. Fstatistic.zip : F statistics of the instrumental variables in the MR analyses. Data sources The uploaded data are processed and formatted versions of publicly available GWAS summary statistics; the original sources are listed in Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx . Ethical approval and informed consent were obtained by the original GWAS studies. Methods Instrumental variables were selected at P < 5 × 10⁻⁸ for smoking and obesity traits, P < 1 × 10⁻⁵ (effect allele frequency > 0.01) for gut microbial features, and P < 1 × 10⁻⁸ (cis, within 1 Mb) or P < 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ (trans) for methylation quantitative trait loci of CpG sites (GoDMC). Variants were clumped at r² < 0.001 within 10,000 kb windows using PLINK with the 1000 Genomes European reference panel, and instruments with F < 10 were excluded. The multiplicative random-effects inverse-variance weighted method (Wald ratio for single-SNP instruments) was used as the primary MR method. Sensitivity analyses included the fixed-effects inverse-variance weighted method, MR-Egger, weighted median, simple and weighted mode, Cochran’s Q test, the MR-Egger intercept test, MR-PRESSO and the Steiger directionality test. Reverse causation was assessed by MR in the reverse direction. Indirect associations were estimated by two-step MR using the product-of-coefficients method with delta-method standard errors. Colocalization was assessed with coloc (p1 = p2 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, p12 = 1 × 10⁻⁵) within ±1 Mb windows and with HyPrColoc for three traits (prior.1 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, prior.c = 0.02).  Acknowledgements We thank UK Biobank ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ ), GSCAN ( https://genome.psych.umn.edu/index.php/GSCAN ), the GIANT consortium ( https://giant-consortium.web.broadinstitute.org/index.php/GIANT_consortium ), GERA ( https://cg.bsc.es/gera_summary_stats/ ), GoDMC ( http://mqtldb.godmc.org.uk/about ), the Dutch Microbiome Project ( https://dutchmicrobiomeproject.molgeniscloud.org/menu/main/home ), the IEU OpenGWAS project ( https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/ ) and the GWAS Catalog ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/ ) for providing the publicly available genetic data used in this research. We acknowledge the research teams, participants and consortia behind these datasets for their commitment to open science.

summary: Urban design relies on judgments about existing and anticipated needs, while the available evidence ranges from lived experience and historical records to geospatial observation, statistical estimation, and computational simulation. Contemporary developments in geospatial artificial intelligence, agent-based modeling, urban digital twins, and computational search expand the means of inquiry while raising questions about inferential validity and methodological compatibility. This paper develops a question-guided framework for identifying and evaluating candidate urban needs through the reconstruction of spatial, temporal, social, ecological, and infrastructural relations. Two complementary inquiry pathways are distinguished: hypothesis-driven assessment of specified candidate needs and exploratory search for candidates emerging from observed or simulated relational patterns. Both pathways are connected to explicit procedures of evidential appraisal, causal examination where identifiable, participatory scrutiny, and post-intervention evaluation. A provisional formal interface is proposed in which generative–relational (GR) subjects have question-dependent spacetime-supported representations, heterogeneous evidence is linked by category-theoretic constructions, and selected event structures are encoded through algebraic-topological invariants of labeled two-complexes. Evolutionary updates of these representations and spin-foam-inspired cellular initializations are considered as exploratory modeling options, with the physical meaning of quantum-gravity spin foams kept separate from urban research. The framework is intended to guide methodological comparison and further model development; its empirical adequacy requires case-specific operationalization and validation.
title: Identifying and Evaluating Urban Needs Through Relational Reconstruction: A Preliminary Generative and Evolutionary Formal Model in an Algebraic Framework

summary: Code accompanying the paper Benchmarking DFT and Machine Learning Potentials for Heat of Formation and Combustion of High-Energy Materials . For a target molecule the script enumerates isodesmic reactions against a curated library of small reference species and ranks them. Bond conservation is encoded as bond signatures (bond order together with the hybridisation and aromaticity of the connected atoms) and solved with a linear programming solver under random cost-vector perturbations, so that many distinct valid schemes are found. A secondary ring-breaking relaxation is applied where strict conservation is impossible for fused ring systems. Candidates are ranked by an IsoScore that balances chemical simplicity, Tanimoto structural similarity to the reference library, and stoichiometric cost. The repository contains the generator, the input file with the twenty high-energy materials of the benchmark set, and a README.
title: Automated isodesmic reaction generator for high-energy materials

summary: This record is the reference implementation released with COES-CD, built from the method and evaluation protocol described in the accompanying manuscript (Sections 5-6 and Appendices B/D). It is a clean implementation that follows the manuscript and the appendix, with fixed seeds, documented configurations and a uniform evaluation pipeline, and every measured number reported in this record was produced by running the code shipped here; values transcribed from the manuscript are marked as the manuscript's. The package contains the model source (coes_cd/), the experiment configurations (configs/), a deterministic synthetic data generator with fixed seeds (data_generation/, scripts/generate_data.py), acquisition scripts for the baselines actually obtained, and the scripts that rebuild the 10 tables and the 6 figures that README's asset table assigns a generation script to. NOTEARS and DAGMA are fetched at pinned commits by the shipped scripts; CSL-HNTS, DyCAST, Meta-D2AG and SPACETIME are not integrated, for the reasons given in Section 0 of docs/BASELINES.md. The pipeline is a six-step chain: generate the datasets, train stage 1, run the stage-2 stability readout, evaluate both stages into results/raw_results.csv, collect the training costs, and rebuild the assets. README's Quick start gives the exact commands, and its asset table lists the seeds and the measured per-run costs. Fixed hyperparameters, the seeds and the dataset count for each setting are listed in docs/HYPERPARAMETERS.md; the per-dataset checksums are stored in the manifests under data/synthetic/. No result files are shipped: the package has no results/ directory. Every asset whose README asset-table row names a generation script is produced by that script from the chain above; assets marked 'no generator in this release' are not, and any stored row whose source lies outside this release is identified in that table's note. summary: The KV cache is the bottleneck of long-context LLM inference.  Every modern serving system —  vLLM, SGLang, Mooncake  — is, at its core, a memory manager for the cache that grows one token at a time as the model decodes.  PagedAttention, RadixAttention , and the various  prefix caching  schemes each solve a piece of the problem, but none of them is  lock-free , none of them is  position-keyed , and none of them uses  structural sharing  to handle both beam-search branching and multi-tenant prefix sharing at the same time. This book introduces the  persistent rope  — a single data structure that does all of these things, derived from two pieces of prior art that were never combined before: the  persistent vector  (which gives the rope its branching semantics) and the  Bw-tree  (which gives the rope its lock-free properties). The book is a design document and API reference for the rope, written for engineers who build serving systems, GPU kernels, and lock-free data structures.  It is  not  a benchmark paper,  not  a tutorial, and  not  a complete serving system. The Python reference implementation is  correct but not lock-free ; the  lock-free Rust port is scaffolded in the repository  and described in detail in Chapter 22. The book covers the design (Ch 1–9), the Python reference (Ch 10–11), the verification (Ch 12–14), the public API (Ch 15–19), and the honest framing of what works, what doesn't, and what's left for future work (Ch 20–23). The appendices include a full  glossary, references, and index . Read it in order if you want to understand the design end-to-end; jump to Chapters 10–19 if you want to use the Python reference; read Chapter 22 if you're planning the Rust port.
title: The Persistent Rope: Position-Keyed Indexing for the LLM KV Cache

summary: Resilience in psychology and public health is usually assessed through recovery or maintained functioning, outcomes that do not reveal whether desirable states have become self-maintaining or still depend on external support. Drawing on coerced-regime theory from social-ecological systems research, we develop aided mental health resilience (AMHR), a framework for desirable mental health states established or maintained through external inputs of resources, organisation, political capital and trust. We make three contributions. First, we frame population mental health as a dimension of social-ecological system states and define the external maintenance subsidy required to sustain desirable conditions. Second, using a dialectical reading of regime change, we distinguish reversion, permanent subsidy and sublation, in which the function initially supplied by aid becomes reproduced through reorganised capacities, practices or institutions. Displacement of harm is treated as a cross-cutting failure mode. Four cases illustrate these dynamics and their limits. Third, drawing on strange loop ethics, we argue that paradoxical outcomes should trigger review not only of intervention instruments but also of the premises that define desirable states and authorise intervention. We outline disconfirmation conditions and a research agenda centred on longitudinal evaluation, subsidy accounting, displacement monitoring and recursive premise review.
title: Aided mental health resilience: governing desirable states that cannot sustain themselves

summary: This paper establishes the mathematical and methodological foundations of the GCT-STL research program on the P versus NP problem, using the decision Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP_dec) as a canonical NP-complete representative and its polynomial reduction to 3-SAT with an exact materialized 3-CNF artifact. The framework organizes nine provenance-controlled descriptors (D1–D9) across three computational-information domains: semantic/geometric (S), temporal/computational (T), and logical/syntactic (L). These descriptors form the canonical raw Valiant–González tensorial signature (R0), supported by explicit SourceMap and Provenance Bundle contracts and three foundational entropy results. Paper I-A situates R0 within a branched four-representation architecture: R1 is a componentwise logarithmic scale complement, R2 is the canonical entropic/information representation, and R3 is the exact-envelope normalized representation. The Full STL Tensorial Coupling Principle remains an open and falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established obstruction theorem. The logical-complexity architecture distinguishes the internal classes P_STL and NP_STL and the conditional F1–F4 route toward the classical P versus NP problem. F1 and F2 remain open mathematical obligations. Empirical robustness, tensorial diagnostics, and candidate obstructions do not constitute universal computational lower bounds. Accordingly, Paper I-A does not prove P ≠ NP. It establishes the representational, logical, methodological, and formal-certification foundations for subsequent research within the GCT-STL program.
title: Three-Dimensional Entropic Domains for TSP Complexity via 3-SAT: Foundations of the GCT-STL Research Program on P versus NP

summary: This deliverable presents practical and adaptable protocols for scaling citizen science initiatives, developed through a user-centred design (UCD) process informed by co-design and validation workshops, interviews with citizen science experts, researchers, and practitioners, and a literature review. Rather than proposing a single, one-size-fits-all model, the protocols are organised around five CROPS scaling strategies: institutional scaling (driving policy and governance change), expansion and replication scaling (extending reach and participation), transformative change scaling (influencing values, attitudes, and behaviours), downscaling (reducing scope while maintaining impact), and combined scaling (pursuing multiple pathways simultaneously). These strategies reflect a multidimensional understanding of scaling that extends beyond geographic or numerical growth. To support projects in deciding whether and how to scale, the deliverable also highlights the CROPS Scalability Framework, a diagnostic tool built around nine constructs relating to the intrinsic characteristics of a project, the scaling process itself, and the target context. This is complemented by a six-step Strategic Scaling Decision process that helps projects determine whether scaling is not only feasible but strategically appropriate. In this deliverable, the protocols are first presented through concise, visually structured informative briefs, providing accessible overviews of guidance for each scaling strategy. These are followed by more detailed guidance, including summary tables of protocols, pillars, and objectives, illustrative examples, and practical dos and don'ts. Additional resources, tools, and guidelines support implementation. The protocols are designed to be adopted in full or in part, depending on a project's context, resources, and objectives, and are intended to remain useful not only for scaling but also for the design of new citizen science initiatives from the outset. Ethical considerations, including privacy, inclusivity, fairness, and transparency, are treated as a cross-cutting requirement throughout. The primary audience for the protocols is the citizen science practitioner community, represented through personas developed as part of the UCD process, alongside researchers, policymakers, EU and international organisation representatives, and other stakeholders engaged in scaling citizen science, particularly in relation to the Horizon Europe EU Missions. The CROPS protocols are intended as an evolving, non-prescriptive resource rather than a definitive model for scaling. Their value lies in providing a structured basis for reflection, planning, and decision-making, while recognising that successful scaling also depends on a broader enabling ecosystem of institutional readiness, sustainable funding, and supportive technical and policy infrastructure. The methodology underpinning protocol development, including persona creation and the wider UCD process, is described in detail in Section 7 and the accompanying annexes.
title: D3.1: User-centred Design Protocols for Scaling Citizen Science

summary: tc-cwi is a lightweight Python toolbox for Environmental and Operational Condition (EoC) compensation in ultrasonic Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) using Coda Wave Interferometry (CWI) and the Time-Stretching method . Developed within the  USES2 project (Work Package 3, Deliverable D3.3), it estimates the relative velocity stretch factor ( eps ) and/or time shift ( dt ) that best realign a measured ultrasonic signal with a baseline reference (fixed or moving-average) and reports the remaining decorrelation. summary: This record contains the experimental datasets supporting the technical Key Performance Indicator (KPI) evaluation of the DETO-XR (Dynamic Edge Tracking Optimization for XR) use case developed within the 6G-PATH (6G Pilots and Trials Through Europe) project, Open Call 2. DETO-XR investigates a distributed edge–cloud architecture combining environment sensing, Multiple Object Tracking (MOT), GPU-accelerated cloud processing, and remote rendering for interactive Mixed Reality applications. The proposed MOT-as-a-Service (MOTaaS) concept enables multiple independent tracking sessions to access shared cloud processing resources. The dataset provides raw measurement traces, processed results, experimental configurations, and verification scripts covering five technical KPIs: Dataset Description KPI-1: Frame Drop Streaks HoloLens 2 client-side video-selection telemetry collected during 5G experiments, including a selected stable operating interval and a supplementary retrospective 30 Hz frame-availability analysis. KPI-2: Jitter Buffer and Frame Availability Evaluation of video-frame availability with a configured 30 ms jitter buffer, including per-stream frame-selection events, timestamped records, and full measurement-stage context. KPI-3: Pose Staleness Comparative experiments evaluating a tracking pose-staleness proxy using different cloud-based object-detection configurations. KPI-4: GPU Duty-Cycle Reduction GPU utilization measurements comparing continuous object detection with periodic detection refresh, supporting the evaluation of computational resource efficiency. KPI-5: Concurrent MOT Sessions Application traces and GPU monitoring data collected during experiments with one, two, and three concurrent MOT sessions sharing GPU-backed cloud services. The experiments were conducted between 18 October and 4 November 2026 , including measurements associated with the 6G-INCOGNICO experimentation environment in Greece. Dataset Organization Each KPI is documented in a dedicated directory containing the relevant raw and processed measurement data. The archive also includes: Detailed README files explaining the experimental setup, measurement methodology, and interpretation of results. A data dictionary describing measurement fields, timestamps, and derived metrics. Source provenance information and mappings between reported KPI results and supporting evidence. SHA-256 checksums and Python verification scripts supporting data integrity and reproducibility. Measurement Scope The KPI-1/KPI-2 dataset includes a retrospectively selected 5G operating interval evaluated using a 30 Hz frame-availability model, together with the original 13-minute measurement-stage records. The alternative frame-availability metric is distinct from native 60 Hz display-frame-loss measurements and does not establish full-run compliance with the original KPI targets. Similarly, KPI-3 uses a model-based pose-staleness proxy rather than direct HoloLens display measurements, while KPI-4 and KPI-5 evaluate specific GPU utilization and concurrency configurations. The datasets are intended to support reproducible performance evaluation, independent analysis, and further research into distributed object tracking, cloud-assisted XR applications, and efficient GPU resource utilization. title: 6G-PATH OC2 [DETO-XR]: Technical KPI Evaluation Datasets

summary: Nicomachean Algorethics: Principles, Limits and Verification of Human and Artificial Transformative Decision-Making This monograph develops a philosophical and formal framework for examining the legitimacy, responsibility and verifiability of transformative decisions made by human agents, institutions and artificial systems. Drawing on Aristotelian practical philosophy, contemporary ethics, epistemology, decision theory and the challenges of artificial intelligence governance, Nicomachean Algorethics addresses a fundamental question: under what conditions may an agent legitimately make decisions that transform the lives, opportunities and futures of others? The proposed framework is organised around twelve normative laws and a Recognition Matrix designed to distinguish technical possibility, epistemic justification, normative admissibility and legitimate authority. Rather than attempting to calculate or optimise the Good, the framework investigates the conditions under which decisions may be justified, contested, corrected or withheld. Particular attention is given to uncertainty, the limitations of representation, delegated authority, corrigibility, reversibility, capability preservation, the distribution of responsibility, value pluralism and the prevention of harm. The work introduces formal definitions, mathematical formulations, verification contracts and operational procedures intended to make normative assumptions and decision-making constraints explicit. Its methodological approach distinguishes conceptual arguments, formal propositions, computational verification, illustrative examples and empirical claims, without treating these different forms of evidence as interchangeable. The monograph also examines recognition as a philosophical and practical problem, investigating the relationship between distinction, otherness, interpretation and responsibility in human and artificial decision-making. Through theoretical analysis and selected case studies, it explores how artificial systems and institutions may improve not only their decisions but also their capacity to identify, explain and correct errors. The work comprises twenty-three chapters, an epilogue and five technical appendices addressing verification contracts, retrospective analysis, comparative protocols, canonical terminology and formal mechanisation. Nicomachean Algorethics is intended as a contribution to moral philosophy, philosophy of technology, artificial intelligence ethics and the interdisciplinary study of responsible decision-making. Its central thesis is that responsibility requires more than selecting among available alternatives: it requires recognising who may be affected, what authority may legitimately be exercised and which possibilities must remain open to others and to future generations.

summary: Visual geo-localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in GNSS-denied environments remains challenging due to the lack of datasets with trajectory continuity, broad scene and geographic coverage, multimodal UAV imagery, wide altitude and geometric variation, and sufficient scale. Here we present UAV-VisLoc, a dataset for UAV geo-localization through image retrieval between UAV imagery and geo-referenced satellite tiles. UAV-VisLoc contains 14,998 UAV images organized into 30 flight trajectories, spanning six continents and seven scene types. The dataset preserves contiguous observations along each trajectory, enabling trajectory-level studies under realistic sequential flight conditions. It includes RGB and Infrared UAV imagery and covers altitudes from 160 to 2,500 m. The dataset comprises 21 real UAV flights collected across multiple provinces in China and 9 synthetic flights built from OpenAerialMap imagery for regions outside China. The dataset also provides image-level flight metadata and more than 120,000 geo-referenced satellite tiles. Baseline retrieval experiments and accompanying scripts are provided to validate data organization, ground-truth annotations, and benchmark usability under diverse real-world conditions.
title: UAV-VisLoc: A Large-scale UAV Dataset with Continuous Trajectories for Visual Geo-localization

summary: This paper examines the effectiveness of Uzbekistan's tax reforms in reducing the shadow economy. Drawing on macroeconomic indicators, firm-level data, and econometric estimates, the analysis reports model-based shadow-economy estimates of approximately 38.9–39.6% of GDP for 2025, alongside reductions in statutory tax rates. The reported average firm-level tax burden was 27.3%, compared with a macroeconomic indicator of 18.3%. Econometric findings suggest a conditional tax-burden benchmark of 19–20% of GDP. The study concludes that sustainable formalization may be supported by tax-rate optimization, equitable taxation, simplified compliance procedures, improved VAT administration, and effective institutional enforcement. summary: This Zenodo repository contains the data for the following article: Molecular Signatures of Pressure-Induced Phase Transitions in a Lipid Bilayer (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcb.5c08607) by Yanna Gautier, Guillaume Stirnemann, and Jérôme Hénin   Abstract: Understanding how lipid bilayers respond to pressure is essential for interpreting the coupling between membrane proteins and their native environments. Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics to examine the pressure–temperature behavior of model membranes composed of dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) or its cis-unsaturated analogue Δ9-cis-PC. Within the studied range (288–308 K, 1–2000 bar), DMPC undergoes a liquid–gel transition, while Δ9-cis-PC remains fluid due to unsaturation. The CHARMM36 force field reproduces experimental boundaries with high fidelity: simulated DMPC transitions fall within 5–10 K and 100–300 bar of experimental values, and Δ9-cis-PC exhibits no transition. Hysteresis is modest but most pronounced when starting from low-temperature gels; we propose a split-phase simulation protocol that alleviates the hysteresis problem. We identify the area per lipid, bilayer thickness, and acyl-chain gauche fractions as sensitive phase markers; among these, the gauche fraction provides the most robust signature. Simulations indicate that an interdigitated gel is the equilibrium structure under finite-size conditions, and we propose a novel metric to quantify the extent of this phenomenon. However, at low temperature and high pressure, interdigitation decreases, consistent with the experimental lamellar gel phase. This long-lived interdigitation critically impacts standard order parameters, specifically, area per lipid and membrane thickness. Finally, we discuss in detail how finite-size effects influence phase transition and interdigitation. Overall, these results underscore the accuracy of modern force fields and highlight how simulations are essential to mechanistically complement experimental studies of pressure-sensitive membranes. Keywords : Molecular Dynamics, DMPC, lipid phase transition, high pressure, phase diagram   Detailed content of the repository: The directories contain the all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulation data generated for the different systems and simulation protocols investigated in this study. All atoms are retained in the trajectory files. To limit the overall size of the repository, the trajectories have been subsampled, with one frame retained for every three frames. DRPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic Δ9-cis-PC bilayer, which was used as the control system. Pressure_temperature_ramp : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer subjected to a pressure and temperature ramp. These simulations were performed for comparison with the pressure and temperature jump simulations used as reference. DMPC_Large_Small_Bilayers : Contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for periodic DMPC bilayers with different system sizes, corresponding to twice and half the size of the reference bilayer, respectively. The reference system consists of 57 DMPC molecules per leaflet. DMPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations used to construct the DMPC phase diagram. The directory is organized into subdirectories, with one folder per simulation replicate.  gel_to_fluid_simulations : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations performed to investigate the gel-to-fluid phase transition. The transition, starting from final gel phase configurations obtained from the DMPC simulations, was induced by independently varying either the pressure or the temperature

summary: Description This record contains the data, code and source data supporting a Mendelian randomization (MR) study of smoking and obesity traits, with DNA methylation (CpG sites) and gut microbial features (species and pathways) as candidate mediators. Files Processed and formatted GWAS summary statistics (instrumental variables and outcome data) used in the analyses. Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx : sources of the original GWAS summary statistics (also listed in Table S1 of the article). Codes.zip : R code for instrument selection, two-sample MR and sensitivity analyses, mediation analysis, colocalization and the figures, with a README describing each script and the run order, software versions and R session information. Source_data.zip : source data underlying the main and supplementary figures. Fstatistic.zip : F statistics of the instrumental variables in the MR analyses. Data sources The uploaded data are processed and formatted versions of publicly available GWAS summary statistics; the original sources are listed in Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx . Ethical approval and informed consent were obtained by the original GWAS studies. Methods Instrumental variables were selected at P < 5 × 10⁻⁸ for smoking and obesity traits, P < 1 × 10⁻⁵ (effect allele frequency > 0.01) for gut microbial features, and P < 1 × 10⁻⁸ (cis, within 1 Mb) or P < 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ (trans) for methylation quantitative trait loci of CpG sites (GoDMC). Variants were clumped at r² < 0.001 within 10,000 kb windows using PLINK with the 1000 Genomes European reference panel, and instruments with F < 10 were excluded. The multiplicative random-effects inverse-variance weighted method (Wald ratio for single-SNP instruments) was used as the primary MR method. Sensitivity analyses included the fixed-effects inverse-variance weighted method, MR-Egger, weighted median, simple and weighted mode, Cochran’s Q test, the MR-Egger intercept test, MR-PRESSO and the Steiger directionality test. Reverse causation was assessed by MR in the reverse direction. Indirect associations were estimated by two-step MR using the product-of-coefficients method with delta-method standard errors. Colocalization was assessed with coloc (p1 = p2 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, p12 = 1 × 10⁻⁵) within ±1 Mb windows and with HyPrColoc for three traits (prior.1 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, prior.c = 0.02).  Acknowledgements We thank UK Biobank ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ ), GSCAN ( https://genome.psych.umn.edu/index.php/GSCAN ), the GIANT consortium ( https://giant-consortium.web.broadinstitute.org/index.php/GIANT_consortium ), GERA ( https://cg.bsc.es/gera_summary_stats/ ), GoDMC ( http://mqtldb.godmc.org.uk/about ), the Dutch Microbiome Project ( https://dutchmicrobiomeproject.molgeniscloud.org/menu/main/home ), the IEU OpenGWAS project ( https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/ ) and the GWAS Catalog ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/ ) for providing the publicly available genetic data used in this research. We acknowledge the research teams, participants and consortia behind these datasets for their commitment to open science.
title: Causal Relationships Between Smoking and Obesity Mediated by Epigenetic Modifications and Altered Gut Microbiota

summary: Replication data and code for the article "Measuring Internet Controls in Central Asia: Network Interference, Legal Frameworks and Digital Sovereignty in Five Post-Soviet States, 2020–2026". The deposit covers Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, January 2020 – October 2026. All measurement data were retrieved passively from the public OONI aggregation API (web connectivity test and six service tests), with Germany, the Netherlands, the United States and Canada as reference countries. No probes were run and no personal data were collected. The deposit contains: Python scripts for collection, classification of blocking, sensitivity analysis, validation (evidence sample, manual review, Censored Planet comparison, domain-by-network rule), tables and figures; processed monthly aggregates by country, domain and network; the classification of every country–domain–month observation; raw OONI API responses, with SHA-256 hashes in the collection state files; and a manifest of the legal texts consulted. See README.md for the file list and the order in which to run the scripts. Citizen Lab test-list categories are not redistributed; the article uses commit 607fcb7523c3ed7bac9b24594f2b3291db6d005a. Version 2: legal-texts manifest extended (Tajikistan's Law No. 1808 on Countering Terrorism and Law No. 56 on Electric Communications, from the parliament's websites); second-coder protocol added. Data, classification and results are unchanged. Version 3: completed second-coder sheet and agreement results added (the two independent coders agree on 27/27 cases; each agrees with the automatic rule on 23/27, Cohen's kappa = 0.68); co-authors added. Data, classification and results are unchanged.

summary: This record accompanies Working Paper No. 9 of the Independent FAIR Evaluation Series of the ATLAS Framework , entitled Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation . The study examines the concentration of computational AACF susceptibility profiles derived from frozen PaccMann and DRPreter predictions for 95 unique registered configurations across 970 matched cancer cell-line profiles . Scores are transformed into normalized weights using a softmax transformation favouring lower AACF indices, with fixed model-specific reference scales. Profile characterization includes Shannon entropy, normalized entropy, effective configuration counts, and leading configuration weights. The evaluation addresses five normalization-scale multipliers, the effect of retaining 97 registered labels instead of 95 unique configurations, lineage comparisons covering 953 profiles in 21 groups, and variability across ten DRPreter checkpoints. It also distinguishes entropy calculated after median index aggregation from the median of checkpoint-wise entropies. At the reference scales, median normalized entropy was 0.9346 for PaccMann and 0.9528 for the DRPreter median consensus . These aggregate differences coexisted with weak cross-model agreement in cell-line entropy rankings ( Spearman ρ = −0.0788 ) and only six shared profiles among the 97 most concentrated profiles identified by each model. Normalization and checkpoint aggregation affected concentration summaries and rankings, demonstrating that entropy requires an explicitly specified computational representation. The accompanying computational materials document the six-stage workflow through analysis scripts, frozen input resources, configuration and profile mappings, normalization policies, numerical tables and arrays, saved bootstrap draws, and provenance and validation records. A README explains the directory structure, principal outputs, reproduction workflow, and interpretation limits. Resources inherited from ATLAS Working Papers 06–08 retain their upstream licensing and attribution requirements. The final technical audit recorded 2,363 passed checks and no failed checks , reviewing 206 distinct files in the selected analysis chain. This audit supports technical consistency and traceability within the implemented checks; it does not constitute independent experimental or clinical validation. The results establish entropy as a conditional descriptor of computational profile concentration . They do not establish therapeutic efficacy, measured mixture responses, biological mechanisms, or malignant-versus-normal selectivity. The materials support transparent inspection, reanalysis, and further methodological evaluation of the ATLAS framework.
title: Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation

summary: This paper establishes the mathematical and methodological foundations of the GCT-STL research program on the P versus NP problem, using the decision Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP_dec) as a canonical NP-complete representative and its polynomial reduction to 3-SAT with an exact materialized 3-CNF artifact. The framework organizes nine provenance-controlled descriptors (D1–D9) across three computational-information domains: semantic/geometric (S), temporal/computational (T), and logical/syntactic (L). These descriptors form the canonical raw Valiant–González tensorial signature (R0), supported by explicit SourceMap and Provenance Bundle contracts and three foundational entropy results. Paper I-A situates R0 within a branched four-representation architecture: R1 is a componentwise logarithmic scale complement, R2 is the canonical entropic/information representation, and R3 is the exact-envelope normalized representation. The Full STL Tensorial Coupling Principle remains an open and falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established obstruction theorem. The logical-complexity architecture distinguishes the internal classes P_STL and NP_STL and the conditional F1–F4 route toward the classical P versus NP problem. F1 and F2 remain open mathematical obligations. Empirical robustness, tensorial diagnostics, and candidate obstructions do not constitute universal computational lower bounds. Accordingly, Paper I-A does not prove P ≠ NP. It establishes the representational, logical, methodological, and formal-certification foundations for subsequent research within the GCT-STL program.
title: Three-Dimensional Entropic Domains for TSP Complexity via 3-SAT: Foundations of the GCT-STL Research Program on P versus NP

summary: This record contains the experimental datasets supporting the technical Key Performance Indicator (KPI) evaluation of the DETO-XR (Dynamic Edge Tracking Optimization for XR) use case developed within the 6G-PATH (6G Pilots and Trials Through Europe) project, Open Call 2. DETO-XR investigates a distributed edge–cloud architecture combining environment sensing, Multiple Object Tracking (MOT), GPU-accelerated cloud processing, and remote rendering for interactive Mixed Reality applications. The proposed MOT-as-a-Service (MOTaaS) concept enables multiple independent tracking sessions to access shared cloud processing resources. The dataset provides raw measurement traces, processed results, experimental configurations, and verification scripts covering five technical KPIs: Dataset Description KPI-1: Frame Drop Streaks HoloLens 2 client-side video-selection telemetry collected during 5G experiments, including a selected stable operating interval and a supplementary retrospective 30 Hz frame-availability analysis. KPI-2: Jitter Buffer and Frame Availability Evaluation of video-frame availability with a configured 30 ms jitter buffer, including per-stream frame-selection events, timestamped records, and full measurement-stage context. KPI-3: Pose Staleness Comparative experiments evaluating a tracking pose-staleness proxy using different cloud-based object-detection configurations. KPI-4: GPU Duty-Cycle Reduction GPU utilization measurements comparing continuous object detection with periodic detection refresh, supporting the evaluation of computational resource efficiency. KPI-5: Concurrent MOT Sessions Application traces and GPU monitoring data collected during experiments with one, two, and three concurrent MOT sessions sharing GPU-backed cloud services. The experiments were conducted between 18 October and 4 November 2026 , including measurements associated with the 6G-INCOGNICO experimentation environment in Greece. Dataset Organization Each KPI is documented in a dedicated directory containing the relevant raw and processed measurement data. The archive also includes: Detailed README files explaining the experimental setup, measurement methodology, and interpretation of results. A data dictionary describing measurement fields, timestamps, and derived metrics. Source provenance information and mappings between reported KPI results and supporting evidence. SHA-256 checksums and Python verification scripts supporting data integrity and reproducibility. Measurement Scope The KPI-1/KPI-2 dataset includes a retrospectively selected 5G operating interval evaluated using a 30 Hz frame-availability model, together with the original 13-minute measurement-stage records. The alternative frame-availability metric is distinct from native 60 Hz display-frame-loss measurements and does not establish full-run compliance with the original KPI targets. Similarly, KPI-3 uses a model-based pose-staleness proxy rather than direct HoloLens display measurements, while KPI-4 and KPI-5 evaluate specific GPU utilization and concurrency configurations. The datasets are intended to support reproducible performance evaluation, independent analysis, and further research into distributed object tracking, cloud-assisted XR applications, and efficient GPU resource utilization. Funding The 6G-PATH project has received funding from the Smart Networks and Services Joint Undertaking (SNS JU) under the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under Grant Agreement No. 101139172 . This dataset reflects only the authors' views. The European Commission is not responsible for any use that may be made of the information it contains.
title: 6G-PATH OC2 [DETO-XR]: Technical KPI Evaluation Datasets

summary: Reproducibility data and executable source for Accuracy, Storage, and Update Cost in Reference-Assisted Sensor Calibration , by Oleksandr Kuznetsov. Version 1.1.0 adds the completed seven-model common-fixture campaign: two validated sessions each on Mega2560, ESP32-C3 and ESP32-S3, 480 timing records and 42 numerical-accuracy checks. It preserves the three original acquisition ZIPs, firmware images, raw serial logs, source/image hashes and an executable audit. All models use one frozen synthetic distorted-NTC fixture; no coefficients, seeds or hyperparameters were retuned. The captured S3 executable uses native float32 instructions. The 4.2% polynomial-Horner timing advantage over LUT32 is specific to the recorded S3 build; optimization-level and code-layout robustness were not measured. The original 1.0.0 evidence archive is retained unchanged. It contains the matched synthetic calibration/adaptation records, cross-validation and sensitivity analyses, historical MCU fixtures and paired refinements using 32-pair block least squares and decaying NLMS. Earlier reanalysis reused separate development and confirmation seeds; it is not a new untouched holdout. Historical fixtures remain separate from the V2 frontier. This is an implementation and resource-cost study. Accuracy and drift are controlled synthetic quantities. Physical boards establish execution time and numerical agreement. No physical NTC/LDR calibration, S3 update timing, measured energy, WCET, peak stack or between-board uncertainty is claimed. The author photograph illustrates the development boards, not a sensor-calibration setup. Immutable V2 audit and results: commit df19065 . Each component archive supplies exact code provenance and SHA-256 manifests. The cleaned English documentation preserves all numerical evidence and the frozen benchmark source set. Author-created data and research documentation: CC BY 4.0. Software retains its included MIT license; third-party components retain their own terms. This is a dataset/software evidence release, not an accepted journal publication.
title: Accuracy, Storage, and Update Cost in Reference-Assisted Sensor Calibration: Reproducibility Data

summary: This archive contains the complete, reproducible analysis pipeline accompanying the article by Bentounsi, Achour and Boufaida, currently under review. Purpose Clinical datasets often present expert labels as if they applied a published guideline. This work proposes an audit method that (i) measures the gap between a guideline-derived reference rule base and the expert labels, (ii) attributes the disagreements to an implicit criterion (Algorithm 1), and (iii) tests whether that criterion can be reconstructed out of sample, using an explicit acceptance criterion: an agreement gain of at least 5 points over the majority baseline, the same rule selected in at least 4 of 5 folds, and a family-wise permutation p-value below 0.01. The method is applied to an Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) dataset (270 records, six labels) and replicated on the UCI Cardiotocography dataset (2,126 segments) against the FIGO 2015 guideline. Contents src/ : Python modules (thresholds and protocol constants, data loading with hash check, generated rule trace, rules–expert gap and Algorithm 1, threshold and interval enumerations with permutation tests, learning control and Shapley attribution, cardiotocography replication, robustness analyses, figures). results/ : every result file used in the manuscript (CSV, TXT, JSON). figures/ : Figures 1–5 (PDF and PNG). tests/ : pytest suite (equivalence of fast and direct enumerations, regression tests on the published tables, checks of the FIGO rule base, and a test that every key figure of the manuscript matches the recomputed results). PROTOCOL.md : analysis protocol, including Amendment 1 for the replication.  PROTOCOL2.sha256 records the hash of Protocol 2. run_all.sh , requirements.txt (pinned versions with hashes, Python 3.13). Data (not redistributed) The input datasets are not included and must be downloaded from their original sources; the code refuses to run on any other version of the files. ABPM: Douibi K, Benabid MM, Settouti N, Chikh MA. Data for: An analysis of Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) . Mendeley Data, V1, 2017. https://doi.org/10.17632/y4dh3b3tfx.1 . File ABPM-dataset.arff , SHA-256 0ea0a53c86bd2564117913fe99dd6699579fc03b23acd118c0b33822db911e07 . Cardiotocography: Campos D, Bernardes J. Cardiotocography . UCI Machine Learning Repository, 2000. https://doi.org/10.24432/C51S4N . File CTG.xls , SHA-256 d6aa62e82625e59f9d5b05bc8fc52af9ea67bdf2a23f1faca8511d5618fcb421 . Reproduction Place both files in data/raw/ , then run: python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt ./run_all.sh The script verifies the dataset hashes, runs all modules, regenerates every result file and figure, and runs the test suite (about twelve minutes on an ordinary laptop). All randomness uses a fixed seed (0); the rule trace is deterministic. Licence Code released under the MIT licence. The datasets remain under the terms set by their authors.
title: Code and results for: Auditing Expert Annotations against Published Guidelines: Measuring, Attributing and Reconstructing Implicit Labelling Criteria in Clinical Datasets

Applicability diagnostics of predictions: every predicted pixel gets DModXPS (distance to the model) and T²PS, with the 0.99 limits from the training data and a summary (share of pixels above the limits, mean prediction within and outside them). Model runs store the projection data they need ( prediction_model : x_mean , x_std , rotations , loadings , score_variances , s0 , limits); models fitted before have no maps until they are fitted again. Prediction.dmodx_map , .t2_map , .diagnostics , .provenance . Wavelength warning at prediction: when the scan and the model both have a real wavelength axis and they differ, the prediction logs a warning with the largest difference and records it in provenance["wavelength_warning"] (Predict summary: Wavelengths ); it never blocks or changes the prediction. enginir.prediction.wavelength_mismatch . Viewer: Layer selector in the Predict map (Prediction, DModX, T²) with the pixels above the limit marked, and the applicability summary. AsLS baseline correction (asymmetric least squares, as in SIMCA): enginir.preprocessing.AsLSBaseline and PreprocessingRecipe(asls=True, asls_lambda=..., asls_p=..., asls_iterations=...) , first in the recipe order, as is in absorbance and flipped in reflectance and DN. Scripts only; the viewer shows and keeps it. SavitzkyGolay(edges="drop") and PreprocessingRecipe.output_wavelengths . Fixed Viewer: a new project (and an exported CSV) gets its extension ( .h5 , .csv ) when the name was typed without one; the file dialog did not add it on some platforms, and the open dialog, filtering on .h5 , then hid the project. The open dialog also offers All files . Project.create documents that it replaces an existing file. summary: Version 1.8.3 carries the manuscript as resubmitted after the major revision and pairs with code tag v1.1.2 . Release identities are now also classified with tag evidence from the time of each change: an archive visit or an immutable release dates a tag binding, while a mutable release record does not ( reports/release_timing.json , release-timing-v2). The matched-control comparison covers months 13-18 ( reports/control_comparison.json ), and reports/revision_checks.json adds the tail window after day 540, the repository-month units of the repository share, commit-level ratios of the second wave and the dependents list against the measured endpoint. The results archive now also holds, under data/ , the cached API responses, stage-freeze scripts, source-frame files and run manifests that the full formal entry point ( python -m pintrace.formal_stats --working ) checks, so it runs from the code tag and the two archives. JOIN_MEASUREMENTS.md corrects the verification directory and the part names and adds a streaming extraction. reproduce.py with expected.json runs the whole reproduction in an empty working directory and compares every output with the archived bytes. The measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. Version 1.8.2 (superseded by 1.8.3) carries the manuscript as resubmitted after the major revision: the pipeline's precision and recall by class against the annotators' consensus, the timing of the annotator replacements, the second wave qualified as carried by organization-owned repositories, and corrected denominators. It adds a note on line endings with the list of files whose implementation hashes were recorded with CRLF line endings ( docs/crlf_hashed_files.txt ). The manuscript sources moved to paper/jsep_v2/ . All data and result files are unchanged from version 1.8.1, and the measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. Version 1.8.1 carries the final revised manuscript (data and code availability, design history, and wording of the second wave) and adds means to the covariate summaries of the coverage audit. All other data are unchanged from version 1.8.0, and the measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. Version 1.8 accompanies the major revision of the manuscript. The results archive adds the dependency-graph coverage audit with its crawl, sample and eligibility records, the stratified sensitivity of the two waves, and the independent two-annotator validation of 400 items (packets, codebook, freeze records, the final annotators' pseudonymous answers, consensus and score). It also archives the cohort baselines, maintenance-scope entries and three table files that these analyses bind. The measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. The record contains two archives. pintrace-measurements-v1.tar.zst holds the per-repository measurement snapshots for 457 measured repositories and 301 matched control repositories, the archived upstream release evidence and the matched-control assignments. pintrace-results-v1.tar.zst holds the published result files, the formal-statistics outputs, the 150-item gold set, the research documentation, the manuscript PDF and LaTeX source, and the claim ledger that maps every rendered number to a result file and JSON pointer. Each archive includes a SHA-256 manifest and a README with extraction and reproduction instructions. The measurement files contain repository identifiers but no commit author names, commit messages, e-mail addresses or credentials. The code is at https://github.com/JunjieChen0/PinTrace under the MIT license. Replication data and results are released under CC BY 4.0. The study has no comparison group shielded from the incident, so the reported quantities describe timing, targets and persistence rather than an incident effect.
title: PinTrace: two waves of SHA pinning in GitHub Actions (replication data and results)
