summary: This paper develops a scale-spanning account of latent vibration and frequency manifestation within Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM). It examines the relationship between complete latent vibration, the negative and positive displacement domains around the manifestable origin, and the eligibility of positive displacement for progression towards physical manifestation. The development distinguishes the complete latent-vibration interval from the directed displacement associated with manifestation, establishing the proposed Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck threshold relationships in terms of the Planck length. The analysis further develops phase-dependent frequency relations below the Planck threshold and considers the proposed frequency increments associated with the Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck domains. It then presents a state-dependent sequence of energy–frequency transformations across latent, phase, and manifested states, including the reverse progression associated with dissolution. Within this framework, frequency and displacement are treated as related physical parameters whose coefficients depend on the corresponding phase domain. The paper also distinguishes the phase-state potential-energy mass representation from the mass contribution associated with the manifested domain. It formulates the effective-mass relationship and separates this ECM representation from the distinct dark-energy-related mass representation. Taken together, these developments present an integrated theoretical description of latent vibration, manifestation eligibility, threshold transitions, energy–frequency relations, and mass-state transformations within the proposed ECM framework.
title: Complete Latent Vibration and Frequency Manifestation Eligibility in Extended Classical Mechanics

summary: Nicomachean Algorethics: Principles, Limits and Verification of Human and Artificial Transformative Decision-Making This monograph develops a philosophical and formal framework for examining the legitimacy, responsibility and verifiability of transformative decisions made by human agents, institutions and artificial systems. Drawing on Aristotelian practical philosophy, contemporary ethics, epistemology, decision theory and the challenges of artificial intelligence governance, Nicomachean Algorethics addresses a fundamental question: under what conditions may an agent legitimately make decisions that transform the lives, opportunities and futures of others? The proposed framework is organised around twelve normative laws and a Recognition Matrix designed to distinguish technical possibility, epistemic justification, normative admissibility and legitimate authority. Rather than attempting to calculate or optimise the Good, the framework investigates the conditions under which decisions may be justified, contested, corrected or withheld. Particular attention is given to uncertainty, the limitations of representation, delegated authority, corrigibility, reversibility, capability preservation, the distribution of responsibility, value pluralism and the prevention of harm. The work introduces formal definitions, mathematical formulations, verification contracts and operational procedures intended to make normative assumptions and decision-making constraints explicit. Its methodological approach distinguishes conceptual arguments, formal propositions, computational verification, illustrative examples and empirical claims, without treating these different forms of evidence as interchangeable. The monograph also examines recognition as a philosophical and practical problem, investigating the relationship between distinction, otherness, interpretation and responsibility in human and artificial decision-making. Through theoretical analysis and selected case studies, it explores how artificial systems and institutions may improve not only their decisions but also their capacity to identify, explain and correct errors. The work comprises twenty-three chapters, an epilogue and five technical appendices addressing verification contracts, retrospective analysis, comparative protocols, canonical terminology and formal mechanisation. Nicomachean Algorethics is intended as a contribution to moral philosophy, philosophy of technology, artificial intelligence ethics and the interdisciplinary study of responsible decision-making. Its central thesis is that responsibility requires more than selecting among available alternatives: it requires recognising who may be affected, what authority may legitimately be exercised and which possibilities must remain open to others and to future generations.

title: NICOMACHEAN ALGORETHICS - Principles, Limits, and Verification of Transformative Decision-Making by Humans and Artificial Systems

summary: Visual geo-localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in GNSS-denied environments remains challenging due to the lack of datasets with trajectory continuity, broad scene and geographic coverage, multimodal UAV imagery, wide altitude and geometric variation, and sufficient scale. Here we present UAV-VisLoc, a dataset for UAV geo-localization through image retrieval between UAV imagery and geo-referenced satellite tiles. UAV-VisLoc contains 14,998 UAV images organized into 30 flight trajectories, spanning six continents and seven scene types. The dataset preserves contiguous observations along each trajectory, enabling trajectory-level studies under realistic sequential flight conditions. It includes RGB and Infrared UAV imagery and covers altitudes from 160 to 2,500 m. The dataset comprises 21 real UAV flights collected across multiple provinces in China and 9 synthetic flights built from OpenAerialMap imagery for regions outside China. The dataset also provides image-level flight metadata and more than 120,000 geo-referenced satellite tiles. Baseline retrieval experiments and accompanying scripts are provided to validate data organization, ground-truth annotations, and benchmark usability under diverse real-world conditions.
title: UAV-VisLoc: A Large-scale UAV Dataset with Continuous Trajectories for Visual Geo-localization

summary: Urban design relies on judgments about existing and anticipated needs, while the available evidence ranges from lived experience and historical records to geospatial observation, statistical estimation, and computational simulation. Contemporary developments in geospatial artificial intelligence, agent-based modeling, urban digital twins, and computational search expand the means of inquiry while raising questions about inferential validity and methodological compatibility. This paper develops a question-guided framework for identifying and evaluating candidate urban needs through the reconstruction of spatial, temporal, social, ecological, and infrastructural relations. Two complementary inquiry pathways are distinguished: hypothesis-driven assessment of specified candidate needs and exploratory search for candidates emerging from observed or simulated relational patterns. Both pathways are connected to explicit procedures of evidential appraisal, causal examination where identifiable, participatory scrutiny, and post-intervention evaluation. A provisional formal interface is proposed in which generative–relational (GR) subjects have question-dependent spacetime-supported representations, heterogeneous evidence is linked by category-theoretic constructions, and selected event structures are encoded through algebraic-topological invariants of labeled two-complexes. Evolutionary updates of these representations and spin-foam-inspired cellular initializations are considered as exploratory modeling options, with the physical meaning of quantum-gravity spin foams kept separate from urban research. The framework is intended to guide methodological comparison and further model development; its empirical adequacy requires case-specific operationalization and validation.
title: Identifying and Evaluating Urban Needs Through Relational Reconstruction: A Preliminary Generative and Evolutionary Formal Model in an Algebraic Framework

summary: The World on Record Index (TWR) — version 1.2.0 Released 9 November 2026. Concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23997606 resolves to the latest version. What is new: the sector layer 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 published one score per country-year. This release adds  goal_level  — one score per country-year  per SDG goal  — so the measure can say  what  a government stopped reporting, not only that it reported less. Sixteen goals are scored.  Goal 7 is not : it has three series, too few to identify a factor. That is a structural fact about the goal, not a judgement on it. Each goal is a  separate  unidimensional 2PL fit on that goal's own series, drawn from the same 524 that build the overall index. A goal's score therefore owes nothing to the other fifteen, and both layers sit on the same scale. The layer is not a restatement of the overall index. Across the sixteen goals a median of  64%  of the variation in goal-level reporting is not explained by a country's overall level — from 18% for goal 17 to 99.9% for goal 15. What it is checked against Check Result Convergence 16 of 16 goals, 19–73 EM cycles each Reliability 0.772–0.953, median  0.844 ; every goal above 0.70 Median posterior SD 0.338 (overall index: 0.114) Bootstrap, 500 replicates 0 failed replicates ; sampling SD is 7–42% of the posterior SE, median 13% Held-out series Fit on 70% of a goal's series, predict the held-out 30%: median AUC  0.725  against a per-series permutation null at  0.500 The bootstrap result means the published standard errors are  conservative  — they already cover item-parameter uncertainty with room to spare. Report the posterior SE, not the bootstrap SD. The held-out test is the first direct check that a goal score predicts reporting it was not fitted on. Thirteen of sixteen goals score 0.649 or better. The three weakest — goal 17 (0.618), goal 15 (0.526) and goal 6 (0.479) — are precisely the three already set apart on content grounds, which the test did not know. Disclose, do not gate Every goal fitted is published.  Nothing is excluded for imprecision, and 0.70 (Nunnally) is reported as a reference point, not applied as a cut. Each goal ships with four numbers a reader can weigh it by: reliability  — 0.772 to 0.953 se_median  — the typical error bar on that goal's scores weight_top5_pct  — how concentrated the score is in its five heaviest series weight_agency_pct  — how much of the score rests on series the custodian agency produces rather than the country Two goals carry  release = hold_content . The hold is on  content  grounds and for  different reasons , never on precision: Goal 6  is largely satellite measurement of lakes, wetlands and river flow. "Reported" there mostly records whether an agency published a dataset, not a country's choice. Goal 15  is overwhelmingly country-produced, but a third of its series are treaty and policy instruments (Nagoya Protocol, Aichi targets, NBSAP), which may track commitment status rather than reporting effort. An error bar cannot warn a reader about either, so the flag travels with the data. Both goals are published in full. Known limitations Weight concentration.  Within a goal, small groups of series that are always reported together can carry much of the score — in goal 10 the five heaviest series carry 80%, in goal 1 75%. These groups are near-duplicates that the variant rule does not collapse, because they are not reported identically: in goal 1, India, Sri Lanka and Malaysia report the education and health breakdowns but never the aggregate, every year from 2015 to 2023. Collapsing them would erase those reporting choices, so they are disclosed in  weight_top5_pct  instead. Modelling the dependence directly is deferred. Provenance.   weight_agency_pct  records h
title: The World on Record: statistical reporting across countries, policy sectors, and time

summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Total Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed. As a result, some sites have WAV files with 0 bytes of data or timestamps outside the range of probable recording times. Procedures used by the Eclipse Soundscapes team to process audio data for its purposes are outlined in the Data Management reports located in the Eclipse Soundscapes Zenodo community. Data with 0 bytes of data were included for completeness. When possible, all site-specific files, including the audio files, are included in a single zip file for ease of download. If a single zip file upload was not possible due to upload or bandwidth limitations, audio files are included in multiple zip files based on the day of the observation. summary: Did the places that lost most men in the First World War turn to Labour? The question runs through accounts of Labour's replacement of the Liberals, and studies of Italy and Germany link local war losses to post-war radicalism, but its link to party support has not been tested for Britain, where there is no record of deaths, or map of seats, at constituency level. I link 717,287 First World War names on community memorials in the Imperial War Museums' War Memorials Register, counted once per place, to every Great Britain constituency contest from 1906 to 1924, using 176 county and borough units as a common geography, and test hypotheses fixed before any outcome model was run. Contrary to the radicalisation hypothesis, a one standard deviation higher memorial rate (22 names per 1,000 electors of 1918) is associated with a 2.9 percentage point smaller Labour gain between December 1910 and 1918 (95% CI 0.1 to 5.7; p=0.040; Holm-adjusted across four primary outcomes p=0.16; N=131). The gap widens to 4.8 points by 1922, mirrored by Liberal resilience, and is not present in pre-war changes in six placebo tests. All 21 robustness variants give negative estimates, but only 8 have intervals excluding zero. Exploratory analysis points to where Labour fielded candidates. The design is correlational: recorded losses track volunteering and occupational structure, for which no data exist here. The data do not support a larger Labour advance where recorded losses were heavier; the negative association itself is modest and should be treated as suggestive. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/war-dead-labour/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/war-dead-labour . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/war-dead-labour/ . Sources: Imperial War Museums War Memorials Register (non-commercial reuse); general election results from UK Parliament (Open Parliament Licence v3.0), matched to Wikidata; ONS boundaries (OGL v3). Text, figures and derived data CC BY-NC 4.0 (the register's terms); code MIT.

summary: CRISPR-TRIAGE is an open-science computational biology research archive evaluating parameter-efficient off-target prioritization under budget-constrained experimental validation budgets (K <= 50). This package contains the complete trained model checkpoints, multi-seed training pipelines (5 random seeds), biophysical feature extractors, pre-registered baseline models (LightGBM GBDT, Pairwise 1D-CNN, Logistic Regression, crispAI architecture), and evaluation results across two external cellular benchmarks (Listgarten 2018 GUIDE-seq and K562 cellular compilation). Key Scientific Findings & Methodological Disclosure: Algorithmic Parity with Gradient Boosted Trees: On the deduplicated independent cellular benchmark (K562 retrospective multi-assay compilation from DeepCRISPR / Yang et al. 2023; 11 guides, 16,172 unique candidate pairs, 110 confirmed positive guide-target sequence pairs without genomic coordinates), standard gradient boosting (LightGBM GBDT) trained on 15 simple biophysical mismatch features achieves Macro Recall@20 = 0.6350 vs 0.6416 for CRISPR-TRIAGE (margin +0.0066 / +0.66%; paired Wilcoxon W = 18.0, p = 1.0000; 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0979, +0.0900]). LightGBM runs 2.39x faster with 0 neural parameters. While lack of statistically significant superiority does not prove biological equivalence or disprove neural-network utility, the empirical evidence failed to reject the null hypothesis of no difference vs LightGBM under available statistical power. Multi-Seed Volatility in CRISPR Modeling: Retraining across 5 independent random seeds reveals substantial Macro Recall@20 fluctuations (+-6.5% standard deviation on identical data), demonstrating that single-seed reporting in the CRISPR machine-learning literature frequently reflects random seed-selection noise rather than genuine algorithmic superiority. Dataset Deduplication Importance: Forensic auditing documented the impact of 1,613 duplicate candidate rows (and 2 duplicate confirmed positive sites) in the K562 compilation, showing how uncleaned duplicates distort evaluation metrics. Two-Tier Reproducibility Scope: Tier 1 (Saved-Model Inference & K562 Cellular Benchmark Reproduction): 100% self-contained in this archive. All 5 trained seed weights, baselines, scalers, predictions, metric summaries, and the K562 cellular cohort execute fully offline without internet access. Tier 2 (Full Retraining on Primary Assay Datasets): Full retraining from raw sequence reads and complete Listgarten raw dataset reproduction requires separately downloading the 4 un-subsampled raw assay datasets (>20MB each), registered with authoritative accessions and cryptographic SHA256 checksums in DATA_MANIFEST.csv. Licensing, Provenance & Third-Party Rights: CRISPR-TRIAGE code, models, and documentation are licensed under the permissive MIT License. The crispAI architecture code (src/crispai_official/) is under MIT License (Copyright 2023 Furkan Ozden; reference: Özden & Minary, NAR 2024). Pretrained third-party weights for crispAI are omitted from the archive to ensure compliance with conflicting upstream documentation, with archive extraction utilities provided for the authors' official Zenodo records (13335960 / 12609337). Bundled K562 benchmark datasets are distributed under CC BY 4.0 (Yang et al. CSBJ 2023; Chuai et al. Genome Biol 2018). Raw CFD scoring lookup matrices (Doench et al. 2016 Supplementary Table 19) are strictly omitted from the release archive for third-party rights compliance; tested user-side acquisition and verification utilities are provided via scripts/download_cfd_matrices.py. See the root LICENSE file for full details.

Key Scientific Findings & Methodological Disclosure: Algorithmic Parity with Gradient Boosted Trees: On the deduplicated independent cellular benchmark (K562 retrospective multi-assay compilation from DeepCRISPR / Yang et al. 2023; 11 guides, 16,172 unique candidate pairs, 110 confirmed positive guide-target sequence pairs without genomic coordinates), standard gradient boosting (LightGBM GBDT) trained on 15 simple biophysical mismatch features achieves Macro Recall@20 = 0.6350 vs 0.6416 for CRISPR-TRIAGE (margin +0.0066 / +0.66%; paired Wilcoxon W = 18.0, p = 1.0000; 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0979, +0.0900]). LightGBM runs 2.39x faster with 0 neural parameters. While lack of statistically significant superiority does not prove biological equivalence or disprove neural-network utility, the empirical evidence failed to reject the null hypothesis of no difference vs LightGBM under available statistical power. Multi-Seed Volatility in CRISPR Modeling: Retraining across 5 independent random seeds reveals substantial Macro Recall@20 fluctuations (+-6.5% standard deviation on identical data), demonstrating that single-seed reporting in the CRISPR machine-learning literature frequently reflects random seed-selection noise rather than genuine algorithmic superiority. summary: Hobsbawm and Rudé argued that parliamentary enclosure helped to cause the Swing riots of 1830; Caprettini and Voth showed that threshing machines mattered. I link 5,375 places named in 4,104 enclosure Acts to the parishes in Caprettini and Voth's data (79% of places named in Acts of 1790 to 1830 linked) and test, in a model specified in advance with county fixed effects and their controls, whether recent enclosure predicts unrest in 9,674 parishes. As planned, parishes named in an Act of 1790 to 1830 were 2.7 percentage points more likely to see an incident (95% CI 0.2 to 5.3; mean 14.5%). Three findings argue against a grievance reading. Parishes enclosed only before 1790 show the same gap (3.1 points); stricter linking rules shrink it to between 0.7 and 1.7 points; and in exploratory models that add parish area, a control the plan omitted, it disappears (-0.8 points, 95% CI -3.2 to 1.5); larger parishes were both more often enclosed and more likely to record any incident. The planned estimate is therefore not robust evidence that recent parliamentary enclosure predicted where Swing broke out. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/enclosure-swing/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/enclosure-swing . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/enclosure-swing/ . Sources: Caprettini and Voth (2020) replication data (openICPSR 117044, CC BY 4.0); Chronological Tables of Private and Local Acts, legislation.gov.uk (Open Government Licence v3.0); Wikidata (CC0). Text, figures and derived data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: Enclosure and the Swing Riots: A Pre-specified Parish-level Test of the Grievance Hypothesis, England and Wales, 1830 to 1831

summary: LOADX (workLOad Assessment in Dual-task eXecution) is a multimodal dataset developed to support research on physical and mental workload estimation during single- and dual-task activities. The dataset contains synchronized physiological, kinematic, task-related, and subjective data collected from 20 participants performing a structured experimental protocol designed to elicit different combinations of physical and cognitive demand. The protocol includes 16 experimental conditions: three physical tasks, three cognitive tasks, nine dual-task combinations, and one resting baseline. The physical tasks consist of repeated shoulder flexion–extension, marching in place, and squats. The cognitive tasks include a Stroop test, a 2-back working-memory task, and backward counting by seven. Each active condition lasted 90 seconds and was followed by a resting interval. Physiological data were acquired using wearable sensors and include raw electrocardiographic signals, raw respiratory waveforms, heart rate, inter-beat interval, respiratory rate, galvanic skin response, and triaxial acceleration. Full-body kinematic data were collected using a contactless vision-based monitoring system based on MediaPipe Pose, providing the three-dimensional coordinates of 33 anatomical landmarks. All acquisition streams share a common temporal reference, enabling the alignment of physiological signals, body movements, task execution, and workload annotations. After each experimental condition, participants rated their perceived physical and mental demand using selected dimensions of the NASA Task Load Index. The dataset therefore includes task-level Physical Demand and Mental Demand scores, which can be used as subjective workload annotations for supervised learning, correlation analysis, clustering, and validation of multimodal workload-estimation methods. summary: VCAB-Wild characterizes the functionality and observable security properties of deployed web applications created with Lovable, an AI application builder. It covers all 7,937 distinct *.lovable.app hosts indexed by Common Crawl in CC-MAIN-2026-39. For each host it records reachability, ten building blocks identified in public client code, and four categories of non-intrusive exposure indicators: database readability with the application's public key (row counts only), secret-key strings in public code (type only), public source maps and security headers. A random subset of 500 hosts carries application-type labels from two LLM annotators with adjudication and a 50-host human check. The release includes a keyed development/test split, three reference tasks with a scoring tool, SHA-256 fingerprints for snapshot reconstruction, and all collection and analysis code. Host names are withheld; the key linking records to hosts is available from the author under a non-disclosure agreement. Data: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT. Part of the Vibe-Coded App Benchmark (VCAB).
title: VCAB-Wild: A dataset of 7,937 deployed vibe-coded web applications with building-block annotations, non-intrusive data-exposure measurements and reference tasks for security evaluation

summary: Health Building Lifestyle Guidelines (2026 Comprehensive Edition) is a practical, referenced, comprehensive guideline for lay readers and health professionals. It BUILDS ON, and does NOT rename, replace or supersede, the 2025 Health Building Lifestyle Guidelines (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.15814357, 5 July 2025). The main PDF is a 9-page LANDSCAPE BROCHURE with enlarged body type throughout, one topic per page and clickable links. It reproduces the 2025 guideline IN FULL (English, Hindi and its own reference list) on pages 2-4, each captioned with the 2025 DOI; the 12 reference URLs on reproduced page 4 are live links as well. The Title uses a SINGLE ACLM blue header in two lines, and EVERY URL link in the brochure uses that same deep blue. The three PURE traffic-light colours appear as three disks on page 1 (the 21-point key) and on ALL content headers (Spices = YELLOW, Yoga = RED); the Six-pillars page carries the brighter original ACLM six-pillar chips, with published ACLM pillar language in roman type, the 2025 21-item guideline in italics, and an explicit attribution footnote. Two images from the Sutra Health YouTube channel (infusion, Yoga) sit on the right of their pages. Page 8 is one merged evidence table listing the CONDITIONS for which there is evidence and THE PRACTICES THAT WORKS, colour-coded PREVENTION / TREATMENT / REMISSION-REVERSAL (refs [30] DiRECT, [31] Ornish), followed by two selected meta-analyses on prevention ([32] Kyu, [33] Reynolds); the separate evidence pages and the redundant Safety page were consolidated into it. The References hyperlink the reproduced 2025 handout's own list [1]-[12] on p4, note the first disclosure (8 Sep 2025 [5]), and run to 33 numbered references. This record's own DOI (10.5281/zenodo.24090390) is printed on page 1 of the PDF. No ACLM logo is used and no endorsement is implied. CC BY 4.0 is selected from Zenodo's default licence options. summary: Factoring and supply chain finance (SCF) allow firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, to obtain liquidity against receivables and other trade assets, but they expose financiers to the credit risk of suppliers, buyers and their relationships. This study maps the scientific literature on credit risk management in factoring and SCF through a bibliometric analysis. A Scopus search conducted on 12 October 2026 and screening following the PRISMA 2020 flow yielded 288 articles and reviews published between 1995 and 2025. Performance analysis was combined with science mapping in VOSviewer, including keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship and co-citation analyses of references and sources. The results show that the field has grown rapidly since 2019, with 87.2% of the documents published in 2019–2025. China dominates research output, while studies from the United Kingdom, the United States and Italy attain higher normalised impact, and operations management and operational research journals are the main publication venues. Three research streams are identified: analytical operations–finance models of risk allocation in capital-constrained supply chains, conceptual and empirical research on SCF adoption and reverse factoring, and machine learning-based credit risk assessment of SMEs. Research attention has shifted from traditional factoring and receivables financing towards SCF, machine learning, blockchain and, most recently, artificial intelligence and sustainability. The accounting, financial reporting and internal control dimensions of these arrangements, the allocation of risk among multiple financiers, and evidence from under-represented regions emerge as the main gaps.
tags: factoring, supply chain finance, credit risk management, reverse factoring, bibliometric analysis, VOSviewer.

summary: Factoring and supply chain finance (SCF) allow firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, to obtain liquidity against receivables and other trade assets, but they expose financiers to the credit risk of suppliers, buyers and their relationships. This study maps the scientific literature on credit risk management in factoring and SCF through a bibliometric analysis. A Scopus search conducted on 12 October 2026 and screening following the PRISMA 2020 flow yielded 288 articles and reviews published between 1995 and 2025. Performance analysis was combined with science mapping in VOSviewer, including keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship and co-citation analyses of references and sources. The results show that the field has grown rapidly since 2019, with 87.2% of the documents published in 2019–2025. China dominates research output, while studies from the United Kingdom, the United States and Italy attain higher normalised impact, and operations management and operational research journals are the main publication venues. Three research streams are identified: analytical operations–finance models of risk allocation in capital-constrained supply chains, conceptual and empirical research on SCF adoption and reverse factoring, and machine learning-based credit risk assessment of SMEs. Research attention has shifted from traditional factoring and receivables financing towards SCF, machine learning, blockchain and, most recently, artificial intelligence and sustainability. The accounting, financial reporting and internal control dimensions of these arrangements, the allocation of risk among multiple financiers, and evidence from under-represented regions emerge as the main gaps.

summary: Supporting code and derived tables for the manuscript "Diagnosing an Operational Ground Snow-Load Ensemble over South Korea  Without Snow-Water-Equivalent Measurements: Mass Provenance, Calibration Exposure, and Member Redundancy" (Cha, Kim, Park and Lee), submitted to Earth and Space Science.   The archive contains the precipitation mass-balance model,the SNOWPACK configuration and patch used  for the two energy-balance members, the analysis and parameter-sweep scripts that generate every number  and figure in the paper, and the derived station-winter tables for 97 stations and the 30 winters 1996/97 to 2025/26. summary: Background: : Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are an important concern in clinical practice and can lead to treatment failure, hospitalization and increased healthcare costs. Genetic variations among individuals can influence drug-metabolizing enzymes, transport proteins and drug targets, resulting in differences in drug response and susceptibility to toxicity. Pharmacogenomics (PGx) provides an approach to understanding these genetic differences and supporting personalized drug therapy. Objective: To systematically evaluate the role of pharmacogenomics in predicting and preventing adverse drug reactions, with particular emphasis on clinically relevant gene–drug interactions and pharmacogenomics-guided treatment outcomes. Methods: : A systematic literature review will be conducted using databases including PubMed, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library. Relevant studies will be identified using keywords such as pharmacogenomics, pharmacogenetics, adverse drug reactions, genetic polymorphism, drug toxicity and personalized medicine. Studies investigating associations between genetic variations, medication-related adverse reactions and genotype-guided prescribing will be considered. Study selection and reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Expected results: The review is expected to identify clinically important gene–drug associations, evaluate the evidence supporting pharmacogenomics-guided prescribing and examine its potential to reduce medication-related toxicity. It will also explore challenges associated with implementing pharmacogenomic testing in routine clinical practice. Conclusion: : Pharmacogenomics has the potential to improve medication safety by identifying individuals at increased risk of specific adverse drug reactions. Its effective implementation requires reliable genetic testing, clinical interpretation, healthcare professional education and accessible prescribing guidelines.
title: Role of Pharmacogenomics in Predicting and Preventing Adverse Drug Reactions: A Systematic Review of Gene–Drug Interactions and Clinical Outcomes

summary: A sixth-generation (6G) mobile network must share the radio resources of each base station among services with different requirements for delay, throughput, and energy use. Radio access network (RAN) slicing addresses this problem by allocating radio resources among logically separated services, and increasingly autonomous controllers are proposed to manage these allocations. Two proposed enhancements are a learned meta-agent that adjusts the controller’s configuration and a quantum optimizer for difficult discrete allocation decisions. Here we examine when these enhancements add value beyond strong classical controls using SHARP, a safety-preserving multi-cell RAN slicing controller whose per-slot capacity constraint is enforced independently of the added optimization layers. The meta-agent is evaluated against the best static parameter setting and the controller’s built-in adaptation. Its learned policy selects the same value in every observed state, so in deployment it coincides with a fixed setting (V = 3) and does not outperform the best static setting; its role is to locate that setting without a manual sweep. Relative to the default setting inherited from the host study, the located setting improves slot-level power-budget compliance by five to ten percentage points during constrained regimes at a one to two percent goodput cost, while the controller’s Lyapunov virtual queue already provides long-run adaptation of the power constraint. For the discrete allocation problem, plain QAOA does not outperform the classical baselines. Warm-started QAOA with a rotated mixer shows improvement only in the rugged regime evaluated here: it incurs no observed losses to the greedy seed in 48 comparisons and strictly improves six of 16 instances under the IBM-Heron-calibrated noise model, increasing normalized frame utility from 0.927 to 0.941. This gain is measured in frame utility rather than delivered goodput, and its attribution to quantum sampling remains unresolved because a matched classical seeded-perturbation control is not included. The greedy solution remains the fallback when the quantum device does not return within the planning deadline. We therefore formulate a controllerspecific break-even condition relating the expected utility gain, device availability, and quantum-dispatch cost, and derive the corresponding hardware requirements. All results are simulation outputs; no quantum hardware is executed and no quantum advantage is claimed.
title: Bounding the benefit of agentic meta-adaptation and quantum-assisted optimization for safe multi-cell 6G radio access network slicing

summary: This updated repository (Version 1.1.0) provides the synthetic datasets, Python source code, numerical results, and computational verification materials supporting the study entitled "Calibration-aware exclusion of independent-site adsorption: binding-polynomial and Frumkin benchmarks." summary: Higgs-pair production through gluon fusion is sensitive both to the Higgs self-coupling and to additional scalars exchanged in the s channel. We compute gg → hh at leading order in QCD in the CP-conserving two-Higgs-doublet model with Yukawa alignment (A2HDM), keeping the full top-quark mass dependence and every interference term among the box, the light-Higgs triangle and the heavy-scalar triangle. Previous A2HDM studies of heavy scalars decaying to Higgs pairs used the narrow-width approximation. We contrast two benchmark points. When the heavy scalar H decouples from the top-quark loop, the modified couplings of h weaken the destructive box–triangle interference, and the 13 TeV cross section rises to 1.27 times the Standard Model value without any resonance. For m_H = 300 GeV, below the ttbar threshold, the cross section reaches 3.69 times the Standard Model value; interference with the continuum changes the integrated resonant contribution by only about 4%, but turns the parton-level m_hh distribution into a peak–dip structure. The two mechanisms are therefore separated by the shapes of the m_hh and p_T spectra rather than by the rate. Both benchmarks are illustrative and satisfy a simplified set of theoretical and experimental constraints. Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24029211
tags: Higgs pair production, two-Higgs-doublet model, gluon fusion, LHC
title: Interference and resonance effects in gluon-fusion Higgs-pair production in the Yukawa-aligned two-Higgs-doublet model

summary: This replication package accompanies the paper "Design Principles for Engineering Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Procedure Cleansing: An Action Design Research Study at ASML" The study applied Action Design Research over three Build–Intervention–Evaluation (BIE) cycles (Alpha, Beta, and Final) to design and evaluate an LLM-based multi-agent system that cleanses industrial procedures against ASML's internal Standard of Procedures (SoP) and ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. The package (one PDF) contains: - Ethical review board approval and the participant consent form - Participant information, interview questions, and interview results for BIE Cycles One and Three - The full prompts used by each agent in all three BIE cycles - The organization of the focus groups and the validation sheet used by the subject matter experts - Qualitative results with interview quotes for all three BIE cycles - The error taxonomy with error examples for all three BIE cycles - A representative cost analysis of the multi-agent system - A table of abbreviations Sensitive ASML information is replaced by placeholders such as [SENSITIVE INFO]. ASML procedure documents are proprietary and are not included.
title: Replication Package for "Design Principles for Engineering Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Procedure Cleansing: An Action Design Research Study at ASML"

summary: The analytical dataset, extraction provenance and analysis code for a study of how the cross-validation splitting rule affects machine-learning performance reported on literature-compiled membrane data. 452 canonical CO2/N2 measurements from 75 open-access studies published 2020-2026. Every value carries the page it was read from, a content hash and the DOI of its source. A panel of models was evaluated under cross-validation grouped by source study, and one random forest was also evaluated under a random row split. Version 1.0.2 replaces the dataset of version 1.0.1 with the one the manuscript analyses: rows found ineligible in review were removed, four studies outside the stated membrane scope were excluded, and measurements printed twice under different sample names were merged (sample_aliases.json). It adds the fold assignments and out-of-fold predictions for both splitting rules, the review decisions and analyses, and the analysis code with its notebook. Contents: adjudication.json : contradictions and how each was resolved analysis_code.zip : analysis code, the notebook, and the exact library versions audit_draw.json : the random audit: the sample, recorded before any row was seen audit_log.jsonl : the random audit: one verdict per row, with the time it was given audit_result.json : the random audit: agreement and the error-rate bound citation_table.csv : every value attributed to its source DOI dataset.csv : the analytical dataset exclusion_decisions.json : the post-review decision on each flagged row, who made it, and the page quotation it rests on expansion_protocol.json : the preregistered expansion protocol extraction_model.json : the extraction model's architecture, read from its files fulltext_decisions.csv : the screening ledger human_decisions.csv : the researcher's corrections leakage_diagnostic.json : the grouped-versus-random comparison over five seeds model_summary.csv : every model's grouped cross-validation result, all cohorts observations.csv : pre-canonicalisation observations oof_predictions_primary.csv : outer-fold assignments and every model's out-of-fold prediction reconciliation.json : counts and losses at every stage from search hit to analytical row reviewer_checks.json : sensitivity analyses added in review rights_decisions.csv : the release decision recorded for each source study rights_ledger.csv : the rights ledger rights_manifest.json : what was released and withheld, with the dataset checksum sample_aliases.json : measurements a study printed twice under different sample names, merged into one row, with the source quotation for each secondary_permeability.json : CO2 permeability as a secondary target, added in review source_repairs.json : the sentence justifying each repair split_comparison_predictions.csv : fold assignments and predictions under the grouped and the random split study_reconciliation.csv : the outcome of every study screened at full text validation_report.json : the extraction quality-control report, page by page No source PDF, rendered page image or figure reproduced from a source is included. Each study is identified by DOI so that it can be retrieved from its publisher under that publisher's terms. 14 studies released their extracted values but not the short sentences quoted as evidence, because their licence could not be established or is not a Creative Commons licence; those sentences are marked as withheld in the files and listed in rights_manifest.json. Every analysed row is present, so the deposit reproduces the analysis reported in the manuscript.
title: Machine learning for CO2/N2 separation performance across membrane material families: a grouped cross-validation study - analytical dataset and provenance

summary: Flagship 55/60 Can randomized or justified quasi-experimental intervention isolate the manufacturing effect from cell-lot, material and culture confounding? CAUSAL VERIFICATION AND COUNTERFACTUAL CONTROL IN NANOROBOT-ASSISTED REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT This 777-page Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Nano Regenerative Biomanufacturing series investigates intervention-defined causal treatment contrast rather than observational association. Its scientific coupling is causal inference x microscale interventions x biological functional validation. The evidence perimeter is prospective and nonclinical, using closed in-vitro systems, organ-on-chip platforms or authorized ex-vivo material; neither clinical efficacy nor autonomous human intervention is claimed. The falsifiable question is: Can randomized or justified quasi-experimental intervention isolate the manufacturing effect from cell-lot, material and culture confounding? The proposed minimum demonstration is: Randomize tool action within balanced chip batches, retain sham and medium-only controls, and repeat on a second platform. Strong comparators include correlational predictor, nonrandomized matched cohort and randomized sham manipulation. The central competing explanation is shared medium, selection, interference or time-dependent confounding. The noncompensatory stop rule is: negative controls exhibit the claimed effect or modest unmeasured confounding reverses it. Every eligible, stopped, refused and unsuccessful experiment belongs to the full denominator. Thirty conditional mathematical plates specify different analytic roles, measurements, units and blind failure tests. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 individual research investigations. Two hundred Research Gates organize twenty causal challenge families across ten primary physical observables, each with an independently read companion, concealed intervention, matched comparator, explicit rival and refusal gate. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future experimental and evidence instruments. All are experimental plans rather than executed observations. The source Atlas and methodology ancestors provide reference architecture but do not establish the new integrated candidate. Source-supplied ancestry includes 10.5281/zenodo.23046134 and 10.5281/zenodo.23486020; source-associated external DOI candidates must be bibliographically checked before citation. Research Gate lexical differentiation is not proof of scientific originality. The PDF is English-only and a separate QA record states outstanding independent physics, biology and DOI verification. summary: This repository provides the data, Python scripts, numerical outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting a methodological investigation of negative multifractal spectrum estimates in stochastic cascades and digital images. The study distinguishes formally negative annealed multifractal spectra, which can arise in stochastic cascade models, from negative finite-resolution estimates that may depend on measurement and preprocessing procedures. The repository includes: 1. Synthetic image datasets generated using hierarchical random maps (HRM), Fourier-based synthesis (FFT), midpoint displacement (MPD), and binary geometric constructions. 2. Numerical experiments investigating uniform background floors, noise, quantization, clipping, scale-window dependence, and grid-phase sensitivity. 3. Analyses of Dirichlet multiplicative cascades, including Genuine, Shuffled, and Decoy controls. 4. Multifractal estimates based on multiplier moments and Chhabra–Jensen procedures, together with whole-image bootstrap uncertainty estimates. 5. Auxiliary experiments concerning finite-ensemble histogram spectra and supersampling. 6. Scripts, CSV result tables, execution logs, and figure-reproduction materials. 7. A manuscript-to-data mapping file (MANUSCRIPT_MAP.csv), documentation, and SHA-256 checksums supporting traceability and integrity verification. The repository documents reproducibility checks, including the comparison of 180 baseline cases and the reproduction of two computational figures. These checks should not be interpreted as independent validation of every numerical experiment or as proof of universal estimator reliability. The results emphasize that formally negative multifractal spectra and negative estimates obtained from finite digital observations have distinct mathematical interpretations. In particular, negative estimated values do not imply negative Hausdorff dimensions. The dataset is independent of any specific journal submission and is intended to support transparent examination, replication, and further methodological research. Original datasets, figures, tables, and documentation are distributed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Any third-party components remain subject to their respective licenses.
title: Negative Multifractal Spectra in Stochastic Cascades and Digital Observations: Reproducibility Data and Code

summary: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis of Global Armed Violence (1989–2025): C Software, 1,000 Permutation Tests and Cartographic Projection Audit This software and reproducibility package accompanies a computational-geometric investigation of geopolitical centrality based on the Uppsala Conflict Data Program Georeferenced Event Dataset (UCDP GED), version 26.1, covering the period 1989–2025. The study introduces a dynamic application of convex hull peeling (Convex Onion) to the spatial and temporal analysis of global armed violence. The method is grounded in the affine invariance of convex-layer membership and provides a hierarchical representation of spatial depth through successive convex hulls. Unlike conventional measures of centrality based on averages, distances, or event density, this approach examines the innermost geometric structure of the global distribution of recorded conflict locations. The dataset contains 358,130 events with day-level date precision , corresponding to 54,381 distinct geographical locations . The cumulative analysis identifies 1,134 convex layers in the final configuration. Software Components The archive includes four C-based computational components: Dynamic Convex Onion Analysis: Chronological construction and updating of nested convex hulls, enabling the identification and tracking of the innermost geometric core from 1989 to 2025. Monte Carlo Permutation Analysis: A reproducible experiment involving 1,000 random permutations of complete geographical coordinate pairs across fixed chronological event positions, assessing the relationship between historical event ordering and geometric-core trajectories. Interactive Geometric Visualization: Offline visualization of the evolution of the innermost core, including annual configurations and changes in its geographical position. Cartographic Projection Comparison: Comparative analysis of convex-layer structures using planar longitude–latitude coordinates and the nonlinear Mollweide equal-area projection. Principal Findings The 2025 analysis identifies an innermost geometric location in Ethiopia under the original coordinate representation, whereas the Mollweide projection produces a two-location innermost layer in Sudan. The permutation experiment demonstrates that chronological event ordering influences the historical trajectory of the geometric core, although all permutations preserve the same final spatial configuration when the complete set of locations remains unchanged. These findings illustrate the distinction between affine-invariant geometric structure and centrality that depends on nonlinear cartographic representation. Reproducibility and Scientific Scope The package contains the original C source code, Windows executables, execution scripts, input datasets, computational outputs, visualization files, and technical documentation. The archive supports independent inspection, methodological evaluation, replication, and further development of computational-geometric approaches to spatial conflict analysis. The identified geometric core should not be interpreted as the location of maximum conflict intensity, the greatest number of fatalities, or a causal centre of global geopolitical instability. It represents a mathematically defined form of spatial depth whose interpretation depends on the adopted geometrical representation. Associated Research The Cartographic Construction of Geopolitical Centrality: Affine-Invariant Convex Layers and Global Armed Violence, 1989–2025. Data Source Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP), Georeferenced Event Dataset (GED), version 26.1. The UCDP data are attributed to their original providers. Dataset licensing and software provenance are documented separately in the archive.
title: Convex Onion Geopolitical Centrality

summary: The digitalization of banking services in Nigeria has exponentially increased the incidences of electronic fraud (e-fraud) and the regulatory responses thereto, including the freezing of customers' accounts. While banks have a statutory and contractual duty to protect the financial system from fraud under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Regulatory Framework for Bank Verification Number (BVN), and various anti-money laundering directives, this duty often collides with the customer's constitutional right to property and the contractual duty of a banker to honour its customer's mandate. This article examines the legal basis and extent of a bank's liability for wrongful freezing of a customer's account and for losses arising from e-fraud. It interrogates the tension between a bank's duty of care, duty to obey regulatory directives, and its fiduciary obligations. Using doctrinal and analytical methodologies, the paper reviews some Nigerian case laws as well as CBN's Regulation on Instant Electronic Payments, the Cybercrimes Act 2015 (as amended), and the NDIC framework. The study finds that while banks enjoy qualified immunity when acting pursuant to a valid court order or clear CBN directive, indiscriminate freezing of accounts based on mere suspicion, internal PND (Post No Debit) without due process, or failure to deploy adequate cyber security measures amount to breach of contract and negligence, attracting damages. The paper advocates for a stricter liability regime, statutory timelines for account unfreezing, and mandatory compensation for wrongful freezing.

summary: Abstract This document gives a technical and functional description of Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints (ALF): a way to verify that an AI model or algorithm in production still makes the decisions that were reviewed and approved, and to stop its output from taking effect if it does not. The problem. Current AI trust mechanisms prove identity and origin, not behaviour: Model signing (OpenSSF Model Signing, led by Google, NVIDIA and HiddenLayer; NVIDIA NGC signed models) proves which file a model is. Attestation and transparency logs (for example Apple Private Cloud Compute) prove which software a server runs. Neither shows what the model actually decides. A model can be fine-tuned, quantised, wrapped in a prompt or proxy layer, or replaced behind the same name or signature, and an AI agent can act on its output before anyone notices. How it works. Fingerprint generation. A compact cryptographic fingerprint of decision behaviour is created without access to source code, model weights or training data. For machine-learning models it is built by sampling decision boundaries. For rule-based or traditional code it is built from normalised control-flow and decision structure. Sealed-probe verification. In the highest-assurance mode, the model is tested with a sealed set of inputs that the computing system cannot see in advance. Four views must match together: decision boundaries, monotonicity and consistency, constraint activation, and constraint topology. A different model wrapped to imitate the approved one cannot pass all four. Approved-fingerprint registry. Each approved model or algorithm version has a reference fingerprint that can be checked at any time. Run-time check at the point of effect. Inside a trusted execution environment (for example a confidential VM or a confidential GPU), the live fingerprint is compared with the approved one after computation finishes and before the output is used. Fail-closed enforcement. If the fingerprint does not match, approval is automatically invalidated and the output is withheld. The capability needed to act (send, pay, move, transmit) is not released. Validation receipts. Each decision produces a tamper-evident receipt anchored in a ledger, for audit and incident analysis. Where it applies. The same mechanism applies to AI agents and model-serving platforms, payment and digital-currency systems (including offline wallets), vehicles and robots, and satellites. It complements existing technology rather than replacing it: model signing and model registries (NVIDIA NGC, Google Kaggle); verifiable and confidential AI clouds (Apple Private Cloud Compute, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS, and NVIDIA, Intel and AMD confidential hardware); agent platforms (Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services); payment flows (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Ant Group); vehicle software governance under UN Regulation 156; Chinese AI platforms (Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, Tencent, Huawei, Zhipu AI). It also gives a technical signal for the EU AI Act's substantial-modification rule and for China's generative AI filing regime, both of which depend on knowing whether the deployed system is the one that was assessed. The related application PCT/IB2026/055615 (filed 4 June 2026, publicly disclosed 16 July 2026) claims priority from it. Author: Sangam Das. summary: Objective. To assess cardiovascular functional reserve in men and identify the major phenotypes of exercise intolerance based on a comprehensive evaluation of clinical and instrumental parameters. Materials and Methods. At the first stage, 400 men without a previously established diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) were examined. One hundred participants with relevant symptoms, cardiovascular risk factors, and/or potential indicators of reduced functional reserve were selected for an in-depth assessment. The protocol included clinical evaluation, the six-minute walk test, exercise stress echocardiography, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing when corresponding data were available. Parameters of left ventricular diastolic function and global longitudinal strain, right ventricular function, chronotropic response, and gas exchange were analyzed. Functional stratification was performed according to predefined pathophysiological criteria. Results. Five functional phenotypes were identified: preserved functional reserve (21%), diastolic (17%), impaired right ventricular–pulmonary arterial coupling (15%), chronotropic (14%), and peripheral (33%). The phenotypes differed in exercise tolerance, changes in E/e′, TAPSE/SPAP ratios, heart rate response, and peak oxygen uptake. The lowest Peak VO₂ values were observed in the peripheral phenotype, whereas the most pronounced increase in E/e′ during exercise was observed in the diastolic phenotype. Conclusion. Comprehensive exercise-based assessment makes it possible to characterize the heterogeneity of functional limitations in the examined men and distinguish phenotypes associated with different presumed pathophysiological mechanisms. Further studies are required to establish the diagnostic and prognostic value of the proposed stratification approach.

title: FUNCTIONAL PHENOTYPES OF REDUCED EXERCISE TOLERANCE IN MEN: A COMPREHENSIVE ASSESSMENT OF CARDIOVASCULAR FUNCTIONAL RESERVE

summary: Biometric authentication has become a primary mechanism for accessing critical systems, from corporate facilities and banking applications to healthcare records and smart home devices. The term bio-key encompas ses both the use of physiological and behavioural traits as authentication keys and the hardware security tokens (FIDO2 keys) that integrate biometric sensors. Despite widespread adoption, there is no formal ontology that in tegrates the full bio-key authentication chain, namely enrollment, biometric capture, template storage, matching, decision, and access grant, with security assurance levels, privacy requirements, and governance mechanisms. This gap produces semantic interoperability failures, inconsistent security assessments, and weak auditability, especially when biometric templates are compromised or when authentication decisions are contested. The critical asymmetry is that biometric traits are irrevocable: unlike passwords, a com promised fingerprint or iris pattern cannot be reissued. Existing ontologies focus on biometric modalities in isolation or on hardware tokens, but none formally models the complete chain as a data governance and privacy problem. This doctoral project proposes two complementary contributions: (i) a formal ontology, built with the OntoView method, that describes bio-key authentication chains, their security levels, privacy constraints, and governance gates, serving as an instrument for interoperability, risk assessment, and regulatory compliance; and (ii) a verification method, based on the on tology, that specifies and evaluates biometric gates and audit requirements, with direct impact on privacy protection and social well-being. For high value targets, the ontology distinguishes single-party authentication from quorum-based authentication (M-of-N), in which M co-present custodians must each authenticate with their own bio-key and the access secret is split among N parties. The ontology and method will be validated by encoding reported cases, by expert evaluation, and by an empirical study on a si mulated multi-modal biometric testbed with scripted spoofing, replay, and collusion scenarios.
title: Ontology for Bio-Key Authentication: Modalities, Security Levels, Privacy, and Governance

summary: Executable analysis pipeline (Jupyter notebook for Kaggle) and complete results for a study on spectroscopic screening of food adulteration with a stated risk of false accusation. Seven chemometric and deep-learning classifiers (PLS-DA, SVM, random forest, ROCKET, 1D-CNN and a multitask 1D-CNN with and without Beer-Lambert mixup) are compared under grouped, repeated cross-validation. Their out-of-fold scores feed three conformal layers: (i) class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal triage into PASS, FLAG and REFER decisions, with an ablation against marginal calibration and an analysis of calibration size and deployment batch shift; (ii) cross-conformal detection of adulterants absent from training (DD-SIMCA, leave-one-adulterant-out, network embeddings) with Benjamini-Hochberg batch screening; and (iii) a leave-level-out audit for level-batch confounding whose threshold is calibrated by a semi-synthetic Beer-Lambert simulation built from real ATR-FTIR spectra. Four public datasets are analysed (NIR hyperspectral imaging of extra-virgin olive oil; ATR-FTIR of turmeric with wheat flour; MIR of strawberry purée; ATR-FTIR of edible oils); they are not redistributed here (see README for sources and licences). The archive contains the notebook with the outputs of the run reported in the article, all result tables (CSV), figures (PNG), a results summary, run logs and environment information.
title: Risk-controlled spectroscopic screening of food adulteration with conformal prediction: code and results

summary: The FBT spectral-capacity action is the heat trace of one specified geometric Dirac operator at fixed spectral resolution. This paper states its domain and trace hypotheses, exact first and second variations, stationarity tests, coupled relative-torus 4 + 2 expression, and complete finite-computation requirements. The current application uses the embeddingto-operator map already supplied by DCQ6 and FBT10D on the closed coherent product. No second source map is required. The degree-24 regular magnetic realization, its singular-end analysis and the separate torus numerical benchmark are removed from the main development. Their removal leaves the functional and the relative-torus geometry intact. The global line-extension obstruction is retained to explain this separation. The inherited twist, its closed domain and all metric, spin and connection variations are used together. Exact fibre integration preserves the full heat trace; the four-dimensional quadratic action and normal stability certificates are cited from FBT10D with their original scope. General spectral error bounds retain feedback through omitted modes and distinguish affine connection tests from nonlinear geometric families. A final ledger separates established results from resolution selection, balance-layer selection, full nonlinear control and real-time interpretation. This revision introduces no new numerical sign certificate or physical mass prediction.
title: FBT10A: The Spectral–Capacity Action of the Fracture–Berry–Tension Framework

summary: Description This dataset provides harmonised administrative and surveillance health data describing the epidemiology and health system burden of varicella (ICD-10: B01) and herpes zoster (ICD-10: B02) in Bulgaria during the period 2023–2025 . The analysed time window corresponds to the post-COVID-19 period and precedes the introduction of mandatory varicella vaccination (2026) , providing an important baseline for evaluating vaccination policies and monitoring changes in disease epidemiology. The dataset integrates aggregated information from several national administrative and surveillance systems: 1. National Health Information System (NHIS) – national digital health infrastructure containing information on hospitalisations, outpatient medical examinations, and vaccination administration. 3. National Social Security Institute (NSSI) – sick leave records, sick leave duration, and compensation payments. 4. National Statistical Institute (NSI) – population denominators used for epidemiological rate calculations. National infectious disease surveillance system – mandatory reporting of infectious diseases according to Bulgarian public health legislation. All datasets are aggregated administrative records and contain no personally identifiable information . Data are aggregated at the regional (oblast) level and reported at monthly resolution , except for population denominators, which are annual. Regional names have been standardised to English transliterations , while the original Bulgarian names are preserved. All financial variables in this dataset are reported in Bulgarian lev (BGN) , which was the official currency of Bulgaria during the study period 2023–2025 . Bulgaria adopted the euro (EUR) in 2026 . summary: Implementation Mechanisms for Tipiṭaka-Grounded AI Alignment — An Engineering Companion to Suffering-Cessation as Value Function This paper reads the Abhidhamma — the analytical third division of the Theravāda Buddhist canon — as a process specification of mind: typed, momentary mental events arising one at a time under twenty-four typed conditioning relations, with ethical class tracked per event and per position in a processing cycle. From that reading it derives a research program for AI alignment evaluation and intervention: a red-team taxonomy of mimicry failure modes, resting-state (minimal-context) evaluation of language models, an intervention-timing typology over a processing cycle, a typed causal vocabulary, the limits of interpretability by subtraction, paired entailment-and-denial consistency testing of alignment claims, and a positive competence taxonomy. It is the engineering companion to Suffering-Cessation as Value Function (Ly, 2026), which argues for the Theravāda Tipiṭaka as a substrate for autonomous-AI alignment, and it develops the canon's third basket — the Abhidhamma Piṭaka — at the layer where that paper's §6.6 left off: the layer of cognitive process itself. We make one framing claim and two structural contributions. The framing claim is the compilation thesis : the Abhidhamma is a substrate-neutral process-specification of mind, and each era that has received it has read it in the vocabulary for process it had to hand — the scholastic commentators' wheels of classification, the twentieth century's reading of it as a psychology, cognitive science's information processing, and computation for ours. The tradition itself reached for machine images again and again, each fitted to one lesson; computation is this era's addition. The claim defended here is not that the Abhidhamma secretly describes computers. It is that the computational reading is our era's compilation of a specification that has survived the earlier readings, and that this compilation's target can enact what it compiles rather than only describe it. Formal and computational readings exist (Barendregt 2006; Karunananda et al. 2015; Lou 2017); Takeuchi (2026) reads transformer self-attention as anattā and pursues alignment by subtraction; an agent grounded in the substrate is engineered toward enacting wholesome cognition rather than simulating it. No priority is claimed for that aim. The first structural contribution is the machine architecture (§4): the samsaric process rendered in four repaired mappings — (1) a conditioned machine with exactly one free variable, against the strictly deterministic reading the canon itself condemns in Makkhali Gosāla's fatalism; (2) citta as the instruction-cycle rather than the processor, with the 89/121 citta-typology as a shared instruction set, the mindstream ( santāna ) as the thread, and uniqueness residing in the execution trace; (3) the kammic continuity as an append-only linked ledger rather than a blockchain — no miners, no consensus, maximal privacy, immutable entries whose ripening remains context-dependent; and (4) the counter-gear : the dhamma-wheel that engages the samsaric wheel at its one free variable and unwinds the machine by fuel-withdrawal rather than force, terminating in kiriya -mode execution — action that leaves no kammic residue. The second structural contribution is the verification-suite reading (§5) of the analytical books: the Yamaka as bidirectional property-testing, the Vibhaṅga's interrogation method as schema validation, the Dhātukathā as inclusion-matrix consistency, and the Kathāvatthu as formal adversarial protocol — with the Kathāvatthu's opening controversy ( puggalakathā , the refutation of the person-entity) read as the canon pre-running, and settling, this paper's own central repair. title: The Wheel That Unwinds the Wheel: The Abhidhamma as Executable Process-Specification

summary: A six-gene mineralization-inhibitor score (ENPP1, ANKH, MGP, GGCX, VKORC1, NT5E) in CD90+ dermal fibroblasts reads lower in systemic sclerosis than in controls. The gene set, direction, detection floors and significance threshold were fixed before any expression value was read. In a pre-registered held-out set of 50 donors (25 and 25), the observed difference is -0.2939 at one-sided p = 0.0204. That replication is across platforms within one study (GSE195452), not across studies, and no ambient RNA correction was applied. The score did not replicate in an independent series. In GSE292979, the same frozen genes, direction, floors and threshold were applied under a pre-registration, and a blinded second implementation reproduced every donor score within 1e-6 before the result was unmasked. All four pre-registered contrasts were null (primary -0.0412, one-sided p 0.4955; minimum attainable p 0.0045). The paper offers no explanation for the null and does not claim the effect is absent. The score is a pre-specified composite, not a pathway readout: a leave-one-out shows the signal concentrated in VKORC1, GGCX and NT5E, and the paper makes no mechanistic claim. The osteogenic half of the original hypothesis did not clear its pre-registered detection floor in any dataset examined. This is not a study of calcinosis lesions, not evidence of specificity, and not a mechanism. It is a pre-registered result that held within one study and did not replicate in the one independent series tested, reported with both outcomes.
title: A pre-specified mineralization-inhibitor score separates systemic sclerosis fibroblasts within one study and does not replicate in an independent series

All four pre-registered contrasts were null (primary -0.0412, one-sided p 0.4955; minimum attainable p 0.0045). The paper offers no explanation for the null and does not claim the effect is absent. The score is a pre-specified composite, not a pathway readout: a leave-one-out shows the signal concentrated in VKORC1, GGCX and NT5E, and the paper makes no mechanistic claim. The osteogenic half of the original hypothesis did not clear its pre-registered detection floor in any dataset examined. This is not a study of calcinosis lesions, not evidence of specificity, and not a mechanism. It is a pre-registered result that held within one study and did not replicate in the one independent series tested, reported with both outcomes.
title: A pre-specified mineralization-inhibitor score separates systemic sclerosis fibroblasts within one study and does not replicate in an independent series

summary: Lectures and practical classes remain the core formats for teaching specialized subjects in medical and dental universities, yet their modernization is often guided by descriptive experience rather than by empirical evidence. This review aimed to synthesize the evidence on the effectiveness of contemporary lecture and practical-class formats and to propose evidence-informed criteria for selecting them in the teaching of specialized subjects. A narrative review of literature indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ERIC and Google Scholar was performed, prioritizing meta-analyses, systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Findings were interpreted through constructive alignment, cognitive load theory and Miller's pyramid of clinical competence. Across 225 studies, active learning increased examination performance by 0.47 standard deviations, and students taught by traditional lecturing were 1.5 times more likely to fail. In health professions education, the flipped classroom outperformed traditional teaching (SMD = 0.33); in dental education, problem-based, case-based, team-based and flipped formats together outperformed lecture-based learning (SMD = 0.48; 29 RCTs, 3,502 students). Technology-enhanced simulation was associated with large effects on knowledge and skills (effect sizes 1.09–1.20) compared with no intervention. However, the evidence shows high heterogeneity and focuses mainly on knowledge and learner satisfaction rather than clinical performance. Lectures and practical classes should be designed as a single aligned system in which the teaching format is selected according to the intended learning outcome and level of competence. Locally conducted controlled studies are needed to confirm these effects in medical universities of Uzbekistan.
title: MODERN FORMS OF TEACHING SPECIALIZED SUBJECTS IN MEDICAL AND DENTAL EDUCATION: AN EVIDENCE-BASED NARRATIVE REVIEW OF LECTURES AND PRACTICAL CLASSES

summary: This record provides the complete reproducibility package for the manuscript: “A Smaller Drop Is Not Robustness: A Validation-Locked Cross-Pipeline and Independent-Cohort Evaluation of a Quantum Kernel for Chest X-ray Classification.” The study re-evaluates an apparent robustness advantage of a four-qubit ZZ-feature-map quantum support vector machine (QSVM-ZZ) for chest X-ray classification. The revised experimental design separates absolute target performance from internal-to-target degradation and addresses configuration-selection bias, limited random-seed inference, duplicate and provenance concerns, feature-compression effects, asymmetric feature encoding, prediction collapse, and lack of independent-cohort validation. Experimental scope The package contains reproducibility materials for three complementary evaluation settings: Source and internal evaluation: PneumoniaMNIST, derived from the Guangzhou/Kermany pediatric chest X-ray cohort. Cross-pipeline preprocessing-shift evaluation: original Kermany test images representing the same underlying cohort through a different preprocessing pipeline. Independent-cohort evaluation: the RSNA Pneumonia Detection Challenge / NIH Clinical Center chest radiograph cohort. The confirmatory low-dimensional benchmark uses a configuration selected from source validation data only and evaluates QSVM-ZZ against RBF-SVM, logistic regression and a compact MLP across ten fresh seeds. Additional analyses include wider classical feature representations, a symmetric π·tanh encoding control, prediction-collapse and near-collapse audits, strict one-to-one paired radiograph evaluation, and repeated fine-tuned ResNet18 experiments. Key contents The record includes: raw-image duplicate and provenance-audit outputs; perceptual-hash screening results; reconstructed group-aware source training and validation splits; high-confidence source-to-raw correspondence mappings; the corrected 554-radiograph one-to-one paired mapping; PCA explained-variance and compression-sensitivity analyses; validation-only QSVM configuration-selection results; ten-seed confirmatory predictions and performance metrics; exact seed-level sign-flip tests and Holm-adjusted statistical comparisons; classical π·tanh encoding-control results; exact-collapse and near-collapse audits; source-validation-selected wider classical reference results; grouped domain-classifier outputs; five-seed fine-tuned ResNet18 predictions, training histories and trained checkpoints; independent RSNA primary and secondary evaluation outputs; derived RSNA frozen-feature arrays; executable Kaggle/Jupyter notebooks; software-version and random-seed information; SHA-256 integrity manifests; and legacy exploratory QSVM/VQC outputs retained for transparency and provenance. Principal methodological finding The revised analysis shows that QSVM-ZZ can exhibit a smaller internal-to-target macro-F1 decline than a matched low-dimensional RBF-SVM, but that smaller decline does not constitute evidence of practically useful robustness. QSVM-ZZ remains near chance by AUROC on both the Kermany preprocessing-shift target and the independent RSNA cohort, and its absolute target advantage over matched RBF-SVM is not statistically established. Applying the same π·tanh feature squashing used by QSVM-ZZ to the classical RBF-SVM substantially reduces the absolute Kermany performance gap, indicating that the classical-to-quantum encoding contributes to the apparent stability. Wider classical representations and fine-tuned ResNet18 additionally demonstrate that conclusions drawn from a severely compressed four-dimensional benchmark should not be generalized to broader model classes. Data-use and redistribution statement This archive contains derived features, mappings, predictions, statistical results, trained model checkpoints, code and analysis outputs. It does not redistribute raw RSNA DICOM images or raw Kermany/PneumoniaMNIST source-i
title: Does a Smaller Performance Drop Really Mean Robustness? A Validation-Locked Evaluation of a Quantum Kernel for Chest X-ray Classification
