summary: Acute respiratory infections in children comprise etiologically and clinically heterogeneous diseases with overlapping early manifestations, whereas the risk of respiratory failure and other adverse outcomes varies according to age, premorbid conditions, and the causative pathogen. This review aims to analyze current approaches to etiological diagnosis and evidence-based risk factors for severe disease in children. An analytical search covered PubMed/MEDLINE and documents issued by the World Health Organization and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence for 2015-2026. Priority was given to guidelines, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, diagnostic accuracy studies, and large cohorts. Clinical assessment identifies the anatomical level of respiratory involvement and current severity but cannot reliably establish viral etiology. Nucleic acid amplification remains the most sensitive method for detecting most respiratory viruses. Diagnostic value depends on the timing and quality of specimen collection, panel composition, and clinical context; a positive multiplex result does not establish the causal contribution of every detected agent. Serology has a limited role in an acute episode. Consistently reported baseline risk factors include young age, prematurity, chronic lung disease, hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, neurological disorders, immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive treatment, and malnutrition. Hypoxemia, apnea, progressive respiratory distress, feeding inability, altered consciousness, and impaired perfusion indicate evolving organ dysfunction and require immediate assessment. Reliable prediction should integrate baseline risk factors with dynamic clinical variables. Any prediction model requires independent validation in the pediatric population for which its use is intended.
title: Acute Respiratory Infections in Children: Current Approaches to Etiological Diagnosis and Prediction of Severe Disease (Literature Review).

A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. summary: This paper outlines a comparative structural framework for analyzing how judicial rulings from supranational courts (specifically the CJEU under Article 267 TFEU preliminary references and the ECHR) systematically transform domestic policy parameters without explicit legislative mandates.   Adapted specifically to the institutional mechanics of the French legal order, the framework operationalizes four key structural components:   Judicial Displacement (JD): The structural mechanism through which supranational courts assume primary interpretative authority over national policy, constrained in France by Article 55 of the Constitution.   Administrative Gradualism (AG): The incremental realignment of domestic policy through an iterative sequence of secondary executive and regulatory instruments (décrets, arrêtés, circulaires, and administrative guidance) issued by ministries and independent regulatory bodies (e.g., CNIL, ARCOM).   The Mandate Scale (M_0–M_3): A heuristic metric assessing the spectrum of explicit democratic authorization present within electoral manifestos, winning coalitions, or direct referendums regarding supranational constraints.   Four-Step Operational Cycle: A recurring sequence mapping the trajectory from supranational judicial trigger \rightarrow national administrative response (expanding, reclaiming, or accommodating) \rightarrow democratic legitimacy deficits (input, throughput, output) \rightarrow systemic political outcomes (evolutionary pushback via contrôle de conventionnalité or systemic backlash).   The paper includes a comparative matrix contrasting UK statutory mechanism (HRA 1998, Statutory Instruments) against French constitutional pathways (Sarran, Nicolo, Article 38 ordonnances), along with a rigorous methodology defining a "True-Negative Profile" to test boundary conditions against selection bias.  Note on Origin & Systemic Scope: This publication represents an operational draft outline designed to establish baseline terminology, structural mechanics, and theoretical metrics for ongoing comparative legal research.   This work is a direct spin-off and structural adaptation of the foundational framework established in: Davidson, C. K. S., Judicial Displacement and Administrative Gradualism, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24023708.    While the original benchmark paper evaluated these dynamics within a dualist, parliamentary context (specifically United Kingdom immigration policy and prisoner voting rights under ECHR jurisprudence), this adaptation recalibrates the core analytical model to the monist-leaning, semi-presidential institutional architecture of the French Fifth Republic under Article 55 of the 1958 French Constitution.    This draft serves as the immediate European adaptation within a broader comparative research agenda, with future planned adaptations extending the framework to examine administrative realignments, executive rule-making, and judicial review dynamics within the United States constitutional framework.

title: Supranational Integration, Administrative Gradualism, and Democratic Legitimacy — A Comparative European Structural Model (French Adaptation)

summary: This analysis examines how computational configuration choices shape resource efficiency in confidential genomic collaboration across institutions. A descriptive secondary analysis uses 14 PRINCESS benchmark configurations published in 2017, comprising seven batch sizes evaluated with compression enabled and disabled across three sites. Matched runtime differences, ratios and joint memory comparisons identify configuration tradeoffs. With compression enabled, increasing batch size from 100 to 10,000 variants reduces runtime by 75.49 percent, while expansion to one million variants provides only 0.38 percent further improvement despite requiring 32.69 times as much memory. Without compression, runtime reaches its observed minimum at 8,000 variants and subsequently increases. Compression enabled records longer enclave runtime in every matched pair. These patterns reveal diminishing processing gains and configuration dependent resource tradeoffs, without isolating their underlying mechanisms. The contribution is a comparative interpretation distinguishing faster execution from economical resource use. The findings refine a resource constraint perspective and support joint evaluation of execution time and memory when configuring protected genomic workflows, with numerical recommendations bounded by the observed benchmark environment.
title: BENCHMARKING CONFIDENTIAL GENOMIC COMPUTING EFFICIENCY THROUGH BATCH SIZE, COMPRESSION, AND MEMORY USE ACROSS COLLABORATIVE SITES

summary: This paper proposes Recursive Anticipatory Argumentation-Control Theory (RAACT), an interdisciplinary framework for representing argumentative discourse as a dynamic, par- tially observed, and recursively updated interaction system. Its central mechanism, Recur- sive Anticipatory Argument-Path Interception (RAAPI), combines contextual observation, pragmatic-linguistic encoding, argument reconstruction, opponent-state estimation, proba- bilistic argument-path forecasting, formal refutation verification, anticipatory intervention, and feedback-based model revision. The framework is developed around the Pre-emptive Refutation Fork Case (PRFC), a primary analytical case in which one participant forecasts an opponent's possible argumenta- tive move and presents a logically evaluated counterargument before that move is explicitly advanced. Subsequent responses are classified into continuation, substitution, qualification, forecast challenge, clarification, and novel argumentative pathways. The mathematical specification introduces latent-state models, observation functions, categorical predictive distributions, Bayesian belief updating, intervention-utility functions, estimation errors, and forecast-evaluation metrics. Conditional mathematical propositions identify what can be established under explicit assumptions, while empirical hypotheses dis- tinguish predictive accuracy from intervention effectiveness and strategic response restriction. RAACT is presented as a formal theoretical architecture and a research program, not as an empirically validated universal law. Its principal scientific obligations are to demonstrate incremental predictive value, establish causal effects under an identifiable research design, prove specific mathematical claims under stated assumptions, and identify boundary conditions through counterexamples and independent replication. Keywords: argumentation theory; linguistic pragmatics; anticipatory reasoning; pre-emptive refutation; cybernetics; feedback control; state estimation; Bayesian forecasting; formal logic; strategic discourse; falsifiability.

summary: Replication materials for “AI and Intergenerational Spirals in Repair Knowledge” by Laurentiu Guinea. The paper develops a three-period overlapping-generations model in which young people choose independent practice or AI delegation, middle-aged people correct mistaken learning beliefs and rebuild skills, and older people repair goods and transmit instructions. The package reproduces the intergenerational spiral, partial-diffusion and stochastic extensions, and the two-product analysis. It contains MATLAB and R scripts, independent Python verification, numerical outputs, manuscript sources and figures, and a descriptive analysis of Open Repair Alliance data. Model parameters are illustrative; the repair records do not estimate or causally test the behavioural mechanism. Instructions and software requirements are included in the README files. summary: Two Hamiltonian systems that share almost nothing in their physical origins turn out to behave identically once their local structure near a 2:1 internal resonance is examined. One system models a pair of flexural modes in a micromechanical resonator through coupled Duffing oscillators. The other models the stretch–bend Fermi resonance of a molecule such as carbon dioxide through a Morse oscillator coupled to a harmonic bend. Both possess an elliptic equilibrium, equal Krein signatures, a frequency ratio close to 2:1, and a cubic resonant coupling. These shared features place them in the same resonant normal-form type, a difference resonance that confines energy exchange rather than driving escape. On the conserved polyad fixed by an initial excitation that places nearly all the energy in the higher-frequency mode, the truncated normal form of any such system collapses to a one-degree-of-freedom problem that depends on only two numbers: a scaled detuning and a scaled anharmonic curvature. Consequently the largest fraction of energy that can be transferred to the lower mode is given by a universal curve whose edges are independent of the curvature. All of the necessary invariants are computed directly from each Hamiltonian before any trajectory is integrated. Numerical integration then confirms the predictions. When the curvature is small the systems follow the one-parameter curve; when it is large they follow the two-parameter curve to high accuracy. A beam whose quartic coefficient is deliberately softened until its curvature matches that of the molecular model reproduces the molecular exchange curve directly, even though the remaining normal-form coefficients differ. An ensemble of sixty randomly drawn members of the same type likewise collapses onto the appropriate universal curve. The residual discrepancy grows roughly linearly with excitation amplitude, as expected from the truncation of the normal form. Two controls mark the boundaries of the result. Reversing one Krein signature converts the same frequency window from bounded exchange into unbounded escape. Weak viscous damping reduces the transferred fraction in the manner predicted by a correspondingly damped reduced model. A quantum treatment of the truncated normal form introduces the polyad number as a third invariant; the lowest Fermi dyad therefore follows a distinct quantum curve rather than the classical one. The findings remain local, confined to two-mode models, and classical except where the quantum analogue is stated explicitly. Within those limits they demonstrate that a dimensionless exchange relation established for one physical system can be transferred to an unrelated system once both have been rescaled by invariants computed from their own Hamiltonians.
title: The Beam That Behaves Like a Molecule

summary: This archive holds the data and code behind the manuscript “Five Inexpensive Checks for Machine-Learned Enzyme Turnover-Number Predictors” by Fatih Aktas and Farida Rahayu. The protocol defines five checks for machine-learned predictors of the enzyme turnover number. They use supplied prediction columns and one measured panel. The five checks are a scale audit, the mutation-response ratio, a kinetics-untrained baseline floor, transfer to external data, and a calibration check. The protocol is applied to six published predictors. The data span 1,571 variants from 130 database-derived campaigns, 23,500 variants from eight deep mutational scans, and two panels of measured turnover numbers. The archive contains the analysis scripts, the JSON output of each script, the extracted datasets, the tables and figures, a README with the execution order, a REPRODUCE guide, and a dated pre-specification note. All kinetic measurements and all model predictions come from the EnzyArena benchmark (Zeng et al., bioRxiv 2026, doi:10.64898/2026.03.29.715152). No new measurements were made. The benchmark release is not redistributed here. Software: Python 3.13, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, RDKit 2026.9.1, Matplotlib 3.11.
title: Data and code for five checks on machine-learned enzyme kcat predictors

summary: This repository contains the analytical datasets, Python scripts, numerical outputs, plots and reproducibility documentation accompanying the manuscript Can strontium isotopes track changing mobility patterns? Evidence from La Tène Central Europe. The repository is intended to support transparent evaluation, replication and further comparative research on Iron Age mobility, life histories and the relationship between human movement and regional geological environments. The repository supports reproduction of the downstream statistical analyses, including: Cemetery-level isotope distributions and local/non-local classifications. Individual-level mobility estimates using two complementary classification rules: Rule A (any sampled tooth potentially non-local) and Rule B (one predefined permanent reference tooth). Mixed-effects logistic models evaluating chronological, demographic and burial material-group associations while accounting for repeated teeth from the same individual. Sensitivity analyses, paired-tooth comparisons and reconstruction of childhood strontium exposure histories. Cross-cemetery isotope comparisons and relationships between lithological diversity and strontium variability at 1, 5, 10 and 20 km spatial scales. Reproducible analytical plots and numerical verification against the published supplementary results.
title: Strontium isotopes and mobility in La Tène Central Europe: analytical data, Python code and reproducibility materials

summary: forelint is an open-source Python library that checks what a forecasting backtest score hides, before anyone acts on it. Leakage between related series: GroupTimeSplit holds out the future of entities the model never saw, and split_optimism reports how much random, group and time-only splits overstate accuracy against it. Run-to-run noise floor: noise_floor measures the spread of repeated runs and the smallest difference that exceeds it. Model comparison across many series: Diebold-Mariano with the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction on long-format panels, and the model confidence set of Hansen, Lunde and Nason (2011). Backtest audit: per-item bias, tracking signal, error concentration, MASE and RMSSE, and forecast value added against a baseline, broken down by demand class (smooth, erratic, intermittent, lumpy), with stockout periods excluded from scoring. On one store of the public M5 data, backtested at ten non-overlapping forecast origins, a gradient-boosting model was 3.9% worse than a 28-day moving average on absolute error and worse on 58% of items. By demand class it added +5.0% on smooth items and lost −10.5% on intermittent and −9.2% on lumpy ones. Source: github.com/davidmashiah/forelint . Author: David Mashiah .
title: forelint: lint your forecast backtests before you trust a score

summary: Dataset of the paper Toward universal excited-state machine-learned potentials: a local excitation Hamiltonian for size consistency and transferability (P. Friederich). TD-DFT (ωB97X-D/6-31G*, full linear response, TURBOMOLE 7.5.1) labels for 303,061 geometries of 106,933 closed-shell organic molecules with C, H, N, O, F (and S in some dyes and ladder molecules): S0 energies and forces, the ten lowest singlet excitation energies with oscillator strengths, and analytic S1, S2, and S3 forces. Geometries: QCDGE minima, thermal geometries from GFN2-xTB dynamics at 300–1000 K, geometries from model-driven S1/S2 dynamics (four active-learning rounds), and test molecules beyond the training distribution (larger molecules from ZINC, dyes from two experimental databases, homologous ladder series up to 30 heavy atoms). Also included: S1–S3 forces at equilibrium geometries of 2,499 test molecules; pairs of molecules at 2.5–20 Å with TD-DFT dimer spectra; twelve TD-ωB97X-D S1 reference trajectories with initial conditions and a validity flag; Löwdin hole and electron populations and charge-transfer numbers of the ten roots for 25,808 geometries; and the TURBOMOLE input and output files (without MO files) of 200,445 calculations. The file README.md describes all files, fields, units, and splits.
title: TD-ωB97X-D excited-state energies and forces of 106,933 molecules at equilibrium, thermal, and excited-state geometries

summary: Delay-Doppler (DD) modulations, such as Zak-transform-based orthogonal time frequency space (Zak-OTFS) modulation, represent the channel as a sparse set of delay and Doppler shifts, which makes them well suited for radar sensing. Sensing with a single DD frame, however, is unambiguous only when the channel spread factor, i.e., the product of the delay and Doppler spreads, is less then one. Long-range mobility scenarios, including drones, airplanes, low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites, and underwater acoustic links, typically violate this crystallization condition, so that a single frame aliases the target delays, Doppler shifts, or both. Existing methods add a time-frequency pilot to a conventional DD frame, resolve the aliasing in only one dimension, and assume integer delays and Doppler shifts. We propose a frame design that combines multiple DD bases with different delay and Doppler periods, which together cover an overspread channel with fractional delays and Doppler shifts, using the same bandwidth and frame size. We show that modular arithmetic on the peak positions uniquely recovers each target by pairing the peaks through their common projection and their gains, and we derive the condition under which this pairing is ambiguous. We implement the design with two superimposed Zak-OTFS frames and propose two receivers: dual-frame sensing (DS), which performs the joint detection directly, and DS with cross-pilot cancellation (DS-XC), which additionally cancels the cross-pilot interference, re-estimates the gains by joint least squares, and removes ghost targets. Both receivers maintain a detection rate close to one as the spread factor grows, and DS-XC also achieves the lowest false-alarm rate and channel estimation error among all the compared systems. In a 100 km drone scenario, DS-XC outperforms all baselines, with a complexity that grows near-linearly with the time-bandwidth product.
title: Sensing Fast and Distant Targets in Fractional Overspread Channels with Zak-OTFS and Modular Arithmetic

summary: The scarcity of labeled underwater acoustic data limits the development of data-driven models for marine acoustic monitoring, motivating the use of self-supervised learning to exploit the abundance of unlabeled recordings. However, large-scale data alone does not guarantee effective representation learning, because model performance is strongly influenced by the distribution of the training data. To facilitate such training data, this study introduces a scalable curation pipeline that curates 3,000 hours from 41 years of raw NOAA hydrophone recordings, producing MarineSet, a large-scale and diverse dataset designed for underwater acoustic learning. A baseline model, MarineNet, trained on MarineSet achieves competitive performance on marine mammal call and ship-type classification, highlighting the value of systematic data curation for developing self-supervised learning models in underwater acoustics.
title: MarineSet: Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Data Curation and evaluation

summary: The transmission of shock waves generated by underwater electrical foil explosions across solid materials with varying acoustic impedances and thicknesses is investigated. Copper foils with thicknesses of 10 and 18 $μ$m are exploded on planar substrates of aluminum, copper, and 3D-printed PLA with thicknesses up to 5 mm using a multi-gigawatt pulsed-power electrical discharge. The resulting shocks are visualized in water using high-speed shadowgraphy at 5 million frames per second, while high-resolution fiber optic hydrophone measurements provide direct quantitative measurements of shock strength after transmission through the impedance-mismatched materials. One-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations are used to reproduce the foil explosion dynamics and provide insight into the thermodynamic, acoustic, and electrical properties of the foil during the explosion. The results show that shock transmission is governed not only by the impedance mismatch at the solid--water interface but also by the finite thickness and dynamic response of the supporting material. These findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding and controlling shock transmission in underwater electrical foil explosions and establish the feasibility and limitations of using solid substrates as structural supports in complex shock-generating geometries.
title: Shock wave transmission across solid-water interfaces in underwater electrical foil explosions

summary: This dataset provides the numerical inputs, source code, reference results, and reproduction workflow accompanying “Light in Light Bubbles — Gravitational Light in the Phraqtal Field” ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23652779 ). Version 2.0 preserves the numerical baseline of version 0.2: stationary-core calculations, regime-channel coupling, integrated gravitational-source calculations, static three-knot comparisons, constrained-curvature diagnostics, and analytical examples for tension-front energy, arrival geometry, and conditional golden-ratio relations. Original numerical programs, input fields, parameters, dependencies, and comparison tolerances remain unchanged. The historical Google Colab replay of October 27, 2026, passed 11 comparison groups and 3,055 checks within the declared tolerances. Its verification records are retained as historical evidence, not presented as a newly executed version-2.0 numerical replay. The extension adds the complete expanded German manuscript and 110 finite exact algebraic controls for magnetic twist organization, the constitutive magnetization readout, source variations, and a conditional magnetic–gravitational response. These controls distinguish directed organization from quadratic source contributions and retain the direct source term in the response calculation. No new core, regime-chain, numerical field-response, or physical-time field-evolution calculations were performed for this extension. The magnetic readout remains an explicit constitutive model choice; its physical calibration and validation against measurements remain open. The algebraic controls do not establish a measured magnetic response or derive the numerical value of Newton’s gravitational constant. The single-cell Colab notebook defaults to integrity checks and the new algebraic extension. Replaying the historical numerical calculations is optional. Release instructions and the new executable interface are in English. The expanded manuscript is in German; the original English manuscript is also retained. The package includes checksums, claim-to-material mappings, and separate historical and extension verification records.
title: Light in Light Bubbles — Reproduction Data and Code for Gravitational Light in the Phraqtal Field

summary: When a phone fails and its owner keeps the messaging account running on a second device, the account's history can end up in two archives, each intact and each missing what the other holds. We call this Temporal Communication Fragmentation (TCF), a loss by non-union: no message is deleted, but the platform offers no operation that joins the two halves. WhatsApp's own documentation states that old and new chats cannot be merged. We define TCF by three jointly necessary and sufficient conditions and specify CARTA 1.1, a framework for reconstructing one archive from several. CARTA is an output contract owed to a reader who cannot check the result. Records that cannot be read unambiguously are quarantined with a typed reason, and a report gives each record's provenance, the conflicts and deduplication ambiguities found, and every setting used. We evaluated a reference implementation, CHAMP-Pipeline, on synthetic fragment sets with known ground truth. With its declared date inference it reproduced the ground truth in all 4,500 configurations of a parameter sweep; the invariants and the predicted outcome held in all 5,000 random configurations of two to four fragments; and reconstruction stayed exact at one million messages. A zone-offset advisory, frozen before testing, flagged all 2,800 misdeclared zones in a designed test of overlapping fragment pairs and 1,470 of 1,542 in random configurations, and raised false alarms in 2 of 600 correctly declared runs. A systematic search found 60 chat-merging tools; none fully provides more than 2 of the five output properties CARTA specifies. With a fragment's time zone left undeclared, every benchmarked tool and CHAMP-Pipeline produce the same duplicated and misdated records, and only CHAMP-Pipeline's report says so. All data are synthetic; no real archive has been reconstructed.
title: When Chats Split Apart: Formalizing Temporal Communication Fragmentation and the CARTA Reconstruction Framework

summary: Code, input-distribution parameters, and all Monte Carlo and sensitivity outputs for the manuscript "A multilayer probabilistic influence model of train driver human error probability and system-level failure probability: Monte Carlo simulation and input-factor sensitivity analysis" (submitted to Reliability Engineering & System Safety). The package reproduces every table and figure of the paper. It contains the 17 input distributions of Table 1 (params/inputs.yaml), the link coefficients of Eqs. (3)-(13) (params/links.yaml), the point values of the three deterministic case studies (params/cases.yaml), the model itself (src/model.py), and the scripts for the Latin hypercube Monte Carlo simulation (300,000 iterations, fixed seed), the one-at-a-time and Sobol' sensitivity analyses, the threshold analysis, and the parametric interval analysis. Version 1.1 adds the analyses of the revised manuscript: the decomposition of the mean output, the convergence and bootstrap intervals of the Sobol' indices, the scenario analysis of the structural estimates, a simplified barrier layer (params/comparison.yaml), and a comparison with 27 events from published investigation reports (params/incident_cases.yaml). Running src/run_all.py regenerates all outputs in under two minutes; tests/test_cases.py and tests/test_tables.py check the results against the values reported in the manuscript. Every parameter is traceable to a published open statistic or a literature effect coefficient, listed with its source and access date in data/sources.csv. summary: We propose the interrogative investment hypothesis: the basic interrogative forms can serve as units for describing how individuals come to differ in cognitive competence. These forms fall into two levels. Questions of object (what, where, who, when, how many) carve reality into aspects; questions of reason (how, why) relate these aspects and underlie methods of inquiry such as the historical and scientific methods. Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences offers a rich description of these differences; we propose a complementary developmental mechanism that may help explain how its profiles take shape. In line with Hayes's (1962) motivational-experiential theory of intelligence, we suggest that its domains are strengthened, at least in part, through investment. A spontaneous preference for one kind of question draws attention and time toward it; because time is scarce, this produces cumulative practice, growing competence and increasing reward, which strengthens the preference in turn. We discuss where such preferences may come from: inherited dispositions, early ability, the answers children receive, and culture. Hayes's experience-producing drives were never operationalised; we suggest that question preferences could provide one possible behavioural indicator of them. We propose a simple task to capture these preferences, a pilot study with explicit criteria for failure, and five testable predictions. Finally, we draw implications for education: questions show where a child's attention goes before competence is visible, one object can be taught through many questions, and the way adults answer may shape which questions grow. The proposal is theoretical; no data have been collected.   Version 5. Adds a section on the origins of question preferences with a fifth prediction, a pilot study with criteria for failure, and a section on implications for education.
title: Questions as Units of Cognitive Investment: An Interrogative Investment Hypothesis of Individual Differences

summary: Code and derived data for the measurement of Monte Carlo ensembles of a fire-front-oriented wildfire cellular automaton on commodity processors. summary: Version 4.0.0 provides code and numerical evidence supporting manuscript V13, "Auditing Integrity Enforcement in Biometric Verification". It contains the unchanged original service, a separately identified strict verification path, portable execution and reanalysis, two paired five-seed campaigns with FaceNet and OpenCV SFace, target-attributed offline audit, structural checks, measured HTTP latency and authenticated-log scaling, scientific figures and Appendices A-F. Each backend has 4,840 scored responses across four configurations. Each configuration has 1,100 specified fault attempts; detected/enforced counts are 51/51 (minimal), 400/400 (conventional subset), 650/550 (full original) and 1,100/1,100 (strict). Clean requests and two trust-boundary negative-control classes are reported separately. The primary records retain coarse collector flags; final analysis explicitly attributes the B10 composed log-rollback alarm to the targeted history. Raw primary responses are unchanged, and collection-time analysis is preserved. The current strict path has 620 complete scored normal-return traces. The median paired strict-minus-minimal latency is 173.90 ms for FaceNet and 83.35 ms for SFace on the recorded CPU host. The study evaluates one application family and a selected scenario set under trusted application code, keys and reference state. It does not establish population attack probabilities, production-cloud security, presentation liveness, durable distributed state or hostile-host attestation. The separately implemented auditor is part of the same AI-assisted study, not an independent laboratory replication. Earlier historical campaigns and engineering pilots are not pooled with the new experiments. No source photographs, reusable biometric vectors, pretrained weights, private keys or private author contact sheet are included. Inputs are acquired separately from documented upstream sources and identified by SHA-256. AT&T Laboratories Cambridge is acknowledged. Available records contain no institutional ethics approval/waiver for this secondary ORL analysis and no original participant consent documentation; no approval, waiver or unrestricted image redistribution permission is claimed. Historical original inputs remain at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23820425. Earlier V12 analysis is at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24043762. summary: Claims about acoustic keystroke side channels, attacks that infer typed content from the sound of a keyboard, are difficult to compare because studies differ in recording conditions, data splits, and how defenses are tested. This paper presents OpenKeystroke, an open source research platform for authorized acoustic side-channel experiments and privacy-defense evaluation. The platform measures how much class information survives in short acoustic transients, and how much signal transformations (defenses) reduce it, under a strict evaluation protocol: session, device, and environment-disjoint splits with leakage checks, train-only fitting of preprocessing statistics, validation-only model selection, cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired comparisons across repeated seeds. Defenses are labelled effective only when they produce a significant accuracy drop, over at least three seeds, against both a static attacker and an adaptive attacker who knows the defense is applied. The platform ships eight classification models and six defenses behind one experiment lifecycle shared by a command line interface, a Python API, and an interactive dashboard. On a synthetic benchmark, headline accuracy degrades materially under domain shift, and several defenses that appear strong against a static attacker largely fail against an adaptive one, which is exactly the gap the platform exists to expose. OpenKeystroke operates only on predefined, non-sensitive acoustic categories in controlled or explicitly consented data. It does not reconstruct typed text, passwords, or messages.
title: OpenKeystroke: An Open Research Platform for Acoustic Side-Channel Experiments and Privacy-Defense Evaluation

summary: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) to infer particle formation rate J(t) and size-dependent growth rate GR(d, t) from parallel differential mobility analyzer (DMA) particle size distribution counts measured in the CERN CLOUD (Cosmics Leaving OUtdoor Droplets) chamber experiments. The PINN is trained on measured counts and constrained by the aerosol general dynamic equation (GDE), with nucleation expressed as a boundary flux at 1.7 nm. For baseline benchmark comparison, the notebook also includes a Python re-implementation of the Julia-based extended Kalman filter and fixed-interval smoother from Ozon et al. (2021). Both methods are evaluated on four simulated cases with known truth (0000_00 to 0000_03) and the three CLOUD experiments (1802_01, 1952_02, 1906_03). For the CLOUD runs, results are compared with the independent PSM (J) and INSIDE (GR) estimates reported in the paper. BAYROSOL 1.1 data is downloaded directly from Zenodo within the notebook (Ozon, Stolzenburg and Dada, 2021, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4450492 , MIT license), so no additional data files are appended.
title: PINN Inference of Aerosol Formation and Growth Rates from CLOUD Chamber Data

summary: Pre-specified reanalysis of public human arteriovenous fistula single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE305423) along with bulk RNA-sequencing data (GSE220796, GSE119296). The repository contains the analysis pipeline, fixed random seed (2611), pinned environment, all result tables cited in the article, and a numeric-provenance assertion script that re-derives every number quoted in the manuscript from the result files. Main findings: apparent transcriptional signatures of maturation failure are dominated by changes in cell composition (including ambient-RNA-driven artefacts) rather than cell-intrinsic reprogramming; myofibroblast abundance, fate bias and matrisome programmes are unchanged within the detectable effect range.
title: Analysis code for: Cell composition accounts for much of the transcriptomic difference between failed and matured human arteriovenous fistulas

F152 | MICROSCALE NONINVASIVE CELL-MEMBRANE-POTENTIAL READOUT AT THE LIMIT — Treats noninvasive cell-membrane voltage as an inverse measurement problem; tests capacitive loading, optical reporting lag, transmembrane polarity, geometry and membrane-surrogate leakage against direct voltage truth. F153 | QUANTUM MAGNETOMETRY AND NEURAL ELECTRICAL SIGNAL COUPLING AT THE LIMIT — Compares magnetometer responses to independently known neural-like current sources while testing coil leakage, cross-axis sensitivity, gradiometer common-mode noise, timing uncertainty and localization ambiguity. summary: STARLI | FLAGSHIP 13 FISSION Ten Research Design Monographs | Flagships 141-150 / 300 Author: 33  |  White Rainbow Epoch  |  Research Design Working Edition v1.2 This ten-volume STARLI series examines trustworthy AI-assisted micro/nanorobotic experiments and nano-quantum measurement systems. The common research question is how to bind physical observation, decision authority, calibration uncertainty, and independently reconstructable evidence without mistaking computational confidence for experimental proof. Each volume is a 777-page English, nonclinical prospective research design containing 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 separately paginated research studies, 200 Research Gates with six mechanistic annotations, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Across the ten volumes, the collection contains 300 research plates, 820 chapters, 4,100 study pages, 2,000 Research Gates, and 330 Phoenix candidates. Research scope by flagship F141 | Microrobotic Autonomous Control Authority Envelope at the Limit — Defines physical authority envelopes for microrobotic control, including credential expiry, actuator veto, permission transfer, and independently observed safe stopping. F142 | AI Nano-Quantum System Trustworthy Refusal Decision at the Limit — Studies when an AI-guided nano-quantum system must refuse action, separating calibrated abstention from indiscriminate rejection and unsafe confidence. F143 | Microscale Autonomous Experimental Design at the Limit — Examines autonomous microscale experimental design under specimen, information, energy, and permission budgets, with causal identification and independent replication. F144 | AI Quantum Sensing Uncertainty Calibration at the Limit — Investigates calibration of quantum-sensing uncertainty, including shared drift, covariance, phase ambiguity, photon budgets, and fair classical comparisons. F145 | Nanorobotic Closed-Loop Control Replayability at the Limit — Tests whether nanorobotic closed-loop decisions can be replayed from raw sensor data, actuator histories, calibration versions, and unselected failures. F146 | AI-Driven Microscale Active Sampling at the Limit — Designs AI-driven active sampling experiments that jointly measure analyte recovery, physical disturbance, resource cost, and contamination under blinded controls. F147 | Nano-Quantum System Human Review Mechanism at the Limit — Evaluates human review of nano-quantum decisions through signed authority, contradictory permissions, case-level uncertainty, and independent physical vetoes. F148 | AI Autonomous Research Agent Safety Boundary at the Limit — Defines safety boundaries for autonomous research agents across instrument access, sample authorization, unsafe tool composition, and immutable evidence. F149 | Microrobotic Autonomous System Interlaboratory Generalization at the Limit — Tests transfer of frozen microrobotic protocols between laboratories with different geometries, materials, calibration trees, operators, and failure environments. F150 | AI Nano-Quantum Trustworthy Autonomous Laboratory at the Limit — Integrates sample custody, microrobotic actuation, quantum/classical readouts, controlled autonomy, human oversight, and cross-site evidence reconstruction. Scientific boundary and publication status These books provide falsifiable research questions, candidate mathematical models, prospective blinded tests, competing explanations, negative-result criteria, and successor research interfaces. They do not report performed experiments or establish clinical efficacy, autonomous deployment safety, or quantum advantage. Independent expert verification of physical assumptions, formula applicability, all bibliographic relationships, and the scientific independence of closely related designs remains necessary. summary: STARLI | F131–F140 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · AI-Guided Micro/Nanosystems, Sampling and Validation Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.1 / Gate Annotation v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview These ten STARLI flagship monographs form an AI, nanosystems and microfluidic research-design collection in the second volume of the Flagship 13 Fission atlas. The studies connect adaptive sampling, counterfactual inference, autonomous calibration, hybrid physical-learning models, failure prediction, interpretable quantum sensing, closed-loop latency, multi-agent coordination, external digital-twin validation and biological signal drift. Each volume defines a prospective measurement target and competing explanation. No result is claimed to be experimentally demonstrated. The collection contains ten separately authored 777-page English working editions: 300 prospective mathematical plates, 820 chapter openers, 4,100 separately paginated study positions, 2,000 Research Gates with six annotation fields per Gate, and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. These counts describe the publication structure, not validated scientific novelty. A companion publication ZIP includes the ten original PDFs and ten per-book Zenodo introductions. The Ten Research Directions F131  AI-Driven Microfluidic Sampling Strategy Optimization At The Limit — Examines recoverable analyte as a fraction of input under fixed sampling resources. Expert tuning with equal trials is the comparator; hidden human intervention is the rival. Blind recovery audits and out-of-distribution refusal test whether AI planning adds genuine value. F132  Nano-Quantum System Counterfactual Inference At The Limit — Tests held-out, intervention-specific counterfactual prediction error while retaining constraint-violation safeguards. Frozen open-loop policies anchor comparison; training-test leakage and nonreplayable observation-to-action chains can invalidate apparent autonomy. F133  AI-Driven Microrobotic Autonomous Calibration At The Limit — Uses blind-standard calibration bias after autonomous correction as a physical measurement target. Preregistered experimental design is the baseline. Extra experimental trials and any action outside the authority envelope defeat a claimed improvement. F134  Microscale Physical Model and Neural Network Coupling At The Limit — Challenges coupled learning and physical models against independently measured conservation residuals under withheld shifts. Matched expert tuning and hidden manual intervention are alternative explanations; unsafe confidence outside the tested domain is a stop condition. F135  AI-Driven Nanoscale Sampling Failure Prediction At The Limit — Proposes prospective fault warning lead time, in seconds, at a fixed false-alarm rate. Frozen open-loop policies and unselected failure cases distinguish early warning from hindsight leakage. Recovery outcomes and complete action replay remain necessary. F136  Quantum Sensor Interpretable AI At The Limit — Asks whether AI explanations agree with mechanism-specific physical ablations, rather than merely producing plausible narratives. The proposed witness is an agreement fraction, with counterfactual error and calibrated sensing as safeguards. More experimental trials are a competing account. F137  Microrobotic Closed-Loop Control Latency At The Limit — Measures the full sensor-to-physical-action delay, in seconds, inside a declared operating envelope. Expert-tuned controls under matched resources establish the comparison. Hidden human intervention and high-confidence out-of-domain action must be ruled out. F138  AI Multi-Agent Sampling Mission Coordination At The Limit — Evaluates calibration-adjusted joint sampling mission completion as a fraction under fairness and safety vetoes. Frozen open-loop coordination and identical observation

summary: Reproducibility materials for "Operating Constraints Shape Portfolio Value in Phased Metro Flood Protection", version 1.3.2. This version adds Supplemental Notes A–E to the original Supplemental Materials. The combined PDF contains 40 pages: the original 33-page material with Tables S1–S35, Figs. S1–S4, and Supplementary Methods, followed by seven pages of additional data and operating evidence, identification checks, sequencing comparisons, annualization sensitivities, and tail diagnostics. The first 33 pages and their numerical results are unchanged from version 1.3.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23969774). The unchanged computational addendum contains protocols, code, seeds, selected station sets, unrounded results, and verification records. It supplements the baseline analysis (version 1.1.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22969483). The original LaTeX source archive constructs the original 33-page part; the editable Word source for the appended seven-page Notes is supplied separately. A release README and SHA-256 checksums document the complete file set. The annualized quantity represents the service deficit of an annual-maximum three-hour representative storm under a common exposure; it is not calibrated cumulative passenger loss. Population is a demand proxy. Station response, dependence, protection, and short-turn service are model assumptions. Source attribution and the original license terms are retained.

summary: This package contains the Python code used to obtain, process, and analyze the data for the article "Coca, Armed Violence, and Drug Seizures in Colombia: Spatial and Temporal Evidence on Territorial Security". The study examines how coca cultivation, recorded armed violence, and drug seizures were related across 1,121 Colombian municipal units between 2020 and 2024, with an extended window from 2016. It combines spatial autocorrelation analysis (global and local Moran statistics with permutation inference and false discovery rate control) with Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood models that include municipality and year fixed effects. Data. The package does not redistribute data. All inputs are public official sources downloaded by the code itself: - Coca area by municipality (Ministry of Justice and Law / UNODC Integrated Illicit Crops Monitoring System, datos.gov.co). - Homicides, terrorism acts, cocaine and coca base seizures, and manual eradication (Ministry of National Defense, datos.gov.co). - Presumed homicides, definitive figures (National Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, datos.gov.co). - Armed conflict events (National Center for Historical Memory, SIEVCAC, datos.gov.co). - PDET municipalities (Territorial Renewal Agency, datos.gov.co). - Population projections, census-based poverty index, and 2023 municipal boundaries (DANE). The download script records the access date and SHA-256 hash of every file. Open-data portals are updated continuously, so later downloads may include revised records. The analyses reported in the article used files downloaded on November 7, 2026. Contents: - scripts/01_download.py: downloads the official datasets. - scripts/02_inspect.py: audits the raw files (structure, periods, codes, units, duplicates). - scripts/03_build_panel.py: builds the municipality-year panel (DANE DIVIPOLA codes, 2015–2024) and a data-quality report. - scripts/04_spatial_prep.py: prepares municipal geometries and spatial weights (queen contiguity and six nearest neighbors). - scripts/05_analysis.py: descriptive statistics, spatial autocorrelation, fixed-effects Poisson models, robustness checks, and seizure analyses. - scripts/08_revision_analyses.py: contrasts for concrete changes in coca area, exploratory equivalence tests, within/between (correlated random effects) models, first-difference models, extended-window sensitivity, and sample composition. - scripts/10_revision2_analyses.py: composition of the armed conflict event index, contiguity-constrained spatial clusters for robust inference, and alternative population specifications. - requirements.txt and README.md: software requirements and run instructions. Usage. Install Python 3.12 and the packages in requirements.txt, then run the scripts in numerical order from the package folder. Results are written as CSV files to results/ and logs to logs/. Inference is descriptive and associational. The code does not identify causal effects.
title: Replication code: coca cultivation, armed violence, and drug seizures in Colombian municipalities, 2016–2024

summary: Overview Part 20 of 20. This is version 2 of the dataset. The source list, the tar file names and the split into parts are the same as in version 1. All images were generated again with a new model, EBGSv2. The dataset contains 2,981,033 synthetic Euclid VIS images. Each image corresponds to one source in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. The sources lie in the Euclid DR1 footprint, and most of them are BGS Bright and BGS Faint photometric targets. The model input is the DESI r- and z-band cutout. Changes from version 1 Item Version 1 This version Model EBGS: trained on DESI–Euclid cutout pairs centred on BGS targets (66,359 training pairs) EBGSv2: trained on patches cut from full Euclid Q1 MER tiles (not centred on galaxies) PSF conditioning None DESI r- and z-band PSF size as input; Euclid PSF fixed to one reference PSF Sampling 10 reverse steps; 3 trajectories share the first 70% of the steps and then run independently; the released image is the mean of the 3 trajectories 50 reverse steps; one trajectory HDUs Prediction, DESI_IMG, PREDICTION_STD Prediction, DESI_IMG; no PREDICTION_STD WCS None In both HDUs Noise model None Parameters in the header give a 1σ uncertainty for each pixel File organisation The dataset has 1,235 tar archives, grouped by HEALPix pixel (nside = 64, NESTED ordering). The archive names, the sources in each archive and the part that holds each archive are the same as in version 1. Each archive holds flat FITS files named <RA>_<DEC>.fits , in decimal degrees. This record holds 52 archives with 127,059 files, covering RA 349.8° to 99.9° (across RA = 0) and Dec −66.8° to −35.7°. It starts from the DESI r-band image and is conditioned on the DESI z-band image. The training data come from 304 Euclid Q1 MER tiles. A further 16 tiles were used for validation and 24 tiles were held out for testing. None of these 40 tiles was used in training. The training target is the background-subtracted MER VIS mosaic (BGSUB). The generated images have the same pixel units, with an AB zero point of 24.6. We use the EMA weights at training step 68,931. This checkpoint has the lowest reduced χ² on the validation set. summary: Event-level Sentinel-2 burned-area dataset of western Canada and the results of a leave-one-province-out benchmark of fourteen segmentation configurations (revised study, version 2.0). Contents: 135 windows of about 20 x 20 km at 10 m in Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan (120 windows centred on large fires of 2022-2024 and 15 fire-free windows), each a single post-fire Sentinel-2 Level-2A scene stacked as nine layers (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, NDVI, NBR, NDMI; GeoTIFF, 32-bit float) with a reference raster derived from the National Burned Area Composite (burned / unburned / ignored) and a no-data mask; the window manifest with scene provenance (product identifiers, processing baseline, clear and masked fractions, fire identifiers); the fold file of the three leave-one-province-out folds (training, validation and test role of every window); the per-window results of every configuration and label-free rule; and the predicted burned-unburned maps of all 1,890 window-model pairs. Code, environment specification and summary tables are in the companion GitHub repository; the trained models are in a separate Zenodo record. Sources: Copernicus Sentinel-2 data (ESA), National Burned Area Composite (Natural Resources Canada, Canadian Forest Service; Open Government Licence - Canada). Files. data_postfire_AB.tar, data_postfire_BC.tar, data_postfire_SK.tar (one per province, 45 windows each, 6.9-7.1 GB each): for every window <window_id>_S2.tif (nine layers, float32, masked pixels NaN), <window_id>_label.tif (0 unburned, 1 burned, 255 ignored) and <window_id>_scl.tif (scene classification layer), plus manifest.csv. data_prefire_AB.tar, data_prefire_BC.tar, data_prefire_SK.tar (6.8-6.9 GB each): the pre-fire scene of every window used by the dNBR baselines, <window_id>_S2pre.tif and <window_id>_scl_pre.tif, plus manifest_prefire.csv. predicted_maps.tar.gz (74 MB): the predicted burned-unburned maps of the 1,890 window-model pairs, maps/<run>/<window_id>_pred.tif (8-bit). results_and_manifests.zip : the per-window results of every configuration and label-free rule, the summary tables, the run ledger and both manifests. burned-area-segmentation-western-canada-v2.0.zip : snapshot of the companion repository at tag v2.0 (code, fold file, manifests, per-window results, tables). SHA256SUMS_release.txt : SHA-256 of every file in this record and in the checkpoint record. Companion to the manuscript "Remote sensing of burned-area delineation with Sentinel-2: a leave-one-province-out multi-model semantic segmentation benchmark across western Canada" (M. S. Khan, H. Afzaal, G. S. Randhawa, A. A. Farooque; in revision at Computers & Geosciences).
title: Sentinel-2 burned-area segmentation benchmark for western Canada (v2.0): dataset, reference rasters, fold file, per-window results and predicted maps

Two five-theme research units contain ten English 777-page working editions: 300 mathematical model plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study designs, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The third-pass Gate edition separately addresses causal mechanisms, orthogonal physical witnesses, masked refutation, competing explanations, hard failure evidence and successor experiments. Structural counts do not certify scientific novelty or physical validation. Research Unit I · F221–F225 F221 OPTICAL PHASE CONTROL AND MICROSCALE LOCALIZATION AT THE LIMIT — Challenges interferometric optical-phase localization with independently registered fiducials, wavefront reversals, detector reference drift and photon-matched free-space baselines. Reports phase and position residuals alongside photothermal rise; apparent field enhancement is not by itself a localization gain. F222 NANOMATERIALS QUANTUM DEFECT ENGINEERING AT THE LIMIT — Tests defect creation, charge states, spin coherence, surface passivation and unselected emitter yield against a geometry-matched classical materials stack. Annealing, sorting bias, substrate strain and thermal cross-sensitivity are live rivals. A bright selected specimen cannot establish manufacturing yield. F223 MICROSCALE PHOTOTHERMAL CONVERSION SAFETY AT THE LIMIT — Constrains photothermal conversion in sealed microfluidic reference systems through spatially independent microthermometry, absorbed-power accounting, duty-cycle variation and physical shutdown tests. Geometry, convection and detector lag compete with any proposed material advantage; local temperature and dose vetoes are noncompensable. F224 QUANTUM OPTICAL MICROROBOTIC NAVIGATION AT THE LIMIT — Compares optically tracked microrobot navigation with free-space reference localization at equal photon and motion budgets. Beacon-phase drift, image interpolation, occlusion, flow reversal and independent trajectory truth challenge seemingly superior tracking; phase stability cannot replace physical pose evidence. F225 NANOPHOTONIC MATERIALS SURFACE AGING AT THE LIMIT — Investigates biofluid, humidity, salt, photooxidation and package-stress ageing of nanophotonic material surfaces. Tracks chemical state, adhesion, insertion loss, intrinsic versus loaded quality factor and functional yield on unselected devices. Survivor selection and bulk-index drift remain rival explanations. SECOND RESEARCH UNIT / SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE & SUCCESSION Research Unit II · F226–F230 F226 PHOTONIC-CRYSTAL MICROFLUIDIC SENSING AT THE LIMIT — Tests photonic-crystal microfluidic sensing against a commercial chip under equal optical power using concealed pressure, ionic and fouling challenges. Separate chemical standards, cavity linewidth, insertion loss and complete sensor-array yield distinguish analyte binding from channel deformation, thermal drift or bulk-index change. F227 NANO-OPTICAL FIELD MULTI-TARGET MANIPULATION AT THE LIMIT — Examines whether optical-field control can manipulate several microscale targets without hidden collision, cross-trap force, laser dose or thermal burden. Independent trap stiffness, site-resolved power and trajectory evidence challenge field interference, hydrodynamic coupling and postselected successful handoffs. F228 QUANTUM-MATERIAL BIOINTERFACE DECOHERENCE AT THE LIMIT — Tests quantum-emitter and spin-defect coherence during controlled biofluid exposure, distinguishing interfacial magnetic noise or redox chemistry from optical blinking, microwave heating, matrix aggregation and strain. Spin relaxation, emission spectra and chemical fate require independent witnesses under unselected lot transfer. F229 MICROSCALE OPTICAL READOUT CROSSTALK AT THE LIMIT — Measures spectral, spatial, polarization, electronic and thermal crosstalk in multiplexed optical readouts. Masked reference-channel swaps, dark controls, detector-bias perturbations and leakage spectra separate real target sensing from optical spillover, ADC alias and common laser noise. F230 NANOPHOTONIC SENSOR AUTONOMOUS CALIBRATION AT THE LIMIT — Challenges autonomous photonic sensor calibration with concealed wavelength-standard ageing, swapped physical references, out-of-distribution laser drift and held-out chips. Independent laboratories must reproduce the calibration accept/abstain decision; clock, package and photon-budget artefacts remain possible rivals. Physical Scope, Falsifiability & Evidence Status All proposals are restricted to synthetic standards, traceable materials, closed chips, authorized ex-vivo references, microfluidic phantoms and bench-scale tests. Comparators should be optimized under matched sample, photon, energy, time and analysis budgets. An unselected trial denominator, calibrated orthogonal witnesses, concealed perturbations and non-negotiable stop conditions are essential. A favorable optical signal never overrides photothermal injury, sample identity loss, physical uncertainty or evidence-provenance failure. Published mechanisms, mathematical relations and candidate flagship claims are kept distinct. The mother research-design source, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23318840, is editorial and methodological ancestry, not experimental verification. External article DOI anchors originate from the flagship atlas; title, author, publication metadata and source-to-claim relevance still require independent confirmation. The original atlas sometimes pairs a mathematical formula with an endpoint that does not directly follow from that formula; specialist physical reconciliation, unit review and per-claim literature verification remain pending. Research Gate Evolution & QA Boundary First-pass questions were challenged by rival mechanism designs before a third-pass rewrite of six scientific annotations. Across 2,000 final Gates, exact textual checks found no fully duplicated questions or complete six-panel notes; two closely similar question texts and recurring shared scientific-method sentences remain on the QA review list. Text novelty cannot establish physical mechanism independence. These volumes report research designs, not measured performance. summary: Does the governance of climate money behave like the governance of a ration card? The Map of Maps of Governance (Tailwinds 2026-02) proposed seven rules for how success and failure move through Indian institutions. This companion to Tailwinds 2026-10 takes the rules out of India for the first time and tests them, in a registered analysis, on the full portfolio of the Green Climate Fund (372 projects, frozen 12 October 2026). Three rules could be tested on the Fund's records; four were declared untestable before any result was seen. One rule holds. Islands: work moved out of the routine, high-discretion track succeeds, and projects on the Fund's Simplified Approval Process reach first disbursement 5.4 months sooner than regular proposals (8.8 against 14.1 months; 90 percent interval −7.3 to −2.9), in every run. Two rules fail. Downhill: delay does not fall harder on the most vulnerable countries (+0.6 months, −2.0 to 2.8). Broker: international intermediaries do not carry more of the money where vulnerability is higher; they carry about four-fifths of it everywhere (79.6 against 81.4 percent). The fast lane is faster, and it is not fairer: inside it, the most vulnerable third of countries waits 1.4 months longer than the least, against 0.2 months on the regular track. The rules travel in part. Where they fail, they fail for a reason the map can use: between countries, a fund's queue runs through its intermediaries, which serve every country alike. The tail that Downhill predicts lies inside countries, where the Fund's record cannot see.
title: The fast lane and the long chain: Why the Green Climate Fund's simplified track speeds money to the ground but does not make it fairer, and what the Map of Maps of Governance learns from its first test outside India

summary: The release behind the five-seed ablation study and its paper. It adds multi-epoch training, an epsilon schedule derived from episode counts, the re-flip restriction and a Gallager-B baseline; it carries the ablation's configurations, generated records and analysis scripts, and the weights of the paper's final policy, so every table, figure and number of the paper regenerates from the repository. The new mechanisms are opt-in, but the 64x128 curricula changed (see Changed), so results are not comparable bit for bit with the 1.1.x series: regenerate rather than mix. Added Five-seed ablation. The design is frozen in docs/ablation/PROTOCOL.md , with the record of how it was run. scripts/make_ablation_configs.py writes its 41 cells under config/ablation_config/ : curriculum and replay seeding crossed, at one and three epochs, on five seeds, plus a one-seed control that holds epsilon at its floor after the first epoch. scripts/aggregate_ablation.py writes docs/ablation/RESULTS.md and RESULTS.json ; scripts/analyze_ablation_details.py writes DETAILS.md , DETAILS.json and learning_curves.csv . config/ablation_checks/ holds the replicate that reproduced a suspended cell bit for bit. Evaluation-only configurations. The pipeline now evaluates a config with no model when it enables baselines explicitly, scoring those alone. Three generated trees use it: config/epoch_eval/ scores the earlier epoch checkpoints of the three-epoch cells ( scripts/make_epoch_eval_configs.py ), config/baseline_eval/ scores Gallager-B on every seed's held-out splits ( scripts/make_baseline_eval_configs.py ), and config/final_eval/ re-scores the final policy from its saved weights ( scripts/make_final_eval_configs.py ). Gallager-B baseline. Hard-input message passing in src/advanced/gallager_b.py , exposed as the gallager_b agent. Its flip thresholds are chosen on training words by scripts/select_gallager_b_thresholds.py , recorded in docs/ablation/GALLAGER_B_SELECTION.md . Decoder cost benchmark. scripts/benchmark_decoders.py measures latency on GPU and CPU, operations per frame and batched throughput for the agent and the baselines, after checking each sampled frame against the recorded evaluation; records go to docs/ablation/benchmark/ . Agent and Min-Sum combined. scripts/cascade_minsum_agent.py runs Min-Sum, the agent on Min-Sum's failures and Min-Sum again; scripts/cascade_controls.py replaces the agent with cheaper alternatives. Records go to docs/ablation/cascade/ . Minimum-distance certificate. scripts/verify_min_distance.py proves $d_{\min} = 14$ for 64x128 by exhaustive enumeration on two information sets, in about a second. The same check identifies the matrix as the CCSDS (128,64) telecommand code. The paper's generators. scripts/paper/ writes every table, figure and quoted number of the paper from the records under docs/ablation/ , in seconds and without a GPU; its README maps the condition IDs to the paper's names. scripts/summarize_development_chain.py , scripts/record_wall_clock.py and scripts/extract_example_episode.py write the remaining records it reads. Final-policy weights. The five trained networks of NoC_NoE3ep (18 MB) under models/ablation/ , so the final policy's evaluation, the cost benchmark and the Min-Sum combination rerun without training. max_errors on uniform_ber . An opt-in cap: the generator redraws any pattern heavier than it, so a BER model can be held inside the code's correction radius. Every 64x128 dataset config sets it to 6. Epochs as a first-class axis. Training is partitioned by (epoch, phase) segment, every training episode carries a run-global episode_id and its epoch , and the training analyses report per epoch. Epsilon fields accept one row per epoch. training.save_epoch_checkpoints keeps the weights at each epoch boundary so epochs can be scored separately. epsilon_decay: "auto_episodes" . Sets epsilon from the fraction of each phase completed, counted in episodes, reaching epsilon_min after epsilon_anne
title: LDPC Decoding via Deep Reinforcement Learning

summary: The 42 trained model checkpoints of the leave-one-province-out burned-area segmentation benchmark for western Canada (revised study, version 2.0): fourteen configurations (U-Net, DeepLabV3, PSPNet and DeepLabV3+ with ResNet-50 encoders, UPerNet with a ConvNeXt-T encoder, SegFormer MiT-B2, SAM-LoRA ViT-B, Mask2Former Swin-L, Prithvi-EO-2.0 300M fully fine-tuned and with LoRA adapters, TerraMind-1.0 base, and the plain-cross-entropy contrast of U-Net, DeepLabV3 and PSPNet) trained once in each of the three folds F-AB, F-BC and F-SK on single post-fire Sentinel-2 scenes with National Burned Area Composite reference labels. Each checkpoint (best validation epoch, PyTorch state dictionary) comes with its run configuration, normalisation statistics, training log and SHA-256 checksum. The dataset, fold file and results are in a separate Zenodo record; the code that loads and applies the checkpoints is in the companion GitHub repository. Files. <run>_best.pt for the 42 runs (<configuration>_F-AB, _F-BC and _F-SK; the suffix _C2 marks the plain-cross-entropy contrast runs), 98 MB to 1.3 GB each and 16.1 GB in total: PyTorch checkpoints holding the model state dictionary, the epoch and the validation score of the best epoch. run_folders.zip : config.json (all arguments and the training, validation and test window lists), norm_stats.json, log.csv (per-epoch log) and ledger.json of every run, and run_ledger.csv (best validation F1, epochs, SHA-256 of the checkpoint, finishing time, wall time, GPU). burned-area-segmentation-western-canada-v2.0.zip : snapshot of the companion repository at tag v2.0, whose models.py builds each architecture and whose eval.py loads a checkpoint and predicts a window. SHA256SUMS_release.txt : SHA-256 of every file in this record and in the dataset record. Companion to the manuscript "Remote sensing of burned-area delineation with Sentinel-2: a leave-one-province-out multi-model semantic segmentation benchmark across western Canada" (M. S. Khan, H. Afzaal, G. S. Randhawa, A. A. Farooque; in revision at Computers & Geosciences).
title: Sentinel-2 burned-area segmentation benchmark for western Canada (v2.0): trained model checkpoints

summary: Code and data that build a corpus of 1.84 million research articles from 256 engineering journals (2015-2025) from OpenAlex, recover missing abstracts, measure word use in abstracts and in a sample of full texts, and estimate departures from pre-2023 trends after the release of ChatGPT.
title: Replication package: What Changed in Engineering Writing After Generative AI Chat Assistants

summary: Medical microbiology occupies an unusual position in the medical curriculum: its objects are almost never seen directly, yet graduates must reason about them from stains, colonies, reaction patterns, and laboratory reports. Methodological guidance in Uzbekistan and the wider Russian-language literature typically responds with lists of criteria for choosing teaching technologies. This article argues that such lists, however sound their individual items, conceal a structural problem, because they treat criteria of different logical kinds as if they could be traded against one another. Using a conceptual model-building design, the study derives eight selection criteria from the literature, sorts them into three tiers (non-compensatory gates, discipline-specific epistemic criteria, and calibration criteria) and applies an explicit 0–2 affordance appraisal to ten teaching technologies. Two of the eight criteria proved relational: they describe a match between a technology and an outcome or a cohort and cannot be scored as properties of the technology. Of the 60 attributable judgements, 26 were conditional rather than direct. Additive totals favoured case analysis, problem-based tasks, and laboratory work, yet only concept mapping and comparison tables cleared both the feasibility and the assessability thresholds unconditionally. The resulting coupling principle holds that a technology chosen for its inferential demand should be paired with one that leaves an assessable trace. The model is offered as an analytic proposal for empirical testing, not as evidence of differential effectiveness.
title: TEACHING THE INVISIBLE: A CONSTRAINT-FIRST DECISION MODEL FOR SELECTING PEDAGOGICAL TECHNOLOGIES IN MEDICAL MICROBIOLOGY

summary: Replication code for the reanalysis reported in the Nature Food manuscript "Strong El Nino events and thin inventories drive concentrated tropical crop losses and uneven world price transmission". Version 1.2.0 reconciles the early-warning record: the earlier v1 episode table (5/8, P=0.118) is renamed superseded_v1_episode_binomial_tests.csv and the current RONI result (RONI_episode_binomial_tests.csv, 2/8, P=0.85) is the reported figure, with the key findings and README updated accordingly, and the deprecated PART 1 of task15_analysis.py marked. The archive contains scripts for the official NOAA RONI and ONI (ERSSTv6), five-season event classification, local projections with block bootstrap, production and phenology regressions, smallholder income decomposition, farm-gate pass-through, macro controls and robustness checks, plus result tables. All inputs are public and no data were generated by the authors.
title: Replication code: Strong El Nino events and thin inventories drive concentrated tropical crop losses and uneven world price transmission

summary: A product hook in copy-data.mjs , and the 0.15.003 plant counts base scripts only (found by CEFOP_DinHot's adoption of 0.15.004: it adapted copy-data.mjs to ship a benchmark document, model metrics and released model cards, and the plant refused its test of that script). The plants are in tests/adversarial/test_adoption_defects_0_15_005.py ; requirements CT-041 and CT-042. Added frontend/scripts/copy-data.mjs calls an optional, product-owned module frontend/scripts/copy-data.product.mjs once, after the declared files are copied into the rebuilt overlay, with { derived, out, repo, readiness } ( readiness is the parsed readiness document or null ). It returns { copied, absent, problems } , arrays of strings: the paths (relative to public/data ) it copied, the paths it leaves out as declared absent (each printed as a WARN line), and the problems that stop the build. The build stops with exit 1 on a problem, on a throw, on a result of another shape, on a reported path that is absolute or leaves public/data , and on a copied file that is not there; the summary line counts what the hook copied. A declared file that is missing still stops the build before the hook runs. No module: the output is that of 0.15.004. frontend/src/lib/copy-data.test.ts , a base test of the script (it says "A product takes this file verbatim"): one case per behaviour above. summary: Data and code for computational prioritization of MYB–NFIB and MYBL1–NFIB junction peptides in adenoid cystic carcinoma. The primary analysis screens 284 public RNA-sequencing libraries and evaluates 3,746 observations representing 3,122 peptide–HLA pairs from 63 reconstructed contexts. Same-observation affinity-percentile and unflanked eluted-ligand rank cutoffs of ≤2% select 57 pairs (34 sequences) supported by 27 libraries, including an 11-pair provisional testing panel. The corrected analysis uses a consistent donor-frame translation rule. A separately reported HLA suffix-relaxed analysis evaluates 7,370 observations and selects 111 pairs, including a 26-pair sensitivity panel. Normal-peptide controls, native-flank comparisons, source annotations, conditional donor-support analyses and reconstruction checks retain their respective scopes; the resource does not provide complete native-context scoring of every normal-control combination or definitive donor attribution. This package includes the checked manuscript and supplement with updated public data links, 133 scientific tables with a 135-sheet workbook, figures, analysis code, saved prediction outputs and reproduction checks. Scientific data, code and outputs are unchanged from the clean 5 November package. Licensed executables, model weights, bulk sequencing reads and accession-linked genetic comparisons are not redistributed. Predictions prioritize experimental testing.
title: Selecting MYB–NFIB and MYBL1–NFIB junction peptides for experimental testing in adenoid cystic carcinoma

summary: Version 5.1.0 reproducibility package for “Feasibility and Portability of Model-Based Duty-Cycle Grades for Marine Fuel Cells” by Eun-Hye Park, Hyo-Chan Kwon and Eun-Joo Park. This complete archive contains executable Python sources, synthetic inputs, frozen computational protocols, numerical tables, selected actual simulated waveforms, first-party figures, provenance and independent numerical checks. It preserves all 827 files of the version-5 numerical baseline at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24037253 and adds 16 disclosure and verification files. No scientific model, input, physical threshold, representative selection or original numerical result is changed. New in v5.1: - Complete five-setting, eight-seed stationary non-Gaussian diagnostic results for 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1 Hz plus exact identity transfer, with signed prediction-error means and seed ranges for both telegraph processes and their phase-randomized controls. At 0.01 Hz, the symmetric and asymmetric telegraph mean errors are +94.2606% and +120.1515%. These separate periodic distribution tests are counterexamples to a general Gaussian absolute-increment accuracy claim, not error bounds for physically screened voyages or estimates of physical aging error. - Explicit calculation conventions: 131,072 samples at 4 Hz, the ideal continuous transfer on the periodic Fourier grid, all circular one-second increments at a 0.25-second stride, and no final voyage-reporting Butterworth filter. The final constrained grades continue to use directly evaluated voyage increments and dwell times. - A fresh isolated execution of the unchanged diagnostic. Its 160 raw rows, 20 summary rows and metadata matched the baseline byte for byte; independent reaggregation from the raw moments had a maximum discrepancy of 1.11e-16 in fractional prediction error. - Clarified field-evidence wording: MS Mariella supports ferry installation and ship-network commissioning tests; the separate Pa-X-ell land-module aging observation is not an at-sea aging slope. - Explicit remaining limitations: universal single-coordinate EMS sufficiency and measured aging equivalence are not established; compatible empirical marine coefficient calibration, confidence intervals and covariance are unavailable; the original PLECS project remains unavailable, and no new OpenModelica/PLECS execution has been performed. Start with README_v5_1.md and ADDENDUM_v5_1_EN.md or ADDENDUM_v5_1_KO.md. Run “python -B verify_v5_1.py” for file integrity. Run “python -B disclosure_v5_1/reproduce_diagnostic.py --scratch ../diagnostic_fresh” for a fresh diagnostic; the scratch directory must be new and outside the extracted archive. Integrity checks do not execute scientific calculations. Original numerical exceptions, failure records and previous-version metadata remain preserved. Publication-status clarification: this ZIP is deposited byte-for-byte as prepared before publication. The “local submission supplement”, “no new DOI” and null publication-identifier statements in README_v5_1.md, release_metadata_v5_1.json and the two ADDENDUM_v5_1 files record that preparation-time state. This Zenodo version publishes those identical v5.1 bytes and supersedes only that historical publication-status wording. The version-5 DOI above continues to identify the earlier numerical baseline; the DOI assigned to this record identifies this version-5.1 archive. The record’s current access and publication state are authoritative. Scope: finite synthetic computational assessment under a phenomenological scalar loss index, a lossless battery and reduced oxygen dynamics. No measured vessel dataset, physical stack-aging validation, hardware qualification or universal grade claim is supplied. Manuscripts, response letters and third-party full papers or standards are excluded; included PDF files are first-party computational figures and overviews. License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.
title: Reproducibility package for Feasibility and Portability of Model-Based Duty-Cycle Grades for Marine Fuel Cells
