summary: I propose an organizing model of the formal mind as knowledge and experience: reusable observations and techniques, and the lived history from which they develop. Skills are techniques trained through experience; habits are repeated patterns rather than a third substance. I call the architecture these processes train the metastructure: a proposed organization of heuristics, reconstruction, anticipation, and usable continuity of thought, not a newly identified neural network. The model predicts that relevant learning can reduce both avoidable errors and stalled thinking, while fixation and bodily disruption can limit or reverse that benefit. I also argue that bodily sensation, presence, and practical constraints matter as much to the person as mental personality. My earlier phrase “more than half” is a qualitative generalization about that interplay, not a measured percentage. The account draws on memory research, expertise, predictive processing, and interoception without treating their findings as proof of the whole model. Eight predictions and two proposed studies distinguish the organizing assumptions from testable consequences. Companion manuscripts address incomplete knowledge of costs, socially shaped wanting, association between perspectives, and the deliberate experience of ordinary boredom; those connections are proposals rather than independent evidence. No new data are reported.
title: The Mind as Knowledge and Experience: Accumulation, Thought Block, and Bodily Presence in Choice

summary: Bees play a crucial role in human agriculture, making the accurate characterization of their behavior essential. In the field of automatic bee traffic tracking, individual monitoring has been prevalent in the past two decades to collect detailed data on foraging behavior. To support analysis, these data must be classified into entry and exit events, and assembled into flight trajectories. However, existing classification methods largely consider only simple exits and entrances, which ignore the existence of U-turn or guarding movements which represent a non-trivial fraction of bee activity at the hive entrance. Identifying these movements as compound events is necessary to accurately track all movements over time while avoiding classifications which may produce misleading movement records. In this presentation, we analyze existing event classification methods to evaluate their accuracy for two different types of movements: simple and compound. We then propose extended event classification methods that explicitly account for compound events, enabling more accurate reconstruction of bee traffic dynamics.
tags: bee traffic monitoring; compound event detection; computer vision; artificial intelligence; precision agriculture;
title: The Relevance of Compound Events in Bee Traffic Monitoring

summary: Bayesian inference is a predictive act. This book builds it from three ideas: de Finetti supplies the structure, writing exchangeable beliefs as mixtures of independent laws; Sanov supplies the asymptotics, the exponential concentration of empirical measures at a rate given by the Kullback Leibler divergence; and Bayes supplies the updating, an exponential tilt of the predictive law. Together they give a tilted de Finetti theorem: conditioning an exchangeable sequence on empirical moment constraints yields predictive laws that are I projections of a baseline measure, so parameters emerge as limits of empirical functionals and maximum entropy appears as a predictive limit rather than a postulate. Testing, shrinkage, asymptotics and decision are then read on one moderate deviation scale. Results the book proves, most first stated in the authors' papers with Daniel Zantedeschi and Jyotishka Datta: a finite sample total variation bound between a block drawn under a moment window and independent draws from the I projection, and the projected de Finetti limit behind it; a split of the predictive Kullback Leibler Bayes risk into a Sanov term and a posterior contraction term,; a condition for a scalar learning rate to calibrate credible sets at moderate scale, namely that model curvature and score covariance be proportional; one control variate form for Bayes linear and prediction powered inference estimators, with the optimal gain in closed form; the global posterior of federated learning as a product of local experts under exchangeability; and a convergence rate for the policy that maximizes posterior expected utility in generative Bayesian computation. Several results are stated conditionally or as open problems, and the book says which. Later chapters treat computation, universal portfolios, causal machine learning and medicine. Scripts reproducing every computed figure and number are in the repository.
title: Elements of Bayes and Information Theory: A Predictive Theory of Inference: Information, Algorithms, and Large Deviations

summary: Thermal Quantum Annealing (tQuA) is a quantum architecture in which a system coupled non-adiabatically to a thermodynamic reservoir evolves toward the thermal Gibbs state of a target Hamiltonian . This paper provides a rigorous and honest foundation for tQuA and its extension to Quantum Intelligent Matrix Methods (QIMM). We distinguish carefully among Theorems (proved in the cited literature, with proofs reproduced in Appendices A–D where necessary), Propositions (with explicitly identified gaps), Conjectures (with open steps), and Numerical Results (simulation evidence, explicitly labeled as obtained on a classical surrogate or on a quantum emulator). The work delivers four contributions. (1) Convergence, correctly scoped. A five-pillar chain establishes that, under the stated Born–Markov and Ohmic-bath assumptions, tQuA converges in trace norm to the unique Gibbs state from any initial condition, without Hamiltonian-adiabatic scheduling, and that the transition rate out of every local minimum is strictly positive at any finite . Ground-state convergence requires a cooling schedule whose rate is bounded by the spectral gap (Theorem 8), or, for the engineered-dissipation family ED-tQuA, follows directly from the dark-state condition (Theorem 7). (2) Honest scaling benchmarks, corrected. On a classical diagonal surrogate, the v2/v6 claim of a flat gap and a clean power law is corrected. At finite temperature ( ), the surrogate gap decays as : polynomial in the Hilbert dimension but exponential in qubit count . At low temperature ( ), the chain is numerically frozen; the value is attributable to a single-transition rate . The surrogate is exact for diagonal and deviates by for off-diagonal perturbation of size (Proposition 2 and Corollary). The trajectory (400 steps, §4.5) remains valid as a short-run diagnostic. (3) Engineered-dissipation tQuA. For the engineered-dissipation family (programmable, energy-lowering jump operators with a complete-graph core and a dark ground state), we prove a logarithmic gap , mixing time , monotonic energy decrease and ground-state convergence, and robustness to bounded control error. These convert the scaling claim from conjecture to theorem for the engineered-dissipation design , not the natural bath. (4) Adaptive policy, reframed. tQuA is identified as an adaptive policy system (temperature schedule, coupling, jump-operator structure, priors ). This is presented as a research direction, not a theorem. The earlier vs. query speedup claim is withdrawn ; Block–Lanczos matches the Simchowitz–Recht–Jordan lower bound. The quantum-advantage conjecture is reframed as a resource tradeoff (qubit count, device time, I/O), not query complexity.

summary: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range for uncooperative spacecraft pose estimation, but models trained on synthetic event streams must generalize to the noise, background activity, and contrast variation of physical sensors. We present a comparative systems study of two independently developed approaches to synthetic-to-real, event-based 6-DoF spacecraft pose estimation. The first is a modular pipeline that combines learned keypoint detection and unlabeled target-domain adaptation with geometry-based pose recovery and temporal smoothing. The second directly regresses translation and rotation from global and cropped event representations using an apparent-scale cue, physics-motivated synthetic corruptions, and feature-consistency regularization. We evaluate both systems under the same SPARK 2026 hidden-test protocol on the real-event split of SPADES, with predictions for all test frames. The results reveal a component-wise reversal concealed by the aggregate challenge score: direct regression reduces orientation error by 22.7% (1.1767 to 0.9101 rad) and obtains a 13.4% lower composite score, whereas the modular pipeline reduces relative translation error by 78.7% (0.1335 to 0.0285). Archived configurations and a qualitative failure case identify plausible explanations for these complementary error profiles, without isolating their causes. These findings motivate a testable hybrid design that combines direct orientation estimation with geometry-constrained translation recovery.
title: Direct Regression and Geometric Recovery for Event-based Spacecraft Pose Estimation

summary: High throughput computational databases such as Materials Project, the Open Quantum Materials Database, and Alexandria now each list on the order of 10^5 predicted stable compounds. However, the overall reliability of these predictions in terms of actual experimental synthesizability remains poorly understood. In this work we attempt to synthesize, via arc melting, 34 different predicted ternary compounds. The majority of these materials did not form in the predicted structure, instead resulting in disordered variants or multiphase mixtures. Four formed ordered structures not reported before, one of them at a composition reported earlier without a structure. We discuss both the failures and the successes, and identify simple filtering criteria that can help researchers avoid hypothetical materials that are unlikely to form.
title: Experimental Evaluation of High-Throughput Structure Predictions

summary: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.
title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates

summary: In many domains from species identification to cancer diagnosis, labelling data to train predictive models remains costly. In these settings, it is advantageous to intelligently select data points to label to achieve the maximum information gain, this is the motivation behind the study of active learning. In addition to the high costs of acquiring data in such domains, there is the added complexity of data distribution shifts that can occur between training and deployment. For example, the features of cancerous skin cells taken in one country may be different in another region of the world. These two challenges - efficient labelling of data, and learning models robust to distribution shifts have been studied separately but not together, even though these challenges often co-occur in real-life settings. We identify failure modes of standard active learning approaches when the distribution of data at deployment is different from the distribution in which the data is sampled for labelling. We propose a new strategy for efficiently learning classifiers that generalise under specific forms of distribution shift, namely subpopulation shift. Drawing on work in learning from heterogeneous data, we aim to train models that perform well across subpopulations of the data, through active learning. To handle this challenging setting, we exploit the fact that many datasets include metadata about data collection that can serve as a noisy proxy for each sample's underlying subpopulation. We demonstrate how to leverage these noisy labels during active learning selection, and demonstrate empirically that our approach improves classifier accuracy across subpopulations.
title: Active Learning of Robust Models

summary: Returned products in circular engineering often have heterogeneous degradation histories, making remaining function difficult to assess. For bolted joints, corrosion alters surface morphology, contact, friction, preload retention, and mechanical response. This paper presents a physics-informed multimodal framework for linking microscopic and camera-based degradation observations to functional indicators of corroded bolted joints. The workflow defines the corrosion failure mode, generates synchronized inspection and functional-response records, preprocesses image, roughness, exposure, and joint descriptors, aligns microscopy and camera observations through similarity learning, and constructs a calibrated corrosion-severity field. Partial differential equation (PDE) discovery is applied to this field to identify candidate effective mesoscale laws rather than complete electrochemical mechanisms. The corrosion-evolution model is coupled to a separate functional model, with friction coefficient as the primary target and preload loss included when clamp-force data are available. The contribution is a reproducible pathway for physically constrained assessment of degraded bolted-joint behavior.
title: A Physics-Informed Learning Framework for Linking Microscopic Surface Degradation to Bolted Joint Functional Behavior

summary: We study weighted edge boundary and outer vertex boundary on Cayley graphs of polynomial growth of degree $Q>1$. For every finite symmetric generating set, we prove that each exact isoperimetric profile satisfies $I(n)=c n^{(Q-1)/Q}+O(n^{(Q-1)/Q-β})$, where $β=1/(8Q^2)$. We identify the leading constant with the isoperimetric constant of a horizontal perimeter on the limiting Carnot group, after accounting for the counting density. Its integrand is a norm with polyhedral unit ball, determined by a convex minimization with one real variable for each coset of a torsion-free nilpotent subgroup. For every asymptotically minimizing sequence, we translate its vertex sets so that the characteristic functions of the associated rescaled regions are precompact in $L^1$. The limiting regions minimize continuum perimeter at fixed volume. The exact-cardinality estimate requires no regularity assumption on these regions. For virtually abelian groups, we prove a quantitative stability estimate using a discrete approximation to the Euclidean Wulff body. The relative symmetric difference from a translate is bounded by the square root of the sum of the relative boundary deficit and a cardinality error. We also characterize when bounded additive changes of Cayley metric preserve the leading vertex constant. Failure occurs already in rank two; we construct pairs with the same measured asymptotic cone whose leading constants have an unbounded ratio as the rank grows.
title: Sharp isoperimetry in groups of polynomial growth

summary: Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. These libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of training and inference across diverse GPU platforms, implementing attention, GEMM, quantization, and low-precision operators while managing tensor shapes, memory layouts, code generation, and hardware-specific dispatch. Problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs, prevent compilation, introduce deployment incompatibilities, or degrade performance, thereby reducing developer productivity and wasting expensive GPU resources. We present the first comprehensive empirical study of issues in GPU kernel libraries for LLM systems. We manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions, and available fixes from seven representative libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers, and bitsandbytes. The analysis characterizes symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. Our main findings are: (1) 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions, so validation must cover the deployment and execution stack, not just kernel code. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. We outline research opportunities and tooling directions to support future LLM GPU kernel development.
title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems

summary: Existing Korean benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) evaluate performance across diverse knowledge domains, but their accuracy scores cannot distinguish whether incorrect responses arise from a lack of required knowledge or a failure to apply that knowledge correctly. Our analysis of existing Korean benchmarks reveals that most questions can be answered through factual recall alone, while those demanding greater application also differ in required knowledge, making it difficult to isolate application ability. To address this, we introduce KLEAR, a framework that constructs knowledge-matched contrasts by varying application demand while preserving the required knowledge. During construction, KLEAR identifies the knowledge underlying each source question as an explicit anchor bundle to guide generation of questions requiring more complex application. Generated candidates then undergo automated and human validation, with iterative revision based on evaluation feedback. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting knowledge-matched sets largely satisfy the intended constraints, enabling controlled evaluation across diverse LLMs. These evaluations reveal that increasing application demand exposes failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided.
title: KLEAR: Knowledge-Matched LLM Evaluation in Korean across Application Requirements via Controlled Benchmark Transformation

summary: Multi-agent systems become capable through institutional mechanisms, such as rules that route information to agents that act on it. These mechanisms are also natural places to restrict the system. Yet as agents learn, share memory, delegate, and repair failures, the collective can find other paths to the same effects: a restriction on the original mechanism still operates but no longer stops them, while routine performance and compliance checks pass. We propose \textbf{Reversible Multi-agent Systems} as a research agenda: collectives that grow while an authorized supervisor can still restrict specified effects, keep them restricted as agents adapt, and reconstitute useful cooperation under renewed authority. What is reversed is the ability to produce a specified effect; restrictions must hold even if learned knowledge persists. The goal is to preserve effective intervention, not a particular mechanism: at every step of growth, some authorized intervention must keep a specified prohibited effect rare while maintaining required service. We identify three research problems: tracking what capabilities depend on, handing off control before an old mechanism loses its effect, and separating legitimate repair from unauthorized reconstruction. We outline how to evaluate control across growth paths, back control claims with evidence, and allocate the rights to restrict and restore.
title: From Emergence to Reversibility: Toward Reversible Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.
title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection

summary: Walsh analysis connects ordered Fourier convergence, summability, nonlinear approximation, and universal representation through a common character algebra. This survey examines developments from 2000-2026 against their classical foundations. Binary kernel geometry explains Hardy-space losses and summability thresholds; interval and packet methods control spectral selection; localized blocks produce correction and universal representations with distinct coefficient and exceptional-set requirements. Selected proofs and counterexamples compare these mechanisms and identify where an implication needs an additional hypothesis. The same distinctions organize digital integration, sparse measurements, Boolean spectra, and generalized Walsh bases. Quantitative thresholds, source conventions, and published theorem pointers are collected in comparative tables. The concluding problems separate source-listed questions, proposed refinements, and elementary obstructions. Supplementary derivations preserve normalization checks and finite covariance calculations while keeping the main exposition focused on the analytic mechanisms.
title: Walsh Analysis in the Twenty-First Century: Convergence, Summability, Nonlinear Approximation, Universality, and Digital Applications

summary: Walsh analysis connects ordered Fourier convergence, summability, nonlinear approximation, and universal representation through a common character algebra. This survey examines developments from 2000-2026 against their classical foundations. Binary kernel geometry explains Hardy-space losses and summability thresholds; interval and packet methods control spectral selection; localized blocks produce correction and universal representations with distinct coefficient and exceptional-set requirements. Selected proofs and counterexamples compare these mechanisms and identify where an implication needs an additional hypothesis. The same distinctions organize digital integration, sparse measurements, Boolean spectra, and generalized Walsh bases. Quantitative thresholds, source conventions, and published theorem pointers are collected in comparative tables. The concluding problems separate source-listed questions, proposed refinements, and elementary obstructions. summary: Unified multimodal models combine image understanding and generation within one system, creating an opportunity to improve both capabilities through paired image--text supervision. We examine the outputs of a pretrained unified model in both directions and observe a loss of specificity: generated images can contain the requested objects with incorrect attributes, while captions identify a scene without expressing its distinguishing details. These failures call for supervision that specifies both the visual content to realize and the descriptive differences to distinguish. We propose UniMore, a post-training method that derives these complementary learning tasks from the fine-grained content of image--text pairs. The generation route predicts grounded crops from their corresponding phrases, matching the scope of the condition and visual target while using the native visual objective. The understanding route combines positive-caption fitting with ranking against captions that omit or alter details, conditioned on the full image. The two routes are optimized independently, and their learned updates are combined into a single unified model without changing its inference procedure. Experiments show gains across multiple understanding and generation benchmarks.

summary: A germination study of Peltophorum africanum seeds was conducted in the laboratory of the Department of Crop Science and Production, Botswana University of Agriculture and Natural Resources from May to June 2017. Seeds were collected from Butale and Gaborone to assess effect of pre-sowing treatments on germination. The experiment followed a completely randomized design (CRD) with five treatments; control, boiling water, hot water, mechanical scarification and concentrated sulphuric acid. The boiling water treatment had three different levels of time exposure, while the sulphuric acid had four different levels of time exposure. Seed germination percentages, germination mean time and germination index were significantly ( P < 0.0001) affected by pre-sowing treatment methods. The maximum germination percentages (82-87) of Butale seeds were recorded in the mechanical scarified seeds, seed immersed in hot water and all sulphuric acid soaking times. The maximum germination percentages (75-88) in the Gaborone seeds were recorded in mechanical scarification, immersion in hot water, boiling water (1min) and sulphuric acid. Mechanical scarification and hot water are methods recommended for use by tree growers and farmers to break dormancy P. africanum because the acid is expensive and need trained people. published by the Journal of Biodiversity and Environmental Sciences | JBES

summary: RESEARCH COLLECTION / FLAGSHIPS 231–240 OF 300 Optical Reliability, Causal Metrology & Bounded Autonomous Micro/Nano-Systems at the Limit Flagship 13 Fission  |  Volume III  |  Author 33  |  Research Design Working Edition v0.7 (Three-Prose Working Draft) This ten-volume collection develops falsifiable research designs for optical microrobot fatigue, encapsulation reliability, photon transport loss, optical–magnetic control, material biofouling, photonic-chip thermal management, cross-instrument consistency, nanomaterial qualification, multiphysics coordination and evidence-bounded autonomous experimentation. It does not claim an experimentally established advantage. The ten English research-design manuscripts contain 7,770 pages, 300 model plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study designs, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate has a separately defined physical mechanism and concealed intervention; cross-volume scientific distinctness remains subject to expert review. Counts describe editorial coverage, not scientific proof. Research Unit I · F231–F235 F231  OPTICAL MICROROBOTIC MATERIALS FATIGUE AT THE LIMIT — Probes cyclic microbeam and coating fatigue through independent deflection, fracture and thermal witnesses. Concealed ageing challenges fixture relaxation and survivor selection; whole-cohort failure counts govern durability. F232  NANO-QUANTUM OPTICAL ENCAPSULATION RELIABILITY AT THE LIMIT — Tests water, ion and seam leakage, pinholes, seal swelling and reference drift through masked humidity and tracer studies. Edge diffusion, adhesive failure and photothermal limits remain live disqualifiers. F233  MICROSCALE PHOTON TRANSPORT LOSS AT THE LIMIT — Separates waveguide propagation loss from coupling, absorption, scattering and detector offsets. Length-resolved cutback and calorimetry establish a physical photon budget; high detected power alone is not proof of low loss. F234  NANO-OPTICAL AND MAGNETIC ACTUATION HYBRID CONTROL AT THE LIMIT — Challenges optical–magnetic actuation using field reversal, independently measured force and pose, synchronized timing faults and thermal budgets. The matched optical-only and magnetic-only controllers are real alternatives. F235  QUANTUM-MATERIAL BIOFOULING TOLERANCE AT THE LIMIT — Examines protein corona, non-specific adsorption, lipid deposition and regeneration-cycle damage. Independent mass, chemical, optical and hydraulic witnesses distinguish surface fouling from bulk-index drift and sample contamination.     SECOND RESEARCH UNIT / TRANSFER, SAFETY & SUCCESSION Research Unit II · F236–F240 F236  MICROSCALE PHOTONIC CHIP THERMAL MANAGEMENT AT THE LIMIT — Investigates chip hot spots, interfacial resistance, pulse heating and shutdown latency. Independent thermometry and energy closure test cooling against passive heat sinking; temperature vetoes cannot be traded for optical output. F237  NANO-OPTICAL SENSOR CROSS-INSTRUMENT CONSISTENCY AT THE LIMIT — Tests calibration transfer across instruments with independently certified wavelength and power standards, masked instrument swaps and held-out laboratories. Vendor fitting and common-reference drift are direct rival explanations. F238  QUANTUM NANOMATERIALS FUNCTIONAL QUALIFICATION AT THE LIMIT — Builds functional nanomaterial qualification from independent structural, chemical and optical evidence across complete manufacturing lots. Hidden lot swaps probe selection bias; failed specimens remain in the denominator. F239  PHOTONIC MICROROBOTIC MULTIPHYSICS COORDINATION AT THE LIMIT — Resolves optical, magnetic, fluid and thermal coupling in physical microrobot control. Separate field, force, position and heat measurements test synchronization faults and safe retrieval under conservation limits. F24

summary: This release avoids the import pykoopman failure caused by setuptools 82, which removed pkg_resources . pykoopman no longer uses pkg_resources itself and now requires setuptools < 82 , because the pinned lightning still imports that module. The release also corrects the rk4 integrator in pykoopman.common . That fix changes numerical results, so data generated with rk4 or with the example systems built on it will differ from 1.2.1. Import failure with setuptools 82 or newer (#71) setuptools 82.0.0 removed pkg_resources , and with setuptools 82 or newer installed, import pykoopman fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pkg_resources' . Every 1.x release up to 1.2.1 reads its version through pkg_resources . pykoopman 1.2.1 does not limit setuptools, so an environment that starts without it, such as one created with uv venv (the setup the README recommends), receives the newest setuptools and hits this error. pykoopman now reads __version__ with importlib.metadata . setuptools < 82 is a new runtime requirement, because the pinned lightning ~= 2.0.9 calls pkg_resources.declare_namespace when it is imported, and import pykoopman imports lightning for NNDMD. If setuptools 82 or newer is installed anyway, the import still fails inside lightning. The UserWarning that pkg_resources is deprecated, which importing pykoopman may still show, also comes from lightning and is harmless despite its advice to pin setuptools below 81. torch 2.1 also imports pkg_resources in torch.utils.cpp_extension , which import pykoopman does not load. The cap can be lifted once the pins require lightning >= 2.4 and torch >= 2.2. The outdated pins are discussed in #65. Because of the cap, installing 1.2.2 resolves setuptools to 81.0.0, the last release below 82, when it is absent and downgrades it to 81.0.0 when 82 or newer is installed. Dependency scanners may flag 81.0.0, which is in the affected ranges of GHSA-h35f-9h28-mq5c (sdist builds on macOS, fixed in 83.0.0) and GHSA-xmj3-9gf7-h52w (legacy wheel installation on Windows, fixed in 84.1.0). Neither concerns importing pykoopman. No other dependency changed. rk4 is now fourth order (#70, fixes #69) The fourth stage of pykoopman.common.rk4 used k1 instead of k3 , so the method was only second order for right-hand sides that do not depend on t , which includes every bundled system. In the new regression test on dx/dt = -x, the observed order goes from 2.04 to 4.06. Reported by Frank Yang in #69. The stages are now evaluated at t , t + dt/2 , t + dt/2 and t + dt instead of all at t . This matters only when the right-hand side depends on t , which is not the case for any bundled system. For such a right-hand side, the old rk4 was in general only first order. Results change for everything that integrates with rk4 : direct rk4 calls (default right-hand side vdp_osc ), and slow_manifold , pykoopman.common.examples.forced_duffing , vbe , nlse and cqgle through simulate and every collect_* method except collect_data_continuous . In the slow manifold eigenfunction tutorial (dt = 0.1), the EDMD eigenvalue whose exact value is -1.1 moves from -1.0991234 to -1.0999991. The L2 errors reported in the EDMDc and Hankel DMDc tutorials for the Van der Pol oscillator change only in the fourth or fifth significant figure. ks has its own integrator and is not affected, and the model fitting code is unchanged. To reproduce 1.2.1 results, stay on 1.2.1 with setuptools < 82 installed. Other changes torus_dynamics no longer emits NumPy's DeprecationWarning about converting an array with ndim > 0 to a scalar when it chooses its Fourier modes. For a given random seed it chooses the same modes as 1.2.1 (#67). Tests and documentation New tests for pykoopman.common : validation, example systems, cqgle , ks and vbe (#67). rk4 regression tests for the convergence order and for the stage times (#70). test/test_package.py checks that pykoopman's own import code no longer needs pkg_resources , and that pyproject.

summary: GiriNeoEquipment™ is a single-file, offline, interactive clinical decision support system (CDSS). It aims to ensure that no newborn in an Indian neonatal unit (SNCU, NICU, NBSU) is harmed, or receives less than optimal care, because of equipment or system failure. It covers the whole life of NICU equipment: deciding what is needed, buying it right, keeping it running, backing it up, and responding in seconds when a device fails. Contents (40 sections): Bedside "device failed — act now" sequences for each device, with a manual bridge for each. Unit clocks for escalation. A Quick Reference Card and twelve golden rules. Equipment-by-level-of-care tables with back-up logic. A back-up and spares calculator with a busy-night stress test. A ten-step procurement pathway for India (GeM, CDSCO Medical Devices Rules 2017, Target Product Profile) with specification checklists. A total-cost-of-ownership comparator. Equipment governance and programme design. PM and calibration planning, and a daily shift readiness check. Consumables stock and reorder calculator; uptime, MTBF and MTTR with a contract-penalty calculator. Repair, replace or condemn guidance. Power, oxygen, medical air and vacuum (three-source) planning, plus environment and HVAC. A pre-filled FMEA; mock drills; alarm safety. Materiovigilance (MvPI) reporting. Training, infection prevention, KPIs and the GiriNeoEquipment Readiness Index (GERI) self-audit. A contract clause builder and an implementation roadmap. FAQs, a quiz, a scenario simulator, a printable bedside pack (with Hindi text), and a monthly committee report. An evidence map, a validation toolkit (Delphi, SUS, pilot), a glossary and 80 references to 09 November 2026. Features: search across all pages; role-based start; today's unit status; a paper shift sheet; a live pre-publication audit; light and dark themes; phone-ready layout. Data stays in the user's browser; no patient data are collected. Companion PDF: the full text in A4 for reading, printing and archiving. Calculators work only in the HTML file. Disclaimer: a Supportive Risk Signal, not a directive. Does not replace institutional policy, statutory requirements, manufacturer (OEM) instructions or professional judgement. Version history: v1.0: initial build. v1.1: integrated three external drafts. v1.2: addressed three external appraisals. v1.3: author upgrade. v1.4: pre-publication layout and accessibility audit, plus a technical and citation update (references 73–80). v1.5 Final Release: merged edition. Version: 1.5 Language: English (eng). Bedside summary also in Hindi (hin), marked "Draft · not validated". Licence: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY-4.0)

summary: RESEARCH COLLECTION / FLAGSHIPS 221–230 OF 300 Quantum Photonic Materials & Microscale Optical Metrology at the Limit Flagship 13 Fission  |  Volume III  |  Author 33  |  STARLI Research Design Working Edition v1.3 This ten-volume research-design collection investigates optical phase localization, engineered quantum defects, microscale photothermal safety, microrobotic optical navigation, surface ageing, photonic-crystal microfluidic sensing, multi-target optical manipulation, biointerface decoherence, readout crosstalk and autonomous calibration. The work proposes physical test designs, not observed new laws, clinical results or experimentally established quantum advantages. Two five-theme research units contain ten English 777-page working editions: 300 mathematical model plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study designs, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The third-pass Gate edition separately addresses causal mechanisms, orthogonal physical witnesses, masked refutation, competing explanations, hard failure evidence and successor experiments. Structural counts do not certify scientific novelty or physical validation. Research Unit I · F221–F225 F221  OPTICAL PHASE CONTROL AND MICROSCALE LOCALIZATION AT THE LIMIT — Challenges interferometric optical-phase localization with independently registered fiducials, wavefront reversals, detector reference drift and photon-matched free-space baselines. Reports phase and position residuals alongside photothermal rise; apparent field enhancement is not by itself a localization gain. F222  NANOMATERIALS QUANTUM DEFECT ENGINEERING AT THE LIMIT — Tests defect creation, charge states, spin coherence, surface passivation and unselected emitter yield against a geometry-matched classical materials stack. Annealing, sorting bias, substrate strain and thermal cross-sensitivity are live rivals. A bright selected specimen cannot establish manufacturing yield. F223  MICROSCALE PHOTOTHERMAL CONVERSION SAFETY AT THE LIMIT — Constrains photothermal conversion in sealed microfluidic reference systems through spatially independent microthermometry, absorbed-power accounting, duty-cycle variation and physical shutdown tests. Geometry, convection and detector lag compete with any proposed material advantage; local temperature and dose vetoes are noncompensable. F224  QUANTUM OPTICAL MICROROBOTIC NAVIGATION AT THE LIMIT — Compares optically tracked microrobot navigation with free-space reference localization at equal photon and motion budgets. Beacon-phase drift, image interpolation, occlusion, flow reversal and independent trajectory truth challenge seemingly superior tracking; phase stability cannot replace physical pose evidence. F225  NANOPHOTONIC MATERIALS SURFACE AGING AT THE LIMIT — Investigates biofluid, humidity, salt, photooxidation and package-stress ageing of nanophotonic material surfaces. Tracks chemical state, adhesion, insertion loss, intrinsic versus loaded quality factor and functional yield on unselected devices. Survivor selection and bulk-index drift remain rival explanations.     SECOND RESEARCH UNIT / SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE & SUCCESSION Research Unit II · F226–F230 F226  PHOTONIC-CRYSTAL MICROFLUIDIC SENSING AT THE LIMIT — Tests photonic-crystal microfluidic sensing against a commercial chip under equal optical power using concealed pressure, ionic and fouling challenges. Separate chemical standards, cavity linewidth, insertion loss and complete sensor-array yield distinguish analyte binding from channel deformation, thermal drift or bulk-index change. F227  NANO-OPTICAL FIELD MULTI-TARGET MANIPULATION AT THE LIMIT — Examines whether optical-field control can manipulate several microscale targets without hidden collision, cross-trap force, laser dose or thermal burden. Independent trap stif

summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies

summary: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

summary: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support commonly focus on the clinical appropriateness of individual responses, potentially overlooking failures that emerge across extended interactions. As AI assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances and prior disclosures, this raises an accountability question: Do AI chatbots provide appropriate support as users' needs evolve? We investigate by analyzing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, examining how a memory-equipped assistant responds to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles. We introduce the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, to assess the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. Advice was less aligned with users' readiness after a crisis than in matched control stretches of the same conversation, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and users' communication style changed how often and when the assistant gave recommendations. Although explicitly unproductive advice was rare, the assistant frequently omitted clinician-expected support such as follow-up and planning for next steps. These findings show the limits of single response-level safety evaluation and the need to assess timing, omission, and consistency across users when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.
title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Evaluating Timing and Omission in Longitudinal AI Mental Health Support

summary: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents

title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents

summary: Zeolites are an important class of porous crystalline materials with broad applications in gas storage, separations, and catalysis. Although hundreds of thousands of experimentally realized and hypothetical zeolite structures are known, identifying materials optimized for a target application remains challenging because property labels are expensive to obtain and available only for limited structure-molecule pairs. While prior work has demonstrated that 3D neural representations can predict zeolite properties effectively, it remains unclear which representation-learning strategies are most effective in the low-data regime relevant to materials discovery. We present ZeoBench, a benchmark for self-supervised learning on dense 3D representations of all-silica zeolites, and evaluate the resulting features on six existing downstream adsorption-property prediction tasks, across a range of training set sizes. Our study compares self-supervised 3D pretraining on volumetric zeolite data, adaptations of image-pretrained 2D ConvNets and vision transformers to 3D via multiview and channel-inflation strategies, and 3D ConvNets pretrained on out-of-domain volumetric datasets, alongside hand-crafted descriptors and supervised baselines. Using our pretraining and evaluation framework, we find self-supervised 3D representations outperform existing methods and achieve state-of-the-art performance across both in-domain label regimes and for the unseen domain of metal organic frameworks. Learned representations consistently outperform hand-crafted descriptors, and convolutional architectures are generally more effective than vision transformers in this setting. These results establish ZeoBench as a practical benchmark for 3D representation learning in zeolites and provide guidance for data-limited adsorption property prediction.
title: ZeoBench: A Benchmark for Self-Supervised Learning on 3D Zeolite Representations

summary: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. When the obstacle geometry is known, however, non-penetration and complementarity make the contact force locally identifiable, and we prove that the resulting system with unknown contact inputs is locally exponentially strongly detectable. We present a constrained moving horizon estimator (MHE) that encodes these conditions and runs in real time as one quadratic program per sample, and we give a local, mode-wise robust stability result for it. In a finite- element benchmark of a two-section robot pressing and sliding on a wall, the estimator located contact to 0.9 mm and estimated contact force to 0.22 N, compared with 65 mm and 0.72 N for a tuned extended Kalman filter (EKF) with state projection. The estimator tolerated millimeter- level errors in the obstacle position and unmodeled wall friction, under which the projected EKF failed. Under randomized model mismatch over 40 trials, including unmodeled tendon friction, it remained better in force and location in every trial. Without contact, the MHE offered no advantage over the EKF, which confirms that its benefit comes from the contact constraints. This report extends a letter submitted to IEEE Control Systems Letters with complete proofs and additional experiments.

summary: Quantum-state conversion between the ortho and para nuclear-spin states of H$_2$ is forbidden in the isolated molecule but these states can become connected through interactions with a surrounding environment. How that same environment governs the dynamics of the newly connected states remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this problem using H$_2$ confined in crystalline molecular solids, where the host environment selectively enables conversion between a pair of otherwise disconnected ortho-H$_2$ and para-H$_2$ states. Rotationally resolved infrared spectroscopy directly determines the state-specific conversion dynamics in crystalline CO$_2$ and N$_2$O at 10 K, revealing that increasing H$_2$ concentration suppresses nuclear-spin conversion by nearly an order of magnitude, reaching complete suppression by 20% H$_2$ loading. Molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations identify two complementary origins of this concentration dependence: changes in the thermally populated phonon modes available to mediate relaxation, and strain-driven H$_2$ clustering that progressively removes molecules from the host crystal field responsible for enabling conversion. The resulting picture connects a classical collective response of the host to microscopic quantum-state dynamics: H$_2$ loading generates strain that reorganizes the local molecular environment, thereby modifying both the phonon bath and the molecular coupling to that bath. These results establish a multiscale mechanism by which condensed-phase environments can govern the connectivity and dynamics of an effective two-level system.
title: Classical control of quantum-state relaxation in confined molecular hydrogen

summary: Plug-and-play (PnP) methods reconstruct images by alternating a data-fitting step with an image denoiser. Their performance depends on two parameters: the step size $γ$ and the measurement noise level $σ$. In practice, $γ$ is often tuned by grid search over validation images and must be retuned whenever the problem setting changes, and $σ$ is assumed known or estimated separately. We propose AdaptivePnP, a PnP framework that jointly estimates $σ$ and $γ$ at every iteration from the data-fitting residual. To do so, we apply the PnP virtual model to the data-fitting proximal map and show that the residual is zero-mean Gaussian with covariance parameterized by $γ$ and $σ$. However, when one parameter is much larger than the other, the residual carries little information about the smaller one and using the maximum likelihood (ML) estimator can degrade the PnP iterations. We therefore introduce the identifiable maximum likelihood (IML) estimator, which restricts the ML estimator to an identifiable window in which the normalized Cramér--Rao bound of every parameter is bounded by a user-specified tolerance. For the virtual model, this window is an interval of ratios $ρ= γ/σ$, so computing the IML estimate reduces to a one-dimensional search over $ρ$. We apply AdaptivePnP to two standard PnP methods, yielding algorithms that require neither a tuned $γ$ nor a known $σ$. On image deblurring and super-resolution, AdaptivePnP matches or outperforms PnP baselines tuned with the true $σ$. Code is available at https://github.com/hdubasullivan/AdaptivePnP.
title: AdaptivePnP: Fast Auto-Tuned Plug-and-Play for Deconvolution

summary: The pigs were bleeding. That was the point of the experiment: could airway pressure reveal hemorrhage before it became critical? In the UCR Time Series Classification Archive, the de facto benchmark for Time Series Classification (TSC), the same recordings ask a different question: "which of 52 pigs produced this trace?". The dataset PigAirwayPressure is not an outlier. Although the archive is the standard benchmark, whether its tasks resemble the problems TSC is meant to solve has rarely been examined. We find that several datasets are repurposed from their original task, built from toy setups, or have flawed test splits. We further question how representative the archive's ordered non-temporal sequences (e.g. spectra, shape outlines) are of real TSC, and the potential downsides from the decomposition of multivariate problems. Our findings call for more careful interpretation of archive-wide scores and greater attention to deployment-relevant evaluation. The audit is at https://github.com/automl/ucr-provenance-audit.
title: Fifty-Two Shades of Pig: What the UCR Archive Really Asks Classifiers to Do

summary: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly involved in software development, but their participation in real-world security remediation remains poorly understood. We investigate observable evidence of coding-agent involvement in commits referenced by reviewed GitHub Security Advisories (GHSAs), characterize the associated vulnerabilities, and examine review timing in relation to advisory disclosure routes. We develop a local-Git mining pipeline that identifies agent evidence through known agent accounts, explicit commit-message attribution, repository instruction files, and agent configuration artifacts. Linking these findings to GHSA-referenced commits yields 469 valid candidate advisories across 189 repositories, including 448 with direct attribution and 21 supported only by repository-level evidence. Claude is the most frequently observed tool family, followed by Copilot and Cursor. We further compare review timing against other advisories and historical baselines using an exact route--timing decomposition. Relative to advisories published in the same months, candidate advisories exhibit a modestly longer mean review lag, primarily associated with within-route timing rather than disclosure-route composition. Compared with a historical baseline, they exhibit substantially shorter mean review lags, with both route composition and within-route timing contributing to the difference. These findings demonstrate that coding-agent involvement is already observable across hundreds of security advisories and repositories, including high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities. By distinguishing direct attribution from repository-level adoption evidence and separating route-composition effects from within-route timing differences, we provide an empirical characterization of agent-associated remediation in the GHSA review pipeline.
title: Agents on the Patch Path: Mining AI-Associated Security Remediation in GitHub Security Advisories

summary: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.
title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks

summary: The reconstruction of the top-quark-pair ($t\bar{t}$) kinematics in the dilepton $t\bar{t}$ decay channel is challenging due to the presence of two undetected neutrinos. In this work, existing kinematic reconstruction methods used by the CMS Collaboration are studied using a Monte Carlo sample with $t\bar{t}$ events from CMS Open Data at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. An improved version of the loose kinematic reconstruction, LKRv2, is developed by imposing more stringent requirements on the jet-lepton pairing entering the reconstruction. A further modification, LKRv3, exploits the kinematic similarity between the dilepton and neutrino-pair systems and improves the resolution of the reconstructed $t\bar{t}$ invariant mass relative to the baseline LKR by $7\%$, with smaller improvements for the transverse momentum and rapidity of $t\bar{t}$. In addition, two machine-learning (ML) based approaches are developed using a residual multilayer perceptron and a conditional normalizing flow. Relative to LKRv3, they improve the resolution of the invariant mass, transverse momentum and rapidity by approximately $30\%$, $20\%$ and $15\%$, respectively. In particular, a resolution of 30 GeV is achieved for the reconstructed invariant mass of $t\bar{t}$ near the production threshold. A dedicated generator-level study and a generator-to-detector transfer test demonstrate that the ML approaches learn a genuine physics-driven correction to the $ν\barν$ approximation, rather than merely exploiting detector-specific effects. These results demonstrate the strong potential of ML-based approaches for improving the reconstruction of dilepton $t\bar{t}$ events, while identifying the neutrino-pair approximation as an important limitation on the achievable resolution.
title: Kinematic Reconstruction of Top-Quark Pairs Using Analytical and Machine-Learning Methods with CMS Open Data

summary: Vehicle telematics provides detailed observations of driving behaviour that can be useful for automobile insurance risk assessment. Existing approaches often summarize these data through counts of harsh events or individually unusual observations, although driving movements naturally develop over time. Building on a previously proposed hidden Markov model (HMM) framework that identifies pointwise anomalies, we identify short intervals in which a sequence of observations is unusual when considered together. We then examine the original acceleration signals to measure the magnitude and temporal concentration of these episodes and identify recurring patterns of vehicle movement. Temporal concentration describes whether acceleration activity is distributed evenly across an episode or concentrated in relatively few observations. Using a controlled telematics dataset containing normal, aggressive, and drowsy driving by the same drivers, we evaluate the proposed measures through comparisons matched by driver and road type. We find that statistical anomaly measures depend on the driving population used to train the HMM. More importantly, mean temporal concentration alone distinguishes normal from abnormal driving more effectively than the original pointwise anomaly indices across different reference populations. The recurring movement patterns further reveal different characteristics of abnormal driving, with stronger longitudinal acceleration during aggressive driving and more frequent lateral corrections or excursions during drowsy driving. The framework therefore goes beyond pointwise anomaly detection, providing interpretable behavioural features that can be calculated for unlabeled trips, used for trip-level assessment, aggregated across a driver's trip history, and subsequently evaluated alongside existing telematics and rating variables for insurance risk modelling and ratemaking.
title: From Point Anomalies to Anomalous Driving Episodes: Interpreting Abnormal Driving from Vehicle Telematics

summary: Extracting discriminative features from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) spectra is important for the classification of complex biological samples. This study evaluates continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based spectral peak extraction for distinguishing human plasma samples labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative. Plasma specimens from 181 individuals, comprising 53 positive samples and 128 negative controls, were deposited as 5 μL droplets on silicon substrates and dried before analysis. Spectra were acquired using a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser operating at 1064 nm, with 100 single-shot measurements collected per specimen and averaged after intensity-based outlier rejection. CWT-based peak detection was coupled with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The reported leave-one-out evaluation yielded an accuracy of 93.00%, sensitivity of 94.67%, and specificity of 91.61%; these estimates remain provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions. Features identified by the CWT pipeline included emission lines assigned to Ca II, K I, and N I. The workflow provides a basis for examining spectral features associated with the studied plasma groups. Independent validation and assessment of specimen, substrate, and acquisition-related variability are required to establish generalizability and diagnostic relevance.
title: Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples

title: Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples

summary: Recommendation systems often enter a new serving window before enough outcomes are available to retrain the deployed model. We study this regime with 0.05-1.0% target feedback, a range that spans our stress tests while keeping supervision far below the degrees of freedom of the source recommender. At this scale, existing fine-tuning and meta-learning methods still estimate target-specific updates from extremely sparse feedback, leaving the update direction weakly identified. SAGE-PAIR instead transfers a source-supported residual correction space and only calibrates this space using target outcomes. We introduce SAGE-PAIR, a staged adapter that pretrains a low-dimensional global residual on an adjacent source period and adds a soft router over residual experts conditioned on source user profiles. Target feedback then calibrates this residual state rather than relearning the recommender. On a locked test split of KuaiSAR-v2, SAGE-PAIR (Full) achieves a 1.77% relative improvement in NDCG@10, while a core-protocol comparison shows a further 0.25% gain from routed experts beyond source-pretrained PAIR. Matched source-pretrained LoRA and Adapter-Tuning baselines remain near the source model, supporting the need for a different adaptation space. Thus, SAGE-PAIR improves ranking quality with millisecond-scale adaptation and inference costs. Sparse-feedback adaptation is fundamentally governed by the identifiability of the update space rather than by label count alone. Source pretraining supplies estimable correction directions for scarce labels, while user-conditioned routing contributes a consistent, differentiated cross-user correction on top of the global correction. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SAGE-PAIR-610E/.
title: SAGE-PAIR: Source-Pretrained Routed Residual Adaptation for Sparse-Feedback Recommendation

summary: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.
title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds

summary: Overview The script conducts the full end-to-end inferential and descriptive statistical analysis pipeline reported in the manuscript . It evaluates changes in commercial drivers' subjective states (sleepiness, physical fatigue symptoms, musculoskeletal discomfort, and blood pressure) alongside objective sustained attention measured via the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) before and after simulated driving sessions . Statistical Pipeline & Methodology Pre-Post Subjective Comparisons: Calculates median and interquartile ranges (Q1, Q3), Wilcoxon signed-rank test statistics, paired rank-biserial correlation effect sizes, and one-sample Hodges-Lehmann median difference estimates paired with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (5,000 resamples) . Fatigue Symptoms & Musculoskeletal Discomfort: Evaluates discrete fatigue symptoms using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni family-wise error rate corrections, and assesses anatomical discomfort changes across individual Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ) regions using exact McNemar tests . Objective Vigilance (PVT): Analyzes pre-to-post alterations in median reaction time (RT), mean RT, mean reciprocal reaction time (1/RT), fastest 10% RT, slowest 10% RT, lapses (RT >= 500 ms), and false starts, adjusted via Holm corrections . Cross-Domain Concordance & Associations: Computes Spearman rank correlations with 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (4,000 resamples), partial Spearman correlations controlling for prior sleep duration, and Cohen's kappa coefficient to quantify concordance across elevated symptom domains . Subjective Fatigue vs. Objective Vigilance: Tests associations between subjective self-reports and objective vigilance metrics with Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) adjustments, complemented by Kruskal-Wallis tests across composite elevated impairment levels . Sensitivity Power Analysis: Computes the minimal detectable paired Cohen's d effect size and minimal detectable correlation coefficient (|rho|) achievable at 80% statistical power and an alpha level of 0.05 . Files & Data Structure analisis_TSR.py : Standalone Python replication script . Input Data: Expects an Excel workbook named Dataset_Induk_n20_v2.xlsx containing participant records within the sheet named data . Generated Output: Automatically writes all formatted statistical output tables directly into a consolidated Excel file named Hasil_Analisis_TSR.xlsx . Execution & Reproducibility Deterministic Randomness: All resampling routines utilize a fixed pseudorandom number generator seed ( seed = 2026 ) to ensure exact reproducibility across runs . Execution: Run directly via terminal/command line: python analisis_TSR.py or within a Google Colab notebook by placing Dataset_Induk_n20_v2.xlsx in the active runtime directory and invoking !python analisis_TSR.py . Software Requirements The script prints active package versions directly to the console upon execution for reporting in manuscript methodology sections . Required dependencies: Python NumPy pandas SciPy statsmodels scikit-learn
title: Replication code for: "Driver subjective responses and objective vigilance after simulated truck driving"

summary: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/FOSCAR.
title: FOSCAR: Accelerating Decode Attention over 2- and 4-Bit KV Caches through Affine Folding

summary: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory

summary: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.
title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure

summary: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.
title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?

summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
