summary: A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with someone else's and measures the drop in accuracy. But this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch. We examine this problem with a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, using histories from similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without history. Removing history only at evaluation makes this gain appear larger, at 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen during training and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence for an advantage remains inconclusive. A small movie-tagging experiment with one training seed also finds no advantage over other users' histories. These findings show why personalization should be evaluated on unseen users, with histories of similar content and a model trained without history as comparisons. We also find that adding gated cross-attention improves on a prefix-only model under our training setup; whether this holds more broadly remains open.
title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control

summary: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.
title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression

summary: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
title: TimeOmni-Live: Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding with Long-Term Memory

summary: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
title: TimeOmni-Live: Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding with Long-Term Memory

summary: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.
title: ENGRAM: From Agent Experience to Weights through Verified Consolidation

summary: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as \texttt{BF16} and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama~3.1~8B~Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52$\times$ and 1.48$\times$ over the fastest baseline on an RTX~4060~Ti and an RTX~5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43~bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.
title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models

summary: We study time-fractional diffusion on real hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$, $n\ge2$, with Caputo order $0<α<1$. We establish global two-sided pointwise estimates for the homogeneous fundamental kernel $Z_{\mathbb H}(t,r)$ and the inhomogeneous (Duhamel) kernel $Y_{\mathbb H}(t,r)$, uniformly over all $t>0$ and positive geodesic distances $r$. By combining inverse-stable subordination with global bounds for the hyperbolic heat kernel, we distinguish a short-time local regime, a large-time interior region, and an exterior region governed by a saddle-point problem with parameter $r/t$. Both kernels have the same exterior exponential rate, while their amplitudes are related by an explicit saddle-point factor. The estimates are uniformly comparable on the interfaces between regimes, recover the Euclidean time-fractional singularities at small scales, and identify the influence of hyperbolic geometry on large-scale decay. The kernel $Z_{\mathbb H}$ also describes the one-time marginal density of hyperbolic Brownian motion under an independent inverse stable clock. This representation yields a radial limit law, moment and quantile asymptotics, and a change in the mean square displacement from order $t^α$ at small times to order $t^{2α}$ at large times.
title: Global Two-Sided Estimates for Time-Fractional Diffusion Kernels on Hyperbolic Space

summary: We establish an exact curved-background Weyl double copy for the doubly spinning Pomeransky--Sen'kov black ring. Its full Weyl tensor is a quadratic form in two source-free Maxwell fields: one generated by the stationary Killing vector, the other a flux-carrying magnetic field obtained by linearizing the dipole-ring gauge potential about its vacuum limit. The mixed Maxwell bilinear is essential: no spacetime-independent real or complex change of field basis removes it. We identify the inverse $S_{IJ}$ of the Weyl coefficient matrix as a matrix zeroth copy. The same matrix arises independently from a weighted limit of the inner products of two Killing vectors in a six-dimensional Ricci-flat parent and satisfies $\Box_g S_{IJ}=-\tfrac12 F_{I\,ab}F_J{}^{ab}$. The singly spinning limit recovers the diagonal two-field Weyl double copy of the Emparan--Reall ring.
title: The Double Copy of the Doubly Spinning Black Ring

summary: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. Existing training-free video editing methods, however, assume full offline access to the entire sequence, while streaming approaches either rely on additional training or are limited to specific editing techniques. We show that this limitation can be removed by analyzing the self-attention dynamics of DMD-distilled autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. We uncover a key asymmetry: queries and keys remain stable and aligned with their source counterparts across denoising timesteps, while values diverge and encode the evolving content. Inherited from the non-distilled bidirectional teacher, this asymmetry is strongest at high noise, where few-step streaming models operate. The resulting mechanism is simple: a single forward pass suffices to capture source identity in the value features, which can be reused throughout generation. Starting from pure Gaussian noise and injecting only these source values reconstructs the input with fidelity matching or surpassing inversion-based methods, effectively eliminating inversion. Based on this insight, we introduce AR-Edit, a training-free, inversion-free method that caches source values once and selectively injects them during denoising. Across multiple AR backbones, AR-Edit enables real-time streaming editing with superior source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.
title: AR-Edit: Training-Free Autoregressive Video Editing without Inversion

summary: We consider Box-Cox transformations of correlation matrices, $Φ_α(C)=\mathrm{vecl}\{(C^α-I)/α\}$, with Jacobian $J_α$. The family nests the raw correlations at $α=1$, the generalised Fisher transformation (GFT), $C\mapsto\mathrm{vecl}(\log C)$, at $α=0$, and the negated off-diagonal concentration coordinates at $α=-1$. The inverse problem is a strictly convex program for every $α$, so every member is injective. The map is onto $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d=n(n-1)/2$, if and only if $α\le0$, such that $α=0$ defines the boundary for unrestricted parametrizations. For $α>0$ the image is bounded. The conditioning obeys the bound $κ(J_α)\leκ(C)^{|1-α|}$, where $κ(C)=λ_{\max}(C)/λ_{\min}(C)$, and on the surjective range the exponent is smallest at $α=0$. Under Gaussian sampling with $n\geq3$, the asymptotic covariance of the transformed sample correlations is the identity at independence for every member, but only $α=0$ retains the identity to first order in the correlations, whereas the leading joint third cumulant at independence vanishes only at $α=1/3$. Finally, applying the transformation to the diagonal rescaling of $C$ that makes the result hollow adds a new family to the existing correlation parametrizations. For every $α$ the rescaling solves a strictly convex problem and the inverse is explicit, and the scaled coordinates are unrestricted exactly when $α=0$, where they recover the known global normal coordinates, centred at independence, for the efficient information metric of the correlations.
title: Box-Cox Transformations of Correlation Matrices

summary: Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$. Recently, Fiat-Naor's solution to this problem has seen significant traction in theoretical computer science, and allowed for several conjectures related to meta-complexity and the 3SUM problem to be broken. In this paper, we consider the natural extension of the function inversion problem that we call preimage reporting. Here, instead of having to report only one $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$, the whole set $f^{-1}(y)$ must be found. We present a new general method to convert any arbitrary function inversion scheme into an efficient corresponding preimage reporting scheme. In particular, if $Δ$ is the maximal indegree of $f$, we show that we can perform preimage reporting using space $S$ in time $T$ for any $T$ and $S$ satisfying $TS^2=N^2 Δ$, matching a variant of a tradeoff obtained by Fiat and Naor for function inversion. This last result implies an improvement over the corresponding function inversion scheme itself, which constitutes the first function inversion scheme whose query time is inversely proportional to $|f^{-1}(y)|$. We derive new simple solutions for the $k$SUM-indexing with reporting and Jumbled indexing with reporting problems.
title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting

summary: We study a Bayesian inverse problem in EUV reflectometry, where optical constants and layer thicknesses are inferred from angle- and wavelength-resolved reflection measurements. The physical process is modeled and evaluated using an efficient forward model based on the transfer matrix method. As an alternative to computationally expensive sampling-based inference, we employ an Eulerian, entropically regularized Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler divergence via proximal steps in the Wasserstein space. Using the Benamou--Brenier dynamic formulation and a Hopf-Cole transform, each JKO step is reformulated as a pair of heat equations coupled only through their initial and terminal conditions, enabling an efficient fixed-point solver. The resulting high-dimensional densities are discretized on tensor-product grids and represented in tensor-train format, exploiting Kronecker structure for scalable computation. Preconditioning based on estimated posterior moments further improves tractability. We test the method with numerical experiments on EUV reflectometry data for a ruthenium--silicon ($\ce{Ru}$ on $\ce{Si}$) specimen and compare the learned tensor-train posterior to ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) reference samples. We demonstrate a use case in which we are able to reuse the tensor-train posterior to obtain samples for shifted target distributions with less computational effort than a comparable MCMC method.
title: Bayesian Inverse Problems for EUV reflectometry with regularized JKO scheme

summary: Local response measurements track how perturbations spread in quantum simulators and nonequilibrium many-body systems. Locality bounds constrain the propagation speed, but do not determine whether the response can distinguish computational outcomes at fixed measurement precision as the distance increases. Here we construct time-independent dynamics with bounded nearest-neighbor interactions in which a fixed single-site detector responds to a remote bond phase after a time proportional to their separation. The susceptibility has a positive lower bound independent of distance. With product-state preparations, estimating this susceptibility to constant additive accuracy is complete for bounded-error quantum polynomial time (BQP), with a decision gap independent of distance. Two source-phase settings give the susceptibility with a distance-independent shot count at fixed accuracy and confidence. Inverse-polynomially weak local couplings between the computational register and the chain carrying the excitation preserve the gap. The leading correction vanishes when exchanging the two internal states of the excitation reverses the interaction. Varying the source and observation time makes all bond phases locally identifiable near the zero-phase reference setting. We also prove a conditional quantum advantage for distribution-free response prediction.
title: BQP-Complete Susceptibilities Observable at Ballistic Times in Local Quantum Dynamics

summary: In this article, we use the PBNF-transform, or Polynomial Boolean Normal Form, described in the two earlier articles and now extended to higher arity, to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT), which are part of the P versus NP problem. SAT consists of a conjunction of clauses, and in our SAT-solving models, we dualize the logical equations by inverting the problem: we multiply letters (literals) in the transferred clauses and use a binary iterated composition based on adding polynomials for the conjunctions in our solution formula. We obtain Polynomial Boolean Equations, PBE=0, by also renaming the truth value T=0. With reversed literal repetition, we get the CNF as the sum of the transformed clauses. In fact, we can always reduce to multiplication in and addition out of clauses, as we do not look for the entire kernel of PBE for a YES instance for SAT.
title: SAT Solving by Multiplication in and Addition out of Clauses

summary: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.
title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming

summary: Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.
title: Know What You Need: Efficient Activation Checkpointing

summary: The natural environments habitable to life are inseparable from dissipative and entropic forces, which mandate active matter to operate on constant fluxes of energy and momentum to survive and propagate through spacetime. In contrast to fundamental particles which are characterized by energy and momentum, we postulate that energy expenditure rate and momentum generation rate are the fundamental dynamical quantities driving this evolution of swimming active matter and accordingly construct the corresponding Lagrangian and Hamiltonian of motion of the active matter. Furthermore, living systems broadly employ periodic, non-repeating motion for both locomotion and various biological functions, with meaningful information stored in the periods of these functions. Consequently, analyzing these dynamics in the Fourier space lands us at the familiar tools of the operator based, quantum mechanics. This is accomplished by introducing a complex field to describe the evolving probability distribution of a single unit, as well as the population density of mutually non-interacting active particles under the constraint of scarce resources. The resulting single-unit wavefunction evolves analogously to the Dirac equation with minimal coupling, wherein gauge symmetry reflects the generality of the governing equations across arbitrary resource landscapes. Additionally, we present a Schrödinger-like equation where the effective potential term represents the environmentally mandated, non-motile base metabolic rate. Finally, we formalize the bidirectional coupling between active swimmers and the surrounding fluid via a multipole expansion of the active force with an emphasis on force monopoles and dipoles, where each pole corresponds to a distinct mode of active motility.
title: A Quantum Mechanical Description of Active Matter

summary: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and schedule
title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part IV : Two Independent Checks and Endpoint-Side Reconstruction to Prevent Tool Misuse, Memory Poisoning, Unauthorized Delegation and Unlawful Data Use — Supporting EU AI Act Record-Keeping, Human Oversight and Cybersecurity, GDPR Purpose Limitation and DORA

summary: Replication package for the paper “Sharp bounds for a mean under bounded response-probability ratios” by Michael Bücker. It contains the R scripts for all simulations, numerical checks and the application to earnings in the 2024 Annual Social and Economic Supplement to the Current Population Survey; the results files from which the manuscript reads every number; the Quarto sources of the manuscript and the supplementary material; and a script that runs everything with the arguments that produced the deposited results. README.md gives the requirements, the run order and the run times. MAP.csv links each results file to the script that writes it and to the parts of the manuscript that read it. SHA256SUMS lists checksums of all files. Not included: the Current Population Survey data (US Census Bureau, public domain) and the Biometrika LaTeX class (licensed for use with Oxford University Press papers only). Scripts in scripts/ download both and verify their checksums. Code: MIT License. Results files: CC BY 4.0. Manuscript sources: all rights reserved.

summary: This repository contains the analysis code accompanying the SPiCe paper (Genome Biology; secrierlab/SPiCe). It has three components. (i) merfish_analysis/ implements the graph neural network (GNN) framework. For each sample of the MERFISH mouse cortex dataset, it builds a spatial k-nearest-neighbour cell graph (k = 20, Euclidean-distance edge weights). It then holds out one cell type at a time and trains a three-layer graph convolutional network (PyTorch Geometric) on one-hot cell-type features to predict which remaining cells sit next to the removed type. Evaluation is inductive, on held-out tissue sections, and performance is measured by ROC-AUC. Predictions are interpreted with Integrated Gradients (Captum) for node-level (cell-type) importance, tested against a permutation baseline with Mann–Whitney U tests and multiple-testing correction. GNNExplainer is used for edge-level (cell-type-pair) importance. (ii) spatial_regression/ contains Python and R notebooks that model spatially varying relationships in Xenium breast cancer data. They regress an EMT hallmark score on tumour-microenvironment and CNV-derived predictors, such as distances to neighbouring cell populations and principal components. The notebooks fit spatial error models (spreg), geographically weighted regression (mgwr) and multiscale GWR (GWmodel in R), with VIF/correlation filtering and variable-specific bandwidth selection. (iii) figure_plotting/ holds the notebook and conda environment that reproduce the paper’s GNN performance, node/edge importance and network figures from the saved outputs. Conda environment files ( base_env_gnn.yml , figures_paper_gnn.yml ) specify the dependencies. The other notebooks show analyses regarding the generalisability, contender frameworks, etc.
title: Integrative Spatial Modelling of Cellular Plasticity using Graph Neural Networks and Geostatistics

summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can adapt O-RAN slice allocations to changing traffic and interference, but episode-average URLLC cost can hide failures during short traffic surges. We audit the maximum traffic-group mean cost; because the groups partition an episode, this worst-group constraint already implies the mean constraint. In a single-cell benchmark with burst traffic, selective jamming, impaired KPMs, and 105 discrete actions, 57 static actions satisfy the mean limit by point estimate but only 46 satisfy the worst-group limit on 100 fresh episodes; interval estimates classify 45 as supported, 10 as uncertain, and 50 as violating. The validation-selected mean-feasible action is worst-group uncertain on those traces. Across five seeds of PPO-Lagrangian, recurrent PPO-Lagrangian, and DQN, bootstrap intervals classify 13 of 15 final states as violating and two as uncertain; every recurrent final policy reduces to a constant catalogue action. A privileged oracle and a delayed-load heuristic, both a two-action rule tuned on validation episodes, safely recover about 4.2 return of adaptive headroom on training-matched and constant-jammer traces, which no evaluated learner or shield does. A calibrated risk ensemble has five supported evaluated runs on both scenarios, yet it loses return to the best safe static action and to the heuristic. Under an unseen sweep jammer, only 50% URLLC reservation remains supported. The resulting audit establishes traffic group, seed, checkpoint, and distribution shift as distinct dimensions of O-RAN DRL safety evaluation.
title: Auditing Deep Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Network Slicing: Worst-Group Safety under Traffic Bursts and Jamming

summary: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education requires sound instruments for identifying faculty development needs. This study reports the Portuguese adaptation and measurement-model evaluation of the Generative AI Competency Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers and Researchers (GAICS-TR), a 35-item self-report instrument designed to assess academics’ perceived self-efficacy in relation to GenAI competencies. The scale comprises nine dimensions conceptually organised into four domains: Basic GenAI Understanding, Teaching with GenAI, Research with GenAI, and Professional Engagement with GenAI. The Portuguese version was developed through a pragmatic, team-based translation and adaptation procedure informed by established cross-cultural adaptation guidance. The procedure included translation of the items, review of their wording and contextual suitability, discussion of discrepancies, and consensus within the PRODIGIA research team. The items were administered on a five-point agreement scale to faculty and researchers from three partner universities, yielding 105 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLSSEM) was used to assess indicator reliability, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The retained measurement model met the reported reliability and validity criteria, with the exception of the discriminant validity between GPD and GKG, which yielded a correlation of 0.923 (exceeding the standard 0.90 threshold). Item GPD2 was removed after presenting a loading of 0.482; after its removal, the professional-development dimension reached an Average Variance Extracted of 0.708 and a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.790. This item-level result should be interpreted cautiously because it may reflect wording, translation, or sample-specific effects. The adapted scale provides evidence for assessing self-reported GenAI competency self-efficacy in the participating institutions and for informing the diagnostic phase of PRODIGIA. Replication in larger, independent samples is needed.
title: Validating a Generative AI competency self-efficacy scale for higher education faculty: A PLS-SEM study

summary: Version 1.8.1 carries the final revised manuscript (data and code availability, design history, and wording of the second wave) and adds means to the covariate summaries of the coverage audit. All other data are unchanged from version 1.8.0, and the measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. Version 1.8 accompanies the major revision of the manuscript. The results archive adds the dependency-graph coverage audit with its crawl, sample and eligibility records, the stratified sensitivity of the two waves, and the independent two-annotator validation of 400 items (packets, codebook, freeze records, the final annotators' pseudonymous answers, consensus and score). It also archives the cohort baselines, maintenance-scope entries and three table files that these analyses bind. The measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. The record contains two archives. pintrace-measurements-v1.tar.zst holds the per-repository measurement snapshots for 457 measured repositories and 301 matched control repositories, the archived upstream release evidence and the matched-control assignments. pintrace-results-v1.tar.zst holds the published result files, the formal-statistics outputs, the 150-item gold set, the research documentation, the manuscript PDF and LaTeX source, and the claim ledger that maps every rendered number to a result file and JSON pointer. Each archive includes a SHA-256 manifest and a README with extraction and reproduction instructions. The measurement files contain repository identifiers but no commit author names, commit messages, e-mail addresses or credentials. The code is at https://github.com/JunjieChen0/PinTrace under the MIT license. Replication data and results are released under CC BY 4.0. The study has no comparison group shielded from the incident, so the reported quantities describe timing, targets and persistence rather than an incident effect.

summary: Current research in the food industry highlights the importance of alternative protein sources in the context of global population growth and the need to reduce the negative impact of raising animals, producing animal proteins, on the environment. Plant proteins represent a sustainable, affordable and beneficial option for health, with high potential to replace animal proteins in the food industry. Plant sources rich in protein include legumes, cereals, pseudocereals, oilseeds, green leaves, algae and, more recently, insects. They differ considerably in protein content and amino acid profile, and their strategic combination can ensure a balanced intake of essential nutrients. Legumes offer high protein content, but are deficient in sulfur amino acids. Cereals, although lower in protein, bring technological benefits and can complement the amino acids missing from legumes. Pseudocereals have a higher nutritional value than conventional cereals, while green leaves and algae offer a high proteins intake and compounds with antioxidant potential, although they require advanced technologies to overcome extraction limitations. Extraction methods play a decisive role in the yield and quality of plant proteins. Conventional techniques are efficient but can cause denaturation and provide low yields. On the other hand, emerging methods allow the recovery of proteins in larger quantities, preserving their functional and technological properties.
title: Plant-based proteins: sources, extraction methods and functional perspectives for the sustainable food industry

summary: Replication package for a staged empirical study of whether a dependency upgrade changes the conclusions of machine-learning comparisons. Six scikit-learn classifiers (LR, SVC, kNN, RF, GB, HGB) were evaluated on all 63 eligible OpenML-CC18 tasks with frozen splits (6 × 5-fold cross-validation), across two real upgrades: 0.21.3 → 0.22.2.post1 (changed defaults) and 1.8.0 → 1.9.1 (negative control). The package contains: the frozen study protocol (v2.2.5) and pre-run amendment (v2.2.6), with SHA-256 manifests; the frozen plan (folds and seeds), environment lock files and provenance records for each scikit-learn release; the frozen changelog-coding frame used for blinding; all fold-level results (balanced accuracy and prediction hashes) and analysis reports; post-review analyses G0–G3 with all raw outputs: restoration of historical defaults, boosting interventions, bootstrap and winner-margin sensitivity, and the corrected six-estimator explicit map E2; scripts that verify every stored file and recompute every number and figure in the paper. Quick check, with no experiments required: python3 paper/verify_results.py and python3 postreview/verify_postreview.py --zip VersionShift_replication.zip . The attached VersionShift_replication.zip (SHA-256 5eb716b64c21ded6f979b0b1610bb68aee46ad2f24889a0d3b133bd430c6ff7d) is the frozen original-study archive that the post-review kits require. The OpenML-CC18 datasets are not redistributed. The scripts rebuild them from OpenML and check them against the frozen hashes.
tags: dependency upgrades; default arguments; breaking changes; scikit-learn; reproducibility; conclusion stability; empirical software engineering
title: When a Library Upgrade Changes the Verdict: Default-Configuration Drift and the Stability of Machine-Learning Comparisons

summary: This record contains the data of the CascadeFQN Study, which asks when a language model is needed to resolve the fully qualified names of types in Java snippets that lack their import statements. It holds a SQLite database with the 467 runs of the study (predictions, costs, and gold labels) and a cache of the model replies, so the LLM runs can be repeated without cost. It also holds FQNs4J, a new benchmark of 1,224 snippets from code created in 2025 or later, together with StatType-SO and ThaliaType, and the dictionaries, usage statistics, trained scorers, and library jars the pipeline uses. The outputs of the external baselines (CKTyper, Scitix, SnR) and the repair rounds of ZS4C on our test parts are included, and the accompanying code repository ( https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cascade-fqn-replication/ ) regenerates every table and number of the paper from these files.
title: Datasets for the CascadeFQN Study

summary: Photonic Neural Networks (PNNs) are projected to be the next-generation AI platform, driving significant advances in compute energy and area efficiency by leveraging light’s parallelism across space, wavelength, and time. Here we present a Photonic Integrated Tensor Core (PITC) architecture that combines an Arrayed Waveguide Grating Router (AWGR)-enabled PNN with a SiGe electro-absorption modulator (EAM) array following a chiplet-based silicon photonic (SiPho) accelerator setup for multi-wavelength data and weight encoding. The 8×8 PITC architectural layout, was experimentally validated in two AI benchmark workloads at 20 Gbaud, successfully classifying the IRIS and MNIST datasets yielding Cohen’s kappa-scores of 0.8438 and 0.7421, respectively.

summary: Code accompanying the paper Benchmarking DFT and Machine Learning Potentials for Heat of Formation and Combustion of High-Energy Materials . For a target molecule the script enumerates isodesmic reactions against a curated library of small reference species and ranks them. Bond conservation is encoded as bond signatures (bond order together with the hybridisation and aromaticity of the connected atoms) and solved with a linear programming solver under random cost-vector perturbations, so that many distinct valid schemes are found. A secondary ring-breaking relaxation is applied where strict conservation is impossible for fused ring systems. Candidates are ranked by an IsoScore that balances chemical simplicity, Tanimoto structural similarity to the reference library, and stoichiometric cost. The repository contains the generator, the input file with the twenty high-energy materials of the benchmark set, and a README.
title: Automated isodesmic reaction generator for high-energy materials

summary: Simultaneous tolerance certification asks whether every component of a dense latent vector lies within its prescribed range. This preprint studies noisy unit-norm linear measurements under pathwise resource budgets, with tolerances calibrated to a fixed prior membership probability. For independent Gaussian priors, every fixed linear channel is uniformly asymptotically equivalent, for the membership decision, to a coordinate-precision design at no greater total precision. A marked Poisson limit characterizes the complete family of feasible limiting experiments. The resulting allocation theory gives exact Brier-optimal designs and proves that every classification-optimal allocation has zero plus at most one positive normalized precision level. The global classification problem therefore reduces to a one-dimensional coverage choice. At low budgets, no allocation is most informative for every decision loss. At fixed row precision, adaptive screening yields a squared-logarithmic reduction in the order of measurements required for prescribed positive decision gain. For classification, sharp high-accuracy constants distinguish the inverse-square risk dependence of fixed designs from the logarithmic dependence of adaptive acquisition. Bounded-spectrum Gaussian dependence preserves the fixed-design frontier. Matching resource orders extend to exponential-power priors, including Laplace and lighter tails. A frozen Gaussian simulation, combined with certified deterministic bounds, establishes a finite-dimensional advantage over all fixed linear designs under the same affine acquisition budget, with one-sided 95% Monte Carlo confidence. This record contains the preprint, proof supplement, editable LaTeX sources, and a reproducibility archive with programs, experimental protocols, and saved results. The manuscript and proof supplement are licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0; original software is licensed under MIT. Third-party components retain their own licenses.
title: Simultaneous Tolerance Certification: Limit Experiments and Sharp Resource Laws

summary: Research code accompanying the paper Data-proximal null-space networks for inverse problems by Jürgen Frikel, Simon Göppel and Markus Haltmeier. Data-proximal networks extend null-space networks by learned corrections whose additional change of the predicted data is explicitly controlled. The repository contains the implementation of the synthetic limited-angle computed tomography study: ellipse phantom generation, the discrete Radon operator and the numerical row-space projection, Tikhonov and total-variation initializations, the residual (RES), null-space (NSN) and data-proximal (DP1, DP2) networks, Float64 training with checkpointing, the frozen evaluator, the public inference entry point for published checkpoints, and the compact scientific export from which the paper tables and figures are regenerated with scripts/reproduce_paper.py . Trained weights, the row-space basis, the operator and the sample data are not part of this record; they are intended for separate data records. The program code is licensed under GPL-3.0-only; see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for the U-Net attribution.

summary: Version 5: Documentation corrections only; code, data, and results are unchanged from v4. Version 4  adds the analyses of the second revision: time-ordered and cross-project evaluation, structured label noise, a drop-one process-feature ablation, a Random Forest hyperparameter check, and label-provenance analyses (results/r2_experiments/), with the per-row revision metadata and commit dates they need. All Java runners now read the datasets from a configurable data directory (JML_DATA_DIR). Everything in v3 is otherwise unchanged; the audit labels are the same as in v3. Version 3. Supersedes version 2 (distributed as package v1.1) and version 1 (package v1.0). Prepared for the revised submission to Science of Computer Programming. Figures from earlier versions should not be cited. Manual validation re-run with a two-rater protocol. Estimated commit-level SZZ label precision is now  49.5% (197/398) with inter-rater agreement Cohen's κ = 0.799 , replacing the 29.2% reported in versions 1 and 2, which came from a single-rater audit with no documented agreement statistic. Per-project precision: Kafka 57.1%, Gson 48.5%, Commons-IO 42.9%. Both raters' blind passes, the disagreement-resolution record for the 10 conflicting cases, and a per-instance false-positive taxonomy of all 201 false positives are included. The labelling question changed, so labels are not directly comparable across versions. The is_valid_fix column has been renamed is_true_bic . The earlier audit recorded whether a candidate was itself a valid fix; the current audit records whether the candidate introduced the defect that its traced fix later repaired. These are different questions, and the resulting labels cannot be compared row by row with earlier versions. A central claim has been withdrawn. Earlier versions of the paper argued that feature-engineering quality has a stronger influence on predictive performance than label purity. A label-noise sensitivity experiment, included here, does not support that claim: adding 20 percentage points of label noise erases more MCC than the entire static-to-hybrid feature-engineering gain, in every project. The claim has been removed from the manuscript and replaced with the measured finding that process features hold a consistent advantage over static features at the observed noise level, while performance remains sensitive to further label degradation. Ablation and significance results re-derived from logged runs. All values now come from 270 independently seeded 10-fold cross-validation runs (30 seeds × 3 projects × 3 feature sets), with per-seed raw results, runner scripts and exact seeds included. The reported Hybrid-over-Static improvement on Commons-IO is 55%, not the 128% stated previously; Static-only MCC on Commons-IO is +0.166, not negative. Statistical testing is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test paired by seed with Cliff's delta and Holm-Bonferroni correction over nine comparisons per metric. MCC replaces F1 as the primary metric, and class prevalence, trivial baselines and confusion matrices are now reported. Prevalence differs by a factor of ~2.7 across the three projects (55.4% / 44.9% / 20.9%), so F1 is not comparable across them; all trivial baselines have MCC = 0. The reported pipeline does not use SMOTE. A direct comparison, included here, shows no benefit in any project and a measurable cost on Commons-IO. SMOTE remains available as a configuration option in the framework. Runtime and energy figures are measured, not extrapolated: 30.6 minutes wall-clock across all three projects for the reported configuration, with per-phase timings and logs. New in this version: the label-noise sensitivity sweep; an AGE-feature ablation; confusion matrices and specificity per project and feature set; a Process-versus-Static significance test; a read-only exporter for the SZZ fix-to-BIC mapping, which the original pipeline did not persist; and a replication configuration annotated with the exact s

summary: Se estudia la variante del algoritmo de Collatz que aplica 3m+1 a los impares congruentes con 1 módulo 4 y 3m−1 a los congruentes con 3 módulo 4, introducida por el autor en 2019. La regla equivale a elegir, entre 3m−1 y 3m+1, el término divisible por 4, de modo que cada paso impar va seguido al menos de dos divisiones por 2. Se demuestra que la distancia al punto fijo 1 se contrae al menos en el factor 3/4 en cada transición entre impares. De ello se siguen la convergencia a 1 de toda órbita, una cota explícita para el número de términos impares y una cota logarítmica para la longitud total de la trayectoria. Se establecen dos acoplamientos exactos. El primero relaciona, en un solo paso, la variante con la aplicación de Collatz acelerada y sitúa su diferencia en una única valuación 2-ádica. El segundo la relaciona con la permutación considerada por Collatz en 1932: sobre cada impar, la inversa de la permutación realiza en un paso el resultado de tres pasos elementales de la variante, y los retornos impares de ambos sistemas difieren en una potencia de 3 determinada por la valuación 2-ádica del paso. Se demuestra que el retorno impar de la permutación es biyectivo y que la variante se obtiene suprimiendo los factores de 3 de su resultado, y se precisa que esta factorización no es una conjugación. Se señalan además obstáculos a la conjugación de la variante con la aplicación de Collatz y con el retorno de la permutación. El resultado central es de naturaleza simbólica. El lenguaje de paridades de la variante es exactamente el conjunto de palabras binarias que evitan el factor 11, con entropía topológica igual al logaritmo de la razón áurea, y la densidad de las clases residuales que realizan cada palabra viene dada por una medida de Markov explícita y no uniforme. Ello contrasta con el teorema de paridades de Terras y Lagarias para la aplicación de Collatz, donde todas las palabras se realizan con la misma densidad. Se plantea como problema abierto la geometría de las clases residuales asociadas a cada palabra, con datos de enumeración exhaustiva. El escrito discute con precisión qué no se sigue de estos resultados acerca de la conjetura de Collatz, y propone controles positivos y negativos para evaluar argumentos generales. Los enunciados efectivos se han comprobado computacionalmente, y el suplemento contiene el programa en Python que reproduce esas comprobaciones con aritmética entera, junto con sus resultados. Versión 2. Se añaden un índice, las referencias a los escritos del autor sobre la permutación de Collatz de 1932 y sobre los filtros bilaterales de los mínimos de sus órbitas, y un suplemento computacional formado por el programa de verificación, un resumen de sus resultados y la tabla de las pruebas sobre las clases residuales. La sección de verificación numérica se reescribe para describir ese suplemento.
title: Una variación en el algoritmo de la conjetura de Collatz.

summary: This record is the reference implementation released with COES-CD, built from the method and evaluation protocol described in the accompanying manuscript (Sections 5-6 and Appendices B/D). It is a clean implementation that follows the manuscript and the appendix, with fixed seeds, documented configurations and a uniform evaluation pipeline, and every measured number reported in this record was produced by running the code shipped here; values transcribed from the manuscript are marked as the manuscript's. The package contains the model source (coes_cd/), the experiment configurations (configs/), a deterministic synthetic data generator with fixed seeds (data_generation/, scripts/generate_data.py), acquisition scripts for the baselines actually obtained, and the scripts that rebuild the 10 tables and the 6 figures that README's asset table assigns a generation script to. NOTEARS and DAGMA are fetched at pinned commits by the shipped scripts; CSL-HNTS, DyCAST, Meta-D2AG and SPACETIME are not integrated, for the reasons given in Section 0 of docs/BASELINES.md. The pipeline is a six-step chain: generate the datasets, train stage 1, run the stage-2 stability readout, evaluate both stages into results/raw_results.csv, collect the training costs, and rebuild the assets. README's Quick start gives the exact commands, and its asset table lists the seeds and the measured per-run costs. Fixed hyperparameters, the seeds and the dataset count for each setting are listed in docs/HYPERPARAMETERS.md; the per-dataset checksums are stored in the manifests under data/synthetic/. No result files are shipped: the package has no results/ directory. Every asset whose README asset-table row names a generation script is produced by that script from the chain above; assets marked 'no generator in this release' are not, and any stored row whose source lies outside this release is identified in that table's note. NetSim is a public benchmark and is not redistributed; data/prepare_netsim.py records its public identity and implements the preprocessing, but the manuscript's N = 18 / K = 3 subset is not identified, so it is not re-run. Satellite telemetry is access-restricted and is not redistributed; the package ships the preprocessing procedure, the variable and regime schema, and a synthetic demo that exercises the pipeline end to end without the restricted input. Tables and figures that README's asset table does not list are not generated by this release. External baseline code is cloned at install time and is not redistributed with this record. Every measured cell in the rebuilt assets is the output of the code shipped here, and where an asset also carries a value transcribed from the manuscript, that value appears in a column marked as such. The measurement path of each cell (forward chain, stage-2 readout, gate, dataset coverage) and the protocol used for it are documented in README and in the table notes generated by the code. How the released runs differ from the submitted experiments: the released tables are measured at 800 epochs on a consumer GPU with one training seed per dataset and 10 datasets per setting, while the submitted tables were measured at 2000 epochs on an RTX 3090 with five training seeds and 20 datasets per setting. Where a table carries a manuscript column, it is marked as such, and each comparison can be read directly off the table. Table 5 and Table 6 are rebuilt and compared cell by cell in the table notes. summary: The KV cache is the bottleneck of long-context LLM inference.  Every modern serving system —  vLLM, SGLang, Mooncake  — is, at its core, a memory manager for the cache that grows one token at a time as the model decodes.  PagedAttention, RadixAttention , and the various  prefix caching  schemes each solve a piece of the problem, but none of them is  lock-free , none of them is  position-keyed , and none of them uses  structural sharing  to handle both beam-search branching and multi-tenant prefix sharing at the same time. This book introduces the  persistent rope  — a single data structure that does all of these things, derived from two pieces of prior art that were never combined before: the  persistent vector  (which gives the rope its branching semantics) and the  Bw-tree  (which gives the rope its lock-free properties). The book is a design document and API reference for the rope, written for engineers who build serving systems, GPU kernels, and lock-free data structures.  It is  not  a benchmark paper,  not  a tutorial, and  not  a complete serving system. The Python reference implementation is  correct but not lock-free ; the  lock-free Rust port is scaffolded in the repository  and described in detail in Chapter 22. The book covers the design (Ch 1–9), the Python reference (Ch 10–11), the verification (Ch 12–14), the public API (Ch 15–19), and the honest framing of what works, what doesn't, and what's left for future work (Ch 20–23). The appendices include a full  glossary, references, and index . Read it in order if you want to understand the design end-to-end; jump to Chapters 10–19 if you want to use the Python reference; read Chapter 22 if you're planning the Rust port.
title: The Persistent Rope: Position-Keyed Indexing for the LLM KV Cache

summary: This record accompanies Working Paper No. 9 of the Independent FAIR Evaluation Series of the ATLAS Framework , entitled Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation . The study examines the concentration of computational AACF susceptibility profiles derived from frozen PaccMann and DRPreter predictions for 95 unique registered configurations across 970 matched cancer cell-line profiles . Scores are transformed into normalized weights using a softmax transformation favouring lower AACF indices, with fixed model-specific reference scales. Profile characterization includes Shannon entropy, normalized entropy, effective configuration counts, and leading configuration weights. The evaluation addresses five normalization-scale multipliers, the effect of retaining 97 registered labels instead of 95 unique configurations, lineage comparisons covering 953 profiles in 21 groups, and variability across ten DRPreter checkpoints. It also distinguishes entropy calculated after median index aggregation from the median of checkpoint-wise entropies. At the reference scales, median normalized entropy was 0.9346 for PaccMann and 0.9528 for the DRPreter median consensus . These aggregate differences coexisted with weak cross-model agreement in cell-line entropy rankings ( Spearman ρ = −0.0788 ) and only six shared profiles among the 97 most concentrated profiles identified by each model. Normalization and checkpoint aggregation affected concentration summaries and rankings, demonstrating that entropy requires an explicitly specified computational representation. The accompanying computational materials document the six-stage workflow through analysis scripts, frozen input resources, configuration and profile mappings, normalization policies, numerical tables and arrays, saved bootstrap draws, and provenance and validation records. A README explains the directory structure, principal outputs, reproduction workflow, and interpretation limits. Resources inherited from ATLAS Working Papers 06–08 retain their upstream licensing and attribution requirements. The final technical audit recorded 2,363 passed checks and no failed checks , reviewing 206 distinct files in the selected analysis chain. This audit supports technical consistency and traceability within the implemented checks; it does not constitute independent experimental or clinical validation. The results establish entropy as a conditional descriptor of computational profile concentration . They do not establish therapeutic efficacy, measured mixture responses, biological mechanisms, or malignant-versus-normal selectivity. The materials support transparent inspection, reanalysis, and further methodological evaluation of the ATLAS framework.
title: Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation

summary: Resilience in psychology and public health is usually assessed through recovery or maintained functioning, outcomes that do not reveal whether desirable states have become self-maintaining or still depend on external support. Drawing on coerced-regime theory from social-ecological systems research, we develop aided mental health resilience (AMHR), a framework for desirable mental health states established or maintained through external inputs of resources, organisation, political capital and trust. We make three contributions. First, we frame population mental health as a dimension of social-ecological system states and define the external maintenance subsidy required to sustain desirable conditions. Second, using a dialectical reading of regime change, we distinguish reversion, permanent subsidy and sublation, in which the function initially supplied by aid becomes reproduced through reorganised capacities, practices or institutions. Displacement of harm is treated as a cross-cutting failure mode. Four cases illustrate these dynamics and their limits. Third, drawing on strange loop ethics, we argue that paradoxical outcomes should trigger review not only of intervention instruments but also of the premises that define desirable states and authorise intervention. We outline disconfirmation conditions and a research agenda centred on longitudinal evaluation, subsidy accounting, displacement monitoring and recursive premise review.
title: Aided mental health resilience: governing desirable states that cannot sustain themselves

summary: This paper establishes the mathematical and methodological foundations of the GCT-STL research program on the P versus NP problem, using the decision Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP_dec) as a canonical NP-complete representative and its polynomial reduction to 3-SAT with an exact materialized 3-CNF artifact. The framework organizes nine provenance-controlled descriptors (D1–D9) across three computational-information domains: semantic/geometric (S), temporal/computational (T), and logical/syntactic (L). These descriptors form the canonical raw Valiant–González tensorial signature (R0), supported by explicit SourceMap and Provenance Bundle contracts and three foundational entropy results. Paper I-A situates R0 within a branched four-representation architecture: R1 is a componentwise logarithmic scale complement, R2 is the canonical entropic/information representation, and R3 is the exact-envelope normalized representation. The Full STL Tensorial Coupling Principle remains an open and falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established obstruction theorem. The logical-complexity architecture distinguishes the internal classes P_STL and NP_STL and the conditional F1–F4 route toward the classical P versus NP problem. F1 and F2 remain open mathematical obligations. Empirical robustness, tensorial diagnostics, and candidate obstructions do not constitute universal computational lower bounds. Accordingly, Paper I-A does not prove P ≠ NP. It establishes the representational, logical, methodological, and formal-certification foundations for subsequent research within the GCT-STL program.
title: Three-Dimensional Entropic Domains for TSP Complexity via 3-SAT: Foundations of the GCT-STL Research Program on P versus NP

summary: This deliverable presents practical and adaptable protocols for scaling citizen science initiatives, developed through a user-centred design (UCD) process informed by co-design and validation workshops, interviews with citizen science experts, researchers, and practitioners, and a literature review. Rather than proposing a single, one-size-fits-all model, the protocols are organised around five CROPS scaling strategies: institutional scaling (driving policy and governance change), expansion and replication scaling (extending reach and participation), transformative change scaling (influencing values, attitudes, and behaviours), downscaling (reducing scope while maintaining impact), and combined scaling (pursuing multiple pathways simultaneously). These strategies reflect a multidimensional understanding of scaling that extends beyond geographic or numerical growth. To support projects in deciding whether and how to scale, the deliverable also highlights the CROPS Scalability Framework, a diagnostic tool built around nine constructs relating to the intrinsic characteristics of a project, the scaling process itself, and the target context. This is complemented by a six-step Strategic Scaling Decision process that helps projects determine whether scaling is not only feasible but strategically appropriate. In this deliverable, the protocols are first presented through concise, visually structured informative briefs, providing accessible overviews of guidance for each scaling strategy. These are followed by more detailed guidance, including summary tables of protocols, pillars, and objectives, illustrative examples, and practical dos and don'ts. Additional resources, tools, and guidelines support implementation. The protocols are designed to be adopted in full or in part, depending on a project's context, resources, and objectives, and are intended to remain useful not only for scaling but also for the design of new citizen science initiatives from the outset. Ethical considerations, including privacy, inclusivity, fairness, and transparency, are treated as a cross-cutting requirement throughout. The primary audience for the protocols is the citizen science practitioner community, represented through personas developed as part of the UCD process, alongside researchers, policymakers, EU and international organisation representatives, and other stakeholders engaged in scaling citizen science, particularly in relation to the Horizon Europe EU Missions. The CROPS protocols are intended as an evolving, non-prescriptive resource rather than a definitive model for scaling. Their value lies in providing a structured basis for reflection, planning, and decision-making, while recognising that successful scaling also depends on a broader enabling ecosystem of institutional readiness, sustainable funding, and supportive technical and policy infrastructure. The methodology underpinning protocol development, including persona creation and the wider UCD process, is described in detail in Section 7 and the accompanying annexes.
title: D3.1: User-centred Design Protocols for Scaling Citizen Science

summary: tc-cwi is a lightweight Python toolbox for Environmental and Operational Condition (EoC) compensation in ultrasonic Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) using Coda Wave Interferometry (CWI) and the Time-Stretching method . Developed within the  USES2 project (Work Package 3, Deliverable D3.3), it estimates the relative velocity stretch factor ( eps ) and/or time shift ( dt ) that best realign a measured ultrasonic signal with a baseline reference (fixed or moving-average) and reports the remaining decorrelation. The package provides both clean Python functions ( stretch , shift , find_optimum , MovingAverageReference ) and a 1:1 MATLAB-compatible dispatch interface ( tc_cwi("findeps", ...) ). PyPI Package: https://pypi.org/project/tc-cwi/ ( pip install tc-cwi ) Source Repository (GitHub): https://github.com/aderaema/tc-cwi Workflows (EWSHM 2026): https://github.com/Zensor-BE/tc-cwi-workflows GitLab Entry Point: https://gitlab.com/uses2project/wp3/tc-cwi

It is a reconstruction, not the original experiment code; the original code was developed iteratively and was not maintained as a release-ready artifact. It depended on internal paths and an undocumented environment and was not kept in a state that could be independently verified. This record therefore provides a clean implementation that follows the manuscript and the appendix, with fixed seeds, documented configurations, and a uniform evaluation pipeline. Every measured number reported in this record was produced by running the code shipped here; values transcribed from the manuscript are marked as the manuscript's. The package contains the model source (coes_cd/), the experiment configurations (configs/), a deterministic synthetic data generator with fixed seeds (data_generation/, scripts/generate_data.py), acquisition scripts for the baselines actually obtained, and the scripts that rebuild the 10 tables and the 6 figures that README's asset table assigns a generation script to. NOTEARS and DAGMA are fetched at pinned commits by the shipped scripts; CSL-HNTS, DyCAST, Meta-D2AG and SPACETIME are not integrated, for the reasons given in Section 0 of docs/BASELINES.md. The pipeline is a six-step chain: generate the datasets, train stage 1, run the stage-2 stability readout, evaluate both stages into results/raw_results.csv, collect the training costs, and rebuild the assets. README's Quick start gives the exact commands, and its asset table lists the seeds and the measured per-run costs. Fixed hyperparameters, the seeds and the dataset count for each setting are listed in docs/HYPERPARAMETERS.md; the per-dataset checksums are stored in the manifests under data/synthetic/. No result files are shipped: the package has no results/ directory. Every asset whose README asset-table row names a generation script is produced by that script from the chain above; assets marked 'no generator in this release' are not, and any stored row whose source lies outside this release is identified in that table's note. NetSim is a public benchmark and is not redistributed; data/prepare_netsim.py records its public identity and implements the preprocessing, but the manuscript's N = 18 / K = 3 subset is not identified, so it is not re-run. summary: This paper develops a scale-spanning account of latent vibration and frequency manifestation within Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM). It examines the relationship between complete latent vibration, the negative and positive displacement domains around the manifestable origin, and the eligibility of positive displacement for progression towards physical manifestation. The development distinguishes the complete latent-vibration interval from the directed displacement associated with manifestation, establishing the proposed Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck threshold relationships in terms of the Planck length. The analysis further develops phase-dependent frequency relations below the Planck threshold and considers the proposed frequency increments associated with the Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck domains. It then presents a state-dependent sequence of energy–frequency transformations across latent, phase, and manifested states, including the reverse progression associated with dissolution. Within this framework, frequency and displacement are treated as related physical parameters whose coefficients depend on the corresponding phase domain. The paper also distinguishes the phase-state potential-energy mass representation from the mass contribution associated with the manifested domain. It formulates the effective-mass relationship and separates this ECM representation from the distinct dark-energy-related mass representation. Taken together, these developments present an integrated theoretical description of latent vibration, manifestation eligibility, threshold transitions, energy–frequency relations, and mass-state transformations within the proposed ECM framework.
title: Complete Latent Vibration and Frequency Manifestation Eligibility in Extended Classical Mechanics

summary: Nicomachean Algorethics: Principles, Limits and Verification of Human and Artificial Transformative Decision-Making This monograph develops a philosophical and formal framework for examining the legitimacy, responsibility and verifiability of transformative decisions made by human agents, institutions and artificial systems. Drawing on Aristotelian practical philosophy, contemporary ethics, epistemology, decision theory and the challenges of artificial intelligence governance, Nicomachean Algorethics addresses a fundamental question: under what conditions may an agent legitimately make decisions that transform the lives, opportunities and futures of others? The proposed framework is organised around twelve normative laws and a Recognition Matrix designed to distinguish technical possibility, epistemic justification, normative admissibility and legitimate authority. Rather than attempting to calculate or optimise the Good, the framework investigates the conditions under which decisions may be justified, contested, corrected or withheld. Particular attention is given to uncertainty, the limitations of representation, delegated authority, corrigibility, reversibility, capability preservation, the distribution of responsibility, value pluralism and the prevention of harm. The work introduces formal definitions, mathematical formulations, verification contracts and operational procedures intended to make normative assumptions and decision-making constraints explicit. Its methodological approach distinguishes conceptual arguments, formal propositions, computational verification, illustrative examples and empirical claims, without treating these different forms of evidence as interchangeable. The monograph also examines recognition as a philosophical and practical problem, investigating the relationship between distinction, otherness, interpretation and responsibility in human and artificial decision-making. Through theoretical analysis and selected case studies, it explores how artificial systems and institutions may improve not only their decisions but also their capacity to identify, explain and correct errors. The work comprises twenty-three chapters, an epilogue and five technical appendices addressing verification contracts, retrospective analysis, comparative protocols, canonical terminology and formal mechanisation. Nicomachean Algorethics is intended as a contribution to moral philosophy, philosophy of technology, artificial intelligence ethics and the interdisciplinary study of responsible decision-making. Its central thesis is that responsibility requires more than selecting among available alternatives: it requires recognising who may be affected, what authority may legitimately be exercised and which possibilities must remain open to others and to future generations.
