summary: Reproducibility data and executable source for Accuracy, Storage, and Update Cost in Reference-Assisted Sensor Calibration , by Oleksandr Kuznetsov. Version 1.1.0 adds the completed seven-model common-fixture campaign: two validated sessions each on Mega2560, ESP32-C3 and ESP32-S3, 480 timing records and 42 numerical-accuracy checks. It preserves the three original acquisition ZIPs, firmware images, raw serial logs, source/image hashes and an executable audit. All models use one frozen synthetic distorted-NTC fixture; no coefficients, seeds or hyperparameters were retuned. The captured S3 executable uses native float32 instructions. The 4.2% polynomial-Horner timing advantage over LUT32 is specific to the recorded S3 build; optimization-level and code-layout robustness were not measured. The original 1.0.0 evidence archive is retained unchanged. It contains the matched synthetic calibration/adaptation records, cross-validation and sensitivity analyses, historical MCU fixtures and paired refinements using 32-pair block least squares and decaying NLMS. Earlier reanalysis reused separate development and confirmation seeds; it is not a new untouched holdout. Historical fixtures remain separate from the V2 frontier. This is an implementation and resource-cost study. Accuracy and drift are controlled synthetic quantities. Physical boards establish execution time and numerical agreement. No physical NTC/LDR calibration, S3 update timing, measured energy, WCET, peak stack or between-board uncertainty is claimed. The author photograph illustrates the development boards, not a sensor-calibration setup. Immutable V2 audit and results: commit df19065 . Each component archive supplies exact code provenance and SHA-256 manifests. The cleaned English documentation preserves all numerical evidence and the frozen benchmark source set. Author-created data and research documentation: CC BY 4.0. Software retains its included MIT license; third-party components retain their own terms. This is a dataset/software evidence release, not an accepted journal publication.

summary: Visual geo-localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in GNSS-denied environments remains challenging due to the lack of datasets with trajectory continuity, broad scene and geographic coverage, multimodal UAV imagery, wide altitude and geometric variation, and sufficient scale. Here we present UAV-VisLoc, a dataset for UAV geo-localization through image retrieval between UAV imagery and geo-referenced satellite tiles. UAV-VisLoc contains 14,998 UAV images organized into 30 flight trajectories, spanning six continents and seven scene types. The dataset preserves contiguous observations along each trajectory, enabling trajectory-level studies under realistic sequential flight conditions. It includes RGB and Infrared UAV imagery and covers altitudes from 160 to 2,500 m. The dataset comprises 21 real UAV flights collected across multiple provinces in China and 9 synthetic flights built from OpenAerialMap imagery for regions outside China. The dataset also provides image-level flight metadata and more than 120,000 geo-referenced satellite tiles. Baseline retrieval experiments and accompanying scripts are provided to validate data organization, ground-truth annotations, and benchmark usability under diverse real-world conditions.
title: UAV-VisLoc: A Large-scale UAV Dataset with Continuous Trajectories for Visual Geo-localization

summary: This paper examines the effectiveness of Uzbekistan's tax reforms in reducing the shadow economy. Drawing on macroeconomic indicators, firm-level data, and econometric estimates, the analysis reports model-based shadow-economy estimates of approximately 38.9–39.6% of GDP for 2025, alongside reductions in statutory tax rates. The reported average firm-level tax burden was 27.3%, compared with a macroeconomic indicator of 18.3%. Econometric findings suggest a conditional tax-burden benchmark of 19–20% of GDP. The study concludes that sustainable formalization may be supported by tax-rate optimization, equitable taxation, simplified compliance procedures, improved VAT administration, and effective institutional enforcement. summary: This Zenodo repository contains the data for the following article: Molecular Signatures of Pressure-Induced Phase Transitions in a Lipid Bilayer (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcb.5c08607) by Yanna Gautier, Guillaume Stirnemann, and Jérôme Hénin   Abstract: Understanding how lipid bilayers respond to pressure is essential for interpreting the coupling between membrane proteins and their native environments. Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics to examine the pressure–temperature behavior of model membranes composed of dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) or its cis-unsaturated analogue Δ9-cis-PC. Within the studied range (288–308 K, 1–2000 bar), DMPC undergoes a liquid–gel transition, while Δ9-cis-PC remains fluid due to unsaturation. The CHARMM36 force field reproduces experimental boundaries with high fidelity: simulated DMPC transitions fall within 5–10 K and 100–300 bar of experimental values, and Δ9-cis-PC exhibits no transition. Hysteresis is modest but most pronounced when starting from low-temperature gels; we propose a split-phase simulation protocol that alleviates the hysteresis problem. We identify the area per lipid, bilayer thickness, and acyl-chain gauche fractions as sensitive phase markers; among these, the gauche fraction provides the most robust signature. Simulations indicate that an interdigitated gel is the equilibrium structure under finite-size conditions, and we propose a novel metric to quantify the extent of this phenomenon. However, at low temperature and high pressure, interdigitation decreases, consistent with the experimental lamellar gel phase. This long-lived interdigitation critically impacts standard order parameters, specifically, area per lipid and membrane thickness. Finally, we discuss in detail how finite-size effects influence phase transition and interdigitation. Overall, these results underscore the accuracy of modern force fields and highlight how simulations are essential to mechanistically complement experimental studies of pressure-sensitive membranes. Keywords : Molecular Dynamics, DMPC, lipid phase transition, high pressure, phase diagram   Detailed content of the repository: The directories contain the all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulation data generated for the different systems and simulation protocols investigated in this study. All atoms are retained in the trajectory files. To limit the overall size of the repository, the trajectories have been subsampled, with one frame retained for every three frames. DRPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic Δ9-cis-PC bilayer, which was used as the control system. Pressure_temperature_ramp : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer subjected to a pressure and temperature ramp. These simulations were performed for comparison with the pressure and temperature jump simulations used as reference. DMPC_Large_Small_Bilayers : Contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for periodic DMPC bilayers with different system sizes, corresponding to twice and half the size of the reference bilayer, respectively. The reference system consists of 57 DMPC molecules per leaflet. DMPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations used to construct the DMPC phase diagram. The directory is organized into subdirectories, with one folder per simulation replicate.  gel_to_fluid_simulations : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations performed to investigate the gel-to-fluid phase transition. The transition, starting from final gel phase configurations obtained from the DMPC simulations, was induced by independently varying either the pressure or the temperature
title: Molecular Signatures of Pressure-Induced Phase Transitions in a Lipid Bilayer

summary: This archive contains the complete, reproducible analysis pipeline accompanying the article by Bentounsi, Achour and Boufaida, currently under review. Purpose Clinical datasets often present expert labels as if they applied a published guideline. This work proposes an audit method that (i) measures the gap between a guideline-derived reference rule base and the expert labels, (ii) attributes the disagreements to an implicit criterion (Algorithm 1), and (iii) tests whether that criterion can be reconstructed out of sample, using an explicit acceptance criterion: an agreement gain of at least 5 points over the majority baseline, the same rule selected in at least 4 of 5 folds, and a family-wise permutation p-value below 0.01. The method is applied to an Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) dataset (270 records, six labels) and replicated on the UCI Cardiotocography dataset (2,126 segments) against the FIGO 2015 guideline. summary: Description This record contains the data, code and source data supporting a Mendelian randomization (MR) study of smoking and obesity traits, with DNA methylation (CpG sites) and gut microbial features (species and pathways) as candidate mediators. Files Processed and formatted GWAS summary statistics (instrumental variables and outcome data) used in the analyses. Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx : sources of the original GWAS summary statistics (also listed in Table S1 of the article). Codes.zip : R code for instrument selection, two-sample MR and sensitivity analyses, mediation analysis, colocalization and the figures, with a README describing each script and the run order, software versions and R session information. Source_data.zip : source data underlying the main and supplementary figures. Fstatistic.zip : F statistics of the instrumental variables in the MR analyses. Data sources The uploaded data are processed and formatted versions of publicly available GWAS summary statistics; the original sources are listed in Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx . Ethical approval and informed consent were obtained by the original GWAS studies. Methods Instrumental variables were selected at P < 5 × 10⁻⁸ for smoking and obesity traits, P < 1 × 10⁻⁵ (effect allele frequency > 0.01) for gut microbial features, and P < 1 × 10⁻⁸ (cis, within 1 Mb) or P < 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ (trans) for methylation quantitative trait loci of CpG sites (GoDMC). Variants were clumped at r² < 0.001 within 10,000 kb windows using PLINK with the 1000 Genomes European reference panel, and instruments with F < 10 were excluded. The multiplicative random-effects inverse-variance weighted method (Wald ratio for single-SNP instruments) was used as the primary MR method. Sensitivity analyses included the fixed-effects inverse-variance weighted method, MR-Egger, weighted median, simple and weighted mode, Cochran’s Q test, the MR-Egger intercept test, MR-PRESSO and the Steiger directionality test. Reverse causation was assessed by MR in the reverse direction. Indirect associations were estimated by two-step MR using the product-of-coefficients method with delta-method standard errors. Colocalization was assessed with coloc (p1 = p2 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, p12 = 1 × 10⁻⁵) within ±1 Mb windows and with HyPrColoc for three traits (prior.1 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, prior.c = 0.02).  Acknowledgements We thank UK Biobank ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ ), GSCAN ( https://genome.psych.umn.edu/index.php/GSCAN ), the GIANT consortium ( https://giant-consortium.web.broadinstitute.org/index.php/GIANT_consortium ), GERA ( https://cg.bsc.es/gera_summary_stats/ ), GoDMC ( http://mqtldb.godmc.org.uk/about ), the Dutch Microbiome Project ( https://dutchmicrobiomeproject.molgeniscloud.org/menu/main/home ), the IEU OpenGWAS project ( https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/ ) and the GWAS Catalog ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/ ) for providing the publicly available genetic data used in this research. We acknowledge the research teams, participants and consortia behind these datasets for their commitment to open science.
title: Causal Relationships Between Smoking and Obesity Mediated by Epigenetic Modifications and Altered Gut Microbiota

summary: Urban design relies on judgments about existing and anticipated needs, while the available evidence ranges from lived experience and historical records to geospatial observation, statistical estimation, and computational simulation. Contemporary developments in geospatial artificial intelligence, agent-based modeling, urban digital twins, and computational search expand the means of inquiry while raising questions about inferential validity and methodological compatibility. This paper develops a question-guided framework for identifying and evaluating candidate urban needs through the reconstruction of spatial, temporal, social, ecological, and infrastructural relations. Two complementary inquiry pathways are distinguished: hypothesis-driven assessment of specified candidate needs and exploratory search for candidates emerging from observed or simulated relational patterns. Both pathways are connected to explicit procedures of evidential appraisal, causal examination where identifiable, participatory scrutiny, and post-intervention evaluation. A provisional formal interface is proposed in which generative–relational (GR) subjects have question-dependent spacetime-supported representations, heterogeneous evidence is linked by category-theoretic constructions, and selected event structures are encoded through algebraic-topological invariants of labeled two-complexes. Evolutionary updates of these representations and spin-foam-inspired cellular initializations are considered as exploratory modeling options, with the physical meaning of quantum-gravity spin foams kept separate from urban research. The framework is intended to guide methodological comparison and further model development; its empirical adequacy requires case-specific operationalization and validation.
title: Identifying and Evaluating Urban Needs Through Relational Reconstruction: A Preliminary Generative and Evolutionary Formal Model in an Algebraic Framework

AsLS baseline correction (asymmetric least squares, as in SIMCA): enginir.preprocessing.AsLSBaseline and PreprocessingRecipe(asls=True, asls_lambda=..., asls_p=..., asls_iterations=...) , first in the recipe order, as is in absorbance and flipped in reflectance and DN. Scripts only; the viewer shows and keeps it. SavitzkyGolay(edges="drop") and PreprocessingRecipe.output_wavelengths . Fixed Viewer: a new project (and an exported CSV) gets its extension ( .h5 , .csv ) when the name was typed without one; the file dialog did not add it on some platforms, and the open dialog, filtering on .h5 , then hid the project. The open dialog also offers All files . Project.create documents that it replaces an existing file. Viewer on Linux: the file dialogs' toolbar buttons (back, up, new folder, list or detail view) show their icons again; the theme's button padding left no room for them. summary: Replication data and code for the article "Measuring Internet Controls in Central Asia: Network Interference, Legal Frameworks and Digital Sovereignty in Five Post-Soviet States, 2020–2026". The deposit covers Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, January 2020 – October 2026. All measurement data were retrieved passively from the public OONI aggregation API (web connectivity test and six service tests), with Germany, the Netherlands, the United States and Canada as reference countries. No probes were run and no personal data were collected. The deposit contains: Python scripts for collection, classification of blocking, sensitivity analysis, validation (evidence sample, manual review, Censored Planet comparison, domain-by-network rule), tables and figures; processed monthly aggregates by country, domain and network; the classification of every country–domain–month observation; raw OONI API responses, with SHA-256 hashes in the collection state files; and a manifest of the legal texts consulted. See README.md for the file list and the order in which to run the scripts. Citizen Lab test-list categories are not redistributed; the article uses commit 607fcb7523c3ed7bac9b24594f2b3291db6d005a. Version 2: legal-texts manifest extended (Tajikistan's Law No. 1808 on Countering Terrorism and Law No. 56 on Electric Communications, from the parliament's websites); second-coder protocol added. Data, classification and results are unchanged. Version 3: completed second-coder sheet and agreement results added (the two independent coders agree on 27/27 cases; each agrees with the automatic rule on 23/27, Cohen's kappa = 0.68); co-authors added. Data, classification and results are unchanged.
title: Replication data and code for "Measuring Internet Controls in Central Asia: Network Interference, Legal Frameworks and Digital Sovereignty in Five Post-Soviet States, 2020–2026"

summary: # Changes from version 1 Version 2 is the version that matches the revised paper. Version 1 is kept on the record for reference. ## Corrected - `Data/Models Data/imputer_pairs.csv` now has the 364 session pairs described in the paper. Version 1 contained an earlier table of 86 rows. The three deposited models were trained on the 364-row table; retraining on it reproduces them exactly (`Code/train_models.py`). - Layer 3 in `Code/SPAC/SPAC.py` now uses the weights of the paper (OS 0.30, Python version 0.30, packages 0.40). Version 1 used 0.10, 0.20 and 0.70, which gave different Layer 3 values and different totals for the Table 5 pairs. - The README, the training summary and the licence file were rewritten. They described a different file layout, feature set and hyperparameters and carried placeholders. - The docstring and comments of `Code/synthetic_generator.py` no longer state that the three thresholds are published values. They are design choices of the framework. - The title, author line and citation now match the paper. - Comments and explanatory strings in `Code/04_collect_pairs.py`, `Code/SPAC/SPAC.py`, `Code/synthetic_generator.py` and `Code/weight_deriver.py` that cited works outside the paper's reference list, or described a BLAS or floating-point mechanism that the paper no longer claims, were corrected or marked as development notes. ## Added - `analysis/`: scripts for the analyses added in the revision (grouped cross-validation and baselines, unified versus separate models, weight and threshold sensitivity, Layer 1 and Layer 2 sensitivity, scoring of the 42 additional pairs, recomputation of Table 5) and their printed outputs. - `replay/`: replay of the OpenClimate sort order under numpy 1.26.4 and 2.3.2. - `Code/train_models.py`: the training and cross-validation of `02_Imputer_Train.py` without Streamlit. - `Code/weight_deriver.py` and `Code/synthetic_generator.py`: the weight derivation and the synthetic data generator (the generator reproduces `run_pairs.csv` byte for byte). - `Data/Revision Pairs/`: the 42 additional pairs with a manifest. - `Data/Testing Data/`: the session files behind Table 5, as plain folders. ## Removed - Archives that duplicated unpacked folders (`Code.rar`, `Data.rar`, `Models Data.rar` and the nested archives in the test data). - The second copy of the three model files (they remain in `Code/SPAC/models/`). - Screenshots of the scoring page and sessions recorded on a local machine, which are not part of the study.

summary: The World on Record Index (TWR) — version 1.2.0 Released 9 November 2026. Concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23997606 resolves to the latest version. What is new: the sector layer 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 published one score per country-year. This release adds  goal_level  — one score per country-year  per SDG goal  — so the measure can say  what  a government stopped reporting, not only that it reported less. Sixteen goals are scored.  Goal 7 is not : it has three series, too few to identify a factor. That is a structural fact about the goal, not a judgement on it. Each goal is a  separate  unidimensional 2PL fit on that goal's own series, drawn from the same 524 that build the overall index. A goal's score therefore owes nothing to the other fifteen, and both layers sit on the same scale. The layer is not a restatement of the overall index. Across the sixteen goals a median of  64%  of the variation in goal-level reporting is not explained by a country's overall level — from 18% for goal 17 to 99.9% for goal 15. What it is checked against Check Result Convergence 16 of 16 goals, 19–73 EM cycles each Reliability 0.772–0.953, median  0.844 ; every goal above 0.70 Median posterior SD 0.338 (overall index: 0.114) Bootstrap, 500 replicates 0 failed replicates ; sampling SD is 7–42% of the posterior SE, median 13% Held-out series Fit on 70% of a goal's series, predict the held-out 30%: median AUC  0.725  against a per-series permutation null at  0.500 The bootstrap result means the published standard errors are  conservative  — they already cover item-parameter uncertainty with room to spare. Report the posterior SE, not the bootstrap SD. The held-out test is the first direct check that a goal score predicts reporting it was not fitted on. Thirteen of sixteen goals score 0.649 or better. The three weakest — goal 17 (0.618), goal 15 (0.526) and goal 6 (0.479) — are precisely the three already set apart on content grounds, which the test did not know. Disclose, do not gate Every goal fitted is published.  Nothing is excluded for imprecision, and 0.70 (Nunnally) is reported as a reference point, not applied as a cut. Each goal ships with four numbers a reader can weigh it by: reliability  — 0.772 to 0.953 se_median  — the typical error bar on that goal's scores weight_top5_pct  — how concentrated the score is in its five heaviest series weight_agency_pct  — how much of the score rests on series the custodian agency produces rather than the country Two goals carry  release = hold_content . The hold is on  content  grounds and for  different reasons , never on precision: Goal 6  is largely satellite measurement of lakes, wetlands and river flow. "Reported" there mostly records whether an agency published a dataset, not a country's choice. Goal 15  is overwhelmingly country-produced, but a third of its series are treaty and policy instruments (Nagoya Protocol, Aichi targets, NBSAP), which may track commitment status rather than reporting effort. An error bar cannot warn a reader about either, so the flag travels with the data. Both goals are published in full. Known limitations Weight concentration.  Within a goal, small groups of series that are always reported together can carry much of the score — in goal 10 the five heaviest series carry 80%, in goal 1 75%. These groups are near-duplicates that the variant rule does not collapse, because they are not reported identically: in goal 1, India, Sri Lanka and Malaysia report the education and health breakdowns but never the aggregate, every year from 2015 to 2023. Collapsing them would erase those reporting choices, so they are disclosed in  weight_top5_pct  instead. Modelling the dependence directly is deferred. Provenance.   weight_agency_pct  records h

summary: CRISPR-TRIAGE is an open-science computational biology research archive evaluating parameter-efficient off-target prioritization under budget-constrained experimental validation budgets (K <= 50). This package contains the complete trained model checkpoints, multi-seed training pipelines (5 random seeds), biophysical feature extractors, pre-registered baseline models (LightGBM GBDT, Pairwise 1D-CNN, Logistic Regression, crispAI architecture), and evaluation results across two external cellular benchmarks (Listgarten 2018 GUIDE-seq and K562 cellular compilation). Key Scientific Findings & Methodological Disclosure: Algorithmic Parity with Gradient Boosted Trees: On the deduplicated independent cellular benchmark (K562 retrospective multi-assay compilation from DeepCRISPR / Yang et al. 2023; 11 guides, 16,172 unique candidate pairs, 110 confirmed positive guide-target sequence pairs without genomic coordinates), standard gradient boosting (LightGBM GBDT) trained on 15 simple biophysical mismatch features achieves Macro Recall@20 = 0.6350 vs 0.6416 for CRISPR-TRIAGE (margin +0.0066 / +0.66%; paired Wilcoxon W = 18.0, p = 1.0000; 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0979, +0.0900]). LightGBM runs 2.39x faster with 0 neural parameters. While lack of statistically significant superiority does not prove biological equivalence or disprove neural-network utility, the empirical evidence failed to reject the null hypothesis of no difference vs LightGBM under available statistical power. Multi-Seed Volatility in CRISPR Modeling: Retraining across 5 independent random seeds reveals substantial Macro Recall@20 fluctuations (+-6.5% standard deviation on identical data), demonstrating that single-seed reporting in the CRISPR machine-learning literature frequently reflects random seed-selection noise rather than genuine algorithmic superiority. Dataset Deduplication Importance: Forensic auditing documented the impact of 1,613 duplicate candidate rows (and 2 duplicate confirmed positive sites) in the K562 compilation, showing how uncleaned duplicates distort evaluation metrics. Two-Tier Reproducibility Scope: Tier 1 (Saved-Model Inference & K562 Cellular Benchmark Reproduction): 100% self-contained in this archive. All 5 trained seed weights, baselines, scalers, predictions, metric summaries, and the K562 cellular cohort execute fully offline without internet access. Tier 2 (Full Retraining on Primary Assay Datasets): Full retraining from raw sequence reads and complete Listgarten raw dataset reproduction requires separately downloading the 4 un-subsampled raw assay datasets (>20MB each), registered with authoritative accessions and cryptographic SHA256 checksums in DATA_MANIFEST.csv. Licensing, Provenance & Third-Party Rights: CRISPR-TRIAGE code, models, and documentation are licensed under the permissive MIT License. The crispAI architecture code (src/crispai_official/) is under MIT License (Copyright 2023 Furkan Ozden; reference: Özden & Minary, NAR 2024). Pretrained third-party weights for crispAI are omitted from the archive to ensure compliance with conflicting upstream documentation, with archive extraction utilities provided for the authors' official Zenodo records (13335960 / 12609337). Bundled K562 benchmark datasets are distributed under CC BY 4.0 (Yang et al. CSBJ 2023; Chuai et al. Genome Biol 2018). Raw CFD scoring lookup matrices (Doench et al. 2016 Supplementary Table 19) are strictly omitted from the release archive for third-party rights compliance; tested user-side acquisition and verification utilities are provided via scripts/download_cfd_matrices.py. See the root LICENSE file for full details.
title: CRISPR-TRIAGE: Evaluation of Parameter-Efficient Bi-Modal Off-Target Prioritization Under Budget-Constrained Screening

summary: Hobsbawm and Rudé argued that parliamentary enclosure helped to cause the Swing riots of 1830; Caprettini and Voth showed that threshing machines mattered. I link 5,375 places named in 4,104 enclosure Acts to the parishes in Caprettini and Voth's data (79% of places named in Acts of 1790 to 1830 linked) and test, in a model specified in advance with county fixed effects and their controls, whether recent enclosure predicts unrest in 9,674 parishes. As planned, parishes named in an Act of 1790 to 1830 were 2.7 percentage points more likely to see an incident (95% CI 0.2 to 5.3; mean 14.5%). Three findings argue against a grievance reading. Parishes enclosed only before 1790 show the same gap (3.1 points); stricter linking rules shrink it to between 0.7 and 1.7 points; and in exploratory models that add parish area, a control the plan omitted, it disappears (-0.8 points, 95% CI -3.2 to 1.5); larger parishes were both more often enclosed and more likely to record any incident. The planned estimate is therefore not robust evidence that recent parliamentary enclosure predicted where Swing broke out. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/enclosure-swing/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/enclosure-swing . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/enclosure-swing/ . Sources: Caprettini and Voth (2020) replication data (openICPSR 117044, CC BY 4.0); Chronological Tables of Private and Local Acts, legislation.gov.uk (Open Government Licence v3.0); Wikidata (CC0). Text, figures and derived data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: Enclosure and the Swing Riots: A Pre-specified Parish-level Test of the Grievance Hypothesis, England and Wales, 1830 to 1831

summary: LOADX (workLOad Assessment in Dual-task eXecution) is a multimodal dataset developed to support research on physical and mental workload estimation during single- and dual-task activities. The dataset contains synchronized physiological, kinematic, task-related, and subjective data collected from 20 participants performing a structured experimental protocol designed to elicit different combinations of physical and cognitive demand. The protocol includes 16 experimental conditions: three physical tasks, three cognitive tasks, nine dual-task combinations, and one resting baseline. The physical tasks consist of repeated shoulder flexion–extension, marching in place, and squats. The cognitive tasks include a Stroop test, a 2-back working-memory task, and backward counting by seven. Each active condition lasted 90 seconds and was followed by a resting interval. Physiological data were acquired using wearable sensors and include raw electrocardiographic signals, raw respiratory waveforms, heart rate, inter-beat interval, respiratory rate, galvanic skin response, and triaxial acceleration. Full-body kinematic data were collected using a contactless vision-based monitoring system based on MediaPipe Pose, providing the three-dimensional coordinates of 33 anatomical landmarks. All acquisition streams share a common temporal reference, enabling the alignment of physiological signals, body movements, task execution, and workload annotations. After each experimental condition, participants rated their perceived physical and mental demand using selected dimensions of the NASA Task Load Index. The dataset therefore includes task-level Physical Demand and Mental Demand scores, which can be used as subjective workload annotations for supervised learning, correlation analysis, clustering, and validation of multimodal workload-estimation methods. The dataset is organized into one folder for each participant, identified through an anonymized numerical code such as S01, S02, and so forth. Each participant folder contains: Sxx.csv: synchronized physiological, kinematic, task-related, and subjective data; Sxx_ecg.csv: raw ECG waveform; Sxx_breath.csv: raw respiratory waveform; Sxx_nasa.xlsx: task-level NASA-TLX Physical Demand and Mental Demand ratings. LOADX can support research on multimodal workload assessment, physiological and movement-signal processing, sensor fusion, feature extraction, task recognition, modality-ablation analysis, subject-independent validation, and the development of adaptive human–machine interaction systems. The inclusion of physical-only, cognitive-only, and dual-task conditions enables the investigation of how physical and mental demands interact and how they are reflected in complementary sensing modalities. LOADX should be considered a structured multimodal research dataset rather than a population-level normative dataset. Inter-individual variability was intentionally retained to support the investigation of personalized and subject-independent workload-estimation approaches.
title: LOADX Dataset: workLOad Assessment in Dual-task eXecution through multimodal monitoring

summary: VCAB-Wild characterizes the functionality and observable security properties of deployed web applications created with Lovable, an AI application builder. It covers all 7,937 distinct *.lovable.app hosts indexed by Common Crawl in CC-MAIN-2026-39. For each host it records reachability, ten building blocks identified in public client code, and four categories of non-intrusive exposure indicators: database readability with the application's public key (row counts only), secret-key strings in public code (type only), public source maps and security headers. A random subset of 500 hosts carries application-type labels from two LLM annotators with adjudication and a 50-host human check. The release includes a keyed development/test split, three reference tasks with a scoring tool, SHA-256 fingerprints for snapshot reconstruction, and all collection and analysis code. Host names are withheld; the key linking records to hosts is available from the author under a non-disclosure agreement. Data: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT. Part of the Vibe-Coded App Benchmark (VCAB).
title: VCAB-Wild: A dataset of 7,937 deployed vibe-coded web applications with building-block annotations, non-intrusive data-exposure measurements and reference tasks for security evaluation

summary: Health Building Lifestyle Guidelines (2026 Comprehensive Edition) is a practical, referenced, comprehensive guideline for lay readers and health professionals. It BUILDS ON, and does NOT rename, replace or supersede, the 2025 Health Building Lifestyle Guidelines (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.15814357, 5 July 2025). The main PDF is a 9-page LANDSCAPE BROCHURE with enlarged body type throughout, one topic per page and clickable links. It reproduces the 2025 guideline IN FULL (English, Hindi and its own reference list) on pages 2-4, each captioned with the 2025 DOI; the 12 reference URLs on reproduced page 4 are live links as well. The Title uses a SINGLE ACLM blue header in two lines, and EVERY URL link in the brochure uses that same deep blue. The three PURE traffic-light colours appear as three disks on page 1 (the 21-point key) and on ALL content headers (Spices = YELLOW, Yoga = RED); the Six-pillars page carries the brighter original ACLM six-pillar chips, with published ACLM pillar language in roman type, the 2025 21-item guideline in italics, and an explicit attribution footnote. Two images from the Sutra Health YouTube channel (infusion, Yoga) sit on the right of their pages. Page 8 is one merged evidence table listing the CONDITIONS for which there is evidence and THE PRACTICES THAT WORKS, colour-coded PREVENTION / TREATMENT / REMISSION-REVERSAL (refs [30] DiRECT, [31] Ornish), followed by two selected meta-analyses on prevention ([32] Kyu, [33] Reynolds); the separate evidence pages and the redundant Safety page were consolidated into it. The References hyperlink the reproduced 2025 handout's own list [1]-[12] on p4, note the first disclosure (8 Sep 2025 [5]), and run to 33 numbered references. This record's own DOI (10.5281/zenodo.24090390) is printed on page 1 of the PDF. No ACLM logo is used and no endorsement is implied. CC BY 4.0 is selected from Zenodo's default licence options. Contents: (1) The updated 21-item traffic-light Health Building Lifestyle Guidelines is being made available for open, public use with the CLARIFICATION that the first seven (red, "avoid") items are reverse-scored / negatively counted; all cross-references use colour-disc group-relative numbering (Red 1-7, Green 1-7, Yellow 1-7); a link to the deposited 21-item-assessment.csv (21 bilingual items, one point each, with a TOTAL column showing the maximum score of 21); and a link to the free public online 21-point assessment at https://www.lifequality.org.in/assessment (a self-assessment, monitoring and provider-administered tool that anyone can fill). (2) The six pillars of lifestyle medicine are listed on Page - 7. The published language follows the American College of Lifestyle Medicine (ACLM) protocol [6]. (3) Guideline-backed, general benefit statements for diet, physical activity / Yoga, sleep, stress, connection and substance avoidance, each cited to national and international guidelines and systematic reviews, are linked to ACLM pillars. (4) The 20-item Yoga asana and pranayama protocol, an elaboration of Yellow 1, with two safety sub-points, with a link to https://www.lifequality.org.in/services/therapeutic-yoga/yoga-asana-protocol, an archive video link (https://archive.org/details/surya-yoga-sequence) and its references - remission / reversal evidence is described as programme-level input (Yoga in combination), not Yoga stand-alone. summary: Factoring and supply chain finance (SCF) allow firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, to obtain liquidity against receivables and other trade assets, but they expose financiers to the credit risk of suppliers, buyers and their relationships. This study maps the scientific literature on credit risk management in factoring and SCF through a bibliometric analysis. A Scopus search conducted on 12 October 2026 and screening following the PRISMA 2020 flow yielded 288 articles and reviews published between 1995 and 2025. Performance analysis was combined with science mapping in VOSviewer, including keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship and co-citation analyses of references and sources. The results show that the field has grown rapidly since 2019, with 87.2% of the documents published in 2019–2025. China dominates research output, while studies from the United Kingdom, the United States and Italy attain higher normalised impact, and operations management and operational research journals are the main publication venues. Three research streams are identified: analytical operations–finance models of risk allocation in capital-constrained supply chains, conceptual and empirical research on SCF adoption and reverse factoring, and machine learning-based credit risk assessment of SMEs. Research attention has shifted from traditional factoring and receivables financing towards SCF, machine learning, blockchain and, most recently, artificial intelligence and sustainability. The accounting, financial reporting and internal control dimensions of these arrangements, the allocation of risk among multiple financiers, and evidence from under-represented regions emerge as the main gaps.

summary: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. A canonical example is a mobility operator that orchestrates a fleet of vehicles to meet customer demand. The stochastic and time-varying nature of these problems calls for learning approaches, yet existing MARL algorithms do not scale: learning assignment and routing jointly over the full state-action space becomes prohibitive as the number of agents grows. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. Since learning occurs at the single-agent level, SALT scales to fleet sizes where MARL baselines become intractable and transfers without retraining to fleet sizes unseen during training. In a vehicle-delivery experiment on the southern Manhattan road network, where MARL baselines are computationally prohibitive, SALT improves travel time by 15-21% over a shortest-path routing heuristic. In stochastic grid worlds, SALT reduces average travel times by 23-61% relative to MARL baselines and scales to population sizes where these methods fail.
title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

summary: LLMs excel at language tasks, but long-meeting QFS remains difficult due to complex speaker dynamics, sparse key information, and limited data. Meetings involve disfluencies, long transcripts and complex discourse. QFS have high risk of information omission, hallucination, even for advanced models such as GPT-4-mini and Gemini. Existing end-to-end methods compress retrieval, evidence extraction, and summary generation into a single pass, failing to handle the complex reasoning required for targeted meeting summaries. We propose ReSUM, a modular multi-LLM framework coordinated by a planner that orchestrates retrieval and summarization agents. By distilling teacher reasoning into query- and plan-conditioned retrievers and summarizers, ReSUM enhances long-context robustness, minimizes irrelevant exploration, and generates more faithful and comprehensive query-focused summaries. Experiments show consistent gains on query-focused meeting summarization benchmarks.
title: ReSUM: Reasoning-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Query-Focused Summarization

summary: Geometric assembly requires fine spatiotemporal coordination to place parts without causing collisions or deadlocks under tight clearances. To address this, we present an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that treats each part as an agent and learns a shared policy for continuous assembly control. A graph neural network represents the pieces, their target poses, and their spatial relationships, and predicts translational and angular velocities for each component. Per-agent proximal policy optimization with a centralized graph critic directly learns motion and temporal coordination within a single feedback policy. We study this formulation through planar Tangram assembly, where pieces must slide and rotate into a given configuration while remaining on the assembly surface. Procedural generation of target configurations and randomized initial arrangements support training and evaluation across diverse assembly problems. Our experiments isolate the roles of relational structure and multi-agent optimization, and compare learned control with sampling-based planning. We demonstrate concurrent assembly in simulation and transfer the policy to sequential execution on a real robot, as our object-centric formulation decouples learned assembly coordination from low-level physical control. Project page: https://tangrambench.org/

summary: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.

summary: Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.
title: s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL

summary: Overview The Earth Surface Anomaly dataset (v1.0) is a five-class, event-grouped Sentinel-2 benchmark for immediate disaster and surface-anomaly detection. It contains 622 samples grouped into 46 event or spatiotemporal observation units (17 source-named/inventory units and 29 observation groups, 2017–2025, globally distributed): 129 fire, 58 flood-context, 54 landslide, 204 crop-residue-burning and 177 retrogressive-thaw-slump samples. 595 samples carry source polygon-derived binary masks; 27 carry weak point inventories only; all 54 landslide samples include pre/post paired observations. Industrial heat sources (208 candidates) are excluded from this release and 17 visually ambiguous candidates are withheld, both enumerated in quality/excluded_samples.csv . Sample structure Each sample ( data/CODE/EVENT/SAMPLE/ ) provides a six-band Sentinel-2 L2A chip (declared bands B2, B3, B4, B8, B11, B12; aligned grid spacing does not imply native 10 m for every band), a 0/1 binary mask, RGB/NIR/SWIR previews, annotation.json and measured facts.json (CRS, transform, WGS84 bounds, geometry statistics, spectral indices, SHA256 checksums). Annotation-conditioned vision-language tasks (4–6 per sample depending on label strength and pairing) cover event classification, factual captioning, spatial reasoning, visual grounding, spectral comparison, and for suitable samples temporal reasoning and label provenance. Splits Group splits are precomputed: default splits/event_disjoint (443/102/77 train/val/test) and inherited splits/site_disjoint (433/114/75). Event-disjointness does not guarantee site-disjointness (1 measured case); use site_disjoint when required. Never randomly split patches from the same event. Screening and quality All 639 non-industrial candidates underwent AI-assisted visual screening of RGB, SWIR and target crops with review sheets and per-sample geometry/text audits retained in the release ( quality/ , visual_review.csv ). This is not independent expert pixel adjudication, field validation, or new external verification of every event identity. Limitations (documented in README, README_zh and DATA_DICTIONARY) Flood-context masks often follow existing river channels; no paired baseline establishes incremental inundation. Fire annotations can cover smoke, scars or hotspots and are not universally burned-area boundaries. Crop-residue burning is a source label; imagery alone does not establish fuel identity. Thaw mechanism/onset and landslide onset cannot be established from the supplied views alone. Point inventories (27 samples) are weak localization, not segmentation truth; polygon provenance does not guarantee exact pixel boundaries. Radiometric scale/offset and the inherited non-landslide band mapping have not been independently traced to every source product; facts.json indices are stored-DN calculations, not validated physical reflectance. External event-match references in index/external_verification_ledger.csv were not newly re-verified during release preparation. License and third-party terms CC BY 4.0 applies to the project-original annotations, revisions and documentation. Sentinel/Copernicus imagery is used under modified-data attribution terms and COOLR landslide inventories retain their original conditions; see LICENSE , licenses/ and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . No ESA or European Union endorsement is implied. Access The metadata and preview figures of this record are public. The files are distributed on an approved-request basis: use the Request access button on this record page and state your affiliation and intended use; requests are reviewed by the authors. summary: Overview The Earth Surface Anomaly dataset (v1.0) is a five-class, event-grouped Sentinel-2 benchmark for immediate disaster and surface-anomaly detection. It contains 622 samples grouped into 46 event or spatiotemporal observation units (17 source-named/inventory units and 29 observation groups, 2017–2025, globally distributed): 129 fire, 58 flood-context, 54 landslide, 204 crop-residue-burning and 177 retrogressive-thaw-slump samples. 595 samples carry source polygon-derived binary masks; 27 carry weak point inventories only; all 54 landslide samples include pre/post paired observations. Industrial heat sources (208 candidates) are excluded from this release and 17 visually ambiguous candidates are withheld, both enumerated in quality/excluded_samples.csv . Sample structure Each sample ( data/CODE/EVENT/SAMPLE/ ) provides a six-band Sentinel-2 L2A chip (declared bands B2, B3, B4, B8, B11, B12; aligned grid spacing does not imply native 10 m for every band), a 0/1 binary mask, RGB/NIR/SWIR previews, annotation.json and measured facts.json (CRS, transform, WGS84 bounds, geometry statistics, spectral indices, SHA256 checksums). Annotation-conditioned vision-language tasks (4–6 per sample depending on label strength and pairing) cover event classification, factual captioning, spatial reasoning, visual grounding, spectral comparison, and for suitable samples temporal reasoning and label provenance. Splits Group splits are precomputed: default splits/event_disjoint (443/102/77 train/val/test) and inherited splits/site_disjoint (433/114/75). Event-disjointness does not guarantee site-disjointness (1 measured case); use site_disjoint when required. Never randomly split patches from the same event. Screening and quality All 639 non-industrial candidates underwent AI-assisted visual screening of RGB, SWIR and target crops with review sheets and per-sample geometry/text audits retained in the release ( quality/ , visual_review.csv ). This is not independent expert pixel adjudication, field validation, or new external verification of every event identity. Limitations (documented in README, README_zh and DATA_DICTIONARY) Flood-context masks often follow existing river channels; no paired baseline establishes incremental inundation. Fire annotations can cover smoke, scars or hotspots and are not universally burned-area boundaries. Crop-residue burning is a source label; imagery alone does not establish fuel identity. Thaw mechanism/onset and landslide onset cannot be established from the supplied views alone. Point inventories (27 samples) are weak localization, not segmentation truth; polygon provenance does not guarantee exact pixel boundaries. Radiometric scale/offset and the inherited non-landslide band mapping have not been independently traced to every source product; facts.json indices are stored-DN calculations, not validated physical reflectance. External event-match references in index/external_verification_ledger.csv were not newly re-verified during release preparation. summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Total Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed. As a result, some sites have WAV files with 0 bytes of data or timestamps outside the range of probable recording times. Procedures used by the Eclipse Soundscapes team to process audio data for its purposes are outlined in the Data Management reports located in the Eclipse Soundscapes Zenodo community. Data with 0 bytes of data were included for completeness. When possible, all site-specific files, including the audio files, are included in a single zip file for ease of download. If a single zip file upload was not possible due to upload or bandwidth limitations, audio files are included in multiple zip files based on the day of the observation. summary: Attention to notable people rises sharply when they die and then fades, but how far it fades, and for whom, has rarely been measured at scale. I follow the English Wikipedia articles of 16,397 people who died between 2016 and 2023 (a 30% hash sample of Wikidata), measuring monthly user pageviews (looking someone up, not remembering them) as a share of all English Wikipedia traffic relative to each person's own level in the year before death. In an analysis pre-specified in a written plan, the median peak is 16.5 times the pre-death level. The decay is best described by two phases, with half-lives of about 11 days and 6.9 months, although a power law predicts later cohorts slightly better. Two to three years after death, the median person receives 0.98 (95% CI 0.97 to 0.99) of their pre-death share; an exploratory comparison with the drift before death places this about 5% above a no-death path. Age at death is the strongest correlate: people who died under 50 retain 63% more long-run attention than those who died at 65 to 79 (95% CI 51 to 77), a gap absent at a placebo date and present in all 21 robustness checks. Performers are the only occupational group whose typical attention settles above its baseline, but placebo tests show that the occupational gaps partly predate the deaths. Estimates for women and for citizens of English-speaking countries depend on specification and are not robust. The design is descriptive and observational. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/fame-half-life/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/fame-half-life . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/fame-half-life/ . Sources: English Wikipedia pageviews (Wikimedia pageviews API, CC0); Wikidata (CC0); Natural Earth (public domain). Text, figures and data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.

summary: Version 1.8.4 carries the manuscript as resubmitted after the major revision and pairs with code tag v1.1.2 . It adds an ethics statement on the independent annotators to the manuscript (Section 3.9 and the Declarations) and updates expected.json for the new results archive. All data, results, code and reproduce.py are unchanged from version 1.8.3; only the manuscript files in the results archive differ. Version 1.8.3 (superseded by 1.8.4) carries the manuscript as resubmitted after the major revision and pairs with code tag v1.1.2 . Release identities are now also classified with tag evidence from the time of each change: an archive visit or an immutable release dates a tag binding, while a mutable release record does not ( reports/release_timing.json , release-timing-v2). The matched-control comparison covers months 13-18 ( reports/control_comparison.json ), and reports/revision_checks.json adds the tail window after day 540, the repository-month units of the repository share, commit-level ratios of the second wave and the dependents list against the measured endpoint. The results archive now also holds, under data/ , the cached API responses, stage-freeze scripts, source-frame files and run manifests that the full formal entry point ( python -m pintrace.formal_stats --working ) checks, so it runs from the code tag and the two archives. JOIN_MEASUREMENTS.md corrects the verification directory and the part names and adds a streaming extraction. reproduce.py with expected.json runs the whole reproduction in an empty working directory and compares every output with the archived bytes. The measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. Version 1.8.2 (superseded by 1.8.3) carries the manuscript as resubmitted after the major revision: the pipeline's precision and recall by class against the annotators' consensus, the timing of the annotator replacements, the second wave qualified as carried by organization-owned repositories, and corrected denominators. It adds a note on line endings with the list of files whose implementation hashes were recorded with CRLF line endings ( docs/crlf_hashed_files.txt ). The manuscript sources moved to paper/jsep_v2/ . All data and result files are unchanged from version 1.8.1, and the measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. Version 1.8.1 carries the final revised manuscript (data and code availability, design history, and wording of the second wave) and adds means to the covariate summaries of the coverage audit. All other data are unchanged from version 1.8.0, and the measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. Version 1.8 accompanies the major revision of the manuscript. The results archive adds the dependency-graph coverage audit with its crawl, sample and eligibility records, the stratified sensitivity of the two waves, and the independent two-annotator validation of 400 items (packets, codebook, freeze records, the final annotators' pseudonymous answers, consensus and score). It also archives the cohort baselines, maintenance-scope entries and three table files that these analyses bind. The measurement archive is unchanged from version 1.4. The record contains two archives. pintrace-measurements-v1.tar.zst holds the per-repository measurement snapshots for 457 measured repositories and 301 matched control repositories, the archived upstream release evidence and the matched-control assignments. pintrace-results-v1.tar.zst holds the published result files, the formal-statistics outputs, the 150-item gold set, the research documentation, the manuscript PDF and LaTeX source, and the claim ledger that maps every rendered number to a result file and JSON pointer. Each archive includes a SHA-256 manifest and a README with extraction and reproduction instructions. The measurement files contain repository identifiers but no commit author names, commit messages, e-mail addresses or credentials. summary: arXiv:2109.12244 is the preprint of this work. This record holds the revised paper, the data of its figures and tables, and the fitted profile parameters. Major findings If a halo grows self-similarly, with mass and radius both proportional to time at fixed concentration c, mass conservation fixes the mean radial velocity inside it for any density profile: outward in the core and inward beyond about twice the scale radius. For an NFW halo the net radial momentum vanishes at c 0 = 3.48. Growth adds surface and kinetic terms to the virial balance. At c 0 they give an effective virial exponent n e = −1.42 instead of −1. A halo radius that grows by random accretion events follows geometric Brownian motion. For a simple osmotic flow the particle Fokker–Planck solution is a generalized gamma profile that contains the Einasto profile as a special case. Tested on composite haloes (all haloes with the same particle number, 4–6326 particles) of a 256 3 SCDM simulation, the generalized gamma profile fits the cumulative mass profiles with a median rms residual of 0.006 dex and a r /b r = 1.41 ± 0.05; the flat inner part lies within about one softening length. The measured mean radial velocity is inward at all resolved radii, between −0.39 H r and −1.24 H r, where self-similar growth predicts about +0.53 H r at the scale radius. The radial velocity dispersion exceeds the isotropic Jeans value by 1.11–1.90 times. Self-similar growth describes the profile shapes, but not the instantaneous kinematics, of these haloes. Contents. P21_revised.pdf (the paper) and csv/ (15 files: the data of Figs 2–9, Fig. A1 and the composite-halo fit tables). The dark matter flow statistics of the simulation are in 10.5281/zenodo.6541231 (Part I), 10.5281/zenodo.6757654 (Part II) and 10.5281/zenodo.6586213 (full dataset).
title: Inverse mass cascade in dark matter flow and effects on halo deformation, energy, size, and density profiles

Major findings If a halo grows self-similarly, with mass and radius both proportional to time at fixed concentration c, mass conservation fixes the mean radial velocity inside it for any density profile: outward in the core and inward beyond about twice the scale radius. For an NFW halo the net radial momentum vanishes at c 0 = 3.48. Growth adds surface and kinetic terms to the virial balance. At c 0 they give an effective virial exponent n e = −1.42 instead of −1. A halo radius that grows by random accretion events follows geometric Brownian motion. For a simple osmotic flow the particle Fokker–Planck solution is a generalized gamma profile that contains the Einasto profile as a special case. Tested on composite haloes (all haloes with the same particle number, 4–6326 particles) of a 256 3 SCDM simulation, the generalized gamma profile fits the cumulative mass profiles with a median rms residual of 0.006 dex and a r /b r = 1.41 ± 0.05; the flat inner part lies within about one softening length. The measured mean radial velocity is inward at all resolved radii, between −0.39 H r and −1.24 H r, where self-similar growth predicts about +0.53 H r at the scale radius. The radial velocity dispersion exceeds the isotropic Jeans value by 1.11–1.90 times. Self-similar growth describes the profile shapes, but not the instantaneous kinematics, of these haloes. Contents. P21_revised.pdf (the paper) and csv/ (15 files: the data of Figs 2–9, Fig. A1 and the composite-halo fit tables). The dark matter flow statistics of the simulation are in 10.5281/zenodo.6541231 (Part I), 10.5281/zenodo.6757654 (Part II) and 10.5281/zenodo.6586213 (full dataset).

summary: Analysis data and code for the Cochrane systematic review CD016067, Postoperative rehabilitation interventions in adults after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction . The package contains the data of every meta-analysis as entered in RevMan Web (with the RoB 2 judgement of each result), a Python script that reads these data from the RevMan Web API, and the R (metafor) code run outside RevMan: re-analysis of all meta-analyses with validation against RevMan, the sensitivity analyses of Additional table 5 (including Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman intervals), prediction intervals, forest plots and tests for small-study effects. Version 1.1 adds the RoB 2 assessment file (RoB2_CD016067_Consensus_final_2026-11-09.xlsx): the consensus responses to the signalling questions and the domain and overall judgements for every result assessed in the review, the judgements that depart from the RoB 2 algorithm with the reasons, and the justifications for consensus judgements. The analysis data and code are unchanged from version 1.0.

summary: Manuscript and CSV data behind the figures and tables of Xu (2026), Inverse energy cascade in self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow and effects of halo shape , arXiv:2110.13885 . The earlier data record of this work is zenodo.org/records/6640331 . Contents: the manuscript (P17_revised.pdf) and the folder csv/ with the data plotted in the figures and tables of the paper: subsystem energies, flux functions of the specific energies, halo-group energies and coherent motion, virial ratios and halo shapes at z = 0. The statistics of the simulation are in the dark matter flow datasets, doi:10.5281/zenodo.6541231 and doi:10.5281/zenodo.6757654 , and the full dataset is doi:10.5281/zenodo.6586213 . Major findings (Einstein–de Sitter simulation of 256³ particles): The flux of any specific quantity V through the halo mass scale is ε V = −(μ + λ V − s) M h H⟨V⟩, where M h ∝ a μ is the mass in haloes, ⟨V⟩ ∝ a λ V its mass-weighted mean and s the growth exponent of V in haloes of fixed mass; with the measured exponents it reproduces every energy flux to within 2 per cent at z < 2. Kinetic energy, both of the motion of haloes and of the motion inside them, is carried to larger haloes (inverse cascade), while the inter- and intra-halo potential energies are carried to smaller haloes (direct cascade); the fluxes are independent of halo mass for haloes of up to a few hundred particles, only at z ≤ 0.3. The steady state of the cascade picture, in which M h ∝ a 1/2 and the energies grow as a 3/2 , is not reached by z = 0: M h grows as a 1/2 only near z = 0 (local exponent 0.47), and the total kinetic and potential energies grow as a 1.13 and a 1.19 at z ≈ 0. The simplest steady-state exponents fail for the inter-halo potential and for the radial kinetic energy of the haloes, so the measured exponents are needed in the flux formula. Haloes are elongated, with r λ3 /r λ1 ≈ 2–3, but their moment of inertia exceeds that of a sphere of equal volume only by a median factor 1.60 (1,674,583 haloes at z = 0). The spin axis lies within 30° of the plane perpendicular to the major axis for 70 per cent of haloes with n p ≥ 20 (isotropic: 50 per cent). Shape change therefore cannot drive the energy cascade; mass accretion does.
title: Inverse energy cascade in self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow and effects of halo shape

Continuous Band Embedding: Embedding the internal 861-node Johnson graph into a three-dimensional Bravais lattice broadens its discrete spectral levels into continuous energy bands, simultaneously generating a gapless acoustic Goldstone branch that defines the speed of light and a protected roton gap that structurally stabilizes the emergent vacuum against collapse .
