summary: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.
title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data

summary: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.
title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion

summary: The goal of this paper is to investigate the following question: what geometric restrictions does the existence of a transitive family of constant mean curvature hyperspheres impose on a Riemannian metric on $\mathbb S^n$? The notion of a transitive family can be made precise through the theory of Zoll families developed by Ambrozio, Marques, and Neves. Within this framework, we partially extend their local rigidity theorem for even conformal factors on $\mathbb S^3$ to every dimension $n\ge4$, assuming each hypersphere in the minimal Zoll family has the area of a round equator. Moreover, we give a partial answer to the following higher-dimensional version of a question posed by Robert Bryant: must a metric on $\mathbb S^n$, conformal to the round metric and admitting a Zoll family of hyperspheres with a common nonzero constant mean curvature, have constant sectional curvature? Finally, we also investigate inverse problems in the spirit of Hangan, asking which metrics make a fixed family of geodesic spheres have a common prescribed mean curvature.
title: Spheres with transitive families of CMC hypersurfaces

summary: Reconstructing turbulent flow fields from sparse and irregular measurements remains challenging because the underlying inverse problem is severely underdetermined. Here we present MANTRA, a manifold-based tensor framework that represents each velocity component in a continuous tensor-product space while constraining its coefficient tensor to a low-rank Tucker manifold. This structure provides a compact, data-adaptive representation without requiring gridded observations or governing equations. Riemannian optimization and adaptive selection of rank and basis complexity enable the model to exploit coordinate-wise spatiotemporal correlations. In simulations of forced isotropic turbulence and flow over a cylinder, MANTRA recovers multiscale structures at sampling densities orders of magnitude below the underlying grids and remains accurate under Gaussian noise up to 20% of the peak velocity. It also recovers leading coordinate-wise correlation structures from sparse observations. Applied to experimental particle-tracking velocimetry of an oscillating impinging jet, MANTRA reveals time-evolving structures that are not apparent from the scattered measurements alone.
title: Low-Rank Tensor Manifolds for Turbulent Field Reconstruction from Sparse Data

summary: We prove a logarithmic central limit theorem for a tagged particle in infinite-dimensional Dyson Brownian motion at inverse temperature $β=2$, starting from the sine$_2$ point process. The fluctuation is of order $\sqrt{\log t}$, which is subdiffusive and substantially slower than the polynomial fluctuations of classical short-range interacting particle systems, reflecting the rigidity induced by long-range logarithmic repulsion. We further identify the scaling limit as the singular Gaussian field corresponding to the zero-Hurst parameter, which provides a realisation of the singular Gaussian field as a scaling limit of a tagged particle raised by Dürr, Goldstein and Lebowitz (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 38 (1985)).
title: The singular Gaussian scaling limit for a tagged particle in the infinite-dimensional Dyson model at $β=2$

summary: AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale. A compression is accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete, and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. We evaluate both ends with two label-free fidelities from our prior work: the local fidelity $L$ at 10 neighbors and the global fidelity $G$ at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach an $L$ of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme; PCA with 8-bit codes, at an $L$ of 0.77, moves 1.7 percent. Rescoring leaves the stored codes, and thus $G$, unchanged. We prove that across the $G$ band, $1-ν_k$ is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and that this rate follows the distance noise of the compression (correlation 0.979). Our locality-aware quantization (LAQ) turns the bound into a hinge objective on the codebooks of an OPQ index, keeping its bytes, rotation, and search. To our knowledge, LAQ is the first quantizer whose objective comes from a proven bound on the far end. Reconstruction alone raises $G$ in 0 of 52 held-out runs; the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises $G$ in all 52 ($p=8.5\times 10^{-4}$ over 13 memory-encoder groups), including the external FinDER memory, has the highest $G$ of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages, and keeps evidence recall.
title: Enhancing Local and Global Structure in Compressed AI Agent Memory

summary: Two-phase designs provide a cost-effective framework for biomarker studies and have been widely used to reduce the burden of collecting expensive biomarker measurements. Most methodological research has focused on efficient Phase II sampling and estimation of biomarker--outcome associations. A natural subsequent step, however, is to incorporate identified biomarkers into risk prediction models, where measures of predictive performance become important inferential targets. Even for binary outcomes, methodological developments for two-phase designs that jointly address association parameters and predictive performance remain limited. Building on classical case-control and matched case-control designs developed primarily for association inference with binary outcomes, we propose a risk-matched case-control (RMCC) design that uses a scalar disease-risk score constructed from Phase I variables to define matching strata and guide Phase II sampling. To address the limitations of existing likelihood-based approaches, which typically require correct specification of the nuisance distribution of biomarkers, we develop a unified design-based inference framework based on inverse probability weighting for both association parameters and predictive performance measures, including positive predictive value and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. We further introduce target-specific weight scaling and calibration procedures and derive variance estimators that account for sampling variability in both phases. Simulation studies demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of the proposed design and inference procedures, and an application to a Taiwanese oral cancer cohort illustrates their potential utility.
title: Risk-matched case-control sampling and semiparametric weight calibration for efficient biomarker assessment with binary outcomes

summary: We study the coherent transfer of circulation between two weakly coupled lattice rings of ultracold bosons, in which a persistent current initially prepared in one ring oscillates back and forth between the rings without net transfer of particles. Combining Bose--Hubbard simulations with their Gross--Pitaevskii and quantum phase model limits, we show that similar current oscillations arise from two distinct microscopic mechanisms. At weak interactions, particles in each occupied momentum mode tunnel independently between the rings, leading to a transfer time inversely proportional to the inter-ring tunnelling, extensive particle-number fluctuations and entanglement distributed over many Schmidt components; this mode-exchange dynamics is suppressed by self-trapping as the interactions increase. At stronger interactions and large filling, in the phase-dominated regime, circulation is instead transferred through a second-order collective process between many-body persistent-current states, with a transfer time scaling as the inverse square of the inter-ring tunnelling in the weak-link limit. Number fluctuations then remain of order one instead of growing with the particle number, and within each number sector the system evolves into coherent superpositions of two many-body configurations, distinguished by which ring carries the circulation. The entanglement accessible under number-conserving operations therefore reaches up to approximately one bit. We propose a quench protocol to prepare the initial state and estimate transfer times within reach of current ring-lattice experiments, identifying coupled rings as a platform to study coherent quantum phase slips and to manipulate persistent-current states.
title: Coherent phase slips in coupled rings: from weak to strong interactions

summary: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies. Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. The attack operates on intermediate communication representations subject to channel effects, with perturbations generated through a learned mapping applied at test time. It is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination. These results reveal a clear trade-off between SemCom gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, motivating the need for secure relay designs that account for insider threats.
title: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities

summary: This work identifies a fundamental, controller-independent limitation in reusable launch vehicle powered descent: a sudden $180^\circ$ phase transition in the open-loop transfer functions from the control inputs to the lateral drift and drift rate. The transition occurs inside the flight envelope, reverses the effective control direction, and can destabilize the closed loop system under uncertainty. An analytical condition governing this transition is derived, its physical mechanism is established, and its dependence on vehicle mass, aerodynamic properties, and geometry is characterized. An Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI)-based control architecture is then developed to inherently address this limitation and is tuned via $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Closed Loop Shaping to provide local robustness and performance guarantees. The internal dynamics introduced by the INDI inversion are analytically derived and proven to be stable throughout the flight envelope. The proposed controller is compared against a robust gain-scheduled baseline controller through linear stability analysis and an extensive nonlinear Monte Carlo campaign. Both controllers achieve 100% success across the considered Monte Carlo campaign, though the INDI-based controller provides improved tracking performance, superior nominal and dispersed stability margins, requires fewer controller design points, and reduces controller tuning complexity.
title: Overcoming Fundamental Control Limitations in Powered Descent Flight through Robust Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion

summary: Abstract The Laser Cognition (LC) is a proposed multilevel theoretical framework for investigating how selective attention, conscious access, curiosity-guided inquiry, associative recruitment, and representational integration may contribute to the emergence and evaluation of novel ideas. Its central explanatory metaphor is laser illumination: a complex cognitive field contains multiple thoughts, memories, representations, and potential relationships, while a selected cognitive target receives processing priority. The framework uses this metaphor to organize a proposed mechanism linking cognitive-field activation, attentional targeting, awareness-mediated processing, focus regulation, associative recruitment, integrative recombination, candidate generation, and metacognitive evaluation. LC retains the distinction between the full theory, its default mechanism, and its canonical primary case. The primary case is the Laser-Spotlight Cognitive Genesis Case (LSCGC); the proposed default mechanism is the Laser Cognition Default Mechanism (LC-DM); and its principal operational cycle is the Laser-Guided Cognitive Integration Cycle (LGCIC). The framework is formalized using a weighted cognitive graph, a dual-route attentional-targeting model, a normalized attentional-allocation function, a focus-stability measure, an associative-recruitment equation, a cognitive-integration index, a probabilistic candidate-emergence model, and a feedback-control representation. The mathematical expressions constitute proposed model specifications, not established equations of human neural operation. Awareness, attention, curiosity, affective engagement, cognitive flexibility, and metacognitive monitoring are treated as related but conceptually distinct constructs. The architecture includes eighteen layers, a multidomain research structure, eight initial research hypotheses, explicit falsifiability requirements, a cross-system functional generalization framework, a fourteen-step research protocol, and a twenty-part manuscript structure. Human cognition is the primary explanatory domain. Applications to artificial intelligence, large language models, artificial general intelligence, and possible artificial superintelligence are framed as hypotheses about functional or computational correspondence rather than established claims of shared consciousness or identical mechanisms. LC is presented as a theory-development and validation framework. Its explanatory value, novelty, causal assumptions, parameter identifiability, empirical adequacy, and cross-domain applicability remain subject to systematic literature review, mathematical audit, empirical testing, model comparison, and replication.

summary: Аннотация. В статье представлен комплексный лингвистический и историко-дипломатический анализ письма вице-губернатора крепости Анапа Сеид-Махмуда Мусселима от 29 марта 1817 года, которое адресовано русскому адмиралу Алексею Самуиловичу Грейгу. Этот документ рассматривается как важнейшее локальное историческое открытие, который на данный момент формирует вокруг себя уникальный контекст пограничной российско-османской коммуникации и одновременно вписывается в макроконтекст реализации условий Бухарестского мирного договора 1812 г. В ходе исследования подробно изучена композиционная структура документа, выявлены системные графические, орфографические и грамматические девиации во французском тексте. Исследование позволяет реконструировать уровень османских адъютантов и специфику функционирования французского языка как инструмента дипломатии.   Abstract. The article presents a complex linguistic and historical-diplomatic analysis of the letter of the vice-governor of the fortress Anapa Seyid-Mahmud Mousselim dated 29 March 1817, which was addressed to the Russian admiral Alexey Samuilovitch Greig. This document is regarded as the most important local historical discovery, which at the moment forms around it a unique context of the Russian border -Ottoman communication and at the same time fits into the macro context of the implementation of the terms of the Treaty of Bucharest (1812). In the course of the study, the compositional structure of the document was thoroughly examined, systematic graphical, orthographic, and grammatical deviations in the French text were identified. The study allows for a reconstruction of the level of Ottoman adjutants and the specificity of the functioning of the French language as an instrument of diplomacy.

summary: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.
title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care

summary: We study an extremal problem involving three disks inside the unit disk. Two disks are initially placed so that they are tangent to each other and internally tangent to the unit circle. A third disk of maximum possible radius is then inserted, subject to tangency with both original disks. We prove that the minimum possible sum of the areas of the three disks is 11π/18, attained when their radii are 1/2, 1/2, and 1/3. Surprisingly, the minimizing configuration does not consist of three equal disks, despite the symmetry of the problem. Three different proofs are presented, based on Descartes' circle theorem, geometric inversion, and a parametrization using tangency points.
tags: Circle packing; Descartes' circle theorem; inversion; extremal geometry; geometric optimization
title: Three Circles in a Unit Disk: Three Solutions to an Extremal Problem

summary: This dataset supports the manuscript “Assessing the Interpretability of QM/MM Interaction Energies: A Representation-Aware Diagnostic Framework,” submitted to the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling (ci-2026-038804). The numerical data describe three retrospective peptide–enzyme case studies: prolyl endopeptidase (PEP; primary nine-peptide electronic-energy analysis, 82 retained configurations), historical beta-secretase 1 (BACE1; 63 audited snapshots, 52 retained after cleaning), and reconstructed angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE; 131 valid QM/MM decompositions, with a distinct 73-configuration GIF/IP/LP core comparison). These data support question-specific representation diagnostics and descriptive configurational-contrast analysis; they do not establish universal applicability or external affinity-prediction performance. Version v4 adds recovered simulation input files, topology and parameter files, preparation and analysis scripts, and file-level provenance manifests. The input supplement contains 8,597 recovered source files, together with the unchanged earlier numerical archive and verification records (8,740 regular files in total). It includes GROMACS run inputs for PEP and BACE1, ACE OpenMM production configurations and Amber input files, Zn-model parameterisation/validation inputs, ORCA component inputs with their coordinate and point-charge dependencies, and separately identified sensitivity, matched-perturbation, and unsuccessful diagnostic branches. The earlier numerical archive is also retained as a separate top-level download for continuity. No scientific numerical results were changed. The computational representations differ among the case studies. Primary PEP uses mixed AMBER03/CHARMM27 production protocols and inherited embedding charges. Historical BACE1 uses dynamically selected gas-phase receptor clusters and is retained for representation auditing. Corrected ACE uses snapshot-specific electrostatic embedding with a documented receptor-QM definition. The three enzymes do not share a single fixed-fragment computational representation. The original structural-analysis program that produced the historical 4 Å contact subsets C–E was not recovered. Curated subset memberships and scripts reproducing the statistics from those memberships are provided. Additional historical provenance limitations, evidence levels, and relocated source paths are documented in the supplement README and manifests. MD trajectories and bulk simulation outputs are not included. File recovery and integrity checks do not imply that the full historical simulation workflow has been rerun in a fresh environment. Third-party force-field distribution files retain their original attribution and licensing terms.
title: Data for: Assessing the Interpretability of QM/MM Interaction Energies: A Representation-Aware Diagnostic Framework

summary: Fusion Pilot Plants (FPPs) need control systems that survive diagnostic and actuator failures . We present DIII-D experiments  validating real-time, ML-enabled controllers in FPP-relevant scenarios under both imposed diagnostic dropouts and real in-shot hardware failures. Conventional equilibrium reconstruction fails when key diagnostics drop out. Our ML-based RTCAKENN recovers plasma profiles under simulated failures of Thomson Scattering (TS), Charge Exchange Recombination (CER), and Motional Stark Effect (MSE) and maintains accuracies above 90%. ECHO, a fault-robust ML controller, coordinates electron cyclotron heating (ECH) by reallocating gyrotron power s and steering across surviving gyrotrons when units fail mid-shot. In a Hybrid scenario with real ECH dropouts, we mitigated heavy-Z impurity accumulation (argon proxy) using core ECH power tracking a real-time ML radiated-power (Bolo-NN) model for pumpout , and Electron Cyclotron Current Drive (ECCD) steering onto the 3/2 tearing mode for MHD amplitude control. Coordinated ML-controlled gyrotron power adjustments (>0.5MW) avoided argon accumulation and MHD-induced confinement collapse. We also accessed Resonant Magnetic Perturbation (RMP) Edge Localized Mode (ELM)-suppressed plasmas at reduced RMP coil current where large sawteeth would otherwise break ELM suppression. The approach was to reduce sawtooth magnitude (and increase frequency) by holding ECCD inside q=1. Control held through the same TS dropouts and ECH failures, with RTCAKENN providing q=1 localization while ECHO maintained aiming. These first-of-a-kind results show integrated ML-enabled fault-tolerant control sustaining FPP-relevant operating points through imposed and unscripted failures, foundational for resilient burning-plasma control.
title: ML-Enabled Fault Resistant Plasma Control on DIII-D

Its scientific coupling is causal inference x microscale interventions x biological functional validation. The evidence perimeter is prospective and nonclinical, using closed in-vitro systems, organ-on-chip platforms or authorized ex-vivo material; neither clinical efficacy nor autonomous human intervention is claimed. Two hundred Research Gates organize twenty causal challenge families across ten primary physical observables, each with an independently read companion, concealed intervention, matched comparator, explicit rival and refusal gate. summary: This repository provides the data, Python scripts, numerical outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting a methodological investigation of negative multifractal spectrum estimates in stochastic cascades and digital images. The study distinguishes formally negative annealed multifractal spectra, which can arise in stochastic cascade models, from negative finite-resolution estimates that may depend on measurement and preprocessing procedures. The repository includes: 1. Synthetic image datasets generated using hierarchical random maps (HRM), Fourier-based synthesis (FFT), midpoint displacement (MPD), and binary geometric constructions. 2. Numerical experiments investigating uniform background floors, noise, quantization, clipping, scale-window dependence, and grid-phase sensitivity. 3. Analyses of Dirichlet multiplicative cascades, including Genuine, Shuffled, and Decoy controls. 4. Multifractal estimates based on multiplier moments and Chhabra–Jensen procedures, together with whole-image bootstrap uncertainty estimates. 5. Auxiliary experiments concerning finite-ensemble histogram spectra and supersampling. 6. Scripts, CSV result tables, execution logs, and figure-reproduction materials. 7. A manuscript-to-data mapping file (MANUSCRIPT_MAP.csv), documentation, and SHA-256 checksums supporting traceability and integrity verification. The repository documents reproducibility checks, including the comparison of 180 baseline cases and the reproduction of two computational figures. These checks should not be interpreted as independent validation of every numerical experiment or as proof of universal estimator reliability. The results emphasize that formally negative multifractal spectra and negative estimates obtained from finite digital observations have distinct mathematical interpretations. In particular, negative estimated values do not imply negative Hausdorff dimensions. The dataset is independent of any specific journal submission and is intended to support transparent examination, replication, and further methodological research. Original datasets, figures, tables, and documentation are distributed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Any third-party components remain subject to their respective licenses.
title: Negative Multifractal Spectra in Stochastic Cascades and Digital Observations: Reproducibility Data and Code

summary: This article examines a method for developing students' chemical language through digital storytelling. The proposed methodological solution involves a sequence of activities in which students not only create a digital story but also translate the content of a chemical phenomenon from its observed form into a verbal explanation, a microcosm model, and a symbolic notation. The method includes setting up a chemical situation, identifying the linguistic core of the topic, a sequential description of the process, peer review of the scenario, creation of a digital story, and reverse transformation of the information. To evaluate the results, criteria for terminological and symbolic accuracy, understanding of the meaning of chemical notation, logical explanation, and coherence of chemical language are identified. The proposed approach can be used in studying exchange reactions, electrolytic dissociation, oxidation-reduction, and organic reactions.
tags: chemical language, digital storytelling, chemical symbols, nomenclature, chemical formulas, reaction equations, chemistry teaching.
title: METHOD OF DEVELOPING CHEMICAL LANGUAGE IN STUDENTS BASED ON DIGITAL STORYTELLING

summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript "Right Ventricular Function and the Mechanical Power–Mortality Gradient During Invasive Ventilation: A Candidate Echo-Informed Ventilator Tolerance Phenotype." Contents: SQL extraction queries (Charlson comorbidity index; plateau-pressure–based "strict" mechanical power), Python analysis code (primary logistic models with stratum-specific estimates and multiplicative interaction; adjustment ladder; RERI; RV-stratified restricted cubic splines; simulation-based power analysis; main-effects-versus-interaction decomposition), and aggregate-level derived results. No patient-level data are included; source data (MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-ECHO, and the hour-resolution respiratory-support dataset) are available to credentialed users via PhysioNet. Version v2026-11 (Revision 1): this version accompanies the first revision of the manuscript submitted to BMC Pulmonary Medicine. It retains the original v2026-08 code and aggregate outputs unchanged (code/, data_aggregate/, README_v2026-08.md) and adds revision_2026-11/, containing hourly respiratory-support and treatment extraction scripts; the frozen primary model (pre-echo SOFA and vasopressor use in the 24 h before echocardiography, with the original model retained as a sensitivity analysis); prespecified sensitivity analyses; RV-dysfunction text-to-category mapping (aggregate counts only); risk-scale RERI with bootstrap CIs; simulation-based power; figure and table code; aggregate outputs; and FROZEN_SPEC_and_AUDIT.md documenting frozen variable definitions and timing audits. No patient-level data are included. Final version (2026-11-07): updates the earlier v2026-11 upload. An independent implementation rebuilt all 1,903 analytic stays from source data and reproduced the exposure within the specified tolerance, RV grades and mortality outcomes under the calendar-day rule (code and aggregate results in revision_2026-11/independent_validation/). Revised analyses now use age at hospital admission rather than MIMIC-IV anchor age (417 ages changed; 00_age_at_admission.py); exposure-hour counts and recomputation checks use invasive-ventilation hours only; and 28-day mortality is explicitly defined in calendar days. All revised outputs were regenerated. No patient-level data are included. Clean-copy verification on macOS (2026-11-07): the age-corrected package was extracted into an empty local directory, supplied only with the two authorised local cohort inputs, and rerun through scripts 00, 01, 02, 04, 07, 08, 09, 10 (500 simulations for each of 1.20, 1.25 and 1.30), 11 and 12. All hourly and treatment intermediates were re-extracted from source. The comparator reported "11/11 files match." with Python 3.9.6, NumPy 2.0.2, pandas 2.3.3 and matplotlib 3.9.4. The primary interaction was OR 1.14 (95% CI 0.93–1.40), P=0.221. README run commands and REPRODUCTION_LOG.md document the procedure and scope; this analysis rerun is distinct from source reconstruction and does not constitute independent confirmation by the cohort-building author. The deposit remains a draft pending final author approval.

summary: Analysis package for a study of copy-specific assignment at the two 23S rRNA copies of Helicobacter pylori . The package contains the seventeen supplementary tables, the analysis and figure code, the recorded software versions, the reconstruction log for the long-read alignments, and a per-read phase-evidence table. What is reproducible. The six-criterion classification of 103 matched isolates is re-runnable and every verdict was re-derived from the counts with zero mismatches. The reference metadata for all cited works is captured from Europe PMC and every DOI was verified against its record. The figures are generated by script and each passes a programmatic overlap, clipping and text-on-line audit before export. The short-read counts at the two A2143 coordinates are reproduced from the archived alignment, whose header records the exact command and tool versions. What is not. The original NCBI query string and its date were not retained, so the cohort cannot be rebuilt verbatim; per-accession inclusion flags are given instead. The barrnap installation originally used on the analysis machine is missing a Perl module and does not run; the rRNA copy numbers were therefore archived values in earlier versions and are re-derived with barrnap 1.10.5 in this version. The original parameter sets for two of the three long-read procedures were not retained; those procedures were re-run and both original and re-run values are reported side by side and never pooled. One cell of the long-read table reproduces exactly; the others do not, and this is stated in the manuscript. Changes in version 4. The package matches the manuscript. All thirteen supplementary tables are present, including Supplementary Tables S12 and S13, which were absent from the previous version, and Supplementary Table S1 now carries the genome length and assembly level of all 1,483 retained genomes rather than leaving those columns empty. A new Supplementary Table S1b lists the seven excluded genomes that could be recovered from local storage, with their lengths; the genome-length window is 1.5 to 1.7 Mb and this version states the evidence that fixes its bounds. Three new scripts are included: the marker-control experiment (scripts 26 and 27), in which the single copy-differentiating base of the isolate was set to A in both copies, to C in both, to T in both, and exchanged between them, with the reads realigned to each control; and the structural diagnostic of the two 26695 23S copies (script 28), which reports that copy 1 contains no ambiguous base while copy 2 contains one N at genome position 1,475,696. The four control reference sequences are deposited under results/marker_control/. Changes in version 6. This version restores the complete file set. The previous version was published from an incomplete upload, so most of the figures, several of the supplementary tables and part of the analysis code were missing from that record. Zenodo caps a record at 100 files and this package has 134, so the package is now deposited as a single archive, hp23s_copy_assignment_package.zip , which holds every file at the path it occupies in the source repository; this README, the SHA-256 manifest and the archive of rRNA calls and copy sequences are additionally placed loose in the record. From version 10 the manuscript itself is not deposited, in the archive or loose. Every member of the archive is listed in SHA256SUMS.txt with its SHA-256, and that manifest is regenerated here, which corrects the entry for this README (the previous manifest had been computed before the last edit of the file). DOI.txt now lists the version DOIs, and the data-availability sentence in the manuscript names the concept DOI rather than one version, so that it cannot point at a superseded record. Changes in version 7. This version is a manuscript round: the text is rebuilt from the same locked data by the same script, and no reported value changes. Three defects in the supplementary apparatus are correcte
title: Long reads assign a 23S rRNA resistance allele to one of the two copies in Helicobacter pylori; a complete short-read assembly does not

summary: Vacuum is an absolutely static reference system. When light propagates in a vacuum, it moves in an absolutely static reference system. The propagation speed of light in a medium is a constant, which has nothing to do with the motion state of the light source, the observer or the receiver. When light propagates in a medium, it is dragged by the inertia of the medium. While light propagates in a vacuum, the vacuum is absolutely static, which cannot drag the light to move, and the speed, position, and direction of light in a vacuum are fixed. Based on this theory, a light interference experiment can be performed as proof, using a Michelson interferometer. The principle of the experiment is to split the laser into two beams of light at a half-reflecting mirror,one of which passes through a vacuum quartz tube and reaches the Mirror M1,The light reflects back from M1,Passing through a vacuum quartz tube,Project onto the screen through a half mirror; The other beam of light does not pass through the vacuum quartz tube,reaches the Mirror M2,The light reflects back from M2,Project onto the screen through a half mirror.however, both of the beams converge on the screen, forming interference fringes.Because the speed, position, and direction of light in a vacuum are fixed and the absolute motion of the earth will drive the vacuum quartz tube to move,when the absolute direction of the earth's motion and the direction of light propagation are parallel to each other,light will have an extra optical path in the tube; when they are perpendicular to each other, light will not have the extra optical path in the tube, so after the instrument has turned 90 degrees, the interference fringes will move. The key to this experiment is to create a vacuum. The structure of the experiment is simple that I hope someone could make an experimental verification. According to this theory, it can be concluded that the essence of Fizeau experiment , sagnac effect and Hoek experiment is the same. The reverse process of Fizeau experiment is sagnac effect, vice versa. According to this theory, the Fizeau experiment has a calculated result of movement at 0.236 fringes and a measured value at 0.23 fringes; in the case of Ruyong Wang's experiment "Generalized Sagnac Effect", the moving phase difference has a calculated result at 0.000251 and measured value at 0.000246 in the experiment. Obviously, this theory is more consistent with the experimental measurement results and the theoretical explanation is more real and natural. The sagnac effect, Mach-Zehnder interferometer and Michelson interferometer can all be used to conduct experiments based on this principle to verify whether there is an absolutely stationary reference system. Among them, the sagnac effect has the highest accuracy, the Mach-Zehnder interferometer the second and the Michelson interferometer the lowest. If Michelson and Morley had used a 11m-long vacuum quartz tube for the experiment, they might have observed a movement of 0.373 interference fringesand there might have no so-called "dark clouds". This experiment is actually to measure the sagnac effect of the Earth's rotation by using a Michelson interferometer.

title: A HypotheticalExperimental Approach to Prove the Existence of an AbsolutelyStationary Reference Frame by Using the Michelson Interferometer

summary: The study aimed to optimize preoperative modeling and the individualized selection of surgical treatment for genital prolapse in women of childbearing age. Materials and methods: A retrospective-prospective descriptive comparative analysis of clinical and functional data from 85 fertile women (Group 1: n=45 with connective tissue dysplasia markers; Group 2: n=40 without manifest CTD) was conducted. Anatomical defects were quantified using the international POP-Q system, levator muscle tone was evaluated via perineometry and 3D/4D pelvic floor ultrasound, and systemic connective tissue dysplasia was assessed using clinical risk scores. Results: Standardized objective quantification using POP-Q, integration of obstetric history, levator defect scoring, and metabolic/CTD markers allowed for the development of a predictive mathematical risk matrix. Custom laparoscopic reconstructive techniques (pectopexy and laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy with autologous/mesh organ-preserving repair) yielded 95.6% 2-year anatomical success compared to 77.5% in standard vaginal repair. Conclusion: Personalized surgical strategies and preoperative modeling based on multiple functional, anatomic, and connective tissue parameters significantly improve long-term outcomes, preserve reproductive capacity, and minimize recurrence in fertile women with pelvic floor dysplasia

summary: Implementation Mechanisms for Tipiṭaka-Grounded AI Alignment — An Engineering Companion to Suffering-Cessation as Value Function This paper reads the Abhidhamma — the analytical third division of the Theravāda Buddhist canon — as a process specification of mind: typed, momentary mental events arising one at a time under twenty-four typed conditioning relations, with ethical class tracked per event and per position in a processing cycle. From that reading it derives a research program for AI alignment evaluation and intervention: a red-team taxonomy of mimicry failure modes, resting-state (minimal-context) evaluation of language models, an intervention-timing typology over a processing cycle, a typed causal vocabulary, the limits of interpretability by subtraction, paired entailment-and-denial consistency testing of alignment claims, and a positive competence taxonomy. It is the engineering companion to Suffering-Cessation as Value Function (Ly, 2026), which argues for the Theravāda Tipiṭaka as a substrate for autonomous-AI alignment, and it develops the canon's third basket — the Abhidhamma Piṭaka — at the layer where that paper's §6.6 left off: the layer of cognitive process itself. We make one framing claim and two structural contributions. The framing claim is the compilation thesis : the Abhidhamma is a substrate-neutral process-specification of mind, and each era that has received it has read it in the vocabulary for process it had to hand — the scholastic commentators' wheels of classification, the twentieth century's reading of it as a psychology, cognitive science's information processing, and computation for ours. The tradition itself reached for machine images again and again, each fitted to one lesson; computation is this era's addition. The claim defended here is not that the Abhidhamma secretly describes computers. It is that the computational reading is our era's compilation of a specification that has survived the earlier readings, and that this compilation's target can enact what it compiles rather than only describe it. Formal and computational readings exist (Barendregt 2006; Karunananda et al. 2015; Lou 2017); Takeuchi (2026) reads transformer self-attention as anattā and pursues alignment by subtraction; an agent grounded in the substrate is engineered toward enacting wholesome cognition rather than simulating it. No priority is claimed for that aim. The first structural contribution is the machine architecture (§4): the samsaric process rendered in four repaired mappings — (1) a conditioned machine with exactly one free variable, against the strictly deterministic reading the canon itself condemns in Makkhali Gosāla's fatalism; (2) citta as the instruction-cycle rather than the processor, with the 89/121 citta-typology as a shared instruction set, the mindstream ( santāna ) as the thread, and uniqueness residing in the execution trace; (3) the kammic continuity as an append-only linked ledger rather than a blockchain — no miners, no consensus, maximal privacy, immutable entries whose ripening remains context-dependent; and (4) the counter-gear : the dhamma-wheel that engages the samsaric wheel at its one free variable and unwinds the machine by fuel-withdrawal rather than force, terminating in kiriya -mode execution — action that leaves no kammic residue. The second structural contribution is the verification-suite reading (§5) of the analytical books: the Yamaka as bidirectional property-testing, the Vibhaṅga's interrogation method as schema validation, the Dhātukathā as inclusion-matrix consistency, and the Kathāvatthu as formal adversarial protocol — with the Kathāvatthu's opening controversy ( puggalakathā , the refutation of the person-entity) read as the canon pre-running, and settling, this paper's own central repair. title: The Wheel That Unwinds the Wheel: The Abhidhamma as Executable Process-Specification

summary: Where is the place of the human being in the physical picture of the world? This question is usually answered from one of two camps: consciousness is a product of the brain and nothing more; or consciousness is immaterial and does not depend on the body. This work takes a different path — forward from the physical foundation, step by step — and looks at where it leads. The foundation is the work “The Birth of Dimensions: A Formal Skeleton” (BD). It contains nothing but a single assumption: everything is a process, an ideal sine wave, and its centre is the observer. Dimensions are born by squaring: first time, then, by iterating the same square, space and mass. Elementary particles turn out to be a resonance of at least three dimensions — time, space and mass. From the same assumption BD obtains the rules of quantum mechanics, the Lorentz transformations and the masses of particles from the speed of light alone. If the foundation is right, its rule should show up everywhere — including in the work of the brain. And it does: the main ranges of brain rhythms approximately form a ladder of squares — 2–3, 4–9, 16–81 Hz — built in the same way as the tower of levels in BD: the width of the levels in logarithms doubles with every step, and the alpha rhythm falls on the boundary between levels. The rhythm bands are blurred, but that is how it should be: the electroencephalogram is a projection of a higher-frequency process onto a single dimension, and within one level the process is smooth. What matters is something else — resonance between frequencies, and in the brain it was measured long ago. This leads to an assumption: the body is a resonator, and since bodies are alike, this answers the question of why different observers see one common world. Consciousness is then built like an elementary particle — as an agreement of three frequencies linked by squares — only on a higher-frequency level. That is why we see its work but cannot weigh it with instruments of our level; and that is why the world is perceived as three-dimensional. The structure is examined: the “I” is the observer; consciousness is time, the “here and now”; the subconscious is space, the “self” and its history; superconsciousness, intuition, is mass, which is born in self-reflection. From this follows an assumption about the meaning of life as the cultivation of intuition. If consciousness is like a particle, the reverse is also true: every particle may contain what we call consciousness. In the calculations of BD the Milky Way is the image of a neutron, and we live inside it; there are neutrons in almost every atom of our body. And the Universe, if it is like a black hole — part of a particle of a larger world — may be an observer. This is a hypothesis, not a proof. At the end there is a list of ways to test it, and what is established is separated from what is assumed. Revisions as of 07.11.2026:  The list of related works has been corrected.       Где в физической картине мира место человеку? Обычно на этот вопрос отвечают из двух лагерей: сознание — порождение мозга, и только; или сознание нематериально и от тела не зависит. Эта работа идёт другим путём — от физической основы вперёд, шаг за шагом, и смотрит, куда она приводит. Основа — работа «Рождение измерений: формальный скелет» (РИ). В ней нет ничего, кроме одного допущения: всё есть процесс, идеальный синус, а его центр — наблюдатель. Измерения рождаются возведением в квадрат: сначала время, затем, итерациями того же квадрата, пространство и масса. summary: This data set contains raw SPECT projection data acquired on a variety of scanners and for a variety of isotopes. summary: This paper proposes Recursive Anticipatory Argumentation-Control Theory (RAACT), an interdisciplinary framework for representing argumentative discourse as a dynamic, par- tially observed, and recursively updated interaction system. Its central mechanism, Recur- sive Anticipatory Argument-Path Interception (RAAPI), combines contextual observation, pragmatic-linguistic encoding, argument reconstruction, opponent-state estimation, proba- bilistic argument-path forecasting, formal refutation verification, anticipatory intervention, and feedback-based model revision. The framework is developed around the Pre-emptive Refutation Fork Case (PRFC), a primary analytical case in which one participant forecasts an opponent's possible argumenta- tive move and presents a logically evaluated counterargument before that move is explicitly advanced. Subsequent responses are classified into continuation, substitution, qualification, forecast challenge, clarification, and novel argumentative pathways. The mathematical specification introduces latent-state models, observation functions, categorical predictive distributions, Bayesian belief updating, intervention-utility functions, estimation errors, and forecast-evaluation metrics. Conditional mathematical propositions identify what can be established under explicit assumptions, while empirical hypotheses dis- tinguish predictive accuracy from intervention effectiveness and strategic response restriction. RAACT is presented as a formal theoretical architecture and a research program, not as an empirically validated universal law. Its principal scientific obligations are to demonstrate incremental predictive value, establish causal effects under an identifiable research design, prove specific mathematical claims under stated assumptions, and identify boundary conditions through counterexamples and independent replication. Keywords: argumentation theory; linguistic pragmatics; anticipatory reasoning; pre-emptive refutation; cybernetics; feedback control; state estimation; Bayesian forecasting; formal logic; strategic discourse; falsifiability.

summary: This paper develops a scale-spanning account of latent vibration and frequency manifestation within Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM). It examines the relationship between complete latent vibration, the negative and positive displacement domains around the manifestable origin, and the eligibility of positive displacement for progression towards physical manifestation. The development distinguishes the complete latent-vibration interval from the directed displacement associated with manifestation, establishing the proposed Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck threshold relationships in terms of the Planck length. The analysis further develops phase-dependent frequency relations below the Planck threshold and considers the proposed frequency increments associated with the Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck domains. It then presents a state-dependent sequence of energy–frequency transformations across latent, phase, and manifested states, including the reverse progression associated with dissolution. Within this framework, frequency and displacement are treated as related physical parameters whose coefficients depend on the corresponding phase domain. The paper also distinguishes the phase-state potential-energy mass representation from the mass contribution associated with the manifested domain. It formulates the effective-mass relationship and separates this ECM representation from the distinct dark-energy-related mass representation. Taken together, these developments present an integrated theoretical description of latent vibration, manifestation eligibility, threshold transitions, energy–frequency relations, and mass-state transformations within the proposed ECM framework.
title: Complete Latent Vibration and Frequency Manifestation Eligibility in Extended Classical Mechanics

summary: This dataset supports 121 benchmark tasks for evaluating coding agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment. summary: Fuente del Salín (Cantabria, Spain) is one of the few decorated caves where a large assemblage of hand stencils is associated with a Gravettian occupation, including a hearth and evidence of pigment processing. Using a 3D reconstruction of the cave’s Palaeolithic state, GIS-based measurements and multivariate statistics, we analysed the spatial organisation of its 55 hand stencils. All are located near the entrance, in accessible, visible spaces able to accommodate several people, unlike the only other motif, deeper in the cave. The assemblage nonetheless includes distinct spatial groups, compositions and unusual orientations. The hearth could have lit more than half of the hands, and both kernel density analysis and hierarchical clustering single out the group surrounding it. These results strengthen the hypothesis that the hands and the occupation were contemporaneous and, together with Gargas, suggest that hand stencils could be produced in spaces also used for everyday activities.
title: By the Light of the Fire: Characterisation and Spatial Organisation of the Hand Stencils at Fuente del Salín in Relation to their Archaeological Context

summary: This repository contains the analytical datasets, Python scripts, numerical outputs, plots and reproducibility documentation accompanying the manuscript Can strontium isotopes track changing mobility patterns? Evidence from La Tène Central Europe. The repository is intended to support transparent evaluation, replication and further comparative research on Iron Age mobility, life histories and the relationship between human movement and regional geological environments. The repository supports reproduction of the downstream statistical analyses, including: Cemetery-level isotope distributions and local/non-local classifications. Individual-level mobility estimates using two complementary classification rules: Rule A (any sampled tooth potentially non-local) and Rule B (one predefined permanent reference tooth). Mixed-effects logistic models evaluating chronological, demographic and burial material-group associations while accounting for repeated teeth from the same individual. Sensitivity analyses, paired-tooth comparisons and reconstruction of childhood strontium exposure histories. Cross-cemetery isotope comparisons and relationships between lithological diversity and strontium variability at 1, 5, 10 and 20 km spatial scales. Reproducible analytical plots and numerical verification against the published supplementary results.
title: Strontium isotopes and mobility in La Tène Central Europe: analytical data, Python code and reproducibility materials

summary: When a phone fails and its owner keeps the messaging account running on a second device, the account's history can end up in two archives, each intact and each missing what the other holds. We call this Temporal Communication Fragmentation (TCF), a loss by non-union: no message is deleted, but the platform offers no operation that joins the two halves. WhatsApp's own documentation states that old and new chats cannot be merged. We define TCF by three jointly necessary and sufficient conditions and specify CARTA 1.1, a framework for reconstructing one archive from several. CARTA is an output contract owed to a reader who cannot check the result. Records that cannot be read unambiguously are quarantined with a typed reason, and a report gives each record's provenance, the conflicts and deduplication ambiguities found, and every setting used. We evaluated a reference implementation, CHAMP-Pipeline, on synthetic fragment sets with known ground truth. With its declared date inference it reproduced the ground truth in all 4,500 configurations of a parameter sweep; the invariants and the predicted outcome held in all 5,000 random configurations of two to four fragments; and reconstruction stayed exact at one million messages. A zone-offset advisory, frozen before testing, flagged all 2,800 misdeclared zones in a designed test of overlapping fragment pairs and 1,470 of 1,542 in random configurations, and raised false alarms in 2 of 600 correctly declared runs. A systematic search found 60 chat-merging tools; none fully provides more than 2 of the five output properties CARTA specifies. With a fragment's time zone left undeclared, every benchmarked tool and CHAMP-Pipeline produce the same duplicated and misdated records, and only CHAMP-Pipeline's report says so. All data are synthetic; no real archive has been reconstructed.
title: When Chats Split Apart: Formalizing Temporal Communication Fragmentation and the CARTA Reconstruction Framework

summary: The triangular Lagrange point of the restricted three-body problem and the radial motion of a charged particle in a Penning trap are both equilibria held at a maximum of an effective potential by a gyroscopic force. Each possesses one mode of negative energy, and each loses linear stability when its two frequencies collide—one at Routh’s mass ratio, the other at the trapping limit. Both systems belong to a single family of planar gyroscopic Hamiltonians. On every level of the conserved angular-momentum invariant, the degree-four normal form of any member at such a collision coincides with the reduced Hamiltonian of an axisymmetric Penning trap whose detuning is shifted by a term proportional to the invariant and whose quartic coefficient is fixed by a single normal-form invariant. On the level containing orbits that start at rest, this reduction yields closed-form laws for the largest excursion, the escape threshold, and the escape time. These laws depend only on the sign of the quartic coefficient and on scaled variables. At the triangular point the coefficient is positive, placing the collision in the soft class: orbits remain confined after stability is lost, with an excursion that grows like the square root of the distance past the critical value. Direct integration confirms the soft law to a fraction of a percent at the smallest detunings tested. Two traps whose quartic coefficient matches that of the triangular point reproduce the same law. Traps with the opposite sign escape at the predicted threshold and in the predicted times. A randomized ensemble of members confirms the classification by the sign of the coefficient. Two further results hold for every member of the family. Before the collision the linear transient gain is exactly the inverse square root of the frequency splitting. With isotropic velocity damping the first-order growth rates depend only on the undamped frequencies, and at the collision they scale with the square root of the damping rate. The first of these explains earlier reports of apparent escape just below Routh’s value as ordinary linear transients that reach a fixed radius. The second recovers the classical magnetron-instability formula as a special case. The results are local, planar, and classical. What transfers between the asteroid and the trap is the normal-form dynamics on each level of the invariant, the transient gain, and the damped linear rates. What does not transfer without further work is the behaviour beyond the normal-form neighbourhood, where the gravitational terms of every order cause the triangular point to deviate from any purely quartic trap.
title: An Asteroid in a Penning Trap

summary: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) to infer particle formation rate J(t) and size-dependent growth rate GR(d, t) from parallel differential mobility analyzer (DMA) particle size distribution counts measured in the CERN CLOUD (Cosmics Leaving OUtdoor Droplets) chamber experiments. The PINN is trained on measured counts and constrained by the aerosol general dynamic equation (GDE), with nucleation expressed as a boundary flux at 1.7 nm. For baseline benchmark comparison, the notebook also includes a Python re-implementation of the Julia-based extended Kalman filter and fixed-interval smoother from Ozon et al. (2021). Both methods are evaluated on four simulated cases with known truth (0000_00 to 0000_03) and the three CLOUD experiments (1802_01, 1952_02, 1906_03). For the CLOUD runs, results are compared with the independent PSM (J) and INSIDE (GR) estimates reported in the paper. BAYROSOL 1.1 data is downloaded directly from Zenodo within the notebook (Ozon, Stolzenburg and Dada, 2021, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4450492 , MIT license), so no additional data files are appended.
title: PINN Inference of Aerosol Formation and Growth Rates from CLOUD Chamber Data

summary: STARLI | FLAGSHIP 13 FISSION Ten Research Design Monographs | Flagships 141-150 / 300 Author: 33  |  White Rainbow Epoch  |  Research Design Working Edition v1.2 This ten-volume STARLI series examines trustworthy AI-assisted micro/nanorobotic experiments and nano-quantum measurement systems. The common research question is how to bind physical observation, decision authority, calibration uncertainty, and independently reconstructable evidence without mistaking computational confidence for experimental proof. Each volume is a 777-page English, nonclinical prospective research design containing 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 separately paginated research studies, 200 Research Gates with six mechanistic annotations, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Across the ten volumes, the collection contains 300 research plates, 820 chapters, 4,100 study pages, 2,000 Research Gates, and 330 Phoenix candidates. Research scope by flagship F141 | Microrobotic Autonomous Control Authority Envelope at the Limit — Defines physical authority envelopes for microrobotic control, including credential expiry, actuator veto, permission transfer, and independently observed safe stopping. F142 | AI Nano-Quantum System Trustworthy Refusal Decision at the Limit — Studies when an AI-guided nano-quantum system must refuse action, separating calibrated abstention from indiscriminate rejection and unsafe confidence. F143 | Microscale Autonomous Experimental Design at the Limit — Examines autonomous microscale experimental design under specimen, information, energy, and permission budgets, with causal identification and independent replication. F144 | AI Quantum Sensing Uncertainty Calibration at the Limit — Investigates calibration of quantum-sensing uncertainty, including shared drift, covariance, phase ambiguity, photon budgets, and fair classical comparisons. F145 | Nanorobotic Closed-Loop Control Replayability at the Limit — Tests whether nanorobotic closed-loop decisions can be replayed from raw sensor data, actuator histories, calibration versions, and unselected failures. F146 | AI-Driven Microscale Active Sampling at the Limit — Designs AI-driven active sampling experiments that jointly measure analyte recovery, physical disturbance, resource cost, and contamination under blinded controls. F147 | Nano-Quantum System Human Review Mechanism at the Limit — Evaluates human review of nano-quantum decisions through signed authority, contradictory permissions, case-level uncertainty, and independent physical vetoes. F148 | AI Autonomous Research Agent Safety Boundary at the Limit — Defines safety boundaries for autonomous research agents across instrument access, sample authorization, unsafe tool composition, and immutable evidence. F149 | Microrobotic Autonomous System Interlaboratory Generalization at the Limit — Tests transfer of frozen microrobotic protocols between laboratories with different geometries, materials, calibration trees, operators, and failure environments. F150 | AI Nano-Quantum Trustworthy Autonomous Laboratory at the Limit — Integrates sample custody, microrobotic actuation, quantum/classical readouts, controlled autonomy, human oversight, and cross-site evidence reconstruction. Scientific boundary and publication status These books provide falsifiable research questions, candidate mathematical models, prospective blinded tests, competing explanations, negative-result criteria, and successor research interfaces. They do not report performed experiments or establish clinical efficacy, autonomous deployment safety, or quantum advantage. Independent expert verification of physical assumptions, formula applicability, all bibliographic relationships, and the scientific independence of closely related designs remains necessary. These counts describe the publication structure, not validated scientific novelty. A companion publication ZIP includes the ten original PDFs and ten per-book Zenodo introductions. The Ten Research Directions F131  AI-Driven Microfluidic Sampling Strategy Optimization At The Limit — Examines recoverable analyte as a fraction of input under fixed sampling resources. Expert tuning with equal trials is the comparator; hidden human intervention is the rival. Blind recovery audits and out-of-distribution refusal test whether AI planning adds genuine value. F132  Nano-Quantum System Counterfactual Inference At The Limit — Tests held-out, intervention-specific counterfactual prediction error while retaining constraint-violation safeguards. Frozen open-loop policies anchor comparison; training-test leakage and nonreplayable observation-to-action chains can invalidate apparent autonomy. F133  AI-Driven Microrobotic Autonomous Calibration At The Limit — Uses blind-standard calibration bias after autonomous correction as a physical measurement target. Frozen open-loop policies and unselected failure cases distinguish early warning from hindsight leakage. Recovery outcomes and complete action replay remain necessary. summary: Overview Part 20 of 20. This is version 2 of the dataset. The source list, the tar file names and the split into parts are the same as in version 1. All images were generated again with a new model, EBGSv2. The dataset contains 2,981,033 synthetic Euclid VIS images. Each image corresponds to one source in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. The sources lie in the Euclid DR1 footprint, and most of them are BGS Bright and BGS Faint photometric targets. The model input is the DESI r- and z-band cutout. Changes from version 1 Item Version 1 This version Model EBGS: trained on DESI–Euclid cutout pairs centred on BGS targets (66,359 training pairs) EBGSv2: trained on patches cut from full Euclid Q1 MER tiles (not centred on galaxies) PSF conditioning None DESI r- and z-band PSF size as input; Euclid PSF fixed to one reference PSF Sampling 10 reverse steps; 3 trajectories share the first 70% of the steps and then run independently; the released image is the mean of the 3 trajectories 50 reverse steps; one trajectory HDUs Prediction, DESI_IMG, PREDICTION_STD Prediction, DESI_IMG; no PREDICTION_STD WCS None In both HDUs Noise model None Parameters in the header give a 1σ uncertainty for each pixel File organisation The dataset has 1,235 tar archives, grouped by HEALPix pixel (nside = 64, NESTED ordering). The archive names, the sources in each archive and the part that holds each archive are the same as in version 1. Each archive holds flat FITS files named <RA>_<DEC>.fits , in decimal degrees. This record holds 52 archives with 127,059 files, covering RA 349.8° to 99.9° (across RA = 0) and Dec −66.8° to −35.7°. Metadata files in this record: checksums.tsv : size, SHA256, MD5 and number of files for all 1,235 archives. ebgsv2_nfe50_index.csv and ebgsv2_nfe50_index.fits : one row per archive, with sky range, list of HEALPix pixels, part number and checksums. record_20_archives.txt : the archives in this record. ebgsv2_nfe50_files.csv.gz : one row per file (file name, RA, Dec, archive, part). Finding the archive for a sky position (same as version 1): import healpy as hp pix = hp.ang2pix(64, ra_deg, dec_deg, nest=True, lonlat=True) # find the row of the index whose hp64_nested_pixels column contains pix Model and generation settings The model is an Image-to-Image Schrödinger Bridge (I2SB). It starts from the DESI r-band image and is conditioned on the DESI z-band image. The training data come from 304 Euclid Q1 MER tiles. A further 16 tiles were used for validation and 24 tiles were held out for testing. None of these 40 tiles was used in training. The training target is the background-subtracted MER VIS mosaic (BGSUB). The generated images have the same pixel units, with an AB zero point of 24.6. We use the EMA weights at training step 68,931. This checkpoint has the lowest reduced χ² on the validation set. DESI PSF conditioning : the r- and z-band PSF FWHM come from the PSFSZ_R and PSFSZ_Z keywords of the DESI cutout header and enter the model as constant maps. If a cutout has no such keywords, we use the median of its PSFSIZE map. The values used are stored in the DPSF_R and DPSF_Z keywords of each file. Euclid PSF conditioning : all sources use the same reference PSF, the median stack of the Q1 test-set PSFs (header keyword PSFMODE = 'ref'). Sampling : one sample per source, 50 reverse steps, no steps shared with other samples. The random seed is 1024 plus the list index of the first file in the batch, so the results are reproducible. summary: Encounters among heterogeneous epistemic–praxis systems can expose differences in evidence, interpretation, and practical capacities . Some differences become consequential gaps relative to specified concerns; others sustain complementary ways of knowing . This paper develops a provisional account of generative translation through which situated encounters may enable new meanings and, under more demanding conditions, enduring changes in interpretive or practical capacities . A comparative philosophical analysis draws on hermeneutics, semiotics, pragmatism, social epistemology, evolutionary coordination, and procedural justice while preserving their distinct commitments . The discussion distinguishes representational correspondence, practical reconstruction, and generative translation, then separates interpretive affordance from realized meaning, retained capacity, recurrent convention, and possible normative recognition . Each transition requires different evidence; ordinary learning, resource changes, incentives, and institutional interfaces provide competing explanations for apparent co-evolution . Ethical evaluation concerns task-appropriate fidelity, opportunities for participation and refusal, authority over classifications, affected interests, and the review of consequential decisions . Ceva’s interactive justice and Eglash and Garvey’s generative justice inform distinct aspects of the inquiry, with questions of cross-category standing remaining open to separate justification . Constructed cases and proposed research designs indicate ways to evaluate and challenge the framework . The contribution is an integrative research programme connecting translation-mediated meaning formation with causal scrutiny and ethical responsibility .
title: How Meaning Grows Across Epistemic Gaps: A Discussion of Generative Translation and Its Ethics

summary: Data and code for computational prioritization of MYB–NFIB and MYBL1–NFIB junction peptides in adenoid cystic carcinoma. The primary analysis screens 284 public RNA-sequencing libraries and evaluates 3,746 observations representing 3,122 peptide–HLA pairs from 63 reconstructed contexts. Same-observation affinity-percentile and unflanked eluted-ligand rank cutoffs of ≤2% select 57 pairs (34 sequences) supported by 27 libraries, including an 11-pair provisional testing panel. The corrected analysis uses a consistent donor-frame translation rule. A separately reported HLA suffix-relaxed analysis evaluates 7,370 observations and selects 111 pairs, including a 26-pair sensitivity panel. Normal-peptide controls, native-flank comparisons, source annotations, conditional donor-support analyses and reconstruction checks retain their respective scopes; the resource does not provide complete native-context scoring of every normal-control combination or definitive donor attribution. This package includes the checked manuscript and supplement with updated public data links, 133 scientific tables with a 135-sheet workbook, figures, analysis code, saved prediction outputs and reproduction checks. Scientific data, code and outputs are unchanged from the clean 5 November package. Licensed executables, model weights, bulk sequencing reads and accession-linked genetic comparisons are not redistributed. Predictions prioritize experimental testing.
title: Selecting MYB–NFIB and MYBL1–NFIB junction peptides for experimental testing in adenoid cystic carcinoma
