summary: This analysis examines how aggregation and evidence composition shape international comparisons of reported antimalarial treatment failure. Using 244 World Health Organization summaries from 69 countries and territories covering 2010 to 2019, descriptive comparisons assess treatment regimens, parasite species and geographical settings, supplemented by exploratory sample restrictions. The mean reported failure median was 1.87 percent, while 62.30 percent of summaries had zero medians. However, 33.55 percent of zero median summaries contained positive failure maxima, revealing heterogeneity concealed by central values. The ordering of two commonly used regimens reversed across seven country pairs aligned by species, follow up duration and reported study interval bounds. Regional differences persisted within a shared species and treatment category, although means and medians produced different geographical orderings. Restricting observations to summaries representing multiple studies reduced dispersion while preserving a zero median. These findings refine surveillance interpretation by distinguishing favourable central performance from consistency across contributing evidence. International reporting should present distributions, study coverage and comparable analytical groups together to support targeted investigation of elevated failure observations.
title: ASSESSING ASSOCIATIONS BETWEEN ANTIMALARIAL TREATMENT REGIMENS, PARASITE SPECIES, REGIONAL SETTINGS, AND REPORTED MEDIAN TREATMENT FAILURE

summary: This analysis examines whether privacy vulnerability rankings remain consistent across text reconstruction procedures, informing international debates on federated learning security. A descriptive secondary analysis uses 72 published benchmark conditions from 2024, covering three attacks, two transformer configurations, three text benchmarks and four batch sizes. Matched comparisons hold the remaining experimental dimensions constant. DAGER exceeds TAG and LAMP in all 24 matched conditions, with average advantages of 61.62 and 49.79 ROUGE 1 score points, respectively. LAMP exceeds TAG in 23 conditions. Increasing batch size from one to eight coincides with lower reconstruction throughout the TAG and LAMP comparisons, whereas DAGER retains ceiling performance on GPT 2 and deteriorates on BERT. Model rankings consequently reverse across attacks. These patterns indicate that aggregation constrains recoverability conditionally rather than providing uniform protection. The contribution is a comparative synthesis showing that observed vulnerability depends on reconstruction capability and model configuration, without establishing causal mechanisms. Organizations should evaluate multiple attacks under matched conditions and distinguish unigram recovery from comprehensive disclosure when interpreting privacy claims.
title: GRADIENT EXPOSURE CONDITIONS AND TEXT RECONSTRUCTION VULNERABILITY IN FEDERATED FOUNDATION MODELS ACROSS PUBLISHED BENCHMARK EXPERIMENTS

summary: Decentralised peacebuilding councils are widely promoted as a means of rebuilding citizen trust in post-conflict states, yet the evidence base for their effectiveness rests largely on observational comparisons that cannot separate the councils' effects from the selection of communities into them. Using a before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and a residual standard deviation of 4.5, the analysis estimates power across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design achieves 80 per cent power to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 56 clusters, a requirement that exceeds the number of municipal units typically available in a single Ivorian region. The regression-discontinuity approach is defensible in principle but fragile in practice, and that its value lies less in producing a definitive estimate than in disciplining claims about what decentralised peacebuilding can plausibly achieve.
tags: decentralised peacebuilding; citizen trust; regression discontinuity; Côte d'Ivoire; before-after-control-impact; statistical power; municipal governance; post-conflict reconstruction
title: Decentralized peacebuilding councils and citizen trust in Côte d'Ivoire: a regression-discontinuity design at municipal budget thresholds

summary: I study an inverse problem for one-dimensional Brownian-compatible diffusions in which multiple probe responses are observed with independent, unknown multiplicative gains. The central question is whether the shared differential structure of the underlying generator can replace external gain calibration. For a diffusion generator Lq f = q(θ)f ′′(θ) + 1 2 q′(θ)f ′(θ), q > 0, the response to each prescribed probe is available only up to an unknown positive gain. I first estab- lish that a single nonconstant Morse probe uniquely and coercively identifies its gain-weighted dif- fusion coefficient. I then show that two nondegenerate probes determine their relative gain through a scalar compatibility relation implied by the Brownian drift–diffusion constraint. This yields an explicit reconstruction of the diffusion profile up to its unavoidable common scale, represented by a normalized inverse-square-root profile. Under quantitative nondegeneracy assumptions, the recon- structed profile depends locally Lipschitz-continuously on the observations. Numerical experiments illustrate the reconstruction procedure and its behavior under smooth response perturbations. I also describe a conditional connection with planar convex geometry. The results provide a generator-specific mechanism for blind relative-gain calibration and projective identification from probe-response functions without trajectory observations
title: Blind Gain Calibration in Brownian-Compatible Diffusions

summary: Figure 2 Circular maps representing the complete mitochondrial genome structural architecture of three Mudaria species generated via Proksee. summary: Exact finite Gram inversion, ordinary sawtooth least-squares errors and rigorous reciprocal-dilate certificates. The Riemann hypothesis and the limiting reciprocal approximation criterion remain unproved. We solve the finite least-squares problem for ordinary sawtooth dilates by explicit Gram inversion and obtain its exact error and asymptotic constant. For the distinct reciprocal-dilate problem, we derive rational Gram certificates, rigorous residual intervals and Hardy-space zero bounds. The Riemann hypothesis remains open.
title: Exact Gram Inversion for Fractional-Part Approximation

summary: For a Fermat fourfold of odd degree, the rational Hodge classes in middle degree are spanned by character blocks indexed by six-entry Hodge characters. Two direct constructions make such a block algebraic: a contraction of two surface characters, which includes the case of an inverse pair, and an exact 5-standard tuple of Aoki. We call the remaining characters *residual*. We prove that the residual characters at every odd degree are exactly the inflations of six explicit seeds in degrees 33, 39, 45 and 105. The proof is uniform in the degree and uses no computer enumeration. Maximal-order Fourier kernels, a classification of surface characters at odd conductor and an analysis of four points of a five-progression reduce an arbitrary primitive residual conductor to the degrees 15, 21, 33, 39, 45 and 105, which are then settled by the same character equations. An exhaustive census through degree 599, and enumerations at the 103 degrees up to 2001 not covered by the earlier subfamily theorems, give an independent check. Since the seeds are algebraic, the classification yields a proof of the Hodge conjecture for these fourfolds that does not use Kang's refined motivic dimension estimates. That conclusion is also covered by the written proof of Bhattacharjee [5], and the six seeds were first isolated by Jumagulov [8] through degree 199; the new content is the exact positive classification at every odd degree. We also record the all-dimensional consequences for the prime supports $\{3,11\}$ and $\{3,13\}$, and give an explicit family of Fermat characters on which the tensor filtration identity used in Kang's product argument fails. Archival copy of version 4 of this paper, first made public on rStation on 5 November 2026 ( rStation hodge_conjecture paper 104, v4 ; version 1 posted 4 November 2026). paper.md is the manuscript source as posted there (SHA-256 cac9f460be44dd1abe019c6eee5b42d898df8acad458e704a084bec91155cadd); the PDF is typeset from it with the posted title and abstract. supplement.zip contains the reproduction bundles (SHA-256 68e062729bbe49f0e92b435d0f4394fc4f156a82b9b8bc9aa1f503a386d91657). This paper follows the author's preprint The Hodge Conjecture for Odd-Degree Fermat Fourfolds , public on 8 September 2026 (ResearchGate, DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.26853.77288 ). The work was produced largely with AI systems and is released for public human verification; it has not been checked by a human expert.
title: Residual Characters of Odd-Degree Fermat Fourfolds

summary: This deposit accompanies a systematic review submitted to Neurosurgical Review: "Cerebrospinal fluid leak after endoscopic surgery for craniopharyngioma versus tuberculum sellae meningioma". The review asks whether craniopharyngioma (CP) and tuberculum sellae meningioma (TSM) differ in postoperative cerebrospinal fluid leak once the surgical corridor is held constant. Sixty-six endoscopic arms (3,453 patients, 349 leaks) were analysed. Pooled leak was 11.68% (95% CI 9.77-13.91) in CP (48 arms, 3,029 patients, 308 leaks) and 9.58% (6.94-13.08) in TSM (18 arms, 424 patients, 41 leaks); with publication era held constant the two cohorts did not differ (odds ratio 0.906, 95% CI 0.596-1.378). The paper's other finding is a measurement finding: third ventricle opening can be classified strictly in 3 of the 48 CP-EEA series and is stated in none of the 18 TSM-EEA series. Contents. data/ holds the extracted dataset (96 arm rows, each with a verbatim source quotation), the per-record source table, the retrieved records from every executed database, the two independent title-abstract screening sheets with their adjudication ledger, the analysis export, the item-level risk-of-bias coding for all 94 appraised arms, the publication-bias output, the pooled estimates as emitted, the absolute-scale contrast derived from them, the exact intervals and crude risk ratios for the four corridor-histology strata, the coding of what each arm states the outcome to be, the coding of whether each arm grades or dates that outcome, and the per-arm coding of how severe that outcome was where an arm says so. code/ holds every retrieval, screening, analysis, figure and verification script, numbered in execution order. Reproducibility. README.md states, for each number in the article, the script that produces it and the command that runs it, and records what is deliberately absent from the deposit. MANIFEST.json and the integrity section of README.md carry the SHA-256 of every file. The headline quantities (the two pooled proportions with their prediction intervals, the era-adjusted contrast, and Cohen's kappa for the duplicate screening) were re-derived from this exact archive before upload. Screening was performed independently by two reviewers (Cohen's kappa 0.699, 95% CI 0.626-0.772 across 261 records); the 52 disagreements were resolved against the eligibility criteria in Table 1 of the article, and none changed the category it carried at first screening. Extraction was abstract-level and single-reader, and the article declares this. Licence: data under CC BY 4.0, code under MIT.
title: Cerebrospinal fluid leak after endoscopic surgery for craniopharyngioma versus tuberculum sellae meningioma — a systematic review and meta-analysis of proportions, with the corridor held constant

summary: This packet contains the analytical outputs, identity and geometry sources, feature metadata, code, execution receipts and the figure package for a nitrate-specific screening assessment of 207 transboundary river-basin reporting units: a prospectively specified susceptibility index and typology, a river-length-weighted archive-scarcity measure derived from the historical GEMStat Open NO3N record (2005 to 2024), a mean-versus-hotspot aggregation diagnostic, a separately specified evaluation of the fixed index against sampled nitrate concentrations at monitored stations, and the scripts that render the figures of the associated Comment. The prospective specification and its updates are recorded on the Open Science Framework (project hsbg3; registration eg3zc and updated record wyugm). The packet does not contain the manuscript, its Supplementary Information or any correspondence. It does not redistribute third-party inputs (see Inputs not included). Contents 01_typology_outputs: corrected reporting-unit typology (RBU.csv, 207 rows), child level-6 scores (L6.csv and L6.parquet, 16,397 rows), class counts, one-way sensitivity counts, mean-versus-hotspot membership, old-versus-corrected transitions, the run manifest, summary and report, and the runner code. 02_identity_geometry: reporting-unit display names and geometry (GeoPackage), the display-name master table, and the record of the sixteen shared-name groups with their distinct identifiers. 03_feature_metadata: JSON sidecars describing the feature tables used by the index and the monitoring axis (field lists, run parameters, hashes). 04_monitoring_axis: GEMStat NO3N footprint summaries by country, region and globally, and the provider’s output-format README. 05_concentration_evaluation: code (observation adapter and outcome builder, estimators, evaluation pipeline, manifest verifier, EnvStats diagnostic script), validation records, the frozen point-cohort and interval-account tables, station-level dispositions and bounds, execution receipts, numerical supplements, the expected-input manifest, synthetic test inputs, and the support-table scripts. 06_pipeline_code: upstream pipeline scripts (GEMStat harmonization, station snapping, design-matrix construction, archive-scarcity feature builder, susceptibility feature constructor) and tests. 07_data_dictionaries: column inventories for the principal tables. 08_comment_figures: the figure package of the associated Comment (also supplied to the journal as Supplementary Software 1): scripts, verified copies of their source files, rendered figures (PDF, SVG, PNG, JPEG), provenance receipts, and its own README, MANIFEST.json and SHA256SUMS.txt. Added in version 1.1. MANIFEST_SHA256.txt lists the SHA-256 of every file; REPRODUCE.md gives the environment and command sequence; CITATION.cff gives the citation. Key results reproduced by this packet Typology (primary setting, top-52 susceptibility stratum, 50 percent archive-scarcity criterion): Class 1, high score and archive-scarce, 38 units; Class 2, high score and below the scarcity threshold, 14; Class 3, outside the high-score set and archive-scarce, 133; Class 4, outside the high-score set and below the threshold, 22; 171 of 207 units met the archive-scarcity criterion. Mean-versus-hotspot screening shared 26 Class 1 units, with 12 mean-only and 14 hotspot-only units. The output files carry the registered class labels (surveillance-priority blind spot, supported hotspot, under-observed lower-modeled-concern basin, monitored lower-modeled-concern basin for Classes 1 to 4); the Comment describes the same classes by their defining conditions, because the archive axis measures submission to one open archive rather than monitoring in place. Archive operator: of 16,287 valid-length reference level-6 units, 15,180 had no NO3N record in the fixed extract and were exactly the flagged set; in this extract the minimum-rank percentile rule reduced to a record-presence rule. Concentration eval
title: Shared Rivers, Uneven Records: data and reproducibility packet for the transboundary nitrate susceptibility and archive-scarcity typology

summary: We prove Critch–Morton Conjecture 8 (SIGMA 10 (2014), 095, Section 2, p. 6): every consecutive three-site improper marginalization is birational for open-boundary, translation-invariant, binary bond-two matrix product states of length N at least four. An explicit rational inverse over the complex numbers is given on a nonempty principal open domain, with both inverse identities on the affine Zariski closures. A four-by-four linear system reconstructs a three-site representation, and inverse boundary contractions restore omitted sites. Consequences include rationality in dimension seven, reconstruction from every longer consecutive block with arbitrary fixed nonzero site-dependent coherent contractions, minimality of three retained amplitude indices, and exact equations characterizing the reconstruction chart.
title: Proof of Critch–Morton Conjecture 8 (SIGMA 10 (2014), 095, Section 2, p. 6): reconstruction from any consecutive three-site improper marginal

summary: Code and data behind the paper "Data-Driven Extraction of Multi-Exponential Thermal Kernels for Integrated Circuit Thermal Analysis" by B. Ali, I. Bruce, C. L. Trinh, X. Jin, C. He, and D. Chen, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) Systems. The method extracts a compact three-component exponential kernel from steady-state 3D-ICE temperature maps and predicts the temperature rise by convolving the kernel with the power map. Even reflection across the die edges handles the adiabatic side faces. thermal_kernel_code.zip: MATLAB and Python code of the kernel extraction, the evaluation, and the analyses of the paper, the 3D-ICE input generator and run script, and the HotSpot bare-die adaptation with the comparison scripts. Its README.txt gives the script and settings behind the tables, the figures, and the numbers in the text of the paper. thermal_kernel_data.zip: the 88 steady-state 3D-ICE temperature maps of the paper with their floorplan and stack files (base floorplan, final test sets A and B, Floorplan B, two further cooling conditions, single-cell impulses), the fitted kernel, the HotSpot inputs and fields of the comparisons, the inner problems of the solver cross-check, and the values of the paper's tables as CSV files. Unzip both files into the same folder. The README.txt of each archive describes its contents. The kernel describes the thermal response of the simulated die stack and cooling condition from which it is extracted. A change in the package structure, the layer thicknesses or materials, or the cooling alters that response and requires a new extraction from maps of the new system. All maps in this record are simulated. Copyright (c) 2026 Iowa State University. Code: MIT License. Data: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. The HotSpot material in the code archive keeps HotSpot's license (see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt).
title: Code and Data for Data-Driven Extraction of Multi-Exponential Thermal Kernels for Integrated Circuit Thermal Analysis

summary: Stenometopiellus dzhungaricus Mityaev, 1971 Figs 4, 12, 23–24, 33–36, 65–87 S. stepposus Mityaev, 1971: 153, 170, syn. n. S. ersinicus Vilbaste, 1980: 88–90, syn. n. Material examined. Many specimens from several localities in southern and southeastern Kazakhstan and northern Kyrgyzstan. Signals of seven males from the environs of Altynemel, 75 km south of Taldykorgan, Kazakhstan recorded on 17. VI. 2022 at 25 and 34 oC; signals of one male from the foothills of Dzhungarian Alatau Mtn. Range, 6 km east of Sarkand, Kazakhstan recorded on 17. VI. 2019 at 28 oC. Description. Coloration typical, pale with dark pattern (Fig. 4). 1 st sternal apodemes situated in transverse plane of body, wide, rounded, separated by deep, narrow, more or less parallel-sided notch (Figs 65–68). 2 nd apodemes broad, as long as their width at base or slightly longer, with widened and rounded apices, separated by narrow notch, sometimes with inner edges touching each other (Figs 69–72). Apical halves of subgenital plates oval, with slightly pointed tips (Figs 73–74). Aedeagus with rather short and high basal part and uniformly curved shaft. Middle part of posterior outline of aedeagus straight or only slightly concave (Figs 75–80). Body length: ♂, 2.6–2.9 mm; ♀, 2.9–3.3 mm. Differs from all species except S. turkestanicus in wide 1 st sternal apodemes situated in transverse plane of body. Differs from S. turkestanicus in shape of notch between 1 st apodemes (cf. Figs 65–68 and 88–90) and wider 2 nd apodemes separated by narrower notch (cf. Figs 69–72 and 91–93). Distribution. Southeastern and eastern Kazakhstan up to the Kazakh part of Altai Mts., Kyrgyzstan (North and Central Tien Shan), South Siberia (Tyva). Remarks. Mityaev (1971) briefly described in a key two closely related species, S. dzhungaricus and S. stepposus . According to his description, in S. dzhungaricus , the posterior outline of the aedeagus shaft is straight near the middle, while the anterior outline is vertical to the base (shown by thin arrow on Figs 81–82). In S. stepposus , the posterior outline near the middle is noticeably concave (shown by thick arrow on Figs 83–84), while the anterior outline is located at an acute angle to the base (shown by thin arrow on Figs 83–84). In the drawings in the key, these differences are quite clear (cf. Figs 81–82 and 83–84). However, a study of numerous specimens from different localities in southeastern Kazakhstan (Figs 75–80) showed that these taxa represent only extreme variants of a continuous variation range. For this reason, most specimens cannot be reliably assigned to either species; also, in some specimens, the anterior outline of the aedeagus is vertical as in S. dzhungaricus or even situated at a somewhat inverse angle to the base, while the posterior outline is slightly concave as in S. stepposus (Fig. 78). Moreover, males with different aedeagus shape sometimes were collected in the same biotope. On this basis, I consider these species to be synonyms and, as the first reviser, select S. dzhungaricus as the valid name. According to Mityaev (2002), the ranges of S. dzhungaricus and S. stepposus overlap almost completely, which also supports the established synonymy. Vilbaste (1980) provided a detailed and well-illustrated description of S. ersinicus from southern Tyva, South Siberia (Figs 85–87). A comparison of his description, particularly the drawing of the 2 nd sternal apodemes (Fig. 86), with my specimens from Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan leaves no doubt that S. ersinicus is a junior synonym of S. dzhungaricus . Since S. dzhungaricus is distributed as far east as the Kazakh Altai, its discovery in the adjacent part of Siberia seems quite natural.
title: Stenometopiellus dzhungaricus Mityaev 1971

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24060703 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the importance of artemisinin resistance and points out a gap in current understanding of its population-level consequences. The research objective is to examine whether increasing Kelch13 mutation prevalence is associated with malaria incidence across 16 Ugandan districts. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The longitudinal ecological design and negative binomial regression are well-suited for examining population-level associations. The authors also included several climatic, malaria-control, and resistance-related factors. However, the use of forward variable selection raises questions about model robustness. It would be helpful to find out whether the findings remain consistent under alternative model specifications and clarify how temporal correlation between monthly observations was handled. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The results support a positive association between Kelch13 mutation prevalence and malaria incidence after adjustment (aIRR = 1.131, 95% CI: 1.090–1.174). However, the ecological study design can't establish causation and the association may be bidirectional. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The tables and figures are well-organized. Figure 2 shows district-specific trends in mutation prevalence and malaria incidence, while figure 3 provides a clear visualization of the adjusted association. However, the apparent decline in predicted incidence at very high Kelch13 prevalence is not quite sure because there were only two observations above 60%. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Somewhat clearly The discussion provides biological explanations for the observed associations and acknowledges some important limitations, including possible reverse causation, residual confounding, and differences in the time scales of the data. However, the model-selection uncertainty and specific sensitivity analyses are not mentioned. Is the preprint likely to advance academic knowledge? Somewhat likely This preprint adds useful evidence about the relationship between antimalarial resistance markers and population-level malaria incidence. It contributes to the integration of molecular surveillance with epidemiological, climatic, and malaria-control data in a high-burden setting. Would it benefit from language editing? No This preprint is clear. Some statements could be more precise. For example, the authors sometimes use "malaria transmission" when the measured outcome is reported malaria incidence. Would you recommend this preprint to others? Yes, but it needs to be improved I would recommend this preprint to researchers interested in malaria epidemiology, antimalarial resistance, and molecular surveillance. The study shows an important public health question and provides useful population-level evidence. Is it ready for attention from an editor, publisher or broader audience? Yes, after minor changes I think this preprint is worth editorial consideration because it addresses an important research question and provides useful findings. However, before publication, I would recommend additional clarification of the statistical model, sensitivity analyses for variable selection. Competing interests The author declares that they have no competing interests. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they did not use generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
title: Structured PREreview of "Expanding Kelch13 artemisinin resistance markers are associated with higher malaria incidence in Uganda"

summary: This dataset offers computational information that underpins the research titled “Integrated computational and experimental characterization of I49R substitution in monomeric M-MLV reverse transcriptase reveals increased soluble recovery and RNA-dependent DNA synthesis.” The dataset comprises inputs for molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, structural models, numerical analysis outcomes, and computational documentation pertaining to Natural-type and I49R variations of Moloney murine leukemia virus reverse transcriptase (M-MLV RT). The initial simulations were conducted with GROMACS 2022 alongside the CHARMM36 force field from July 2022. Each protein variation was examined for 400 ns under periodic boundary conditions at 315 K and 1 bar. The dataset comprises the following elements: Structural models: Beginning and concluding protein configurations for Natural-type and I49R M-MLV RT. Simulation parameters: GROMACS configuration files, topology data, and production simulation setup files. Structural dynamics: Quantitative metrics for root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF), radius of gyration (Rg), and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA). Conformational assessment: Principal component analysis (PCA), free-energy landscape information, dynamic cross-correlation matrices (DCCM), and structural variability evaluations. Convergence evaluation: Temporal comparisons and geographical analyzes employed to evaluate the stationarity of chosen structural observables during the prolonged simulations. Protein–RNA complexes: Computationally generated structural representations of Natural-type and I49R reverse transcriptase interacting with RNA, alongside protein-only cluster-center conformations acquired from RNA-inclusive simulation systems. Reproducibility records: GROMACS procedural details, analytical notebooks, and ancillary documentation. The dataset aims to promote repeatability, autonomous analysis, and additional inquiries into the correlation between amino acid alterations, protein structural behavior, soluble protein extraction, and enzymatic activity. The computational findings enhance the experimental data of augmented soluble protein recovery and RNA-dependent DNA synthesis linked to the I49R mutation.
title: Computational Dataset for Molecular Dynamics Analysis of the I49R Substitution in Monomeric M-MLV Reverse Transcriptase

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: The triangular Lagrange point of the restricted three-body problem and the radial motion of a charged particle in a Penning trap are both equilibria held at a maximum of an effective potential by a gyroscopic force. Each possesses one mode of negative energy, and each loses linear stability when its two frequencies collide—one at Routh’s mass ratio, the other at the trapping limit. Both systems belong to a single family of planar gyroscopic Hamiltonians. On every level of the conserved angular-momentum invariant, the degree-four normal form of any member at such a collision coincides with the reduced Hamiltonian of an axisymmetric Penning trap whose detuning is shifted by a term proportional to the invariant and whose quartic coefficient is fixed by a single normal-form invariant. On the level containing orbits that start at rest, this reduction yields closed-form laws for the largest excursion, the escape threshold, and the escape time. These laws depend only on the sign of the quartic coefficient and on scaled variables. At the triangular point the coefficient is positive, placing the collision in the soft class: orbits remain confined after stability is lost, with an excursion that grows like the square root of the distance past the critical value. Direct integration confirms the soft law to a fraction of a percent at the smallest detunings tested. Two traps whose quartic coefficient matches that of the triangular point reproduce the same law. Traps with the opposite sign escape at the predicted threshold and in the predicted times. A randomized ensemble of members confirms the classification by the sign of the coefficient. Two further results hold for every member of the family. Before the collision the linear transient gain is exactly the inverse square root of the frequency splitting. With isotropic velocity damping the first-order growth rates depend only on the undamped frequencies, and at the collision they scale with the square root of the damping rate. The first of these explains earlier reports of apparent escape just below Routh’s value as ordinary linear transients that reach a fixed radius. The second recovers the classical magnetron-instability formula as a special case. The results are local, planar, and classical. What transfers between the asteroid and the trap is the normal-form dynamics on each level of the invariant, the transient gain, and the damped linear rates. What does not transfer without further work is the behaviour beyond the normal-form neighbourhood, where the gravitational terms of every order cause the triangular point to deviate from any purely quartic trap.
title: An Asteroid in a Penning Trap

summary: For a Fermat fourfold of odd degree, the rational Hodge classes in middle degree are spanned by character blocks indexed by six-entry Hodge characters. Two direct constructions make such a block algebraic: a contraction of two surface characters, which includes the case of an inverse pair, and an exact 5-standard tuple of Aoki. We call the remaining characters *residual*. We prove that the residual characters at every odd degree are exactly the inflations of six explicit seeds in degrees 33, 39, 45 and 105. The proof is uniform in the degree and uses no computer enumeration. Maximal-order Fourier kernels, a classification of surface characters at odd conductor and an analysis of four points of a five-progression reduce an arbitrary primitive residual conductor to the degrees 15, 21, 33, 39, 45 and 105, which are then settled by the same character equations. An exhaustive census through degree 599, and enumerations at the 103 degrees up to 2001 not covered by the earlier subfamily theorems, give an independent check. Since the seeds are algebraic, the classification yields a proof of the Hodge conjecture for these fourfolds that does not use Kang's refined motivic dimension estimates. That conclusion was previously stated in the author's earlier preprint [11] (8 September 2026), before the written proof of Bhattacharjee [5] (October 2026), and the six seeds were first isolated by Jumagulov [8] through degree 199; the new content is the exact positive classification at every odd degree. We also record the all-dimensional consequences for the prime supports $\{3,11\}$ and $\{3,13\}$, and give an explicit family of Fermat characters on which the tensor filtration identity used in Kang's product argument fails. Archival copy of version 6 of this paper, public on rStation on 9 November 2026 ( rStation hodge_conjecture paper 104, v6 ; version 1 posted 4 November 2026). paper.md is the manuscript source as posted (SHA-256 7dd045e569c13c11c09510e016aa2889f517f1d2201bf1aa37b87e80736101ad); the PDF is typeset from it with the posted title and abstract. supplement.zip contains the reproduction bundles (SHA-256 68e062729bbe49f0e92b435d0f4394fc4f156a82b9b8bc9aa1f503a386d91657). Changes from the previous Zenodo version (rStation v4): the abstract and Section 1 now state that the all-odd-degree algebraicity conclusion was previously stated in the author's preprint The Hodge Conjecture for Odd-Degree Fermat Fourfolds (8 September 2026; ResearchGate, DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.26853.77288 ), before Bhattacharjee's written proof (October 2026). Theorems, proofs and computational bundles are unchanged. The work was produced largely with AI systems and is released for public human verification; it has not been checked by a human expert.
title: Residual Characters of Odd-Degree Fermat Fourfolds

summary: Dataset Description This dataset contains experimental X-ray computed tomography (CT) and Angular Segmented Gamma Scanning (ASGS) measurements of radioactive waste drum mockups, collected for research into three-dimensional radionuclide activity reconstruction. The measurements were used in the development and evaluation of SARUMAN (Spatial Activity Reconstruction Using Machine-learning Algorithms for Nuclear Waste) , a Bayesian machine-learning framework for reconstructing spatial activity distributions from gamma spectrometry and CT-derived attenuation information. Dataset Contents The dataset comprises nine experimental configurations: Six homogeneous mockups (HOM-1 to HOM-6) , containing different source arrangements within homogeneous filling materials, including bark and potting soil. Three heterogeneous mockups (HET-1 to HET-3) , designed to investigate activity reconstruction under more complex material and source distributions. Each configuration is provided as an individual ZIP archive, containing: CT/ : A reconstructed X-ray CT volume in MetaImage format ( reconstructionFloat.mhd and reconstructionFloat.raw ). ASGS/ : Gamma spectrometry acquisition files ( .asr , .asw , and .srf ) corresponding to the segmented angular measurements. The original spectrometry file formats are preserved to retain the experimental acquisition information. Intended Use These measurements are provided to support reproducibility, methodological comparisons, and further research into radiological waste characterization, gamma-ray transport modelling, uncertainty quantification, and Bayesian inverse problems. The dataset can be used with SARUMAN or adapted for other reconstruction and data-analysis approaches. Reference Publication Users are strongly encouraged to read the associated scientific publication before using or interpreting this dataset: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306454926007383 The publication provides the scientific context for the experimental measurements, the associated reconstruction methodology, and the considerations relevant to their interpretation. Researchers wishing to reproduce the original analyses or adapt the methodology to other applications should consult this publication alongside the SARUMAN source code and documentation. Scope and Limitations The measurements originate from a specific experimental characterization system. Their interpretation requires appropriate knowledge of the detector geometry, acquisition configuration, calibration procedures, and CT attenuation modelling. The associated SARUMAN implementation includes detector-efficiency and CT attenuation models developed for this experimental setup. These models should not be assumed valid for different instruments without appropriate adaptation and validation. The dataset is provided for scientific research purposes and does not constitute a universally validated characterization benchmark. Associated Software SARUMAN — Spatial Activity Reconstruction Using Machine-learning Algorithms for Nuclear Waste https://github.com/vcasasmo/SARUMAN Dataset preparation and software development: Victor J. Casas Molina.
title: SARUMAN: Experimental CT and Angular Segmented Gamma Scanning Dataset for Radioactive Waste Drum Mockups

summary: I propose an organizing model of the formal mind as knowledge and experience: reusable observations and techniques, and the lived history from which they develop. Skills are techniques trained through experience; habits are repeated patterns rather than a third substance. I call the architecture these processes train the metastructure: a proposed organization of heuristics, reconstruction, anticipation, and usable continuity of thought, not a newly identified neural network. The model predicts that relevant learning can reduce both avoidable errors and stalled thinking, while fixation and bodily disruption can limit or reverse that benefit. I also argue that bodily sensation, presence, and practical constraints matter as much to the person as mental personality. My earlier phrase “more than half” is a qualitative generalization about that interplay, not a measured percentage. The account draws on memory research, expertise, predictive processing, and interoception without treating their findings as proof of the whole model. Eight predictions and two proposed studies distinguish the organizing assumptions from testable consequences. Companion manuscripts address incomplete knowledge of costs, socially shaped wanting, association between perspectives, and the deliberate experience of ordinary boredom; those connections are proposals rather than independent evidence. No new data are reported.
title: The Mind as Knowledge and Experience: Accumulation, Thought Block, and Bodily Presence in Choice

summary: Bees play a crucial role in human agriculture, making the accurate characterization of their behavior essential. In the field of automatic bee traffic tracking, individual monitoring has been prevalent in the past two decades to collect detailed data on foraging behavior. To support analysis, these data must be classified into entry and exit events, and assembled into flight trajectories. However, existing classification methods largely consider only simple exits and entrances, which ignore the existence of U-turn or guarding movements which represent a non-trivial fraction of bee activity at the hive entrance. Identifying these movements as compound events is necessary to accurately track all movements over time while avoiding classifications which may produce misleading movement records. In this presentation, we analyze existing event classification methods to evaluate their accuracy for two different types of movements: simple and compound. We then propose extended event classification methods that explicitly account for compound events, enabling more accurate reconstruction of bee traffic dynamics.
tags: bee traffic monitoring; compound event detection; computer vision; artificial intelligence; precision agriculture;
title: The Relevance of Compound Events in Bee Traffic Monitoring

summary: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range for uncooperative spacecraft pose estimation, but models trained on synthetic event streams must generalize to the noise, background activity, and contrast variation of physical sensors. We present a comparative systems study of two independently developed approaches to synthetic-to-real, event-based 6-DoF spacecraft pose estimation. The first is a modular pipeline that combines learned keypoint detection and unlabeled target-domain adaptation with geometry-based pose recovery and temporal smoothing. The second directly regresses translation and rotation from global and cropped event representations using an apparent-scale cue, physics-motivated synthetic corruptions, and feature-consistency regularization. We evaluate both systems under the same SPARK 2026 hidden-test protocol on the real-event split of SPADES, with predictions for all test frames. The results reveal a component-wise reversal concealed by the aggregate challenge score: direct regression reduces orientation error by 22.7% (1.1767 to 0.9101 rad) and obtains a 13.4% lower composite score, whereas the modular pipeline reduces relative translation error by 78.7% (0.1335 to 0.0285). Archived configurations and a qualitative failure case identify plausible explanations for these complementary error profiles, without isolating their causes. These findings motivate a testable hybrid design that combines direct orientation estimation with geometry-constrained translation recovery.
title: Direct Regression and Geometric Recovery for Event-based Spacecraft Pose Estimation

summary: Multi-agent systems become capable through institutional mechanisms, such as rules that route information to agents that act on it. These mechanisms are also natural places to restrict the system. Yet as agents learn, share memory, delegate, and repair failures, the collective can find other paths to the same effects: a restriction on the original mechanism still operates but no longer stops them, while routine performance and compliance checks pass. We propose \textbf{Reversible Multi-agent Systems} as a research agenda: collectives that grow while an authorized supervisor can still restrict specified effects, keep them restricted as agents adapt, and reconstitute useful cooperation under renewed authority. What is reversed is the ability to produce a specified effect; restrictions must hold even if learned knowledge persists. The goal is to preserve effective intervention, not a particular mechanism: at every step of growth, some authorized intervention must keep a specified prohibited effect rare while maintaining required service. We identify three research problems: tracking what capabilities depend on, handing off control before an old mechanism loses its effect, and separating legitimate repair from unauthorized reconstruction. We outline how to evaluate control across growth paths, back control claims with evidence, and allocate the rights to restrict and restore.
title: From Emergence to Reversibility: Toward Reversible Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

summary: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support commonly focus on the clinical appropriateness of individual responses, potentially overlooking failures that emerge across extended interactions. As AI assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances and prior disclosures, this raises an accountability question: Do AI chatbots provide appropriate support as users' needs evolve? We investigate by analyzing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, examining how a memory-equipped assistant responds to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles. We introduce the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, to assess the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. Advice was less aligned with users' readiness after a crisis than in matched control stretches of the same conversation, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and users' communication style changed how often and when the assistant gave recommendations. Although explicitly unproductive advice was rare, the assistant frequently omitted clinician-expected support such as follow-up and planning for next steps. These findings show the limits of single response-level safety evaluation and the need to assess timing, omission, and consistency across users when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.
title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Evaluating Timing and Omission in Longitudinal AI Mental Health Support

summary: The reconstruction of the top-quark-pair ($t\bar{t}$) kinematics in the dilepton $t\bar{t}$ decay channel is challenging due to the presence of two undetected neutrinos. In this work, existing kinematic reconstruction methods used by the CMS Collaboration are studied using a Monte Carlo sample with $t\bar{t}$ events from CMS Open Data at a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. An improved version of the loose kinematic reconstruction, LKRv2, is developed by imposing more stringent requirements on the jet-lepton pairing entering the reconstruction. A further modification, LKRv3, exploits the kinematic similarity between the dilepton and neutrino-pair systems and improves the resolution of the reconstructed $t\bar{t}$ invariant mass relative to the baseline LKR by $7\%$, with smaller improvements for the transverse momentum and rapidity of $t\bar{t}$. In addition, two machine-learning (ML) based approaches are developed using a residual multilayer perceptron and a conditional normalizing flow. Relative to LKRv3, they improve the resolution of the invariant mass, transverse momentum and rapidity by approximately $30\%$, $20\%$ and $15\%$, respectively. In particular, a resolution of 30 GeV is achieved for the reconstructed invariant mass of $t\bar{t}$ near the production threshold. A dedicated generator-level study and a generator-to-detector transfer test demonstrate that the ML approaches learn a genuine physics-driven correction to the $ν\barν$ approximation, rather than merely exploiting detector-specific effects. These results demonstrate the strong potential of ML-based approaches for improving the reconstruction of dilepton $t\bar{t}$ events, while identifying the neutrino-pair approximation as an important limitation on the achievable resolution.
title: Kinematic Reconstruction of Top-Quark Pairs Using Analytical and Machine-Learning Methods with CMS Open Data

summary: Recommendation systems often enter a new serving window before enough outcomes are available to retrain the deployed model. We study this regime with 0.05-1.0% target feedback, a range that spans our stress tests while keeping supervision far below the degrees of freedom of the source recommender. At this scale, existing fine-tuning and meta-learning methods still estimate target-specific updates from extremely sparse feedback, leaving the update direction weakly identified. SAGE-PAIR instead transfers a source-supported residual correction space and only calibrates this space using target outcomes. We introduce SAGE-PAIR, a staged adapter that pretrains a low-dimensional global residual on an adjacent source period and adds a soft router over residual experts conditioned on source user profiles. Target feedback then calibrates this residual state rather than relearning the recommender. On a locked test split of KuaiSAR-v2, SAGE-PAIR (Full) achieves a 1.77% relative improvement in NDCG@10, while a core-protocol comparison shows a further 0.25% gain from routed experts beyond source-pretrained PAIR. Matched source-pretrained LoRA and Adapter-Tuning baselines remain near the source model, supporting the need for a different adaptation space. Thus, SAGE-PAIR improves ranking quality with millisecond-scale adaptation and inference costs. Sparse-feedback adaptation is fundamentally governed by the identifiability of the update space rather than by label count alone. Source pretraining supplies estimable correction directions for scarce labels, while user-conditioned routing contributes a consistent, differentiated cross-user correction on top of the global correction. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SAGE-PAIR-610E/.
title: SAGE-PAIR: Source-Pretrained Routed Residual Adaptation for Sparse-Feedback Recommendation

summary: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.
title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds

summary: We study time-fractional diffusion on real hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$, $n\ge2$, with Caputo order $0<α<1$. We establish global two-sided pointwise estimates for the homogeneous fundamental kernel $Z_{\mathbb H}(t,r)$ and the inhomogeneous (Duhamel) kernel $Y_{\mathbb H}(t,r)$, uniformly over all $t>0$ and positive geodesic distances $r$. By combining inverse-stable subordination with global bounds for the hyperbolic heat kernel, we distinguish a short-time local regime, a large-time interior region, and an exterior region governed by a saddle-point problem with parameter $r/t$. Both kernels have the same exterior exponential rate, while their amplitudes are related by an explicit saddle-point factor. The estimates are uniformly comparable on the interfaces between regimes, recover the Euclidean time-fractional singularities at small scales, and identify the influence of hyperbolic geometry on large-scale decay. The kernel $Z_{\mathbb H}$ also describes the one-time marginal density of hyperbolic Brownian motion under an independent inverse stable clock. This representation yields a radial limit law, moment and quantile asymptotics, and a change in the mean square displacement from order $t^α$ at small times to order $t^{2α}$ at large times.
title: Global Two-Sided Estimates for Time-Fractional Diffusion Kernels on Hyperbolic Space

summary: We establish an exact curved-background Weyl double copy for the doubly spinning Pomeransky--Sen'kov black ring. Its full Weyl tensor is a quadratic form in two source-free Maxwell fields: one generated by the stationary Killing vector, the other a flux-carrying magnetic field obtained by linearizing the dipole-ring gauge potential about its vacuum limit. The mixed Maxwell bilinear is essential: no spacetime-independent real or complex change of field basis removes it. We identify the inverse $S_{IJ}$ of the Weyl coefficient matrix as a matrix zeroth copy. The same matrix arises independently from a weighted limit of the inner products of two Killing vectors in a six-dimensional Ricci-flat parent and satisfies $\Box_g S_{IJ}=-\tfrac12 F_{I\,ab}F_J{}^{ab}$. The singly spinning limit recovers the diagonal two-field Weyl double copy of the Emparan--Reall ring.
title: The Double Copy of the Doubly Spinning Black Ring

summary: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. Existing training-free video editing methods, however, assume full offline access to the entire sequence, while streaming approaches either rely on additional training or are limited to specific editing techniques. We show that this limitation can be removed by analyzing the self-attention dynamics of DMD-distilled autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. We uncover a key asymmetry: queries and keys remain stable and aligned with their source counterparts across denoising timesteps, while values diverge and encode the evolving content. Inherited from the non-distilled bidirectional teacher, this asymmetry is strongest at high noise, where few-step streaming models operate. The resulting mechanism is simple: a single forward pass suffices to capture source identity in the value features, which can be reused throughout generation. Starting from pure Gaussian noise and injecting only these source values reconstructs the input with fidelity matching or surpassing inversion-based methods, effectively eliminating inversion. Based on this insight, we introduce AR-Edit, a training-free, inversion-free method that caches source values once and selectively injects them during denoising. Across multiple AR backbones, AR-Edit enables real-time streaming editing with superior source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.
title: AR-Edit: Training-Free Autoregressive Video Editing without Inversion

summary: We consider Box-Cox transformations of correlation matrices, $Φ_α(C)=\mathrm{vecl}\{(C^α-I)/α\}$, with Jacobian $J_α$. The family nests the raw correlations at $α=1$, the generalised Fisher transformation (GFT), $C\mapsto\mathrm{vecl}(\log C)$, at $α=0$, and the negated off-diagonal concentration coordinates at $α=-1$. The inverse problem is a strictly convex program for every $α$, so every member is injective. The map is onto $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d=n(n-1)/2$, if and only if $α\le0$, such that $α=0$ defines the boundary for unrestricted parametrizations. For $α>0$ the image is bounded. The conditioning obeys the bound $κ(J_α)\leκ(C)^{|1-α|}$, where $κ(C)=λ_{\max}(C)/λ_{\min}(C)$, and on the surjective range the exponent is smallest at $α=0$. Under Gaussian sampling with $n\geq3$, the asymptotic covariance of the transformed sample correlations is the identity at independence for every member, but only $α=0$ retains the identity to first order in the correlations, whereas the leading joint third cumulant at independence vanishes only at $α=1/3$. Finally, applying the transformation to the diagonal rescaling of $C$ that makes the result hollow adds a new family to the existing correlation parametrizations. For every $α$ the rescaling solves a strictly convex problem and the inverse is explicit, and the scaled coordinates are unrestricted exactly when $α=0$, where they recover the known global normal coordinates, centred at independence, for the efficient information metric of the correlations.
title: Box-Cox Transformations of Correlation Matrices

summary: Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$. Recently, Fiat-Naor's solution to this problem has seen significant traction in theoretical computer science, and allowed for several conjectures related to meta-complexity and the 3SUM problem to be broken. In this paper, we consider the natural extension of the function inversion problem that we call preimage reporting. Here, instead of having to report only one $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$, the whole set $f^{-1}(y)$ must be found. We present a new general method to convert any arbitrary function inversion scheme into an efficient corresponding preimage reporting scheme. In particular, if $Δ$ is the maximal indegree of $f$, we show that we can perform preimage reporting using space $S$ in time $T$ for any $T$ and $S$ satisfying $TS^2=N^2 Δ$, matching a variant of a tradeoff obtained by Fiat and Naor for function inversion. This last result implies an improvement over the corresponding function inversion scheme itself, which constitutes the first function inversion scheme whose query time is inversely proportional to $|f^{-1}(y)|$. We derive new simple solutions for the $k$SUM-indexing with reporting and Jumbled indexing with reporting problems.
title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting

summary: We study a Bayesian inverse problem in EUV reflectometry, where optical constants and layer thicknesses are inferred from angle- and wavelength-resolved reflection measurements. The physical process is modeled and evaluated using an efficient forward model based on the transfer matrix method. As an alternative to computationally expensive sampling-based inference, we employ an Eulerian, entropically regularized Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler divergence via proximal steps in the Wasserstein space. Using the Benamou--Brenier dynamic formulation and a Hopf-Cole transform, each JKO step is reformulated as a pair of heat equations coupled only through their initial and terminal conditions, enabling an efficient fixed-point solver. The resulting high-dimensional densities are discretized on tensor-product grids and represented in tensor-train format, exploiting Kronecker structure for scalable computation. Preconditioning based on estimated posterior moments further improves tractability. We test the method with numerical experiments on EUV reflectometry data for a ruthenium--silicon ($\ce{Ru}$ on $\ce{Si}$) specimen and compare the learned tensor-train posterior to ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) reference samples. We demonstrate a use case in which we are able to reuse the tensor-train posterior to obtain samples for shifted target distributions with less computational effort than a comparable MCMC method.
title: Bayesian Inverse Problems for EUV reflectometry with regularized JKO scheme

summary: Local response measurements track how perturbations spread in quantum simulators and nonequilibrium many-body systems. Locality bounds constrain the propagation speed, but do not determine whether the response can distinguish computational outcomes at fixed measurement precision as the distance increases. Here we construct time-independent dynamics with bounded nearest-neighbor interactions in which a fixed single-site detector responds to a remote bond phase after a time proportional to their separation. The susceptibility has a positive lower bound independent of distance. With product-state preparations, estimating this susceptibility to constant additive accuracy is complete for bounded-error quantum polynomial time (BQP), with a decision gap independent of distance. Two source-phase settings give the susceptibility with a distance-independent shot count at fixed accuracy and confidence. Inverse-polynomially weak local couplings between the computational register and the chain carrying the excitation preserve the gap. The leading correction vanishes when exchanging the two internal states of the excitation reverses the interaction. Varying the source and observation time makes all bond phases locally identifiable near the zero-phase reference setting. We also prove a conditional quantum advantage for distribution-free response prediction.
title: BQP-Complete Susceptibilities Observable at Ballistic Times in Local Quantum Dynamics

summary: In this article, we use the PBNF-transform, or Polynomial Boolean Normal Form, described in the two earlier articles and now extended to higher arity, to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT), which are part of the P versus NP problem. SAT consists of a conjunction of clauses, and in our SAT-solving models, we dualize the logical equations by inverting the problem: we multiply letters (literals) in the transferred clauses and use a binary iterated composition based on adding polynomials for the conjunctions in our solution formula. We obtain Polynomial Boolean Equations, PBE=0, by also renaming the truth value T=0. With reversed literal repetition, we get the CNF as the sum of the transformed clauses. In fact, we can always reduce to multiplication in and addition out of clauses, as we do not look for the entire kernel of PBE for a YES instance for SAT.
title: SAT Solving by Multiplication in and Addition out of Clauses

summary: Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.
title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming

summary: The natural environments habitable to life are inseparable from dissipative and entropic forces, which mandate active matter to operate on constant fluxes of energy and momentum to survive and propagate through spacetime. In contrast to fundamental particles which are characterized by energy and momentum, we postulate that energy expenditure rate and momentum generation rate are the fundamental dynamical quantities driving this evolution of swimming active matter and accordingly construct the corresponding Lagrangian and Hamiltonian of motion of the active matter. Furthermore, living systems broadly employ periodic, non-repeating motion for both locomotion and various biological functions, with meaningful information stored in the periods of these functions. Consequently, analyzing these dynamics in the Fourier space lands us at the familiar tools of the operator based, quantum mechanics. This is accomplished by introducing a complex field to describe the evolving probability distribution of a single unit, as well as the population density of mutually non-interacting active particles under the constraint of scarce resources. The resulting single-unit wavefunction evolves analogously to the Dirac equation with minimal coupling, wherein gauge symmetry reflects the generality of the governing equations across arbitrary resource landscapes. Additionally, we present a Schrödinger-like equation where the effective potential term represents the environmentally mandated, non-motile base metabolic rate. Finally, we formalize the bidirectional coupling between active swimmers and the surrounding fluid via a multipole expansion of the active force with an emphasis on force monopoles and dipoles, where each pole corresponds to a distinct mode of active motility.
title: A Quantum Mechanical Description of Active Matter

summary: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and schedule
title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part IV : Two Independent Checks and Endpoint-Side Reconstruction to Prevent Tool Misuse, Memory Poisoning, Unauthorized Delegation and Unlawful Data Use — Supporting EU AI Act Record-Keeping, Human Oversight and Cybersecurity, GDPR Purpose Limitation and DORA

summary: Current research in the food industry highlights the importance of alternative protein sources in the context of global population growth and the need to reduce the negative impact of raising animals, producing animal proteins, on the environment. Plant proteins represent a sustainable, affordable and beneficial option for health, with high potential to replace animal proteins in the food industry. Plant sources rich in protein include legumes, cereals, pseudocereals, oilseeds, green leaves, algae and, more recently, insects. They differ considerably in protein content and amino acid profile, and their strategic combination can ensure a balanced intake of essential nutrients. Legumes offer high protein content, but are deficient in sulfur amino acids. Cereals, although lower in protein, bring technological benefits and can complement the amino acids missing from legumes. Pseudocereals have a higher nutritional value than conventional cereals, while green leaves and algae offer a high proteins intake and compounds with antioxidant potential, although they require advanced technologies to overcome extraction limitations. Extraction methods play a decisive role in the yield and quality of plant proteins. Conventional techniques are efficient but can cause denaturation and provide low yields. On the other hand, emerging methods allow the recovery of proteins in larger quantities, preserving their functional and technological properties.
title: Plant-based proteins: sources, extraction methods and functional perspectives for the sustainable food industry

summary: Simultaneous tolerance certification asks whether every component of a dense latent vector lies within its prescribed range. This preprint studies noisy unit-norm linear measurements under pathwise resource budgets, with tolerances calibrated to a fixed prior membership probability. For independent Gaussian priors, every fixed linear channel is uniformly asymptotically equivalent, for the membership decision, to a coordinate-precision design at no greater total precision. A marked Poisson limit characterizes the complete family of feasible limiting experiments. The resulting allocation theory gives exact Brier-optimal designs and proves that every classification-optimal allocation has zero plus at most one positive normalized precision level. The global classification problem therefore reduces to a one-dimensional coverage choice. At low budgets, no allocation is most informative for every decision loss. At fixed row precision, adaptive screening yields a squared-logarithmic reduction in the order of measurements required for prescribed positive decision gain. For classification, sharp high-accuracy constants distinguish the inverse-square risk dependence of fixed designs from the logarithmic dependence of adaptive acquisition. Bounded-spectrum Gaussian dependence preserves the fixed-design frontier. Matching resource orders extend to exponential-power priors, including Laplace and lighter tails. A frozen Gaussian simulation, combined with certified deterministic bounds, establishes a finite-dimensional advantage over all fixed linear designs under the same affine acquisition budget, with one-sided 95% Monte Carlo confidence. This record contains the preprint, proof supplement, editable LaTeX sources, and a reproducibility archive with programs, experimental protocols, and saved results. The manuscript and proof supplement are licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0; original software is licensed under MIT. Third-party components retain their own licenses.
title: Simultaneous Tolerance Certification: Limit Experiments and Sharp Resource Laws

summary: Resilience in psychology and public health is usually assessed through recovery or maintained functioning, outcomes that do not reveal whether desirable states have become self-maintaining or still depend on external support. Drawing on coerced-regime theory from social-ecological systems research, we develop aided mental health resilience (AMHR), a framework for desirable mental health states established or maintained through external inputs of resources, organisation, political capital and trust. We make three contributions. First, we frame population mental health as a dimension of social-ecological system states and define the external maintenance subsidy required to sustain desirable conditions. Second, using a dialectical reading of regime change, we distinguish reversion, permanent subsidy and sublation, in which the function initially supplied by aid becomes reproduced through reorganised capacities, practices or institutions. Displacement of harm is treated as a cross-cutting failure mode. Four cases illustrate these dynamics and their limits. Third, drawing on strange loop ethics, we argue that paradoxical outcomes should trigger review not only of intervention instruments but also of the premises that define desirable states and authorise intervention. We outline disconfirmation conditions and a research agenda centred on longitudinal evaluation, subsidy accounting, displacement monitoring and recursive premise review.
title: Aided mental health resilience: governing desirable states that cannot sustain themselves
