summary: This paper develops a scale-spanning account of latent vibration and frequency manifestation within Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM). It examines the relationship between complete latent vibration, the negative and positive displacement domains around the manifestable origin, and the eligibility of positive displacement for progression towards physical manifestation. The development distinguishes the complete latent-vibration interval from the directed displacement associated with manifestation, establishing the proposed Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck threshold relationships in terms of the Planck length. The analysis further develops phase-dependent frequency relations below the Planck threshold and considers the proposed frequency increments associated with the Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck domains. It then presents a state-dependent sequence of energy–frequency transformations across latent, phase, and manifested states, including the reverse progression associated with dissolution. Within this framework, frequency and displacement are treated as related physical parameters whose coefficients depend on the corresponding phase domain. The paper also distinguishes the phase-state potential-energy mass representation from the mass contribution associated with the manifested domain. It formulates the effective-mass relationship and separates this ECM representation from the distinct dark-energy-related mass representation. Taken together, these developments present an integrated theoretical description of latent vibration, manifestation eligibility, threshold transitions, energy–frequency relations, and mass-state transformations within the proposed ECM framework.
title: Complete Latent Vibration and Frequency Manifestation Eligibility in Extended Classical Mechanics

summary: This archive contains the complete, reproducible analysis pipeline accompanying the article by Bentounsi, Achour and Boufaida, currently under review. Purpose Clinical datasets often present expert labels as if they applied a published guideline. This work proposes an audit method that (i) measures the gap between a guideline-derived reference rule base and the expert labels, (ii) attributes the disagreements to an implicit criterion (Algorithm 1), and (iii) tests whether that criterion can be reconstructed out of sample, using an explicit acceptance criterion: an agreement gain of at least 5 points over the majority baseline, the same rule selected in at least 4 of 5 folds, and a family-wise permutation p-value below 0.01. The method is applied to an Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) dataset (270 records, six labels) and replicated on the UCI Cardiotocography dataset (2,126 segments) against the FIGO 2015 guideline. Contents src/ : Python modules (thresholds and protocol constants, data loading with hash check, generated rule trace, rules–expert gap and Algorithm 1, threshold and interval enumerations with permutation tests, learning control and Shapley attribution, cardiotocography replication, robustness analyses, figures). results/ : every result file used in the manuscript (CSV, TXT, JSON). figures/ : Figures 1–5 (PDF and PNG). tests/ : pytest suite (equivalence of fast and direct enumerations, regression tests on the published tables, checks of the FIGO rule base, and a test that every key figure of the manuscript matches the recomputed results). PROTOCOL.md : analysis protocol, including Amendment 1 for the replication.  PROTOCOL2.sha256 records the hash of Protocol 2. run_all.sh , requirements.txt (pinned versions with hashes, Python 3.13). Data (not redistributed) The input datasets are not included and must be downloaded from their original sources; the code refuses to run on any other version of the files. ABPM: Douibi K, Benabid MM, Settouti N, Chikh MA. Data for: An analysis of Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) . Mendeley Data, V1, 2017. https://doi.org/10.17632/y4dh3b3tfx.1 . File ABPM-dataset.arff , SHA-256 0ea0a53c86bd2564117913fe99dd6699579fc03b23acd118c0b33822db911e07 . Cardiotocography: Campos D, Bernardes J. Cardiotocography . UCI Machine Learning Repository, 2000. https://doi.org/10.24432/C51S4N . File CTG.xls , SHA-256 d6aa62e82625e59f9d5b05bc8fc52af9ea67bdf2a23f1faca8511d5618fcb421 . Reproduction Place both files in data/raw/ , then run: python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt ./run_all.sh The script verifies the dataset hashes, runs all modules, regenerates every result file and figure, and runs the test suite (about twelve minutes on an ordinary laptop). summary: Description This record contains the data, code and source data supporting a Mendelian randomization (MR) study of smoking and obesity traits, with DNA methylation (CpG sites) and gut microbial features (species and pathways) as candidate mediators. Files Processed and formatted GWAS summary statistics (instrumental variables and outcome data) used in the analyses. Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx : sources of the original GWAS summary statistics (also listed in Table S1 of the article). Codes.zip : R code for instrument selection, two-sample MR and sensitivity analyses, mediation analysis, colocalization and the figures, with a README describing each script and the run order, software versions and R session information. Source_data.zip : source data underlying the main and supplementary figures. Fstatistic.zip : F statistics of the instrumental variables in the MR analyses. Data sources The uploaded data are processed and formatted versions of publicly available GWAS summary statistics; the original sources are listed in Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx . Ethical approval and informed consent were obtained by the original GWAS studies. Methods Instrumental variables were selected at P < 5 × 10⁻⁸ for smoking and obesity traits, P < 1 × 10⁻⁵ (effect allele frequency > 0.01) for gut microbial features, and P < 1 × 10⁻⁸ (cis, within 1 Mb) or P < 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ (trans) for methylation quantitative trait loci of CpG sites (GoDMC). Variants were clumped at r² < 0.001 within 10,000 kb windows using PLINK with the 1000 Genomes European reference panel, and instruments with F < 10 were excluded. The multiplicative random-effects inverse-variance weighted method (Wald ratio for single-SNP instruments) was used as the primary MR method. Sensitivity analyses included the fixed-effects inverse-variance weighted method, MR-Egger, weighted median, simple and weighted mode, Cochran’s Q test, the MR-Egger intercept test, MR-PRESSO and the Steiger directionality test. Reverse causation was assessed by MR in the reverse direction. Indirect associations were estimated by two-step MR using the product-of-coefficients method with delta-method standard errors. Colocalization was assessed with coloc (p1 = p2 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, p12 = 1 × 10⁻⁵) within ±1 Mb windows and with HyPrColoc for three traits (prior.1 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, prior.c = 0.02).  Acknowledgements We thank UK Biobank ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ ), GSCAN ( https://genome.psych.umn.edu/index.php/GSCAN ), the GIANT consortium ( https://giant-consortium.web.broadinstitute.org/index.php/GIANT_consortium ), GERA ( https://cg.bsc.es/gera_summary_stats/ ), GoDMC ( http://mqtldb.godmc.org.uk/about ), the Dutch Microbiome Project ( https://dutchmicrobiomeproject.molgeniscloud.org/menu/main/home ), the IEU OpenGWAS project ( https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/ ) and the GWAS Catalog ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/ ) for providing the publicly available genetic data used in this research. We acknowledge the research teams, participants and consortia behind these datasets for their commitment to open science.
title: Causal Relationships Between Smoking and Obesity Mediated by Epigenetic Modifications and Altered Gut Microbiota

summary: Urban design relies on judgments about existing and anticipated needs, while the available evidence ranges from lived experience and historical records to geospatial observation, statistical estimation, and computational simulation. Contemporary developments in geospatial artificial intelligence, agent-based modeling, urban digital twins, and computational search expand the means of inquiry while raising questions about inferential validity and methodological compatibility. This paper develops a question-guided framework for identifying and evaluating candidate urban needs through the reconstruction of spatial, temporal, social, ecological, and infrastructural relations. Two complementary inquiry pathways are distinguished: hypothesis-driven assessment of specified candidate needs and exploratory search for candidates emerging from observed or simulated relational patterns. Both pathways are connected to explicit procedures of evidential appraisal, causal examination where identifiable, participatory scrutiny, and post-intervention evaluation. A provisional formal interface is proposed in which generative–relational (GR) subjects have question-dependent spacetime-supported representations, heterogeneous evidence is linked by category-theoretic constructions, and selected event structures are encoded through algebraic-topological invariants of labeled two-complexes. Evolutionary updates of these representations and spin-foam-inspired cellular initializations are considered as exploratory modeling options, with the physical meaning of quantum-gravity spin foams kept separate from urban research. The framework is intended to guide methodological comparison and further model development; its empirical adequacy requires case-specific operationalization and validation.
title: Identifying and Evaluating Urban Needs Through Relational Reconstruction: A Preliminary Generative and Evolutionary Formal Model in an Algebraic Framework

summary: Factoring and supply chain finance (SCF) allow firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, to obtain liquidity against receivables and other trade assets, but they expose financiers to the credit risk of suppliers, buyers and their relationships. This study maps the scientific literature on credit risk management in factoring and SCF through a bibliometric analysis. A Scopus search conducted on 12 October 2026 and screening following the PRISMA 2020 flow yielded 288 articles and reviews published between 1995 and 2025. Performance analysis was combined with science mapping in VOSviewer, including keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship and co-citation analyses of references and sources. The results show that the field has grown rapidly since 2019, with 87.2% of the documents published in 2019–2025. China dominates research output, while studies from the United Kingdom, the United States and Italy attain higher normalised impact, and operations management and operational research journals are the main publication venues. Three research streams are identified: analytical operations–finance models of risk allocation in capital-constrained supply chains, conceptual and empirical research on SCF adoption and reverse factoring, and machine learning-based credit risk assessment of SMEs. Research attention has shifted from traditional factoring and receivables financing towards SCF, machine learning, blockchain and, most recently, artificial intelligence and sustainability. The accounting, financial reporting and internal control dimensions of these arrangements, the allocation of risk among multiple financiers, and evidence from under-represented regions emerge as the main gaps.

title: CREDIT RISK MANAGEMENT IN FACTORING AND SUPPLY CHAIN FINANCE: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF SCIENTIFIC PUBLICATIONS

summary: arXiv:2109.12244 is the preprint of this work. This record holds the revised paper, the data of its figures and tables, and the fitted profile parameters. Major findings If a halo grows self-similarly, with mass and radius both proportional to time at fixed concentration c, mass conservation fixes the mean radial velocity inside it for any density profile: outward in the core and inward beyond about twice the scale radius. For an NFW halo the net radial momentum vanishes at c 0 = 3.48. Growth adds surface and kinetic terms to the virial balance. At c 0 they give an effective virial exponent n e = −1.42 instead of −1. A halo radius that grows by random accretion events follows geometric Brownian motion. For a simple osmotic flow the particle Fokker–Planck solution is a generalized gamma profile that contains the Einasto profile as a special case. Tested on composite haloes (all haloes with the same particle number, 4–6326 particles) of a 256 3 SCDM simulation, the generalized gamma profile fits the cumulative mass profiles with a median rms residual of 0.006 dex and a r /b r = 1.41 ± 0.05; the flat inner part lies within about one softening length. The measured mean radial velocity is inward at all resolved radii, between −0.39 H r and −1.24 H r, where self-similar growth predicts about +0.53 H r at the scale radius. The radial velocity dispersion exceeds the isotropic Jeans value by 1.11–1.90 times. Self-similar growth describes the profile shapes, but not the instantaneous kinematics, of these haloes. Contents. P21_revised.pdf (the paper) and csv/ (15 files: the data of Figs 2–9, Fig. A1 and the composite-halo fit tables). The dark matter flow statistics of the simulation are in 10.5281/zenodo.6541231 (Part I), 10.5281/zenodo.6757654 (Part II) and 10.5281/zenodo.6586213 (full dataset).
title: Inverse mass cascade in dark matter flow and effects on halo deformation, energy, size, and density profiles

summary: Manuscript and CSV data behind the figures and tables of Xu (2026), Inverse energy cascade in self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow and effects of halo shape , arXiv:2110.13885 . The earlier data record of this work is zenodo.org/records/6640331 . Contents: the manuscript (P17_revised.pdf) and the folder csv/ with the data plotted in the figures and tables of the paper: subsystem energies, flux functions of the specific energies, halo-group energies and coherent motion, virial ratios and halo shapes at z = 0. The statistics of the simulation are in the dark matter flow datasets, doi:10.5281/zenodo.6541231 and doi:10.5281/zenodo.6757654 , and the full dataset is doi:10.5281/zenodo.6586213 . Major findings (Einstein–de Sitter simulation of 256³ particles): The flux of any specific quantity V through the halo mass scale is ε V = −(μ + λ V − s) M h H⟨V⟩, where M h ∝ a μ is the mass in haloes, ⟨V⟩ ∝ a λ V its mass-weighted mean and s the growth exponent of V in haloes of fixed mass; with the measured exponents it reproduces every energy flux to within 2 per cent at z < 2. Kinetic energy, both of the motion of haloes and of the motion inside them, is carried to larger haloes (inverse cascade), while the inter- and intra-halo potential energies are carried to smaller haloes (direct cascade); the fluxes are independent of halo mass for haloes of up to a few hundred particles, only at z ≤ 0.3. The steady state of the cascade picture, in which M h ∝ a 1/2 and the energies grow as a 3/2 , is not reached by z = 0: M h grows as a 1/2 only near z = 0 (local exponent 0.47), and the total kinetic and potential energies grow as a 1.13 and a 1.19 at z ≈ 0. The simplest steady-state exponents fail for the inter-halo potential and for the radial kinetic energy of the haloes, so the measured exponents are needed in the flux formula. Haloes are elongated, with r λ3 /r λ1 ≈ 2–3, but their moment of inertia exceeds that of a sphere of equal volume only by a median factor 1.60 (1,674,583 haloes at z = 0). The spin axis lies within 30° of the plane perpendicular to the major axis for 70 per cent of haloes with n p ≥ 20 (isotropic: 50 per cent). Shape change therefore cannot drive the energy cascade; mass accretion does.
title: Inverse energy cascade in self-gravitating collisionless dark matter flow and effects of halo shape

summary: Changing an objective does not automatically revise agents' earlier plans or delegated tasks. Acknowledgment can coexist with obsolete execution, while misleading instructions can redirect work or discard retained constraints. We present a Strategic World simulation testbed that separates authoritative objectives, local plans, notice receipt, and consequential action. Six intervention families vary objectives, conditions, authority, membership, and communication. Matched protocols and deadlines establish feasibility for the tested disturbances. Controlled trajectories demonstrate that identical completion and acknowledgment summaries can conceal uninformed obsolete work, obsolete work after receipt, or blocked unsafe intent. Local language-model trials and instructed action probes reveal competence limits that constrain interpretation of dynamic failures. A further 16-episode comparison evaluates an engineered guard that prioritizes pending notice submissions over local work. It completes 4/4 held-out settings, compared with 1/4 for a calibrated assisted baseline. Each episode contains one large language model actor and two fixed peers. These results establish diagnostic distinctions and bounded policy feasibility under explicit simulation assumptions; they do not establish frontier-model reliability or autonomous team adaptation.
title: When the Plan Changes: A Strategic World Testbed for Dynamic Multi-Agent Coordination

summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems solve complex tasks through collaboration, but their growing, simultaneously resident key-value (KV) caches create a memory bottleneck. Applying single-model quantization policies independently ignores differences in agents' precision needs, potentially degrading collective reasoning. We introduce Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization (CoMixKV), which combines online sensitivity estimation with joint agent-layer bit-width allocation under a shared memory budget. To our knowledge, CoMixKV is the first mixed-precision KV-cache quantization framework to jointly allocate precision across simultaneously resident agent caches under such a budget. The estimator derives sensitivity from a local attention-error bound using recent queries, keys, and values, without calibration data, trial quantization, or additional model passes. A shared controller combines these scores with remaining quantizable capacity and byte-level storage costs to minimize total estimated error. Allocations are refreshed as agents start or finish and new observations become available. Selected widths apply only to newly quantized blocks; recent states retain native precision and previously quantized blocks remain unchanged. Across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones at average 2-bit, 3-bit, and 4-bit settings, CoMixKV achieves strong accuracy against the evaluated quantization baselines. At the average 3-bit setting on Gemma-4-31B-it, it achieves 68.35% average accuracy, exceeding the strongest quantized baseline by 0.59%. On Qwen3-32B, it reduces peak KV-cache memory by 32.08% and achieves a 1.38x inference speedup over FullKV.
title: Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization for Efficient LLM-based Multi-agent Systems

summary: Local-first security tools let organizations analyze code without sending it to third-party services, but the small language models they can run locally are weaker than hosted ones and are hard to improve without breaching the privacy guarantee that motivates them. We present Tantular Cyber, an open-source, read-only repository security analyzer that keeps deterministic scanner findings authoritative and confines a locally served language model to advisory explanations in Bahasa Indonesia. We report its measured v0.3.0 baseline on a synthetic, ground-truth benchmark: combining Semgrep with an interprocedural call-graph scanner yields precision 0.843 and recall 0.915 (Semgrep alone: 0.818 and 0.766). The advisory layer is the weak point: 57% of explanations met an evidence-grounding check, against 95% for a different 8B model under identical prompts. A forensic re-scoring of retained outputs shows that every grounding failure cites a code identifier absent from the evidence shown, and that a prompt change which appeared to raise grounding from 0.56 to 0.72 did so partly by citing nothing. We document two evaluation-validity hazards we encountered: silent model-file migration during a run and non-reproducible published figures. Building on these lessons and on constraint-aware evaluation from security operations research, we propose a governed self-improvement loop (code-free feedback, curated data, a cheapest-first intervention ladder from prompts to LoRA and weight-space edits, hard gates, and human release approval) and preregister the protocol by which its first cycle will be judged. We report no results for the loop itself.

summary: Visuomotor policies can handle many robot manipulation tasks, but understanding their failures remains difficult. Unfamiliar conditions and small action errors can lead to failure, yet watching the robot alone tells us little about what went wrong inside the policy. We introduce MIND (Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Diagnosis), a method that looks inside a trained policy to detect failures during execution and identify the internal concepts involved. MIND uses a sparse autoencoder to break down the policy's internal activations into features that can be studied individually. We give meaning to these features by linking their activity to the robot's position, movement, and surroundings, and by steering their activations to examine how they affect the robot's actions. From successful and failed executions, we learn how the features behave on the way to a failure. During execution, MIND flags deviations from these patterns and uses the meaningful features contributing most to the change to describe the problem. Experiments in simulation and on a physical robot show that changes in these internal features help detect and explain failures. By using the same features for detection and diagnosis, MIND connects failure signals to understandable changes inside the policy.
title: Detecting and Explaining Robot Policy Failures from Sparse Internal Features

summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are an important tool for fMRI prediction, where empirical functional connectivity matrices serve both as features and for graph construction. However, recent studies and our own experiments show that these methods often fail to outperform simpler graph-agnostic baselines. We propose a statistical explanation for this failure by formulating connectome prediction as an errors-in-variables (EIV) problem: the true connectome is latent, while the observed covariance matrix is a noisy finite-time-series estimate. In a linear asymptotic setting, we decompose the effect of graph convolution into three mechanisms: smoothing-induced bias and variance reduction, graph estimation error, and a double-dipping effect arising when the same noisy matrix determines both graph and features. Under a latent community model adapted to neuroscience, we identify a narrow favorable regime, set by the brain community structure, the predictive signal, the graph construction and the recording length, in which message passing can improve prediction. Simulations validate this decomposition, while real-data experiments illustrate that connectome GNN pipelines often fall outside this regime. Our results provide a first step towards explaining when graph convolutions can help brain connectome prediction, and why they often do not.
title: Bias, Measurement Error, and Double-Dipping: When Can GNN Convolutions Help Brain Connectome Prediction?

summary: Long-term conversational question answering can require several separated dialogue turns that support an answer only together. We introduce EviCover, a retrieval approach designed to retain this complementary evidence. It converts questions into observable evidence requirements, checks requirement coverage using retrieved source identifiers, and selects turns jointly. We track annotated support sets - the benchmark-labeled dialogue turns associated with each question - through retrieval, reranking, and final answer-generation context. We evaluate the baseline memory pipeline on generated, human-verified LoCoMo conversations and human-written REALTALK conversations, and examine EviCover on REALTALK's 108 multi-hop questions. Compared with the hybrid lexical/dense baseline, support-turn recall among 60 candidate turns rises from 0.526 to 0.575, and recall in the final ten-turn context rises from 0.349 to 0.379. The evidence funnel identifies separate discovery and selection failures, while paired answer evaluation shows that greater evidence recall does not yet establish a correctness gain. This analysis locates where complementary evidence is lost and distinguishes evidence retrieval from its use in answer generation.

We track annotated support sets - the benchmark-labeled dialogue turns associated with each question - through retrieval, reranking, and final answer-generation context. We evaluate the baseline memory pipeline on generated, human-verified LoCoMo conversations and human-written REALTALK conversations, and examine EviCover on REALTALK's 108 multi-hop questions. Compared with the hybrid lexical/dense baseline, support-turn recall among 60 candidate turns rises from 0.526 to 0.575, and recall in the final ten-turn context rises from 0.349 to 0.379. The evidence funnel identifies separate discovery and selection failures, while paired answer evaluation shows that greater evidence recall does not yet establish a correctness gain. This analysis locates where complementary evidence is lost and distinguishes evidence retrieval from its use in answer generation.

Local information and normalized total correlation give the characteristic local and global lengths. summary: Reflections: BELIEF, DISBELIEF. SPIRIT and MATTER. Skrynnik Sergey Nikolaevich Republic of Kazakhstan, Almaty, science@ast-1c.kz Abstract This work is a philosophical and theoretical study aimed at building a holistic model of reality that unites the physical and subjective aspects of being. It is the original, “manifesto” part of a cycle of eleven articles; it is here that the ideas developed in the subsequent works were first formulated. The work consists of two parts. The first (“Faith, Unbelief”) examines the essence of man and the meaning of life outside the categories of good and evil: questions of immortality, of imperfection as a source of striving, of reason, of freedom of choice and of the idea of the Creator. The main conclusion of this part is that the principle of life is preserved regardless of what a person believes in. The second part (“Spirit and Matter”) draws on the physical model of the work “The Birth of Dimensions: A Formal Skeleton” and draws analogies between the physical and the spiritual: consciousness is considered as a resonant structure that cannot be reduced to matter but is inseparably connected with it. Consciousness and matter appear as different frequency manifestations of a single process, which suggests a possible way of overcoming the traditional opposition of the “spiritual” and the “material”. The structure of the observer, the connection between consciousness and the brain, the soul, attention and the role of life as the medium in which the observer develops are discussed. The work is interdisciplinary and hypothetical in character and is open to critical analysis. Revision dated 2026-11-10: A chapter “Esotericism and Psychology: The Search for Balance” has been added after the chapter “Man and Woman: The Family as a Structure” — an analysis based on the author’s own example. Esotericism and psychology often describe the same things in different languages, and BD can serve as a bridge between the approaches from the side of spirit and from the side of matter. Esotericists can suggest the direction of development, but understanding what they say often comes after the fact, through experience, which is not a failure but the very process of development. From any source the author keeps only what withstands analysis and looks like a manifestation of balance. The chapter “Man and Woman” now notes that the roles of man and woman can intertwine: a woman can be a muse, and a man the one who gives birth to an idea or a work.       Размышления: ВЕРА, НЕВЕРИЕ. Она является исходной, «манифестной» частью цикла из одиннадцати статей; именно здесь впервые сформулированы идеи, развитые в последующих работах. Работа состоит из двух частей. В первой («Вера, неверие») рассматриваются суть человека и смысл жизни вне категорий добра и зла: вопросы бессмертия, несовершенства как источника стремления, разума, свободы выбора и идеи Создателя. Основной вывод части — принцип жизни сохраняется независимо от того, во что верит человек. Вторая часть («Дух и материя») опирается на физическую модель работы «Рождение измерений: формальный скелет» и проводит аналогии между физическим и духовным: сознание рассматривается как резонансная структура, не сводимая к материи, но неразрывно связанная с ней. It is the original, “manifesto” part of a cycle of eleven articles; it is here that the ideas developed in the subsequent works were first formulated. The work consists of two parts. The first (“Faith, Unbelief”) examines the essence of man and the meaning of life outside the categories of good and evil: questions of immortality, of imperfection as a source of striving, of reason, of freedom of choice and of the idea of the Creator. The main conclusion of this part is that the principle of life is preserved regardless of what a person believes in. The second part (“Spirit and Matter”) draws on the physical model of the work “The Birth of Dimensions: A Formal Skeleton” and draws analogies between the physical and the spiritual: consciousness is considered as a resonant structure that cannot be reduced to matter but is inseparably connected with it. Consciousness and matter appear as different frequency manifestations of a single process, which suggests a possible way of overcoming the traditional opposition of the “spiritual” and the “material”. The structure of the observer, the connection between consciousness and the brain, the soul, attention and the role of life as the medium in which the observer develops are discussed. The work is interdisciplinary and hypothetical in character and is open to critical analysis. summary: This record provides supporting numerical data and code for the study "Entry, reciprocity, and severity in self-consistent wrong-motion optical flow." The study investigates a known optical-flow failure in which mutually consistent forward and backward estimates can correspond to an incorrect motion layer. Using controlled two-layer translations, it separately evaluates appearance-dependent alternate-side assignment, reciprocal wrong-motion consistency, and conditional error severity under near alternate-layer substitution. The supporting materials include source-level and pair-level numerical tables, plotted data, representative example arrays, figure-generation scripts, frozen experimental specifications, selected generator and evaluation code, verification scripts, and SHA-256 references to archived experimental results. The experiments use pretrained RAFT-Small, RAFT-Large, and GMFlow with STL-10 and BSDS500 image appearances. Reproducibility scope: The deposited materials support figure regeneration and examination of reported numerical summaries. Complete model prediction archives, original image archives, pretrained model checkpoints, and a complete inference environment are not included. Full prediction-to-metric verification requires the separately identified experimental archives. Original third-party image datasets remain subject to their respective providers' terms. No nuclear-decommissioning footage is included. File access is restricted pending review of publication rights and licensing.

summary: LLM-based agents extend LLMs with tool calls, memory, planning, and retrieval to act in external environments, but they are vulnerable to attacks at different workflow steps. Existing defenses, including prompt engineering and post-training alignment, primarily improve LLM-only safety and often overlook risks that arise from multi-step execution. External verification adds guardrails to check each step separately, but it typically ignores how risks can propagate across steps. We argue that we should consider risk transitions across dependent steps through the agent workflow, rather than separate verification on a single step. summary: We study group-conditional conformal risk control (CRC) for disjoint and overlapping groups under bounded monotone losses. For disjoint groups, we establish exact finite-sample conditional risk control, two-sided bounds on the group-restricted risk, and fundamental limitations arising from local support and calibration-rank granularity. For overlapping groups, we study two exactly valid approaches: group-restricted calibration followed by union deployment, and direct calibration of the deployed prediction-set family. We characterize the union's limiting reconciliation gap, identify conditions for its disappearance, and establish sharp lower bounds for structured losses in specified product-form models. We also demonstrate a strict size advantage for direct calibration in an ordinal model. Experiments show that direct calibration can reduce prediction-set size, but its efficiency depends on group structure, loss type, and shape fitting. Results on historical diabetic-retinopathy scores further illustrate these tradeoffs. Overall, local support, reconciliation slack, and threshold heterogeneity determine efficiency, with neither approach uniformly dominating.
title: Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control: Exact Guarantees, Limits, and Overlapping Extensions

summary: Information-flow control (IFC) is a promising approach to enforce policy in agentic AI systems. However, IFC suffers from label creep, a phenomenon where monotonically increasing security labels propagate through a system and progressively limit its utility. Label creep in agentic AI systems can be mitigated using two major strategies: (1) improved system design and (2) label declassification. In this paper, we characterize how far system design alone can mitigate label creep in agentic systems. Specifically, we measure how system topology, scale, and agent composition affect utility loss and security enforcement cost proxies for conservative IFC enforcement in a stateful agentic system simulator. We develop a pipeline to systematically vary these features and measure their impacts on label propagation. Our results demonstrate strong associations between structural graph features and our IFC utility loss metric (up to a Spearman correlation $|ρ|$ of $0.96$) and show that system size and tool allocation substantially affect how labels propagate. These findings identify design choices to reduce IFC utility loss, but they also demonstrate that system design alone cannot fully prevent utility loss due to monotonic label propagation. This motivates the development of label declassification mechanisms that aid these design choices and diminish IFC utility cost.
title: The Limits of Information-Flow Control Enforcement for Agentic Systems

summary: Supervised fine-tuning over a large pool of heterogeneous tasks is often computationally expensive, leading practitioners to train language models on a fixed training budget of carefully chosen SFT tasks. Thus, achieving strong downstream performance hinges on selecting an effective subset of tasks, or equivalently, identifying an optimal task mixture under a fixed budget constraint. In practice, supervised finetuning mixtures are often determined using simple heuristics (e.g., uniform or size-proportional sampling) that ignore task interactions, which can hurt transfer and waste budget on redundant task sources. We introduce TASKMIXPGM, a framework for learning continuous task mixtures through energy-based modelling over SFT tasks. Each task forms a node in a Markov random field, with unary potentials capturing task utility and pairwise potentials modelling inter-task relationships via behavioral divergences between predictive distributions of single-task fine-tuned models. Optimizing this objective yields task mixtures that balance utility, coverage, and redundancy. We further show that the induced set function defined over the set of such tasks is weakly submodular under budget constraints, enabling approximation guarantees for discrete task selection. Empirically, we provide a fixed, benchmark-independent mixture that improves over heuristic mixing across multiple model families and different training budgets. TASKMIXPGM also uncovers interpretable structure in task interactions, revealing complementarities and redundancies that inform effective SFT mixtures.
title: From Task Affinities to Optimal Allocations: Probabilistic Graphical Modelling for Supervised Finetuning

summary: Supervised fine-tuning over a large pool of heterogeneous tasks is often computationally expensive, leading practitioners to train language models on a fixed training budget of carefully chosen SFT tasks. Thus, achieving strong downstream performance hinges on selecting an effective subset of tasks, or equivalently, identifying an optimal task mixture under a fixed budget constraint. In practice, supervised finetuning mixtures are often determined using simple heuristics (e.g., uniform or size-proportional sampling) that ignore task interactions, which can hurt transfer and waste budget on redundant task sources. We further show that the induced set function defined over the set of such tasks is weakly submodular under budget constraints, enabling approximation guarantees for discrete task selection. Empirically, we provide a fixed, benchmark-independent mixture that improves over heuristic mixing across multiple model families and different training budgets. TASKMIXPGM also uncovers interpretable structure in task interactions, revealing complementarities and redundancies that inform effective SFT mixtures.

summary: Wildland urban interface (WUI) fires increasingly threaten communities and infrastructure, motivating the need for rapid visual assessment. Recent research has focused primarily on detecting fire and assessing post-event damage. However, structure-level fire threat identification during active WUI fire events remains underexplored. This study evaluates Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct for this active-fire decision using two separately scored tracks: 1,824 synthetic images from 491 designed WUI scenarios and 45 frames from a controlled-burn experiment conducted in collaboration with Columbus Fire & EMS Department. Under zero-shot prompting, the model returned valid target fields for 1,808 synthetic images and 39 controlled-burn frames. Accuracy among valid outputs was 94.0% for the synthetic track and 69.2% for the controlled-burn track, compared with a 16.0% random-selection baseline for the latter. On the synthetic track, the model generally identified the intended target across varied designed WUI scenarios when the relevant fire-spread cues were visually distinct. Controlled-burn performance was well above random selection, but errors showed difficulty interpreting spatial relations in complex scenes. The dual-track protocol provides scalable stress testing in designed scenarios and a controlled-burn reference for assessing model behavior under physical fire conditions. Future work can use the synthetic data for VLM post-training and then evaluate the adapted models on larger and more diverse real WUI fire datasets.

summary: Widely used dimensionality reduction methods prioritize neighborhood or distance 1 preservation, yet planar coordinates alone cannot certify the homological type or 2 sample-level support of higher-order structures. Obtaining this evidence directly 3 is costly because simplicial complexes grow rapidly with dimension. We propose 4 Certified Homology-Aware Reverse-scale Mapping (CHARM), which combines 5 two-dimensional coordinates with certified homology records and sample-level 6 localization. Diffusion coordinates guide cover proposals; safe contractions and a 7 Cover Quotient Tower reduce the domain of structural computation; exact algebra 8 certifies and tracks homology representatives; and reverse-scale layout places their 9 supports in shared coordinates. Safe contraction preserves the homotopy type of 10 the input flag complex. The quotient tower is multiplicatively 3-interleaved with 11 the coarse-graph hop-distance Rips filtration. Verifiable distance-distortion bounds 12 give an additive guarantee between the original Euclidean and coarse-graph Rips 13 filtrations, and composite multiplicative guarantees for the tower on positive scales. 14 Across 22 datasets and 41,637 samples under a fixed configuration, CHARM 15 ranks among the top two on all 15 sample-weighted metrics for nonsynthetic data, 16 including the smallest values on all four Euclidean persistence-diagram distances. 17 It also provides 957 traceable support records across the full benchmark. On a 18 spherical shell, one certified H2 record identifies 1,578 original samples in the 19 two-dimensional view. CHARM thus combines geometric exploration with explicit 20 evidence of homological type and location.

summary: Transparent-interface reconstruction must recover glass surfaces even when most observed color comes from the scene behind them. We present ClearForm, a shared-planar-Gaussian method for jointly reconstructing transparent interfaces and the appearance seen through them. We identify and analyze the Geometry-Appearance Compositing Dilemma (GACD): when the same transparency-dependent alpha controls both color and geometry, revealing the background can weaken a transparent surface's contribution to geometric reconstruction. We derive its effect on plane-based depth estimation, identify a mechanism that can weaken geometric learning, and quantify the loss of interface support through controlled comparisons. To address this conflict, we develop geometry-preserving dual-opacity surface reconstruction. Shared planar Gaussians retain interface contributions in geometry compositing while modeling transmission and sparse reflection in RGB, supported by transparency-aware geometric constraints. To manage the different primitive-visibility requirements of these compositors, we introduce Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL), which retains Gaussians supported by multi-view geometry or RGB reconstruction evidence. On 3D-FRONT-T, ClearForm achieves 27.05 mm Chamfer distance (CD) and 0.928 F1, compared with 59.18 mm CD for our PGSR reproduction and the reported 34 mm CD and 0.836 F1 for GLINT. On TransLab, it achieves 1.65 mm CD, 0.963 F1, and 40.14 dB PSNR. In matched ablations, dual-opacity compositing reduces CD from 59.25 to 27.09 mm, while DEL improves PSNR by 2.06 dB. Our project page is available at https://hajeongx.github.io/clearform/.
title: ClearForm: Shared-Surface Gaussian Splatting for Transparent and Opaque Scenes

summary: Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition (OV-MLR) aims to identify all queried semantic concepts present in an image. Existing methods mainly improve global image-text matching or text-side representations, leaving local prediction largely under-explored. In this paper, we revisit local prediction and reveal that it can serve as a strong discriminative branch once two properties are properly handled: spatial consistency of local visual features and compatibility-aware local competition. This perspective is motivated by local semantic sparsity: each image region is related to only a small subset of queried concepts, while compatible concepts of different granularities or types may still coexist locally. We instantiate this perspective with LoCo, a selective Local Competition framework for OV-MLR. LoCo adopts a spatially consistent visual encoder to reduce local feature entanglement, and introduces Selective Softmax to impose competition only among locally incompatible categories while preserving compatible responses. Multi-scale inference further improves local prediction at different scales. LoCo can also be ensembled with an existing global predictor to provide complementary image-level context. Experiments on four multi-label benchmarks show that standalone LoCo improves average F1-score and mAP over TagCLIP by 3.4% and 3.8%, respectively. LoCo + DualPrompt achieves the highest averages among the compared methods, with gains of 4.8% and 5.2% over TagCLIP. Our results suggest that local semantic sparsity offers a useful basis for developing more discriminative open-vocabulary multi-label recognition methods. The code is available at https://github.com/lee-plus-plus/LoCo.

summary: Estimating long-term treatment effects is essential in regulatory and healthcare decision-making, yet the limited follow-up duration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) poses a significant challenge. Open-label extension studies attempt to capture additional information for treated subjects, but there is often significant systematic censoring and selection bias due to placebo crossover. While supplementing RCTs with real-world evidence is a common strategy, existing methods often rely on restrictive exchangeability assumptions that fail under latent confounding. We propose a novel proximal framework to integrate real-world evidence into an RCT with an open-label extension to estimate the long-term continued-control trajectory. Our approach successfully identifies long-term effects even in the presence of time-varying latent confounding effects and inter-study outcome drift. We provide a doubly robust locally efficient estimator that provides further resilience to model misspecification. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework maintains validity in complex data-generating processes where standard approaches may be biased.
title: Proximal Difference-in-Differences for Causal Learning under Confounding and Outcome Drift

summary: We conduct a retrospective exploratory pilot analysis of paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 surface plasmon resonance (SPR) trajectories, examining retained response, dual-marker fusion, and additional early-shape information. Numerical matching links the original exports to previously quality-selected data: 69 files represent 68 distinct source column pairs from 10 cancer and 10 healthy study patients. Existing exclusions and truncations are preserved. All 20 patients contribute to development and exploration; no independent validation cohort is available. Because historical per-scan manual alignment offsets are unavailable, the numerical comparisons are conditional on separately documented candidate response-transition intervals rather than verified injection-event times. Patient-level paired comparisons, leave-pair-out internal assessment, empirical false-positive budgets, and timing sensitivity are implemented in reproducible Python code. Under candidate alignment, the dual-marker retained-response sum has an apparent AUC of 0.570, with a fixed-score bootstrap 95% interval of [0.300, 0.820]. In the nested 13-patient shape subset, retention alone and the fixed 85:15 retention-shape score both have AUC 0.619; the small paired increment changes direction across the -1,0,+1 minute shift scenarios. At a same-sample budget of two false positives among ten controls, dual-marker retention identifies four cancer cases, compared with two for PD-L1 and three for Siglec-15. Analytical bounds describe feature stability under stated measurement assumptions but do not identify the cause of weak discrimination. The study provides a traceable analysis framework and operating-point hypotheses for independent evaluation; the small development cohort does not establish diagnostic utility or a reliable fusion or shape advantage.
title: An Exploratory Pilot Analysis of Paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 SPR Sensorgrams: Retained Response, Early Shape, and Complementarity

summary: We conduct a retrospective exploratory pilot analysis of paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 surface plasmon resonance (SPR) trajectories, examining retained response, dual-marker fusion, and additional early-shape information. Numerical matching links the original exports to previously quality-selected data: 69 files represent 68 distinct source column pairs from 10 cancer and 10 healthy study patients. Existing exclusions and truncations are preserved. All 20 patients contribute to development and exploration; no independent validation cohort is available. Because historical per-scan manual alignment offsets are unavailable, the numerical comparisons are conditional on separately documented candidate response-transition intervals rather than verified injection-event times. Patient-level paired comparisons, leave-pair-out internal assessment, empirical false-positive budgets, and timing sensitivity are implemented in reproducible Python code. Under candidate alignment, the dual-marker retained-response sum has an apparent AUC of 0.570, with a fixed-score bootstrap 95% interval of [0.300, 0.820]. In the nested 13-patient shape subset, retention alone and the fixed 85:15 retention-shape score both have AUC 0.619; the small paired increment changes direction across the -1,0,+1 minute shift scenarios. At a same-sample budget of two false positives among ten controls, dual-marker retention identifies four cancer cases, compared with two for PD-L1 and three for Siglec-15. Analytical bounds describe feature stability under stated measurement assumptions but do not identify the cause of weak discrimination. The study provides a traceable analysis framework and operating-point hypotheses for independent evaluation; the small development cohort does not establish diagnostic utility or a reliable fusion or shape advantage.

summary: This software archive contains R and Python scripts, cohort-specific statistical audit scripts, gene-level derived summary tables, figure source comparisons, selected graphical outputs, and integrity checks associated with a secondary analysis of 13 intercalated-disc genes in human dilated cardiomyopathy. Public inputs include GEO studies GSE141910, GSE116250, GSE249925, GSE183852, Broad Single Cell Portal SCP1303, and published left-ventricular proteomics data from Li et al. (PXD018678). The work evaluates bulk myocardial transcriptomic reproducibility, donor-level cardiomyocyte nuclear pseudobulk analyses, CellBender-versus-CellRanger count processing, matched nuclear-versus-bulk modality effects, and published proteomic evidence. Original large datasets and individual-level source matrices are not redistributed. Source-derived proteomics values are credited to Li et al.; the 2,614-protein aggregate re-tabulation is excluded. Original code is MIT-licensed; original author-owned tables, figures, and documentation are CC BY 4.0 licensed. Exact file scopes and source exceptions are listed in LICENSE_MAP.csv and THIRD_PARTY_ATTRIBUTION.md. Earlier project stages included stepwise independent numerical audit and supplementary table checks; a single clean-environment execution from freshly downloaded raw source data through every figure has not been demonstrated. This archive is intended for research transparency and documents its specific reproducibility limits. Version 1.0.1 update: Corrected the direction_concordant annotations for eight genes in Supplementary Table S9 and updated the README to reflect the Zenodo release. The strict replication results and scientific conclusions remain unchanged.

summary: Replication package of the paper on SpecDetect4ML, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. SpecDetect4ML detects ML code smells in Python ML pipeline code. Each smell is written as a short rule in a declarative DSL, and the rules run on a code property graph (CPG) that links syntax, control flow, data flow, imports, aliases and wrappers across the files of a project.  Requirements: Python 3.11 or newer, packages pinned in requirements.txt. Docker only for the web app. License: the source code of the tool and the scripts is under the MIT license (see LICENSE).
title: SpecDetect4ML: replication package

summary: Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent's constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle's information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms $27$ baselines by $+15.0$ Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at https://github.com/EllenYiGe/PatternBloom.
title: PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns

title: PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns

summary: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.

summary: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.
title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction

summary: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
title: ASCENT: Scale-Complementary External State for Frozen Long-Context Language Models

summary: Objective: Using a path length constraint with dual energy computed tomography (DECT) data, a sample can be decomposed into three basis materials. We aim to analyze the stability of such a system by presenting a noise propagation framework for optimizing the contrast to noise ratio (CNR) of virtual monochromatic images (VMIs) and by studying instances where sinogram decompositions are not unique. Approach: We extend a noise propagation framework developed for two-material DECT to three materials. Using the Jacobian of the system, we identify tube voltage pairings with good noise properties and obtain analytical expressions for VMI CNR. We apply spectral theorem to identify the best CNR possible in a linear combination of basis images. By using a reduced two-dimensional problem, we develop the sampling isoline recovery algorithm (SIRA) to study non-unique sinogram decompositions in this system. Main results: Using our noise propagation framework with a realistic breast phantom consisting of adipose, glandular tissue, and iodine, we find an ideal tube pairing of 34 kVp and 69 kVp, and a maximum VMI CNR of a spiculated lesion of 9.9. By allowing arbitrary linear combinations of basis material images, we find a CNR of 10.2 can be achieved. In a realistic phantom with a cardiac plaque, we find non-unique water, bone and iodine decompositions, and show that qualitatively accurate reconstructions can be obtained using SIRA. Significance: We developed a framework for direct optimization of VMI CNR in a three-material DECT decomposition and showed that an arbitrary linear combination of basis material images can achieve a higher CNR than a strict VMI. We demonstrate the presence of non-unique sinogram decompositions in three-material DECT with a data constraint.

summary: Kramers nodal lines (KNLs) are predicted in all achiral, non-centrosymmetric crystal structures, and yet there are very few experimental realizations of KNLs, only in weakly correlated systems. Especially, their realization in strongly correlated systems remains unexplored. Here we investigate KNL topology in the non-centrosymmetric, achiral Kondo lattice CeAuAl$_3$, using magnetotransport, thermodynamic measurements, density functional theory (DFT), and tight-binding toy model calculations. We find that CeAuAl$_3$ hosts KNLs in the $\mathitΓ\text{-}Z$ and $X\text{-}P$ directions, protected by time-reversal and mirror symmetries. Breaking of these crystalline symmetries, along with time-reversal symmetry via spin polarization, lifts the KNL degeneracy, which, in turn, generates Berry curvature resulting in an intrinsic anomalous Hall effect (AHE). More importantly, CeAuAl$_3$ shows large AHE not only below the magnetic ordering temperature $T_N$ but rather below the Kondo temperature. This underscores the role of the Kondo correlations in bringing the KNLs at the Fermi surface rather than at accidental energies, as would be expected without correlations. Our work identifies a new topological state, Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line, with CeAuAl$_3$ being the first compound explicitly identified to host this new correlated topological state, and demonstrating the expected AHE associated with it. More generally, our work outlines the pathway for finding Kondo-KNL systems in all compounds that combine achiral, non-centrosymmetric structure with Kondo correlations.
title: Discovery of Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line Topological State in strongly correlated material CeAuAl$_3$

summary: Multimodal fusion requires not only exchanging information across modalities but also determining which representations should participate in the interaction and how complementary cross-modal views should be combined. We introduce Guided Co-Attention with Adaptive Gating, a fusion framework that integrates token-wise guidance, bidirectional cross-attention, and sample-specific fusion. The proposed method constructs two directional representations: an image-conditioned text representation, obtained by allowing textual tokens to query visual features, and a text-conditioned image representation formed in the reverse direction. Token-wise guidance modulates the representations before cross-attention, while an adaptive gate learns the relative contribution of the two resulting directional representations for each sample. We evaluate the approach using paired chest radiographs and radiology reports as an image-text test bed for binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification. The two cross-attention directions exhibit distinct performance characteristics, demonstrating that reversing the query and source modalities does not produce interchangeable representations. Ablation experiments further show that bidirectional interaction, adaptive gating, and token guidance provide complementary benefits. The proposed model achieves 96.05% accuracy, 96.10% F1-score, 98.37% AUC, 95.60% Sens@95Spec, and 96.51% Spec@95Sens, yielding the highest mean performance across all evaluated metrics. These findings support explicitly modeling interaction direction, token relevance, and sample-dependent integration when constructing multimodal representations.

We introduce Guided Co-Attention with Adaptive Gating, a fusion framework that integrates token-wise guidance, bidirectional cross-attention, and sample-specific fusion. The proposed method constructs two directional representations: an image-conditioned text representation, obtained by allowing textual tokens to query visual features, and a text-conditioned image representation formed in the reverse direction. Token-wise guidance modulates the representations before cross-attention, while an adaptive gate learns the relative contribution of the two resulting directional representations for each sample. We evaluate the approach using paired chest radiographs and radiology reports as an image-text test bed for binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification. The two cross-attention directions exhibit distinct performance characteristics, demonstrating that reversing the query and source modalities does not produce interchangeable representations. Ablation experiments further show that bidirectional interaction, adaptive gating, and token guidance provide complementary benefits. The proposed model achieves 96.05% accuracy, 96.10% F1-score, 98.37% AUC, 95.60% Sens@95Spec, and 96.51% Spec@95Sens, yielding the highest mean performance across all evaluated metrics. These findings support explicitly modeling interaction direction, token relevance, and sample-dependent integration when constructing multimodal representations.

summary: Due to supply constraints, replacing damaged automotive components can be expensive and time-consuming, while replacing the entire component can be wasteful when much of it remains usable. This paper presents a pipeline to investigate whether missing geometry can be reconstructed as a repair patch using paired observations of the intact models and synthetically damaged components. Noise-free color, depth, and silhouette images were produced using the camera viewpoints. Depth differences were then used to identify the potential missing regions, while multi-view voxel reconstruction was used to estimate the missing portion. A pretrained DINOv2 model was also added to validate missing candidates and determine whether pretrained visual features could improve reconstruction. We tested the pipeline on 20 automotive CAD models, each with a synthetically removed portion. Each model was tested under four different conditions using two reconstruction methods for a total of 160 trials. The predictions were compared with the missing geometry of the unchanged ground-truth using predefined thresholds of the voxel intersection-over-union over 0.85 and the absolute relative volume error less than 15%. Of the 160 experimental trials, 109 of them satisfied both thresholds. Geometry-only reconstruction passed 16 of 20 components with eight views but only 10 of 20 with four adjacent views. Further analysis showed that 24 out of the 37 failed reconstructions could be categorized as unsuccessful because extra material was incorrectly added to areas that should have been empty. The implementation of DINOv2 into the pipeline did not improve the overall reconstruction accuracy and made prediction generation slower. For 13 verified tests, printing only the repaired sections instead of the entire parts reduced filament use by 93.08% and printing time by 89.39% based on the median results.

summary: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{é}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.

summary: Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) is a key strategy for advancing sustainable urban development by promoting high-density, mixed-use land development within walking distance of public transit stations. However, traditional TOD planning often relies on heuristic methods, making it difficult to efficiently identify quantitatively optimized transit-oriented land use patterns. This paper presents DRL4TOD, a deep reinforcement learning framework that automatically optimizes land use types and floor area ratios (FARs) around transit stations in alignment with TOD principles. DRL4TOD incorporates a graph neural network to capture spatial interdependencies among land parcels, road networks, and metro stations, and uses a DRL-based optimization strategy to assign land-use types and FARs to selected parcels. It jointly optimizes multiple objectives, including land use density, land use diversity, and transit capacity utilization, while minimizing reconstruction costs to account for development feasibility. Applied to two real-world station areas in Shanghai, DRL4TOD consistently outperforms rule-based approaches and genetic algorithms, achieving more effective TOD outcomes with lower reconstruction costs. By adjusting objective weights, the framework enables flexible prioritization, such as placing greater emphasis on cost minimization when financial feasibility is a concern. These results demonstrate DRL4TOD's potential as a decision-support tool for generating coordinated land-use and FAR configurations under planner-specified priorities, rather than prescribing a single fixed design. For policymakers, the framework provides parcel-level, constraint-aware alternatives that make trade-offs among competing objectives explicit and support targeted decisions about development intensity and feasibility.

summary: Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) forms images from incomplete Fourier measurements, shifting acquisition burden to computational reconstruction. Deep unrolled networks interleave learned regularization and data consistency, yet typically estimate the full unmeasured spectrum at every cascade. We propose STAIRS (Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling), which projects intermediate reconstructions onto nested Fourier supports that expand to the full spectrum and conditions each update on its support transition. Conditional increments of a regularized log-determinant score of training covariance define a normalized spectral coordinate, accounting for dependencies between newly and previously admitted frequencies. Dyadic targets allocate larger coordinate increments to earlier cascades and are mapped to fixed supports before training, enabling coarse-to-fine reconstruction with unchanged sampling masks and data consistency. On fastMRI and Stanford2D, STAIRS improves matched Transformer (HUMUSNet) and convolutional (NAFNet) backbones in single- and multi-coil reconstruction, including radiologist-annotated pathology regions. It also outperforms predictor-based progression with lower parameter overhead and inference latency. Stage-wise analysis shows repeated error correction by projection and lower intermediate reconstruction errors than the backbones alone throughout support expansion. Ablations favor dyadic allocation over uniform expansion for square and line-band supports and over manual front-loading for square windows. Support projection alone improves reconstruction, and transition conditioning strengthens the gain. Cross-dataset evaluation shows improvements for both backbones in both directions. Support allocation thus complements regularizer design in unrolled MRI reconstruction.
title: STAIRS: Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling for Unrolled MRI Reconstruction

We propose STAIRS (Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling), which projects intermediate reconstructions onto nested Fourier supports that expand to the full spectrum and conditions each update on its support transition. Conditional increments of a regularized log-determinant score of training covariance define a normalized spectral coordinate, accounting for dependencies between newly and previously admitted frequencies. Dyadic targets allocate larger coordinate increments to earlier cascades and are mapped to fixed supports before training, enabling coarse-to-fine reconstruction with unchanged sampling masks and data consistency. On fastMRI and Stanford2D, STAIRS improves matched Transformer (HUMUSNet) and convolutional (NAFNet) backbones in single- and multi-coil reconstruction, including radiologist-annotated pathology regions. It also outperforms predictor-based progression with lower parameter overhead and inference latency. Stage-wise analysis shows repeated error correction by projection and lower intermediate reconstruction errors than the backbones alone throughout support expansion. Ablations favor dyadic allocation over uniform expansion for square and line-band supports and over manual front-loading for square windows. Support projection alone improves reconstruction, and transition conditioning strengthens the gain. Cross-dataset evaluation shows improvements for both backbones in both directions. Support allocation thus complements regularizer design in unrolled MRI reconstruction.

summary: We study anchor reconstruction stability in return-map inverse problems for class $\mathcal O_C$. Local identifiability is governed by the first nonvanishing derivative of the holonomy map $H = T_γ- \text{Id}$. In the non-neutral case, we prove local Lipschitz stability and multiplier estimates. In the neutral regime, using Faà di Bruno equations and Malgrange preparation, we derive quantitative $1/k$-Hölder estimates for order-$k$ anchor perturbations. We also establish finite jet stability, real-analytic dependence, and global $C^0$-stability of order $O(\varepsilon_F^{1/k})$. Numerical benchmarks on circular-core return geometries validate these theoretical convergence rates and square-root laws.
title: Stability in the Non-Neutral and Neutral Regimes of the Holonomy-Based Inverse Problem in the Class \(\mathcal{OC}\)

summary: The advent of Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs) and AC-coupled Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (AC-LGADs) as candidate technologies for four-dimensional tracking has moved part of the reconstruction burden onto the analog waveforms of the sensor, in which the charge shared between electrodes encodes the impact position well below the electrode pitch. Recovering that position is a continuous, non-linear inverse problem. Transient Current Technique measurements characterize this problem at fixed injected charge and high signal-to-noise, whereas a minimum-ionizing beam adds Landau fluctuations in the deposited charge under detector operating conditions. We report test beam results for full-waveform reconstruction of an AC-LGAD of 500 $μ$m pitch read out on a $2\times2$ pad matrix, exposed to the 120 GeV pion beam of the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) and read out alongside a six-plane MIMOSA-26 telescope. The telescope is aligned, and its per-plane resolutions are calibrated in situ, giving a track pointing resolution of about 2.5 $μ$m per axis at the device, so that the measured residual is the sensor response rather than a convolution with the reference. We then compare two analytic estimators, the parameter-free charge-imbalance formula and a fitted linear matrix inversion, with the topology-agnostic transformer developed for resistive silicon sensors. Over the full active pad, the transformer reaches a median total position with up to factor 3 improvement. Within the charge-sharing core, the three methods converge to the floor of this sensor at the achieved signal-to-noise.
title: Test beam results for machine-learning-based reconstruction of resistive silicon sensors

summary: Reflections: BELIEF, DISBELIEF. SPIRIT and MATTER. Skrynnik Sergey Nikolaevich Republic of Kazakhstan, Almaty, science@ast-1c.kz Abstract This work is a philosophical and theoretical study aimed at building a holistic model of reality that unites the physical and subjective aspects of being. It is the original, “manifesto” part of a cycle of eleven articles; it is here that the ideas developed in the subsequent works were first formulated. The work consists of two parts. The first (“Faith, Unbelief”) examines the essence of man and the meaning of life outside the categories of good and evil: questions of immortality, of imperfection as a source of striving, of reason, of freedom of choice and of the idea of the Creator. The main conclusion of this part is that the principle of life is preserved regardless of what a person believes in. The second part (“Spirit and Matter”) draws on the physical model of the work “The Birth of Dimensions: A Formal Skeleton” and draws analogies between the physical and the spiritual: consciousness is considered as a resonant structure that cannot be reduced to matter but is inseparably connected with it. Consciousness and matter appear as different frequency manifestations of a single process, which suggests a possible way of overcoming the traditional opposition of the “spiritual” and the “material”. The structure of the observer, the connection between consciousness and the brain, the soul, attention and the role of life as the medium in which the observer develops are discussed. The work is interdisciplinary and hypothetical in character and is open to critical analysis.
