summary: Transparent-interface reconstruction must recover glass surfaces even when most observed color comes from the scene behind them. We present ClearForm, a shared-planar-Gaussian method for jointly reconstructing transparent interfaces and the appearance seen through them. We identify and analyze the Geometry-Appearance Compositing Dilemma (GACD): when the same transparency-dependent alpha controls both color and geometry, revealing the background can weaken a transparent surface's contribution to geometric reconstruction. We derive its effect on plane-based depth estimation, identify a mechanism that can weaken geometric learning, and quantify the loss of interface support through controlled comparisons. To address this conflict, we develop geometry-preserving dual-opacity surface reconstruction. Shared planar Gaussians retain interface contributions in geometry compositing while modeling transmission and sparse reflection in RGB, supported by transparency-aware geometric constraints. To manage the different primitive-visibility requirements of these compositors, we introduce Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL), which retains Gaussians supported by multi-view geometry or RGB reconstruction evidence. On 3D-FRONT-T, ClearForm achieves 27.05 mm Chamfer distance (CD) and 0.928 F1, compared with 59.18 mm CD for our PGSR reproduction and the reported 34 mm CD and 0.836 F1 for GLINT. On TransLab, it achieves 1.65 mm CD, 0.963 F1, and 40.14 dB PSNR. In matched ablations, dual-opacity compositing reduces CD from 59.25 to 27.09 mm, while DEL improves PSNR by 2.06 dB. Our project page is available at https://hajeongx.github.io/clearform/.
title: ClearForm: Shared-Surface Gaussian Splatting for Transparent and Opaque Scenes

summary: Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition (OV-MLR) aims to identify all queried semantic concepts present in an image. Existing methods mainly improve global image-text matching or text-side representations, leaving local prediction largely under-explored. In this paper, we revisit local prediction and reveal that it can serve as a strong discriminative branch once two properties are properly handled: spatial consistency of local visual features and compatibility-aware local competition. This perspective is motivated by local semantic sparsity: each image region is related to only a small subset of queried concepts, while compatible concepts of different granularities or types may still coexist locally. We instantiate this perspective with LoCo, a selective Local Competition framework for OV-MLR. LoCo adopts a spatially consistent visual encoder to reduce local feature entanglement, and introduces Selective Softmax to impose competition only among locally incompatible categories while preserving compatible responses. Multi-scale inference further improves local prediction at different scales. LoCo can also be ensembled with an existing global predictor to provide complementary image-level context. Experiments on four multi-label benchmarks show that standalone LoCo improves average F1-score and mAP over TagCLIP by 3.4% and 3.8%, respectively. LoCo + DualPrompt achieves the highest averages among the compared methods, with gains of 4.8% and 5.2% over TagCLIP. Our results suggest that local semantic sparsity offers a useful basis for developing more discriminative open-vocabulary multi-label recognition methods. The code is available at https://github.com/lee-plus-plus/LoCo.
title: LoCo: Selective Local Competition for Discriminative Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition

summary: Estimating long-term treatment effects is essential in regulatory and healthcare decision-making, yet the limited follow-up duration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) poses a significant challenge. Open-label extension studies attempt to capture additional information for treated subjects, but there is often significant systematic censoring and selection bias due to placebo crossover. While supplementing RCTs with real-world evidence is a common strategy, existing methods often rely on restrictive exchangeability assumptions that fail under latent confounding. We propose a novel proximal framework to integrate real-world evidence into an RCT with an open-label extension to estimate the long-term continued-control trajectory. Our approach successfully identifies long-term effects even in the presence of time-varying latent confounding effects and inter-study outcome drift. We provide a doubly robust locally efficient estimator that provides further resilience to model misspecification. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework maintains validity in complex data-generating processes where standard approaches may be biased.
title: Proximal Difference-in-Differences for Causal Learning under Confounding and Outcome Drift

summary: We conduct a retrospective exploratory pilot analysis of paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 surface plasmon resonance (SPR) trajectories, examining retained response, dual-marker fusion, and additional early-shape information. Numerical matching links the original exports to previously quality-selected data: 69 files represent 68 distinct source column pairs from 10 cancer and 10 healthy study patients. Existing exclusions and truncations are preserved. All 20 patients contribute to development and exploration; no independent validation cohort is available. Because historical per-scan manual alignment offsets are unavailable, the numerical comparisons are conditional on separately documented candidate response-transition intervals rather than verified injection-event times. Patient-level paired comparisons, leave-pair-out internal assessment, empirical false-positive budgets, and timing sensitivity are implemented in reproducible Python code. Under candidate alignment, the dual-marker retained-response sum has an apparent AUC of 0.570, with a fixed-score bootstrap 95% interval of [0.300, 0.820]. In the nested 13-patient shape subset, retention alone and the fixed 85:15 retention-shape score both have AUC 0.619; the small paired increment changes direction across the -1,0,+1 minute shift scenarios. At a same-sample budget of two false positives among ten controls, dual-marker retention identifies four cancer cases, compared with two for PD-L1 and three for Siglec-15. Analytical bounds describe feature stability under stated measurement assumptions but do not identify the cause of weak discrimination. The study provides a traceable analysis framework and operating-point hypotheses for independent evaluation; the small development cohort does not establish diagnostic utility or a reliable fusion or shape advantage.
title: An Exploratory Pilot Analysis of Paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 SPR Sensorgrams: Retained Response, Early Shape, and Complementarity

summary: This software archive contains R and Python scripts, cohort-specific statistical audit scripts, gene-level derived summary tables, figure source comparisons, selected graphical outputs, and integrity checks associated with a secondary analysis of 13 intercalated-disc genes in human dilated cardiomyopathy. Public inputs include GEO studies GSE141910, GSE116250, GSE249925, GSE183852, Broad Single Cell Portal SCP1303, and published left-ventricular proteomics data from Li et al. (PXD018678). The work evaluates bulk myocardial transcriptomic reproducibility, donor-level cardiomyocyte nuclear pseudobulk analyses, CellBender-versus-CellRanger count processing, matched nuclear-versus-bulk modality effects, and published proteomic evidence. Original large datasets and individual-level source matrices are not redistributed. Source-derived proteomics values are credited to Li et al.; the 2,614-protein aggregate re-tabulation is excluded. Original code is MIT-licensed; original author-owned tables, figures, and documentation are CC BY 4.0 licensed. Exact file scopes and source exceptions are listed in LICENSE_MAP.csv and THIRD_PARTY_ATTRIBUTION.md. Earlier project stages included stepwise independent numerical audit and supplementary table checks; a single clean-environment execution from freshly downloaded raw source data through every figure has not been demonstrated. This archive is intended for research transparency and documents its specific reproducibility limits. Version 1.0.1 update: Corrected the direction_concordant annotations for eight genes in Supplementary Table S9 and updated the README to reflect the Zenodo release. The strict replication results and scientific conclusions remain unchanged.
title: Analysis Code and Audit Tables for Cross-Cohort and Cross-Omics Investigation of Intercalated-Disc Changes in Human Dilated Cardiomyopathy

summary: Replication package of the paper on SpecDetect4ML, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. SpecDetect4ML detects ML code smells in Python ML pipeline code. Each smell is written as a short rule in a declarative DSL, and the rules run on a code property graph (CPG) that links syntax, control flow, data flow, imports, aliases and wrappers across the files of a project.  Requirements: Python 3.11 or newer, packages pinned in requirements.txt. Docker only for the web app. License: the source code of the tool and the scripts is under the MIT license (see LICENSE).
title: SpecDetect4ML: replication package

summary: Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent's constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle's information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms $27$ baselines by $+15.0$ Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at https://github.com/EllenYiGe/PatternBloom.
title: PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns

summary: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.
title: Hibana: Fast Agentic Inference on Unified-Memory Devices

summary: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.
title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction

summary: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
title: ASCENT: Scale-Complementary External State for Frozen Long-Context Language Models

summary: Objective: Using a path length constraint with dual energy computed tomography (DECT) data, a sample can be decomposed into three basis materials. We aim to analyze the stability of such a system by presenting a noise propagation framework for optimizing the contrast to noise ratio (CNR) of virtual monochromatic images (VMIs) and by studying instances where sinogram decompositions are not unique. Approach: We extend a noise propagation framework developed for two-material DECT to three materials. Using the Jacobian of the system, we identify tube voltage pairings with good noise properties and obtain analytical expressions for VMI CNR. We apply spectral theorem to identify the best CNR possible in a linear combination of basis images. By using a reduced two-dimensional problem, we develop the sampling isoline recovery algorithm (SIRA) to study non-unique sinogram decompositions in this system. Main results: Using our noise propagation framework with a realistic breast phantom consisting of adipose, glandular tissue, and iodine, we find an ideal tube pairing of 34 kVp and 69 kVp, and a maximum VMI CNR of a spiculated lesion of 9.9. By allowing arbitrary linear combinations of basis material images, we find a CNR of 10.2 can be achieved. In a realistic phantom with a cardiac plaque, we find non-unique water, bone and iodine decompositions, and show that qualitatively accurate reconstructions can be obtained using SIRA. Significance: We developed a framework for direct optimization of VMI CNR in a three-material DECT decomposition and showed that an arbitrary linear combination of basis material images can achieve a higher CNR than a strict VMI. summary: Kramers nodal lines (KNLs) are predicted in all achiral, non-centrosymmetric crystal structures, and yet there are very few experimental realizations of KNLs, only in weakly correlated systems. Especially, their realization in strongly correlated systems remains unexplored. Here we investigate KNL topology in the non-centrosymmetric, achiral Kondo lattice CeAuAl$_3$, using magnetotransport, thermodynamic measurements, density functional theory (DFT), and tight-binding toy model calculations. We find that CeAuAl$_3$ hosts KNLs in the $\mathitΓ\text{-}Z$ and $X\text{-}P$ directions, protected by time-reversal and mirror symmetries. Breaking of these crystalline symmetries, along with time-reversal symmetry via spin polarization, lifts the KNL degeneracy, which, in turn, generates Berry curvature resulting in an intrinsic anomalous Hall effect (AHE). More importantly, CeAuAl$_3$ shows large AHE not only below the magnetic ordering temperature $T_N$ but rather below the Kondo temperature. This underscores the role of the Kondo correlations in bringing the KNLs at the Fermi surface rather than at accidental energies, as would be expected without correlations. Our work identifies a new topological state, Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line, with CeAuAl$_3$ being the first compound explicitly identified to host this new correlated topological state, and demonstrating the expected AHE associated with it. More generally, our work outlines the pathway for finding Kondo-KNL systems in all compounds that combine achiral, non-centrosymmetric structure with Kondo correlations.
title: Discovery of Kondo-Kramers Nodal Line Topological State in strongly correlated material CeAuAl$_3$

summary: Multimodal fusion requires not only exchanging information across modalities but also determining which representations should participate in the interaction and how complementary cross-modal views should be combined. We introduce Guided Co-Attention with Adaptive Gating, a fusion framework that integrates token-wise guidance, bidirectional cross-attention, and sample-specific fusion. The proposed method constructs two directional representations: an image-conditioned text representation, obtained by allowing textual tokens to query visual features, and a text-conditioned image representation formed in the reverse direction. Token-wise guidance modulates the representations before cross-attention, while an adaptive gate learns the relative contribution of the two resulting directional representations for each sample. We evaluate the approach using paired chest radiographs and radiology reports as an image-text test bed for binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification. The two cross-attention directions exhibit distinct performance characteristics, demonstrating that reversing the query and source modalities does not produce interchangeable representations. Ablation experiments further show that bidirectional interaction, adaptive gating, and token guidance provide complementary benefits. The proposed model achieves 96.05% accuracy, 96.10% F1-score, 98.37% AUC, 95.60% Sens@95Spec, and 96.51% Spec@95Sens, yielding the highest mean performance across all evaluated metrics. These findings support explicitly modeling interaction direction, token relevance, and sample-dependent integration when constructing multimodal representations.
title: Guided Co-Attention with Adaptive Gating for Multimodal Medical Data Fusion

summary: Due to supply constraints, replacing damaged automotive components can be expensive and time-consuming, while replacing the entire component can be wasteful when much of it remains usable. This paper presents a pipeline to investigate whether missing geometry can be reconstructed as a repair patch using paired observations of the intact models and synthetically damaged components. Noise-free color, depth, and silhouette images were produced using the camera viewpoints. Depth differences were then used to identify the potential missing regions, while multi-view voxel reconstruction was used to estimate the missing portion. A pretrained DINOv2 model was also added to validate missing candidates and determine whether pretrained visual features could improve reconstruction. We tested the pipeline on 20 automotive CAD models, each with a synthetically removed portion. Each model was tested under four different conditions using two reconstruction methods for a total of 160 trials. The predictions were compared with the missing geometry of the unchanged ground-truth using predefined thresholds of the voxel intersection-over-union over 0.85 and the absolute relative volume error less than 15%. Of the 160 experimental trials, 109 of them satisfied both thresholds. Geometry-only reconstruction passed 16 of 20 components with eight views but only 10 of 20 with four adjacent views. Further analysis showed that 24 out of the 37 failed reconstructions could be categorized as unsuccessful because extra material was incorrectly added to areas that should have been empty. The implementation of DINOv2 into the pipeline did not improve the overall reconstruction accuracy and made prediction generation slower. For 13 verified tests, printing only the repaired sections instead of the entire parts reduced filament use by 93.08% and printing time by 89.39% based on the median results.
title: AI-Driven Repair of Missing Automotive Components

summary: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{é}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.
title: Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction

summary: Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) is a key strategy for advancing sustainable urban development by promoting high-density, mixed-use land development within walking distance of public transit stations. However, traditional TOD planning often relies on heuristic methods, making it difficult to efficiently identify quantitatively optimized transit-oriented land use patterns. This paper presents DRL4TOD, a deep reinforcement learning framework that automatically optimizes land use types and floor area ratios (FARs) around transit stations in alignment with TOD principles. DRL4TOD incorporates a graph neural network to capture spatial interdependencies among land parcels, road networks, and metro stations, and uses a DRL-based optimization strategy to assign land-use types and FARs to selected parcels. It jointly optimizes multiple objectives, including land use density, land use diversity, and transit capacity utilization, while minimizing reconstruction costs to account for development feasibility. Applied to two real-world station areas in Shanghai, DRL4TOD consistently outperforms rule-based approaches and genetic algorithms, achieving more effective TOD outcomes with lower reconstruction costs. By adjusting objective weights, the framework enables flexible prioritization, such as placing greater emphasis on cost minimization when financial feasibility is a concern. These results demonstrate DRL4TOD's potential as a decision-support tool for generating coordinated land-use and FAR configurations under planner-specified priorities, rather than prescribing a single fixed design. For policymakers, the framework provides parcel-level, constraint-aware alternatives that make trade-offs among competing objectives explicit and support targeted decisions about development intensity and feasibility.
title: Transit-Oriented Land Use Planning Using Deep Reinforcement Learning

summary: Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) forms images from incomplete Fourier measurements, shifting acquisition burden to computational reconstruction. Deep unrolled networks interleave learned regularization and data consistency, yet typically estimate the full unmeasured spectrum at every cascade. We propose STAIRS (Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling), which projects intermediate reconstructions onto nested Fourier supports that expand to the full spectrum and conditions each update on its support transition. Conditional increments of a regularized log-determinant score of training covariance define a normalized spectral coordinate, accounting for dependencies between newly and previously admitted frequencies. Dyadic targets allocate larger coordinate increments to earlier cascades and are mapped to fixed supports before training, enabling coarse-to-fine reconstruction with unchanged sampling masks and data consistency. On fastMRI and Stanford2D, STAIRS improves matched Transformer (HUMUSNet) and convolutional (NAFNet) backbones in single- and multi-coil reconstruction, including radiologist-annotated pathology regions. It also outperforms predictor-based progression with lower parameter overhead and inference latency. Stage-wise analysis shows repeated error correction by projection and lower intermediate reconstruction errors than the backbones alone throughout support expansion. Ablations favor dyadic allocation over uniform expansion for square and line-band supports and over manual front-loading for square windows. Support projection alone improves reconstruction, and transition conditioning strengthens the gain. Cross-dataset evaluation shows improvements for both backbones in both directions. Support allocation thus complements regularizer design in unrolled MRI reconstruction.
title: STAIRS: Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling for Unrolled MRI Reconstruction

summary: We study anchor reconstruction stability in return-map inverse problems for class $\mathcal O_C$. Local identifiability is governed by the first nonvanishing derivative of the holonomy map $H = T_γ- \text{Id}$. In the non-neutral case, we prove local Lipschitz stability and multiplier estimates. We also establish finite jet stability, real-analytic dependence, and global $C^0$-stability of order $O(\varepsilon_F^{1/k})$. Numerical benchmarks on circular-core return geometries validate these theoretical convergence rates and square-root laws.

summary: The advent of Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs) and AC-coupled Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (AC-LGADs) as candidate technologies for four-dimensional tracking has moved part of the reconstruction burden onto the analog waveforms of the sensor, in which the charge shared between electrodes encodes the impact position well below the electrode pitch. Recovering that position is a continuous, non-linear inverse problem. Transient Current Technique measurements characterize this problem at fixed injected charge and high signal-to-noise, whereas a minimum-ionizing beam adds Landau fluctuations in the deposited charge under detector operating conditions. We report test beam results for full-waveform reconstruction of an AC-LGAD of 500 $μ$m pitch read out on a $2\times2$ pad matrix, exposed to the 120 GeV pion beam of the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) and read out alongside a six-plane MIMOSA-26 telescope. The telescope is aligned, and its per-plane resolutions are calibrated in situ, giving a track pointing resolution of about 2.5 $μ$m per axis at the device, so that the measured residual is the sensor response rather than a convolution with the reference. We then compare two analytic estimators, the parameter-free charge-imbalance formula and a fitted linear matrix inversion, with the topology-agnostic transformer developed for resistive silicon sensors. Over the full active pad, the transformer reaches a median total position with up to factor 3 improvement. Within the charge-sharing core, the three methods converge to the floor of this sensor at the achieved signal-to-noise.
title: Test beam results for machine-learning-based reconstruction of resistive silicon sensors

summary: Reflections: BELIEF, DISBELIEF. SPIRIT and MATTER. Skrynnik Sergey Nikolaevich Republic of Kazakhstan, Almaty, science@ast-1c.kz Abstract This work is a philosophical and theoretical study aimed at building a holistic model of reality that unites the physical and subjective aspects of being. It is the original, “manifesto” part of a cycle of eleven articles; it is here that the ideas developed in the subsequent works were first formulated. The work consists of two parts. The first (“Faith, Unbelief”) examines the essence of man and the meaning of life outside the categories of good and evil: questions of immortality, of imperfection as a source of striving, of reason, of freedom of choice and of the idea of the Creator. The main conclusion of this part is that the principle of life is preserved regardless of what a person believes in. The second part (“Spirit and Matter”) draws on the physical model of the work “The Birth of Dimensions: A Formal Skeleton” and draws analogies between the physical and the spiritual: consciousness is considered as a resonant structure that cannot be reduced to matter but is inseparably connected with it. Consciousness and matter appear as different frequency manifestations of a single process, which suggests a possible way of overcoming the traditional opposition of the “spiritual” and the “material”. The structure of the observer, the connection between consciousness and the brain, the soul, attention and the role of life as the medium in which the observer develops are discussed. The work is interdisciplinary and hypothetical in character and is open to critical analysis. Revision dated 2026-11-10: The chapter “Man and Woman” now specifies what the reverse combination of roles means and what price the system pays for the rearrangement; it adds that roles can intertwine: a woman as muse gives the impulse, and a man gives birth to an idea or a work — birth passes to the next level. These roles are not tied to sex and must be balanced by the manifestation of our phase.     Размышления: ВЕРА, НЕВЕРИЕ. ДУХ и МАТЕРИЯ. Скрынник Сергей Николаевич Республика Казахстан, г. Алматы, science@ast-1c.kz Аннотация Настоящая работа представляет собой философско-теоретическое исследование, направленное на построение целостной модели реальности, объединяющей физические и субъективные аспекты бытия. Она является исходной, «манифестной» частью цикла из одиннадцати статей; именно здесь впервые сформулированы идеи, развитые в последующих работах. Работа состоит из двух частей. В первой («Вера, неверие») рассматриваются суть человека и смысл жизни вне категорий добра и зла: вопросы бессмертия, несовершенства как источника стремления, разума, свободы выбора и идеи Создателя. Основной вывод части — принцип жизни сохраняется независимо от того, во что верит человек. Вторая часть («Дух и материя») опирается на физическую модель работы «Рождение измерений: формальный скелет» и проводит аналогии между физическим и духовным: сознание рассматривается как резонансная структура, не сводимая к материи, но неразрывно связанная с ней. Сознание и материя предстают как различные частотные проявления единого процесса, что предлагает возможный путь к преодолению традиционного противопоставления «духовного» и «материального». Обсуждаются структура наблюдателя, связь сознания и мозга, душа, внимание и роль жизни как среды развития наблюдателя. Работа носит междисциплинарный и гипотетический характер и открыта для критического анализа. Правки от 10.11.2026:  В главе «Мужчина и женщина» уточнено, что такое обратная комбинация ролей и какую цену система платит за перестановку; добавлено, что роли могут переплетаться: женщина-муза даёт импульс, а мужчина рождает идею или произведение — рождение переходит на следующий уровень. Эти роли не закре
title: Reflections: BELIEF, DISBELIEF. SPIRIT and MATTER.

summary: Pyralysis (PYthon Radio Astronomy anaLYSis and Image Synthesis) is an open-source Python library for radio-interferometric simulation, gridding, and image reconstruction. Imaging is stated as an explicit optimization problem — chi-squared (and closure / bispectrum terms) plus regularizers you choose — solved with modern first-order methods (e.g. FISTA, L-BFGS, SDMM). It is not a black-box CLEAN imager.

summary: Museum of One working paper · Version 1.0 · 10 November 2026 · 16 pages · 21 references A work can retain its title and historical date even when its materials, arrangement, or means of presentation have changed. This working paper examines four Korean archival and museum cases: Kim Yong-Ik’s Plane Object photographs and the history of “plain” and “place”; the differing production years assigned to Park Suk-won’s Jeok–Eungnyeok; the 1975 historical reference and 2016 materials of Lee Kang-so’s Untitled 75031; and Kim Kulim’s Mediator, used by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, to exemplify compound dating. MMCA’s acquisition narrative and publication guidance acknowledge remaking as part of collecting an experimental past. The paper reads that institutional practice alongside scholarship on the relations among images, material traces, and artwork identity. Aga Wielocha’s discussion of Danh Vo’s chandeliers provides a particularly revealing comparison: a title can date an object’s removal and transformation into art rather than its fabrication, just as a museum’s leading year can identify an earlier work rather than the age of its present components. These different histories require the event dated by each title or caption to remain explicit. Neither artist authorisation nor institutional recognition settles every claim about an earlier condition. The paper credits the overlapping demonstrations in the author’s Relational Archival Investigation papers and develops their implications for collecting, editorial preference, and historical inference. Its contribution is a comparative account of how names and dates sustain continuity without making the evidence for that continuity interchangeable. Evidence limits. The source base is documentary. Physical artworks, original versos, complete printing proofs and object-specific acquisition and conservation dossiers remain unexamined. Park’s two published dates establish a discrepancy without determining the original year or a sequence of database changes. A shared series title cannot identify an individual Kim Yong-Ik work. The eight- and ten-image accounts do not establish a sequence of additions to Lee’s work. Jung Eun Young is cited through the published abstracts. The four selected cases establish no national rate of discrepancy. This working paper has not undergone independent peer review. Relationship to Relational Archival Investigation. The RAI main paper , Documentary Supplement and Extended Case Studies already report the shared naming and date comparisons, the limits of series-title identification, and the difference between Lee’s photographic accounts. This paper extends that work through MMCA’s acquisition narrative and compound dating of Mediator , a sustained comparison with Korean scholarship and conservation research, and analysis of what later objects and records establish about earlier works. Its bibliography points to the cited OSF file versions. 김용익(평면 오브제), 박석원(적-응력), 이강소(무제 75031), 김구림(매개항)의 사례를 통해 한국 실험미술에서 작품의 제목과 연대, 재제작, 소장 기록이 어떤 역사적 주장을 뒷받침하는지 살핀다. 작품의 역사적 정체성과 현존 구성 요소의 제작 시기를 구분하며, 네 사례의 자료 범위와 기존 RAI 연구와의 관계를 명시한다.
title: Titles, Dates, and Reconstructed Works: Four Documentary Histories of Korean Experimental Art

summary: Manuscript and CSV data behind the figures and tables of Xu (2021), Halo mass functions from maximum entropy distributions in collisionless dark matter flow, arXiv: 2110.09676 . Contents: the manuscript (PDF) and 19 CSV files with the data of the figures and of the tables that are generated from the simulation data. Companion datasets: doi:10.5281/zenodo.6541231 (Part I, halo-based statistics) and doi:10.5281/zenodo.6757654 (Part II, correlation-based statistics). The earlier record of this work is zenodo.org/records/6640325 . Major findings (friends-of-friends halos of a cosmological N-body simulation, z = 0 unless stated): The velocity distribution that maximises the entropy of a self-gravitating collisionless system (the X distribution) is a scale mixture of Gaussians of halo groups; without halo motion its mixing distribution is exactly the generalised inverse Gaussian distribution H∞. H∞ is a maximum entropy distribution only for potential exponent n = 0, not for gravity. A Gaussian mixture built from the measured halo-particle dispersions reproduces the velocity distribution of the halo particles to 0.03 dex (rms over |v| < 6σ 0 ) and its kurtosis (5.10 against 5.12), yet no halo particle has a total dispersion below 0.51σ 0 ², where H∞ places 0.28–0.34 of the particles. For any halo velocity dispersion bounded away from zero, the exact equation for the mass function has no solution; its push-forward solution leaves a fraction 0.27 of the mixture unassigned. The simulated mass function in ν = σ v ²/σ̄ h ² is described by the two-parameter P form with rms 0.18 in ln f, comparable to the fitted double-λ (0.18) and Sheth–Tormen (0.21) forms. The mass function is not independent of redshift: the mean ν rises from 0.56 at z = 2 to 1.14 at z = 0.
title: Halo mass functions from maximum entropy distributions in collisionless dark matter flow

summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) integrate information across modalities, but become unreliable when those modalities disagree. Under conflicting inputs, MLLMs may favor modalities that are not the most reliable for the task, thus motivating inference-time control of modality arbitration. We identify a small set of attention heads, termed arbitration heads, that causally influence whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight, training-free intervention that biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time. The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalize across settings, and steering them enables effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks. Our findings identify an effective control mechanism to align MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.
title: Beyond Modality Preference: Controlling Multimodal Arbitration under Modality Conflict in MLLMs

summary: We compute the cubic and $C_3\wedge X_8$ caracteristic class contributions to the trial anomaly polynomial of supersymmetric $AdS_3\times M_8$ backgrounds with $M_8=P(\mathcal O \oplus \mathcal L)\to B_6$. Including the Abelian currents descending from $C_3$, we identify the projective invariant $J$ as the denominator arising from their elimination by $c$-extremization and recover the central charge $c^{(0)}=-I_3+3I_+I_-/J$. The $X_8$ push-forward determines the pure R-symmetry, mixed R--Betti and gravitational anomalies. Evaluating it at the classical extremum gives the associated central-charge corrections, linear in the overall unshifted flux. The mixed term contributes equally to both central charges and is required in general. We evaluate these formulae for three flux-quantized backgrounds, including non-polynomial solutions. Direct projective fibre integration reproduces the mixed coefficient obtained by localization. On the wrapped-$M5$ $S^4$ bundle, the same couplings reproduce the independently known field-theory anomaly through orders $N^3$ and $N$. Their interpretation as full CFT central charges requires a unitary SCFT with a normalizable vacuum, suitable supersymmetric boundary conditions, a complete mixing sector of global currents and control of omitted anomaly sectors. A conditional Euclidean relative-equivariant interpretation is discussed separately.
title: M-theory anomaly localization and holographic $c$-extremization

summary: Recently, a new coordinate-based normalization has been introduced in [1] to represent tetrahedral similarity classes by normalized coordinates, enabling the study of LEB orbits as a discrete dynamical system. However, the uniqueness of this representation is not guaranteed when two or more edges adjacent to the selected longest edge have the same minimum length and remain admissible under the normalization criteria. In this paper, we demonstrate that different admissible choices may lead to distinct normalized coordinate representations of the same tetrahedral similarity class. We first present an explicit counterexample in which two admissible vertex labelings yield different normalized coordinate representations related by reflection, despite corresponding to the same similarity class. We then provide a systematic classification of the nine possible edge configurations arising in the selection of the canonical face when the longest edge of the tetrahedron is unique, and analyze the corresponding geometric and algebraic conditions. Our analysis identifies the configurations in which the normalization is non-unique and distinguishes them from those in which the ambiguity is resolved by the length criterion, angle criterion, or geometric symmetries. We further show that this non-uniqueness leads to an overcounting of distinct similarity classes.

summary: In this paper, we study the inverse problem of determining the coefficient $q$ and the nonlinearity $F$ in the semilinear biharmonic equation $Δ^2 u+q(x)u=F(x,u)$ with Navier boundary data. The measurement consists of $\partial_νu(x_0)$ at a fixed boundary point $x_0$. We apply the mixed variation approach to linearize the nonlinear problem and construct semiclassical boundary-localized solutions for the linearized equation. Under suitable analyticity, nonresonance, and nondegeneracy assumptions on $q$ and $F$, we prove that this boundary point measurement uniquely determines both $q$ and $F$. We also establish boundary determination of all normal derivatives of $q$ and of the first nonzero Taylor coefficient of $F$ on a nonempty relatively open subset of the boundary. When the linear potential $q$ is known, we prove that either component of the Navier boundary input alone suffices to determine $F$, and that the polynomial nonlinearity can be uniquely determined without requiring any analyticity conditions. For suitable finite-dimensional classes of nonanalytic potentials, we also obtain, for fixed $F$, the stable determination of $q$ from finitely many boundary inputs and the associated point measurements. In addition, as an important supplement, we provide nontrivial examples verifying the main assumptions, as well as counterexamples concerning the recovery of the linear coefficient. Finally, we present numerical experiments that demonstrate the theoretical results.
title: Single-point determination of a potential and a nonlinearity in a semilinear biharmonic equation

When the linear potential $q$ is known, we prove that either component of the Navier boundary input alone suffices to determine $F$, and that the polynomial nonlinearity can be uniquely determined without requiring any analyticity conditions. For suitable finite-dimensional classes of nonanalytic potentials, we also obtain, for fixed $F$, the stable determination of $q$ from finitely many boundary inputs and the associated point measurements. In addition, as an important supplement, we provide nontrivial examples verifying the main assumptions, as well as counterexamples concerning the recovery of the linear coefficient. title: Single-point determination of a potential and a nonlinearity in a semilinear biharmonic equation

summary: Answer accuracy alone does not distinguish failures in acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application. AuDiR (Audio Diagnostic Reasoning) examines these distinctions through controlled input interventions. Each item contains an audio clip, a multiple-choice question, a task-general rule, and a textual description of the acoustic observations needed to answer. Three conditions progressively supply the rule and observations; a fourth removes the audio while retaining the question and rule. The first correct diagnostic condition assigns an operational response label, without identifying a unique internal cause. The current benchmark contains 201 items in 18 families drawn from 9 sources, with answer references documented separately from percept extraction. In a preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash, accuracy is 29.3% without supplied information, 31.3% with the rule, and 98.5% with the observations also supplied. No-audio accuracy is 23.9%, with a confidence interval containing the 25.0% chance rate. A family-level knowledge probe associates incomplete rule recall with larger gains from rule provision. These results show the benefit of supplying acoustic observations as text, while incomplete validation, possible recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit stronger failure-attribution claims.

summary: As modern text-to-speech systems become increasingly intelligible and natural, evaluation is shifting from detecting gross synthesis failures to identifying subtle departures from lifelike human delivery. Because large-scale listening tests are costly and slow, speech reward models can serve as scalable automatic judges for comparing generated utterances, curating data, and supporting iterative TTS development. Existing speech reward models can predict scores or pairwise preferences and may generate natural-language rationales, but their supervision is typically defined at the utterance or pair level. The connection between local acoustic phenomena and the final preference therefore remains implicit. We introduce REAL, a framework for Reward modeling through Evidence-linked Analysis of Lifelikeness in generated speech. Its central idea is to supervise not only the final pairwise preference but also a structured account of its supporting observations, linking local audio spans to perceptual phenomena, affected dimensions, and the overall judgment. Specifically, REAL-Jury constructs these evidence-linked reports through timestamp alignment, multi-model analysis, and dispute-oriented deliberation. REAL-Judge learns to generate them from paired audio inputs. REAL-Eval assesses preference prediction in two tiers, from salient perceptual differences to subtle distinctions among strong TTS systems. Instantiated with MiMo-Audio, REAL-Judge improves pairwise preference accuracy over its backbone by 16.01 and 11.41 percentage points on the two tiers, respectively, and outperforms the open-source speech reward models SpeechJudge and UniSRM on both tiers.
title: REAL: Reward Modeling through Evidence-Linked Analysis of Lifelikeness in Generated Speech

summary: A family ${\mathcal A}\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ is \emph{uncomplemented} if it contains no set together with its complement. Families ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t$ are \emph{strongly incomparable} if every set in one family is incomparable with every set in another family. In 1976, Hilton conjectured that if ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ are uncomplemented and strongly incomparable, then $$\sum_{i=1}^t |{\mathcal A}_i|\le 2^{n-1}.$$ We confirm this conjecture by a matrix rank argument that encodes incomparability and uncomplementedness in the same matrix, which is quite different from the earlier methods on this problem. We also study weak incomparability, in which the same set may occur in different families. Goldwasser, Hilton and Zheng conjectured an upper bound in this setting and claimed that their conjecture is equivalent to Hilton's conjecture. We give counterexamples to their conjecture for every $t\ge3$ and identify the error in the claimed equivalence. We then propose a replacement conjecture and confirm it when $t$ is large. The upper bound $2^{n-1}$ in Hilton's conjecture can be attained if some families are allowed to by empty. It is natural to consider the maximum size of $\sum_{i=1}^t |{\mathcal A}_i|$ for uncomplemented and strongly incomparable families ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ when all families are required to be non-empty. Denote this maximum number by $M(n,t)$. We show that \[ 2^{n-1}-1\le M(n,t)\le 2^{n-1} \] for $n\ge3$ and $3\le t\le n$.
title: Hilton's Conjecture on Uncomplemented Incomparable Families

summary: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured. To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations. Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

summary: Vision-language Models (VLMs) can generate natural language explanations for complex decision-making scenarios. However, these explanations can sometimes be misleading, sounding convincing while containing incorrect or unsupported information. Automated explanation-quality metrics help researchers and practitioners evaluate large collections of explanations, but their scores alone provide limited support for identifying failure cases and understanding the reliability of these metrics. This paper presents a case study on how interactive visualizations can help researchers and practitioners evaluate both AI-generated explanations and automated explanation-quality metrics across large datasets. Based on formative interviews with nine AI researchers and practitioners, we designed an interactive visualization tool named ExCritique, situated in the task of Visual Question Answering (VQA). ExCritique visualizes the distributions of multiple automated quality metrics, allows users to explore thousands of data items, filter items and inspect the evidence behind individual scores. We compared ExCritique with a baseline interface without interactive visualizations in a controlled study involving 16 AI researchers and practitioners. Our findings suggest that the interactive visualizations in ExCritique helped users identify explanation-quality issues more efficiently and better understand automated quality metrics, supporting an effective way to measure the reliability of AI-generated explanations.
title: ExCritique: An Interactive Visual Interface to Evaluate AI-Generated Explanations at Scale

Automated explanation-quality metrics help researchers and practitioners evaluate large collections of explanations, but their scores alone provide limited support for identifying failure cases and understanding the reliability of these metrics. This paper presents a case study on how interactive visualizations can help researchers and practitioners evaluate both AI-generated explanations and automated explanation-quality metrics across large datasets. Based on formative interviews with nine AI researchers and practitioners, we designed an interactive visualization tool named ExCritique, situated in the task of Visual Question Answering (VQA). ExCritique visualizes the distributions of multiple automated quality metrics, allows users to explore thousands of data items, filter items and inspect the evidence behind individual scores. We compared ExCritique with a baseline interface without interactive visualizations in a controlled study involving 16 AI researchers and practitioners. Our findings suggest that the interactive visualizations in ExCritique helped users identify explanation-quality issues more efficiently and better understand automated quality metrics, supporting an effective way to measure the reliability of AI-generated explanations.
title: ExCritique: An Interactive Visual Interface to Evaluate AI-Generated Explanations at Scale

summary: Salient and camouflaged object detection (SOD and COD) both recover foreground support, yet most joint methods output only a binary mask and therefore cannot distinguish the type. USC12K distinguishes the two types, but its baseline USCNet still binds foreground existence to the type within a single normalization, so the failure source cannot be attributed. Our cross-task study shows that foreground localization transfers between SOD and COD, whereas type discrimination does not: a COD-only model recovers foreground on SOD images but its type judgement follows the training distribution rather than the foreground-background relation, so the two decisions require separate mechanisms. SegDis factorizes the output into an explicit foreground probability and a conditional type probability given foreground: FLR provides high-quality task-agnostic support, and RTA refines the SOD/COD assignment from the foreground-background relation without a task identifier. Because support is explicit, each ground-truth foreground pixel is classified as correct-type, type-swapped, or missed, so foreground-recovery and type-assignment errors are diagnosed separately. With PVT-v2-B2, SegDis attains 68.98% FG-mIoU and 78.35% mIoU on USC12K at about one-eighth of USCNet's parameters; CSCS is 5.75.

summary: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.
title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction

Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.

summary: For a bounded coherent complex of graded modules over the Raynaud ring $R$, we compare three descriptions of finite torsion: Ekedahl's pieces $A_f^2$ and $A_{\SSpart}^1$ of the biduality filtration, the nilpotent and semisimple parts of the torsion of the Illusie--Raynaud cœur, and the corresponding parts of the finite torsion $t^1$ of Ekedahl's diagonal cohomology. We show that finite torsion in bidegree $(0,i+1)$ measures the failure of the $i$th flat Artin--Mazur formal group to be smooth; we deduce that all flat Artin--Mazur formal groups of a Mazur--Ogus variety are smooth. For a smooth projective surface, we identify the three possible dual pairs in terms of the $p$-primary torsion of the geometric Néron--Severi group and the local-local and local-étale parts of the finite Picard quotient.
title: Finite torsion in Hodge--Witt cohomology groups

summary: Reproducibility in large language model (LLM) agent evaluation depends on replay fidelity: which parts of an execution trace are reconstructed, controlled, and compared. This matters for agent debugging, failure analysis, and counterfactual evaluation of stateful tool use. We audit all 71 unsuccessful executions in a fixed historical AppWorld corpus using 284 isolated fixed-code replay attempts. Reconstructed declared settings admit 42 cases under printed-output, pre-oracle database-delta, and native-verdict/test-count checks; resetting the random-number generator before each interaction admits 68. The 26-case gap contracts to four under database/oracle checks, with one endpoint unknown. Mechanism studies identify four materialized-state discrepancies despite matching outputs and verdicts. In one admitted endpoint pair, an identical API call yields matching responses but different row effects; common future Python RNG removes that deterministic difference in two paired repetitions. A separate JWT credential-equality program and alignment controls expose authentication/write differences, with missing repetitions retained. For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained output trackers restores the reference comparison without changing original cached contents. A purposeful 12-case BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested public-state, return, and verdict checks. We preserve resource censoring and infrastructure deviations. The contribution is a bounded empirical characterization of replay eligibility, hidden state, and test-oracle integration, without estimating debugger accuracy, repair gains, or method-ranking distortion.
title: Replay Fidelity in LLM Agent Evaluation: Randomness, Hidden State, and Test Oracles in AppWorld

summary: In this article, we study heavy-tailed alternatives to Gaussian-process surrogates, namely Student-$t$ processes, $α$-stable processes and Gaussian processes with heavy-tailed noise. These are Gaussian scale mixtures, and the position of the mixing variable decides whether the tails can be learned from a single realization. For process-level mixtures with a free amplitude, the profile likelihood of the mixing law is data-free and is maximized by the Gaussian law, the plug-in predictive is a data-free transformation of the Gaussian-process predictive, and no estimator can be consistent for the mixing law over the model along one path. For observation-level mixtures with symmetric $α$-stable noise, the tail index is identifiable. Further, for one-dimensional inputs under fixed-domain asymptotics with $α_0<2$ and compact hyperparameter sets, a cross-fitted plug-in estimator and the Laplace marginal-likelihood estimate computed at the global posterior mode attain the efficiency bound of the model with a known regression function, also for Matérn-$5/2$ sample paths. We also characterize small-sample failures of the Laplace approximation as folds of a posterior-mode branch and give a diagnostic. Finally, in a repeated Bayesian optimization study, observation-level tails reduced regret under gross outliers, as did Student-$t$ noise, and no degradation was detected under Gaussian noise.
title: Heavy tails in Gaussian-process surrogates: process-level profiling degeneracy versus observation-level identifiability

summary: Reproducible pipeline for the in silico screening of a 104-compound library of benzofuroxan, oxadiazole and hydrazone derivatives against five molecular targets related to alcohol-associated liver fibrosis: HDAC6, HDAC8, MAO-B, AT1R and KDM1A. This deposit accompanies the manuscript submitted to AppliedChem (MDPI) and is the repository to which its Data Availability Statement refers. Contents: the command-line scripts organised by stage, in a Spanish and an English edition; the desktop application that runs them; the per-phase user guides; the pinned environment specification; the provenance files of each run; and the intermediate result tables cited in the manuscript. The pipeline covers library canonicalisation and InChIKey assignment, biological activity spectrum prediction, molecular target prediction, cross-screening against the indexed literature, receptor and ligand preparation, molecular docking, interaction profiling, structural selection criteria, ADMET consensus across three platforms, multiparameter weighting, and the integration of the structural and ADMET criteria.
title: LIFFT in silico screening pipeline v3.0.3: scripts, desktop application, result tables and figure code

This deposit accompanies the manuscript submitted to AppliedChem (MDPI) and is the repository to which its Data Availability Statement refers. Contents: the command-line scripts organised by stage, in a Spanish and an English edition; the desktop application that runs them; the per-phase user guides; the pinned environment specification; the provenance files of each run; and the intermediate result tables cited in the manuscript. The pipeline covers library canonicalisation and InChIKey assignment, biological activity spectrum prediction, molecular target prediction, cross-screening against the indexed literature, receptor and ligand preparation, molecular docking, interaction profiling, structural selection criteria, ADMET consensus across three platforms, multiparameter weighting, and the integration of the structural and ADMET criteria.

summary: Code, cached results and preprint for Words to Coordinates (W2C), an uncertainty-aware NLP-geospatial framework that links what firms disclose about physical climate risk to what their assets face: taxonomy-aligned extraction (IFRS S2 with crosswalks to ESRS E1 and GRI 305) with provenance, geocoding with explicit precision classes, hazard-ensemble overlay and the Disclosure Gap Index with disclosure-exposure quadrants. The simulation study uses the real locations of 11,107 power plants (Global Power Plant Database v1.3.0) with synthetic hazards and disclosures, confirms a closed-form relation between geolocation error and exposure fidelity, and propagates extraction, geolocation and hazard-model uncertainty by Monte Carlo. Companion software to the preprint "Words to Coordinates: An Uncertainty-Aware NLP-Geospatial Framework for Measuring the Gap Between Disclosed and Physical Climate Risk".

summary: This work looks at the Riemann hypothesis from the standpoint of the Birth of Dimensions model (BD). The number line is treated as an arrow with the observer, the unit, at its centre; prime numbers as the only irreducible boundaries; and everything else as oscillations of their interaction. The main idea: the line 1/2 is the level of lost phase. When waves add without a common phase, their intensities add, and the deviation from balance grows as a square root — with exponent 1/2. Unique factorization makes the frequencies of the primes incommensurable, so their phases never agree. The oscillation of each prime is an exact cycle without amplitude; amplitude arises as a phenomenon of the relation to the observer. Each prime builds a triangle “observer — end 1/p”, and the line 1/2 is the common midline of all such triangles: that is why it is one for all primes. The mirror x → 1/x itself swaps 0 and ∞ — the two poles of one sphere; for phase its centre is the unit circle, for intensity the line 1/2. In the end 1/2 is read four times — through phase, amplitude, energy and geometry — and each time it is a root, a step towards the centre. The zeros of the zeta function are the points where the relation 1/ζ goes to infinity, and at the same time points of balance without phase. On the arrow itself there is one such infinity; their multitude is born of phase, one for each frequency, and on the mirror phase disappears and the function becomes real. In this language the Riemann hypothesis says that the loss of phase among the primes is complete: no oscillation rises above this level, and the infinity of each frequency does not split but stands on the mirror. All formulations reduce to one: at each frequency the balance is unique, and a unique balance coincides with its reflection and therefore stands at 1/2. The open part lies not in the primes themselves but in their relations. This is an interpretation, not a proof. Every step carries a status tag, as in BD: [K] — known mathematical fact, [H] — hypothesis or the author's interpretation, [O] — open question. The conclusion states exactly where the chain does not yet close. Version 4. Section 8, “Planned development: a standing wave between the small and large ends”, is added — a link to the physics of the series. The real part σ sets the longitudinal direction (scale, motion towards the small or large end), and the imaginary part t the transverse one (frequency and phase). On the line 1/2 the wave coincides with its reflection, and a pure standing wave arises; its nodes are the zeros of the zeta function. Off the line the amplitudes of the wave and its reflection differ, and the wave is partly travelling. Levels on the mirror are described through Gram points: N(T) = θ(T)/π + 1 + S(T) — there are as many zeros as levels, plus a small oscillation around the limit. Inside a level there is a straight line without phase; transitions are abrupt and dictated by balance. The section is marked as a plan for developing the idea, not a result. The reference list is extended.         Работа предлагает взгляд на гипотезу Римана со стороны модели «Рождение измерений» (РИ). Числовая ось рассматривается как стрела с наблюдателем-единицей в центре, простые числа — как единственные неразложимые границы, а всё остальное — как колебания их взаимодействия. Главная мысль: прямая 1/2 — это уровень потерянной фазы. Когда волны складываются без общей фазы, складываются их интенсивности, и отклонение от баланса растёт как корень — в степени 1/2. Единственность разложения на простые делает их частоты несоизмеримыми, поэтому фазы простых не согласуются. Колебание каждого простого — точный цикл без амплитуды; амплитуда возникает как явление связи с наблюдателем. Каждое простое строит треугольник «наблюдатель — конец 1/p»,
title: The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2: The Riemann Hypothesis in the Light of the Birth of Dimensions Model

summary: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. summary: Hybrid reasoning models interleave attention with recurrent mixers such as Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, whose state is cached between decoding steps. Prior work showed that storing this state in FP16 or INT8 with round-to-nearest (RTN) makes Mamba-2 and GDN hybrids more verbose, and that stochastic rounding (SR) fixes it. We study the other 16-bit format that serving engines expose, bf16, on six open hybrid reasoning models and 590 competition-math problems. With bf16 RTN state, five of six models reason longer (geometric-mean length 1.07x to 1.27x; also under greedy decoding in the two models tested) and hit the 32K token cap more often. On Qwen3.5-9B, cap hits rise from 118 to 223 and accuracy falls from 85.6% to 70.8%. On LiveCodeBench, both models tested also reason longer and lose 12.6 and 13.4 points of pass@1. Rerunning the capped items with a 128K budget halves the accuracy gap but does not close it (93.6% vs. 86.6%): bf16 runs that never finish are twice as common, and 85% of them are exact repetition loops. On Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2, by contrast, 30 of 31 extra caps finish at 128K, so the cost there is mostly extra tokens (exploratory). Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of five affected models, restores Qwen3.5-9B to 87.6% and brings code length and pass@1 near FP32 levels, so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution. With an integer-hash random generator, SR on Qwen3.5-9B matches FP32 on cap hits and accuracy (113 vs. 118; 85.6% for both) at the memory and decoding speed of bf16 RTN. In the Nemotron-Nano-v2 lineage, SR on 25% of heads (an intermediate-decay band) removes the effect, while random heads and the top teacher-forced-KL octiles do not; in Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5-9B the effect is spread across heads. We recommend that evaluations of hybrid models report the state dtype, cap rate and output length alongside accuracy.

summary: Hybrid reasoning models interleave attention with recurrent mixers such as Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, whose state is cached between decoding steps. Prior work showed that storing this state in FP16 or INT8 with round-to-nearest (RTN) makes Mamba-2 and GDN hybrids more verbose, and that stochastic rounding (SR) fixes it. We study the other 16-bit format that serving engines expose, bf16, on six open hybrid reasoning models and 590 competition-math problems. With bf16 RTN state, five of six models reason longer (geometric-mean length 1.07x to 1.27x; also under greedy decoding in the two models tested) and hit the 32K token cap more often. On Qwen3.5-9B, cap hits rise from 118 to 223 and accuracy falls from 85.6% to 70.8%. On LiveCodeBench, both models tested also reason longer and lose 12.6 and 13.4 points of pass@1. Rerunning the capped items with a 128K budget halves the accuracy gap but does not close it (93.6% vs. 86.6%): bf16 runs that never finish are twice as common, and 85% of them are exact repetition loops. On Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2, by contrast, 30 of 31 extra caps finish at 128K, so the cost there is mostly extra tokens (exploratory). Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of five affected models, restores Qwen3.5-9B to 87.6% and brings code length and pass@1 near FP32 levels, so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution. With an integer-hash random generator, SR on Qwen3.5-9B matches FP32 on cap hits and accuracy (113 vs. 118; 85.6% for both) at the memory and decoding speed of bf16 RTN. In the Nemotron-Nano-v2 lineage, SR on 25% of heads (an intermediate-decay band) removes the effect, while random heads and the top teacher-forced-KL octiles do not; in Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5-9B the effect is spread across heads. We recommend that evaluations of hybrid models report the state dtype, cap rate and output length alongside accuracy.

summary: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.
title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
