title: CRISPR-TRIAGE: Evaluation of Parameter-Efficient Bi-Modal Off-Target Prioritization Under Budget-Constrained Screening

summary: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation

summary: Overview The Earth Surface Anomaly dataset (v1.0) is a five-class, event-grouped Sentinel-2 benchmark for immediate disaster and surface-anomaly detection. It contains 622 samples grouped into 46 event or spatiotemporal observation units (17 source-named/inventory units and 29 observation groups, 2017–2025, globally distributed): 129 fire, 58 flood-context, 54 landslide, 204 crop-residue-burning and 177 retrogressive-thaw-slump samples. 595 samples carry source polygon-derived binary masks; 27 carry weak point inventories only; all 54 landslide samples include pre/post paired observations. Industrial heat sources (208 candidates) are excluded from this release and 17 visually ambiguous candidates are withheld, both enumerated in quality/excluded_samples.csv . Sample structure Each sample ( data/CODE/EVENT/SAMPLE/ ) provides a six-band Sentinel-2 L2A chip (declared bands B2, B3, B4, B8, B11, B12; aligned grid spacing does not imply native 10 m for every band), a 0/1 binary mask, RGB/NIR/SWIR previews, annotation.json and measured facts.json (CRS, transform, WGS84 bounds, geometry statistics, spectral indices, SHA256 checksums). Annotation-conditioned vision-language tasks (4–6 per sample depending on label strength and pairing) cover event classification, factual captioning, spatial reasoning, visual grounding, spectral comparison, and for suitable samples temporal reasoning and label provenance. Splits Group splits are precomputed: default splits/event_disjoint (443/102/77 train/val/test) and inherited splits/site_disjoint (433/114/75). Event-disjointness does not guarantee site-disjointness (1 measured case); use site_disjoint when required. Never randomly split patches from the same event. Screening and quality All 639 non-industrial candidates underwent AI-assisted visual screening of RGB, SWIR and target crops with review sheets and per-sample geometry/text audits retained in the release ( quality/ , visual_review.csv ). This is not independent expert pixel adjudication, field validation, or new external verification of every event identity. Limitations (documented in README, README_zh and DATA_DICTIONARY) Flood-context masks often follow existing river channels; no paired baseline establishes incremental inundation. Fire annotations can cover smoke, scars or hotspots and are not universally burned-area boundaries. Crop-residue burning is a source label; imagery alone does not establish fuel identity. Thaw mechanism/onset and landslide onset cannot be established from the supplied views alone. Point inventories (27 samples) are weak localization, not segmentation truth; polygon provenance does not guarantee exact pixel boundaries. Radiometric scale/offset and the inherited non-landslide band mapping have not been independently traced to every source product; facts.json indices are stored-DN calculations, not validated physical reflectance. External event-match references in index/external_verification_ledger.csv were not newly re-verified during release preparation. License and third-party terms CC BY 4.0 applies to the project-original annotations, revisions and documentation. Sentinel/Copernicus imagery is used under modified-data attribution terms and COOLR landslide inventories retain their original conditions; see LICENSE , licenses/ and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . No ESA or European Union endorsement is implied. Access The metadata and preview figures of this record are public. The files are distributed on an approved-request basis: use the Request access button on this record page and state your affiliation and intended use; requests are reviewed by the authors. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0 for research use, subject to the third-party imagery conditions listed in licenses/ and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Citation Zhao, W., & Wang, Q. (2026). title: Earth Surface Anomaly Dataset (v1.0): Five-Class Event-Grouped Sentinel-2 Observations for Immediate Disaster and Surface-Anomaly Detection

summary: Data and code for the manuscript "Auditing source dependence in clinical variant interpretation benchmarks" (under peer review).   The archive (one zip file) contains the frozen inputs (ClinGen Evidence Repository records retrieved on 29 August 2026; GeneBe output captured on 29 August 2026, reduced to the applied criteria with strengths, point sums and verdicts; ClinVar review status; per-variant extracts of ten annual ClinVar GRCh38 archives, 2017-2025), a per-variant identifier table (ClinGen Allele Registry and ClinVar identifiers, GRCh38 coordinates, HGVS descriptions), per-variant and per-target result tables, source masks, the historical-archive and source-intervention outputs for BIAS-2015 and InterVar, the BRCA2, LDLR and GCK functional extensions, the pre-registration of the temporal analysis, and the analysis, verification and figure code with replay instructions.   README.md maps the folders to the analyses and gives the commands that reproduce the results. THIRD_PARTY_SOURCES.md identifies the third-party code and data that were used but are not redistributed (BIAS-2015, InterVar, raw ClinVar releases, author functional datasets) by location, version and SHA-256.   Only public, de-identified variant records are included; there are no patient data.   Files are restricted during peer review; reviewers receive an access link through the journal's submission system. summary: The paper derives the discrete architecture of the vacuum from a scale-free, compressible primordial quantum fluid, demonstrating that spatial order emerges dynamically through spectral softening and topological condensation: Phonon-Roton Spectral Softening: Long-range dipolar velocity fields generated by solenoidal vortex rings induce intermediate-scale softening in the collective excitation spectrum, producing a stable roton minimum that selects a preferred spatial scale while precluding tachyonic vacuum decay. Analytical Scale Hierarchy: The ratio between the emergent lattice spacing and the microscopic vortex core radius is fixed to the inverse fine-structure constant through the self-consistent equilibrium between hydrodynamic circulation tension and conserved axial chiral twist charge, eliminating empirical fine-tuning. Helicity Invariance and Condensation: Total kinetic helicity is proven to be an exact constant of motion under compressible flow with quantum gradient pressure; acoustic radiation emitted during vortex filament reconnections carries away excess energy, driving Taylor relaxation into a stable, force-free Beltrami lattice. Continuous Band Embedding: Embedding the internal 861-node Johnson graph into a three-dimensional Bravais lattice broadens its discrete spectral levels into continuous energy bands, simultaneously generating a gapless acoustic Goldstone branch that defines the speed of light and a protected roton gap that structurally stabilizes the emergent vacuum against collapse .
title: Dynamical Emergence of Vacuum Structure: Phonon–Roton Spectral Organization and Topological Condensation in Primordial Turbulence

summary: Local large language model (LLM) inference is often described as private, verified, or reproducible without separating the technical claims behind those terms. This paper presents Caleta, an Apache-2.0 process supervisor and evidence layer around llama.cpp rather than a new inference engine. Caleta combines versioned manifests, exact-size and SHA-256 verification, controlled backend construction, a restricted OpenAI-compatible proxy, prompt-free execution records, benchmark reports, and a small conformance suite. Its contribution is the composition of these mechanisms into explicit contracts that distinguish integrity from authenticated provenance and privacy controls from operating-system isolation. We evaluate the implementation through static checks, 22 unit tests, deterministic end-to-end tests on Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows, and a pinned real-model experiment on Windows CPU using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct Q4_K_M and llama.cpp b11981. The real experiment validates artifact verification, startup, model listing, non-streaming and server-sent-event chat, and conformance. Three independent benchmark invocations produced fifteen successful warm requests with no failures. In this single configuration, median time to first token was 18.066 ms and median decode throughput was 54.394 tokens/s. These descriptive measurements do not establish cross-engine superiority, output quality, energy efficiency, or hardware-general performance. Raw JSON, commands, and environment metadata are published. Remaining challenges include signed manifests, time-of-check/time-of-use replacement, operating-system containment, proxy-overhead measurement, and broader experimental matrices.
title: Caleta: An Evidence-Oriented Trust Layer for Reproducible Local Large Language Model Inference

summary: Long-term conversational question answering can require several separated dialogue turns that support an answer only together. We introduce EviCover, a retrieval approach designed to retain this complementary evidence. It converts questions into observable evidence requirements, checks requirement coverage using retrieved source identifiers, and selects turns jointly. We track annotated support sets - the benchmark-labeled dialogue turns associated with each question - through retrieval, reranking, and final answer-generation context. We evaluate the baseline memory pipeline on generated, human-verified LoCoMo conversations and human-written REALTALK conversations, and examine EviCover on REALTALK's 108 multi-hop questions. Compared with the hybrid lexical/dense baseline, support-turn recall among 60 candidate turns rises from 0.526 to 0.575, and recall in the final ten-turn context rises from 0.349 to 0.379. The evidence funnel identifies separate discovery and selection failures, while paired answer evaluation shows that greater evidence recall does not yet establish a correctness gain. This analysis locates where complementary evidence is lost and distinguishes evidence retrieval from its use in answer generation.
title: Where Did the Evidence Go? Diagnosing Proof-Set Loss in Long-Term Conversational Memory

summary: # A Spectral Construction of Natural-Number Arithmetic [Archival DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22512592) ## Arithmetic with its construction history retained This paper constructs natural-number arithmetic from a correlation spectrum and then resolves its values into the expressions by which they are generated. Its central achievement is to connect three levels that are usually studied separately: arithmetic values, the histories of arithmetic operations, and an evolution acting on those histories. The resulting system retains both the familiar numerical laws and information that numerical evaluation alone removes. The source is minimal unbiased compositional change. The least-dimensional faithful irreducible real orthogonal carrier is a rotation plane. Independent composition, exact same-shape self-similarity and unit covariance determine square-root scaling and a Gaussian law. Local information and normalized total correlation give the characteristic local and global lengths. Preservation of constants selects Neumann closure within the stated separated nondegenerate homogeneous local boundary class. Spectral projections are ordered by their Gaussian response before an integer enumeration is introduced. Orientation selects the positive analytic modes. Pointwise modulation and circle-map composition define their addition and multiplication; modulation by the first positive mode defines successor. The paper proves the Peano recursion structure, unique prime factorization and canonical transport under scale and orientation changes. Winding degree certifies the resulting natural-number arithmetic. ## Resolving how a value is generated The next construction retains ordered, bracketed addition and multiplication expressions. Only the specified zero, unit and absorbing reductions are imposed at this level. Arithmetic evaluation identifies expressions with the same value, while each value has a finite expression fibre. This gives a precise space in which the construction of a number can itself be observed. The simplest example is six. Adding six unit leaves and multiplying an additive expression for three by an additive expression for two give the same root value and the same root energy. Their leaf counts are six and five, while their accumulated internal quadratic defects are thirty and thirty-one. In both cases leaf energy plus accumulated defect is thirty-six. The equality at the root coexists with a measurable difference in the construction. A recursive positive law gives equal weight to the admissible root channels and assembles their subhistories independently. This law differs from uniform counting of all complete expressions. Phase invariance determines a finite phase extension. Summing the resolved source over histories and phases recovers the original Gaussian mass of each mode exactly. Expression multiplicity therefore enriches the source without changing its original partition function. Weighted amplitude readout, probability pushforward and conditional expectation have distinct definitions. Exact variance and entropy identities separate the information in the root value from the information remaining within its fibre. The example of six has strictly positive conditional leaf-count variance, giving a concrete instance of information preserved by the resolved construction. ## A complete operator on generation histories The same source weights determine a parent-child assembly response. The paper constructs a nonnegative self-adjoint trace-class operator on the complete counting history space. Its trace tail has an explicit Gaussian bound independent of the number of expressions in each fibre. Finite root cutoffs converge in trace norm, and the full operator generates a contraction evolution with a dissipation identity. The decisive result is a nonzero transfer from an initially invisible history difference to a later value response. A difference supported on the six histories of four has zero initial value readout,

summary: This record provides supporting numerical data and code for the study "Entry, reciprocity, and severity in self-consistent wrong-motion optical flow." The study investigates a known optical-flow failure in which mutually consistent forward and backward estimates can correspond to an incorrect motion layer. Using controlled two-layer translations, it separately evaluates appearance-dependent alternate-side assignment, reciprocal wrong-motion consistency, and conditional error severity under near alternate-layer substitution. The supporting materials include source-level and pair-level numerical tables, plotted data, representative example arrays, figure-generation scripts, frozen experimental specifications, selected generator and evaluation code, verification scripts, and SHA-256 references to archived experimental results. The experiments use pretrained RAFT-Small, RAFT-Large, and GMFlow with STL-10 and BSDS500 image appearances. Reproducibility scope: The deposited materials support figure regeneration and examination of reported numerical summaries. Complete model prediction archives, original image archives, pretrained model checkpoints, and a complete inference environment are not included. Full prediction-to-metric verification requires the separately identified experimental archives. Original third-party image datasets remain subject to their respective providers' terms. No nuclear-decommissioning footage is included. File access is restricted pending review of publication rights and licensing.
title: Supporting data and code for Entry, reciprocity, and severity in self-consistent wrong-motion optical flow

summary: LLM-based agents extend LLMs with tool calls, memory, planning, and retrieval to act in external environments, but they are vulnerable to attacks at different workflow steps. Existing defenses, including prompt engineering and post-training alignment, primarily improve LLM-only safety and often overlook risks that arise from multi-step execution. External verification adds guardrails to check each step separately, but it typically ignores how risks can propagate across steps. We argue that we should consider risk transitions across dependent steps through the agent workflow, rather than separate verification on a single step. In this paper, we propose \textbf{T}ail-risk-aware \textbf{A}gent \textbf{S}afety (TAS), a tail-risk-aware safety framework that models agent workflow safety as a sequence of dependent safety states and constrains the rare but extreme risks (i.e., tail risk) with a shared budget. TAS first models safety-state transitions sequentially along the workflow as an MDP to trace risk propagation, then measures a tail-sensitive risk to target rare but high-cost risks (i.e., tail risk), and constrains the risk with a shared budget to derive a step-wise safety strategy. By constraining tail risk rather than the overall average, TAS suppresses rare high-cost failures while preserving utility in normal cases. Experiments show that TAS achieves better performance compared with eleven baselines across three benchmarks.
title: Tail-risk-aware Agent Safety: Constraining Tail Risks Across Multi-step LLM Agent Workflows

summary: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
title: ASCENT: Scale-Complementary External State for Frozen Long-Context Language Models

summary: Due to supply constraints, replacing damaged automotive components can be expensive and time-consuming, while replacing the entire component can be wasteful when much of it remains usable. This paper presents a pipeline to investigate whether missing geometry can be reconstructed as a repair patch using paired observations of the intact models and synthetically damaged components. Noise-free color, depth, and silhouette images were produced using the camera viewpoints. Depth differences were then used to identify the potential missing regions, while multi-view voxel reconstruction was used to estimate the missing portion. A pretrained DINOv2 model was also added to validate missing candidates and determine whether pretrained visual features could improve reconstruction. We tested the pipeline on 20 automotive CAD models, each with a synthetically removed portion. Each model was tested under four different conditions using two reconstruction methods for a total of 160 trials. The predictions were compared with the missing geometry of the unchanged ground-truth using predefined thresholds of the voxel intersection-over-union over 0.85 and the absolute relative volume error less than 15%. Of the 160 experimental trials, 109 of them satisfied both thresholds. Geometry-only reconstruction passed 16 of 20 components with eight views but only 10 of 20 with four adjacent views. Further analysis showed that 24 out of the 37 failed reconstructions could be categorized as unsuccessful because extra material was incorrectly added to areas that should have been empty. The implementation of DINOv2 into the pipeline did not improve the overall reconstruction accuracy and made prediction generation slower. For 13 verified tests, printing only the repaired sections instead of the entire parts reduced filament use by 93.08% and printing time by 89.39% based on the median results.
title: AI-Driven Repair of Missing Automotive Components

summary: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{é}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.
title: Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction

summary: Museum of One working paper · Version 1.0 · 10 November 2026 · 16 pages · 21 references A work can retain its title and historical date even when its materials, arrangement, or means of presentation have changed. This working paper examines four Korean archival and museum cases: Kim Yong-Ik’s Plane Object photographs and the history of “plain” and “place”; the differing production years assigned to Park Suk-won’s Jeok–Eungnyeok; the 1975 historical reference and 2016 materials of Lee Kang-so’s Untitled 75031; and Kim Kulim’s Mediator, used by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, to exemplify compound dating. MMCA’s acquisition narrative and publication guidance acknowledge remaking as part of collecting an experimental past. The paper reads that institutional practice alongside scholarship on the relations among images, material traces, and artwork identity. Aga Wielocha’s discussion of Danh Vo’s chandeliers provides a particularly revealing comparison: a title can date an object’s removal and transformation into art rather than its fabrication, just as a museum’s leading year can identify an earlier work rather than the age of its present components. These different histories require the event dated by each title or caption to remain explicit. Neither artist authorisation nor institutional recognition settles every claim about an earlier condition. The paper credits the overlapping demonstrations in the author’s Relational Archival Investigation papers and develops their implications for collecting, editorial preference, and historical inference. Its contribution is a comparative account of how names and dates sustain continuity without making the evidence for that continuity interchangeable. Evidence limits. The source base is documentary. Physical artworks, original versos, complete printing proofs and object-specific acquisition and conservation dossiers remain unexamined. Park’s two published dates establish a discrepancy without determining the original year or a sequence of database changes. A shared series title cannot identify an individual Kim Yong-Ik work. The eight- and ten-image accounts do not establish a sequence of additions to Lee’s work. Jung Eun Young is cited through the published abstracts. The four selected cases establish no national rate of discrepancy. This working paper has not undergone independent peer review. Relationship to Relational Archival Investigation. The RAI main paper , Documentary Supplement and Extended Case Studies already report the shared naming and date comparisons, the limits of series-title identification, and the difference between Lee’s photographic accounts. This paper extends that work through MMCA’s acquisition narrative and compound dating of Mediator , a sustained comparison with Korean scholarship and conservation research, and analysis of what later objects and records establish about earlier works. Its bibliography points to the cited OSF file versions. 김용익(평면 오브제), 박석원(적-응력), 이강소(무제 75031), 김구림(매개항)의 사례를 통해 한국 실험미술에서 작품의 제목과 연대, 재제작, 소장 기록이 어떤 역사적 주장을 뒷받침하는지 살핀다. 작품의 역사적 정체성과 현존 구성 요소의 제작 시기를 구분하며, 네 사례의 자료 범위와 기존 RAI 연구와의 관계를 명시한다.
title: Titles, Dates, and Reconstructed Works: Four Documentary Histories of Korean Experimental Art

summary: Recently, a new coordinate-based normalization has been introduced in [1] to represent tetrahedral similarity classes by normalized coordinates, enabling the study of LEB orbits as a discrete dynamical system. However, the uniqueness of this representation is not guaranteed when two or more edges adjacent to the selected longest edge have the same minimum length and remain admissible under the normalization criteria. In this paper, we demonstrate that different admissible choices may lead to distinct normalized coordinate representations of the same tetrahedral similarity class. We first present an explicit counterexample in which two admissible vertex labelings yield different normalized coordinate representations related by reflection, despite corresponding to the same similarity class. We then provide a systematic classification of the nine possible edge configurations arising in the selection of the canonical face when the longest edge of the tetrahedron is unique, and analyze the corresponding geometric and algebraic conditions. Our analysis identifies the configurations in which the normalization is non-unique and distinguishes them from those in which the ambiguity is resolved by the length criterion, angle criterion, or geometric symmetries. We further show that this non-uniqueness leads to an overcounting of distinct similarity classes.
title: Non-Uniqueness in the Coordinate-Based Normalization of Tetrahedral Similarity Classes

summary: In this paper, we study the inverse problem of determining the coefficient $q$ and the nonlinearity $F$ in the semilinear biharmonic equation $Δ^2 u+q(x)u=F(x,u)$ with Navier boundary data. The measurement consists of $\partial_νu(x_0)$ at a fixed boundary point $x_0$. We apply the mixed variation approach to linearize the nonlinear problem and construct semiclassical boundary-localized solutions for the linearized equation. Under suitable analyticity, nonresonance, and nondegeneracy assumptions on $q$ and $F$, we prove that this boundary point measurement uniquely determines both $q$ and $F$. We also establish boundary determination of all normal derivatives of $q$ and of the first nonzero Taylor coefficient of $F$ on a nonempty relatively open subset of the boundary. When the linear potential $q$ is known, we prove that either component of the Navier boundary input alone suffices to determine $F$, and that the polynomial nonlinearity can be uniquely determined without requiring any analyticity conditions. For suitable finite-dimensional classes of nonanalytic potentials, we also obtain, for fixed $F$, the stable determination of $q$ from finitely many boundary inputs and the associated point measurements. In addition, as an important supplement, we provide nontrivial examples verifying the main assumptions, as well as counterexamples concerning the recovery of the linear coefficient. Finally, we present numerical experiments that demonstrate the theoretical results.
title: Single-point determination of a potential and a nonlinearity in a semilinear biharmonic equation

summary: A family ${\mathcal A}\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ is \emph{uncomplemented} if it contains no set together with its complement. Families ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t$ are \emph{strongly incomparable} if every set in one family is incomparable with every set in another family. In 1976, Hilton conjectured that if ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ are uncomplemented and strongly incomparable, then $$\sum_{i=1}^t |{\mathcal A}_i|\le 2^{n-1}.$$ We confirm this conjecture by a matrix rank argument that encodes incomparability and uncomplementedness in the same matrix, which is quite different from the earlier methods on this problem. We also study weak incomparability, in which the same set may occur in different families. Goldwasser, Hilton and Zheng conjectured an upper bound in this setting and claimed that their conjecture is equivalent to Hilton's conjecture. We give counterexamples to their conjecture for every $t\ge3$ and identify the error in the claimed equivalence. We then propose a replacement conjecture and confirm it when $t$ is large. The upper bound $2^{n-1}$ in Hilton's conjecture can be attained if some families are allowed to by empty. It is natural to consider the maximum size of $\sum_{i=1}^t |{\mathcal A}_i|$ for uncomplemented and strongly incomparable families ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ when all families are required to be non-empty. Denote this maximum number by $M(n,t)$. We show that \[ 2^{n-1}-1\le M(n,t)\le 2^{n-1} \] for $n\ge3$ and $3\le t\le n$.
title: Hilton's Conjecture on Uncomplemented Incomparable Families

summary: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.
title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction

summary: Reproducible pipeline for the in silico screening of a 104-compound library of benzofuroxan, oxadiazole and hydrazone derivatives against five molecular targets related to alcohol-associated liver fibrosis: HDAC6, HDAC8, MAO-B, AT1R and KDM1A. This deposit accompanies the manuscript submitted to AppliedChem (MDPI) and is the repository to which its Data Availability Statement refers. Contents: the command-line scripts organised by stage, in a Spanish and an English edition; the desktop application that runs them; the per-phase user guides; the pinned environment specification; the provenance files of each run; and the intermediate result tables cited in the manuscript. The pipeline covers library canonicalisation and InChIKey assignment, biological activity spectrum prediction, molecular target prediction, cross-screening against the indexed literature, receptor and ligand preparation, molecular docking, interaction profiling, structural selection criteria, ADMET consensus across three platforms, multiparameter weighting, and the integration of the structural and ADMET criteria.
title: LIFFT in silico screening pipeline v3.0.3: scripts, desktop application, result tables and figure code

summary: This work looks at the Riemann hypothesis from the standpoint of the Birth of Dimensions model (BD). The number line is treated as an arrow with the observer, the unit, at its centre; prime numbers as the only irreducible boundaries; and everything else as oscillations of their interaction. The main idea: the line 1/2 is the level of lost phase. When waves add without a common phase, their intensities add, and the deviation from balance grows as a square root — with exponent 1/2. Unique factorization makes the frequencies of the primes incommensurable, so their phases never agree. The oscillation of each prime is an exact cycle without amplitude; amplitude arises as a phenomenon of the relation to the observer. Each prime builds a triangle “observer — end 1/p”, and the line 1/2 is the common midline of all such triangles: that is why it is one for all primes. The mirror x → 1/x itself swaps 0 and ∞ — the two poles of one sphere; for phase its centre is the unit circle, for intensity the line 1/2. In the end 1/2 is read four times — through phase, amplitude, energy and geometry — and each time it is a root, a step towards the centre. The zeros of the zeta function are the points where the relation 1/ζ goes to infinity, and at the same time points of balance without phase. On the arrow itself there is one such infinity; their multitude is born of phase, one for each frequency, and on the mirror phase disappears and the function becomes real. In this language the Riemann hypothesis says that the loss of phase among the primes is complete: no oscillation rises above this level, and the infinity of each frequency does not split but stands on the mirror. All formulations reduce to one: at each frequency the balance is unique, and a unique balance coincides with its reflection and therefore stands at 1/2. The open part lies not in the primes themselves but in their relations. This is an interpretation, not a proof. Every step carries a status tag, as in BD: [K] — known mathematical fact, [H] — hypothesis or the author's interpretation, [O] — open question. The conclusion states exactly where the chain does not yet close. Version 4. Section 8, “Planned development: a standing wave between the small and large ends”, is added — a link to the physics of the series. The real part σ sets the longitudinal direction (scale, motion towards the small or large end), and the imaginary part t the transverse one (frequency and phase). On the line 1/2 the wave coincides with its reflection, and a pure standing wave arises; its nodes are the zeros of the zeta function. Off the line the amplitudes of the wave and its reflection differ, and the wave is partly travelling. Levels on the mirror are described through Gram points: N(T) = θ(T)/π + 1 + S(T) — there are as many zeros as levels, plus a small oscillation around the limit. Inside a level there is a straight line without phase; transitions are abrupt and dictated by balance. The section is marked as a plan for developing the idea, not a result. The reference list is extended.         Работа предлагает взгляд на гипотезу Римана со стороны модели «Рождение измерений» (РИ). Числовая ось рассматривается как стрела с наблюдателем-единицей в центре, простые числа — как единственные неразложимые границы, а всё остальное — как колебания их взаимодействия. Главная мысль: прямая 1/2 — это уровень потерянной фазы. Когда волны складываются без общей фазы, складываются их интенсивности, и отклонение от баланса растёт как корень — в степени 1/2. Единственность разложения на простые делает их частоты несоизмеримыми, поэтому фазы простых не согласуются. Колебание каждого простого — точный цикл без амплитуды; амплитуда возникает как явление связи с наблюдателем. Каждое простое строит треугольник «наблюдатель — конец 1/p»,
title: The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2: The Riemann Hypothesis in the Light of the Birth of Dimensions Model

summary: Generative agents are game characters whose plans, conversations, and memories are written on the fly by a large language model (LLM). The original Generative Agents demonstration used cloud inference in a custom simulation. We present GARP, a platform for real-time generative agents inside Godot, and describe the Character Behavior System used in GARP 2. The complete loop runs on local hardware using a 3B-parameter open-weight model and no cloud service. Alongside the original planning, memory, and reflection, GARP gives each agent an emotion system driven by LLM appraisal, four graded personality axes drawn from the Big Five that set simulation parameters as well as prompt text, six needs whose urgency grows over time, and pairwise relationships updated after every conversation. The system narrows 50+ candidate actions to typically 3-8, constrains model responses with JSON schemas, and surfaces important memories in decision prompts. A layered optimization strategy (an adjustable game clock, decisions taken ahead of need, multi-tier caching, prompt compression, and fully asynchronous execution) keeps the game responsive while the model thinks. In a nine-scenario evaluation, 25 of 27 runs passed log-based checks. Both failures occurred in the birthday party scenario, where one guest omitted the event from their daily plan.
title: GARP: Real-Time Generative Agents on Local Hardware in a Game Engine

summary: Policy-gradient methods for adaptive linear quadratic control improve the feedback gain of an unknown plant online by gradient-type steps computed from closed-loop data. A recent framework of such methods, policy-gradient adaptive control (PGAC), takes one gradient-type step per sample, which its indirect form computes from an estimated model and its direct form directly from the data. Because data generated by a fixed linear feedback cannot identify the plant, PGAC adds a probing perturbation to the input and leaves its covariance as a design parameter. We study the adaptive LQR problem through a KL-regularized formulation, in which the probing is the randomness of a Gaussian policy kept close to a Gaussian reference policy, so that the cost of the probing is part of the objective. One policy improvement of this formulation gives a gain update together with a probing covariance. We show that, for suitable references centred at the current gain, this gain update is exactly PGAC's Gauss-Newton or natural-gradient update with any step size below a bound. We repeat this policy improvement, each time against a tempered copy of the current policy, and refer to this scheme as KL-regularized policy iteration (KLPI). On a known plant and with tempering, the cost of KLPI's gains converges linearly to the optimal cost, and the probing covariance keeps a floor proportional to the regularization weight. On an estimated plant, under conditions like PGAC's (small updates and sufficiently informative data), the closed loop stays stable, the cost of the gains converges linearly up to a bias, and the probing covariance again keeps this floor. In simulations at equal probing cost, the shape of KLPI's probing covariance, which PGAC can adopt, lowers the extra cost caused by suboptimal gains on nearly all tested plants, whereas KLPI's use of past iterations in its gain update changes this cost little.
title: KL-Regularized Policy Iteration for Adaptive LQR: Gain Updates and Probing from One Policy Improvement

summary: Correlation Matrix Memories (CMMs) store associations as sums of rank-one outer products, providing closed-form addressability, exact deletion, and linear attribution. While classical analyses assume random, orthogonal keys, semantic encoders produce correlated representations. We analyse CMMs under correlated keys using frame-theoretic coherence: (i) capacity bounds yielding an encoder-independent limit $n \le d(1+\varepsilon^2)$ for mean squared crosstalk $\varepsilon^2$; (ii) an exact characterisation of the collateral effect of deleting an association, guaranteeing that deletion never invalidates certified associations; and (iii) a geometric transparency bound demonstrating why attribution requires candidate sets of centred keys. On this basis, we introduce Topology-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Associative Retrieval (TANSAR). TANSAR traverses a directed acyclic association graph, prunes invalid paths via sound ground Horn constraints, and injects a representation derived strictly from the verified path into the residual stream of a frozen language model, guarded by a Clopper--Pearson selective-risk gate. Controlled experiments confirm all theoretical bounds. In multi-hop knowledge editing, Horn pruning reduces answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, whereas Hopfield retrieval incurs 24% contradictions when stale associations remain stored (and 0% if stale associations are removed). An end-to-end edit transaction requires 13.6 ms on a standard CPU and 2.37 ms on GPU. The symbolic component matches gold labels across all 600 ProofWriter theories and achieves 94.0% agreement on FOLIO, demonstrating sound and efficient multi-hop associative retrieval with exact unlearning.
title: TANSAR: Editable and Attributable Correlation Matrix Memories under Correlated Keys, with Rule-Constrained Multi-Hop Knowledge Editing

summary: Stellarators are fusion devices that use externally generated, three-dimensional magnetic fields to confine hot plasma and offer a promising route to commercial fusion. Their electromagnetic coils pose a challenging design problem: they must reproduce the target magnetic field while satisfying engineering constraints and remaining practical and cost-effective to manufacture. Finding suitable geometries is a highly nonlinear inverse problem that generally has neither a closed-form nor a unique solution. This problem lies at the heart of stellarator design. We introduce CoilStellaration, a dataset and benchmark for learning the mapping between coil geometries from target plasma magnetic fields and engineering requirements. The dataset contains 177,000 optimized filamentary coilsets targeting plasma equilibria from ConStellaration, with sampled engineering requirements and achieved geometric and magnetic-field metrics. It spans multiple coil counts and field-period numbers, supporting studies of both specialized and shared models across configurations. The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and requirements on coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field error. We show that magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, with learned models rarely satisfying all requirements simultaneously. However, using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. We release baseline models and evaluation code to support reproducible research on both direct coil generation and learned optimization initializations. By lowering the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to engage with stellarator coil design, we aim to accelerate progress toward practical, cost-effective stellarator power plants.
title: CoilStellaration: A Dataset and Benchmark for Engineering-Aware Stellarator Coilset Generation

summary: Sampling only part of the data reduces the cost of each iteration in an inverse problem, but can make reconstruction updates unreliable. We study stochastic multilevel sampling, which computes updates on a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of correction spaces. The guiding idea is that a small sample may support a reliable coarse-grid update even when it provides insufficient information for a fine-grid update. For quadratic objectives, we identify conditions under which corrections computed from sampled data decrease the full-data objective. In small-batch experiments with computed tomography and periodic deblurring, the stochastic multilevel method improves reconstruction accuracy over matched single-level methods. In an increasingly ill-conditioned CT refinement with a fixed number of projection angles, the single-level error increases as the image dimension grows, whereas a deep hierarchy maintains or improves accuracy and outperforms full-data single-level optimization at the same number of forward and adjoint applications. The gains persist across the tested local solvers and strengthen with deeper hierarchies. A separate known-probe ptychography study provides complementary evidence for the benefit of hierarchical corrections for nonlinear inverse problems.
title: Stochastic Multilevel Sampling for Inverse Problems via Coarse-Space Identifiability

summary: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.
title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity

summary: Recent systems such as the eBPF Certificate Framework (BCF) and Proof-Carrying BPF address the imprecision in the Linux eBPF verifier with proof-carrying code. When the verifier's abstract domains cannot prove a safety condition, an in-kernel proof checker checks an untrusted user-space refutation proof. A single bug in this checker can compromise the security of the entire kernel. While formalizing BCF's in-kernel checker, we discovered 13 bugs such as unsound rewrite rules, silently unchecked proof steps, and memory safety errors. We demonstrate that forged certificates can trick the kernel to accept arbitrary unsafe eBPF programs. To address this problem, we propose Keel, a formally verified in-kernel proof checker for the Linux eBPF verifier. First, we specify the checker as a pure functional program in Lean and prove its soundness against bit-vector semantics. We decouple the steps of the proof certificate checker from the mathematical rewrite rules, which enables us to extend the rewrite rules without the need to change the checker. Second, we implement the checker in EmbC, a deeply embedded C fragment, and prove that our C implementation refines the functional specification without undefined behavior or memory leaks. Third, using an amortized potential argument, we prove linear time and memory bounds for the C checker. Keel is correct-by-construction while also being faster than the BCF checker inside the kernel, 1.3X in total and 2.0X on the slowest 1.4% of certificates.
title: Keel: A Verified In-Kernel Proof Checker for Proof Carrying BPF

summary: The Retriangulation of Great Britain, begun in 1936, left thousands of concrete pillars on British hilltops and gave the country its National Grid. Treating the Ordnance Survey's legacy station list as data, this paper asks four questions, pre-specified in a written plan: how the network is laid out, when it was built, how much is recorded destroyed, and whether a modern open terrain model reproduces the rule that neighbouring stations of the same order must be intervisible. Grouping 31,521 mark records into 24,433 stations (6,573 pillars), I find a clear hierarchy of spacing (median nearest same-order distance 19.6 km for primary stations, 7.1 km for secondary and 4.3 km for third-order pillars), primaries far more regular than random points (Clark and Evans ratio 1.54 against 1.02 to 1.17), and 99.0% of pillars dated 1936 to 1962. Over Terrain Tiles (zoom 9), with curvature and refraction, 228 of 240 nearest-neighbour primary lines are clear (95.0%, 95% CI 91.5 to 97.1), against 16.6% when both ends are moved 1 km and 10.9% for random land pairs of the same lengths. Of the 12 failures, 8 involve a structure without a recorded height and 3 a station observed from a steel tower; one is unexplained. The result depends on using surveyed station heights: with the terrain model's own heights at the ends, only 67.1% of lines are clear, because the model sits a median 22 m below surveyed pillar tops. Pillars are far less often recorded destroyed (6.3%) than other marks. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/trig-network/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/trig-network . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/trig-network/ . Text, figures and derived data CC BY 4.0, except that OS station fields remain under the Open Government Licence v3.0 and the OSM-derived file osm_points.csv is ODbL; code MIT.

summary: In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to space-filling input design for nonlinear system identification, in which an agent learns a control policy that actively drives the system to explore its state space. Classical input design, developed mainly for linear models, minimises the covariance of the estimated parameters. For nonlinear black-box models, however, the dominant error is the bias induced by the model structure over the region of interest, which motivates space-filling strategies that seek to cover the system state space. Existing space-filling approaches rely on predefined input signal classes and require solving explicit optimisation problems. Unlike these methods, the proposed approach requires no input class to be selected and no frequency band to be tuned for the system at hand, satisfies and amplitude bound by construction, and adapts to varying initial conditions through its observation-based policy without re-optimisation. The learned excitation signals exhibit physically meaningful behaviours, such as resonance excitation and amplitude modulation. The approach is evaluated against tuned swept sine and crest-factor-optimised multisine excitations, and against a state-of-the-art space-filling multisine design, on two nonlinear benchmark systems: a mass-spring-damper with nonlinear stiffness and a Van der Pol oscillator. Under the same amplitude bound, the learned policy achieves the best overall space-filling performance on both systems and distributes its samples more uniformly than the state-of-the-art design.

summary: Post-Temporal Physics and the SPARC Galaxy Rotation Data — An Independently Audited Empirical Benchmark A Fourteen-Year Foundational Research Program Reaches a Reproducible Empirical Milestone Post-Temporal Physics (PTP) originated in 2012 as a foundational scientific research program investigating whether physical existence, persistence, causality, interaction, and observable behavior could be reconstructed from principles more primitive than conventional continuous spacetime and geometric descriptions. Its development has involved fourteen years of theoretical investigation, mathematical construction, physical analysis, and successive reformulations aimed at establishing a coherent alternative framework for understanding physical law. The research initially progressed through a substantial transitional program encompassing twenty native physics sectoral expansions (18 Transitonal Sectoral Expansions have not been released due to sever dual-use concern). These investigations explored the implications of the developing theory across multiple physical sectors and exposed the mathematical requirements of constructing a unified foundational system. The subsequent development of Ledgeral Mathematics provided a dedicated finite mathematical architecture through which the physical theory could be reconstructed with explicitly defined primitive objects, operations, admissibility conditions, and verification procedures. This progression culminated in the consolidated formulation of Post-Temporal Physics: The Finite Ledgeral Reconstruction of Existence, Persistence, and Physical Law , supported by Ledgeral Mathematics: A Finite Algebra of Recursion, Admissibility, Projection, and Survivor Structure and the companion Applied Ledgeral Mathematics research program and their respective sectoral and subsectoral expansions. Within this architecture, physical standing is described through finite retained records, admissibility, recursion, projection, survivor formation, residue accounting, and auditable relationships. Conventional physical quantities are admitted through specified recovery procedures, while continuum spacetime and geometric structures are not assigned primitive status within the native formulation. The present empirical release represents a significant milestone in this long-term undertaking. It establishes a reproducible astronomical benchmark through which a specified observational recovery prescription associated with the Post-Temporal Physics research program is evaluated against measured galaxy rotation behavior.   The Empirical Investigation The investigation uses observational data from the SPARC database, originally assembled by Lelli, McGaugh, and Schombert. SPARC provides measured galaxy rotation curves and baryonic mass models suitable for examining the relationship between observed circular velocities and the gravitational contribution attributed to measured baryonic matter. The analysis retains 3,269 usable radial observational records from 163 galaxies. A galaxy-level training and testing procedure separates 114 galaxies, containing 2,216 radial records, from 49 withheld galaxies containing 1,053 observational measurements. A single characteristic acceleration scale is calibrated using the designated training population. The resulting observational recovery prescription is subsequently evaluated against the withheld galaxies without additional galaxy-specific calibration of the principal fitted scale. The recovered predictions achieve a root-mean-square velocity error of approximately 22.91 kilometers per second, compared with approximately 57.52 kilometers per second for the specified fixed baryon-only reference. This corresponds to an approximately 60.2 percent reduction in RMS prediction error. At the individual galaxy level, the tested prescription improves predictive accuracy relative to the baryon-only reference in 45 of the 49 withheld galaxies. summary: Purpose: The aim of this study was to define whether a gesture similarity index (GSI) based on muscle synergies extracted by a wearable device (REMO, Morecognition Ltd, Turin, Italy) provides the same information of clinical outcome measures, after specific training of hand function. The secondary aim was to define whether specific hand tasks could be considered as target tasks for hand function assessment, after stroke.  Methods: REMO is a wearable composed of 8 surface-electromyography (sEMG) sensors able to detect forearm muscles activation in real-time. The acquisition protocol consisted of bilateral execution of wrist and hand movements of the Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA-Hand, maximum score 24 points) using REMO. Then, we applied the Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) algorithm to extract muscle synergies from the sEMG signals. We calculated the GSI which represents the mathematical distance between the muscle synergies extracted from a group of elderly-healthy subjects (as reference model) and from the patient's performance (the lowest distance represented the maximum similarity, GSI=100%). Stroke survivors were assessed before (T0) and after (T1) a specific hand training of 15 sessions (1 hour each, 5 time/week, 3 weeks) (ClinicalTrial.gov ID NCT05815368). After randomization, the patients underwent to a task-specific training (control group, CG) or biofeedback training using REMO (experimental group, EG). We compared the FMA-Hand and GSI results before and after the training, and we calculated Spearman's correlation to investigate the relationship between the level of FMA-Hand and the GSI index.  Results: We collected data from a control group of 4 elderly-healthy subjects (age 74±6.3) and a group of 14 people with diagnosis of stroke (age 64.7±13.8). Overall patients showed a significant hand motor recovery (FMA-Hand: T0=11.8 ± 3.0; T1=15.7 ± 3.7; p=0.002). Based on GSI results, data showed a statistically significant improvement in wrist circumduction movements (T0= 82% ± 4.5%; T1= 85.4% ± 4.3%; p=0.048). No differences between groups were found both in FMA-Hand and in GSI analysis. Then, at the baseline, correlation analysis showed a positive significant correlation between FMA-Hand and GSI value in circumduction movement (r=0.54; p=0.046).  Conclusion(s): The results showed that a specific hand motor training induced a significant improvement in patients’ functional level. GSI results showed that wrist circumduction could be a target movement to describe motor recovery after stroke. Future perspectives will include a wider data collection to confirm the results.
title: Gesture similarity index based on muscle synergies model describing hand recovery after stroke: preliminary results of a randomised controlled trial

summary: Voters often see a candidate's face before learning about the candidate's political positions. Building on evidence that rapid visual impressions predict electoral outcomes, we examine how time pressure and information costs shape political learning and whether these constraints produce distinct patterns of scrutiny for women candidates. We conduct a preregistered three-arm online visual conjoint experiment using photographs and political information drawn from Colombian electoral data. Respondents are randomly assigned to make these choices under a nine-second deadline, an effort cost for accessing political information, or an unconstrained baseline. Candidate pairings, task order, and left-right placement are randomized within respondents. The experiment measures recorded candidate selection, candidate-specific information acquisition, and decision time. Working paper (work in progress). The oTree implementation is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24089204.
title: Faces or Facts? Experimental Evidence on Time Pressure, Information Costs, and Gender Bias in Electoral Choice

summary: How much of Great Britain lay within a day's travel of London, and how did that change between the coaching era and today? I build a multimodal network model on a 2 km grid for five dates (1750, the 1830s, 1850, 1910 and today) from historical GIS of the turnpike roads of England and Wales and the railways of 1851, a reconstruction of the 1910 rail network, and OpenStreetMap. Coach speeds are fitted to scheduled times of London coach services in 1836 (136 destinations) and to twelve cited journeys of 1739 to 1764; train speeds come from published averages; every era is tested on journeys it was not fitted to. The 1830s model reproduces the 1837 mail-coach timetable with a median absolute error of 12%. The 1750 model fails the error threshold set in advance (28% against 25%), so its map is a rough sketch. The 1850 and 1910 models use average train speeds and are slower than documented expresses by a median 46% and 34%, on four and six journeys, so their areas are lower bounds. Leaving Charing Cross at dawn, twelve hours of travel reached 5% of Great Britain's land in 1750, 19% in the 1830s, at least 47% in 1850, at least 72% in 1910 and 97% today. The largest gain per year came between the 1830s and 1850, when the first railways multiplied the area within a day by at least 2.5 in about fifteen years. The surfaces and code are released for reuse. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/day-from-london/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/day-from-london . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/day-from-london/. Sources: turnpike roads and London coach services of 1819 and 1836 (Rosevear, Bogart, Shaw-Taylor and Satchell, openICPSR 195126 and 195128; derived results only); 1851 England, Wales and Scotland rail lines (Satchell et al., UK Data Service ReShare SN 852991, CC BY 4.0); OpenStreetMap contributors via OpenFreeMap (ODbL); train speeds from Leunig (2006). Text, figures and derived data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.

summary: How much of Great Britain lay within a day's travel of London, and how did that change between the coaching era and today? I build a multimodal network model on a 2 km grid for five dates (1750, the 1830s, 1850, 1910 and today) from historical GIS of the turnpike roads of England and Wales and the railways of 1851, a reconstruction of the 1910 rail network, and OpenStreetMap. Coach speeds are fitted to scheduled times of London coach services in 1836 (136 destinations) and to twelve cited journeys of 1739 to 1764; train speeds come from published averages; every era is tested on journeys it was not fitted to. The 1830s model reproduces the 1837 mail-coach timetable with a median absolute error of 12%. The 1750 model fails the error threshold set in advance (28% against 25%), so its map is a rough sketch. The 1850 and 1910 models use average train speeds and are slower than documented expresses by a median 46% and 34%, on four and six journeys, so their areas are lower bounds. Leaving Charing Cross at dawn, twelve hours of travel reached 5% of Great Britain's land in 1750, 19% in the 1830s, at least 47% in 1850, at least 72% in 1910 and 97% today. The largest gain per year came between the 1830s and 1850, when the first railways multiplied the area within a day by at least 2.5 in about fifteen years. summary: This study investigates the inverse domination number and inverse total domination number of Sierpiński Star graphs, contributing to the broader study of domination theory in graph theory. Domination parameters play an important role in understanding graph structures and have practical applications in areas such as computer networks, communication systems, and network security, where efficient selection of primary and backup nodes is essential. Building on previous studies of inverse domination and inverse total domination in various graph classes, this research focuses on the distinctive structural properties of Sierpiński Star graphs, which are constructed based on the Sierpiński triangle. The study examines the relationships between domination sets, inverse dominating sets, and inverse total dominating sets within these graphs. Through mathematical analysis and graph-theoretic techniques, it seeks to establish the corresponding inverse domination parameters and provide results that extend existing knowledge of domination in specially structured graphs. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of domination theory and provide a foundation for further investigations of inverse domination parameters in fractal-related graph structures.

summary: This paper examines the concept of permission within the set-theoretical approach to the logical theory of normative systems. Drawing on Alchourrón and Bulygin’s expressive conception of norms, and Žarnić’s formal reconstruction of von Wright’s later deontic logic, the study argues that the standard interpretation of permission as the derogation of a command fails to capture its pragmatic function. Building on a distinction between prescriptive and descriptive uses of deontic language, the paper develops an alternative reinterpretation of the set-theoretical framework in which permission is treated as an autonomous prescriptive speech act. Within this model, the relations among obligation, prohibition, and permission are expressed through two sets—commanded and permitted act-propositions—and then two perfection properties of ideal normative systems are identified—inner consistency and relational consistency. Finally, the analysis reveals that the notion of permission is even more ambiguous than the literature has so far acknowledged, distinguishing four types—normative, weak (negative), unilateral positive, and bilateral positive—and shows that the principle “Obligation implies permission” is valid only under specific interpretations of positive permission.
title: Four concepts of permission
