summary: The World on Record Index (TWR) — version 1.2.0 Released 9 November 2026. Concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23997606 resolves to the latest version. What is new: the sector layer 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 published one score per country-year. This release adds  goal_level  — one score per country-year  per SDG goal  — so the measure can say  what  a government stopped reporting, not only that it reported less. Sixteen goals are scored.  Goal 7 is not : it has three series, too few to identify a factor. That is a structural fact about the goal, not a judgement on it. Each goal is a  separate  unidimensional 2PL fit on that goal's own series, drawn from the same 524 that build the overall index. A goal's score therefore owes nothing to the other fifteen, and both layers sit on the same scale. The layer is not a restatement of the overall index. Across the sixteen goals a median of  64%  of the variation in goal-level reporting is not explained by a country's overall level — from 18% for goal 17 to 99.9% for goal 15. What it is checked against Check Result Convergence 16 of 16 goals, 19–73 EM cycles each Reliability 0.772–0.953, median  0.844 ; every goal above 0.70 Median posterior SD 0.338 (overall index: 0.114) Bootstrap, 500 replicates 0 failed replicates ; sampling SD is 7–42% of the posterior SE, median 13% Held-out series Fit on 70% of a goal's series, predict the held-out 30%: median AUC  0.725  against a per-series permutation null at  0.500 The bootstrap result means the published standard errors are  conservative  — they already cover item-parameter uncertainty with room to spare. Report the posterior SE, not the bootstrap SD. The held-out test is the first direct check that a goal score predicts reporting it was not fitted on. Thirteen of sixteen goals score 0.649 or better. The three weakest — goal 17 (0.618), goal 15 (0.526) and goal 6 (0.479) — are precisely the three already set apart on content grounds, which the test did not know. Disclose, do not gate Every goal fitted is published.  Nothing is excluded for imprecision, and 0.70 (Nunnally) is reported as a reference point, not applied as a cut. Each goal ships with four numbers a reader can weigh it by: reliability  — 0.772 to 0.953 se_median  — the typical error bar on that goal's scores weight_top5_pct  — how concentrated the score is in its five heaviest series weight_agency_pct  — how much of the score rests on series the custodian agency produces rather than the country Two goals carry  release = hold_content . The hold is on  content  grounds and for  different reasons , never on precision: Goal 6  is largely satellite measurement of lakes, wetlands and river flow. "Reported" there mostly records whether an agency published a dataset, not a country's choice. Goal 15  is overwhelmingly country-produced, but a third of its series are treaty and policy instruments (Nagoya Protocol, Aichi targets, NBSAP), which may track commitment status rather than reporting effort. An error bar cannot warn a reader about either, so the flag travels with the data. Both goals are published in full. Known limitations Weight concentration.  Within a goal, small groups of series that are always reported together can carry much of the score — in goal 10 the five heaviest series carry 80%, in goal 1 75%. These groups are near-duplicates that the variant rule does not collapse, because they are not reported identically: in goal 1, India, Sri Lanka and Malaysia report the education and health breakdowns but never the aggregate, every year from 2015 to 2023. Collapsing them would erase those reporting choices, so they are disclosed in  weight_top5_pct  instead. Modelling the dependence directly is deferred. Provenance.   weight_agency_pct  records h
title: The World on Record: statistical reporting across countries, policy sectors, and time

summary: CRISPR-TRIAGE is an open-science computational biology research archive evaluating parameter-efficient off-target prioritization under budget-constrained experimental validation budgets (K <= 50). This package contains the complete trained model checkpoints, multi-seed training pipelines (5 random seeds), biophysical feature extractors, pre-registered baseline models (LightGBM GBDT, Pairwise 1D-CNN, Logistic Regression, crispAI architecture), and evaluation results across two external cellular benchmarks (Listgarten 2018 GUIDE-seq and K562 cellular compilation). Key Scientific Findings & Methodological Disclosure: Algorithmic Parity with Gradient Boosted Trees: On the deduplicated independent cellular benchmark (K562 retrospective multi-assay compilation from DeepCRISPR / Yang et al. 2023; 11 guides, 16,172 unique candidate pairs, 110 confirmed positive guide-target sequence pairs without genomic coordinates), standard gradient boosting (LightGBM GBDT) trained on 15 simple biophysical mismatch features achieves Macro Recall@20 = 0.6350 vs 0.6416 for CRISPR-TRIAGE (margin +0.0066 / +0.66%; paired Wilcoxon W = 18.0, p = 1.0000; 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0979, +0.0900]). LightGBM runs 2.39x faster with 0 neural parameters. While lack of statistically significant superiority does not prove biological equivalence or disprove neural-network utility, the empirical evidence failed to reject the null hypothesis of no difference vs LightGBM under available statistical power. Multi-Seed Volatility in CRISPR Modeling: Retraining across 5 independent random seeds reveals substantial Macro Recall@20 fluctuations (+-6.5% standard deviation on identical data), demonstrating that single-seed reporting in the CRISPR machine-learning literature frequently reflects random seed-selection noise rather than genuine algorithmic superiority. Dataset Deduplication Importance: Forensic auditing documented the impact of 1,613 duplicate candidate rows (and 2 duplicate confirmed positive sites) in the K562 compilation, showing how uncleaned duplicates distort evaluation metrics. Two-Tier Reproducibility Scope: Tier 1 (Saved-Model Inference & K562 Cellular Benchmark Reproduction): 100% self-contained in this archive. All 5 trained seed weights, baselines, scalers, predictions, metric summaries, and the K562 cellular cohort execute fully offline without internet access. Tier 2 (Full Retraining on Primary Assay Datasets): Full retraining from raw sequence reads and complete Listgarten raw dataset reproduction requires separately downloading the 4 un-subsampled raw assay datasets (>20MB each), registered with authoritative accessions and cryptographic SHA256 checksums in DATA_MANIFEST.csv. Licensing, Provenance & Third-Party Rights: CRISPR-TRIAGE code, models, and documentation are licensed under the permissive MIT License. The crispAI architecture code (src/crispai_official/) is under MIT License (Copyright 2023 Furkan Ozden; reference: Özden & Minary, NAR 2024). Pretrained third-party weights for crispAI are omitted from the archive to ensure compliance with conflicting upstream documentation, with archive extraction utilities provided for the authors' official Zenodo records (13335960 / 12609337). Bundled K562 benchmark datasets are distributed under CC BY 4.0 (Yang et al. CSBJ 2023; Chuai et al. Genome Biol 2018). Raw CFD scoring lookup matrices (Doench et al. 2016 Supplementary Table 19) are strictly omitted from the release archive for third-party rights compliance; tested user-side acquisition and verification utilities are provided via scripts/download_cfd_matrices.py. See the root LICENSE file for full details.
title: CRISPR-TRIAGE: Evaluation of Parameter-Efficient Bi-Modal Off-Target Prioritization Under Budget-Constrained Screening

summary: Overview The Earth Surface Anomaly dataset (v1.0) is a five-class, event-grouped Sentinel-2 benchmark for immediate disaster and surface-anomaly detection. It contains 622 samples grouped into 46 event or spatiotemporal observation units (17 source-named/inventory units and 29 observation groups, 2017–2025, globally distributed): 129 fire, 58 flood-context, 54 landslide, 204 crop-residue-burning and 177 retrogressive-thaw-slump samples. 595 samples carry source polygon-derived binary masks; 27 carry weak point inventories only; all 54 landslide samples include pre/post paired observations. Industrial heat sources (208 candidates) are excluded from this release and 17 visually ambiguous candidates are withheld, both enumerated in quality/excluded_samples.csv . Sample structure Each sample ( data/CODE/EVENT/SAMPLE/ ) provides a six-band Sentinel-2 L2A chip (declared bands B2, B3, B4, B8, B11, B12; aligned grid spacing does not imply native 10 m for every band), a 0/1 binary mask, RGB/NIR/SWIR previews, annotation.json and measured facts.json (CRS, transform, WGS84 bounds, geometry statistics, spectral indices, SHA256 checksums). Annotation-conditioned vision-language tasks (4–6 per sample depending on label strength and pairing) cover event classification, factual captioning, spatial reasoning, visual grounding, spectral comparison, and for suitable samples temporal reasoning and label provenance. Splits Group splits are precomputed: default splits/event_disjoint (443/102/77 train/val/test) and inherited splits/site_disjoint (433/114/75). Event-disjointness does not guarantee site-disjointness (1 measured case); use site_disjoint when required. Never randomly split patches from the same event. Screening and quality All 639 non-industrial candidates underwent AI-assisted visual screening of RGB, SWIR and target crops with review sheets and per-sample geometry/text audits retained in the release ( quality/ , visual_review.csv ). This is not independent expert pixel adjudication, field validation, or new external verification of every event identity. Limitations (documented in README, README_zh and DATA_DICTIONARY) Flood-context masks often follow existing river channels; no paired baseline establishes incremental inundation. Fire annotations can cover smoke, scars or hotspots and are not universally burned-area boundaries. Crop-residue burning is a source label; imagery alone does not establish fuel identity. Thaw mechanism/onset and landslide onset cannot be established from the supplied views alone. Point inventories (27 samples) are weak localization, not segmentation truth; polygon provenance does not guarantee exact pixel boundaries. Radiometric scale/offset and the inherited non-landslide band mapping have not been independently traced to every source product; facts.json indices are stored-DN calculations, not validated physical reflectance. External event-match references in index/external_verification_ledger.csv were not newly re-verified during release preparation. License and third-party terms CC BY 4.0 applies to the project-original annotations, revisions and documentation. Sentinel/Copernicus imagery is used under modified-data attribution terms and COOLR landslide inventories retain their original conditions; see LICENSE , licenses/ and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . No ESA or European Union endorsement is implied. Access The metadata and preview figures of this record are public. The files are distributed on an approved-request basis: use the Request access button on this record page and state your affiliation and intended use; requests are reviewed by the authors. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0 for research use, subject to the third-party imagery conditions listed in licenses/ and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Citation Zhao, W., & Wang, Q. (2026). summary: Local large language model (LLM) inference is often described as private, verified, or reproducible without separating the technical claims behind those terms. This paper presents Caleta, an Apache-2.0 process supervisor and evidence layer around llama.cpp rather than a new inference engine. Caleta combines versioned manifests, exact-size and SHA-256 verification, controlled backend construction, a restricted OpenAI-compatible proxy, prompt-free execution records, benchmark reports, and a small conformance suite. Its contribution is the composition of these mechanisms into explicit contracts that distinguish integrity from authenticated provenance and privacy controls from operating-system isolation. We evaluate the implementation through static checks, 22 unit tests, deterministic end-to-end tests on Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows, and a pinned real-model experiment on Windows CPU using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct Q4_K_M and llama.cpp b11981. The real experiment validates artifact verification, startup, model listing, non-streaming and server-sent-event chat, and conformance. Three independent benchmark invocations produced fifteen successful warm requests with no failures. In this single configuration, median time to first token was 18.066 ms and median decode throughput was 54.394 tokens/s. These descriptive measurements do not establish cross-engine superiority, output quality, energy efficiency, or hardware-general performance. Raw JSON, commands, and environment metadata are published. Remaining challenges include signed manifests, time-of-check/time-of-use replacement, operating-system containment, proxy-overhead measurement, and broader experimental matrices.
title: Caleta: An Evidence-Oriented Trust Layer for Reproducible Local Large Language Model Inference

summary: This record provides supporting numerical data and code for the study "Entry, reciprocity, and severity in self-consistent wrong-motion optical flow." The study investigates a known optical-flow failure in which mutually consistent forward and backward estimates can correspond to an incorrect motion layer. Using controlled two-layer translations, it separately evaluates appearance-dependent alternate-side assignment, reciprocal wrong-motion consistency, and conditional error severity under near alternate-layer substitution. The supporting materials include source-level and pair-level numerical tables, plotted data, representative example arrays, figure-generation scripts, frozen experimental specifications, selected generator and evaluation code, verification scripts, and SHA-256 references to archived experimental results. The experiments use pretrained RAFT-Small, RAFT-Large, and GMFlow with STL-10 and BSDS500 image appearances. Reproducibility scope: The deposited materials support figure regeneration and examination of reported numerical summaries. Complete model prediction archives, original image archives, pretrained model checkpoints, and a complete inference environment are not included. Full prediction-to-metric verification requires the separately identified experimental archives. Original third-party image datasets remain subject to their respective providers' terms. No nuclear-decommissioning footage is included. File access is restricted pending review of publication rights and licensing.
title: Supporting data and code for Entry, reciprocity, and severity in self-consistent wrong-motion optical flow

summary: This software archive contains R and Python scripts, cohort-specific statistical audit scripts, gene-level derived summary tables, figure source comparisons, selected graphical outputs, and integrity checks associated with a secondary analysis of 13 intercalated-disc genes in human dilated cardiomyopathy. Public inputs include GEO studies GSE141910, GSE116250, GSE249925, GSE183852, Broad Single Cell Portal SCP1303, and published left-ventricular proteomics data from Li et al. (PXD018678). The work evaluates bulk myocardial transcriptomic reproducibility, donor-level cardiomyocyte nuclear pseudobulk analyses, CellBender-versus-CellRanger count processing, matched nuclear-versus-bulk modality effects, and published proteomic evidence. Original large datasets and individual-level source matrices are not redistributed. Source-derived proteomics values are credited to Li et al.; the 2,614-protein aggregate re-tabulation is excluded. Original code is MIT-licensed; original author-owned tables, figures, and documentation are CC BY 4.0 licensed. Exact file scopes and source exceptions are listed in LICENSE_MAP.csv and THIRD_PARTY_ATTRIBUTION.md. Earlier project stages included stepwise independent numerical audit and supplementary table checks; a single clean-environment execution from freshly downloaded raw source data through every figure has not been demonstrated. This archive is intended for research transparency and documents its specific reproducibility limits. Version 1.0.1 update: Corrected the direction_concordant annotations for eight genes in Supplementary Table S9 and updated the README to reflect the Zenodo release. The strict replication results and scientific conclusions remain unchanged.
title: Analysis Code and Audit Tables for Cross-Cohort and Cross-Omics Investigation of Intercalated-Disc Changes in Human Dilated Cardiomyopathy

summary: Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent's constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle's information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms $27$ baselines by $+15.0$ Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at https://github.com/EllenYiGe/PatternBloom.
title: PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns

summary: Reproducibility in large language model (LLM) agent evaluation depends on replay fidelity: which parts of an execution trace are reconstructed, controlled, and compared. This matters for agent debugging, failure analysis, and counterfactual evaluation of stateful tool use. We audit all 71 unsuccessful executions in a fixed historical AppWorld corpus using 284 isolated fixed-code replay attempts. Reconstructed declared settings admit 42 cases under printed-output, pre-oracle database-delta, and native-verdict/test-count checks; resetting the random-number generator before each interaction admits 68. The 26-case gap contracts to four under database/oracle checks, with one endpoint unknown. Mechanism studies identify four materialized-state discrepancies despite matching outputs and verdicts. In one admitted endpoint pair, an identical API call yields matching responses but different row effects; common future Python RNG removes that deterministic difference in two paired repetitions. A separate JWT credential-equality program and alignment controls expose authentication/write differences, with missing repetitions retained. For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained output trackers restores the reference comparison without changing original cached contents. A purposeful 12-case BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested public-state, return, and verdict checks. We preserve resource censoring and infrastructure deviations. The contribution is a bounded empirical characterization of replay eligibility, hidden state, and test-oracle integration, without estimating debugger accuracy, repair gains, or method-ranking distortion.
title: Replay Fidelity in LLM Agent Evaluation: Randomness, Hidden State, and Test Oracles in AppWorld

summary: Reproducible pipeline for the in silico screening of a 104-compound library of benzofuroxan, oxadiazole and hydrazone derivatives against five molecular targets related to alcohol-associated liver fibrosis: HDAC6, HDAC8, MAO-B, AT1R and KDM1A. This deposit accompanies the manuscript submitted to AppliedChem (MDPI) and is the repository to which its Data Availability Statement refers. Contents: the command-line scripts organised by stage, in a Spanish and an English edition; the desktop application that runs them; the per-phase user guides; the pinned environment specification; the provenance files of each run; and the intermediate result tables cited in the manuscript. The pipeline covers library canonicalisation and InChIKey assignment, biological activity spectrum prediction, molecular target prediction, cross-screening against the indexed literature, receptor and ligand preparation, molecular docking, interaction profiling, structural selection criteria, ADMET consensus across three platforms, multiparameter weighting, and the integration of the structural and ADMET criteria.
title: LIFFT in silico screening pipeline v3.0.3: scripts, desktop application, result tables and figure code

summary: 1,400 synthetic coronary CT angiography (CCTA) reports in English, 200 in each CAD-RADS category (0, 1, 2, 3, 4A, 4B, 5), each released with the complete clinical scenario that produced it: the vessel, segment, degree of stenosis and plaque composition of every lesion with its per-lesion CAD-RADS grade, the plaque burden, the modifiers, the Agatston score, the patient age and sex, the indication and the sites of any stent, graft or vulnerable plaque. The reports were produced by an open-source deterministic generator that computes the CAD-RADS label from the lesions and imposes it on the language model, so the label and the findings cannot disagree. The archive contains the reports, the rendered prompts, the raw model answers, the result of the automatic checks applied to every report, the configuration used for production and the run provenance (model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, selector deepseek/deepseek-flash, accessed 31 October 2026; seed 42). The corpus is synthetic research material. It contains no patient data, was not derived from patient records, and must not be used for clinical decision-making. Known limitations are documented in README.md. The generator is released separately under the MIT licence.
title: A parameterizable synthetic corpus of 1,400 CAD-RADS coronary CT angiography reports with their generating scenarios

summary: Code, cached results and preprint for Words to Coordinates (W2C), an uncertainty-aware NLP-geospatial framework that links what firms disclose about physical climate risk to what their assets face: taxonomy-aligned extraction (IFRS S2 with crosswalks to ESRS E1 and GRI 305) with provenance, geocoding with explicit precision classes, hazard-ensemble overlay and the Disclosure Gap Index with disclosure-exposure quadrants. The simulation study uses the real locations of 11,107 power plants (Global Power Plant Database v1.3.0) with synthetic hazards and disclosures, confirms a closed-form relation between geolocation error and exposure fidelity, and propagates extraction, geolocation and hazard-model uncertainty by Monte Carlo. Companion software to the preprint "Words to Coordinates: An Uncertainty-Aware NLP-Geospatial Framework for Measuring the Gap Between Disclosed and Physical Climate Risk".
title: words-to-coordinates

summary: The development of deep learning-based medical AI depends on high-quality annotated data. Yet, dataset creation remains constrained by the need for expert radiologist annotations, limiting curated datasets to relatively small cohorts. To overcome this limitation, recent efforts increasingly aggregate disparate public datasets into large-scale dataset collections. However, combining datasets at scale often obscures data provenance, introducing substantial risks of reuse propagation, unintended leakage, bias amplification and distorted data distributions. In this work, we study these problems on a massive collection of 565k 3D radiological images across 1034 public datasets and provide practical resources to address them. Firstly, we formalize dataset collections as a distinct paradigm in medical image analysis and characterize their structural challenges, including reuse propagation, duplication, and provenance fragmentation. Secondly, we perform a large-scale empirical study of duplication on this collection and demonstrate extensive exact and near-duplicate reuse across public datasets via perceptual hashing and manual tracing, identifying a lower bound of 118k duplicate pairs. We make the perceptual hashes publicly accessible for comparison through our website, providing researchers with a standardized reference for identifying potential overlaps and shared provenance. Thirdly, since hashing alone cannot detect all duplicates, we introduce MAP (Metadata for Aggregation and Provenance), a lightweight, portable metadata profile for documenting provenance, known overlaps, and deduplication decisions in dataset collections. Our contributions help dataset collections shift from coarse aggregations to reliable and provenance-aware data scaling mechanisms in medical image analysis. A web tool supporting our work is available at https://mic-dct.dkfz.de/.
title: Dataset Collections: Challenges of Large-Scale Data Aggregation in 3D Medical Image Datasets

summary: The ocean environment is inherently unpredictable, posing significant challenges for the reliable operation of marine energy converters (MECs). A critical step in the design of any WEC is identifying the scenarios that may lead to system failure. One common failure mode in marine energy devices occurs at system joints, such as mechanical hinges, where excessive loads or unfavorable configurations can lead to malfunction or structural breakdown [1]. A typical approach for identifying such failure modes is to perform high-fidelity simulations in which a MEC is subjected to a broad range of loading conditions, including irregular multidirectional waves and slamming events [2]. However, this approach can be prohibitively time consuming. Additionally, identifying high-risk scenarios becomes more difficult as system complexity grows, particularly for MECs, which span a wide range of configurations that complicate the identification of representative conditions. Importantly, MECs failure depends not only on load magnitude, but also on the system configuration at the moment wave forces act.
title: Rapid Identification of Potential Failure Scenarios in Marine Energy Systems

summary: A tape of $n$ cells over three values — equivalently, two-bit cells read through their sum — is read by two headers that enclose a window; at each step a fixed rule, given the window's content and the geometry, chooses one of eight actions: move a header inward or outward, trim a cell from the left, the right or both, or halt. The cost is the number of cell reads, the state is $O(\log n)$ bits, and the question is how the cost must grow with $n$ for each rule. On the evidence the rules fall into three classes — fully linear, semi-linear and superlinear — separated by a worst-case cost and a mean cost. All three are populated: four natural rules are fully linear, one construction is semi-linear ($e=\Theta(n)$ with $g=\Theta(n^2)$), and the remaining seventeen are superlinear. The paper separates the length of a walk from the number of cells it reads, shows the length is a property of the rule rather than of the model, gives machines for every rule in the catalogue, arranges their costs on a ladder from $n^{1/2}$ to $n^3$, and states exactly which rungs are proved, which are conditional and which are conjectural. Negative results included: the certificate bound does not compose (on one tape per-query certificates sum to $1{,}285{,}703$ cells while their union has $1{,}020$), and a bound on the rule's output transfers to the walk only after multiplication by the fraction of queries at which the answer can change the action, measured at $0.104$ and falling like $n^{-0.99}$.
title: A memoryless two-header tape machine: what a window costs, and why two lower-bound techniques fail

summary: Summary of changes in STIR release 6.5 Overall summary This version is 100% backwards compatible with STIR 6.4, aside from bug fixes of course. In particular, the "bucket" information for the Siemens mMR has changed (see below). This is a release with several major updates, including dead-time correction for the Siemens mMR, TOF support with "block" and "generic" scanners, initial support for PETSIRD 0.12, GATE-ROOT support for "block" scanners and support for SimSET block detectors. More detail is below. Main code contributions were by Nikos Efthimiou (UMCG), Alan Osys (LSBU), Daniel Deidda (NPL), Kris Thielemans (UCL). Overall overview and release management was by Kris Thielemans (UCL). Patch release info 6.5.0 released 9 Nov 2026 GitHub Milestone 6.5 Summary for end users (also to be read by developers) Bug fixes Fix incompatibility problem with ROOT 6.38 or later. Previous versions of STIR either crashed or threw an error Entry is null . PR #1741 . Fix GE Signa PET/MR (and other RDF9 scanners?) header reading problem. Previous version of STIR got caught on the \0's present in the header and threw an error and stopped. PR #1777 . Fix ProjMatrixByBinSPECTUB and ProjMatrixByBinPinholeSPECTUB returning an empty LOR for the first bin that is requested in each view (when not all views are kept in the cache). This made forward and back projection inconsistent when they are used one after the other on the same view, as in the gradient of the Poisson log-likelihood. See issue #1576 . New functionality General Initial support for reading PETSIRD 0.12 list-mode data, the proposed standard for PET list-mode data from the Emission Tomography Standardization Initiative (ETSI). Some limitations include single layer, single module type geometry. Dead-time correction for PETSIRD data uses the alive-time fractions per crystal that are stored in the PETSIRD file. Module-pair alive-time fractions are not supported yet. See also STIR2PETSIRD for using STIR to write PETSIRD data. PR #1604 , PR #1770 . Initial support for even number of TOF bins. PR #1604 , but see Issue #1751 . enable TOF for BlocksOnCylindrical/Generic PR #1746 . Enable GATE ROOT support BlocksOnCylindrical . This requires extra keywords in the headers for the ROOT file ( .hroot ). The keywords are the same as in the Interfile header. For example Scanner geometry (BlocksOnCylindrical/Cylindrical/Generic) := BlocksOnCylindrical Distance between crystals in axial direction (cm) := 0.63 Distance between crystals in transaxial direction (cm) := 0.42 Distance between blocks in axial direction (cm) := 3.78 Distance between blocks in transaxial direction (cm) := 3.78 This change makes STIR geometry much closer to GATE ROOT, which for instance allowed us to decrease the tolerances in our tests. Warning: This is currently only supported for GATE scanner type := GATE_Cylindrical_PET Note that the user of "virtual" crystals and block geometry likely will lead to wrong results (and is untested). PR #1746 . New utility conv_SimSET_crystal_pairs_to_STIR and script conv_SimSET_crystal_pairs_to_STIR.sh to convert SimSET block-detector output binned by crystal pair into STIR projection data, for Cylindrical and BlocksOnCylindrical scanners. PR #1774 . Dead-time correction for Siemens mMR (ECAT8) data. lm_to_projdata now writes the singles rates of each time frame to a JSON file ( <output prefix>_f<frame>_singles.json ), which can be given to BinNormalisationFromECAT8 with the keywords use_dead_time and singles filename . See the User's Guide. PR #1770 . summary: Enterprise adoption of agentic systems is often framed as a problem of agent reasoning, tool use, retrieval, or memory. This paper investigates an additional architectural problem: preparing heterogeneous enterprise knowledge into task-appropriate representations that agents can interpret, reuse, and govern. We propose Cognitive Preparation as an explicit architectural lifecycle between authoritative enterprise knowledge and agent execution, with a Cognitive Preparation Compiler (CPC) coordinating representation decisions, compilation, validation, provenance binding, temporal constraints, and publication through a reusable Cognitive Substrate. The contribution is positioned at the architectural and methodological level; no novelty is claimed for ontologies, symbolic predicates, memory mechanisms, provenance, temporal models, or knowledge compilation individually. Recent 2026 preprints on precomputed agent-memory views and enterprise context engineering further narrow the novelty boundary and are treated as close, non-peer-reviewed prior art. We report a staged prototype evaluation implemented in Ver.Test9 on a Ver.Test8 runtime foundation. Deterministic tests examine selected lifecycle controls, while exploratory LLM-assisted evaluations (T17–T22) examine controlled reuse of synthetic operational knowledge through deterministic retrieval. The results provide implementation-level feasibility evidence and preliminary observations of scoped procedural knowledge reuse, including provider- and operation-specific applicability, temporal validity, and version precedence. They do not establish general performance superiority, validated adaptive representation selection, transfer between genuinely independent agents, autonomous learning, production readiness, or economic break-even. The five research questions are retained, with preliminary support strongest for controlled knowledge reuse; preparation effectiveness and evolution receive partial evidence, while adaptive representation selection and reuse economics remain open.

summary: 6.17.0 (2026-11-10) Changes: Add Zarr media-types application/vnd.zarr (including version=2 and version=3 parameters) for directory stores, and application/zarr+zip for zipped stores, with their .zarr and .zarr.zip extensions. The zipped variant is distinguished from a plain application/zip (resolves #1012 ). Convert WPS/OGC API - Processes I/O using only Zarr directory media-types into CWL Directory without format (not applicable for that type), similarly to the handling of application/directory . Handle Zarr directory media-types as directories when returning Job results by-value and when refusing local directory uploads to the Vault from the CLI. Preserve the Zarr media-type declared by a Process output as the type of the resulting Job output when the CWL output is a Directory (instead of reporting it as application/directory ), and report it as Content-Type for directory references when explicitly provided. Offer application/zarr+zip as alternate format of Zarr directory Job outputs, using the ?f={mediaType} result representation to obtain the zipped store (store contents located at the root of the archive). When an explicit version of the Zarr media-type is declared, the generic application/vnd.zarr is also offered, and requesting it returns the same directory store without conversion. Refuse deployment of a Process declaring a Zarr directory media-type on an I/O that is defined as a CWL File , since Zarr stores must be represented by a Directory . Fixes: Fix files without extension in a remote directory listing (e.g.: Zarr chunks such as c/0 ) being renamed with a default extension (e.g.: c/0.txt ) when fetched as part of a directory, which corrupted the directory contents. Fix Job results returned by-value for binary contents (e.g.: zipped Zarr) being decoded as UTF-8 text, which failed for non-text bytes. Raw bytes are now returned as is for single result responses, and as base64 encoded value (with encoding metadata) when embedded in the JSON results document. Run safety dependency checks using its ghcr.io/pyupio/safety Docker image in the Makefile and CI. Move vulnerability exclusions and their reasons into .safety-policy.yml . Remove the Python development dependency and its authlib / marshmallow compatibility pins (relates to pyupio/safety#822 ). Add OGC API - Processes - Part 5: Provenance and Profiles new metadata-profiles conformance class references which provides the semantics of metadata with role , href and a profiled-term rel to annotate the Process itself or at granular I/O definitions, and aligns with dataClasses URIs along the I/O schema (relates to opengeospatial/ogcapi-processes#637 ). Implement GET /processes?metadata[<scope>][<role>]=<profile> query filtering to list only Process summaries that define a matching metadata entry, either in the main process or per inputs/outputs definition of the requested <scope>, and resolving Safe CURIE/URN role / profile references to their long-form URI as necessary. Corresponding HTTP 400/422 error responses are raised when applicable for invald parsing or combinations. Add OGC API - Processes - Part 5: Provenance and Profiles metadata-profiles conformance class references. Implement OPTIONS /processes to advertise supported methods and deployment media types with Allow and Accept-Post headers, as required by the metadata-profiles requirements. Add Vary: Accept, Prefer because process-list response behavior depends on those request headers. Add legacy application/tiff; application=geotiff and application/jp2 media-types (from the OGC API - Processes examples) as dynamically supported equivalents of image/tiff; application=geotiff and image/jp2 respectively. Inputs submitted with them are accepted by any Process that defines the official media-types, without explicitly listing them in its description. The legacy types are never selected when resolving media-types (e.g.: from file extensions). Add keyless allratestoday option for weaver.quota

summary: Phase 6-ter of the consolidation: the full MCP server. Astrocook can be driven by an AI agent through 65 tools: the 48 recipes (each one a tool, generated from the registry), the sessions with undo and redo, the inspection of a session, the notes and gaps of the agent, the log as the text of a methods section, the cancellation of a long recipe, a GUI that follows a session of the server and a headless Docker image. Outputs come from RecipeResult only, and nothing the agent does is lost. A minor version: the interface of the server grows, the results of the recipes do not change but in the two cases below. Numerical results. Unchanged for the benchmark of synthetic spectra (documentation page Accuracy , as for 2.2.0) and for the fits and the identification in general, with two changes decided on purpose (PR 7-quater). (1) Check associated metals ( metals_auto ) refitted the session it started from and lost the ions already found, and kept a trial ion if its fit gave logN >= 12 and 2 <= b <= 50 km/s ( aic_penalty was accepted and not used). It now keeps the ions found, skips the ions whose lines fall outside the spectrum (with a warning) and keeps a trial ion only if its fit does not end at a bound (b or logN) and its AIC change is below -aic_penalty (F111, F121); on a real spectrum (J0103-1305 raw, 215 thousand pixels) the recipe went from 192 ions kept, 67 of them at b = 50 km/s, to 82 and none at the bound, and from 26.7 to 6.4 minutes for the trials. The benchmark of synthetic spectra does not run metals_auto : a targeted test measures it (the SiIV of the mock of the trials is found). (2) A fit of components with no valid pixel around them no longer fits the whole spectrum: the components are not fitted and keep their first values (F111). Published on GitHub with the macOS app; not on PyPI yet (install with pip from GitHub). Changed Using Astrocook from an AI Agent rewritten for the full MCP server (phase 6-ter, closing): installation and Docker, the tools by group, a longer example (a blend fitted with undo and constraints), what a request should say, the review in the GUI and the limits (the automatic recipes, no measure of the fit, z_em and R not estimated, the cost in context of the 65 tools). The server is no longer called a pilot. MCP server for agents (phase 6-ter): every recipe is a tool , named <menu>_<recipe> (e.g. flux_rebin , absorbers_fit_component ), made from the description of the recipe that the GUI dialogs use: the same parameters, defaults, bounds and texts, the values checked as in the GUI; a recipe added to Astrocook becomes a tool with no change of the server. The five tools of the pilot keep their names. Every tool returns what the recipe changed, listed (the components removed with the reason, the components changed, the columns, the properties), with the summaries of the pilot where they apply (continuum, identification, fit). A recipe that opens new sessions in the GUI does so in the server too, each with its own session_id , and leaves the session it ran on unchanged: Identify Absorption Lines now opens a new session (in the pilot it changed the same one). A parameter that names another session (e.g. the reference of Equalize ) takes its session_id . The messages name the tools that provide what is missing ( edit_set_properties , continuum_estimate_auto ). MCP server: tools for the sessions, session_list , session_describe , session_history , session_undo , session_redo , session_duplicate and session_close (phase 6-ter). Every state of a session is kept, as in the GUI: what a recipe removed is had back with session_undo , and the result of such a recipe says so. session_close does not close a session with changes not saved unless asked to discard them. MCP server: tools to look into a session without changing it (phase 6-ter): components_list (the components with their errors, flags, fit groups and constraints, filtered by series, redshift and flags), spectrum_read (the column

summary: Local bus mileage in England outside London has fallen by more than a quarter since 2005, and debate about rural buses relies mostly on counts of routes cut or money spent. This paper measures what remains, place by place. Using the complete set of regional timetables published through the Bus Open Data Service, I count departures on one weekday, one Saturday and one Sunday at 251,790 English bus stops and relate them to 15,012 villages from Wikidata and to all 33,755 small areas (LSOAs). 32.6% of villages have no stop with a weekday bus within 800 m, and 41.4% have no stop with four or more weekday departures. 61.5% have no bus from 19:00 and 67.8% none on Sunday; only 29.8% have a usable weekday service, an evening bus and a Sunday bus. 10.5% of England's population, 6.0 million people, live in small areas without a usable weekday bus, 72% of them in rural areas. In a pre-specified model with rurality and region held fixed, more deprived areas are less likely to lack a usable bus (odds ratio 0.68 per standard deviation, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.78) and areas with older populations more likely (odds ratio 1.28, 1.19 to 1.38). A planned falsification test fails, so these associations partly reflect rural differences the official classification does not capture. The results give a reproducible baseline for measuring rural bus provision. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/bus-deserts/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/bus-deserts . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/bus-deserts/ . Sources: Department for Transport, Bus Open Data Service regional GTFS timetables (Open Government Licence v3.0); Wikidata (CC0); English Indices of Deprivation 2025, MHCLG (OGL v3.0); ONS 2021 Rural Urban Classification and LSOA 2021 boundaries via the geographr R package (OGL v3.0); ONS region and country boundaries (OGL v3.0). Text, figures and data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.

A planned falsification test fails, so these associations partly reflect rural differences the official classification does not capture. The results give a reproducible baseline for measuring rural bus provision. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/bus-deserts/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/bus-deserts . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/bus-deserts/ . summary: The Hydraulic and Electric Reverse Osmosis Wave Energy Converter (HERO WEC) is a 3-kW point-absorber WEC designed to desalinate ocean water using breakwater wave energy. In its electrical configuration, a permanent magnet synchronous generator produces three-phase "wild AC" power that is rectified and regulated by a charge controller to charge a battery bank and power a reverse-osmosis pump. Wave energy presents a uniquely challenging environment for power electronics: energy delivery is pulsed, irregular, and characterized by high peak-to-average power ratios. The HERO WEC originally used an off-the-shelf buck converter charge controller designed for wind, solar, and hydropower. Field deployments to North Carolina revealed two critical limitations: (1) a 32 V cut-in voltage that rendered the controller inoperable during low-energy wave states, and (2) severe current overshoot in energetic waves that exceeded commanded current and threatened system survivability. Together, these constraints produced only a narrow operational window and average battery power of tens of watts, far below the controller’s 1.8 kW rating. This work describes the redesign of the charge controller to address these limitations and expand the operational range of the WEC.
title: Custom Charge Controller Design and Validation for Wave Energy Conversion

Wave energy presents a uniquely challenging environment for power electronics: energy delivery is pulsed, irregular, and characterized by high peak-to-average power ratios. The HERO WEC originally used an off-the-shelf buck converter charge controller designed for wind, solar, and hydropower. Field deployments to North Carolina revealed two critical limitations: (1) a 32 V cut-in voltage that rendered the controller inoperable during low-energy wave states, and (2) severe current overshoot in energetic waves that exceeded commanded current and threatened system survivability. Together, these constraints produced only a narrow operational window and average battery power of tens of watts, far below the controller’s 1.8 kW rating. This work describes the redesign of the charge controller to address these limitations and expand the operational range of the WEC.
title: Custom Charge Controller Design and Validation for Wave Energy Conversion

summary: This dataset contains experimental data supporting the reproducibility of side-channel-assisted secret-key reconstruction attacks against HQC. It provides the vectors used to construct soft spectra from side-channel-derived error-weight estimates for two attack scenarios: Chosen-Ciphertext Attack (CCA) and Known-Ciphertext Attack (KCA). The corresponding estimated error weights, as well as the C implementations of the soft-spectrum construction and secret-key reconstruction algorithms (Simulated Annealing and Depth-First Search), are available in the accompanying GitHub repository. The dataset does not contain raw side-channel traces. Instead, it provides the intermediate experimental data required to reproduce the soft-spectrum-based key-recovery experiments and evaluate reconstruction success rates as a function of the number of observations. The files should be placed in the appropriate data/cca/ and data/kca/ directories of the GitHub repository, as described in its README.
title: Experimental Side-Channel Data for HQC Secret-Key Reconstruction

summary: LLMs excel at language tasks, but long-meeting QFS remains difficult due to complex speaker dynamics, sparse key information, and limited data. Meetings involve disfluencies, long transcripts and complex discourse. QFS have high risk of information omission, hallucination, even for advanced models such as GPT-4-mini and Gemini. Existing end-to-end methods compress retrieval, evidence extraction, and summary generation into a single pass, failing to handle the complex reasoning required for targeted meeting summaries. We propose ReSUM, a modular multi-LLM framework coordinated by a planner that orchestrates retrieval and summarization agents. By distilling teacher reasoning into query- and plan-conditioned retrievers and summarizers, ReSUM enhances long-context robustness, minimizes irrelevant exploration, and generates more faithful and comprehensive query-focused summaries. Experiments show consistent gains on query-focused meeting summarization benchmarks.
title: ReSUM: Reasoning-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Query-Focused Summarization

summary: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation

summary: Attention to notable people rises sharply when they die and then fades, but how far it fades, and for whom, has rarely been measured at scale. I follow the English Wikipedia articles of 16,397 people who died between 2016 and 2023 (a 30% hash sample of Wikidata), measuring monthly user pageviews (looking someone up, not remembering them) as a share of all English Wikipedia traffic relative to each person's own level in the year before death. In an analysis pre-specified in a written plan, the median peak is 16.5 times the pre-death level. The decay is best described by two phases, with half-lives of about 11 days and 6.9 months, although a power law predicts later cohorts slightly better. Two to three years after death, the median person receives 0.98 (95% CI 0.97 to 0.99) of their pre-death share; an exploratory comparison with the drift before death places this about 5% above a no-death path. Age at death is the strongest correlate: people who died under 50 retain 63% more long-run attention than those who died at 65 to 79 (95% CI 51 to 77), a gap absent at a placebo date and present in all 21 robustness checks. Performers are the only occupational group whose typical attention settles above its baseline, but placebo tests show that the occupational gaps partly predate the deaths. Estimates for women and for citizens of English-speaking countries depend on specification and are not robust. The design is descriptive and observational. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/fame-half-life/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/fame-half-life . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/fame-half-life/ . Sources: English Wikipedia pageviews (Wikimedia pageviews API, CC0); Wikidata (CC0); Natural Earth (public domain). Text, figures and data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: The Half-Life of Fame: How Attention to Notable People on English Wikipedia Rises and Decays after Their Deaths

summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems solve complex tasks through collaboration, but their growing, simultaneously resident key-value (KV) caches create a memory bottleneck. Applying single-model quantization policies independently ignores differences in agents' precision needs, potentially degrading collective reasoning. We introduce Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization (CoMixKV), which combines online sensitivity estimation with joint agent-layer bit-width allocation under a shared memory budget. To our knowledge, CoMixKV is the first mixed-precision KV-cache quantization framework to jointly allocate precision across simultaneously resident agent caches under such a budget. The estimator derives sensitivity from a local attention-error bound using recent queries, keys, and values, without calibration data, trial quantization, or additional model passes. A shared controller combines these scores with remaining quantizable capacity and byte-level storage costs to minimize total estimated error. Allocations are refreshed as agents start or finish and new observations become available. Selected widths apply only to newly quantized blocks; recent states retain native precision and previously quantized blocks remain unchanged. Across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones at average 2-bit, 3-bit, and 4-bit settings, CoMixKV achieves strong accuracy against the evaluated quantization baselines. At the average 3-bit setting on Gemma-4-31B-it, it achieves 68.35% average accuracy, exceeding the strongest quantized baseline by 0.59%. On Qwen3-32B, it reduces peak KV-cache memory by 32.08% and achieves a 1.38x inference speedup over FullKV.
title: Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization for Efficient LLM-based Multi-agent Systems

summary: Long-term conversational question answering can require several separated dialogue turns that support an answer only together. We introduce EviCover, a retrieval approach designed to retain this complementary evidence. It converts questions into observable evidence requirements, checks requirement coverage using retrieved source identifiers, and selects turns jointly. We track annotated support sets - the benchmark-labeled dialogue turns associated with each question - through retrieval, reranking, and final answer-generation context. We evaluate the baseline memory pipeline on generated, human-verified LoCoMo conversations and human-written REALTALK conversations, and examine EviCover on REALTALK's 108 multi-hop questions. Compared with the hybrid lexical/dense baseline, support-turn recall among 60 candidate turns rises from 0.526 to 0.575, and recall in the final ten-turn context rises from 0.349 to 0.379. The evidence funnel identifies separate discovery and selection failures, while paired answer evaluation shows that greater evidence recall does not yet establish a correctness gain. This analysis locates where complementary evidence is lost and distinguishes evidence retrieval from its use in answer generation.
title: Where Did the Evidence Go? Diagnosing Proof-Set Loss in Long-Term Conversational Memory

summary: # A Spectral Construction of Natural-Number Arithmetic [Archival DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22512592) ## Arithmetic with its construction history retained This paper constructs natural-number arithmetic from a correlation spectrum and then resolves its values into the expressions by which they are generated. Its central achievement is to connect three levels that are usually studied separately: arithmetic values, the histories of arithmetic operations, and an evolution acting on those histories. The resulting system retains both the familiar numerical laws and information that numerical evaluation alone removes. The source is minimal unbiased compositional change. The least-dimensional faithful irreducible real orthogonal carrier is a rotation plane. Independent composition, exact same-shape self-similarity and unit covariance determine square-root scaling and a Gaussian law. Local information and normalized total correlation give the characteristic local and global lengths. Preservation of constants selects Neumann closure within the stated separated nondegenerate homogeneous local boundary class. Spectral projections are ordered by their Gaussian response before an integer enumeration is introduced. Orientation selects the positive analytic modes. Pointwise modulation and circle-map composition define their addition and multiplication; modulation by the first positive mode defines successor. The paper proves the Peano recursion structure, unique prime factorization and canonical transport under scale and orientation changes. Winding degree certifies the resulting natural-number arithmetic. ## Resolving how a value is generated The next construction retains ordered, bracketed addition and multiplication expressions. Only the specified zero, unit and absorbing reductions are imposed at this level. Arithmetic evaluation identifies expressions with the same value, while each value has a finite expression fibre. This gives a precise space in which the construction of a number can itself be observed. The simplest example is six. Adding six unit leaves and multiplying an additive expression for three by an additive expression for two give the same root value and the same root energy. Their leaf counts are six and five, while their accumulated internal quadratic defects are thirty and thirty-one. In both cases leaf energy plus accumulated defect is thirty-six. The equality at the root coexists with a measurable difference in the construction. A recursive positive law gives equal weight to the admissible root channels and assembles their subhistories independently. This law differs from uniform counting of all complete expressions. Phase invariance determines a finite phase extension. Summing the resolved source over histories and phases recovers the original Gaussian mass of each mode exactly. Expression multiplicity therefore enriches the source without changing its original partition function. Weighted amplitude readout, probability pushforward and conditional expectation have distinct definitions. Exact variance and entropy identities separate the information in the root value from the information remaining within its fibre. The example of six has strictly positive conditional leaf-count variance, giving a concrete instance of information preserved by the resolved construction. ## A complete operator on generation histories The same source weights determine a parent-child assembly response. The paper constructs a nonnegative self-adjoint trace-class operator on the complete counting history space. Its trace tail has an explicit Gaussian bound independent of the number of expressions in each fibre. Finite root cutoffs converge in trace norm, and the full operator generates a contraction evolution with a dissipation identity. The decisive result is a nonzero transfer from an initially invisible history difference to a later value response. A difference supported on the six histories of four has zero initial value readout,
tags: Finite evaluation fibres of arithmetic expressions
Unique factorization on generated arithmetic modes
Exact separation of value and expression-history information
Nontrivial coupling between arithmetic values and expression histories
Trace-class operator from arithmetic expression assembly
Exact memory equation for arithmetic readout
Canonical scale and orientation transport of arithmetic
title: A Spectral Construction of Natural-Number Arithmetic

summary: LLM-based agents extend LLMs with tool calls, memory, planning, and retrieval to act in external environments, but they are vulnerable to attacks at different workflow steps. Existing defenses, including prompt engineering and post-training alignment, primarily improve LLM-only safety and often overlook risks that arise from multi-step execution. External verification adds guardrails to check each step separately, but it typically ignores how risks can propagate across steps. We argue that we should consider risk transitions across dependent steps through the agent workflow, rather than separate verification on a single step. In this paper, we propose \textbf{T}ail-risk-aware \textbf{A}gent \textbf{S}afety (TAS), a tail-risk-aware safety framework that models agent workflow safety as a sequence of dependent safety states and constrains the rare but extreme risks (i.e., tail risk) with a shared budget. TAS first models safety-state transitions sequentially along the workflow as an MDP to trace risk propagation, then measures a tail-sensitive risk to target rare but high-cost risks (i.e., tail risk), and constrains the risk with a shared budget to derive a step-wise safety strategy. By constraining tail risk rather than the overall average, TAS suppresses rare high-cost failures while preserving utility in normal cases. Experiments show that TAS achieves better performance compared with eleven baselines across three benchmarks.
title: Tail-risk-aware Agent Safety: Constraining Tail Risks Across Multi-step LLM Agent Workflows

summary: Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition (OV-MLR) aims to identify all queried semantic concepts present in an image. Existing methods mainly improve global image-text matching or text-side representations, leaving local prediction largely under-explored. In this paper, we revisit local prediction and reveal that it can serve as a strong discriminative branch once two properties are properly handled: spatial consistency of local visual features and compatibility-aware local competition. This perspective is motivated by local semantic sparsity: each image region is related to only a small subset of queried concepts, while compatible concepts of different granularities or types may still coexist locally. We instantiate this perspective with LoCo, a selective Local Competition framework for OV-MLR. LoCo adopts a spatially consistent visual encoder to reduce local feature entanglement, and introduces Selective Softmax to impose competition only among locally incompatible categories while preserving compatible responses. Multi-scale inference further improves local prediction at different scales. LoCo can also be ensembled with an existing global predictor to provide complementary image-level context. Experiments on four multi-label benchmarks show that standalone LoCo improves average F1-score and mAP over TagCLIP by 3.4% and 3.8%, respectively. LoCo + DualPrompt achieves the highest averages among the compared methods, with gains of 4.8% and 5.2% over TagCLIP. Our results suggest that local semantic sparsity offers a useful basis for developing more discriminative open-vocabulary multi-label recognition methods. The code is available at https://github.com/lee-plus-plus/LoCo.
title: LoCo: Selective Local Competition for Discriminative Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition

summary: Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent's constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle's information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms $27$ baselines by $+15.0$ Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at https://github.com/EllenYiGe/PatternBloom.
title: PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns

summary: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.
title: Hibana: Fast Agentic Inference on Unified-Memory Devices

summary: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.
title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction

summary: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
title: ASCENT: Scale-Complementary External State for Frozen Long-Context Language Models

summary: Multimodal fusion requires not only exchanging information across modalities but also determining which representations should participate in the interaction and how complementary cross-modal views should be combined. We introduce Guided Co-Attention with Adaptive Gating, a fusion framework that integrates token-wise guidance, bidirectional cross-attention, and sample-specific fusion. The proposed method constructs two directional representations: an image-conditioned text representation, obtained by allowing textual tokens to query visual features, and a text-conditioned image representation formed in the reverse direction. Token-wise guidance modulates the representations before cross-attention, while an adaptive gate learns the relative contribution of the two resulting directional representations for each sample. We evaluate the approach using paired chest radiographs and radiology reports as an image-text test bed for binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification. The two cross-attention directions exhibit distinct performance characteristics, demonstrating that reversing the query and source modalities does not produce interchangeable representations. Ablation experiments further show that bidirectional interaction, adaptive gating, and token guidance provide complementary benefits. The proposed model achieves 96.05% accuracy, 96.10% F1-score, 98.37% AUC, 95.60% Sens@95Spec, and 96.51% Spec@95Sens, yielding the highest mean performance across all evaluated metrics. These findings support explicitly modeling interaction direction, token relevance, and sample-dependent integration when constructing multimodal representations.
title: Guided Co-Attention with Adaptive Gating for Multimodal Medical Data Fusion

summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.
title: BunshinRL: Splitting Live Agent Workspaces for Memory-Efficient Agentic RL

summary: Recently, a new coordinate-based normalization has been introduced in [1] to represent tetrahedral similarity classes by normalized coordinates, enabling the study of LEB orbits as a discrete dynamical system. However, the uniqueness of this representation is not guaranteed when two or more edges adjacent to the selected longest edge have the same minimum length and remain admissible under the normalization criteria. In this paper, we demonstrate that different admissible choices may lead to distinct normalized coordinate representations of the same tetrahedral similarity class. We first present an explicit counterexample in which two admissible vertex labelings yield different normalized coordinate representations related by reflection, despite corresponding to the same similarity class. We then provide a systematic classification of the nine possible edge configurations arising in the selection of the canonical face when the longest edge of the tetrahedron is unique, and analyze the corresponding geometric and algebraic conditions. Our analysis identifies the configurations in which the normalization is non-unique and distinguishes them from those in which the ambiguity is resolved by the length criterion, angle criterion, or geometric symmetries. We further show that this non-uniqueness leads to an overcounting of distinct similarity classes.
title: Non-Uniqueness in the Coordinate-Based Normalization of Tetrahedral Similarity Classes

summary: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.
title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks

summary: Hybrid reasoning models interleave attention with recurrent mixers such as Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, whose state is cached between decoding steps. Prior work showed that storing this state in FP16 or INT8 with round-to-nearest (RTN) makes Mamba-2 and GDN hybrids more verbose, and that stochastic rounding (SR) fixes it. We study the other 16-bit format that serving engines expose, bf16, on six open hybrid reasoning models and 590 competition-math problems. With bf16 RTN state, five of six models reason longer (geometric-mean length 1.07x to 1.27x; also under greedy decoding in the two models tested) and hit the 32K token cap more often. On Qwen3.5-9B, cap hits rise from 118 to 223 and accuracy falls from 85.6% to 70.8%. On LiveCodeBench, both models tested also reason longer and lose 12.6 and 13.4 points of pass@1. Rerunning the capped items with a 128K budget halves the accuracy gap but does not close it (93.6% vs. 86.6%): bf16 runs that never finish are twice as common, and 85% of them are exact repetition loops. On Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2, by contrast, 30 of 31 extra caps finish at 128K, so the cost there is mostly extra tokens (exploratory). Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of five affected models, restores Qwen3.5-9B to 87.6% and brings code length and pass@1 near FP32 levels, so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution. With an integer-hash random generator, SR on Qwen3.5-9B matches FP32 on cap hits and accuracy (113 vs. 118; 85.6% for both) at the memory and decoding speed of bf16 RTN. In the Nemotron-Nano-v2 lineage, SR on 25% of heads (an intermediate-decay band) removes the effect, while random heads and the top teacher-forced-KL octiles do not; in Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5-9B the effect is spread across heads. We recommend that evaluations of hybrid models report the state dtype, cap rate and output length alongside accuracy.
title: Lost in Rounding: bf16 Recurrent State Makes Hybrid Reasoning Models Think Longer

summary: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.
