title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens

summary: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
title: Planners Exploit Deterministic Error: Dithered Low-Bit World Models

summary: A deployed language model does not merely answer questions. It spends computation, consumes time, consults evidence, exposes memory, invites or avoids human review, and sometimes makes mistakes whose consequences are radically unequal. Yet LLM systems are still commonly compared as if the relevant object were a single model and the relevant outcome were a single benchmark score. This paper argues that the unit of analysis should instead be the deployment policy: the mechanism that decides when to retrieve, when to remember, when to call a larger model, when to verify, and when not to answer at all. We introduce risk-adjusted deployment efficiency (RADE), a system-level objective that scores the utility a deployment delivers net of inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected failure cost, while treating harms that cannot be priced as hard budgets alongside constraints on latency, privacy, and resources. The framework brings selective routing, retrieval and governed memory, efficient specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and human escalation into a common account. We then examine five deployment regimes in which the same nominal LLM capability leads to different rational architectures, and propose a reporting protocol based on risk-coverage behavior, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load. The central claim is modest but consequential: frontier capability should be treated as a resource to allocate, not a default state to maintain. A safe and sustainable system is not the one that always uses the strongest model; it is the one that spends capability where the reduction in risk or increase in utility justifies the cost.
title: RADE: Risk-Adjusted Deployment Efficiency, A Framework for Routing, Memory, and Escalation in Safe LLM Systems

summary: Generative agents are game characters whose plans, conversations, and memories are written on the fly by a large language model (LLM). The original Generative Agents demonstration used cloud inference in a custom simulation. We present GARP, a platform for real-time generative agents inside Godot, and describe the Character Behavior System used in GARP 2. The complete loop runs on local hardware using a 3B-parameter open-weight model and no cloud service. Alongside the original planning, memory, and reflection, GARP gives each agent an emotion system driven by LLM appraisal, four graded personality axes drawn from the Big Five that set simulation parameters as well as prompt text, six needs whose urgency grows over time, and pairwise relationships updated after every conversation. The system narrows 50+ candidate actions to typically 3-8, constrains model responses with JSON schemas, and surfaces important memories in decision prompts. A layered optimization strategy (an adjustable game clock, decisions taken ahead of need, multi-tier caching, prompt compression, and fully asynchronous execution) keeps the game responsive while the model thinks. In a nine-scenario evaluation, 25 of 27 runs passed log-based checks. Both failures occurred in the birthday party scenario, where one guest omitted the event from their daily plan.
title: GARP: Real-Time Generative Agents on Local Hardware in a Game Engine

summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly improve themselves through self-evolution, distilling execution experience into persistent, reusable skills. However, this persistence creates a new attack surface: malicious rules implanted into skills can compromise subsequent agent behavior. Existing skill backdoor attacks typically assume direct manipulation of the victim's skills, which is impractical when skills are constructed internally by a trusted evolver. In this paper, we study a novel problem of task-level backdoor attacks, where the attacker can only inject poisoned evolution tasks, inducing the agent to implant backdoors into its own skills. Since the attacker controls neither skill induction nor downstream execution, a natural approach is to iteratively optimize poisoned tasks based on attack success. However, our preliminary analysis reveals two key challenges: (i) failures at different stages of skill evolution and downstream execution can produce indistinguishable outcomes, providing little guidance for targeted poisoned-task updates; and (ii) unsuccessful updates may undermine earlier progress, while simply discarding them may lead to repeated ineffective updates. To address these challenges, we propose BadEvolve, a failure-aware task-poisoning framework against self-evolving LLM agents. BadEvolve diagnoses attack failures across four stages, i.e., Induction, Activation, Following, and Effect, and directs updates toward the failing stage. It further employs rollback to preserve earlier progress and failure memory to avoid repeating ineffective updates. Extensive experiments across diverse self-evolution frameworks, benchmarks, and backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of BadEvolve. Our code is available at https://github.com/ventr1c/BadEvolve.
title: When Experience Becomes a Backdoor: Poisoning Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Failure-Aware Task Optimization

summary: Latent Diffusion Models dominate generative modeling but face two-stage training complexity and the inherent reconstruction limits of pre-trained autoencoders. Pixel-space Flow Matching offers a simplified end-to-end alternative yet often encounters training difficulties when using the standard $v$-prediction objective. Recent research attributes this difficulty to the off-manifold nature of noised targets, motivating a shift toward $x$-prediction. In this paper, we investigate this explanation through patch-wise Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and identify a bandwidth bottleneck. The velocity in minor components is largely determined by the raw noisy input, requiring deep backbones to preserve information that competes with principal-component modeling. Through controlled experiments and representation analysis, we further examine why $x$-prediction remains effective: its parameterization provides a raw-input bypass, while its learned input representation can spontaneously concentrate on principal directions. Under low-rank observations, our analysis of the induced flow characterizes $x$-prediction as an implicit conditional-mean decoder, reconstructing discarded components from the retained information. These observations motivate the Raw-injected Transformer (RiT), which combines a lightweight raw-conditioned decoder with an output-side shortcut to separate semantic modeling from raw-state propagation. Our method restores effective $v$-prediction and achieves competitive performance on ImageNet $256\times256$, providing a perspective on the interaction between prediction objectives and architectural bandwidth.
title: What kills $v$-prediction? A Patch-wise PCA Perspective on Pixel-Space Flow Matching

summary: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.
title: HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents

summary: AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels.
title: MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning

summary: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
title: $Σ$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control

summary: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.
title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model

summary: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.
title: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?

summary: Correlation Matrix Memories (CMMs) store associations as sums of rank-one outer products, providing closed-form addressability, exact deletion, and linear attribution. While classical analyses assume random, orthogonal keys, semantic encoders produce correlated representations. We analyse CMMs under correlated keys using frame-theoretic coherence: (i) capacity bounds yielding an encoder-independent limit $n \le d(1+\varepsilon^2)$ for mean squared crosstalk $\varepsilon^2$; (ii) an exact characterisation of the collateral effect of deleting an association, guaranteeing that deletion never invalidates certified associations; and (iii) a geometric transparency bound demonstrating why attribution requires candidate sets of centred keys. On this basis, we introduce Topology-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Associative Retrieval (TANSAR). TANSAR traverses a directed acyclic association graph, prunes invalid paths via sound ground Horn constraints, and injects a representation derived strictly from the verified path into the residual stream of a frozen language model, guarded by a Clopper--Pearson selective-risk gate. Controlled experiments confirm all theoretical bounds. In multi-hop knowledge editing, Horn pruning reduces answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, whereas Hopfield retrieval incurs 24% contradictions when stale associations remain stored (and 0% if stale associations are removed). An end-to-end edit transaction requires 13.6 ms on a standard CPU and 2.37 ms on GPU. The symbolic component matches gold labels across all 600 ProofWriter theories and achieves 94.0% agreement on FOLIO, demonstrating sound and efficient multi-hop associative retrieval with exact unlearning.
title: TANSAR: Editable and Attributable Correlation Matrix Memories under Correlated Keys, with Rule-Constrained Multi-Hop Knowledge Editing

summary: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.
title: How Many Exposures Does a World Model Need? Learning Unseen Game Mechanics at Test Time

summary: Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) methods update models online using a stream of unlabeled data to overcome distribution shifts encountered at test time. However, CTTA is often unstable, as it can reinforce biases in early predictions and increasingly predict only a few classes, resulting in drift or even collapse. In this paper, we identify narrowing pseudo-label class usage as an indicator of CTTA instability and quantify this behavior. Most existing methods have attempted to address this issue by either selecting reliable adaptation samples or re-weighting the loss to encourage diverse pseudo-labels, but they do not explicitly enforce a class marginal over a temporal window. Instead, we propose Sinkhorn Class-Marginal Regularization (SCALAR), a simple plug-and-play module that controls the pseudo-label distribution over a short temporal window. SCALAR works by maintaining recent predictions in a buffer, balancing their class distribution via the Sinkhorn algorithm to match a specified target distribution, and using the balanced soft targets for adaptation. Without changing the model architecture, SCALAR maintains the per-step runtime and increases the peak allocated GPU memory by only 10 MB on ImageNet-C. Our method is particularly effective on skewed, non-stationary data with severe distribution shifts, where SCALAR significantly alleviates drift and collapse when combined with existing stabilization methods based on entropy or diversity.
title: Controlling Temporal Pseudo-Label Marginals for Stable Online Test-Time Adaptation

summary: Verbal memory retrieval carries rich diagnostic information for Alzheimer's disease through the order, hesitation, and categorical organization of recalled words, yet computational modeling of this retrieval process remains largely unexplored. A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail. On real-world clinical data, we show that TrajLift outperforms diverse baselines by jointly modeling timing and semantic structure, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative.
title: TrajLift: Lifting Memory Recall Trajectories with Latency-Modulated Heat Diffusion

summary: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.
title: GeoMind: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in Robotic Manipulation

summary: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.
title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation

summary: Multi-view anomaly detection is crucial for industrial inspection to identify defects hidden from single viewpoints. Yet, despite their strong success in single-view applications, reconstruction-based methods remain largely underexplored in multi-view settings. A key challenge in extending these methods lies in generating view-consistent pseudo-anomalies. To address this, we propose PAR, a reconstruction-based framework for enhanced multi-view anomaly detection. First, we introduce a feature perturbation strategy coupled with a consensus aggregation module that integrates these perturbed features across viewpoints to mitigate view-inconsistent anomalies and construct highly aligned pseudo-anomaly representations. Second, we employ a view-specialized multi-decoder architecture; by assigning a dedicated decoder to each view, we increase the model's representational complexity, enabling the generation of highly feasible, localized anomaly maps rather than less precise, view-agnostic reconstructions. Last, we incorporate Fourier attention into the decoders to emphasize global frequency-domain structures over local token evidence, effectively preventing identity mapping. Extensive experiments on the Real-IAD dataset demonstrate that PAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in sample-level, image-level, and pixel-level anomaly detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/SpatialAILab/PAR_mvad.
title: Perturb, Aggregate then Reconstruct: Consensus Aggregation and Fourier-Attended Multi-Decoders for Reconstruction-based Multi-View Anomaly Detection

summary: Combining video generation, dynamic reconstruction and monocular SLAM requires consistent coordinates, explicit handling of missing outputs and predictable memory use. We present AcrossVAM3.0, an offline system that converts text, images or monocular RGB video into a versioned point representation. Frozen components run sequentially on one GPU; map corrections update cameras, points and trajectories together. The coordination layer adds no neural parameters. Three fresh input-mode runs completed with a maximum sampled task-process-tree GPU footprint of 17.14 GB. In a frozen 16-scene video suite, every scene yielded a 4D reconstruction and 15 yielded a non-empty SLAM map. Strict cross-window matching reduced local surface error but lost long-range track coverage on TAP-Vid-DAVIS. We therefore developed multi-hypothesis adaptive surface chaining (MHAC), which retains several candidate matches and an explicit missing state. After selection on disjoint development data, MHAC improved Average Jaccard over a position-only baseline by 0.1394 on a frozen ten-video holdout (95% bootstrap interval [0.1074,0.1689]). Across 265 RoboTAP videos, the mean paired gain was 0.0610 ([0.0510,0.0715]), with 215 wins, one tie and 49 losses. These results support resource-bounded scene construction and an external tracking gain under the tested protocol. They do not establish metric scale, semantic identity or high-fidelity novel-view rendering.
title: ACROSSVAM3.0: Resource-Bounded 4D Scene Construction and Adaptive Surface Association

summary: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.
title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity

summary: Continual instruction tuning often preserves old skills with task-private modules. Inference still requires selecting the right module from the prompt alone. We introduce Task-Isolated Latent Adapter Continual Training (TILA-CT), a replay-free method that makes each task module self-indexing. Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation, the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context. For access, its persistent state provides the routing prototype used by a shared prompt-only router. On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score, with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 acquisition and 64.17 final macro score. Across 6 backbones, final scores remain within 1.5 points of acquisition. Ablations support memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9\%, and oracle routing recovers 1.21 final macro points. These results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it.
title: Self-Indexing Latent Memories for Access-Aware Continual Instruction Tuning of LLMs

summary: Learning neural solvers for spatiotemporal partial differential equations (PDEs) under real-world constraints remains a key challenge in scientific machine learning, especially for inverse tasks with sparse and noisy boundary observations. We present the Aletheia dataset, the first 3D benchmark for learning data-driven solvers in the context of nondestructive testing (NDT). The dataset simulates eddy-current-induced heating in conductive solids and models the resulting transient heat propagation governed by the heat equation. Aletheia contains over 4,700 high-resolution samples across 10 excitation frequencies (1-100,kHz), each providing volumetric heat source and temperature fields over time. It supports both forward prediction of temperature evolution and inverse reconstruction of internal heat sources or defects from surface infrared measurements. Real infrared thermography data from cracked rail specimens are included for calibration and comparison. We define four canonical tasks on both regular and irregular grids and benchmark them using various neural operators. Aletheia establishes a unified platform for evaluating neural PDE solvers under realistic NDT conditions, enabling progress in reliable, data-driven inverse modeling. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://github.com/sherlock-0327/ALETHEIA.
title: ALETHEIA: A Multi-Frequency Eddy Current Pulsed Thermography Dataset for Neural Operator Learning in Nondestructive Testing

summary: Low-bit post-training quantization reduces language-model memory but can sharply degrade downstream task accuracy. Calibration usually relies on generic text, but when task-informed data recover accuracy and which quantizers benefit remain poorly understood. We introduce FragCal-DC, which supplements generic text with training documents from task families with low retention of full-precision accuracy in a two-bit scan. We use a two- to four-bit sweep to locate functional regimes and four-seed calibration comparisons to evaluate six data-dependent methods across six dense models (1.7B-8B) and ten tasks. At their lowest tested functional bit widths, iterative SignRound V2 and OmniQuant improve at two bits, whereas single-pass GPTQ and AWQ show small mean responses at three bits. At two bits, SignRound V2 gains 1.83 percentage points in mean ten-task accuracy over generic-text calibration across six models. At 70 billion parameters, GPTQ and SignRound V2 both improve at two bits, with functional generic-calibration baselines. For two-bit SignRound V2, task-level controls show that recovery concentrates on families included in calibration, while incorrect answer designations retain about 90% of the mean accuracy gain. Changes in reconstruction error do not consistently track accuracy gains. These findings support task-informed calibration as a design principle for preserving downstream accuracy in low-bit quantization.
title: When Calibration Data Matter in Sub-4-Bit Language Model Quantization

summary: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.
title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations

summary: Systematic literature reviews (SRs) remain slow and labor-intensive, and most automation tools address single stages of the workflow. We present PARIS (PRISMA Agentic Research Intelligence System), an open-source framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 specialized large language model (LLM) agents, from scoping a research question to exporting a manuscript draft. Agents are specified declaratively, coordinate exclusively through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before every transition, and delegate retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring to deterministic Python utilities. Three human checkpoints gate study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. We also introduce QualityScore, a pre-synthesis index that aggregates normalized network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores into a 0-100 grade. Two case studies illustrate both: AI chatbots and university students' learning (388 records, 100 included) and AI-assisted SR methods (131 records, 123 included, QualityScore 69.1 recomputed with a proxy network sub-score). They show end-to-end feasibility across domains and the diagnostic use of QualityScore: in the first run, corpus improvements chosen at the corpus-adequacy checkpoint raised the score from 74.6 to 81.9 and the number of pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits of both runs exposed failure modes: incomplete retrieval, counts that drifted between agents, unrecorded or delegated checkpoint decisions and a grade that depends on how citation data are handled. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partially supports 11. Output quality has so far been judged only by an internal reviewer agent; independent validation against human reviews is the next step.
title: PARIS: A multi-agent LLM framework for end-to-end, PRISMA-guided systematic literature reviews with pre-synthesis corpus quality assessment

summary: Recent systems such as the eBPF Certificate Framework (BCF) and Proof-Carrying BPF address the imprecision in the Linux eBPF verifier with proof-carrying code. When the verifier's abstract domains cannot prove a safety condition, an in-kernel proof checker checks an untrusted user-space refutation proof. A single bug in this checker can compromise the security of the entire kernel. While formalizing BCF's in-kernel checker, we discovered 13 bugs such as unsound rewrite rules, silently unchecked proof steps, and memory safety errors. We demonstrate that forged certificates can trick the kernel to accept arbitrary unsafe eBPF programs. To address this problem, we propose Keel, a formally verified in-kernel proof checker for the Linux eBPF verifier. First, we specify the checker as a pure functional program in Lean and prove its soundness against bit-vector semantics. We decouple the steps of the proof certificate checker from the mathematical rewrite rules, which enables us to extend the rewrite rules without the need to change the checker. Second, we implement the checker in EmbC, a deeply embedded C fragment, and prove that our C implementation refines the functional specification without undefined behavior or memory leaks. Third, using an amortized potential argument, we prove linear time and memory bounds for the C checker. Keel is correct-by-construction while also being faster than the BCF checker inside the kernel, 1.3X in total and 2.0X on the slowest 1.4% of certificates.
title: Keel: A Verified In-Kernel Proof Checker for Proof Carrying BPF

summary: A tape of $n$ cells over three values — equivalently, two-bit cells read through their sum — is read by two headers that enclose a window; at each step a fixed rule, given the window's content and the geometry, chooses one of eight actions: move a header inward or outward, trim a cell from the left, the right or both, or halt. The cost is the number of cell reads, the state is $O(\log n)$ bits, and the question is how the cost must grow with $n$ for each rule. On the evidence the rules fall into three classes — fully linear, semi-linear and superlinear — separated by a worst-case cost and a mean cost. All three are populated: four natural rules are fully linear, one construction is semi-linear ($e=\Theta(n)$ with $g=\Theta(n^2)$), and the remaining seventeen are superlinear. The paper separates the length of a walk from the number of cells it reads, shows the length is a property of the rule rather than of the model, gives machines for every rule in the catalogue, arranges their costs on a ladder from $n^{1/2}$ to $n^3$, and states exactly which rungs are proved, which are conditional and which are conjectural. Negative results included: the certificate bound does not compose (on one tape per-query certificates sum to $1{,}285{,}703$ cells while their union has $1{,}020$), and a bound on the rule's output transfers to the walk only after multiplication by the fraction of queries at which the answer can change the action, measured at $0.104$ and falling like $n^{-0.99}$.
title: A memoryless two-header tape machine: what a window costs, and why two lower-bound techniques fail

summary: Enterprise adoption of agentic systems is often framed as a problem of agent reasoning, tool use, retrieval, or memory. This paper investigates an additional architectural problem: preparing heterogeneous enterprise knowledge into task-appropriate representations that agents can interpret, reuse, and govern. We propose Cognitive Preparation as an explicit architectural lifecycle between authoritative enterprise knowledge and agent execution, with a Cognitive Preparation Compiler (CPC) coordinating representation decisions, compilation, validation, provenance binding, temporal constraints, and publication through a reusable Cognitive Substrate. The contribution is positioned at the architectural and methodological level; no novelty is claimed for ontologies, symbolic predicates, memory mechanisms, provenance, temporal models, or knowledge compilation individually. Recent 2026 preprints on precomputed agent-memory views and enterprise context engineering further narrow the novelty boundary and are treated as close, non-peer-reviewed prior art. We report a staged prototype evaluation implemented in Ver.Test9 on a Ver.Test8 runtime foundation. Deterministic tests examine selected lifecycle controls, while exploratory LLM-assisted evaluations (T17–T22) examine controlled reuse of synthetic operational knowledge through deterministic retrieval. The results provide implementation-level feasibility evidence and preliminary observations of scoped procedural knowledge reuse, including provider- and operation-specific applicability, temporal validity, and version precedence. They do not establish general performance superiority, validated adaptive representation selection, transfer between genuinely independent agents, autonomous learning, production readiness, or economic break-even. The five research questions are retained, with preliminary support strongest for controlled knowledge reuse; preparation effectiveness and evolution receive partial evidence, while adaptive representation selection and reuse economics remain open.
title: Cognitive Preparation for Agentic Enterprise Systems: A Knowledge Compilation Architecture and Preliminary Evaluation

summary: 6.17.0 (2026-11-10) Changes: Add Zarr media-types application/vnd.zarr (including version=2 and version=3 parameters) for directory stores, and application/zarr+zip for zipped stores, with their .zarr and .zarr.zip extensions. The zipped variant is distinguished from a plain application/zip (resolves #1012 ). Convert WPS/OGC API - Processes I/O using only Zarr directory media-types into CWL Directory without format (not applicable for that type), similarly to the handling of application/directory . Handle Zarr directory media-types as directories when returning Job results by-value and when refusing local directory uploads to the Vault from the CLI. Preserve the Zarr media-type declared by a Process output as the type of the resulting Job output when the CWL output is a Directory (instead of reporting it as application/directory ), and report it as Content-Type for directory references when explicitly provided. Offer application/zarr+zip as alternate format of Zarr directory Job outputs, using the ?f={mediaType} result representation to obtain the zipped store (store contents located at the root of the archive). When an explicit version of the Zarr media-type is declared, the generic application/vnd.zarr is also offered, and requesting it returns the same directory store without conversion. Refuse deployment of a Process declaring a Zarr directory media-type on an I/O that is defined as a CWL File , since Zarr stores must be represented by a Directory . Fixes: Fix files without extension in a remote directory listing (e.g.: Zarr chunks such as c/0 ) being renamed with a default extension (e.g.: c/0.txt ) when fetched as part of a directory, which corrupted the directory contents. Fix Job results returned by-value for binary contents (e.g.: zipped Zarr) being decoded as UTF-8 text, which failed for non-text bytes. Raw bytes are now returned as is for single result responses, and as base64 encoded value (with encoding metadata) when embedded in the JSON results document. Run safety dependency checks using its ghcr.io/pyupio/safety Docker image in the Makefile and CI. Move vulnerability exclusions and their reasons into .safety-policy.yml . Remove the Python development dependency and its authlib / marshmallow compatibility pins (relates to pyupio/safety#822 ). Add OGC API - Processes - Part 5: Provenance and Profiles new metadata-profiles conformance class references which provides the semantics of metadata with role , href and a profiled-term rel to annotate the Process itself or at granular I/O definitions, and aligns with dataClasses URIs along the I/O schema (relates to opengeospatial/ogcapi-processes#637 ). Implement GET /processes?metadata[<scope>][<role>]=<profile> query filtering to list only Process summaries that define a matching metadata entry, either in the main process or per inputs/outputs definition of the requested <scope>, and resolving Safe CURIE/URN role / profile references to their long-form URI as necessary. Corresponding HTTP 400/422 error responses are raised when applicable for invald parsing or combinations. Add OGC API - Processes - Part 5: Provenance and Profiles metadata-profiles conformance class references. Implement OPTIONS /processes to advertise supported methods and deployment media types with Allow and Accept-Post headers, as required by the metadata-profiles requirements. Add Vary: Accept, Prefer because process-list response behavior depends on those request headers. Add legacy application/tiff; application=geotiff and application/jp2 media-types (from the OGC API - Processes examples) as dynamically supported equivalents of image/tiff; application=geotiff and image/jp2 respectively. Inputs submitted with them are accepted by any Process that defines the official media-types, without explicitly listing them in its description. The legacy types are never selected when resolving media-types (e.g.: from file extensions). Add keyless allratestoday option for weaver.quota
title: crim-ca/weaver:6.17.0

summary: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.
title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery

summary: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.
title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels

summary: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) have emerged as generative models guaranteeing tractable probabilistic inference. However, tractability comes at the price of larger model sizes than in other generative models. As such, to scale PCs to high-dimensional data such as images, previous work has devised several parameter sharing techniques as well as fast evaluation protocols that consider learning PCs on independent image patches. In this work, we revisit this practice to highlight a surprising learnability issue: models that assume independence counterintuitively can yield better likelihoods than models that do not. To break this apparent bottleneck and to scale PCs further, we introduce a recursive parameter sharing construction (RePA) that fosters efficiency without assuming independence. We show empirically that RePA can greatly reduce time and memory consumption while yielding competitive likelihoods. Inspired by these results, we further generalize the approach to data modalities that do not inherently exhibit patch-structure (NoPA), such as tabular data, showing similar efficiency improvements, with marginal changes in likelihoods and sample quality on seven tabular datasets. Code available at https://github.com/april-tools/RePA.
title: Patching Up Circuit Learning via Parameter Sharing

summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.
title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs

The scales, per-dataset diagnostics and iteration count are stored in the fit metadata ( error_scales , dataset_diagnostics , weighting , reweight_iterations ). Optional error floors: visual_error_floor , rv_error_floor . Real-data benchmarks for Capella (Torres et al. 2009) and alpha Cen AB (Akeson et al. 2021), a GL 765 benchmark (Balega et al. 2007), a PySeshat-versus-published comparison, a weighting-sensitivity study and orbit-coverage metrics ( scripts/ , validation/results/ ). The VizieR tables are not redistributed; see the README in each benchmark folder. Third-party licence notice for the bundled ORBIT / ORBIT3 example files ( third_party/ORBIT/NOTICE.md ). Component magnitude differences (e.g. from speckle interferometry) as an SED-fitting constraint: photometry.observations.MagnitudeDifference , photometry.model.synthetic_magnitude_differences , fit_photometry(..., magnitude_differences=...) , PhotometricContext.magnitude_differences , and a magnitude_differences entry in the benchmark files. Tests: tests/test_magnitude_difference.py . photometry.calibration : standard-system zero points following Maíz Apellániz (2006, 2007): Vega's standard magnitudes ( VEGA_STANDARD_MAGNITUDES , Table 4 of Maíz Apellániz 2007, ASP Conf. Ser., 364, 227), the CALSPEC Vega spectrum alpha_lyr_stis_003 (Bohlin 2007; shipped as package data), and vega_zero_points(passbands) , which integrates Vega through the same passbands as the target. Tests: tests/test_photometric_calibration.py , and solar checks (Willmer 2018 magnitudes, Meléndez et al. 2010 Strömgren indices) with a CK04 model and with the observed CALSPEC solar spectrum ( tests/data/ ) in tests/test_synthetic_photometry_sun_calibration.py . Photon-counting passbands: PhotometricPassband.photon_counting , load_passband(..., photon_counting=None) (read from a # detector: photon|energy header line; default energy-integrating), and lambda weighting of photon-counting curves in synthetic_band_flux (Maíz Apellániz 2006, AJ, 131, 1184, Eq. A1). Provenance table: validation/photometry/passbands/README.md . Tests: tests/test_photon_counting_passband.py . fit_visual_orbit_mcmc(..., parameterization="sqrt_e") (also in fit_visual_orbit_mcmc_from_problem ): samples the mean longitude and sqrt(e) sin/cos omega in place of (T0, e, omega), with the Jacobian term, so the posterior is unchanged and near-circular orbits mix far better. The default ( "standard" ) is unchanged; results are returned in the standard elements. pyseshat.inference.reparameterization ; tests: tests/test_sqrt_e_parameterization.py . Fixed Binary MCMC: T0 is now folded to within P/2 of the least-squares T0 (using each sample's P). The model depends on T0 only modulo P; on near-circular orbits the walkers drifted across many periods, which inflated the T0 spread and the autocorrelation times. Tests: tests/test_mcmc_t0_folding.py . Visual-only fits (no RV data) with K1, K2 or V0 flagged as fitted (the OrbitalElements default) counted these parameters in the degrees of freedom, reported zero uncertainties for them, and let them drift without bound in MCMC. They are now held fixed when there are no RV data. The ORBIT-format benchmark inputs were not affected (their flags are read from the files). summary: This repository provides the data, scripts, intermediate products, numerical outputs and documentation supporting the manuscript “Monitoring habitat conservation status and assessing biodiversity: The Dehesa case”. It implements a reproducible framework combining Earth observation, probability sampling and model-assisted estimation to monitor dehesa conservation status, carbon stocks and change, and biodiversity. The repository is organised into two Earth observation preprocessing modules and six numerical examples: EO Sentinel: processing of wet- and dry-season Sentinel-2 imagery and construction of the 10 m auxiliary pixel database. EO LiDAR: processing and validation of PNOA LiDAR data and construction of the reviewed LiDAR candidate-tree dataset. Numerical Example 1: tree condition and temporal change. Numerical Example 2: grassland condition and temporal change. Numerical Example 3: shrubland condition and temporal change. Numerical Example 4: integrated woody carbon-stock accounting, with annual herbaceous biomass-carbon flows reported separately. Numerical Example 5: herbaceous composition and biodiversity. Numerical Example 6: bird composition and biodiversity. After downloading and extracting the archive, readers should begin with the top-level README.md. Each module also contains a README describing its purpose, inputs, analytical workflow, scripts, expected outputs, validation checks and limitations. The module READMEs document the provenance of the Earth observation source data included in the archive and identify any additional inputs needed to run the workflows. The numerical examples illustrate the methods presented in the manuscript and its supplementary materials. Some example data are simulated or use proxies, as specified in the corresponding documentation. The repository is intended to facilitate peer review, reproducibility and adaptation of the monitoring framework to other dehesa areas.

summary: The discovery rate p a of Cuckoo Search sets how much of each solution the abandonment operator rebuilds, and many variants tune it with schedules or online controllers. Using one shared implementation, paired seeds and 70 problem instances (classical functions at D = 10, 30 and 50, shifted-rotated functions, and CEC-2017 F1 and F3–F20 at D = 30 and 50), we show that the best constant p a ranges from 0.02 to 0.80. Much of this dependence reflects separability: rotating the classical functions raises the best level on 6 of 8, as the crossover-rate theory of differential evolution predicts. Early progress is an unreliable guide: the best level after 10% of the budget differs from the best final level on 12 of 35 functions, and on the classical functions choosing it raises the final error a median 12.4-fold. Keeping a spread of rates across the nests avoids this choice. A random per-nest spread alone improves on the default on 13 of 19 CEC-2017 functions at D = 30; self-adaptive (SA- p a ) and success-history (SH- p a ) per-nest rates improve on it on 54 and 47 of 70 instances, with 3 and 5 losses (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests). On CEC-2017 their median error is 0.93 (D = 30) and 1.13 (D = 50) times that of the best constant chosen in hindsight, against 1.76 and 1.67 for the default. The gains vanish at D = 10, and Cuckoo Search remains well behind jDE.
tags: Cuckoo search; Parameter control; Self-adaptation; Discovery rate; Rotation invariance; Separability; Benchmarking
title: A spread of rates, not a schedule: population-level heterogeneity in the discovery rate of Cuckoo Search

summary: EXTRARNAS — Datasets, Software Outputs, and Analysis Scripts Companion material for the CIBB 2026 short paper and an extended manuscript under submission This repository contains research data, RNA annotation outputs, curated references, analysis scripts, and supplementary documentation associated with EXTRARNAS. It supports the original CIBB 2026 short paper, “EXTRARNAS: A Framework for Extracting RNA Structures with Multiple Tools,” and the extended manuscript “EXTRARNAS: Standardized RNA Structure Annotation and Cross-Tool Comparison” (currently under submission). What is new in this version The extended study analyzes eight RNA structures containing triple-helix motifs using seven tools: RNAView, MC-Annotate, RNApolis Annotator, FR3D, X3DNA-DSSR, Barnaba, and BPNet. The archive includes the full tool outputs, standardized BPSEQ/BPSEQE representations, curated structural references, and quantitative comparisons with the references and among the annotators. The extension experiments used EXTRARNAS v1.1.0. The accompanying manifest documents Docker image IDs, tool versions, Git revisions, checksums, and analysis dependencies. The licensed X3DNA-DSSR executable is not redistributed. Repository contents ·   experiment_triple_helices_extension/ — complete eight-structure dataset, seven-annotator outputs, BPSEQ/BPSEQE files, curated references, analysis scripts, quantitative results, figures, and reproducibility instructions. ·   experiment_triple_helices_extension/software_environment/ — version and execution-environment manifest. ·   experiment_triple_helices/ — original CIBB 2026 experiment using three annotators, retained unchanged. ·   additional-experiments/5s-pseudoknot-batch/ — historical batch-processing experiment on 20 5S RNA structures; not included in the extended study’s quantitative evaluation. ·   documentation_CIBB2026/ and README.md — archived original documentation and current repository-wide guide. Reference annotations and reproducibility For the extended study, the PAN2 reference sequence was corrected to match the 3D model and the published structure figure; the original reference remains in the historical material for provenance. Exact cWH Hoogsteen-pair recovery is evaluated against a non-exhaustive curated reference and therefore reported as recovery/recall only, not precision or F1. The included scripts reproduce the raw quantitative comparison results from archived annotation outputs without rerunning the seven tools. Full workflow reproduction additionally requires a compatible software environment and separately licensed components. The original CIBB 2026 experiments were generated with EXTRARNAS v1.0.1-cibb2026. Software repository: https://github.com/bdslab/EXTRARNAS Software DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21238912 Dataset DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21246054

summary: This repository provides supporting research materials for the conceptual manuscript entitled “Financial Stress, Spiritual Coping, and Mental Health Resilience in Emerging Economies: Toward an Integrative Conceptual Framework.” It documents the development of the Financial–Spiritual Resilience Framework (FSRF), which integrates financial adversity, religious and spiritual coping, spiritual struggle, communal meaning-making, psychological distress, and resilience, with particular attention to emerging economies.       The repository contains literature search expressions and scope documentation, a conceptual selection protocol, a reference map of 43 publications, bibliographic and source-access verification records, a claim–evidence correspondence audit covering 56 central statements, six theoretical propositions, a supplementary operationalization and falsification matrix, and the conceptual framework figure.       Project bibliographic exports comprised 491 initial records (221 from Web of Science and 270 from Scopus), with 353 provisionally unique records after bibliographic deduplication. Full-document copies of 39 of the 43 cited works were available for targeted verification; four were not supplied. This documentation supports transparency but does not constitute a systematic literature review, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or exhaustive replication of all reported findings.       The FSRF is a conceptual and testable framework, not an empirically validated intervention. No original participant-level data, copyrighted full-text articles, or proprietary database exports are redistributed. The materials are shared under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

This documentation supports transparency but does not constitute a systematic literature review, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or exhaustive replication of all reported findings.       The FSRF is a conceptual and testable framework, not an empirically validated intervention. No original participant-level data, copyrighted full-text articles, or proprietary database exports are redistributed. The materials are shared under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

summary: emgteach is an open-source Python package that provides a unified PySide6 desktop application for real-time acquisition, offline analysis and maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) normalisation of surface electromyography (sEMG) signals. It is designed for hands-on biopotential acquisition in undergraduate physiology teaching laboratories, and is meant to be set up by instructors with different levels of technical background and used directly by students during a practical session. The application is hardware-agnostic through a common AcquisitionDevice interface and ships with two interchangeable low-cost backends: BITalino (revolution) over Bluetooth, and an Arduino RedBoard Plus + MyoWare 2.0 over USB serial (open firmware included). A single setting switches between them. Main features: Three-tab GUI (Acquisition, Analysis, MVC normalisation) wrapping a reusable, Qt-free analytic core. Bilingual interface (English / Spanish) with automatic start-up language detection and an in-app language switch. Two-channel acquisition (e.g. agonist/antagonist) with a stacked two-channel live view. Automatic contraction-onset detection (baseline + k·SD threshold) stored as EDF+ annotations. Muscle-load analysis (Jonsson APDF): static (P10), median (P50) and peak (P90) %MVC levels, both offline and as a live monitor with warning/danger zones. One-click PDF session and MVC/muscle-load reports. Reliable EDF+ output using a buffered-write pattern that avoids a silent file-corruption artefact during continuous streaming. Assisted selection of significant fragments, with an editable fragment editor (detection parameters and envelope-filter cut-offs) applied to the analysis. CSV export of results and a live signal-quality check during recording. Classroom mode: a read-only live dashboard served over the local network so students follow the session on their phone/tablet browser (no install), with a per-session access code so the follower link only works while the broadcast is running. Kinematics via the BITalino accelerometer (v2.0.0): a movement-versus-EMG analysis panel, a guided force-velocity acquisition wizard (an MVC maximum followed by cued quick lifts, each auto-marked with its load), and a force-velocity study that turns one recording into the load-velocity, Hill force-velocity, power and recruitment curves. Since v3.0.0 the accelerometer's input is a stated convention (muscle on A1, accelerometer on A2) rather than a selectable channel. Configuration by practical (v3.0.0): three practicals — one muscle, agonist/antagonist and muscle kinematics — fix the channel count, the accelerometer and what each tab offers, replacing the settings that were previously chosen one at a time. The session as a single file with its phases marked inside it (v3.0.0): warm-up, calibration repetitions, preparation and recording, so the maximum voluntary contraction every percentage is measured against travels with the signal, and a derived (tuned) recording carries the decisions taken on screen. Teaching layer (v3.0.0): a guided tour over the interface, contextual help on every box, one analysis row per contraction with its electromechanical delay, and an agonist/antagonist co-activation index (Falconer-Winter) computed per marked phase in %MVC. Handling at the laboratory bench (v3.1.0): the fragment editor as a three-step procedure that counts the marked contractions against the protocol and lets each be kept, dropped, split or dragged, with the detection sensitivity set per practical and recorded in the report and the CSV; a single running instance with a start-up splash; pictures of the electrode placement and the calibration in the guided tour; and a printable sheet for each station of the agonist/antagonist practical. Patch 3.1.1: the co-activation of a named window is read on the uncut recording, with each muscle's resting level taken from the whole recording phase, so choosing fragments no longer measures the antagonist against a rest taken from a signal

summary: Wave-powered reverse osmosis (RO) desalination with electricity cogeneration is a promising approach, as both the energy source and the seawater are present at the same location. Hydraulic power take-off (PTO) systems are used because they are well-suited for the low-frequency, high-force requirements of wave energy converters (WECs). Conventional hydraulic PTOs for cogeneration suffer from limitations related to the required power density and cost. In these architectures, the WEC-driven pump and the RO module are connected in parallel to a common pressure rail, forcing the pump to operate at the relatively low pressure of the RO membrane. This limits the power density of the WEC pump, thus increasing the size of the most costly component.
title: Integrated Hydraulic Transformer for Cogeneration of Electricity and Freshwater from Wave Energy

Hydraulic power take-off (PTO) systems are used because they are well-suited for the low-frequency, high-force requirements of wave energy converters (WECs). Conventional hydraulic PTOs for cogeneration suffer from limitations related to the required power density and cost. In these architectures, the WEC-driven pump and the RO module are connected in parallel to a common pressure rail, forcing the pump to operate at the relatively low pressure of the RO membrane. This limits the power density of the WEC pump, thus increasing the size of the most costly component.

summary: The papers of Johann Ludwig Kuefstein, imperial orator at the Porte in 1628–1629 (ELTE University Library, Budapest, Manuscript Collection, G. 4, Fol., Tom. I–XIV), include a page almost wholly in a cipher of graphic signs, Tom. V p. 1461, catalogued as a dispatch of Kuefstein to the Emperor and listed as undeciphered. Regina Donáth reproduced it in Magyar Könyvszemle (1964). Using the key rebuilt from Donáth's printed examples, this preprint gives a provisional German text (about 90% read), an English translation and a commentary. The page is not a dispatch from Kuefstein but an order to him from the Imperial War Council (Hofkriegsrat), dated Vienna, 27 October 1629: the Emperor has heard that the Pasha of Buda (Murtaza Pasha) had been received with, or joined by, about 3,000 Turks, and asks what troops these are, where they came from, and whether they are still assembled. Version 1 is a provisional reading from Donáth's 1964 halftone; a definitive edition will follow once a scan of the original has been obtained. Files: the preprint (PDF) and the reconstructed key (TSV). Donáth's plate is not reproduced. AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) was used in key reconstruction, transcription and drafting and is disclosed in the text.
title: Vienna Asks Constantinople: The Imperial War Council to Johann Ludwig Kuefstein, 27 October 1629 (a provisional decipherment of ELTE G. 4, Tom. V, p. 1461)

summary: Changing an objective does not automatically revise agents' earlier plans or delegated tasks. Acknowledgment can coexist with obsolete execution, while misleading instructions can redirect work or discard retained constraints. We present a Strategic World simulation testbed that separates authoritative objectives, local plans, notice receipt, and consequential action. Six intervention families vary objectives, conditions, authority, membership, and communication. Matched protocols and deadlines establish feasibility for the tested disturbances. Controlled trajectories demonstrate that identical completion and acknowledgment summaries can conceal uninformed obsolete work, obsolete work after receipt, or blocked unsafe intent. Local language-model trials and instructed action probes reveal competence limits that constrain interpretation of dynamic failures. A further 16-episode comparison evaluates an engineered guard that prioritizes pending notice submissions over local work. It completes 4/4 held-out settings, compared with 1/4 for a calibrated assisted baseline. Each episode contains one large language model actor and two fixed peers. These results establish diagnostic distinctions and bounded policy feasibility under explicit simulation assumptions; they do not establish frontier-model reliability or autonomous team adaptation.
title: When the Plan Changes: A Strategic World Testbed for Dynamic Multi-Agent Coordination

summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems solve complex tasks through collaboration, but their growing, simultaneously resident key-value (KV) caches create a memory bottleneck. Applying single-model quantization policies independently ignores differences in agents' precision needs, potentially degrading collective reasoning. We introduce Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization (CoMixKV), which combines online sensitivity estimation with joint agent-layer bit-width allocation under a shared memory budget. To our knowledge, CoMixKV is the first mixed-precision KV-cache quantization framework to jointly allocate precision across simultaneously resident agent caches under such a budget. The estimator derives sensitivity from a local attention-error bound using recent queries, keys, and values, without calibration data, trial quantization, or additional model passes. A shared controller combines these scores with remaining quantizable capacity and byte-level storage costs to minimize total estimated error. Allocations are refreshed as agents start or finish and new observations become available. Selected widths apply only to newly quantized blocks; recent states retain native precision and previously quantized blocks remain unchanged. Across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones at average 2-bit, 3-bit, and 4-bit settings, CoMixKV achieves strong accuracy against the evaluated quantization baselines. At the average 3-bit setting on Gemma-4-31B-it, it achieves 68.35% average accuracy, exceeding the strongest quantized baseline by 0.59%. On Qwen3-32B, it reduces peak KV-cache memory by 32.08% and achieves a 1.38x inference speedup over FullKV.
title: Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization for Efficient LLM-based Multi-agent Systems

summary: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.
title: Hibana: Fast Agentic Inference on Unified-Memory Devices

summary: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.
title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction

summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) integrate information across modalities, but become unreliable when those modalities disagree. Under conflicting inputs, MLLMs may favor modalities that are not the most reliable for the task, thus motivating inference-time control of modality arbitration. We identify a small set of attention heads, termed arbitration heads, that causally influence whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight, training-free intervention that biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time. The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalize across settings, and steering them enables effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks. Our findings identify an effective control mechanism to align MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.
title: Beyond Modality Preference: Controlling Multimodal Arbitration under Modality Conflict in MLLMs
