summary: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.
title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations

summary: Systematic literature reviews (SRs) remain slow and labor-intensive, and most automation tools address single stages of the workflow. We present PARIS (PRISMA Agentic Research Intelligence System), an open-source framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 specialized large language model (LLM) agents, from scoping a research question to exporting a manuscript draft. Agents are specified declaratively, coordinate exclusively through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before every transition, and delegate retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring to deterministic Python utilities. Three human checkpoints gate study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. We also introduce QualityScore, a pre-synthesis index that aggregates normalized network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores into a 0-100 grade. Two case studies illustrate both: AI chatbots and university students' learning (388 records, 100 included) and AI-assisted SR methods (131 records, 123 included, QualityScore 69.1 recomputed with a proxy network sub-score). They show end-to-end feasibility across domains and the diagnostic use of QualityScore: in the first run, corpus improvements chosen at the corpus-adequacy checkpoint raised the score from 74.6 to 81.9 and the number of pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits of both runs exposed failure modes: incomplete retrieval, counts that drifted between agents, unrecorded or delegated checkpoint decisions and a grade that depends on how citation data are handled. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partially supports 11. Output quality has so far been judged only by an internal reviewer agent; independent validation against human reviews is the next step.
title: PARIS: A multi-agent LLM framework for end-to-end, PRISMA-guided systematic literature reviews with pre-synthesis corpus quality assessment

summary: In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to space-filling input design for nonlinear system identification, in which an agent learns a control policy that actively drives the system to explore its state space. Classical input design, developed mainly for linear models, minimises the covariance of the estimated parameters. For nonlinear black-box models, however, the dominant error is the bias induced by the model structure over the region of interest, which motivates space-filling strategies that seek to cover the system state space. Existing space-filling approaches rely on predefined input signal classes and require solving explicit optimisation problems. Unlike these methods, the proposed approach requires no input class to be selected and no frequency band to be tuned for the system at hand, satisfies and amplitude bound by construction, and adapts to varying initial conditions through its observation-based policy without re-optimisation. The learned excitation signals exhibit physically meaningful behaviours, such as resonance excitation and amplitude modulation. The approach is evaluated against tuned swept sine and crest-factor-optimised multisine excitations, and against a state-of-the-art space-filling multisine design, on two nonlinear benchmark systems: a mass-spring-damper with nonlinear stiffness and a Van der Pol oscillator. Under the same amplitude bound, the learned policy achieves the best overall space-filling performance on both systems and distributes its samples more uniformly than the state-of-the-art design.
title: Space-Filling Input Design for Nonlinear System Identification: A Reinforcement Learning Approach

summary: Post-Temporal Physics and the SPARC Galaxy Rotation Data — An Independently Audited Empirical Benchmark A Fourteen-Year Foundational Research Program Reaches a Reproducible Empirical Milestone Post-Temporal Physics (PTP) originated in 2012 as a foundational scientific research program investigating whether physical existence, persistence, causality, interaction, and observable behavior could be reconstructed from principles more primitive than conventional continuous spacetime and geometric descriptions. Its development has involved fourteen years of theoretical investigation, mathematical construction, physical analysis, and successive reformulations aimed at establishing a coherent alternative framework for understanding physical law. The research initially progressed through a substantial transitional program encompassing twenty native physics sectoral expansions (18 Transitonal Sectoral Expansions have not been released due to sever dual-use concern). These investigations explored the implications of the developing theory across multiple physical sectors and exposed the mathematical requirements of constructing a unified foundational system. The subsequent development of Ledgeral Mathematics provided a dedicated finite mathematical architecture through which the physical theory could be reconstructed with explicitly defined primitive objects, operations, admissibility conditions, and verification procedures. This progression culminated in the consolidated formulation of Post-Temporal Physics: The Finite Ledgeral Reconstruction of Existence, Persistence, and Physical Law , supported by Ledgeral Mathematics: A Finite Algebra of Recursion, Admissibility, Projection, and Survivor Structure and the companion Applied Ledgeral Mathematics research program and their respective sectoral and subsectoral expansions. Within this architecture, physical standing is described through finite retained records, admissibility, recursion, projection, survivor formation, residue accounting, and auditable relationships. Conventional physical quantities are admitted through specified recovery procedures, while continuum spacetime and geometric structures are not assigned primitive status within the native formulation. The present empirical release represents a significant milestone in this long-term undertaking. It establishes a reproducible astronomical benchmark through which a specified observational recovery prescription associated with the Post-Temporal Physics research program is evaluated against measured galaxy rotation behavior.   The Empirical Investigation The investigation uses observational data from the SPARC database, originally assembled by Lelli, McGaugh, and Schombert. SPARC provides measured galaxy rotation curves and baryonic mass models suitable for examining the relationship between observed circular velocities and the gravitational contribution attributed to measured baryonic matter. The analysis retains 3,269 usable radial observational records from 163 galaxies. A galaxy-level training and testing procedure separates 114 galaxies, containing 2,216 radial records, from 49 withheld galaxies containing 1,053 observational measurements. A single characteristic acceleration scale is calibrated using the designated training population. The resulting observational recovery prescription is subsequently evaluated against the withheld galaxies without additional galaxy-specific calibration of the principal fitted scale. The recovered predictions achieve a root-mean-square velocity error of approximately 22.91 kilometers per second, compared with approximately 57.52 kilometers per second for the specified fixed baryon-only reference. This corresponds to an approximately 60.2 percent reduction in RMS prediction error. At the individual galaxy level, the tested prescription improves predictive accuracy relative to the baryon-only reference in 45 of the 49 withheld galaxies. title: Post-Temporal Physics and the SPARC Galaxy Rotation Data: An Independently Audited Empirical Benchmark

summary: Purpose: The aim of this study was to define whether a gesture similarity index (GSI) based on muscle synergies extracted by a wearable device (REMO, Morecognition Ltd, Turin, Italy) provides the same information of clinical outcome measures, after specific training of hand function. The secondary aim was to define whether specific hand tasks could be considered as target tasks for hand function assessment, after stroke.  Methods: REMO is a wearable composed of 8 surface-electromyography (sEMG) sensors able to detect forearm muscles activation in real-time. The acquisition protocol consisted of bilateral execution of wrist and hand movements of the Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA-Hand, maximum score 24 points) using REMO. Then, we applied the Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) algorithm to extract muscle synergies from the sEMG signals. We calculated the GSI which represents the mathematical distance between the muscle synergies extracted from a group of elderly-healthy subjects (as reference model) and from the patient's performance (the lowest distance represented the maximum similarity, GSI=100%). Stroke survivors were assessed before (T0) and after (T1) a specific hand training of 15 sessions (1 hour each, 5 time/week, 3 weeks) (ClinicalTrial.gov ID NCT05815368). After randomization, the patients underwent to a task-specific training (control group, CG) or biofeedback training using REMO (experimental group, EG). We compared the FMA-Hand and GSI results before and after the training, and we calculated Spearman's correlation to investigate the relationship between the level of FMA-Hand and the GSI index.  Results: We collected data from a control group of 4 elderly-healthy subjects (age 74±6.3) and a group of 14 people with diagnosis of stroke (age 64.7±13.8). Overall patients showed a significant hand motor recovery (FMA-Hand: T0=11.8 ± 3.0; T1=15.7 ± 3.7; p=0.002). Based on GSI results, data showed a statistically significant improvement in wrist circumduction movements (T0= 82% ± 4.5%; T1= 85.4% ± 4.3%; p=0.048). No differences between groups were found both in FMA-Hand and in GSI analysis. Then, at the baseline, correlation analysis showed a positive significant correlation between FMA-Hand and GSI value in circumduction movement (r=0.54; p=0.046).  Conclusion(s): The results showed that a specific hand motor training induced a significant improvement in patients’ functional level. GSI results showed that wrist circumduction could be a target movement to describe motor recovery after stroke. Future perspectives will include a wider data collection to confirm the results.
title: Gesture similarity index based on muscle synergies model describing hand recovery after stroke: preliminary results of a randomised controlled trial

summary: Voters often see a candidate's face before learning about the candidate's political positions. Building on evidence that rapid visual impressions predict electoral outcomes, we examine how time pressure and information costs shape political learning and whether these constraints produce distinct patterns of scrutiny for women candidates. We conduct a preregistered three-arm online visual conjoint experiment using photographs and political information drawn from Colombian electoral data. Respondents are randomly assigned to make these choices under a nine-second deadline, an effort cost for accessing political information, or an unconstrained baseline. Candidate pairings, task order, and left-right placement are randomized within respondents. The experiment measures recorded candidate selection, candidate-specific information acquisition, and decision time. Working paper (work in progress). The oTree implementation is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24089204.
title: Faces or Facts? Experimental Evidence on Time Pressure, Information Costs, and Gender Bias in Electoral Choice

summary: How much of Great Britain lay within a day's travel of London, and how did that change between the coaching era and today? I build a multimodal network model on a 2 km grid for five dates (1750, the 1830s, 1850, 1910 and today) from historical GIS of the turnpike roads of England and Wales and the railways of 1851, a reconstruction of the 1910 rail network, and OpenStreetMap. Coach speeds are fitted to scheduled times of London coach services in 1836 (136 destinations) and to twelve cited journeys of 1739 to 1764; train speeds come from published averages; every era is tested on journeys it was not fitted to. The 1830s model reproduces the 1837 mail-coach timetable with a median absolute error of 12%. The 1750 model fails the error threshold set in advance (28% against 25%), so its map is a rough sketch. The 1850 and 1910 models use average train speeds and are slower than documented expresses by a median 46% and 34%, on four and six journeys, so their areas are lower bounds. Leaving Charing Cross at dawn, twelve hours of travel reached 5% of Great Britain's land in 1750, 19% in the 1830s, at least 47% in 1850, at least 72% in 1910 and 97% today. The largest gain per year came between the 1830s and 1850, when the first railways multiplied the area within a day by at least 2.5 in about fifteen years. The surfaces and code are released for reuse. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/day-from-london/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/day-from-london . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/day-from-london/. Sources: turnpike roads and London coach services of 1819 and 1836 (Rosevear, Bogart, Shaw-Taylor and Satchell, openICPSR 195126 and 195128; derived results only); 1851 England, Wales and Scotland rail lines (Satchell et al., UK Data Service ReShare SN 852991, CC BY 4.0); OpenStreetMap contributors via OpenFreeMap (ODbL); train speeds from Leunig (2006). Text, figures and derived data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: A Day from London: One-Day Travel Reach across Great Britain in 1750, the 1830s, 1850, 1910 and Today, from a Calibrated Historical Network Model

summary: This study investigates the inverse domination number and inverse total domination number of Sierpiński Star graphs, contributing to the broader study of domination theory in graph theory. Domination parameters play an important role in understanding graph structures and have practical applications in areas such as computer networks, communication systems, and network security, where efficient selection of primary and backup nodes is essential. Building on previous studies of inverse domination and inverse total domination in various graph classes, this research focuses on the distinctive structural properties of Sierpiński Star graphs, which are constructed based on the Sierpiński triangle. The study examines the relationships between domination sets, inverse dominating sets, and inverse total dominating sets within these graphs. Through mathematical analysis and graph-theoretic techniques, it seeks to establish the corresponding inverse domination parameters and provide results that extend existing knowledge of domination in specially structured graphs. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of domination theory and provide a foundation for further investigations of inverse domination parameters in fractal-related graph structures.
title: COMPUTING INVERSE DOMINATION AND INVERSE TOTAL DOMINATION NUMBERS OF SIERPIŃSKI STAR GRAPHS

summary: This paper examines the concept of permission within the set-theoretical approach to the logical theory of normative systems. Drawing on Alchourrón and Bulygin’s expressive conception of norms, and Žarnić’s formal reconstruction of von Wright’s later deontic logic, the study argues that the standard interpretation of permission as the derogation of a command fails to capture its pragmatic function. Building on a distinction between prescriptive and descriptive uses of deontic language, the paper develops an alternative reinterpretation of the set-theoretical framework in which permission is treated as an autonomous prescriptive speech act. Within this model, the relations among obligation, prohibition, and permission are expressed through two sets—commanded and permitted act-propositions—and then two perfection properties of ideal normative systems are identified—inner consistency and relational consistency. Finally, the analysis reveals that the notion of permission is even more ambiguous than the literature has so far acknowledged, distinguishing four types—normative, weak (negative), unilateral positive, and bilateral positive—and shows that the principle “Obligation implies permission” is valid only under specific interpretations of positive permission.
title: Four concepts of permission

summary: Enterprise adoption of agentic systems is often framed as a problem of agent reasoning, tool use, retrieval, or memory. This paper investigates an additional architectural problem: preparing heterogeneous enterprise knowledge into task-appropriate representations that agents can interpret, reuse, and govern. We propose Cognitive Preparation as an explicit architectural lifecycle between authoritative enterprise knowledge and agent execution, with a Cognitive Preparation Compiler (CPC) coordinating representation decisions, compilation, validation, provenance binding, temporal constraints, and publication through a reusable Cognitive Substrate. The contribution is positioned at the architectural and methodological level; no novelty is claimed for ontologies, symbolic predicates, memory mechanisms, provenance, temporal models, or knowledge compilation individually. Recent 2026 preprints on precomputed agent-memory views and enterprise context engineering further narrow the novelty boundary and are treated as close, non-peer-reviewed prior art. We report a staged prototype evaluation implemented in Ver.Test9 on a Ver.Test8 runtime foundation. Deterministic tests examine selected lifecycle controls, while exploratory LLM-assisted evaluations (T17–T22) examine controlled reuse of synthetic operational knowledge through deterministic retrieval. The results provide implementation-level feasibility evidence and preliminary observations of scoped procedural knowledge reuse, including provider- and operation-specific applicability, temporal validity, and version precedence. They do not establish general performance superiority, validated adaptive representation selection, transfer between genuinely independent agents, autonomous learning, production readiness, or economic break-even. The five research questions are retained, with preliminary support strongest for controlled knowledge reuse; preparation effectiveness and evolution receive partial evidence, while adaptive representation selection and reuse economics remain open.
title: Cognitive Preparation for Agentic Enterprise Systems: A Knowledge Compilation Architecture and Preliminary Evaluation

summary: Phase 6-ter of the consolidation: the full MCP server. Astrocook can be driven by an AI agent through 65 tools: the 48 recipes (each one a tool, generated from the registry), the sessions with undo and redo, the inspection of a session, the notes and gaps of the agent, the log as the text of a methods section, the cancellation of a long recipe, a GUI that follows a session of the server and a headless Docker image. Outputs come from RecipeResult only, and nothing the agent does is lost. A minor version: the interface of the server grows, the results of the recipes do not change but in the two cases below. Numerical results. Unchanged for the benchmark of synthetic spectra (documentation page Accuracy , as for 2.2.0) and for the fits and the identification in general, with two changes decided on purpose (PR 7-quater). (1) Check associated metals ( metals_auto ) refitted the session it started from and lost the ions already found, and kept a trial ion if its fit gave logN >= 12 and 2 <= b <= 50 km/s ( aic_penalty was accepted and not used). It now keeps the ions found, skips the ions whose lines fall outside the spectrum (with a warning) and keeps a trial ion only if its fit does not end at a bound (b or logN) and its AIC change is below -aic_penalty (F111, F121); on a real spectrum (J0103-1305 raw, 215 thousand pixels) the recipe went from 192 ions kept, 67 of them at b = 50 km/s, to 82 and none at the bound, and from 26.7 to 6.4 minutes for the trials. The benchmark of synthetic spectra does not run metals_auto : a targeted test measures it (the SiIV of the mock of the trials is found). (2) A fit of components with no valid pixel around them no longer fits the whole spectrum: the components are not fitted and keep their first values (F111). Published on GitHub with the macOS app; not on PyPI yet (install with pip from GitHub). Changed Using Astrocook from an AI Agent rewritten for the full MCP server (phase 6-ter, closing): installation and Docker, the tools by group, a longer example (a blend fitted with undo and constraints), what a request should say, the review in the GUI and the limits (the automatic recipes, no measure of the fit, z_em and R not estimated, the cost in context of the 65 tools). The server is no longer called a pilot. MCP server for agents (phase 6-ter): every recipe is a tool , named <menu>_<recipe> (e.g. flux_rebin , absorbers_fit_component ), made from the description of the recipe that the GUI dialogs use: the same parameters, defaults, bounds and texts, the values checked as in the GUI; a recipe added to Astrocook becomes a tool with no change of the server. The five tools of the pilot keep their names. Every tool returns what the recipe changed, listed (the components removed with the reason, the components changed, the columns, the properties), with the summaries of the pilot where they apply (continuum, identification, fit). A recipe that opens new sessions in the GUI does so in the server too, each with its own session_id , and leaves the session it ran on unchanged: Identify Absorption Lines now opens a new session (in the pilot it changed the same one). A parameter that names another session (e.g. the reference of Equalize ) takes its session_id . The messages name the tools that provide what is missing ( edit_set_properties , continuum_estimate_auto ). MCP server: tools for the sessions, session_list , session_describe , session_history , session_undo , session_redo , session_duplicate and session_close (phase 6-ter). Every state of a session is kept, as in the GUI: what a recipe removed is had back with session_undo , and the result of such a recipe says so. session_close does not close a session with changes not saved unless asked to discard them. MCP server: tools to look into a session without changing it (phase 6-ter): components_list (the components with their errors, flags, fit groups and constraints, filtered by series, redshift and flags), spectrum_read (the column

summary: Local bus mileage in England outside London has fallen by more than a quarter since 2005, and debate about rural buses relies mostly on counts of routes cut or money spent. This paper measures what remains, place by place. Using the complete set of regional timetables published through the Bus Open Data Service, I count departures on one weekday, one Saturday and one Sunday at 251,790 English bus stops and relate them to 15,012 villages from Wikidata and to all 33,755 small areas (LSOAs). 32.6% of villages have no stop with a weekday bus within 800 m, and 41.4% have no stop with four or more weekday departures. 61.5% have no bus from 19:00 and 67.8% none on Sunday; only 29.8% have a usable weekday service, an evening bus and a Sunday bus. 10.5% of England's population, 6.0 million people, live in small areas without a usable weekday bus, 72% of them in rural areas. In a pre-specified model with rurality and region held fixed, more deprived areas are less likely to lack a usable bus (odds ratio 0.68 per standard deviation, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.78) and areas with older populations more likely (odds ratio 1.28, 1.19 to 1.38). A planned falsification test fails, so these associations partly reflect rural differences the official classification does not capture. The results give a reproducible baseline for measuring rural bus provision. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/bus-deserts/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/bus-deserts . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/bus-deserts/ . Sources: Department for Transport, Bus Open Data Service regional GTFS timetables (Open Government Licence v3.0); Wikidata (CC0); English Indices of Deprivation 2025, MHCLG (OGL v3.0); ONS 2021 Rural Urban Classification and LSOA 2021 boundaries via the geographr R package (OGL v3.0); ONS region and country boundaries (OGL v3.0). Text, figures and data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: Bus Deserts: Villages Without a Usable Bus, the Last Bus Home and Who Lives Beyond the Network in England

summary: We present a calibrated search for a coincident plasma enhancement associated with the binary neutron star merger GW170817 using Wind/WAVES quasi-thermal noise measurements.   Using electron density fit_n_e from the WIND_WAVES_QTNFIT dataset via NASA CDAWeb HAPI, we compare a ±60 s window around the GW170817 merger time to 1000 control windows on the same day.   We find a mean density of 10.01 cm^-3 at the event (N=21), versus 10.57 ± 0.83 cm^-3 in controls, yielding z = -0.67, p = 0.50, consistent with no excess.   This null result calibrates the method, establishes the background distribution for radio-plasma searches, and sets the baseline for a targeted search in Jovian decametric emission in Paper 2.   Data: NASA CDAWeb HAPI, WIND_WAVES_QTNFIT, 2017-08-17 10:00-15:00 UTC, 3425 valid points after cleaning fill value -1e31. Method: Event window ±60s around GPS 1187008882.43 (2017-08-17 12:41:04.43 UTC) vs 1000 random control windows on the same day. Reproduction: Run reproduce_paper1.py - it downloads the data from HAPI, cleans it, computes the statistics and regenerates Figure 1. Files: paper1.pdf, reproduce_paper1.py, figure1_wind_lightcurve.png
title: Limits on Plasma Density Enhancement Coincident with GW170817 from Wind/WAVES QTN Measurements

summary: The Hydraulic and Electric Reverse Osmosis Wave Energy Converter (HERO WEC) is a 3-kW point-absorber WEC designed to desalinate ocean water using breakwater wave energy. In its electrical configuration, a permanent magnet synchronous generator produces three-phase "wild AC" power that is rectified and regulated by a charge controller to charge a battery bank and power a reverse-osmosis pump. Wave energy presents a uniquely challenging environment for power electronics: energy delivery is pulsed, irregular, and characterized by high peak-to-average power ratios. The HERO WEC originally used an off-the-shelf buck converter charge controller designed for wind, solar, and hydropower. Field deployments to North Carolina revealed two critical limitations: (1) a 32 V cut-in voltage that rendered the controller inoperable during low-energy wave states, and (2) severe current overshoot in energetic waves that exceeded commanded current and threatened system survivability. Together, these constraints produced only a narrow operational window and average battery power of tens of watts, far below the controller’s 1.8 kW rating. This work describes the redesign of the charge controller to address these limitations and expand the operational range of the WEC.
title: Custom Charge Controller Design and Validation for Wave Energy Conversion

summary: This dataset contains experimental data supporting the reproducibility of side-channel-assisted secret-key reconstruction attacks against HQC. It provides the vectors used to construct soft spectra from side-channel-derived error-weight estimates for two attack scenarios: Chosen-Ciphertext Attack (CCA) and Known-Ciphertext Attack (KCA). The corresponding estimated error weights, as well as the C implementations of the soft-spectrum construction and secret-key reconstruction algorithms (Simulated Annealing and Depth-First Search), are available in the accompanying GitHub repository. The dataset does not contain raw side-channel traces. Instead, it provides the intermediate experimental data required to reproduce the soft-spectrum-based key-recovery experiments and evaluate reconstruction success rates as a function of the number of observations. The files should be placed in the appropriate data/cca/ and data/kca/ directories of the GitHub repository, as described in its README.
title: Experimental Side-Channel Data for HQC Secret-Key Reconstruction

summary: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.
title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery

summary: The discovery rate p a of Cuckoo Search sets how much of each solution the abandonment operator rebuilds, and many variants tune it with schedules or online controllers. Using one shared implementation, paired seeds and 70 problem instances (classical functions at D = 10, 30 and 50, shifted-rotated functions, and CEC-2017 F1 and F3–F20 at D = 30 and 50), we show that the best constant p a ranges from 0.02 to 0.80. Much of this dependence reflects separability: rotating the classical functions raises the best level on 6 of 8, as the crossover-rate theory of differential evolution predicts. Early progress is an unreliable guide: the best level after 10% of the budget differs from the best final level on 12 of 35 functions, and on the classical functions choosing it raises the final error a median 12.4-fold. Keeping a spread of rates across the nests avoids this choice. A random per-nest spread alone improves on the default on 13 of 19 CEC-2017 functions at D = 30; self-adaptive (SA- p a ) and success-history (SH- p a ) per-nest rates improve on it on 54 and 47 of 70 instances, with 3 and 5 losses (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests). On CEC-2017 their median error is 0.93 (D = 30) and 1.13 (D = 50) times that of the best constant chosen in hindsight, against 1.76 and 1.67 for the default. The gains vanish at D = 10, and Cuckoo Search remains well behind jDE.
tags: Cuckoo search; Parameter control; Self-adaptation; Discovery rate; Rotation invariance; Separability; Benchmarking
title: A spread of rates, not a schedule: population-level heterogeneity in the discovery rate of Cuckoo Search

summary: EXTRARNAS — Datasets, Software Outputs, and Analysis Scripts Companion material for the CIBB 2026 short paper and an extended manuscript under submission This repository contains research data, RNA annotation outputs, curated references, analysis scripts, and supplementary documentation associated with EXTRARNAS. It supports the original CIBB 2026 short paper, “EXTRARNAS: A Framework for Extracting RNA Structures with Multiple Tools,” and the extended manuscript “EXTRARNAS: Standardized RNA Structure Annotation and Cross-Tool Comparison” (currently under submission). What is new in this version The extended study analyzes eight RNA structures containing triple-helix motifs using seven tools: RNAView, MC-Annotate, RNApolis Annotator, FR3D, X3DNA-DSSR, Barnaba, and BPNet. The archive includes the full tool outputs, standardized BPSEQ/BPSEQE representations, curated structural references, and quantitative comparisons with the references and among the annotators. The extension experiments used EXTRARNAS v1.1.0. The accompanying manifest documents Docker image IDs, tool versions, Git revisions, checksums, and analysis dependencies. The licensed X3DNA-DSSR executable is not redistributed. summary: This repository provides supporting research materials for the conceptual manuscript entitled “Financial Stress, Spiritual Coping, and Mental Health Resilience in Emerging Economies: Toward an Integrative Conceptual Framework.” It documents the development of the Financial–Spiritual Resilience Framework (FSRF), which integrates financial adversity, religious and spiritual coping, spiritual struggle, communal meaning-making, psychological distress, and resilience, with particular attention to emerging economies.       The repository contains literature search expressions and scope documentation, a conceptual selection protocol, a reference map of 43 publications, bibliographic and source-access verification records, a claim–evidence correspondence audit covering 56 central statements, six theoretical propositions, a supplementary operationalization and falsification matrix, and the conceptual framework figure.       Project bibliographic exports comprised 491 initial records (221 from Web of Science and 270 from Scopus), with 353 provisionally unique records after bibliographic deduplication. Full-document copies of 39 of the 43 cited works were available for targeted verification; four were not supplied. This documentation supports transparency but does not constitute a systematic literature review, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or exhaustive replication of all reported findings.       The FSRF is a conceptual and testable framework, not an empirically validated intervention. No original participant-level data, copyrighted full-text articles, or proprietary database exports are redistributed. The materials are shared under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

summary: emgteach is an open-source Python package that provides a unified PySide6 desktop application for real-time acquisition, offline analysis and maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) normalisation of surface electromyography (sEMG) signals. It is designed for hands-on biopotential acquisition in undergraduate physiology teaching laboratories, and is meant to be set up by instructors with different levels of technical background and used directly by students during a practical session. The application is hardware-agnostic through a common AcquisitionDevice interface and ships with two interchangeable low-cost backends: BITalino (revolution) over Bluetooth, and an Arduino RedBoard Plus + MyoWare 2.0 over USB serial (open firmware included). A single setting switches between them. Main features: Three-tab GUI (Acquisition, Analysis, MVC normalisation) wrapping a reusable, Qt-free analytic core. Bilingual interface (English / Spanish) with automatic start-up language detection and an in-app language switch. Two-channel acquisition (e.g. agonist/antagonist) with a stacked two-channel live view. Automatic contraction-onset detection (baseline + k·SD threshold) stored as EDF+ annotations. Muscle-load analysis (Jonsson APDF): static (P10), median (P50) and peak (P90) %MVC levels, both offline and as a live monitor with warning/danger zones. One-click PDF session and MVC/muscle-load reports. Reliable EDF+ output using a buffered-write pattern that avoids a silent file-corruption artefact during continuous streaming. Assisted selection of significant fragments, with an editable fragment editor (detection parameters and envelope-filter cut-offs) applied to the analysis. CSV export of results and a live signal-quality check during recording. Classroom mode: a read-only live dashboard served over the local network so students follow the session on their phone/tablet browser (no install), with a per-session access code so the follower link only works while the broadcast is running. Kinematics via the BITalino accelerometer (v2.0.0): a movement-versus-EMG analysis panel, a guided force-velocity acquisition wizard (an MVC maximum followed by cued quick lifts, each auto-marked with its load), and a force-velocity study that turns one recording into the load-velocity, Hill force-velocity, power and recruitment curves. Since v3.0.0 the accelerometer's input is a stated convention (muscle on A1, accelerometer on A2) rather than a selectable channel. Configuration by practical (v3.0.0): three practicals — one muscle, agonist/antagonist and muscle kinematics — fix the channel count, the accelerometer and what each tab offers, replacing the settings that were previously chosen one at a time. The session as a single file with its phases marked inside it (v3.0.0): warm-up, calibration repetitions, preparation and recording, so the maximum voluntary contraction every percentage is measured against travels with the signal, and a derived (tuned) recording carries the decisions taken on screen. Teaching layer (v3.0.0): a guided tour over the interface, contextual help on every box, one analysis row per contraction with its electromechanical delay, and an agonist/antagonist co-activation index (Falconer-Winter) computed per marked phase in %MVC. Handling at the laboratory bench (v3.1.0): the fragment editor as a three-step procedure that counts the marked contractions against the protocol and lets each be kept, dropped, split or dragged, with the detection sensitivity set per practical and recorded in the report and the CSV; a single running instance with a start-up splash; pictures of the electrode placement and the calibration in the guided tour; and a printable sheet for each station of the agonist/antagonist practical. Patch 3.1.1: the co-activation of a named window is read on the uncut recording, with each muscle's resting level taken from the whole recording phase, so choosing fragments no longer measures the antagonist against a rest taken from a signal
title: emgteach: an open-source teaching platform for surface electromyography

summary: Wave-powered reverse osmosis (RO) desalination with electricity cogeneration is a promising approach, as both the energy source and the seawater are present at the same location. Hydraulic power take-off (PTO) systems are used because they are well-suited for the low-frequency, high-force requirements of wave energy converters (WECs). Conventional hydraulic PTOs for cogeneration suffer from limitations related to the required power density and cost. In these architectures, the WEC-driven pump and the RO module are connected in parallel to a common pressure rail, forcing the pump to operate at the relatively low pressure of the RO membrane. This limits the power density of the WEC pump, thus increasing the size of the most costly component.
title: Integrated Hydraulic Transformer for Cogeneration of Electricity and Freshwater from Wave Energy

summary: The papers of Johann Ludwig Kuefstein, imperial orator at the Porte in 1628–1629 (ELTE University Library, Budapest, Manuscript Collection, G. 4, Fol., Tom. I–XIV), include a page almost wholly in a cipher of graphic signs, Tom. V p. 1461, catalogued as a dispatch of Kuefstein to the Emperor and listed as undeciphered. Regina Donáth reproduced it in Magyar Könyvszemle (1964). Using the key rebuilt from Donáth's printed examples, this preprint gives a provisional German text (about 90% read), an English translation and a commentary. The page is not a dispatch from Kuefstein but an order to him from the Imperial War Council (Hofkriegsrat), dated Vienna, 27 October 1629: the Emperor has heard that the Pasha of Buda (Murtaza Pasha) had been received with, or joined by, about 3,000 Turks, and asks what troops these are, where they came from, and whether they are still assembled. Version 1 is a provisional reading from Donáth's 1964 halftone; a definitive edition will follow once a scan of the original has been obtained. Files: the preprint (PDF) and the reconstructed key (TSV). Donáth's plate is not reproduced. AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) was used in key reconstruction, transcription and drafting and is disclosed in the text.
title: Vienna Asks Constantinople: The Imperial War Council to Johann Ludwig Kuefstein, 27 October 1629 (a provisional decipherment of ELTE G. 4, Tom. V, p. 1461)

summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.
title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.
title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading

summary: Electric heavy goods vehicle (eHGV) fleet coordination requires each vehicle to choose driving, charging and resting actions whose consequences depend on shared infrastructure. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods mainly represent current states, leaving action-specific futures and resource interactions to be learned indirectly. We develop Horizon-Preview and Graph-Coordinated Proximal Policy Optimisation (HGC-PPO), which integrates horizon preview and candidate-resource graph coordination into the PPO decision architecture. Horizon preview represents each legal action through its short-horizon operational consequences. Graph message passing then updates these candidates through station, charger-type and time-slot resources shared across the fleet. On the 794km Folkestone-Glasgow task, HGC-PPO achieved the lowest mean charging cost among five RL methods at £504.32 per vehicle, with a fleet completion time of 24.920h. It also completed the task 1.763h faster and cost £36.51 less per vehicle than a replay-verified finite-budget MILP benchmark. Across six unseen routes and fleet sizes from 5 to 20 vehicles, HGC-PPO delivered the lowest macro-average completion time, charging cost and charging frequency among the RL methods. A 2 by 2 ablation showed that the full preview-graph architecture performed best across all four operational metrics. These results show that prospective action information and fleet-wide resource coordination improve eHGV decisions under charging and driver-hours constraints.

summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in groups, each pursuing an individual objective while jointly determining system performance. If an operator controls which agent observes which other agent, but not their payoffs or messages, how should observations be structured to raise collective welfare? We make the information network (who observes whom) a design object, decoupled from the fixed interaction network over which agents act. Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games; by default each observes only an anonymous summary of the group's previous-round outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed observation links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games spanning coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas, and discovery, we ask how much information to share and, at a fixed budget, who should observe whom. Disclosure creates behavioral coupling: observation acts as a contagion channel whose welfare effect depends on the alignment between individually attractive behavior and the collective objective. First, the value of information is alignment-contingent: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual behavior is aligned with the collective goal, but under free-riding or congestion externalities it amplifies collectively harmful behavior; in a public-goods game the group does best with no information at all. We read this sign separation as a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population, not a model-invariant law. Second, at a fixed budget, who observes whom matters primarily when coupling is harmful: a modular "barbell" that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behavior is reliably the worst wiring, reversing the network-reciprocity intuition from human evolutionary game theory. These results argue against a default of full transparency for agent collectives.
title: Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks

summary: We built a hybrid multi-agent trading system that combines large language model (LLM) analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves. We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.
title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents

We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.

summary: Frontline sales staff spend much of their day re-coordinating quotes after customers change quantities, ask for discounts or new payment terms, or costs move. We present LoMASA (Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant), a training-free multi-agent system that runs entirely on one desktop computer. A 35B mixture-of-experts model (System-1) makes each decision in a single forward pass and reads its confidence from the probabilities of the answer options. A 27B dense model (System-2) writes customer replies and escalation briefs and is consulted when System-1 is unsure. Code computes every price, margin and option, and hard pricing rules cannot be overridden. On a test split of 500 simulated episodes with 1512 decisions built from public supply-chain data, the salesperson has to decide only 19.5% of decisions: 38.0% are settled automatically, with a median latency of 2.67 seconds, and 42.5% are escalated to a manager by the hard rules. On the automatically settled decisions LoMASA is as accurate as a rule baseline (0.894 vs.\ 0.894) and makes fewer commitments whose margin later falls below the floor (2.61% vs 4.53%); the price is additional escalations to the manager. Option probabilities are well calibrated without any training, unlike confidence stated in words by the same model. We also report where the design does not help: the 27B model rarely changes a decision.
title: LoMASA: A Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant with Confidence-Gated Delegation for B2B Quoting

summary: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects. In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions. Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.
title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems

summary: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.
title: A Gamified Framework for Conflict-Driven Design: Discovering Strategies for Collaborative Resilience with Multi-Agent Learning

summary: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.

summary: Multi-agent search and coverage is critical to autonomous exploration, search-and-rescue, and defense applications. This paper investigates settings where a mobile sensor network is tasked with coordinating to discover the position of a stationary target within a bounded region. We develop a Bayesian update scheme where agents iteratively combine local uncertainties derived from their sensor measurements through inverse variance weighting to get a better global understanding of where the target may be located given some prior belief. Network agents' trajectories are governed by a primal-dual gradient update rule that simultaneously minimizes the expected sensing uncertainty and enforces network connectivity among the agents. We prove that the belief converges to the target under mild planner conditions, with an explicit exponential rate of false-hypothesis rejection and a bound on expected search time. Simulation results show that we can successfully find the target and collapse belief to the ground truth target location while ensuring connectivity of our sensor network. They also empirically confirm our theoretical bounds and planner conditions. Finally, we compare against a naive lawnmower sweeping strategy, showing that our method locates the target more quickly when the prior is informative.

summary: Networked multi-agent systems coordinating in adversarial environments face compound cyber threats that alternate between false-data injection (FDI), denial-of-service (DoS), and stealthy decoy perturbations designed to mimic benign operational anomalies. Because the switching policy is latent and the plant dynamics evolve continuously, deterministic threshold detectors struggle to isolate deception without causing excessive false alarms. This paper presents an online, data-driven framework that couples distributed continuous time unknown input observers (UIOs) with a topology-aware Hidden Markov Model (HMM) for real-time attack detection and classification under unknown adversarial strategies. By decoupling FDI signals from augmented node states, distributed observers deployed across the network generate local augmented residuals that are discretized into emission sequences. The HMM embeds the underlying directed communication graph into the off-diagonal blocks of its transition probability matrix, explicitly capturing inter-agent attack propagation. Both transition and observation probabilities are updated recursively online via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) scheme, adapting the classifier to evolving threat behaviours without prior offline calibration. Numerical simulations on a directed network demonstrate that incorporating graph topology into the latent transition dynamics resolves the severe classification ambiguity between nominal and decoy modes, outperforming decoupled agent-independent decoders while restricting observer deployment to a sparse subset of nodes.
title: Real-Time Threat Classification in Multi-Agent Systems via Topology-Coupled Hidden Markov Models

summary: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.
title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification

summary: Cryptocurrency perpetual futures form a large-scale online financial market in which automated agents manage interacting asset positions under changing conditions. Policies relying solely on micro-level numerical states may overlook cross-asset relationships and become vulnerable to regime shifts, while macro-level linguistic judgments alone cannot ensure precise measurement or optimize positions under trading costs and risk constraints. Connecting market interpretation to coordinated multi-asset decisions remains challenging. We propose M3FT, a micro-macro-micro framework for multi-agent perpetual futures trading. The first micro stage constructs time-aligned numerical states from exchange and account observations through deterministic processing. The macro stage transforms these measured states into explicit market interpretations without adding external market information. Four asset-specific teams, each comprising a Market Interpreter, an Asset Communicator, and a Risk Reviewer, refine these interpretations through experience retrieval, cross-asset communication, and review of joint-position risks. The final micro stage combines encoded linguistic representations with the original numerical states to learn continuous target positions. We implement this framework with a language-conditioned multi-agent policy: asset actors use global and private numerical states together with linguistic context, while centralized critics evaluate joint actions using portfolio-wide information and shared-account rewards. Experiments on real cryptocurrency perpetual futures data, including comparisons across language models and policy-learning algorithms and component ablations, show that the best-performing M3FT configuration achieves a higher mean test return than the evaluated direct LLM, numerical RL, and rule-based baselines.

summary: Version 3.0 of the Latin Josephus scholarly corpus. The corrected core contains all 166 canonical XML files and 14 citation registries. It includes Greek, Latin and English texts of Antiquitates Judaicae , Bellum Judaicum and Contra Apionem , the Latin Ussani and English Pollard v1.2 editions of De excidio Hierosolymitano , manuscript annotations, textual apparatus and citation structures. The source snapshot of 10 November 2026 restores Greek Antiquitates IX.51–109. The companion contains the French Millet (1556) and Italian Lauro (1544) transcriptions and their Latin passage correspondences, the Froben (1524) Latin transcription with Niese segmentation and recorded gaps, 1,917 released manuscript annotations from 21 witnesses, 527 manuscript catalogue records, 17 medieval library catalogue records, De excidio and Lodge concordances, and the original EEBO-TCP A04680 source for byte locators. The accompanying documentation gives editorial coverage, provenance and stable identifiers. Component rights are recorded in the XML and supplementary file manifests. They include CC BY 4.0, CC BY-SA 4.0, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 International for the covered Pollard translation and notes, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 Italy for the digilibLT textual layer, and CC0 1.0 for the EEBO-TCP source. The core documents the limited Blatt and Loeb quotations and their basis. The full preservation master is a separate object.

summary: NORMA-O (the NORMA Ontology) is an OWL 2 DL ontology for representing legal norms as machine-readable, interoperable data. It describes what a norm requires, forbids or allows, under which conditions, for whom, and on which legal source it rests. Each statement can be traced back to its legal source and to the process that produced it. NORMA-O is part of ongoing research on representing legal norms so that machines can store, query and reason over them while keeping their conditions, exceptions, addressees and legal authority. Version 1.0 introduced deontic types, constitutive rules, conditions and their outcomes, agents, actions, objects, legal sources, annotation provenance and controlled vocabularies. It was designed for norms annotated on BPMN models of regulatory processes. Version 2.0 keeps every term of 1.0 and describes the model independently of any notation or authoring method. Version 2.0 adds the means to state how norms relate to each other and to concrete cases, and to compute what applies, to whom and why: - Standard Deontic Logic grounding: action negation, facultative acts, weak permission, and deontic equivalence, contradiction and conflict between norms. - Hohfeldian legal positions: duty, claim, privilege and no-right, with holder, counterparty, correlatives and opposites. - Roles, parties and cases: legal roles, the parties that occupy them, role assignments and fact patterns. - Defeasibility: exception, conflict and temporal defeaters; lex superior, lex specialis and lex posterior; normative rank, norm strength and a prevalence graph. - Counts-as chaining: when a classification is defeated, every obligation that depends on it is withdrawn. The release also includes the derivation module NORMA-O Deriv (prefix normad, https://w3id.org/def/norma-o/deriv). It records how each derived conclusion was obtained, by which rule and under which assumptions. The release also includes a reference rule set (norma-derivation/1.0) that computes the deontic closure, the legal positions, the prevalence ordering (with cycle detection), applicability to each case and weak permissions. A Python package with the norma command checks annotations, derives conclusions and produces reports. NORMA-O reuses open Semantic Web standards and vocabularies, including OWL 2, RDF, PROV-O, ELI, FOAF and SKOS. It was developed following the LOT methodology. It originated in the NORMA project, whose semantic toolkit uses it to annotate regulations, build RDF graphs and evaluate compliance, but the ontology does not depend on that toolkit. Files: norma-ontology-v2.ttl / .rdf (ontology 2.0), norma-o-deriv.ttl / .rdf (derivation module 1.0), diagrams of both (.svg), and NORMA-O-v2.0.0.zip (a snapshot of the GitHub tag v2.0.0 with the rule set, the engine and the Python package). Documentation: https://w3id.org/def/norma-o · Source: https://github.com/sheyls/NORMA-O

summary: A memory can last for decades, yet the proteins of a synapse are replaced within days. Crick (1984) proposed that the molecules that store a memory restore one another, so that the pattern survives its parts, and several molecular switches of this kind have since been modelled. Here we ask a question that does not depend on the mechanism: what is the longest time that any switch made of $N$ molecules can remember? We consider all switches in which the number of active molecules changes one molecule at a time, with an activation rate per inactive molecule between a spontaneous floor $\varepsilon$ and a catalytic ceiling $k$, and a loss rate per active molecule between the turnover rate $\mu$ and an erasure ceiling $\lambda$. (i) We prove that, for every readout threshold, both the potentiated and the unpotentiated state are retained longest, in the sense of stochastic order, by one and the same switch: a threshold rule that restores at full speed when at least $m$ molecules are active and erases at full speed otherwise. (ii) We give its mean retention times in closed form, as sums of binomial coefficients, and evaluate them in exact rational arithmetic. (iii) When the two contrasts $\kappa=k/\mu$ and $\chi=\lambda/\varepsilon$ are equal to $c$ and $\lambda=\mu$, the longest possible memory $T^*(N)$ satisfies $N^{-1}(\sqrt c/2)^N\le\mu T^*(N)\le\bigl((1+c)/\sqrt c\bigr)^N$ for even $N$; numerically, each added molecule multiplies it by about $(1+c)/(2\sqrt c)$. (iv) With molecules that last 30 hours, no switch of this class holds both states for a mean of a century with fewer than 20 molecules if $c=10$, 12 if $c=30$, 8 if $c=100$ and 4 if $c=1000$, and these numbers are attained; thirty molecules suffice as soon as $c\ge7$, while a single dimer with $c=100$ lasts 50 molecular lifetimes. (v) The retention times of the ideal switch have an increasing failure rate, so that a mean of a hundred centuries guarantees a century with probability above $0.99$, at the price of two to ten more molecules. (vi) Smooth cooperativity is far from the limit: a switch with Hill exponent 2 needs 187 molecules where the ideal one needs 12. In this class, then, a lifetime of memory requires few molecules but a sharp threshold. These are limits for one-variable switches with constant rates, not a model of a particular synapse. This record contains the preprint (PDF, PCI template), its LaTeX source, and the Python code and results file that reproduce every theorem, table and figure (code under the MIT license).

summary: Overview This dataset provides a reproducible local-earthquake tomography framework for investigating the subsurface velocity structure of the Batu Hijau–Elang porphyry Cu–Au district, Sumbawa Island, Indonesia. The archive supports a three-dimensional seismic tomography study based on local earthquake observations, simultaneous inversion of P-wave velocity (Vp) and Vp/Vs structure, resolution-constrained interpretation, and systematic sensitivity testing of inversion damping parameters. The primary objective is to document the computational reproducibility and numerical stability of the reconstructed seismic velocity anomalies while explicitly accounting for limitations in spatial resolution and geological interpretation. Earthquake Dataset and Inversion Configuration The G40 CM117 tomographic inversion uses: 600 selected earthquakes. 60 seismic stations. 11,529 seismic observations. 7,378 P-wave arrival observations. 4,151 S–P differential-time observations. A three-dimensional grid containing 25 × 14 × 12 nodes. A transverse-Mercator coordinate system with central meridian 117°E. Five inversion iterations using SIMUL2023. The reference inversion uses damping parameters of 1100 for Vp and 300 for Vp/Vs. The weighted RMS residual decreases from 0.47223 s to 0.39282 s after five iterations. Computational Reproducibility The original inversion was reproduced using a clean compilation of the archived SIMUL2023 source code and the corresponding inversion inputs. The rebuilt inversion reproduces the historical velocity model at the numerical precision stored in the output file. The only identified textual difference in the final velocity-model file is the computation timestamp. The archive preserves the source-code snapshot, inversion configuration files, model outputs, numerical logs, and provenance information required to document this result. Damping Sensitivity Experiments Four additional inversions were performed to evaluate the sensitivity of the reconstructed velocity anomalies to the damping parameters: Vp damping = 700; Vp/Vs damping = 300. Vp damping = 1600; Vp/Vs damping = 300. Vp damping = 1100; Vp/Vs damping = 200. Vp damping = 1100; Vp/Vs damping = 500. All five inversions use the same input dataset and complete five iterations. The final weighted RMS residuals range from 0.39010 s to 0.39605 s. Resolution-Constrained Evaluation Spatial sensitivity is evaluated using a frozen resolution-supported node mask derived from Vp resolution diagnostics. The evaluation includes: 145 STRICT nodes within the 0–40 km evaluation domain. 113 STRICT nodes within the 5–30 km depth interval. For the 113-node subset, spatial correlations between the reference and alternative models range from: 0.989 to 0.998 for Vp anomalies. 0.985 to 0.996 for Vp/Vs anomalies. Median absolute anomaly differences range from: 0.147 to 0.425 percentage points for Vp. 0.114 to 0.338 percentage points for Vp/Vs. Anomaly-sign agreement is evaluated only at nodes where the absolute reference anomaly is at least 0.1%. All 16 combinations of spatial domain, damping configuration, and velocity parameter passed an independent numerator-and-denominator verification against the node-level CSV data. Archive Contents The reproducibility package includes: SIMUL2023 source-code snapshot and compilation information. Historical reference inversion inputs and velocity-model output. Five inversion configurations and their numerical outputs. Frozen starting velocity model. Geographic node coordinates and resolution-mask information. Machine-readable damping sensitivity tables. Node-level Vp and Vp/Vs anomaly comparisons. Three-dimensional model and resolution-related outputs. Discrete-node visualizations of Vp and Vp/Vs anomalies. summary: Abstract This manuscript presents the Residual-Load Rebound Amplification Framework (RLR-AF), a proposed domain-general framework for analyzing conditions under which temporary relief from a problem may be followed by a recurrence that exceeds a comparable reference level. The framework is organized around a central distinction between observable problem attenuation and sufficient modification of the condition that generates or maintains the problem. It proposes that when an intervention reduces the observable output without adequately resolving the relevant generative condition, residual problem-related states may persist. If the intervention or subsequent systemic changes also modify the conditions governing future responses, the residual state may be expressed more strongly when the relevant constraint, control process, or suppressive influence no longer operates in the same way. The framework does not assume that residual load necessarily produces amplification. Amplified recurrence is a conditional outcome requiring an effective pathway that increases the subsequent expression of the residual state and a net effect that exceeds the system's relevant restorative or control processes. The manuscript introduces the Residual-State Conditional Amplification Principle (RSCAP), the expanded Residual-Load-Compensation-Rebound Mechanism (RLCR+), and the primary case of Emotional-Distress Suppression and Amplified Rebound (EDS-AR). It develops a domain-neutral state-space architecture, operational definitions, conditional propositions, a causal-comparison strategy, candidate amplification pathways, cross-domain mapping rules, counterexamples, and an empirical validation roadmap. The framework is a proposed theoretical contribution rather than an established universal law. Its conceptual coherence, mathematical consistency, causal mechanisms, empirical validity, and applicability to domains beyond its primary case must be evaluated separately. Keywords: Residual load; rebound amplification; temporary relief; systemic reconfiguration; causal inference; state-space modeling; control theory; cognitive science; feedback systems; domain-general theoretical framework.

summary: Abstract The Generalized Evidence-to-System Projection Theory (GESPT) is proposed as an integrative framework for analyzing the relationship between available evidence and claims about a broader target system. Its central concern is the distinction between the accuracy of a description within an observed or otherwise documented reference set and the validity of extending that description to a larger, partially unknown, or temporally extended system. The framework is motivated by a criminal-case observation: records of detected offenders may support accurate descriptions of detected cases, while the same records alone may be insufficient to establish that every offender will eventually be detected. The absence of comparable records for undetected cases does not prove that those cases have any particular outcome. It establishes a limitation on what can be inferred from the available evidence without additional assumptions or information. The proposed framework distinguishes reference-set accuracy, target-system validity, evidence availability, selection, measurement, transformation, inference, projection, labeling, decision-making, and feedback. Its central Evidence-Boundary Non-Entailment Principle (EBNP) states that truth within a reference set does not, by itself, logically entail universal truth within a broader target set. The Reference-Accurate, Target-Underdetermined Mechanism (RATUM) describes the coexistence of an accurate analysis of available data and unresolved uncertainty about the broader system. A formal model is provided using reference and target sets, selection probabilities, estimands, projection gaps, and identifiability conditions. Several propositions follow under explicitly stated assumptions. Applications to statistics, causal inference, systems theory, information processing, cybernetics, network analysis, criminology, sociology, and machine learning are discussed as conditional extensions rather than presumed universal results. The document is a proposed theoretical synthesis, not an already validated universal law. Its originality, empirical performance, and domain-specific scope require systematic comparison with established methods and independent testing. Keywords evidence boundaries; reference sets; target systems; non-entailment; selection; underdetermination; generalization; projection; missing data; feedback; criminal detection
